Accessible Introduction to Computer Science

Accessible Introduction to Computer Science

A living, accessibility-first textbook across programming languages and software domains

This book is a structured introduction to computer science and software development. It is designed with blind and visually impaired learners who use screen readers, braille displays, magnification, keyboard navigation, or combinations of access technologies in mind. It is also intended for sighted learners, educators, and anyone who benefits from explicit, text-first instruction.

The repository contains 13 full language curricula, focused modules in Git, HTML/CSS, Markdown, R, regular expressions, SQL, structured data formats, and web accessibility, and shared Bash and PowerShell terminal tracks. The languages are presented by their common technical uses and ecosystems, not as a hierarchy. No single language is the best choice for every problem.

The textbook is published with mdBook. Markdown files in this repository are the maintained source; mdBook builds them into the navigable online textbook hosted on GitHub Pages. The book is intended to remain a living resource: lessons, examples, exercises, accessibility notes, and teaching materials can be reviewed and improved as learners and educators use them.

Start learning: complete the shared prerequisites, then choose a language curriculum or focused module that aligns with your goals. Each language curriculum includes its own topic index. The shared Programming Code Glossary defines common and language-specific terminology.

Complete the shared prerequisites

Terminal skills

Before beginning a language curriculum, complete the Terminal Skills prerequisite. Choose the Bash track for macOS and Linux or the PowerShell track for Windows. Both tracks teach equivalent foundational workflows using native commands: navigating directories, managing files, reading and searching text, running programs, interpreting errors, and working safely from a project folder. These skills support every language and toolchain in the book.

Computing foundations

Read the Foundations overview and Computing Foundations Primer. These materials introduce concepts and vocabulary that apply across programming languages, operating systems, and development tools.

Development environments

Review the IDE and editor guide and Environment Isolation guide. Visual Studio Code and Theia IDE are the primary editor options discussed for the course. The materials also describe professional IDEs and data platforms—including JetBrains products and Databricks—by their typical roles and use cases, without providing setup procedures for those products.

Project-defined development containers receive particular emphasis when a course requires a consistent compiler, runtime, linter, formatter, test runner, or supporting service. The guides explain the relationship between development containers, Docker, and Podman and how project-level environments support reproducible learning and assessment.

Purpose and learning philosophy

The goal is not simply to teach syntax. Learners should develop the habits used to solve problems with computers: clarify requirements, decompose a task, represent information, design an algorithm, implement it, test it, interpret errors, revise the solution, and explain their decisions.

The curricula share these commitments:

  • Accessibility is part of the design. Core activities use text-based input and output and can be completed through keyboard-accessible tools. Lessons explain code structure and navigation rather than depending on visual scanning.
  • Concepts precede tools. Editors, terminals, runtimes, compilers, interpreters, and libraries are instruments for learning computer science.
  • Practice is central. Short experiments, guided exercises, debugging, and projects provide repeated opportunities to apply concepts.
  • Understanding matters more than typing speed. Learners reason about programs, predict behavior, test assumptions, and explain their decisions.
  • Errors are part of learning. Reading diagnostics and correcting a program are core skills.
  • The resource evolves. Corrections, new examples, and accessibility improvements are welcome through GitHub Discussions, Issues, and Pull Requests.

Who should use this book?

The primary audience includes learners who are blind or visually impaired. It may be used in secondary or postsecondary courses, accessible technology programs, tutoring, independent study, or educator professional development.

No previous programming experience is required for the introductory learning paths. Learners should have, or be developing, basic keyboard and screen-reader or braille-display navigation skills. A teacher can introduce programming and assistive-technology workflows together; lack of advanced screen-reader fluency should not be mistaken for lack of programming ability.

The material is also useful to sighted learners because it emphasizes precise language, semantic structure, explicit feedback, and reproducible text-based workflows.

What learners will develop

By working through a selected curriculum, learners should build the ability to:

  1. Describe what a computer program is and explain a basic software-development cycle.
  2. Use a language runtime, compiler, editor, terminal, and project environment appropriate to the selected technology.
  3. Read code structurally, including identifiers, operators, delimiters, indentation, braces, and nested blocks.
  4. Store, convert, compare, and process values using appropriate data types.
  5. Use expressions, input, output, decisions, and repetition to solve problems.
  6. Organize related values in collections and select suitable data structures.
  7. Decompose programs into functions, methods, modules, or components with clear responsibilities.
  8. Work with files, exceptions, structured data, and external libraries where relevant.
  9. Understand classes, objects, interfaces, memory, concurrency, or other paradigms where the selected language requires them.
  10. Test behavior, diagnose errors, refine a solution, and communicate how it works.
  11. Build text-based applications or domain-appropriate projects and complete the projects specified by the selected path.
  12. Evaluate whether program interaction, prompts, messages, and output are understandable through assistive technology.

Outcomes vary by curriculum and module. These are learning goals, not a claim of professional mastery.

Focused technology modules

Some important technologies are not general-purpose programming languages. They have distinct roles and are included as focused modules:

ModulePrimary usage and roleRepresentative software or platforms

HTML is a markup language and CSS is a style-sheet language; together they form the structure and presentation layer of the web. SQL is a declarative query language for relational data. R is a programming language used extensively in statistics and data analysis. Git is a version control system, Markdown is a documentation markup language, regular expressions are a pattern language embedded in many tools, JSON, YAML, and TOML are structured text formats, and web accessibility is an engineering discipline built on the web platform’s accessibility APIs.

Shared terminal tracks

Bash and PowerShell are shell languages. They support command execution, file and process management, automation, and development workflows. Bash is common on macOS and Linux; PowerShell is central to Windows administration and is also available cross-platform. Both are shared prerequisites rather than alternatives to the application languages above.

Selecting a pathway

Choose a path according to the problem domain, deployment target, ecosystem, and learning objectives:

  • Automation, data analysis, and machine learning: Python; consider R for statistical analysis and Julia for numerical or scientific computing.
  • Web application development: JavaScript and TypeScript, alongside HTML/CSS and the web accessibility module; add SQL when the application stores relational data.
  • Enterprise and JVM applications: Java or Kotlin.
  • Android and Apple platforms: Kotlin is widely used for Android development; Swift is the primary language for modern native Apple-platform development.
  • Operating systems, embedded devices, and systems software: C, C++, or Rust, depending on hardware, ecosystem, performance, and safety requirements.
  • Cloud services and infrastructure tooling: Go, Java, Python, Rust, or C# depending on platform and system requirements.
  • Game development and application scripting: C++, C#, and Lua have distinct roles across engines, application logic, and embedded scripting.
  • Relational data systems: SQL is a companion to application languages, not a replacement for them.
  • Professional workflow skills: the Git, Markdown, regular expressions, and structured data formats modules support every other path in the textbook.

These categories overlap. A real product may use several languages, and a language may serve multiple domains. Selection should reflect the problem being solved, the existing codebase, team expertise, operational constraints, and available libraries.

Each full language curriculum has its own landing page and supporting lesson materials. Depending on the language, it may also include a topic index, teacher’s guide, standardization audit, or validation record. The focused modules provide a narrower introduction to a particular technology. Follow the sequence and scope documented on the corresponding landing page and in the table of contents.

A practical study routine

  1. Preview: read the lesson title, objectives or overview, vocabulary, and prerequisites.
  2. Understand: read the explanation and trace each example. Identify what each statement contributes.
  3. Predict: state what you expect the program to do before running it.
  4. Run: execute the example and inspect its text output.
  5. Experiment: change one input, value, or statement at a time.
  6. Practice: complete the activities without copying a finished solution.
  7. Debug: read the diagnostic, locate the relevant code, form a hypothesis, and test a correction.
  8. Explain: describe the algorithm and the role of important variables, conditions, loops, functions, methods, modules, or objects.
  9. Review: revisit the skills checklist and record concepts that need more practice.

Keep a learning journal or portfolio. Include the problem statement, approach, sample input and output, errors encountered, and what changed.

Accessibility and technology

Recommended editor and development workflow

Visual Studio Code is the primary editor in the setup material. Theia IDE is another option for keyboard-first development. The IDE guide also describes the roles of JetBrains IDEs, Databricks, and other professional tools without giving setup instructions for them.

For projects that require compilers, linters, formatters, test runners, and supporting services, the course emphasizes repository-defined development containers. A containerized project environment can make the toolchain more consistent across learner computers and CI. The environment guide explains the Dev Container model and the roles of Docker and Podman.

Access configurations vary by operating system, screen reader, braille display, editor version, and individual preference. Treat shortcuts and settings in the lessons as starting points; verify them in the learner’s environment.

Dependency and environment management

Use the project-native dependency and build tools documented by each language curriculum. Examples include uv and Python project environments, npm for JavaScript and TypeScript, Maven or Gradle wrappers for JVM projects, and the relevant package and build tools for C, C++, C#, Julia, Swift, Rust, Go, and Lua. Keep dependencies project-scoped where possible, commit lockfiles when the ecosystem supports them, and use the repository’s documented commands rather than relying on undocumented global tools.

A development container can complement these tools; it does not replace language package managers, lockfiles, or build systems. The project should document both the container environment and the commands used to build, lint, test, and run its code.

Shared accessibility practices

  • Use semantic headings, descriptive link text, ordered procedures, and code fences with language identifiers.
  • Enable editor screen-reader support where available and learn navigation by line, word, symbol, file, and diagnostic.
  • Configure speech or braille output for punctuation, indentation, line numbers, and code symbols according to learner preference.
  • Use a terminal or REPL to run examples and inspect text output.
  • Keep examples and output understandable when read sequentially. Label collections, menu options, and results.
  • Avoid relying on syntax highlighting, color, spatial placement, diagrams, or screenshots to communicate essential information.
  • Provide a text description or equivalent activity when a visual resource is included.
  • Allow time for navigation and tool interaction; assess programming reasoning separately from assistive-technology speed.
  • Ask learners which tools and interaction patterns work for them. Do not infer needs from a diagnosis.

A text-only interface is not automatically accessible. Output order, verbosity, prompts, error handling, keyboard operation, and documentation structure all affect usability. Test activities with the actual access technology where possible and revise barriers as they are identified.

Assessment and evidence of learning

Use varied evidence rather than relying only on timed code production:

  • Explain a program or algorithm in the learner’s own words.
  • Predict output before execution and explain any difference.
  • Complete a program or technical task from a clear specification.
  • Find and fix a deliberately introduced bug.
  • Write tests or identify useful test cases.
  • Refactor a program into clearer functions, methods, modules, or data structures.
  • Demonstrate keyboard and assistive-technology workflows used to create, run, and debug the work.
  • Maintain a portfolio with incremental versions and reflections.

Assess correctness, reasoning, testing, clarity, independence, and progress. Provide reasonable accommodations without lowering the underlying learning objective.

Using AI tools thoughtfully

AI-assisted coding tools may help explain unfamiliar concepts, interpret diagnostics, propose test cases, or provide alternative explanations. They can also produce incorrect, insecure, inaccessible, outdated, or overly complicated code. AI output is not evidence that a learner understands a topic.

Follow the instructor’s policy for each activity and assessment. Disclose assistance when required; never submit generated code that the learner cannot explain, test, and modify. Do not share personal, educational-record, credential, or confidential information with public AI systems. Review generated code for correctness, dependencies, security, licensing, and screen-reader usability. Keep a non-AI path available so paid tools or accounts are not prerequisites.

Contributing to this living textbook

Learners, teachers, developers, and accessibility specialists are invited to contribute:

  • Use GitHub Discussions for questions, proposals, and teaching ideas.
  • Use GitHub Issues to report errors, broken links, unclear explanations, outdated setup instructions, or accessibility barriers.
  • Use Pull Requests to propose corrections and additions.

Read CONTRIBUTING.md, follow CODE_STYLE.md, and respect the Code of Conduct. Record textbook-source changes in CHANGES.md.

References and acknowledgments

The Foundations introduction includes a bibliography of introductory computer science texts. Each language landing page and focused technology module includes curated introductory book recommendations, with authors, editions or publication dates where verified, notes on intended use, and links to publisher, author, or free online editions. The Bash and PowerShell tracks also include shell-specific reading recommendations. These bibliographies complement—not replace—the course lessons and official language documentation. Use official documentation to confirm version-sensitive language, API, and tool details.

External resources may change or have different accessibility characteristics over time; evaluate them in the learner’s actual environment. Preserve appropriate attribution when improving or extending material.

Select a curriculum that matches a technical domain or learning objective, complete its prerequisites, and work through its materials in sequence. The goal is to become an independent problem solver who can read, write, test, explain, and improve software using accessible tools.

Terminal Skills: Prerequisite Curriculum

Purpose

This short prerequisite teaches the command-line skills used throughout the programming curricula. Complete it before beginning a language track. The goal is to make learners comfortable navigating projects, creating and inspecting files, running programs, understanding command output, and recovering from common mistakes.

A terminal is a text interface for interacting with the operating system. A shell reads commands and runs programs. The terminal application displays the shell’s input and output. These are related but distinct tools.

Choose the track for your operating system

  • Bash track: macOS and Linux
  • PowerShell track: Windows 11

The tracks teach the same learning outcomes using native commands. Do not try to memorize both syntaxes before beginning programming. Learn the track for the computer you use; consult the other track when collaborating across operating systems.

Prerequisites

  • You can use your computer’s keyboard.
  • You can open a terminal application and move focus to its command prompt.
  • If you use a screen reader or braille display, you can read text output and move by line or character. The lessons include practice for improving this workflow.

No programming experience is required.

Learning outcomes

After completing either track, you should be able to:

  1. Explain the difference between a terminal, a shell, a command, a path, and a process.
  2. Identify the current working directory and navigate between directories.
  3. List, create, copy, move, rename, and remove files and directories.
  4. Read command syntax, options, arguments, and quoted paths containing spaces.
  5. Use tab completion and command history to reduce typing.
  6. Read standard output and error messages, recognize an exit status, and interrupt a running command.
  7. Search for text and inspect file contents without relying on a graphical file manager.
  8. Run a program from its project directory and understand why the working directory matters.
  9. Use help and documentation to investigate an unfamiliar command.
  10. Recognize destructive commands and verify a target before changing or deleting data.

Lesson sequence

LessonTopicEvidence of learning
1Terminal, shell, prompt, and first commandsIdentify the shell and print a working directory
2Paths and directory navigationMove through a practice directory tree
3Files and directoriesCreate, copy, rename, move, and remove practice files
4Command structure and efficient entryUse options, quoting, completion, and history
5Reading, searching, and filtering textInspect a text file and find matching lines
6Running programs and understanding resultsRun a script and interpret output and errors
7Processes, help, and safe troubleshootingInterrupt a process and locate command help
8Integrated practice projectComplete a small file-based workflow independently

How to study

For each lesson:

  1. Read the explanation before entering commands.
  2. Type commands yourself. Do not paste a command you cannot explain.
  3. Predict what a command will do before running it.
  4. Compare the result with the expected behavior.
  5. Change one detail at a time and observe the difference.
  6. Complete the activity in a disposable practice directory.
  7. Explain what each command did in your own words.

Commands are shown in fenced blocks labeled for the intended shell. Text shown as output is illustrative; do not enter it as a command.

Accessibility practices

  • Keep the terminal focused while entering commands; use the keyboard to switch between the editor and terminal.
  • Read command output sequentially. Use screen-reader review commands to revisit earlier output when needed.
  • Prefer short commands and one operation per line while learning.
  • Use descriptive filenames and directories. Avoid relying on color, alignment, or visual location.
  • Learn how your terminal announces the prompt, command line, and output. Terminal behavior varies by application and screen reader.
  • If output is long, redirect it to a file or use a pager only after learning how to exit the pager. The lessons explain this explicitly.
  • Do not assume a command succeeded because it returned to the prompt. Check the output and, where appropriate, its exit status.

Safety rules

  1. Practice in a dedicated folder such as terminal-practice, not in your home directory or a course repository.
  2. Read a command before running it. Be especially cautious with recursive deletion, wildcards, administrator privileges, and commands copied from the internet.
  3. List the target directory before moving or deleting files.
  4. Do not run commands containing unexplained downloads piped directly into a shell.
  5. Do not use elevated privileges to solve an error until you understand why permission was denied.
  6. Keep credentials, access tokens, and private information out of command history and shared terminal transcripts.

Completion standard

You are ready to begin the programming curricula when you can complete the final practice project without following a step-by-step command recipe, explain the commands you chose, and recover from at least one intentional mistake. Use the track’s skills checklist to identify anything that needs more practice.

Reference documentation

  • GNU Bash manual
  • GNU Coreutils manual
  • Apple: Use the command line
  • Microsoft: PowerShell documentation
  • Microsoft: PowerShell about topics

Bash Track: macOS and Linux Terminal Skills

Scope

This track uses Bash syntax and common commands available on macOS and mainstream Linux distributions. macOS commonly opens zsh by default. Most commands in this track also work in zsh, but shell-specific behavior is identified where relevant. Linux distributions may package some utilities differently.

Complete the terminal skills overview first. Work only inside a practice directory you create for these lessons.

Lesson 1: Meet the terminal and shell

Learning objectives

  • Distinguish the terminal application from the shell.
  • Recognize the command prompt and command line.
  • Display the current working directory and identify the shell.

Concepts

The terminal is the application that provides text input and output. Bash is a shell: it interprets commands and starts programs. The prompt is the shell’s invitation to enter a command. Your prompt may contain your username, computer name, current directory, or other information; its appearance is configurable and is not a reliable substitute for checking the directory.

A command generally has a command name followed by options and arguments. Press Enter to run it. A command that finishes normally returns control to the prompt.

Try it

pwd
whoami
uname -s
printf 'Terminal practice is ready.\\n'

Expected behavior

  • pwd prints the absolute path of the current working directory.
  • whoami prints the current account name.
  • uname -s identifies the operating-system kernel.
  • printf prints the supplied text followed by a newline.

The exact paths and account name vary by computer.

Activities

  1. Run each command separately and describe its output.
  2. Run pwd again after opening a new terminal window. Compare the locations.
  3. Explain why the prompt’s appearance does not prove which directory is active.

Lesson 2: Paths and directory navigation

Learning objectives

  • Explain the difference between an absolute and relative path.
  • Move to a directory and return to the home directory.
  • List directory contents.

Concepts

A path identifies a file or directory. An absolute path begins at the filesystem root, written / on macOS and Linux. A relative path is interpreted from the current working directory. A forward slash separates path components.

Special path names include . for the current directory, .. for its parent, and ~ for your home directory. Use quotes around a path containing spaces.

Try it

pwd
ls
ls -la
cd ~
pwd
mkdir -p terminal-practice/first-project
cd terminal-practice/first-project
pwd
cd ..
pwd
cd ~

Expected behavior

The commands list the current directory, move to your home directory, create a nested practice directory, enter it, move to its parent, and return home. The -la options request a detailed listing that includes hidden entries; hidden names conventionally begin with a dot.

Activities

  1. Create terminal-practice/first-project/notes using mkdir -p.
  2. Enter the notes directory using a relative path.
  3. Return to your home directory using cd ~.
  4. Explain the difference between cd .. and cd ~.

Lesson 3: Create and manage files

Learning objectives

  • Create an empty file and a directory.
  • Copy, move, rename, and remove practice items.
  • Verify each change by listing the directory.

Concepts

Use touch to create an empty file, cp to copy, mv to move or rename, and rm to remove a file. Use mkdir to create a directory. These commands act on the paths you provide; they do not ask whether you intended a different target.

For this lesson, use only the practice folder created in Lesson 2.

Try it

cd ~/terminal-practice/first-project
mkdir -p notes
touch notes/todo.txt
cp notes/todo.txt notes/todo-backup.txt
mv notes/todo-backup.txt notes/archive.txt
ls -l notes
rm notes/archive.txt
ls -l notes

Expected behavior

The first listing contains todo.txt and archive.txt. The second contains only todo.txt.

Activities

  1. Create a directory named drafts and an empty file named drafts/idea.txt.
  2. Copy the file to drafts/idea-copy.txt.
  3. Rename the copy to idea-final.txt.
  4. List the directory and verify both files before deleting the copy.
  5. Explain why you should inspect a target before using rm.

Safety: deletion

rm removes files; it does not move them to a graphical trash folder. Recursive deletion with rm -r can remove an entire directory tree. Do not use rm -rf, wildcards, or recursive deletion in these introductory exercises. Never experiment with deletion from the filesystem root, your home directory, or a repository.

Lesson 4: Command structure and efficient entry

Learning objectives

  • Identify command names, options, and arguments.
  • Quote paths containing spaces.
  • Use tab completion and command history.

Concepts

Options modify command behavior. Many short options begin with one hyphen, such as -l; long options often begin with two, such as --all. Exact options depend on the command. Arguments identify the data or location on which the command operates.

Quotes keep spaces and shell-special characters inside one argument. The shell expands an unquoted wildcard such as *.txt to matching filenames before the command runs. This is useful but can affect more files than expected.

Press Tab to request completion. Press the Up Arrow to recall a previous command. Use Left Arrow and Right Arrow to edit the command line before pressing Enter.

Try it

cd ~/terminal-practice
mkdir "project notes"
touch "project notes/first draft.txt"
ls -l "project notes"
printf '%s\\n' "A quoted path can contain spaces."

Activities

  1. Create a directory named week one and a file named plan for week one.txt.
  2. Use Tab completion to finish a directory or filename.
  3. Recall a previous harmless command with the Up Arrow, edit one argument, and run it.
  4. Explain why quoting project notes matters.

Lesson 5: Read, search, and filter text

Learning objectives

  • Display a text file.
  • Search for a word or phrase.
  • Understand basic output redirection and pipelines.

Concepts

cat displays a file’s contents. less opens a pager for longer output; press q to exit. grep searches text for a pattern. The vertical bar | sends one command’s standard output to another command as input. The greater-than sign > redirects output to a file and replaces that file’s previous contents; >> appends instead.

Try it

cd ~/terminal-practice
printf 'apple\\nbanana\\napricot\\n' > fruit.txt
cat fruit.txt
grep 'ap' fruit.txt
grep -n 'ap' fruit.txt
cat fruit.txt | grep 'banana'
printf 'grape\\n' >> fruit.txt
cat fruit.txt

Expected behavior

The first search finds apple and apricot. The -n option includes line numbers. The pipeline prints the matching banana line. The final listing includes the appended grape.

Activities

  1. Create a file containing three short lines of your own.
  2. Search for one word and then a word that does not occur.
  3. Use grep -n and explain the line number.
  4. Explain the difference between > and >>.

Lesson 6: Run programs and interpret results

Learning objectives

  • Run a command-line program from a known directory.
  • Distinguish output from an error message.
  • Understand the current working directory’s effect on relative paths.

Concepts

A program is a file or executable command that the shell starts. For a script, the runtime may be named explicitly. For example, python3 hello.py starts Python and asks it to run the file hello.py. A relative filename is resolved from the current working directory, not automatically from the script’s location.

A process may print normal output to standard output or diagnostics to standard error. A nonzero exit status commonly indicates failure. In Bash, $? contains the exit status of the most recently completed command; inspect it immediately because the next command changes it.

Try it

cd ~/terminal-practice
printf "print('Hello from the terminal')\\n" > hello.py
python3 hello.py
printf 'Exit status: %s\\n' "$?"
python3 missing-file.py
printf 'Exit status: %s\\n' "$?"

Expected behavior

The first run prints Hello from the terminal and normally returns status 0. The second run reports that the file cannot be found and normally returns a nonzero status. Exact diagnostic wording varies by Python version.

Activities

  1. Change the greeting and run the program again.
  2. Run the program from a different directory using its absolute path.
  3. Explain why python3 hello.py may fail when run from the wrong directory.
  4. Record the difference between a program’s printed output and its diagnostic.

Lesson 7: Processes, help, and troubleshooting

Learning objectives

  • Interrupt a foreground process.
  • Find built-in help and manual pages.
  • Diagnose a missing command or incorrect path.

Concepts

A running command is a process. Press Ctrl+C to send an interrupt to the foreground process. It usually stops the command, but a program may handle the interrupt differently.

Use command --help when supported. Use man command for a manual page; press q to exit. Not every command implements the same help option. A message such as command not found means the shell could not locate a command with that name in its command search path.

Try it

man ls
man pwd
command -v python3

Activities

  1. Open the manual page for ls and exit with q.
  2. Use command -v to locate python3.
  3. Intentionally enter a misspelled harmless command and read the diagnostic.
  4. Start a long-running command such as sleep 60, then stop it with Ctrl+C.

Lesson 8: Integrated practice project

Goal

Create a small project folder, add a text file and a Python script, inspect the files, run the script, and verify the result.

Requirements

  1. Create terminal-practice/final-project.
  2. Inside it, create data and output directories.
  3. Create data/message.txt with one line of text.
  4. Create hello.py that prints Terminal skills are ready..
  5. List the project files and inspect the message file.
  6. Run the Python script from the project directory.
  7. Record the exit status and explain why it indicates success or failure.
  8. Make a copy of the message file, verify the copy, and remove only that copy.

One possible command sequence

cd ~/terminal-practice
mkdir -p final-project/data final-project/output
printf 'Practice makes progress.\\n' > final-project/data/message.txt
printf "print('Terminal skills are ready.')\\n" > final-project/hello.py
cd final-project
find . -type f
cat data/message.txt
python3 hello.py
printf 'Exit status: %s\\n' "$?"
cp data/message.txt output/message-copy.txt
ls -l output
rm output/message-copy.txt
ls -l output

Reflection

Explain each command in the sequence. Identify which paths are relative, what the current working directory is during the script run, and which command would be dangerous if its target were mistyped.

Bash skills checklist

  • I can open a terminal and identify the shell prompt.
  • I can display and explain the current working directory with pwd.
  • I can navigate with cd, including ~, ., and ...
  • I can list files with ls and recognize hidden entries.
  • I can create directories and files with mkdir and touch.
  • I can copy, move, rename, and safely remove practice files.
  • I can quote paths containing spaces.
  • I can use Tab completion and command history.
  • I can inspect and search text with cat and grep.
  • I understand output redirection and a basic pipeline.
  • I can run a program from its project directory.
  • I can read an error message and inspect an exit status.
  • I can interrupt a foreground process with Ctrl+C.
  • I can find command help and complete the final practice project.

Further reference

  • GNU Bash manual
  • GNU Coreutils manual
  • Apple Terminal User Guide
  • Python command-line documentation

Recommended introductory books

  • Shotts, William. The Linux Command Line: A Complete Introduction, 3rd edition. No Starch Press, 2026. A practical introduction to shell use, files, processes, text tools, scripting, and the Linux command-line environment. Publisher page.

Suggested use: this is the primary supplementary text for the Bash track. The book focuses on Linux; macOS users should expect some differences in available commands and utilities. Follow this course’s Bash examples and your operating system’s manual pages when behavior differs.

PowerShell Track: Windows 11 Terminal Skills

Scope

This track uses PowerShell 7-compatible syntax and commands that are also available in the Windows PowerShell shipped with Windows 11 unless otherwise noted. PowerShell is a command shell and scripting language. The examples use native PowerShell commands rather than Command Prompt syntax.

Complete the terminal skills overview first. Work only inside a practice directory you create for these lessons.

Lesson 1: Meet the terminal and shell

Learning objectives

  • Distinguish the terminal application from the shell.
  • Recognize the PowerShell prompt and command line.
  • Display the current working directory and identify the PowerShell version.

Concepts

Windows Terminal is a terminal application. PowerShell is a shell that interprets commands and starts programs. The prompt commonly displays the current path followed by a greater-than sign. Its appearance is configurable; always check the working directory rather than relying on the prompt’s visual appearance.

A command may be a PowerShell cmdlet, function, alias, script, or external program. Cmdlet names commonly use a Verb-Noun pattern, such as Get-Location. Press Enter to run a command.

Try it

Get-Location
$env:USERNAME
$PSVersionTable.PSVersion
Write-Output "Terminal practice is ready."

Expected behavior

  • Get-Location displays the current working directory.
  • $env:USERNAME displays the current account name.
  • $PSVersionTable.PSVersion displays the installed PowerShell version.
  • Write-Output writes the supplied text to the output stream.

Exact paths, account names, and version numbers vary.

Activities

  1. Run each command separately and describe its output.
  2. Open a new terminal tab and compare its starting directory.
  3. Explain why the prompt’s appearance does not prove which directory is active.

Lesson 2: Paths and directory navigation

Learning objectives

  • Explain the difference between an absolute and relative path.
  • Move to a directory and return to the home directory.
  • List directory contents.

Concepts

A path identifies a file or directory. A Windows absolute path commonly begins with a drive letter, such as C:\Users\Student. A relative path is interpreted from the current working directory. Windows paths conventionally use backslashes, though PowerShell also accepts forward slashes in many path contexts.

The . symbol means the current directory and .. means its parent. The automatic variable $HOME identifies your home directory. Use quotes around paths containing spaces.

Try it

Get-Location
Get-ChildItem
Get-ChildItem -Force
Set-Location $HOME
Get-Location
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "$HOME\terminal-practice\first-project" -Force
Set-Location "$HOME\terminal-practice\first-project"
Get-Location
Set-Location ..
Get-Location
Set-Location $HOME

Expected behavior

The commands list the current directory, move to your home directory, create a nested practice directory, enter it, move to its parent, and return home. -Force includes hidden and system entries where permitted; it does not mean that files are being deleted or overwritten.

Activities

  1. Create terminal-practice\first-project\notes using New-Item.
  2. Enter the notes directory using a relative path.
  3. Return to your home directory using Set-Location $HOME.
  4. Explain the difference between Set-Location .. and Set-Location $HOME.

Lesson 3: Create and manage files

Learning objectives

  • Create an empty file and a directory.
  • Copy, move, rename, and remove practice items.
  • Verify each change by listing the directory.

Concepts

Use New-Item to create a file or directory, Copy-Item to copy, Move-Item to move or rename, and Remove-Item to remove an item. These commands act on the paths you provide; they do not know whether you intended a different target.

For this lesson, use only the practice folder created in Lesson 2.

Try it

Set-Location "$HOME\terminal-practice\first-project"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path notes -Force | Out-Null
New-Item -ItemType File -Path notes\todo.txt
Copy-Item notes\todo.txt notes\todo-backup.txt
Move-Item notes\todo-backup.txt notes\archive.txt
Get-ChildItem notes
Remove-Item notes\archive.txt
Get-ChildItem notes

Expected behavior

The first listing contains todo.txt and archive.txt. The second contains only todo.txt.

Activities

  1. Create a directory named drafts and an empty file named drafts\idea.txt.
  2. Copy the file to drafts\idea-copy.txt.
  3. Rename the copy to idea-final.txt.
  4. List the directory and verify both files before deleting the copy.
  5. Explain why you should inspect a target before using Remove-Item.

Safety: deletion

Remove-Item deletes the specified item. Recursive removal can delete an entire directory tree. Do not use -Recurse, wildcards, or forceful deletion in these introductory exercises. Never experiment with deletion from the root of a drive, your home directory, or a repository.

Lesson 4: Command structure and efficient entry

Learning objectives

  • Identify command names, parameters, and arguments.
  • Quote paths containing spaces.
  • Use tab completion and command history.

Concepts

PowerShell cmdlets commonly use named parameters beginning with a hyphen, such as -Path and -ItemType. A parameter controls command behavior; its argument supplies a value. PowerShell command names are generally case-insensitive.

Quotes keep spaces and special characters inside one argument. Single quotes create literal strings; double quotes allow variable expansion, such as "$HOME\Documents". PowerShell’s wildcard character * can match multiple names, so verify the target before using a wildcard with a command that changes or removes data.

Press Tab to complete a command or path. Press the Up Arrow to recall a previous command. Use Left Arrow and Right Arrow to edit a command before pressing Enter.

Try it

Set-Location $HOME
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "project notes"
New-Item -ItemType File -Path "project notes\first draft.txt"
Get-ChildItem "project notes"
Write-Output 'A quoted path can contain spaces.'

Activities

  1. Create a directory named week one and a file named plan for week one.txt.
  2. Use Tab completion to finish a directory or filename.
  3. Recall a previous harmless command with the Up Arrow, edit one argument, and run it.
  4. Explain the difference between single-quoted and double-quoted strings.

Lesson 5: Read, search, and filter text

Learning objectives

  • Display a text file.
  • Search for a word or phrase.
  • Understand basic output redirection and pipelines.

Concepts

Use Get-Content to display a text file. Use Select-String to search text for a pattern. The vertical bar | sends objects or output from one command to another. The greater-than sign > redirects output to a file and replaces that file’s previous contents; >> appends instead.

PowerShell commands often pass structured objects through a pipeline, not just plain text. For this introductory lesson, focus on the visible results and the role of each command.

Try it

Set-Location $HOME\terminal-practice
"apple", "banana", "apricot" | Set-Content fruit.txt
Get-Content fruit.txt
Select-String -Path fruit.txt -Pattern "ap"
Select-String -Path fruit.txt -Pattern "ap" -List
Get-Content fruit.txt | Select-String -Pattern "banana"
Add-Content fruit.txt "grape"
Get-Content fruit.txt

Expected behavior

The first search finds apple and apricot. The pipeline prints the matching banana line. The final listing includes the appended grape.

Activities

  1. Create a file containing three short lines of your own.
  2. Search for one word and then a word that does not occur.
  3. Use Select-String and explain how it reports matching lines.
  4. Explain the difference between Set-Content and Add-Content.

Lesson 6: Run programs and interpret results

Learning objectives

  • Run a command-line program from a known directory.
  • Distinguish output from an error message.
  • Understand the current working directory’s effect on relative paths.

Concepts

A program is a file or executable command that PowerShell starts. For a Python script, py -3 hello.py starts the Python launcher and asks it to run hello.py. A relative filename is resolved from the current working directory, not automatically from the script’s location.

PowerShell displays errors in the host and exposes the most recent native program exit code through $LASTEXITCODE. For PowerShell cmdlets, inspect the error record and the command’s documented behavior; $LASTEXITCODE is specifically for native programs and scripts that set an exit code.

Try it

Set-Location $HOME\terminal-practice
"print('Hello from the terminal')" | Set-Content -Encoding utf8 hello.py
py -3 hello.py
"Exit status: $LASTEXITCODE"
py -3 missing-file.py
"Exit status: $LASTEXITCODE"

Expected behavior

The first run prints Hello from the terminal and normally returns status 0. The second run reports that the file cannot be found and normally returns a nonzero status. Exact diagnostic wording varies by Python version and launcher installation.

Activities

  1. Change the greeting and run the program again.
  2. Run the program from a different directory using its absolute path.
  3. Explain why py -3 hello.py may fail when run from the wrong directory.
  4. Record the difference between a program’s printed output and its diagnostic.

Lesson 7: Processes, help, and troubleshooting

Learning objectives

  • Interrupt a foreground process.
  • Find built-in help.
  • Diagnose a missing command or incorrect path.

Concepts

A running command is a process. Press Ctrl+C to send an interrupt to the foreground process. It usually stops the command, but a program may handle the interrupt differently.

Use Get-Help CommandName to request help. On a computer without locally installed help files, PowerShell may offer to update them; you can instead use the online help option where supported. Use Get-Command to discover commands and Get-Command python to check whether a command can be found.

Try it

Get-Help Get-ChildItem -Examples
Get-Command py
Get-Command python

Activities

  1. Read the examples for Get-ChildItem and identify one parameter.
  2. Use Get-Command to locate the Python launcher.
  3. Intentionally enter a misspelled harmless command and read the error.
  4. Start a long-running command such as Start-Sleep -Seconds 60, then stop it with Ctrl+C.

Lesson 8: Integrated practice project

Goal

Create a small project folder, add a text file and a Python script, inspect the files, run the script, and verify the result.

Requirements

  1. Create terminal-practice\final-project.
  2. Inside it, create data and output directories.
  3. Create data\message.txt with one line of text.
  4. Create hello.py that prints Terminal skills are ready..
  5. List the project files and inspect the message file.
  6. Run the Python script from the project directory.
  7. Record the exit status and explain why it indicates success or failure.
  8. Make a copy of the message file, verify the copy, and remove only that copy.

One possible command sequence

Set-Location $HOME\terminal-practice
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path final-project\data -Force
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path final-project\output -Force
"Practice makes progress." | Set-Content final-project\data\message.txt
"print('Terminal skills are ready.')" | Set-Content final-project\hello.py
Set-Location final-project
Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File
Get-Content data\message.txt
py -3 hello.py
"Exit status: $LASTEXITCODE"
Copy-Item data\message.txt output\message-copy.txt
Get-ChildItem output
Remove-Item output\message-copy.txt
Get-ChildItem output

Reflection

Explain each command in the sequence. Identify which paths are relative, what the current working directory is during the script run, and which command would be dangerous if its target were mistyped.

PowerShell skills checklist

  • I can open a terminal and identify the PowerShell prompt.
  • I can display and explain the current working directory with Get-Location.
  • I can navigate with Set-Location, including $HOME, ., and ...
  • I can list files with Get-ChildItem and recognize hidden entries.
  • I can create directories and files with New-Item.
  • I can copy, move, rename, and safely remove practice files.
  • I can quote paths containing spaces.
  • I can use Tab completion and command history.
  • I can inspect and search text with Get-Content and Select-String.
  • I understand output redirection and a basic pipeline.
  • I can run a program from its project directory.
  • I can read an error message and inspect a native program’s exit code.
  • I can interrupt a foreground process with Ctrl+C.
  • I can find command help and complete the final practice project.

Further reference

  • Microsoft PowerShell documentation
  • PowerShell about topics
  • Windows Terminal documentation
  • Python on Windows

Recommended introductory books

  • Plunk, Travis, James Petty, Tyler Leonhardt, Don Jones, and Jeffery Hicks. Learn PowerShell in a Month of Lunches, 4th edition. Manning, 2022. A hands-on introduction to PowerShell commands, the help system, the object pipeline, variables, scripts, loops, errors, and debugging. It covers Windows, Linux, and macOS. Publisher page.

Suggested use: this is a practical companion for the PowerShell track and does not require prior scripting experience. Its examples span multiple PowerShell versions and operating systems; use the course’s PowerShell version baseline and current Microsoft documentation when details differ.

Development Editors, IDEs, and Project Development Containers

Purpose and scope

An integrated development environment (IDE) combines source editing with language-aware services such as diagnostics, navigation, refactoring, debugging, testing, and project management. A code editor may provide many of these capabilities through extensions. The practical distinction is the depth of project and language tooling.

This reference identifies the development environments used or discussed in this curriculum and explains their appropriate roles. It is not an installation guide for third-party IDEs. Product descriptions are not instructions to install software, select extensions, configure accounts, or alter operating-system settings. Follow institution-approved technical support and vendor documentation for operational procedures.

The curriculum’s general-purpose editor choices are Visual Studio Code (VS Code) and Eclipse Theia. They are distinct products, not interchangeable names for one application. The recommended project-environment model is to keep the development toolchain reproducible and project-scoped, preferably through a Development Container (Dev Container) when compiler, linter, formatter, test runner, or system-library consistency is important.

Development Containers: the recommended project model

A Development Container, often shortened to Dev Container, is a containerized workspace configured specifically for software development. It is not merely a container that runs the finished application. It provides the language runtime, compiler, SDK, build tools, linters, formatters, test tools, libraries, and supporting command-line utilities needed to work on a repository.

The Development Containers Specification defines a tool-neutral metadata format for describing such environments. A project commonly stores its configuration in .devcontainer/devcontainer.json, alongside an optional Dockerfile, Compose configuration, scripts, and supporting files. A compatible editor or service interprets that metadata and connects the development interface to the environment. The project can therefore document and version the toolchain as part of the repository rather than relying on undocumented differences between learners’ computers. Specification · VS Code overview · Specification-supported tools

Why this is especially useful in a programming course

A course may require a compiler and runtime, a linter, a formatter, a test framework, a debugger, system headers or libraries, and a particular version of each. These tools interact. A learner may otherwise have a correct source file but an incompatible compiler, a missing system library, a linter version that reports different diagnostics, or a test runner that behaves differently from the instructor’s.

A repository-defined Dev Container can standardize:

  • Language toolchains: interpreters, compilers, SDKs, JDKs, and runtime versions.
  • Code quality tools: linters, static analyzers, formatters, and documentation checkers.
  • Build and test tools: build systems, test frameworks, coverage tools, and test data.
  • System dependencies: headers, native libraries, and command-line utilities required by the project.
  • Editor integration: supported language services and project-specific editor customizations.
  • Supporting services: databases, message brokers, or other dependencies when a lesson genuinely requires them.
  • Reproducibility metadata: pinned image versions, feature versions, environment variables that are not secrets, and documented lifecycle commands.

This can make a learning environment more predictable across Windows, macOS, and Linux hosts. The host still supplies the container runtime and operating-system kernel; the container supplies a controlled user-space environment. A container is not a full virtual machine and does not provide a different kernel.

Typical project structure

A project may use a structure such as:

project/
├── .devcontainer/
│   ├── devcontainer.json
│   ├── Dockerfile
│   └── compose.yaml          # optional; for multi-service environments
├── src/
├── tests/
├── scripts/
├── README.md
└── language-specific project and lock files

Not every project needs all these files. A simple project may refer to a maintained development image directly. A project with additional system packages may build from a Dockerfile. A project that depends on multiple services may use Compose. The .devcontainer directory contains the development-environment description; source code and tests remain ordinary project files.

What the configuration describes

A devcontainer.json commonly identifies or builds the development image, configures the workspace location, declares development-container Features, sets a non-root user, defines environment variables, forwards development ports, and describes lifecycle commands. Editor-specific customizations may identify extensions or settings for a compatible editor.

A Dockerfile describes how the image is built: its base image, system packages, users, and other image contents. Compose can describe a group of related services, such as a development workspace and a database. The Dev Container configuration ties the developer’s workspace experience to these container resources.

Illustrative configuration (not a complete course image):

{
  "name": "Course development environment",
  "build": {
    "dockerfile": "Dockerfile"
  },
  "remoteUser": "vscode",
  "forwardPorts": [],
  "customizations": {
    "vscode": {
      "extensions": []
    }
  }
}

This example shows the shape of project metadata only. It does not install a compiler, select a language version, or constitute a ready-to-run environment. A real course repository must provide a maintained Dockerfile or image, explicit tool versions, validation commands, and any required features.

Dev Containers as a teaching and assessment control

For this curriculum, an instructor can publish a known development environment for a language unit or project. The environment can include the exact compiler and linter versions used by automated checks. Learners then run the same project scripts locally inside the container that CI runs in a clean build environment.

A robust project should expose clear commands for tasks such as:

  • formatting checks (for example, verify formatting without silently changing submitted files);
  • linting and static analysis;
  • compilation or build;
  • unit tests and integration tests;
  • expected-output checks for instructional examples;
  • documentation and link validation where applicable.

These commands should be documented in the repository and, where practical, invoked by the same CI workflow. A Dev Container is a development convenience and consistency mechanism; it does not replace continuous integration. CI should independently build and test a clean checkout so that a learner’s persistent container state cannot conceal missing files, undeclared dependencies, or order-dependent tests.

Images, versions, and reproducibility

A development image is a versioned filesystem and toolchain template from which a container is created. For instructional use, avoid relying on floating tags such as latest when a change could alter compiler diagnostics or program behavior without a course revision. Prefer explicit supported release tags or immutable digests for controlled teaching environments. Pin language versions, package manager versions, Dev Container Features, and relevant system dependencies when reproducibility matters.

Rebuilds should be intentional and tested. Updating the base image, compiler, or linter can change warnings, formatting, generated files, or test behavior. Treat such changes as curriculum maintenance: review them, run the validation suite, and record the resulting toolchain baseline.

Dev Containers and accessibility

A container does not automatically make an editor accessible. The editor may run on the host while language servers, compilers, and extensions run inside the container. This separation can improve consistency, but it also creates multiple components that must work together.

Evaluate keyboard navigation, screen-reader announcements, braille output, editor diagnostics, terminal interaction, build output, test results, debugger behavior, and remote-session focus. Check whether the editor’s remote-development extension is accessible in the actual version used. Ensure that essential instructions and results are available as text. Do not require a graphical container dashboard or mouse-only workflow as the only way to complete an assignment.

Risks and operational boundaries

Containers are isolation mechanisms, not guarantees of security. A development container may have access to mounted source files, network resources, credentials, and host resources. Treat untrusted images, Features, package install scripts, and workspace lifecycle commands as executable code.

  • Use trusted base images and inspect their provenance.
  • Prefer a non-root development user.
  • Do not bake access tokens, passwords, SSH private keys, or personal data into an image or repository.
  • Avoid mounting the container runtime’s control socket into a learner’s development container unless the task explicitly requires it and the security implications have been reviewed.
  • Limit privileged mode, Linux capabilities, host networking, and broad host filesystem mounts.
  • Keep source code in version control; do not commit generated container layers, caches, or secrets.
  • Use synthetic data for coursework unless a governed data environment is explicitly approved.
  • Consider resource quotas and lifecycle policies for shared institutional hosts.

Container engines and tools: Docker and Podman

A Dev Container is the development-environment pattern and metadata; Docker and Podman are container engines/tooling that can build and run containers. They solve related but different parts of the workflow. The choice of engine affects compatibility, operations, security boundaries, and platform support.

Docker

Docker is a widely used container platform. Its ecosystem includes the Docker Engine, Docker CLI, Docker Desktop, image registries, build tooling, and Compose. Docker Engine commonly uses a long-running daemon to manage images, containers, networks, and volumes. Docker Desktop packages a managed experience for macOS and Windows, where Linux containers generally run in a lightweight Linux virtual machine.

Docker has broad industry adoption and extensive documentation, image availability, Compose workflows, and integration with developer tooling. VS Code’s Dev Containers documentation primarily describes a Docker-compatible workflow. This makes Docker the most straightforward baseline when an instructional environment is designed around the default VS Code Dev Containers experience.

Docker Desktop licensing and organizational use are subject to Docker’s current terms. Institutional adoption should review licensing, administration, and data-handling requirements rather than assume every deployment has identical terms.

Podman

Podman is an open-source container engine designed to manage OCI containers and images. On Linux it can operate without a central daemon and supports rootless containers, allowing many container operations to run under an ordinary user account. Podman also provides a command-line interface familiar to Docker users and supports pods, image builds, registries, and Compose-oriented workflows through associated tooling.

On macOS and Windows, Linux containers require a Linux environment; Podman commonly uses a managed virtual machine, called a Podman machine. On Linux, rootless operation can reduce the need for a privileged daemon, but it does not eliminate the need to understand user namespaces, storage, networking, and host permissions.

Podman can be attractive for Linux-based teaching labs, organizations prioritizing daemonless and rootless workflows, and teams that prefer open-source container tooling. It supports Docker-compatible interfaces for many common operations, but compatibility is not absolute. Compose behavior, networking, volume permissions, socket/API behavior, build features, and IDE integrations should be tested against the exact versions in use.

Docker and Podman compared

ConcernDockerPodman
Core modelEngine commonly managed by a daemonDaemonless architecture on Linux; API service can be exposed when needed
Rootless useSupported in specific configurationsA major design capability on Linux
macOS / WindowsDocker Desktop provides a managed Linux-container environmentPodman machine provides a managed Linux environment
CLI familiarityNative Docker CLIDocker-like CLI for many operations
Image formatOCI-compatible images and Docker ecosystem formatsOCI-compatible images
Multi-container workflowsDocker Compose is widely usedCompose-compatible workflows are available, but compatibility should be checked
Dev Container integrationCommon baseline for VS Code documentation and workflowsPossible through compatible interfaces/tooling, but validate the specific editor, extension, and runtime versions
Common selection rationaleBroad adoption, mature ecosystem, low-friction editor supportRootless/daemonless model, open-source preference, Linux host integration

Neither engine is universally better. The appropriate choice depends on the operating system, institutional policy, editor integration, desired security model, and the exact development-container features used by the project.

Dev Container compatibility is a separate question

A project may conform to the Development Containers Specification while still depending on implementation-specific behavior. The specification describes metadata; it does not guarantee every editor, service, and container engine supports every property or lifecycle feature in the same way.

  • VS Code: its Dev Containers extension is a mature implementation and its official documentation uses Docker as the standard engine workflow. Podman compatibility can depend on the Docker-compatible API endpoint and extension/runtime versions. Treat Podman as a validated alternative, not an automatic drop-in replacement.
  • Eclipse Theia: Theia is an extensible platform, and support for Dev Containers depends on the specific Theia distribution and extensions included by its provider. Confirm that the deployed Theia product supports the required parts of the specification and the selected container engine.
  • Hosted workspaces and other tools: platforms may implement the specification with managed infrastructure. Users may not control the underlying engine or host. Verify which configuration fields, Features, lifecycle hooks, and Compose patterns are supported.

The Development Containers supporting-tools directory lists implementations and services. Use it as a starting point, then test the actual environment selected for the course.

Curriculum-supported editor choices

Visual Studio Code

Visual Studio Code is a cross-platform source-code editor with an extension ecosystem, integrated terminal, source control interface, language services, debugging interfaces, and workspace features. It is suitable for introductory programming and multi-language projects where learners benefit from a consistent editor across Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, C-family languages, and other supported languages.

VS Code is an editor platform rather than a compiler or runtime. A language extension can provide syntax-aware editing and communicate with a language server, but the relevant compiler, interpreter, SDK, debugger, or external service remains a separate toolchain dependency. Its Dev Containers extension can connect the editor to a project-defined development container.

Accessibility considerations include keyboard operation, editor accessibility support, screen-reader announcements, accessible integrated terminal interaction, and the ability to inspect diagnostics and source-control changes without relying on color or spatial layout. Accessibility is version-, extension-, operating-system-, and assistive-technology-dependent. Validate the complete edit, run, debug, and test workflow with the learner’s actual screen reader or other access technology.

Eclipse Theia

Eclipse Theia is an extensible IDE framework and platform for building desktop or browser-based development environments. It shares some interaction conventions and extension concepts with VS Code, but it is a separate project with its own release, packaging, extension compatibility, and product distribution decisions.

Theia is relevant to hosted development environments, institution-managed workspaces, cloud development platforms, and organizations that need to tailor an IDE experience. Its browser-based form can reduce the need for learners to manage a full local toolchain, but it introduces dependence on network access, remote workspace availability, browser accessibility, and the accessibility of the particular Theia distribution.

Do not assume that every VS Code extension works in every Theia deployment. Do not assume that a hosted Theia environment supports the Dev Containers Specification or a particular engine. Evaluate the actual distribution used by the course or institution.

Other professional development environments

The following products are discussed for professional context. They are not required course dependencies, and this curriculum does not provide setup instructions for them.

JetBrains IDE family

JetBrains develops language- and workflow-focused IDEs. Its products are often selected when deep language intelligence, integrated refactoring, test discovery, framework support, and mature debugging workflows are important.

  • IntelliJ IDEA is a general-purpose IDE particularly associated with Java and Kotlin development, JVM projects, build systems, and enterprise application work.
  • PyCharm focuses on Python development, including project navigation, debugging, testing, virtual environments, scientific workflows, and web frameworks.
  • WebStorm focuses on JavaScript, TypeScript, and web application development, with framework-aware navigation, refactoring, and testing support.
  • CLion targets C and C++ development, including native build systems, debugger integration, and code analysis.
  • Rider focuses on .NET development and is commonly used for C#, ASP.NET Core, and Unity workflows.
  • DataGrip is a database IDE for querying, exploring, and managing relational and other supported data platforms.

JetBrains IDEs are relevant when a sustained project uses a language or ecosystem for which the corresponding IDE provides substantial integrated tooling. Product editions, licensing, supported platforms, and accessibility behavior vary. Assess the specific product and version rather than generalizing from one JetBrains IDE to the entire family.

Databricks workspace and notebooks

Databricks is a data and AI platform, not simply a general-purpose desktop IDE. Its workspace combines collaborative notebooks, data engineering workflows, SQL analytics, machine learning, governed data access, jobs, and managed compute. It is commonly used with Apache Spark and the lakehouse architecture.

Databricks notebooks support exploratory and collaborative work in languages such as Python, SQL, Scala, and R, depending on the runtime and workspace configuration. They are useful for data preparation, distributed processing, analytics, experimentation, and production data pipelines. Notebook execution is stateful: cells may depend on prior execution order and shared session state. This differs from a conventional source file executed as a fresh process. Professional workflows therefore need attention to reproducibility, dependency management, data permissions, compute cost, version control, and the distinction between exploratory analysis and production jobs.

The platform is a managed service with workspace-specific permissions, compute policies, and organizational governance. It is not a prerequisite for this introductory curriculum.

JupyterLab and notebook environments

JupyterLab is a web-based interactive computing environment built around notebooks, consoles, terminals, and file-based project work. It is widely used in education, scientific computing, data analysis, and exploratory research. A notebook interleaves executable code, output, and explanatory text.

Notebook workflows are useful for incremental experimentation and communicating analysis. They can also conceal execution-order dependencies, mutable session state, and hidden environmental assumptions. Learners should understand the underlying language and runtime rather than treating a notebook as a substitute for programming fundamentals. Keyboard and screen-reader accessibility must be assessed with the exact notebook version and extensions in use.

RStudio / Posit

RStudio is an IDE strongly associated with R, statistical analysis, data visualization, Quarto, and reproducible research. It provides an integrated source editor, console, package and project workflows, debugging, and data-oriented tools. Posit also develops products and services for publishing and managing data applications and analytical work.

RStudio is especially relevant to statisticians, researchers, analysts, and teams whose work centers on R. The R language module in this curriculum is introductory; RStudio is contextual information, not a required platform.

Microsoft Visual Studio

Microsoft Visual Studio is a full-featured IDE for Windows-centric development, especially .NET, C#, C++, desktop applications, and enterprise workloads. It is distinct from Visual Studio Code. Visual Studio typically provides a more integrated project-system and debugger experience for supported Microsoft development stacks.

Xcode

Xcode is Apple’s IDE for developing software for Apple platforms, including iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, and tvOS. It integrates Swift and Objective-C editing, Apple SDKs, simulators, signing, testing, and application distribution workflows. Apple-platform application development generally depends on Xcode and the corresponding Apple toolchain.

Eclipse IDE

Eclipse IDE is a long-established extensible IDE platform with a strong history in Java and enterprise development, as well as support for other languages through project-specific tooling. It remains relevant in organizations with established Eclipse-based workflows, plugins, and build systems.

Choosing an environment by task

Work typeTypical environment fitWhy
Introductory multi-language courseworkVS Code or an institution-provided Theia environment with a course Dev ContainerConsistent editor and toolchain across tracks
Java or Kotlin application developmentIntelliJ IDEA; also VS Code or Eclipse in suitable projectsJVM-aware navigation, refactoring, build and test integration
Python application developmentVS Code or PyCharmLanguage services, testing, debugging, and environment awareness
Front-end JavaScript and TypeScriptVS Code or WebStormType-aware editing and web-framework workflows

.NET and C#Visual Studio or Rider; VS Code for lighter workflows.NET project and debugger support
Apple-platform applicationsXcodeApple SDK, simulator, signing, and platform toolchain integration
Statistical analysis in RRStudio / PositStatistical and reproducible-research workflows
Exploratory scientific computingJupyterLabInteractive code, narrative, and results
Enterprise data engineering and analyticsDatabricks workspaceDistributed data processing, governed data, jobs, and collaborative notebooks
Database query and schema workDataGrip or a database-specific clientQuerying, schema exploration, and database-aware tooling

These are common fits, not exclusive rules. A product’s marketing category does not establish that it is appropriate for a particular course, accessible to a particular learner, or approved by an institution.

Accessibility and procurement criteria

When evaluating any editor, IDE, Dev Container, or container runtime, assess the complete workflow rather than the source editor alone:

  1. Keyboard access to files, navigation, search, diagnostics, terminal, debugging, testing, and source control.
  2. Screen-reader announcement of editor text, punctuation, indentation, completion lists, diagnostics, and status changes.
  3. Stable focus order and predictable focus restoration when panels, dialogs, remote sessions, and tool windows open and close.
  4. Ability to inspect errors and warnings as text, navigate between them, and understand their source locations.
  5. Ability to run and debug a program without relying on unlabeled icons, color-only indicators, drag-and-drop, or inaccessible graphical output.
  6. Compatibility with the learner’s operating system, screen reader, braille display, magnification, and keyboard configuration.
  7. Whether the workflow depends on a cloud account, persistent network connection, remote desktop, container VM, or institution-managed permissions.
  8. Whether source files remain accessible on the host and whether container file permissions preserve the learner’s ability to edit and submit work.
  9. Whether the container runtime, image build output, lifecycle commands, and terminal can be operated and understood without visual-only controls.
  10. Whether the organization can provide an equivalent accessible route when a specialized interface is not accessible.

A tool should not be mandated solely because it is popular or used by a professional team. The instructional objective is programming competence; an IDE and container are means of supporting that objective. Provide an equivalent accessible route when a product interface blocks participation.

Course expectation

Students should learn to create and manage source files, understand project folders, run programs, interpret diagnostics, and use version control concepts. Those skills transfer between editors and runtimes. When a course supplies a Dev Container, students should also understand what the environment provides, how to run the documented project checks, and why the environment definition is version-controlled. They are not expected to become container administrators.

The course does not require learners to master every product described here, and it does not prescribe installation or configuration steps for third-party IDEs.
