Lesson 9.5: CSV records

Reading References

  • Official C language guide and standard-library documentation.
  • Corresponding Python course lesson for the shared problem context and learning objective.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain this concept using C terminology.
  • Trace a short program and predict its behavior before execution.
  • Modify and test the example independently.

Concept Explanation

CSV is a delimited text format with quoting rules; splitting every line on commas is not a correct general CSV parser because quoted fields may contain commas, quotes, and newlines. Use a documented CSV library for production data. For the first exercise, read a simple known CSV file and state that the format excludes quoted commas.

Worked Example

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
int main(void)
{
    FILE *file = fopen("students.csv", "r");
    char line[256];
    if (!file) { perror("students.csv"); return 1; }
    if (fgets(line, sizeof line, file)) printf("Columns: %s", line);
    while (fgets(line, sizeof line, file)) printf("Record: %s", line);
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}

Create a header with student_id,first_name,last_name,score,active and at least two rows. The program prints the header and each record line. A production parser must handle CSV quoting correctly.

Expected Behavior or Output

With students.csv in the working directory, containing:

student_id,first_name,last_name,score,active
1,Avery,Student,91,true
2,Jordan,Lee,82,true
3,Casey,Smith,76,false

Output observed when the worked example was run (gcc 13.3, C17; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

Columns: student_id,first_name,last_name,score,active
Record: 1,Avery,Student,91,true
Record: 2,Jordan,Lee,82,true
Record: 3,Casey,Smith,76,false

Common Mistakes

  • Splitting every CSV line on commas despite quoted commas and escaped quotes.
  • Ignoring overlong lines or malformed rows.
  • Assuming every row contains the same number of fields without validating it.

Activities

  1. Create the canonical students.csv header and two data rows.
  2. Test missing file, empty file, and an overlong row.
  3. Add a quoted comma and explain why naive comma splitting is invalid CSV parsing.
  4. Write the expected test result and explain what a failing assertion or diagnostic would indicate.

Lesson 10.2: Text adventure: five rooms and movement

Reading References

  • C language standard library: stdio.h, string.h, and ctype.h.
  • Canonical shared project specification: Python Unit 10, Lesson 10.3.

Learning Objectives

  • Represent all five canonical rooms with C records and integer room indexes.
  • Validate movement before changing the current room.
  • Explain why the treasure room is not reachable until the key puzzle is implemented.

Concept Explanation

Use five fixed room indexes: start_room is 0, tunnel is 1, clearing is 2, locked_door_room is 3, and treasure_room is 4. Each exit stores a destination index or -1 when no exit exists. The graph is start north to tunnel; tunnel south to start and east to clearing; clearing west to tunnel and north to locked_door_room; and locked_door_room south to clearing. Part 1 deliberately has no north exit from locked_door_room.

The command loop reads a line, normalizes it to lowercase, checks the selected exit, and updates the current room only when the destination is valid. End-of-file acts like quit.

Worked Example

#include <ctype.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

typedef struct {
    const char *id;
    const char *description;
    int north, east, south, west;
} Room;

int main(void) {
    Room rooms[5] = {
        {"start_room", "A dimly lit cave. A narrow passage leads north.", 1, -1, -1, -1},
        {"tunnel", "A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.", -1, 2, 0, -1},
        {"clearing", "A quiet clearing. An antechamber lies to the north.", 3, -1, -1, 1},
        {"locked_door_room", "A chamber with a heavy door to the north.", -1, -1, 2, -1},
        {"treasure_room", "You found the treasure. You win!", -1, -1, -1, -1}
    };
    int current = 0;
    char command[80];

    for (;;) {
        printf("---\n%s\nWhat do you want to do?\n", rooms[current].description);
        if (!fgets(command, sizeof command, stdin)) strcpy(command, "quit");
        command[strcspn(command, "\r\n")] = '\0';
        for (size_t i = 0; command[i] != '\0'; ++i)
            command[i] = (char)tolower((unsigned char)command[i]);

        if (strcmp(command, "quit") == 0) {
            puts("Exiting game. Goodbye!");
            break;
        }

        int destination = -1;
        if (strcmp(command, "north") == 0) destination = rooms[current].north;
        else if (strcmp(command, "east") == 0) destination = rooms[current].east;
        else if (strcmp(command, "south") == 0) destination = rooms[current].south;
        else if (strcmp(command, "west") == 0) destination = rooms[current].west;

        if (destination >= 0 && destination < 5) current = destination;
        else puts("You cannot go that way. Enter a listed direction or quit.");
    }
    return 0;
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Enter north, east, north, north, quit. The player reaches tunnel, clearing, and locked_door_room. The second north is rejected and the player remains in locked_door_room. The treasure room is present in the room table but has no incoming exit in Part 1.

Common Mistakes

  • Using -1 as an array index instead of checking it first.
  • Updating the current room before validating the destination.
  • Confusing a room index with the room’s display name.
  • Adding the treasure exit before the key puzzle is implemented.

Activities

  1. Trace north, east, north and record the room index after each command.
  2. Try west from start_room and verify the current room does not change.
  3. Verify every nonnegative exit index is between 0 and 4.
  4. Explain why treasure_room is unreachable in Part 1.

Accessibility Practice

Read the room description and prompt in order. The invalid-movement response explains what happened and how to continue. Compile and run from the terminal, then inspect output sequentially with the learner’s access technology.

Skills Checklist

  • I can represent all five rooms with C records.
  • I can represent missing exits with a sentinel value.
  • I validate an exit before changing rooms.
  • I can reject an invalid direction without changing state.
  • I can explain why the treasure room is not yet reachable.

Lesson 10.3: Text adventure: shiny key and locked door

Reading References

  • C language standard library: stdio.h, string.h, and ctype.h.
  • Canonical shared project specification: Python Unit 10, Lesson 10.3.

Learning Objectives

  • Keep the shiny key in start_room until it is collected.
  • Transfer the key to inventory exactly once.
  • Require the player to use the key in locked_door_room before moving north to treasure_room.
  • End the game after the player reaches treasure_room.

Concept Explanation

Keep the five-room graph from Lesson 10.2. The shiny key begins in start_room. The take shiny key command changes key_in_room to false and has_key to true. The use shiny key command succeeds only when the player is in locked_door_room and has_key is true. North from locked_door_room is blocked while door_locked is true. Reaching treasure_room ends the game.

Worked Example

#include <ctype.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

typedef struct {
    const char *id;
    const char *description;
    int north, east, south, west;
} Room;

int main(void) {
    Room rooms[5] = {
        {"start_room", "A dimly lit cave.", 1, -1, -1, -1},
        {"tunnel", "A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.", -1, 2, 0, -1},
        {"clearing", "A quiet clearing. An antechamber lies to the north.", 3, -1, -1, 1},
        {"locked_door_room", "A chamber with a heavy door to the north.", 4, -1, 2, -1},
        {"treasure_room", "You found the treasure. You win!", -1, -1, -1, -1}
    };
    int current = 0, key_in_room = 1, has_key = 0, door_locked = 1;
    char command[80];

    for (;;) {
        printf("\n%s\n", rooms[current].description);
        if (current == 4) break;
        if (current == 0 && key_in_room) puts("You see: shiny key");
        puts(has_key ? "Your inventory: shiny key" : "Your inventory: empty");
        puts("What do you want to do?");
        if (!fgets(command, sizeof command, stdin)) strcpy(command, "quit");
        command[strcspn(command, "\r\n")] = '\0';
        for (size_t i = 0; command[i] != '\0'; ++i)
            command[i] = (char)tolower((unsigned char)command[i]);

        if (strcmp(command, "quit") == 0) {
            puts("You quit the adventure.");
            break;
        } else if (strcmp(command, "take shiny key") == 0) {
            if (current == 0 && key_in_room) {
                key_in_room = 0;
                has_key = 1;
                puts("You picked up the shiny key.");
            } else puts("There is no shiny key here to take.");
        } else if (strcmp(command, "use shiny key") == 0) {
            if (current != 3) puts("You must be at the locked door to use the key.");
            else if (!has_key) puts("You do not have the shiny key.");
            else {
                door_locked = 0;
                puts("You unlocked the door!");
            }
        } else if (current == 3 && strcmp(command, "north") == 0 && door_locked) {
            puts("The door is locked! You need to use the shiny key here.");
        } else {
            int destination = -1;
            if (strcmp(command, "north") == 0) destination = rooms[current].north;
            else if (strcmp(command, "east") == 0) destination = rooms[current].east;
            else if (strcmp(command, "south") == 0) destination = rooms[current].south;
            else if (strcmp(command, "west") == 0) destination = rooms[current].west;
            if (destination >= 0 && destination < 5) current = destination;
            else puts("Invalid command. Enter north, south, east, west, take shiny key, use shiny key, or quit.");
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Enter north, east, north, north, south, west, south, take shiny key, north, east, north, use shiny key, north. The first north from locked_door_room is rejected. The key is removed from the room and added to inventory. Using it outside locked_door_room is rejected. Using it there unlocks the door; the final north reaches treasure_room and prints the win description. End-of-file acts like quit.

Common Mistakes

  • Allowing the key to be collected more than once.
  • Unlocking the door without checking both room location and inventory.
  • Allowing north movement before door_locked becomes false.
  • Leaving the key listed in start_room after pickup.
  • Treating a failed command as a state change.

Activities

  1. Run the full command sequence and record room, key location, inventory, and door state.
  2. Try taking the key twice; the second attempt must be rejected.
  3. Try using the key in start_room and clearing; both attempts must be rejected.
  4. Try north from locked_door_room before and after unlocking.
  5. Add a help command that lists every supported command.

Accessibility Practice

Announce the room, visible item, inventory, and prompt as separate text lines. Every failed action explains why it failed. Test the full sequence with a screen reader and verify that item and door state are unambiguous.

Skills Checklist

  • I can implement the five-room graph.
  • I can transfer the shiny key to inventory exactly once.
  • I can require key use in the locked-door room.
  • I can block and unlock the north exit.
  • I can end the game in the treasure room.

Lesson 10.4: Command-line to-do manager

Reading References

  • Official C language guide and standard-library documentation.
  • Corresponding Python course lesson for the shared problem context and learning objective.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain this concept using C terminology.
  • Trace a short program and predict its behavior before execution.
  • Modify and test the example independently.

Concept Explanation

Build a command-line to-do tool with a menu loop and separate functions for adding, viewing, completing, saving, and loading tasks. Use the shared task fields and provide confirmations. C has no standard JSON support; for this project either choose a maintained JSON library and document its build instructions, or use a clearly documented simple text format while teaching JSON serialization separately in Lesson 8.5. Do not label a custom text format as JSON.

Worked Example

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
typedef struct { char title[80]; int done; } Task;
void show_tasks(const Task tasks[], size_t count)
{
    if (count == 0) { puts("No tasks in your list."); return; }
    for (size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i)
        printf("%zu. [%c] %s\n", i + 1, tasks[i].done ? 'X' : ' ', tasks[i].title);
}
int main(void)
{
    Task tasks[50] = {0}; size_t count = 0; char line[100];
    for (;;) {
        puts("1 Add task  2 View tasks  3 Quit");
        printf("Choice: ");
        if (!fgets(line, sizeof line, stdin)) break;
        if (line[0] == '1' && count < 50) {
            printf("Task title: ");
            if (!fgets(tasks[count].title, sizeof tasks[count].title, stdin)) break;
            tasks[count].title[strcspn(tasks[count].title, "\n")] = '\0';
            tasks[count++].done = 0; puts("Task added.");
        } else if (line[0] == '2') show_tasks(tasks, count);
        else if (line[0] == '3') break;
        else puts("Invalid choice.");
    }
    return 0;
}

This starter implements add, view, and quit with a fixed capacity of 50 tasks. Extend it with completion and persistence, checking every input and file operation.

Expected Behavior or Output

Output observed when the worked example was run (gcc 13.3, C17; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

1 Add task  2 View tasks  3 Quit
Choice:

Common Mistakes

  • Writing beyond the fixed task array’s capacity.
  • Treating the first character of a menu line as fully validated input.
  • Completing or deleting a task by index without checking the selected range.

Activities

  1. Add two tasks and view them in insertion order.
  2. Complete a task by ID and reject an unknown ID.
  3. Implement save/load and verify data remains after restarting.
  4. Write an acceptance test with the initial project state, user action, expected response, and unchanged state after a rejected action.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate the complete source file by line, word, and character using the learner’s access technology. Read punctuation and indentation, run from the terminal, and inspect standard output and errors sequentially.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain the C rule demonstrated by “Command-line to-do manager” without relying on Python terminology.
  • I can predict and verify the exact behavior of this lesson’s worked example.
  • I can complete the lesson-specific boundary or extension tests above and explain the result.
  • I can recognize the three C-specific failure modes listed in this lesson and apply a correction.
  • I can navigate, compile, run, and inspect the source and output using my chosen access technology.

Lesson 10.5: Accessible UX and validation

Reading References

  • Official C language guide and standard-library documentation.
  • Corresponding Python course lesson for the shared problem context and learning objective.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain this concept using C terminology.
  • Trace a short program and predict its behavior before execution.
  • Modify and test the example independently.

Concept Explanation

Accessible text interfaces use explicit prompts, consistent labels, predictable menu order, and clear confirmations. Validate all input before changing state. On errors, state what was wrong and how to correct it. Do not rely on color, position, or symbols alone to convey task status. For a screen-reader workflow, ensure output is announced in a useful sequence.

Worked Example

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
int main(void)
{
    char line[80], *end;
    long age;
    for (;;) {
        printf("Enter your age as a positive whole number: ");
        if (!fgets(line, sizeof line, stdin)) return 1;
        age = strtol(line, &end, 10);
        if (end != line && age > 0) break;
        puts("Invalid age. Enter a whole number greater than zero.");
    }
    printf("You entered age: %ld\n", age);
    return 0;
}

The program repeats until it receives a positive integer. Improve it by rejecting trailing non-whitespace characters and checking errno for overflow.

Expected Behavior or Output

With these lines typed as standard input:

abc
-4
16

Output observed when the worked example was run (gcc 13.3, C17; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

Enter your age as a positive whole number: Invalid age. Enter a whole number greater than zero.
Enter your age as a positive whole number: Invalid age. Enter a whole number greater than zero.
Enter your age as a positive whole number: You entered age: 16

Common Mistakes

  • Using color or a symbol as the only indication of completion.
  • Displaying an error without telling the user how to correct it.
  • Silently truncating an overlong title or failing to announce a successful operation.

Activities

  1. Complete the menu workflow using keyboard only and read prompts sequentially.
  2. Submit blank, overlong, and invalid menu input and verify corrective instructions.
  3. Test with a named screen reader and OS; record observed results rather than assuming compatibility.
  4. Write an acceptance test with the initial project state, user action, expected response, and unchanged state after a rejected action.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate the complete source file by line, word, and character using the learner’s access technology. Read punctuation and indentation, run from the terminal, and inspect standard output and errors sequentially.

Unit 11: Capstone: Personal Data Manager

Overview

Plan, implement, test, document, and present a C personal-data manager using the shared record fields and required CRUD/persistence behavior. Preserve the Python capstone’s data and functional requirements while using a C-appropriate terminal-first interface.

The Python capstone uses NiceGUI, but that framework is Python-specific. The C course must preserve the same user-facing data-manager requirements without pretending that NiceGUI has a C equivalent. Implement a keyboard-operable terminal interface first; a graphical interface is an optional extension using a separately selected C-compatible toolkit. The core record fields, operations, validation, persistence, tests, and accessibility acceptance criteria remain the same.

Lesson 11.2: Data model and storage

Reading References

  • Official C language guide and standard-library documentation.
  • Corresponding Python course lesson for the shared problem context and learning objective.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain this concept using C terminology.
  • Trace a short program and predict its behavior before execution.
  • Modify and test the example independently.

Concept Explanation

Define a C struct for the shared capstone record and choose a clear ownership strategy for strings. Fixed-size arrays are acceptable for a small beginner project if maximum lengths are documented and input is bounded. For persistent data, use a maintained JSON library and document its version, dependency setup, and error handling. The C standard library does not provide JSON serialization.

Worked Example

#include <stddef.h>
typedef struct {
    int id;
    char title[80];
    char description[240];
    char category[40];
    char created_at[32];
    char updated_at[32];
} DataItem;

The record contains the exact canonical capstone fields. Define which fields are required, how empty strings are handled, and how IDs and timestamps are generated. The serialization layer must preserve all fields when saving and loading.

Expected Behavior or Output

The struct definition prints nothing by itself, and it is not a complete program. The expected result is a written storage design: which fields are required, how empty strings are treated, how IDs and timestamps are produced, and how a save followed by a load preserves every field.

Common Mistakes

  • Using fixed-size fields without documenting maximum lengths and truncation policy.
  • Generating duplicate IDs or inconsistent timestamp formats.
  • Serializing only part of the canonical record or trusting loaded fields without validation.

Activities

  1. Define every C record field and its maximum length or allocation strategy.
  2. Specify ID generation, timestamp format, and string ownership.
  3. Round-trip a record through the chosen JSON library and compare every field.
  4. Add one capstone acceptance-test case to the project test plan, including test data, expected persisted fields, and failure behavior.

Lesson 11.3: Create/read/update/delete

Reading References

  • Official C language guide and standard-library documentation.
  • Corresponding Python course lesson for the shared problem context and learning objective.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain this concept using C terminology.
  • Trace a short program and predict its behavior before execution.
  • Modify and test the example independently.

Concept Explanation

Implement create, read, update, and delete operations as separate functions that operate on the same collection and report success or failure. Validate an identifier before modifying a record. After every operation, refresh the displayed list and persist successful changes. Avoid returning pointers to local stack variables.

Worked Example

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
typedef struct { int id; char title[80]; int done; } Task;
int find_task(const Task tasks[], size_t count, int id)
{
    for (size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i) if (tasks[i].id == id) return (int)i;
    return -1;
}
int main(void)
{
    Task tasks[] = {{1, "Read C lesson", 0}, {2, "Practice arrays", 1}};
    size_t count = sizeof tasks / sizeof tasks[0];
    int index = find_task(tasks, count, 1);
    if (index >= 0) { strcpy(tasks[index].title, "Review C arrays"); tasks[index].done = 1; }
    for (size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i)
        printf("%d: %s (%s)\n", tasks[i].id, tasks[i].title, tasks[i].done ? "done" : "open");
    return 0;
}

Expected state: task 1 is renamed to Review C arrays and marked done; task 2 is unchanged. Add bounds-safe input and implement add/delete operations using the same ID lookup.

Expected Behavior or Output

Output observed when the worked example was run (gcc 13.3, C17; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

1: Review C arrays (done)
2: Practice arrays (done)

Common Mistakes

  • Using an unchecked lookup result as an array index.
  • Copying a title into a fixed-size buffer without checking length.
  • Changing in-memory state before persistence succeeds without a recovery strategy.

Activities

  1. Add two records and verify their stable display order.
  2. Edit one record by ID and confirm unrelated fields remain unchanged.
  3. Delete an existing record, then attempt to delete the same ID again.
  4. Add one capstone acceptance-test case to the project test plan, including test data, expected persisted fields, and failure behavior.

Lesson 11.4: Validation and testing

Reading References

  • Official C language guide and standard-library documentation.
  • Corresponding Python course lesson for the shared problem context and learning objective.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain this concept using C terminology.
  • Trace a short program and predict its behavior before execution.
  • Modify and test the example independently.

Concept Explanation

Validate required fields before creating or updating a record. Test duplicate IDs, empty titles, overlong input, missing files, malformed JSON, and operations on unknown IDs. Keep deterministic logic separate from terminal input so it can be tested. In C, use assertions or a test framework and run with compiler warnings; consider AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer during development.

Worked Example

#include <assert.h>
#include <string.h>
int valid_title(const char *title)
{
    return title != NULL && title[0] != '\0';
}
int main(void)
{
    assert(valid_title("Read C lesson"));
    assert(!valid_title(""));
    assert(!valid_title(NULL));
    return 0;
}

All assertions pass with exit status 0. Add tests for the full CRUD functions and compile a debug build with -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer where supported.

Expected Behavior or Output

Output observed when the worked example was run (gcc 13.3, C17; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

The program prints nothing and exits normally.

Common Mistakes

  • Testing only successful operations and ignoring malformed input or missing files.
  • Ignoring compiler warnings or sanitizer diagnostics.
  • Using assertions for recoverable user input errors in the release application.

Activities

  1. Create a test matrix for valid, boundary, malformed, missing-file, and unknown-ID cases.
  2. Compile with warnings and address every diagnostic.
  3. Run AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer where available and investigate reports.
  4. Add one capstone acceptance-test case to the project test plan, including test data, expected persisted fields, and failure behavior.

Unit 0: Accessible Environment and Toolchain

Course overview

Before you start: complete Unit P: Computing Foundations Primer. It explains the language-neutral vocabulary and concepts used in every language track, using non-visual examples.

Course Overview

C++ is used in game engines, simulation, robotics, finance, desktop software, and performance-critical systems.

This course intentionally parallels the original Python curriculum. It reuses problem contexts—greetings, profiles, a calculator, grade decisions, score collections, inventory, functions, text files, tests, text analysis, CSV, a to-do list, and a personal-data manager—so the principal new learning target is the C++ language. The syntax and implementation remain idiomatic, not a mechanical translation.

Unit 0: Accessible Environment and Toolchain

Overview

Install a C++20 compiler, configure an editor, create a reproducible project workspace, and verify keyboard and assistive-technology access to source code, diagnostics, and terminal output.

Lesson 0.1: Install and Verify C++

Reading References

  • GCC, Clang, or Microsoft C++ compiler installation documentation.
  • C++ language support and compiler-version documentation.

Learning Objectives

  • Identify the compiler and its version.
  • Compile, link, and run a minimal C++20 program.
  • Explain the difference between a compiler diagnostic and program output.

Concept Explanation

C++ is a compiled language. The compiler translates each translation unit; the linker combines object code and required libraries into an executable. The course uses C++20. Keep the compiler, editor language service, and command-line build on the same standard.

Worked Example

#include <iostream>
int main() {
    std::cout << "Hello, C++20!\n";
    return 0;
}

Compile with c++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g main.cpp -o main; run with ./main (or the platform executable form).

Expected Behavior or Output

The compile command prints nothing when there are no warnings. Running the program prints one line:

Hello, C++20!

This output was observed with g++ 13.3 on Linux.

Common Mistakes

  • Installing only editor syntax highlighting and assuming it includes a compiler.
  • Omitting the C++20 standard flag and unknowingly using a different language baseline.
  • Treating a compiler error as output produced by the running program.

Activities

  1. Install GCC, Clang, or MSVC and record its exact version.
  2. Compile and run the example from the terminal.
  3. Remove the semicolon after the output statement, compile again, and locate the diagnostic.
  4. Restore the semicolon and confirm that the build succeeds.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate the source by line, word, and character. Confirm that punctuation, braces, indentation, compiler diagnostics, and terminal output can be read without relying on color or mouse-only controls.

Skills Checklist

  • I can identify the installed compiler and version.
  • I can compile and link a C++20 program from the terminal.
  • I can run the executable and distinguish its output from diagnostics.
  • I can navigate the source and diagnostic text with my access technology.

Lesson 0.2: Workspace and First Run

Reading References

  • Compiler command-line documentation.
  • The shared terminal prerequisite.

Learning Objectives

  • Create a course workspace and source file.
  • Identify the current working directory and executable path.
  • Rebuild and run a program after changing its source.

Concept Explanation

A source file such as main.cpp is input to the compiler; it is not itself the executable. Relative paths are interpreted from the process’s current working directory. Keep source files separate from generated executables and temporary build output.

Worked Example

mkdir -p cpp-course/hello
cd cpp-course/hello
# Save the C++ example as main.cpp
c++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic main.cpp -o hello
./hello

Expected Behavior or Output

Compiling prints nothing when the source is correct, and ./hello prints:

Hello, C++20!

Common Mistakes

  • Running the compile command from a directory that does not contain the source file.
  • Editing one copy of a file while compiling a different copy.
  • Confusing the source filename with the executable filename.

Activities

  1. Create a course folder and a hello subfolder.
  2. Save the first program as main.cpp and compile it to hello.
  3. Change the output text, rebuild, and verify the new output.
  4. List the folder contents and identify source versus generated files.

Accessibility Practice

Use terminal commands to confirm the working directory and list files. Navigate the folder tree with keyboard commands and verify the executable name from text output.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create and navigate a project directory.
  • I can identify the current working directory.
  • I can compile a named source file into a separate executable.
  • I can rebuild after an edit and verify the changed output.

Lesson 0.3: Editor and Accessibility Workflow

Reading References

  • IDE setup lesson.
  • Documentation for the chosen editor’s C++ language extension and screen-reader support.

Learning Objectives

  • Open the project root rather than an individual source file only.
  • Configure C++ language services and compiler selection.
  • Navigate source, diagnostics, terminal, and project files by keyboard.

Concept Explanation

An editor provides text editing; an IDE adds integrated language services, build, debugging, and project navigation. VS Code, VSCodium, and Theia can provide C++ support through extensions, but their extension marketplaces differ. A language server is not a substitute for an installed compiler.

Worked Example

Open the folder containing main.cpp, install the appropriate C++ language extension, select the same compiler used in the terminal, and confirm that diagnostics identify a deliberately introduced syntax error.

Expected Behavior or Output

The editor shows a diagnostic at the syntax error that you introduce, with a line number and message that match what the compiler prints in the terminal. After you fix the error, the editor and the compiler are both clean.

Common Mistakes

  • Opening only a file instead of the project root, preventing project-level configuration from loading.
  • Installing an extension from a marketplace unavailable to the selected editor distribution.
  • Assuming code completion or syntax highlighting proves that the compiler is configured.

Activities

  1. Open the project folder in VS Code, VSCodium, or Theia.
  2. Verify language-server diagnostics and compiler selection.
  3. Navigate to a line, inspect punctuation, and read a diagnostic using the screen reader.
  4. Build and run from the integrated terminal, then repeat from the system terminal.

Accessibility Practice

Test keyboard-only access to the editor, file tree, diagnostics panel, integrated terminal, and output. Adjust punctuation verbosity and indentation announcements to a usable level.

Skills Checklist

  • I can open the project root in my chosen editor.
  • I can identify the C++ extension and compiler configuration.
  • I can navigate diagnostics and terminal output by keyboard.
  • I can complete the build/run workflow without mouse-only actions.

Lesson 0.4: Project Environments, Dependencies, and Terminal Usage

Reading References

  • CMake getting-started documentation.
  • Compiler and linker command-line documentation.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the working directory and the roles of source, header, object, and executable files.
  • Compile and link a multi-file project.
  • Record external dependencies and reproducible build instructions.

Concept Explanation

C++ dependencies may be supplied by the standard library or external libraries. Header lookup happens during preprocessing/compilation; unresolved external symbols are generally linker errors. Larger projects should record build configuration and use an out-of-source build directory such as a CMake build/ folder.

Worked Example

c++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g main.cpp helper.cpp -o app
./app

Expected Behavior or Output

The compile command builds one program from both source files and prints nothing when it succeeds; ./app then runs it. If helper.cpp is left off the command, the linker reports an undefined reference error.

Common Mistakes

  • Running a relative path from the wrong working directory.
  • Treating a missing header as a linker error.
  • Omitting a required implementation file or library from the link command.

Activities

  1. Compile a one-file program from the project root and record the exact command.
  2. Split a program into a header, implementation file, and main.cpp; compile and link all translation units.
  3. Remove one implementation file from the command and interpret the linker diagnostic.
  4. Record compiler version, standard flag, dependencies, and build steps in a README.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate each project file and terminal diagnostic by keyboard. Confirm that build errors can be read sequentially and are not communicated by color alone.

Skills Checklist

  • I can identify the project root and run commands from it.
  • I can explain the difference between a header error and a linker error.
  • I can compile and link a multi-file project.
  • I can document dependencies and reproducible build steps.

Unit 1: Foundations of Computing

Lesson 1.1: Computer science and problem solving

Reading References

  • Official C++ language guide and standard-library documentation.
  • Corresponding Python course lesson for the shared problem context and learning objective.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain this concept using C++ terminology.
  • Trace a short program and predict its behavior before execution.
  • Modify and test the example independently.

Concept Explanation

Computer science and problem solving is taught through the shared course datasets and requirements. The Python curriculum supplies a common problem context, not syntax to translate mechanically. In C++, make the type system, object lifetime, standard-library contracts, ownership, and failure behavior explicit. This lesson focuses on: distinguish an algorithm from its C++ implementation; a clean build does not prove algorithmic correctness.

Worked Example

std::cout << "Computer science turns problems into precise, testable steps.\n";

Trace: predict the output before compiling. Identify declarations, values, control-flow decisions, and state changes in order. Then compile and compare actual output with the prediction. The lesson example is intended to be independently compilable.

Expected Behavior or Output

Output observed when the worked example was run with empty standard input (g++ 13.3, C++20; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

Computer science turns problems into precise, testable steps.

Common Mistakes

  • A successful compile does not establish that the algorithm satisfies the requirement.
  • Distinguish an algorithm from its C++ implementation.
  • A clean build does not prove algorithmic correctness.

Activities

  1. Trace the computer science and problem solving example and predict its output before compiling.
  2. Adapt the example to Avery’s profile and greeting and preserve the same observable requirement using idiomatic C++20.
  3. Add one boundary case and one invalid or missing-data case; state the expected result and implement the handling.
  4. Write a short test or trace table, then explain the C++ type, lifetime, ownership, iterator, or error-handling rule that matters here.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate the complete source file by line, word, and character using the learner’s access technology. Read punctuation and indentation, run from the terminal, and inspect standard output and errors sequentially.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain the concept in C++ terminology.
  • I can trace and predict the example.
  • I can modify and run the code independently.
  • I can identify and correct a common error.
  • I can read source and output accessibly.

Lesson 2.5: Using the Math Library

Reading References

  • C++ standard library documentation for <cmath>.
  • Python Unit 2.5 for the corresponding circle and distance problems.

Learning Objectives

  • Include and use mathematical functions from <cmath>.
  • Calculate a circle’s area and circumference.
  • Calculate distance from the origin using the Pythagorean theorem.

Concept Explanation

C++ provides common mathematical functions through <cmath>, including std::sqrt, std::pow, and std::round. Prefer direct multiplication for simple squares when it improves clarity. Use floating-point types for measurements and check domain constraints before calling functions such as square root.

Worked Example

#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    const double radius = 3.0;
    const double pi = std::acos(-1.0);
    const double area = pi * radius * radius;
    const double circumference = 2.0 * pi * radius;
    const double distance = std::sqrt(3.0 * 3.0 + 4.0 * 4.0);
    std::cout << "Area: " << area << '\n';
    std::cout << "Circumference: " << circumference << '\n';
    std::cout << "Distance: " << distance << '\n';
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Output observed when the worked example was run with empty standard input (g++ 13.3, C++20; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

Area: 28.2743
Circumference: 18.8496
Distance: 5

Common Mistakes

  • Calling a math function without including <cmath> or qualifying it with std::.
  • Using integer variables for measurements and losing fractional precision.
  • Passing a negative value to std::sqrt without defining an error policy.

Activities

  1. Change the radius to 5 and calculate the expected area and circumference before running.
  2. Calculate the distance for coordinates (5, 12), then compare it with the expected 13.
  3. Add a guard for a negative radicand and explain the chosen behavior.
  4. Format the results to two decimal places and compare rounded output with the unrounded values.

Accessibility Practice

Read each intermediate variable and output label in source order. Keep units and labels in text output rather than communicating values through a visual chart.

Skills Checklist

  • I can include and call functions from <cmath>.
  • I can calculate circle area and circumference.
  • I can calculate distance from coordinates using std::sqrt.
  • I can explain floating-point precision and domain validation.
  • I can format calculated measurements with meaningful labels and units.

Lesson 10.2: Text adventure: five rooms and movement

Reading References

  • C++ standard library: map
  • C++ standard library: string
  • Canonical shared project specification: Python Unit 10, Lesson 10.3.

Learning Objectives

  • Represent all five canonical rooms with C++ structs and maps.
  • Validate movement before changing the current room.
  • Explain why the treasure room is not reachable until the key puzzle is implemented.

Concept Explanation

Use the same five-room graph in every language. A Room stores a description and a map from direction strings to room identifiers. The player begins in start_room. Part 1 includes the unconditional connections but leaves the north exit from locked_door_room unavailable. A failed map lookup must not change the current room.

Worked Example

#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <string>

struct Room {
    std::string description;
    std::map<std::string, std::string> exits;
};

int main() {
    const std::map<std::string, Room> rooms{
        {"start_room", {"A dimly lit cave. A narrow passage leads north.", {{"north", "tunnel"}}}},
        {"tunnel", {"A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.", {{"south", "start_room"}, {"east", "clearing"}}}},
        {"clearing", {"A quiet clearing. An antechamber lies to the north.", {{"west", "tunnel"}, {"north", "locked_door_room"}}}},
        {"locked_door_room", {"A chamber with a heavy door to the north.", {{"south", "clearing"}}}},
        {"treasure_room", {"You found the treasure. You win!", {}}}
    };

    std::string current = "start_room";
    std::string command;
    while (true) {
        std::cout << "---\n" << rooms.at(current).description << "\nWhat do you want to do?\n";
        if (!std::getline(std::cin, command)) command = "quit";
        if (command == "quit") {
            std::cout << "Exiting game. Goodbye!\n";
            break;
        }
        const auto& exits = rooms.at(current).exits;
        const auto destination = exits.find(command);
        if (destination != exits.end()) current = destination->second;
        else std::cout << "You cannot go that way. Enter a listed direction or quit.\n";
    }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Enter north, east, north, north, quit. The player reaches tunnel, clearing, and locked_door_room. The second north is rejected and the current room does not change. The treasure room exists but has no incoming exit in Part 1.

Common Mistakes

  • Using map::at for a direction that may not exist.
  • Updating current before checking the map lookup result.
  • Defining a destination that is not one of the five room identifiers.
  • Adding the treasure exit before implementing the key puzzle.

Activities

  1. Trace north, east, north, north and record the current room.
  2. Try west from start_room and verify that the room does not change.
  3. Check every exit destination against the room map.
  4. Explain why treasure_room cannot yet be reached.

Accessibility Practice

Announce the room description and prompt in a consistent order. The invalid-movement response explains what happened and how to continue. Compile and run from the terminal and inspect output sequentially with the learner’s access technology.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model all five canonical rooms.
  • I can use a map to represent exits.
  • I can reject invalid movement without changing state.
  • I can explain why the treasure room is not yet reachable.

Lesson 10.3: Text adventure: shiny key and locked door

Reading References

  • C++ standard library: vector
  • C++ standard library: algorithm
  • Canonical shared project specification: Python Unit 10, Lesson 10.3.

Learning Objectives

  • Place the shiny key in start_room and transfer it to inventory exactly once.
  • Require the key to be used in locked_door_room.
  • Unlock the north exit only after the key puzzle succeeds.
  • End the game when the player reaches treasure_room.

Concept Explanation

Keep the same five-room graph. Each room has a vector of items. Picking up the shiny key removes it from the room and appends it to the inventory. The use command checks both the player’s location and inventory. A north command from locked_door_room is rejected while the door is locked.

Worked Example

#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Room {
    std::string description;
    std::map<std::string, std::string> exits;
    std::vector<std::string> items;
};

int main() {
    std::map<std::string, Room> rooms{
        {"start_room", {"A dimly lit cave.", {{"north", "tunnel"}}, {"shiny key"}}},
        {"tunnel", {"A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.", {{"south", "start_room"}, {"east", "clearing"}}, {}}},
        {"clearing", {"A quiet clearing. An antechamber lies to the north.", {{"west", "tunnel"}, {"north", "locked_door_room"}}, {}}},
        {"locked_door_room", {"A chamber with a heavy door to the north.", {{"south", "clearing"}, {"north", "treasure_room"}}, {}}},
        {"treasure_room", {"You found the treasure. You win!", {}, {}}}
    };

    std::string current = "start_room";
    std::vector<std::string> inventory;
    bool door_locked = true;
    std::string command;

    while (true) {
        Room& room = rooms.at(current);
        std::cout << "\n" << room.description << "\n";
        if (current == "treasure_room") break;
        if (!room.items.empty()) {
            std::cout << "You see: ";
            for (const auto& item : room.items) std::cout << item << " ";
            std::cout << "\n";
        }
        std::cout << "Your inventory: ";
        if (inventory.empty()) std::cout << "empty";
        else for (const auto& item : inventory) std::cout << item << " ";
        std::cout << "\nWhat do you want to do?\n";

        if (!std::getline(std::cin, command)) command = "quit";
        if (command == "quit") {
            std::cout << "You quit the adventure.\n";
            break;
        } else if (command == "take shiny key") {
            auto item = std::find(room.items.begin(), room.items.end(), "shiny key");
            if (item != room.items.end()) {
                room.items.erase(item);
                inventory.push_back("shiny key");
                std::cout << "You picked up the shiny key.\n";
            } else std::cout << "There is no shiny key here to take.\n";
        } else if (command == "use shiny key") {
            if (current != "locked_door_room") std::cout << "You must be at the locked door to use the key.\n";
            else if (std::find(inventory.begin(), inventory.end(), "shiny key") == inventory.end())
                std::cout << "You do not have the shiny key.\n";
            else {
                door_locked = false;
                std::cout << "You unlocked the door!\n";
            }
        } else if (current == "locked_door_room" && command == "north" && door_locked) {
            std::cout << "The door is locked! You need to use the shiny key here.\n";
        } else {
            auto destination = room.exits.find(command);
            if (destination != room.exits.end()) current = destination->second;
            else std::cout << "Invalid command. Enter north, south, east, west, take shiny key, use shiny key, or quit.\n";
        }
    }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Enter north, east, north, north, south, west, south, take shiny key, north, east, north, use shiny key, north. The first north from locked_door_room is rejected. Taking the key removes it from the room and adds it to inventory. Using it outside locked_door_room is rejected. Using it in that room unlocks the door; the final north reaches treasure_room and prints the win description.

Common Mistakes

  • Erasing the key without adding it to inventory, or adding it without erasing it.
  • Unlocking the door without checking the current room.
  • Unlocking the door without checking inventory.
  • Allowing north movement before door_locked becomes false.
  • Using map::at for an unvalidated command.

Activities

  1. Run the complete puzzle sequence and record room, items, inventory, and door state.
  2. Attempt to take the key twice and verify no duplicate is added.
  3. Try to use the key outside locked_door_room.
  4. Try north before and after unlocking.
  5. Add a help command with all supported commands.

Accessibility Practice

Announce the room, visible items, inventory, and prompt as separate text lines. Error messages explain the failed action. Test the complete interaction with keyboard-only input and sequential screen-reader output.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model the five canonical rooms.
  • I can transfer the key from a room to inventory.

C# is a modern managed language for .NET services, web apps, desktop software, cloud systems, and Unity games.

A complete introductory sequence aligned to Python Units 0–11: setup; foundations; numeric computation; control flow; data structures; input and iteration; functions; object-oriented design; files and exceptions; testing and data analysis; projects; and capstone. Environment

Unit 0: Accessible Environment and Toolchain

Course overview

Before you start: complete Unit P: Computing Foundations Primer. It explains the language-neutral vocabulary and concepts used in every language track, using non-visual examples.

Course Overview

C# is a modern managed language for .NET services, web applications, desktop software, cloud systems, and Unity games.

This course intentionally parallels the original Python curriculum. It reuses problem contexts—greetings, profiles, a calculator, grade decisions, score collections, inventory, functions, text files, tests, text analysis, CSV, a to-do list, and a personal-data manager—so the principal new learning target is the C# language. The syntax and implementation remain idiomatic, not a mechanical translation.

Unit 0: Accessible Environment and Toolchain

Overview

Install and verify the .NET SDK, create a reproducible console project, configure an editor, and test the complete keyboard and assistive-technology workflow. The .NET SDK includes the compiler, runtime tooling, project system, and build commands. A C# source file is normally built as part of a project rather than compiled as a standalone script.

Lesson 0.1: Install and Verify C#

Reading References

  • Microsoft Learn: .NET installation and C# language documentation.
  • .NET SDK command-line reference.

Learning Objectives

  • Install and identify the .NET SDK.
  • Create and run a minimal C# console application.
  • Distinguish SDK, runtime, compiler, and program output.

Concept Explanation

Install the .NET 10 SDK using the official installer or supported package manager. Run dotnet --info to inspect installed SDKs and runtimes. Create a project with dotnet new console -n CSharpCourse, enter the project folder, and run dotnet run. Installing an editor extension alone does not install the SDK.

Worked Example

dotnet new console -n CSharpCourse
cd CSharpCourse
dotnet run

Expected default output: Hello, World!

Expected Behavior or Output

dotnet run builds the project and prints the default template output:

Hello, World!

Common Mistakes

  • Installing only C# syntax highlighting without the .NET SDK.
  • Running dotnet commands outside the intended project directory.
  • Confusing the installed runtime with the SDK needed to build applications.

Activities

  1. Install the .NET 10 SDK and record the output of dotnet --info.
  2. Create the CSharpCourse console project and run it unchanged.
  3. Change the output message and rebuild with dotnet run.
  4. Run dotnet --list-sdks and dotnet --list-runtimes; explain the difference.

Accessibility Practice

Use keyboard navigation to reach the terminal, enter each command, and read the complete output sequentially. Confirm that the editor announces punctuation, braces, indentation, and build diagnostics.

Skills Checklist

  • I can install and identify the .NET 10 SDK.
  • I can create a console project with dotnet new.
  • I can run a project with dotnet run.
  • I can distinguish SDK, runtime, compiler, and application output.
  • I can read terminal output and diagnostics using my access technology.

Lesson 0.2: Workspace and First Run

Reading References

  • .NET project and CLI documentation.
  • Shared terminal navigation prerequisite.

Learning Objectives

  • Create and navigate a project workspace.
  • Identify source, project, and generated build files.
  • Run build and execution commands from the project root.

Concept Explanation

A .NET project is described by a .csproj file. Source files such as Program.cs contain C# code; bin contains build output and obj contains intermediate files. The current working directory determines how relative file paths are resolved. Use dotnet build to compile and dotnet run to build and execute.

Worked Example

mkdir csharp-course
cd csharp-course
dotnet new console
dotnet build
dotnet run

Expected Behavior or Output

dotnet build ends with a summary that says the build succeeded, and dotnet run prints the default template output Hello, World!.

Common Mistakes

  • Editing a source file in one folder while building a different project.
  • Deleting or manually editing generated files under bin or obj.
  • Assuming relative data-file paths are resolved from the source file location.

Activities

  1. Create a course workspace and a console project inside it.
  2. Identify Program.cs, the project file, bin, and obj.
  3. Build with dotnet build and run with dotnet run.
  4. Create a text data file and verify how its relative path changes when the working directory changes.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate the project tree using keyboard commands and verify file names through text output. Move between source, terminal, build diagnostics, and project files without mouse-only operations.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create and navigate a .NET project workspace.
  • I can identify source and project files.
  • I can distinguish generated build output from source.
  • I can build and run from the project root.
  • I can explain current-working-directory path behavior.

Lesson 0.3: Editor and Accessibility Workflow

Reading References

  • Shared IDE setup lesson.
  • Documentation for the chosen editor and C# language tooling.

Learning Objectives

  • Configure C# language services in the selected editor.
  • Navigate project files, diagnostics, and terminal output by keyboard.
  • Distinguish editor assistance from compiler validation.

Concept Explanation

A text editor edits source code; an IDE adds integrated project navigation, language services, build, and debugging tools. VS Code, VSCodium, and Theia can support C# through compatible extensions and .NET tooling, but their marketplaces and extension availability differ. A language server provides completion and diagnostics; it is not a substitute for the .NET SDK or a successful build.

Worked Example

Open the project folder, install the C# extension supported by the chosen editor, select the installed .NET SDK, and introduce a temporary syntax error. Navigate to the diagnostic, read its location and message, correct the source, and build from the integrated terminal.

Expected Behavior or Output

The editor underlines the syntax error and lists it with its location and message. The message from dotnet build in the integrated terminal names the same file and line. After you correct the source, the build succeeds.

Common Mistakes

  • Opening an individual source file instead of the project root.
  • Assuming an extension installs the SDK or compiler.
  • Treating syntax coloring or completion as proof that the project builds.

Activities

  1. Open the complete project folder in VS Code, VSCodium, or Theia.
  2. Verify that C# language services recognize the project and target framework.
  3. Navigate to a deliberate syntax error using the keyboard and read its diagnostic.
  4. Correct the error and build from both the integrated and system terminals.

Accessibility Practice

Test file navigation, symbol navigation, punctuation verbosity, indentation announcements, error lists, terminal focus, and build output with the learner’s screen reader, braille display, magnifier, or other access technology.

Skills Checklist

  • I can open the project root in my chosen editor.
  • I can configure C# language services.
  • I can navigate diagnostics and source by keyboard.
  • I can build from an integrated terminal.
  • I can explain why editor assistance is not compiler validation.

Lesson 0.4: Project Environments, Dependencies, and Terminal Usage

Reading References

  • .NET project file and package management documentation.
  • NuGet package management and dotnet CLI references.

Learning Objectives

  • Identify the project target framework and dependency declarations.
  • Restore packages and build reproducibly.
  • Run project commands from the correct directory.

Concept Explanation

A .NET project records its target framework and package references in the .csproj file. NuGet manages external packages; dotnet restore resolves dependencies and creates assets in obj. dotnet build compiles the project, dotnet test runs tests, and dotnet run executes an application. Keep dependencies project-scoped and review package versions rather than installing arbitrary binaries globally.

Worked Example

dotnet restore
dotnet build
dotnet test
dotnet run

Expected Behavior or Output

Each command reports success or failure on its own status lines. dotnet restore and dotnet build prepare and compile the project, dotnet run starts it, and dotnet test runs tests only when the project contains a test project.

Common Mistakes

  • Running restore or build from a directory that does not contain the project or solution.
  • Adding a package without checking its target framework and version compatibility.
  • Editing generated NuGet assets instead of the project file.

Activities

  1. Inspect the target framework and package references in the project file.
  2. Run dotnet restore and identify the generated assets file.
  3. Run dotnet build and dotnet test; distinguish their purposes.
  4. Add one approved package using dotnet add package, then restore and build again.

Accessibility Practice

Read the project file as text and verify that package names and versions are available to assistive technology. Navigate restore/build/test diagnostics by keyboard and retain the exact command output.

Skills Checklist

  • I can identify the target framework in a project file.
  • I can explain the role of NuGet package references.
  • I can restore dependencies with dotnet restore.
  • I can distinguish build, test, and run commands.
  • I can execute project commands from the correct working directory.

Unit 2: Numeric Computations

Overview

This unit covers development process, expressions, assignment, input/output, conversions, arithmetic, math library. Follow the same problem progression as Python so that the main comparison is language syntax and semantics. Use the worked examples as starting points, then complete the activities independently.

Lesson 2.1: Design and tracing

Reading References

  • Official C# language guide and standard-library documentation.
  • Corresponding Python course lesson for the shared problem context and learning objective.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the C# concepts and runtime behavior introduced in this lesson.
  • Trace the worked example and predict its observable result.
  • Apply the shared problem context using appropriate C# types and .NET APIs.

Concept Explanation

C# uses statically typed expressions and the .NET Base Class Library. Follow values from input through conversion and calculation; use explicit types, named intermediate values, and a stated policy for parsing, culture, precision, and formatting.

Worked Example

double bill = 24.50, tipRate = 0.15;
double tip = bill * tipRate, total = bill + tip;
Console.WriteLine($"Bill: {bill:F2}; tip: {tip:F2}; total: {total:F2}");

Trace: identify declarations, expressions, control flow, and observable output. Predict the result, run the example, and compare the actual output with the prediction.

Expected Behavior or Output

Output observed when the worked example was run (.NET 8; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

Bill: 24.50; tip: 3.67; total: 28.18

Common Mistakes

  • Using the wrong numeric type or conversion for the value being processed.
  • Ignoring input parsing failures or culture-dependent formatting.
  • Relying on implicit precedence or rounding without stating the intended calculation.

Activities

  1. Calculate the expected result for the canonical bill, score, or measurement before running the example.
  2. Change one canonical input and verify which intermediate and final values change.
  3. Test malformed text, a boundary value, or a different numeric representation as appropriate.
  4. Explain the selected type, conversion, precedence, or formatting rule in C#.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate the complete source file by line, word, and character using the learner’s access technology. Read punctuation and indentation, run from the terminal, and inspect standard output and errors sequentially.

Lesson 2.5: Using the Math Library

Reading References

  • Microsoft Learn: System.Math API reference.
  • Corresponding Python lesson on mathematical functions and geometric calculations.

Learning Objectives

  • Use System.Math for common mathematical operations.
  • Calculate circle area and circumference using Math.PI.
  • Calculate distance from the origin using Math.Sqrt and Math.Pow.

Concept Explanation

The .NET System.Math class provides mathematical constants and methods such as PI, Pow, Sqrt, Abs, and Round. C# accesses these static members through the Math type. The distance from the origin to (x, y) is the square root of x squared plus y squared. Floating-point values should be formatted or rounded according to an explicit display requirement.

Worked Example

double radius = 3.0;
double area = Math.PI * Math.Pow(radius, 2);
double circumference = 2.0 * Math.PI * radius;
double distance = Math.Sqrt(Math.Pow(3.0, 2) + Math.Pow(4.0, 2));
Console.WriteLine($"Area: {area:F2}; circumference: {circumference:F2}; distance: {distance:F2}");

Trace: area is approximately 28.27, circumference is approximately 18.85, and distance from (3, 4) to the origin is 5.

Expected Behavior or Output

Output observed when the worked example was run (.NET 8; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

Area: 28.27; circumference: 18.85; distance: 5.00

Common Mistakes

  • Using an approximate value of pi when Math.PI is available.
  • Passing a diameter where the formula expects a radius.
  • Taking the square root before adding both squared coordinate values.

Activities

  1. Calculate area and circumference for a circle with radius 3.
  2. Calculate distance from the origin to (3, 4) and verify the 5-unit result.
  3. Change the radius to zero and predict the outputs.
  4. Compare the full double value with F2 formatted output.

Accessibility Practice

Read the complete expressions, including parentheses and method names. Verify that formatted values have explicit labels and units.

Skills Checklist

  • I can locate and use Math.PI, Math.Pow, and Math.Sqrt.
  • I can calculate circle area and circumference.
  • I can calculate distance from the origin.
  • I can explain floating-point precision and formatting.
  • I can test a zero-radius boundary case.

Reading References

Learning Objectives

Concept Explanation

Control flow in C# uses Boolean expressions, if/else, arrays, loops, and immutable string values. Array indexes start at zero; collection lengths and loop bounds must be checked. String methods return new strings rather than mutating the original.

Worked Example

int score = 82;
bool validScore = score >= 0 && score <= 100, passed = validScore && score >= 60;
Console.WriteLine($"Valid: {validScore}; passed: {passed}");

Expected Behavior or Output

Common Mistakes

  • Using an incorrect Boolean boundary or condition order.
  • Assuming array indexes start at one or exceed the valid range.
  • Assuming string operations mutate the original value.

Lesson 4.1: Mutable sequences

Reading References

  • Official C# language guide and standard-library documentation.
  • Corresponding Python course lesson for the shared problem context and learning objective.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the C# concepts and runtime behavior introduced in this lesson.
  • Trace the worked example and predict its observable result.
  • Apply the shared problem context using appropriate C# types and .NET APIs.

Concept Explanation

C# offers generic collections such as List and Dictionary<TKey,TValue>, plus records and structs for data modeling. Select a collection based on whether the problem needs ordered mutable elements, unique keys, or immutable value data.

Worked Example

Unit 5: Input and Iteration

Overview

This unit covers input validation, sentinel loops, while loops, flags, break/continue, infinite-loop prevention. Follow the same problem progression as Python so that the main comparison is language syntax and semantics. Use the worked examples as starting points, then complete the activities independently.

Lesson 5.1: Input and validation

Reading References

  • Official C# language guide and standard-library documentation.
  • Corresponding Python course lesson for the shared problem context and learning objective.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the C# concepts and runtime behavior introduced in this lesson.
  • Trace the worked example and predict its observable result.
  • Apply the shared problem context using appropriate C# types and .NET APIs.

Concept Explanation

Console input is text and must be parsed and validated before use. while, foreach, break, and continue control repetition; every loop needs a clear exit condition and progress toward termination.

Worked Example

var input = new Queue<string>(new[] { "16", "abc", "131" });
while (input.Count > 0) { string candidate = input.Dequeue(); if (int.TryParse(candidate, out int age) && age >= 0 && age <= 130) Console.WriteLine($"Accepted age: {age}"); else Console.WriteLine($"Invalid age: {candidate}"); }

Trace: identify declarations, expressions, control flow, and observable output. Predict the result, run the example, and compare the actual output with the prediction.

Expected Behavior or Output

Output observed when the worked example was run (.NET 8; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

Accepted age: 16
Invalid age: abc
Invalid age: 131

Common Mistakes

  • Treating parsed text as valid domain data without checking it.
  • Failing to update loop state or provide a terminating condition.
  • Using break or continue when the other control-flow operation is intended.

Activities

  1. Trace the input or loop state after each iteration of the worked example.
  2. Test valid input, malformed input, and one domain-boundary value.
  3. Change the sentinel, flag, or attempt limit and predict when the loop terminates.
  4. Explain how the code guarantees progress and avoids an unbounded loop.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate the complete source file by line, word, and character using the learner’s access technology. Read punctuation and indentation, run from the terminal, and inspect standard output and errors sequentially.

Skills Checklist

  • I can parse and validate input before using it.
  • I can implement the required loop or control-flow operation.
  • I can identify the loop’s termination condition.
  • I can test valid and invalid paths.
  • I can explain how the code avoids an infinite loop.

Lesson 6.1: Defining functions

Reading References

  • Official C# language guide and standard-library documentation.
  • Corresponding Python course lesson for the shared problem context and learning objective.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the C# concepts and runtime behavior introduced in this lesson.
  • Trace the worked example and predict its observable result.
  • Apply the shared problem context using appropriate C# types and .NET APIs.

Concept Explanation

C# methods declare parameter and return types. Use parameters to make dependencies explicit, return values to separate computation from presentation, and collection interfaces or params when they improve the method contract.

Worked Example

static double CalculateTotal(double bill, double rate) { double tip = bill * rate; return bill + tip; }
Console.WriteLine($"Total: {CalculateTotal(24.50, 0.15):F2}");

Trace: identify declarations, expressions, control flow, and observable output. Predict the result, run the example, and compare the actual output with the prediction.

Expected Behavior or Output

Output observed when the worked example was run (.NET 8; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

Total: 28.18

Common Mistakes

  • Confusing a parameter with an argument or a returned value with printed output.
  • Choosing a method signature that does not express its input/output contract.
  • Ignoring empty collections, optional values, or variadic edge cases.

Activities

  1. Call the method with the canonical bill/rate or score values and predict its return value.
  2. Add a second call with different arguments, including a named or optional argument where relevant.
  3. Test empty input, zero arguments, or another edge case for the method contract.
  4. Explain the method signature, parameter semantics, and return behavior.

Concept Explanation

C# methods declare parameter and return types. Use parameters to make dependencies explicit, return values to separate computation from presentation, and collection interfaces or params when they improve the method contract.

Worked Example

static int Sum(params int[] values) { int total = 0; foreach (int value in values) total += value; return total; }
Console.WriteLine(Sum(2, 3, 4)); Console.WriteLine(Sum(82, 91, 76, 88));

Expected Behavior or Output

Output observed when the worked example was run (.NET 8; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

9
337

Common Mistakes

  • Confusing a parameter with an argument or a returned value with printed output.
  • Choosing a method signature that does not express its input/output contract.
  • Ignoring empty collections, optional values, or variadic edge cases.

Reading References

Concept Explanation

C# supports classes, records, structs, properties, methods, interfaces, inheritance, and composition. Choose value or reference semantics intentionally and protect invariants through the public API.

Worked Example

var student = new Student("Avery", 16, "Computer Science");
Console.WriteLine($"{student.Name}, {student.Age}, {student.FavoriteSubject}");
record Student(string Name, int Age, string FavoriteSubject);

Avery, 16, Computer Science

Common Mistakes

  • Exposing mutable state that bypasses the type’s invariants.
  • Confusing reference identity with value equality.
  • Using inheritance where an interface or composition better represents the relationship.

  2. Change one property or method input and verify the model invariant remains true.

Lesson 8.1: Reading text files

Reading References

  • Official C# language guide and standard-library documentation.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the C# concepts and runtime behavior introduced in this lesson.
  • Trace the worked example and predict its observable result.

Concept Explanation

The .NET file and serialization APIs provide text I/O, exception handling, deterministic disposal, and JSON persistence. Resolve relative paths from the working directory, handle expected failures, and dispose IDisposable resources.

Worked Example

string path = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), "csharp-notes.txt");
File.WriteAllLines(path, new[] { "First line", "Second line" });
foreach (string line in File.ReadLines(path)) Console.WriteLine(line);

Trace: identify declarations, expressions, control flow, and observable output. Predict the result, run the example, and compare the actual output with the prediction.

Expected Behavior or Output

Output observed when the worked example was run (.NET 8; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

First line
Second line

Common Mistakes

  • Resolving relative paths from the wrong working directory.
  • Overwriting data when append or safe replacement is required.
  • Failing to handle expected I/O/serialization errors or dispose resources.

Activities

  1. Run the file or serialization example using a temporary test file and inspect its contents.
  2. Test a missing file, malformed JSON, or an access failure in a controlled case.
  3. Change the operation from replace to append, or move resource use across its scope.
  4. Explain path resolution, exception handling, serialization, or disposal behavior.

Lesson 9.1: Testing functions

Reading References

Concept Explanation

Testing and analysis should use deterministic inputs where possible. Verify expected results, test state transitions, seed pseudo-random generators when reproducibility matters, and define text/CSV parsing assumptions explicitly.

Worked Example

static int Add(int left, int right) => left + right;
if (Add(2, 3) != 5 || Add(-2, 2) != 0) throw new Exception("Add tests failed");
Console.WriteLine("Add tests passed.");

Common Mistakes

  • Testing only a happy path and omitting boundary or failure cases.
  • Using nondeterministic inputs without a reproducible test strategy.
  • Assuming simple string splitting implements the complete text or CSV standard.

Activities

  1. Predict the expected result before running the test or analysis example.
  2. Add a positive, negative, boundary, or invalid-data test case.

Lesson 9.4: Text analysis

Reading References

Concept Explanation

Testing and analysis should use deterministic inputs where possible. Verify expected results, test state transitions, seed pseudo-random generators when reproducibility matters, and define text/CSV parsing assumptions explicitly.

Worked Example

string sample = "A student studies programming. Programming develops problem-solving skills.";
int letters = sample.Count(char.IsLetter), spaces = sample.Count(char.IsWhiteSpace);
int occurrences = sample.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries).Count(word => word.Trim('.', ',').Equals("programming", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase));
Console.WriteLine($"Letters: {letters}; spaces: {spaces}; programming occurrences: {occurrences}");
