Lesson 10.2: Text adventure: five rooms and movement

Reading References

  • C# collections
  • .NET Dictionary documentation
  • Canonical shared project specification: Python Unit 10, Lesson 10.3.

Learning Objectives

  • Represent all five canonical rooms with C# objects and dictionaries.
  • Validate movement before changing the current room.
  • Explain why the treasure room is not reachable until the key puzzle is implemented.

Concept Explanation

The shared graph has five rooms: start_room, tunnel, clearing, locked_door_room, and treasure_room. A Room object stores a description and a dictionary of exits. The player begins in start_room. The north exit from locked_door_room is not available in Part 1. Use TryGetValue to handle missing directions without changing state.

Worked Example

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var rooms = new Dictionary<string, Room>
{
    ["start_room"] = new("A dimly lit cave. A narrow passage leads north.", new() { ["north"] = "tunnel" }),
    ["tunnel"] = new("A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.", new() { ["south"] = "start_room", ["east"] = "clearing" }),
    ["clearing"] = new("A quiet clearing. An antechamber lies to the north.", new() { ["west"] = "tunnel", ["north"] = "locked_door_room" }),
    ["locked_door_room"] = new("A chamber with a heavy door to the north.", new() { ["south"] = "clearing" }),
    ["treasure_room"] = new("You found the treasure. You win!", new())
};

var current = "start_room";
while (true)
{
    Console.WriteLine("---");
    Console.WriteLine(rooms[current].Description);
    Console.WriteLine("What do you want to do?");
    var command = (Console.ReadLine() ?? "quit").Trim().ToLowerInvariant();
    if (command == "quit")
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Exiting game. Goodbye!");
        break;
    }
    if (rooms[current].Exits.TryGetValue(command, out var destination))
        current = destination;
    else
        Console.WriteLine("You cannot go that way. Enter a listed direction or quit.");
}

record Room(string Description, Dictionary<string, string> Exits);

Expected Behavior or Output

Enter north, east, north, north, quit. The player reaches tunnel, clearing, and locked_door_room. The second north is rejected and the current room does not change. The treasure room exists but has no incoming exit in Part 1.

Common Mistakes

  • Using the dictionary indexer for a direction that may not exist.
  • Updating current before validating the requested exit.
  • Defining a destination that is not one of the five room identifiers.
  • Adding the treasure exit before implementing the key puzzle.

Activities

  1. Trace north, east, north, north and record the current room.
  2. Try west from start_room and verify that the room does not change.
  3. Check every exit destination against the room dictionary.
  4. Explain why treasure_room cannot yet be reached.

Accessibility Practice

Announce the room description and prompt in a consistent order. The invalid-movement response explains what happened and how to continue. Run from the terminal and inspect output sequentially with the learner’s access technology.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model all five canonical rooms.
  • I can represent exits with a dictionary.
  • I can reject invalid movement without changing state.
  • I can explain why the treasure room is not yet reachable.

Lesson 10.3: Text adventure: shiny key and locked door

Reading References

  • C# collections
  • .NET List documentation
  • Canonical shared project specification: Python Unit 10, Lesson 10.3.

Learning Objectives

  • Place the shiny key in start_room and transfer it to inventory exactly once.
  • Require key use in locked_door_room.
  • Unlock the north exit only after the puzzle succeeds.
  • End the game when the player reaches treasure_room.

Concept Explanation

Keep the five-room graph from Lesson 10.2. Room objects also contain item lists. Picking up the shiny key removes it from start_room and adds it to inventory. Using the key succeeds only in locked_door_room when the key is in inventory. The north exit remains blocked until the key is used.

Worked Example

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;

var rooms = new Dictionary<string, Room>
{
    ["start_room"] = new("A dimly lit cave.", new() { ["north"] = "tunnel" }, new() { "shiny key" }),
    ["tunnel"] = new("A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.", new() { ["south"] = "start_room", ["east"] = "clearing" }),
    ["clearing"] = new("A quiet clearing. An antechamber lies to the north.", new() { ["west"] = "tunnel", ["north"] = "locked_door_room" }),
    ["locked_door_room"] = new("A chamber with a heavy door to the north.", new() { ["south"] = "clearing", ["north"] = "treasure_room" }),
    ["treasure_room"] = new("You found the treasure. You win!", new())
};

var current = "start_room";
var inventory = new List<string>();
var doorLocked = true;
while (true)
{
    var room = rooms[current];
    Console.WriteLine();
    Console.WriteLine(room.Description);
    if (current == "treasure_room") break;
    if (room.Items.Count > 0) Console.WriteLine("You see: " + string.Join(", ", room.Items));
    Console.WriteLine("Your inventory: " + (inventory.Count == 0 ? "empty" : string.Join(", ", inventory)));
    Console.WriteLine("What do you want to do?");
    var command = (Console.ReadLine() ?? "quit").Trim().ToLowerInvariant();

    if (command == "quit")
    {
        Console.WriteLine("You quit the adventure.");
        break;
    }
    if (command == "take shiny key")
    {
        if (room.Items.Remove("shiny key"))
        {
            inventory.Add("shiny key");
            Console.WriteLine("You picked up the shiny key.");
        }
        else Console.WriteLine("There is no shiny key here to take.");
    }
    else if (command == "use shiny key")
    {
        if (current != "locked_door_room") Console.WriteLine("You must be at the locked door to use the key.");
        else if (!inventory.Contains("shiny key")) Console.WriteLine("You do not have the shiny key.");
        else
        {
            doorLocked = false;
            Console.WriteLine("You unlocked the door!");
        }
    }
    else if (current == "locked_door_room" && command == "north" && doorLocked)
        Console.WriteLine("The door is locked! You need to use the shiny key here.");
    else if (room.Exits.TryGetValue(command, out var destination))
        current = destination;
    else
        Console.WriteLine("Invalid command. Enter north, south, east, west, take shiny key, use shiny key, or quit.");
}

record Room(string Description, Dictionary<string, string> Exits, List<string> Items)
{
    public Room(string description, Dictionary<string, string> exits) : this(description, exits, new()) { }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Enter north, east, north, north, south, west, south, take shiny key, north, east, north, use shiny key, north. The first north from locked_door_room is rejected. Taking the key removes it from the room and adds it to inventory. Using it outside locked_door_room is rejected. Using it there unlocks the door; the final north reaches treasure_room and prints the win description.

Common Mistakes

  • Leaving the key in the room after adding it to inventory.
  • Unlocking the door outside locked_door_room.
  • Unlocking the door without checking inventory.
  • Allowing north movement before doorLocked becomes false.
  • Treating a failed action as a state change.

Activities

  1. Run the complete puzzle sequence and record room, items, inventory, and door state.
  2. Attempt to take the key twice; the second attempt must be rejected.
  3. Try to use the key outside locked_door_room.
  4. Try north before and after unlocking.
  5. Add a help command listing every supported command.

Accessibility Practice

Announce the room, visible items, inventory, and prompt as separate text lines. Error messages explain the failed action. Test the complete interaction with keyboard-only input and sequential screen-reader output.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model the five canonical rooms.
  • I can transfer the key from a room to inventory.
  • I can prevent duplicate pickup.
  • I can require key use in locked_door_room.
  • I can block and unlock the north exit.
  • I can end the game in treasure_room.

Worked Example

string[] documentation = { "Project: Accessible Personal Data Manager", "Runtime: .NET 10", "Build: dotnet build", "Run: dotnet run", "Test: dotnet test", "Data: JSON file with six documented fields", "Accessibility: keyboard-first commands and explicit text feedback" };

Unit 0: Accessible Environment and Toolchain

Course overview

Before you start: complete Unit P: Computing Foundations Primer. It explains the language-neutral vocabulary and concepts used in every language track, using non-visual examples.

Course Overview

Go is a compiled, statically typed language used for cloud services, network servers, command-line tools, infrastructure, and concurrent systems. This course follows the Python curriculum’s shared examples and datasets while teaching Go idioms: packages and modules, explicit types, slices, maps, structs, interfaces, error values, goroutines, channels, and the standard library.

Toolchain baseline: current stable Go release. Use the official Go distribution, gofmt, modules, and the go command. The examples are self-contained standard-library programs unless a lesson explicitly names a package.

Concept Explanation

A module is described by go.mod. An executable starts in package main and defines func main(). The command go run . builds and runs the package from its module root.

Worked Example

mkdir courseapp\ncd courseapp\ngo mod init example.com/courseapp\nprintf 'package main\\nimport "fmt"\\nfunc main() { fmt.Println("Hello, Go!") }\\n' > main.go\ngo run .

Expected Behavior or Output

Go creates go.mod and runs main.go, printing Hello, Go!.

Common Mistakes

  • Installing Go from an unofficial source or mixing multiple PATH installations.
  • Confusing the editor language server with the Go compiler and toolchain.
  • Running commands outside the intended module root.

Lesson 1.1: Computer science and problem solving

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain computer science and problem solving using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { fmt.Println(“A program is a precise set of instructions.”) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { name := “Avery” fmt.Println(“Hello,”, name) fmt.Println(“This line runs second.”) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { var age int = 16 height := 1.72 active := true fmt.Printf(“age=%d height=%.2f active=%t\n”, age, height, active) } The lesson uses the canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./… as routine development tools.

Worked Example

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	fmt.Println("A program is a precise set of instructions.")
}

Example 1.1.2

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	name := "Avery"
	fmt.Println("Hello,", name)
	fmt.Println("This line runs second.")
}

Example 1.1.3

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	var age int = 16
	height := 1.72
	active := true
	fmt.Printf("age=%d height=%.2f active=%t\n", age, height, active)
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Output observed when each example was run with empty standard input (Go 1.22; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

Example 1:

A program is a precise set of instructions.

Example 2:

Hello, Avery
This line runs second.

Example 3:

age=16 height=1.72 active=true

Common Mistakes

  1. Treating a computer as if it inferred unstated requirements.
  2. Omitting package main or the required main entry point in an executable.
  3. Using a variable without declaring it or misunderstanding inferred types.

Activities

  1. Run the worked example unchanged; trace each declaration, type, function call, and output line.
  2. Change the canonical Avery’s student profile, calculator bill/tip, and grade thresholds data and predict the output before running the program.
  3. Add one boundary case and one malformed or missing-data case; state expected behavior before changing the code.
  4. Refactor one part using the Go feature named in this lesson (computer science and problem solving); run gofmt and go test ./… and explain the result.

Accessibility Practice

Use keyboard navigation to move between the lesson heading, code fence, compiler output, and terminal. With a screen reader, inspect punctuation in Go syntax (:=, &, *, …, {}, and error assignments). Do not rely on syntax highlighting or color to distinguish errors. Read prompts and validation messages in document order; verify output is announced without unexpected focus movement.

Lesson 1.3: Variables, constants, and primitive types

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain variables, constants, and primitive types using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

Go is statically typed: every variable has a type fixed at compile time. var age int = 16 declares the type explicitly, while height := 1.72 declares and infers float64 inside a function. Constants use const, and an unassigned variable holds its type’s zero value (0, “”, false) rather than an undefined value.

	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	var age int = 16
	height := 1.72
	active := true
	fmt.Printf("age=%d height=%.2f active=%t\n", age, height, active)
} The lesson uses the canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./... as routine development tools.

Lesson 2.1: Software design and tracing

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain software design and tracing using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { bill := 24.50 rate := 0.15 tip := bill * rate fmt.Printf(“Tip: %.2f; total: %.2f\n”, tip, bill+tip) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { subtotal := 24.50 taxRate := 0.075 tax := subtotal * taxRate fmt.Printf(“Subtotal %.2f, tax %.2f, total %.2f\n”, subtotal, tax, subtotal+tax) },package main import ( “bufio” “fmt” “os” “strconv” ) func main() { reader := bufio.NewReader(os.Stdin) fmt.Print(“Enter a score: “) text, _ := reader.ReadString(‘\n’) score, err := strconv.Atoi(text) if err != nil { fmt.Println(“Enter a whole number.”) } else { fmt.Println(“Score:”, score) } },package main import ( “fmt” “math” ) func main() { radius := 3.0 area := math.Pi * math.Pow(radius, 2) circumference := 2 * math.Pi * radius fmt.Printf(“area=%.2f circumference=%.2f\n”, area, circumference) },package main import ( “fmt” “math” ) func main() { distance := math.Hypot(3, 4) fmt.Println(“Distance from origin:”, distance) } The lesson uses the canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./… as routine development tools.

Worked Example

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	bill := 24.50
	rate := 0.15
	tip := bill * rate
	fmt.Printf("Tip: %.2f; total: %.2f\n", tip, bill+tip)
}

Example 2.1.2

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	subtotal := 24.50
	taxRate := 0.075
	tax := subtotal * taxRate
	fmt.Printf("Subtotal %.2f, tax %.2f, total %.2f\n", subtotal, tax, subtotal+tax)
}

Example 2.1.3

package main
import (
	"bufio"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"strconv"
)
func main() {
	reader := bufio.NewReader(os.Stdin)
	fmt.Print("Enter a score: ")
	text, _ := reader.ReadString('\n')
	score, err := strconv.Atoi(text)
	if err != nil { fmt.Println("Enter a whole number.") } else { fmt.Println("Score:", score) }
}

Example 2.1.4

package main
import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
)
func main() {
	radius := 3.0
	area := math.Pi * math.Pow(radius, 2)
	circumference := 2 * math.Pi * radius
	fmt.Printf("area=%.2f circumference=%.2f\n", area, circumference)
}

Example 2.1.5

package main
import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
)
func main() {
	distance := math.Hypot(3, 4)
	fmt.Println("Distance from origin:", distance)
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Output observed when each example was run with empty standard input (Go 1.22; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

Example 1:

Tip: 3.67; total: 28.18

Example 2:

Subtotal 24.50, tax 1.84, total 26.34

Example 3:

Enter a score: Enter a whole number.

Example 4:

area=28.27 circumference=18.85

Example 5:

Distance from origin: 5

Common Mistakes

  1. Confusing := declaration with = assignment.
  2. Ignoring errors returned by fmt.Fscan or strconv parsing.
  3. Mixing int and float64 without explicit conversion.

Lesson 2.2: Expressions, operators, and assignment

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain expressions, operators, and assignment using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

An expression produces a value. Go’s arithmetic operators are +, -, *, /, and %; dividing two integers truncates toward zero, so 7 / 2 is 3. Go has no implicit numeric conversion, so an int and a float64 cannot be mixed until one is converted. Assignment stores a result, and += updates a variable in place.

Worked Example

Example 2.2.1

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	bill := 24.50
	rate := 0.15
	tip := bill * rate
	fmt.Printf("Tip: %.2f; total: %.2f\n", tip, bill+tip)
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	subtotal := 24.50
	taxRate := 0.075
	tax := subtotal * taxRate
	fmt.Printf("Subtotal %.2f, tax %.2f, total %.2f\n", subtotal, tax, subtotal+tax)
},package main
import (
	"bufio"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"strconv"
)
func main() {
	reader := bufio.NewReader(os.Stdin)
	fmt.Print("Enter a score: ")
	text, _ := reader.ReadString('\n')
	score, err := strconv.Atoi(text)
	if err != nil { fmt.Println("Enter a whole number.") } else { fmt.Println("Score:", score) }
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
)
func main() {
	radius := 3.0
	area := math.Pi * math.Pow(radius, 2)
	circumference := 2 * math.Pi * radius
	fmt.Printf("area=%.2f circumference=%.2f\n", area, circumference)
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
)
func main() {
	distance := math.Hypot(3, 4)
	fmt.Println("Distance from origin:", distance)
} The lesson uses the canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./... as routine development tools.

Lesson 2.3: Input and output with fmt

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain input and output with fmt using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

The fmt package writes with Println and Printf and reads with Scanln or a bufio.Scanner. Reading returns an error value as well as data, and Go programs check it: at the end of input the error is io.EOF. Typed text is a string, so a number needs strconv.Atoi or strconv.ParseFloat, which also return an error for invalid text.

Lesson 2.4: Numeric conversions and math

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain numeric conversions and math using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

Go converts types explicitly: float64(count) and int(price). Converting a float to an integer discards the fraction and does not round. strconv converts between text and numbers and reports invalid text through an error. Floating-point values are approximations, which is why 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3.

The math package provides Pi, Sqrt, Pow, Floor, and Hypot. Go has a built-in hypotenuse function, so the distance from the origin to (3, 4) is math.Hypot(3, 4), which is exactly 5. Every math function takes and returns float64, so integers must be converted first.

Lesson 3.1: Boolean expressions and if statements

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain boolean expressions and if statements using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { score := 82 fmt.Printf(“score=%d; passing=%t\n”, score, score >= 60) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88, 59} for _, score := range scores { grade := “F” if score >= 90 { grade = “A” } else if score >= 80 { grade = “B” } else if score >= 70 { grade = “C” } else if score >= 60 { grade = “D” } fmt.Printf(“%d: %s\n”, score, grade) } },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88} fmt.Printf(“first=%d last=%d count=%d\n”, scores[0], scores[len(scores)-1], len(scores)) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88} total := 0 for _, score := range scores { total += score } fmt.Printf(“total=%d average=%.1f\n”, total, float64(total)/float64(len(scores))) },package main import ( “fmt” “strings” ) func main() { sample := “A student studies programming.” fmt.Printf(“bytes=%d runes=%d words=%d\n”, len(sample), len([]rune(sample)), len(strings.Fields(sample))) } The lesson uses the canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./… as routine development tools.

Worked Example

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	score := 82
	fmt.Printf("score=%d; passing=%t\n", score, score >= 60)
}

Example 3.1.2

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88, 59}
	for _, score := range scores {
	 grade := "F"
	 if score >= 90 { grade = "A" } else if score >= 80 { grade = "B" } else if score >= 70 { grade = "C" } else if score >= 60 { grade = "D" }
	 fmt.Printf("%d: %s\n", score, grade)
	}
}

Example 3.1.3

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88}
	fmt.Printf("first=%d last=%d count=%d\n", scores[0], scores[len(scores)-1], len(scores))
}

Example 3.1.4

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88}
	total := 0
	for _, score := range scores { total += score }
	fmt.Printf("total=%d average=%.1f\n", total, float64(total)/float64(len(scores)))
}

Example 3.1.5

package main
import (
	"fmt"
	"strings"
)
func main() {
	sample := "A student studies programming."
	fmt.Printf("bytes=%d runes=%d words=%d\n", len(sample), len([]rune(sample)), len(strings.Fields(sample)))
}

88: B
59: F

Example 3:

Example 4:

total=337 average=84.2

Example 5:

bytes=30 runes=30 words=4

Common Mistakes

  1. Assuming Go has while or do-while keywords instead of for forms.
  2. Indexing a slice without checking its length.
  3. Using len(string) when the intended count is Unicode code points.

Lesson 3.2: Chained conditionals and grade classification

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain chained conditionals and grade classification using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

Go chains conditions with else if and ends with else, testing from top to bottom and running only the first branch that is true. The shared grade thresholds are 90, 80, 70, 60, otherwise F, so each later test needs only a lower bound. A switch with no value (switch { case score >= 90: ... }) is an equivalent and often clearer form.

Worked Example

Example 3.2.1

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	score := 82
	fmt.Printf("score=%d; passing=%t\n", score, score >= 60)
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88, 59}
	for _, score := range scores {
	 grade := "F"
	 if score >= 90 { grade = "A" } else if score >= 80 { grade = "B" } else if score >= 70 { grade = "C" } else if score >= 60 { grade = "D" }
	 fmt.Printf("%d: %s\n", score, grade)
	}
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88}
	fmt.Printf("first=%d last=%d count=%d\n", scores[0], scores[len(scores)-1], len(scores))
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88}
	total := 0
	for _, score := range scores { total += score }
	fmt.Printf("total=%d average=%.1f\n", total, float64(total)/float64(len(scores)))
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
	"strings"
)
func main() {
	sample := "A student studies programming."
	fmt.Printf("bytes=%d runes=%d words=%d\n", len(sample), len([]rune(sample)), len(strings.Fields(sample)))

Lesson 3.3: Arrays, slices, and indexing

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain arrays, slices, and indexing using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

An array has a fixed length that is part of its type; a slice is a view of an array that can grow with append. Indexes start at 0, len gives the length, and indexing outside the slice stops the program with a run-time panic. A slice assigned to another variable shares the same underlying elements.

Lesson 3.4: For loops and range

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain for loops and range using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

Go has one loop keyword, for. for i := 0; i < n; i++ counts, for condition {} repeats while a condition holds, and for index, value := range slice visits every element. Use _ for a value you do not need, since an unused variable is a compile error. The range stops at the end of the slice, so no index checks are needed.

	}
}

Lesson 3.5: Strings and common operations

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain strings and common operations using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

A Go string is an immutable sequence of bytes that normally holds UTF-8 text. len counts bytes, not characters, and indexing gives a byte. The strings package supplies ToUpper, ToLower, Contains, Index, Count, TrimSpace, and Fields. Because strings cannot be changed, each function returns a new string.

Lesson 4.1: Slices and collection mutation

Reading References

Concept Explanation

package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { scores := []int{82, 91, 76} scores = append(scores, 88) fmt.Println(scores) },package main import ( “fmt” “slices” ) func main() { scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88} slices.Sort(scores) fmt.Println(“ascending:”, scores) slices.Reverse(scores) fmt.Println(“descending:”, scores) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { type Student struct { Name string; Age int; Score int } s := Student{Name: “Avery”, Age: 16, Score: 82} fmt.Printf(“%s age %d score %d\n”, s.Name, s.Age, s.Score) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { stock := map[string]int{“Notebook”: 3, “Pencil”: 10} count, ok := stock[“Notebook”] if !ok { count = 0 } fmt.Println(“Notebook stock:”, count) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88} passing := make([]int, 0) for _, score := range scores { if score >= 80 { passing = append(passing, score) } } fmt.Println(“Passing:”, passing) } The lesson uses the canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./… as routine development tools.

Worked Example

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76}
	scores = append(scores, 88)
	fmt.Println(scores)
}

Example 4.1.2

	"fmt"
	"slices"
)
func main() {
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88}
	slices.Sort(scores)
	fmt.Println("ascending:", scores)
	slices.Reverse(scores)
	fmt.Println("descending:", scores)
}

Example 4.1.3

	"fmt"
)

	type Student struct { Name string; Age int; Score int }

}

Example 4.1.4

	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	stock := map[string]int{"Notebook": 3, "Pencil": 10}
	count, ok := stock["Notebook"]
	if !ok { count = 0 }
	fmt.Println("Notebook stock:", count)
}

Example 4.1.5

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88}
	passing := make([]int, 0)
	for _, score := range scores { if score >= 80 { passing = append(passing, score) } }
	fmt.Println("Passing:", passing)
}

Common Mistakes

  1. Assuming append always mutates the original backing array in place.
  2. Relying on map iteration order.
  3. Mutating a map or slice while overlooking aliasing through shared references.

The sort package sorts slices in place: sort.Ints, sort.Strings, and sort.Slice with a comparison function. sort.Sort(sort.Reverse(sort.IntSlice(s))) sorts in descending order. To keep the original order, copy the slice first with copy or slices.Clone.

Lesson 4.3: Structs and tuple-like multiple returns

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain structs and tuple-like multiple returns using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

Go has no tuples. A struct groups named fields into one value, and a function can return several values. Returning (x, y) and receiving x, y := point() covers the same need. Struct values are copied on assignment, which makes a struct a good fixed record.

Worked Example

Example 4.3.1

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76}
	scores = append(scores, 88)
	fmt.Println(scores)
}

Example 4.3.2

import (
	"fmt"
	"slices"
)
func main() {
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88}
	slices.Sort(scores)
	fmt.Println("ascending:", scores)
	slices.Reverse(scores)
	fmt.Println("descending:", scores)
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	type Student struct { Name string; Age int; Score int }
	s := Student{Name: "Avery", Age: 16, Score: 82}
	fmt.Printf("%s age %d score %d\n", s.Name, s.Age, s.Score)
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	stock := map[string]int{"Notebook": 3, "Pencil": 10}
	count, ok := stock["Notebook"]
	if !ok { count = 0 }
	fmt.Println("Notebook stock:", count)
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88}
	passing := make([]int, 0)
	for _, score := range scores { if score >= 80 { passing = append(passing, score) } }
	fmt.Println("Passing:", passing)
} The lesson uses the canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./... as routine development tools.

Lesson 4.4: Maps and key-value data

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain maps and key-value data using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

A map holds key-value pairs: map[string]int. Reading a missing key returns the zero value, so the two-value form value, ok := m[key] tells you whether the key exists. delete(m, key) removes a key, and len(m) counts the keys. A nil map can be read but writing to it panics, so create maps with make or a literal.

Lesson 4.5: Collection traversal

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain collection traversal using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

for key, value := range m visits a map, but Go randomizes the iteration order on purpose, so output printed straight from a map can differ between runs. For stable output, collect the keys into a slice, sort it, and then visit the keys in order. Printing a map with fmt is the exception: it prints keys in sorted order.

}

Lesson 5.1: Input and validation

Concept Explanation

package main import ( “bufio” “fmt” “os” “strconv” “strings” ) func main() { reader := bufio.NewReader(os.Stdin) fmt.Print(“Enter age: “) text, _ := reader.ReadString(‘\n’) age, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(text)) if err != nil || age < 0 || age > 120 { fmt.Println(“Enter an age from 0 to 120.”) } else { fmt.Println(“Accepted:”, age) } },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { values := []int{3, 4, 0, 5} count := 0 for _, value := range values { if value == 0 { break }; count++ } fmt.Println(“Read”, count, “values before sentinel.”) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { values := []int{4, 8, -1, 12} found := false for _, value := range values { if value < 0 { found = true; break } } fmt.Println(“negative value found:”, found) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { values := []int{-2, 3, 0, 7, -1, 9} positives := make([]int, 0) for _, value := range values { if value <= 0 { continue }; positives = append(positives, value) } fmt.Println(positives) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { attempts := 0 for attempts < 3 { attempts++; fmt.Println(“attempt”, attempts) } fmt.Println(“stopped after”, attempts, “attempts”) } The lesson uses the canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./… as routine development tools.

Worked Example

package main
import (
	"bufio"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"strconv"
	"strings"
)
func main() {
	reader := bufio.NewReader(os.Stdin)
	fmt.Print("Enter age: ")
	text, _ := reader.ReadString('\n')
	age, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(text))
	if err != nil || age < 0 || age > 120 { fmt.Println("Enter an age from 0 to 120.") } else { fmt.Println("Accepted:", age) }
}

Example 5.1.2

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	values := []int{3, 4, 0, 5}
	count := 0
	for _, value := range values { if value == 0 { break }; count++ }
	fmt.Println("Read", count, "values before sentinel.")
}

Example 5.1.3

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	values := []int{4, 8, -1, 12}
	found := false
	for _, value := range values { if value < 0 { found = true; break } }
	fmt.Println("negative value found:", found)
}

Example 5.1.4

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	values := []int{-2, 3, 0, 7, -1, 9}
	positives := make([]int, 0)
	for _, value := range values { if value <= 0 { continue }; positives = append(positives, value) }
	fmt.Println(positives)
}

Example 5.1.5

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	attempts := 0
	for attempts < 3 { attempts++; fmt.Println("attempt", attempts) }
	fmt.Println("stopped after", attempts, "attempts")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Output observed when each example was run with empty standard input (Go 1.22; the text of the output does not depend on the operating system):

Example 1:

Enter age: Enter an age from 0 to 120.

Example 2:

Read 2 values before sentinel.

Example 3:

negative value found: true

Example 4:

[3 7 9]

Example 5:

attempt 1
attempt 2
attempt 3
stopped after 3 attempts

Common Mistakes

  1. Failing to trim newline and whitespace before parsing.
  2. Choosing a sentinel that may also be valid data.
  3. Writing a loop whose state never changes on one branch.

  2. Change the canonical scores [82, 91, 76, 88] and the shared text sample data and predict the output before running the program.
  3. Add one boundary case and one malformed or missing-data case; state expected behavior before changing the code.

Lesson 5.4: Continue and filtering

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain continue and filtering using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

continue skips the rest of one pass of a for loop and goes to the next. Use it to skip invalid entries, such as scores below 0 or above 100, while still reporting that they were skipped. Be sure that the loop’s counter is updated before continue in a condition-only for loop, or the loop will never end.

Worked Example

Example 5.4.1

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	values := []int{3, 4, 0, 5}
	count := 0
	for _, value := range values { if value == 0 { break }; count++ }
	fmt.Println("Read", count, "values before sentinel.")
}

Example 5.4.2

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	values := []int{4, 8, -1, 12}
	found := false
	for _, value := range values { if value < 0 { found = true; break } }
	fmt.Println("negative value found:", found)
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	values := []int{-2, 3, 0, 7, -1, 9}
	positives := make([]int, 0)
	for _, value := range values { if value <= 0 { continue }; positives = append(positives, value) }
	fmt.Println(positives)
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	attempts := 0
	for attempts < 3 { attempts++; fmt.Println("attempt", attempts) }
	fmt.Println("stopped after", attempts, "attempts")
} The lesson uses the canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./... as routine development tools.

Common Mistakes

  1. Failing to trim newline and whitespace before parsing.
  2. Choosing a sentinel that may also be valid data.
  3. Writing a loop whose state never changes on one branch.

Lesson 5.5: Preventing infinite loops

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain preventing infinite loops using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

An endless loop never makes its condition false. Defend against it with a progress rule and a limit, for example a maximum number of attempts, and stop when input ends. A bare for { ... } is an intentional endless loop that must contain a break or return. Stop a running program from the terminal with Ctrl+C.

	for _, value := range values { if value == 0 { break }; count++ }
	fmt.Println("Read", count, "values before sentinel.")
}

Concept Explanation

package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { greet := func(name string) { fmt.Println(“Hello,”, name) } greet(“Avery”) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { describe := func(name string, score int) { fmt.Printf(“%s scored %d.\n”, name, score) } name := “Avery” describe(name, 82) fmt.Println(“still available:”, name) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { grade := func(score int) string { if score >= 60 { return “pass” }; return “retry” } fmt.Println(grade(82)) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { average := func(scores []int) float64 { total := 0; for _, score := range scores { total += score }; return float64(total)/float64(len(scores)) } scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88} fmt.Printf(“average=%.1f\n”, average(scores)) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { sum := func(values …int) int { total := 0; for _, value := range values { total += value }; return total } fmt.Println(“sum:”, sum(82, 91, 76, 88)) } The lesson uses the canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./… as routine development tools.

Worked Example

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	greet := func(name string) { fmt.Println("Hello,", name) }
	greet("Avery")
}

Example 6.1.2

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	describe := func(name string, score int) { fmt.Printf("%s scored %d.\n", name, score) }
	name := "Avery"
	describe(name, 82)
	fmt.Println("still available:", name)
}

Example 6.1.3

import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	grade := func(score int) string { if score >= 60 { return "pass" }; return "retry" }
	fmt.Println(grade(82))
}

Example 6.1.4

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	average := func(scores []int) float64 { total := 0; for _, score := range scores { total += score }; return float64(total)/float64(len(scores)) }
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88}
	fmt.Printf("average=%.1f\n", average(scores))
}

Example 6.1.5

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	sum := func(values ...int) int { total := 0; for _, value := range values { total += value }; return total }
	fmt.Println("sum:", sum(82, 91, 76, 88))
}

Common Mistakes

  1. Expecting a function to return a value when its signature does not.
  2. Ignoring an error return value.
  3. Confusing variadic arguments with a slice argument; use … to expand a slice.

Lesson 6.2: Parameters and multiple return values

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain parameters and multiple return values using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

Go has no default arguments or keyword arguments. Pass every argument in order, or use a struct as an options value when a call needs many named settings. A function can return several results, written func f() (int, error), and the caller receives them with a, b := f().

Worked Example

Example 6.2.1

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	greet := func(name string) { fmt.Println("Hello,", name) }
	greet("Avery")
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	describe := func(name string, score int) { fmt.Printf("%s scored %d.\n", name, score) }
	name := "Avery"
	describe(name, 82)
	fmt.Println("still available:", name)
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	grade := func(score int) string { if score >= 60 { return "pass" }; return "retry" }
	fmt.Println(grade(82))
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	average := func(scores []int) float64 { total := 0; for _, score := range scores { total += score }; return float64(total)/float64(len(scores)) }
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88}
	fmt.Printf("average=%.1f\n", average(scores))
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	sum := func(values ...int) int { total := 0; for _, value := range values { total += value }; return total }
	fmt.Println("sum:", sum(82, 91, 76, 88))
} The lesson uses the canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./... as routine development tools.

Lesson 6.4: Functions over slices and maps

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain functions over slices and maps using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

A slice passed to a function shares its elements with the caller, so changing an element inside the function changes the caller’s slice; appending may not be visible to the caller unless the slice is returned. A map is passed by reference and can be changed in place. To protect the caller’s data, copy a slice before changing it.

Lesson 6.5: Variadic parameters and scope

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain variadic parameters and scope using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

A final parameter written ...int accepts any number of arguments and arrives in the function as a slice. Pass an existing slice with values.... Variables declared inside a function or block are local to it, and an inner variable with the same name shadows an outer one, which hides the outer value inside that block.

Worked Example

Example 6.5.1

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	greet := func(name string) { fmt.Println("Hello,", name) }
	greet("Avery")
}

Example 6.5.2

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	describe := func(name string, score int) { fmt.Printf("%s scored %d.\n", name, score) }
	name := "Avery"
	describe(name, 82)
	fmt.Println("still available:", name)
}

Example 6.5.3

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	grade := func(score int) string { if score >= 60 { return "pass" }; return "retry" }
	fmt.Println(grade(82))
}

Example 6.5.4

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	average := func(scores []int) float64 { total := 0; for _, score := range scores { total += score }; return float64(total)/float64(len(scores)) }
	scores := []int{82, 91, 76, 88}
	fmt.Printf("average=%.1f\n", average(scores))
},package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	sum := func(values ...int) int { total := 0; for _, value := range values { total += value }; return total }
	fmt.Println("sum:", sum(82, 91, 76, 88))
} The lesson uses the canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./... as routine development tools.

### Worked Example
```go
package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	sum := func(values ...int) int { total := 0; for _, value := range values { total += value }; return total }
	fmt.Println("sum:", sum(82, 91, 76, 88))
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Example 1:

Hello, Avery

Example 2:

Avery scored 82.
still available: Avery

Example 3:

pass

Example 4:

average=84.2

Example 5:

sum: 337

Common Mistakes

  1. Expecting a function to return a value when its signature does not.
  2. Ignoring an error return value.
  3. Confusing variadic arguments with a slice argument; use … to expand a slice.

package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { type Student struct { Name string; Score int } type Status int const ( Active Status = iota; Inactive ) s := Student{Name: “Avery”, Score: 82} state := Active fmt.Printf(“%s: %d; active=%t; inactive=%t\n”, s.Name, s.Score, state == Active, Inactive == Inactive) },package main import ( “fmt” ) type Student struct { Name string; Score int } func (s *Student) AddPoints(points int) { s.Score += points } func main() { s := Student{Name: “Avery”, Score: 82} s.AddPoints(3) fmt.Println(s.Name, “score:”, s.Score) },package main import ( “fmt” ) type Summarizer interface { Summary() string } type Task struct { Title string; Done bool } func (t Task) Summary() string { return fmt.Sprintf(“%s: %t”, t.Title, t.Done) } func main() { var item Summarizer = Task{Title: “Study Go”, Done: false} fmt.Println(item.Summary()) },package main import ( “fmt” ) func main() { type Contact struct { Email string } type Contact struct { Email string } type Student struct { Name string; Contact } s := Student{Name: “Avery”, Contact: Contact{Email: “avery@example.test”}} fmt.Println(s.Name, s.Email) },package main import ( “fmt” ) type Reader interface { Read() string } type Note struct { Text string } func (n Note) Read() string { return n.Text } func display(r Reader) { fmt.Println(r.Read()) } func main() { display(Note{Text: “Composition and interfaces”}) } The lesson uses the canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./… as routine development tools.

Worked Example

package main
import (
	"fmt"
)
func main() {
	type Student struct { Name string; Score int }
	type Status int
	const ( Active Status = iota; Inactive )
	s := Student{Name: "Avery", Score: 82}
	state := Active
	fmt.Printf("%s: %d; active=%t; inactive=%t\n", s.Name, s.Score, state == Active, Inactive == Inactive)
}

Concept Explanation

Go models data with structs and behavior with methods and interfaces. Pointer receivers can mutate a value; interfaces are satisfied implicitly. Embedding promotes fields and methods but is composition, not inheritance. Keep domain types small and make dependencies explicit. The lesson uses canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./… as routine development tools.

	"fmt"
)

	func main() {
	 s := Student{Name: "Avery", Score: 82}
	 s.AddPoints(3)
	 fmt.Println(s.Name, "score:", s.Score)
	}

Expected behavior: The standalone program demonstrates creating values and pointer receivers with shared course example data. It compiles and runs using the standard library. Predict the output first, then compare it with terminal output.

Common Mistakes

  2. Assuming interfaces must be declared as implemented explicitly.
  3. Mistaking embedding for class inheritance or overlooking promoted-field ambiguity.

Lesson 8.1: Reading text files

Reading References

  • The Go Programming Language Specification
  • A Tour of Go
  • Go standard library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain reading text files using Go terminology and type conventions.
  • Select an idiomatic Go construct rather than transliterating Python syntax.
  • Predict, compile, and verify the worked example.
  • Test a relevant boundary condition and explain a common failure.

Concept Explanation

The os and io packages provide file operations. Functions return errors that callers must check. defer schedules cleanup at function return; check Close errors when writes matter. encoding/json handles JSON serialization with struct tags. Production code should avoid panic for expected failures. The lesson uses canonical course data so learners focus on Go semantics rather than a new domain problem. Format with gofmt and use go test ./… as routine development tools.

Worked Example

package main
import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
)
func main() {
 path := "go_read_demo.txt"
 if err := os.WriteFile(path, []byte("Avery,82\n"), 0600); err != nil { panic(err) }
 data, err := os.ReadFile(path)
 if err != nil { panic(err) }
 fmt.Print(string(data))
 if err := os.Remove(path); err != nil { panic(err) }
}

Expected behavior: The standalone program demonstrates reading text files with shared course example data. It compiles and runs using the standard library. Predict the output first, then compare it with terminal output.

Common Mistakes

  1. Ignoring errors from file operations and Close.
  2. Calling defer inside a long-running loop and retaining resources too long.
  3. Using hand-built JSON instead of encoding/json.

	"fmt"
	"os"
)
func main() {
 path := "go_cleanup_demo.txt"
 file, err := os.Create(path)
 if err != nil { panic(err) }
 defer func() { if err := file.Close(); err != nil { fmt.Println("close error:", err) }; _ = os.Remove(path) }()
 if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(file, "closed when function returns"); err != nil { panic(err) }
 fmt.Println("deferred cleanup is scheduled")
}

Expected behavior: The standalone program demonstrates deferred cleanup and resource lifetime with shared course example data. It compiles and runs using the standard library. Predict the output first, then compare it with terminal output.

Common Mistakes

  1. Ignoring errors from file operations and Close.
  2. Calling defer inside a long-running loop and retaining resources too long.
  3. Using hand-built JSON instead of encoding/json.

Activities

  1. Run the worked example unchanged; trace each declaration, type, function call, and output line.
  2. Change the canonical inventory records, file samples, and CSV fields and predict the output before running it.
  3. Add a boundary case and one malformed or missing-data case; define expected behavior before editing the program.

Lesson 10.2: Text adventure: five rooms and movement

Reading References

  • Go maps
  • Go standard library: bufio
  • Canonical shared project specification: Python Unit 10, Lesson 10.3.

Learning Objectives

  • Represent all five canonical rooms with Go structs and maps.
  • Validate movement before changing the current room.
  • Explain why treasure_room is not reachable until the key puzzle is implemented.

Concept Explanation

The shared graph has five rooms: start_room, tunnel, clearing, locked_door_room, and treasure_room. A Room stores its description and valid exits. The player starts in start_room. Part 1 does not provide the north exit from locked_door_room. Map lookup uses the two-result form so a missing direction cannot change state.

Worked Example

package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "strings"
)

type Room struct {
    description string
    exits       map[string]string
}

func main() {
    rooms := map[string]Room{
        "start_room":       {"A dimly lit cave. A narrow passage leads north.", map[string]string{"north": "tunnel"}},
        "tunnel":           {"A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.", map[string]string{"south": "start_room", "east": "clearing"}},
        "clearing":         {"A quiet clearing. An antechamber lies to the north.", map[string]string{"west": "tunnel", "north": "locked_door_room"}},
        "locked_door_room": {"A chamber with a heavy door to the north.", map[string]string{"south": "clearing"}},
        "treasure_room":    {"You found the treasure. You win!", map[string]string{}},
    }
    scanner := bufio.NewScanner(os.Stdin)
    current := "start_room"

    for {
        fmt.Println("---")
        fmt.Println(rooms[current].description)
        fmt.Println("What do you want to do?")
        command := "quit"
        if scanner.Scan() {
            command = strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(scanner.Text()))
        }
        if command == "quit" {
            fmt.Println("Exiting game. Goodbye!")
            break
        }
        if destination, ok := rooms[current].exits[command]; ok {
            current = destination
        } else {
            fmt.Println("You cannot go that way. Enter a listed direction or quit.")
        }
    }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Enter north, east, north, north, quit. The player reaches tunnel, clearing, and locked_door_room. The second north is rejected and the current room does not change. The treasure room exists but has no incoming exit in Part 1.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a map result without checking the boolean.
  • Updating current before validating the destination.
  • Defining a destination that is not one of the five room identifiers.
  • Adding the treasure exit before implementing the key puzzle.

Activities

  1. Trace north, east, north, north and record the current room.
  2. Try west from start_room and verify that the room does not change.
  3. Check every exit destination against the room map.
  4. Explain why treasure_room cannot yet be reached.

Accessibility Practice

Announce the room description and prompt in a consistent order. The invalid-movement response explains what happened and how to continue. Run from the terminal and inspect output sequentially with the learner’s access technology.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model all five canonical rooms.
  • I can represent exits with maps.
  • I can reject invalid movement without changing state.
  • I can explain why the treasure room is not yet reachable.

Lesson 10.3: Text adventure: shiny key and locked door

Reading References

  • Go slices
  • Go standard library: strings
  • Canonical shared project specification: Python Unit 10, Lesson 10.3.

Learning Objectives

  • Place the shiny key in start_room and transfer it to inventory exactly once.
  • Require key use in locked_door_room.
  • Unlock the north exit only after the puzzle succeeds.
  • End the game when the player reaches treasure_room.

Concept Explanation

Keep the five-room graph from Lesson 10.2. Room values contain slices of items. Picking up the shiny key removes it from start_room and appends it to inventory. Using the key succeeds only in locked_door_room when inventory contains it. The north exit remains blocked until the key is used.

Worked Example

package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "strings"
)

type Room struct {
    description string
    exits       map[string]string
    items       []string
}

func contains(items []string, target string) bool {
    for _, item := range items {
        if item == target {
            return true
        }
    }
    return false
}

func main() {
    rooms := map[string]Room{
        "start_room":       {"A dimly lit cave.", map[string]string{"north": "tunnel"}, []string{"shiny key"}},
        "tunnel":           {"A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.", map[string]string{"south": "start_room", "east": "clearing"}, nil},
        "clearing":         {"A quiet clearing. An antechamber lies to the north.", map[string]string{"west": "tunnel", "north": "locked_door_room"}, nil},
        "locked_door_room": {"A chamber with a heavy door to the north.", map[string]string{"south": "clearing", "north": "treasure_room"}, nil},
        "treasure_room":    {"You found the treasure. You win!", map[string]string{}, nil},
    }
    current := "start_room"
    inventory := []string{}
    doorLocked := true
    scanner := bufio.NewScanner(os.Stdin)

    for {
        room := rooms[current]
        fmt.Println()
        fmt.Println(room.description)
        if current == "treasure_room" {
            break
        }
        if len(room.items) > 0 {
            fmt.Println("You see:", strings.Join(room.items, ", "))
        }
        inventoryText := "empty"
        if len(inventory) > 0 {
            inventoryText = strings.Join(inventory, ", ")
        }
        fmt.Println("Your inventory:", inventoryText)
        fmt.Println("What do you want to do?")
        command := "quit"
        if scanner.Scan() {
            command = strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(scanner.Text()))
        }

        switch command {
        case "quit":
            fmt.Println("You quit the adventure.")
            return
        case "take shiny key":
            room = rooms[current]
            if contains(room.items, "shiny key") {
                for i, item := range room.items {
                    if item == "shiny key" {
                        room.items = append(room.items[:i], room.items[i+1:]...)
                        break
                    }
                }
                rooms[current] = room
                inventory = append(inventory, "shiny key")
                fmt.Println("You picked up the shiny key.")
            } else {
                fmt.Println("There is no shiny key here to take.")
            }
        case "use shiny key":
            if current != "locked_door_room" {
                fmt.Println("You must be at the locked door to use the key.")
            } else if !contains(inventory, "shiny key") {
                fmt.Println("You do not have the shiny key.")
            } else {
                doorLocked = false
                fmt.Println("You unlocked the door!")
            }
        case "north":
            if current == "locked_door_room" && doorLocked {
                fmt.Println("The door is locked! You need to use the shiny key here.")
            } else if destination, ok := rooms[current].exits[command]; ok {
                current = destination
            } else {
                fmt.Println("You cannot go that way.")
            }
        case "south", "east", "west":
            if destination, ok := rooms[current].exits[command]; ok {
                current = destination
            } else {
                fmt.Println("You cannot go that way.")
            }
        default:
            fmt.Println("Invalid command. Enter north, south, east, west, take shiny key, use shiny key, or quit.")
        }
    }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Enter north, east, north, north, south, west, south, take shiny key, north, east, north, use shiny key, north. The first north from locked_door_room is rejected. Taking the key removes it from the room and adds it to inventory. Using it outside locked_door_room is rejected. Using it there unlocks the door; the final north reaches treasure_room and prints the win description.

Common Mistakes

  • Updating a local copy of a Room without writing it back into the map.
  • Removing the key without adding it to inventory, or adding it without removing it.
  • Unlocking the door outside locked_door_room.
  • Allowing north movement before doorLocked becomes false.
  • Treating a missing map key as a valid destination.

Activities

  1. Run the complete puzzle sequence and record room, items, inventory, and door state.
  2. Attempt to take the key twice; the second attempt must be rejected.
  3. Try to use the key outside locked_door_room.
  4. Try north before and after unlocking.
  5. Add a help command listing every supported command.

Accessibility Practice

Announce the room, visible items, inventory, and prompt as separate text lines. Error messages explain the failed action. Test the complete interaction with keyboard-only input and sequential screen-reader output.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model the five canonical rooms.
  • I can transfer the key from a room to inventory.
  • I can prevent duplicate pickup.
  • I can require key use in locked_door_room.
  • I can block and unlock the north exit.
  • I can end the game in treasure_room.

)

Introduction to Computer Science with Java

Before you start: complete Unit P: Computing Foundations Primer. It explains the language-neutral vocabulary and concepts used in every language track, using non-visual examples.

Accessible beginner curriculum

The Java curriculum introduces programming, problem-solving, and object-oriented design using the Java language and Java Development Kit (JDK). It is designed for blind and visually impaired learners who use screen readers, braille displays, magnification, keyboard navigation, or combinations of access technologies. It is also appropriate for sighted beginners and mixed-vision classrooms.

Java makes types and program structure explicit. Its compilation process and class-based organization require more syntax than some introductory languages, but they also provide opportunities to teach how programs are organized, how types constrain operations, and how a compiler helps detect errors.

Recommended sequence: work through Units 0–11 in order. The Markdown files group related units; use the headings and lesson numbers inside each document.

Complete lesson sequence

The complete standardized course, including four setup lessons and 53 numbered lessons, is available in lessons.md. The original grouped unit documents remain supplementary reference material. See validation status for example-check coverage and remaining verification.

Course outcomes

By the end of the curriculum, learners should be able to:

  • Explain foundational computer science concepts and the software-development process.
  • Install and verify a JDK and use an editor, terminal, compiler, and Java runtime.
  • Read and write Java source code using classes, the main method, statements, expressions, and comments.
  • Declare variables with primitive and reference types and reason about type conversion.
  • Use arithmetic, input/output, conditionals, loops, and Boolean expressions.
  • Work with arrays, ArrayLists, strings, and introductory collection types.
  • Define and call methods with parameters and return values.
  • Create classes and objects and explain fields, constructors, methods, encapsulation, and inheritance.
  • Read and write files and handle exceptions.
  • Apply introductory data-processing and unit-testing techniques.
  • Plan, implement, test, and explain text-based projects and a capstone.
  • Evaluate prompts, output, compiler diagnostics, and runtime messages for accessibility.

The curriculum establishes a foundation for further Java and computer science study; it does not attempt to cover the full Java platform.

Prerequisites and intended learners

No previous programming experience is required. Learners need a computer that can run a supported JDK, a keyboard-accessible editor or IDE, and a terminal. Basic keyboard and file-management skills are helpful. Screen-reader and braille workflows can develop alongside programming.

The primary audience includes students using NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, Narrator, braille displays, or magnification. The Java teacher’s guide discusses the additional pacing and navigation demands of Java syntax, compiler messages, IDE tooling, and project structure.

Learning sequence

UnitMain topicsEvidence of progress
0. Environment setupJDK, editor and Java tools, project creation, terminal, first programCompile and run a small Java program
1. FoundationsComputer science, problem solving, Java program structure, variables, and primitive typesExplain the role of a class, main, and typed variables
2. Input/output and mathSoftware-development process, Scanner, numeric input, and Math operationsCreate an interactive calculation
3. Control flowBoolean expressions, conditionals, loops, and branchingPredict and implement program paths
4. Arrays and ArrayListsIndexed collections, iteration, and collection operationsStore and process multiple values
5. StringsString operations, comparison, and text processingProcess user-provided text
6. MethodsMethod declarations, parameters, return values, overloading, and decompositionOrganize behavior into reusable methods
7. Object-oriented programmingClasses, objects, constructors, fields, methods, and inheritanceModel a simple domain with objects
8. Files and exceptionsFile input/output and exception handlingPersist information and handle expected failures
9. Collections and testingJava Collections Framework, data analysis, and JUnitChoose a collection and test program behavior
10. Project-based learningRequirements, design, and text-based application developmentImplement a multi-feature program
11. CapstoneIntegration, testing, documentation, and explanationDemonstrate and explain an independent solution

Materials and navigation

  • Units 0–1: Setup and Foundations
  • Units 2–4: Input, Control Flow, and Arrays
  • Units 5–8: Strings, Methods, OOP, and Files
  • Units 9–11: Collections, Testing, and Projects
  • Teacher’s guide: instructor planning, accessible instruction, assessment, and AI guidance

Return to the curriculum overview to compare the independent language pathways. Kotlin is now taught in its own standalone curriculum.

Recommended environment

Use Unit 0 for detailed installation steps. Use JDK 25 LTS as the course baseline. JDK 25 is the latest long-term-support release as of October 30, 2026; later non-LTS feature releases are not required. Keep the course examples within the Java SE 25 language and API level, without preview features. Check Adoptium or the official Oracle Java documentation for current distributions and versions.

Recommended tools include a JDK, Visual Studio Code with the Extension Pack for Java or Theia IDE, a terminal, and the learner’s preferred access technology. Theia is an alternative with keyboard- and screen-reader-oriented workflows; verify Java language support, debugger, test runner, and extension compatibility through Open VSX before using it in class.

Useful verification commands:

java --version
javac --version
jshell

Windows Powershell

java --version
javac --version
jshell

The JDK provides JShell for interactive experiments. Complete programs are compiled and run as described in Unit 0. Build systems such as Maven or Gradle may be introduced when required; they should not be added before learners understand the basic compile/run cycle. When a build system is used, commit its Maven or Gradle Wrapper and run the project-local wrapper (./mvnw / mvnw.cmd or ./gradlew / gradlew.bat) instead of requiring a global build-tool installation.

Java 25 baseline and current conventions

The course targets JDK 25 LTS. Use the latest security update in the JDK 25 line. The examples use standard Java 25 features and avoid preview features so learners can compile them with an ordinary JDK installation.

Follow standard Java conventions: PascalCase class and interface names; camelCase variables, methods, and parameters; UPPER_SNAKE_CASE constants; one public top-level class per matching source file; four-space indentation; explicit imports rather than wildcard imports; braces for all control-flow blocks; and meaningful method names. Prefer interfaces such as List and Map for variable declarations, use generics rather than raw collections, compare String content with equals/equalsIgnoreCase rather than ==, and use try-with-resources for closeable resources. Use var only for local variables when the initializer makes the type immediately obvious; keep explicit types in beginner examples. Avoid preview features and do not adopt a new syntax feature until the course objective requires it.

Accessibility and instructional design

Java uses braces to define blocks, semicolons to terminate statements, and explicit type declarations. Long class and method declarations can be difficult to navigate when heard or read on a narrow braille display. Teach students to navigate by class, method, line, and diagnostic, and keep examples logically organized.

The curriculum emphasizes keyboard-first editor, IDE, and terminal workflows; explicit interpretation of braces, parentheses, brackets, semicolons, generics, and type names; predictable class and method organization; text-based input/output; and compiler diagnostics as a first debugging resource.

IDE features can help with navigation and code completion, but generated project files and visual project explorers must not become the only way to understand or operate a project. Explain file structure and provide terminal equivalents where feasible.

How to study each lesson

  1. Read the overview and identify the concepts and new syntax.
  2. Read the class and method structure before tracing individual statements.
  3. Predict output and identify the types of important values.
  4. Compile and run the example, reading compiler messages and runtime output.
  5. Change one statement or input and predict the effect before testing.
  6. Complete the exercises, using the compiler as feedback rather than as a substitute for reasoning.
  7. When compilation fails, read the diagnostic, identify the file and line, inspect the relevant declaration and use, then recompile.
  8. When a runtime exception occurs, trace the values and method calls that led to it.
  9. Explain why the types, methods, and data structures fit the problem.

Maintain a portfolio with source files, test cases, compiler errors resolved, and short design notes.

Assessment and projects

Use code reading, output prediction, debugging, method implementation, object modeling, test writing, refactoring, and project demonstrations. Assess correctness, reasoning, type safety, decomposition, testing, clarity, and the learner’s ability to explain and modify their work.

The capstone should have a written problem statement, user requirements, class or data design, method responsibilities, text-based input/output, test cases, implementation milestones, and a demonstration or explanation. The student should identify limitations and propose a next improvement.

Teaching with AI

The student-facing AI Policy above and in the lesson file takes precedence over the instructor guidance in this section.

AI assistants may explain compiler messages, suggest test cases, compare method designs, or provide alternative explanations. They can also invent Java APIs, use unsupported language features, omit imports, produce incorrect generic types, mishandle exceptions, or generate a class hierarchy more complex than the learning objective requires.

Follow the instructor’s policy. Students must disclose AI assistance where required and explain, test, and modify every submitted line. Do not share student records, credentials, private source code, or confidential data with public AI services. AI must not replace independent work in assessments intended to measure individual skills. The teacher’s guide contains a fuller protocol.

Recommended introductory books

  • Eck, David J. Introduction to Programming Using Java. A free online textbook introducing programming fundamentals, object-oriented concepts, and data structures. Author-maintained online text.
  • Downey, Allen B., and Chris Mayfield. Think Java: How to Think Like a Computer Scientist, 2nd edition. O’Reilly Media, 2016. A free, structured introduction that develops programming and computer science concepts step by step. Book site and publisher page.
  • Gaddis, Tony. Starting Out with Java: From Control Structures Through Objects, 7th edition. Pearson, 2019. A traditional introductory course text with worked examples and exercises. Publisher catalog.

Suggested use: Eck and Think Java are suitable companions for self-study and conceptual review. Gaddis is an alternative structured textbook. Check the Java version used in any book against the course’s JDK baseline; older editions may use APIs or conventions that differ from the current toolchain.

Further learning

Use the official Java documentation and Java Language Specification as authoritative references. David J. Eck’s Introduction to Programming Using Java is an additional introductory text at math.hws.edu/javanotes.

Java’s explicit types and program structure offer a useful way to deepen understanding of how software is organized. The objective is to build independent problem-solving habits that transfer to other languages and platforms.

GUI, visualization, and workbench accessibility

See the shared GUI, visualization, and workbench accessibility reference for screen-reader support by toolkit, platform-specific activation settings, recommended alternatives, and interfaces that must not be required without an equivalent accessible route.

AI Policy

AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, or generate course code or assessment solutions.
