Lesson 0.2: Setting Up VS Code or Theia IDE

For a new project, create a package manifest with npm init -y. Choose one module system and declare it explicitly: set package.json to { “type”: “commonjs” } for the CommonJS examples in the early lessons, or { “type”: “module” } for the ES module examples later in the course. Do not combine the two syntaxes in one file.

  1. Install Visual Studio Code or Theia IDE. Theia supports many VS Code extensions through Open VSX, but check that the required extensions are available and test them with the learner’s screen reader.
  2. In VS Code, press Ctrl + Shift + X to open Extensions. In Theia, open View → Extensions or run Toggle Extensions View. Install:
    • JavaScript (ES6) code snippets — Handy code shortcuts.
    • ESLint — Catches common errors.
  3. In VS Code, enable Screen Reader Mode: Ctrl + Shift + P → “Toggle Screen Reader Optimized”. In Theia, enable its corresponding screen-reader setting and verify editor, terminal, diagnostics, and extension announcements.

Reading References

  • Visual Studio Code accessibility documentation.
  • Theia IDE documentation and extension marketplace guidance.

Learning Objectives

  • Configure an editor for JavaScript development.
  • Navigate files, editor, terminal, and diagnostics by keyboard.

Concept Explanation

An editor provides source navigation and language tooling; it does not replace the Node.js runtime. Keyboard shortcuts and extension availability can differ between VS Code and Theia.

VS Code Shortcuts for JavaScript (Theia keybindings may differ)

ActionShortcut
Run file (via terminal)Ctrl + \`` then node filename.js`
Command PaletteCtrl + Shift + P
Problems ViewCtrl + Shift + M
Next ErrorF8
Format CodeShift + Alt + F
Go to DefinitionF12

Verify editor tooling and the Node.js project environment

Visual Studio Code

  • JavaScript language support is built in. Confirm that the built-in JavaScript and TypeScript language features are enabled for the workspace.
  • Install ESLint from the Extensions view when the project uses ESLint. The JavaScript snippets extension is optional and is not required to compile or run JavaScript.
  • Open the project root (the folder containing package.json) as the workspace. Open the integrated terminal from that folder and verify that node --version and npm --version report the expected Node.js 26 LTS and npm versions.

Theia IDE

  • Open the Extensions view and use the configured Open VSX registry to find JavaScript/TypeScript language tooling, ESLint integration, and (if needed) Node.js debugging support.
  • Verify availability and compatibility with the installed Theia release before depending on an extension. Do not assume every Visual Studio Marketplace extension is available through Open VSX.
  • Test syntax diagnostics, completion, navigation, terminal operation, debugging (if used), and screen-reader announcements. The editor extension supplies language tooling; Node.js remains the runtime and must be installed and available to the terminal.

Use the project’s local toolchain consistently

  • Keep package.json, package-lock.json, and node_modules in the project root. Install project dependencies locally with npm install or npm install --save-dev package-name; do not install course tools globally.
  • Run project tools with npm run script-name or npx tool-name. Use the integrated terminal opened at the project root so npm resolves the local dependencies.
  • Check that the editor’s integrated terminal and the system terminal resolve the same Node.js installation and version. If they differ, correct the terminal PATH or runtime configuration before continuing.
  • For these terminal-first lessons, run programs with node filename.js from the project root. Do not rely on an editor’s generic Run button until you have verified that it invokes the same Node.js runtime and working directory.

Advanced editor options

Experienced coders may prefer JetBrains IDEs, such as WebStorm. They are advanced alternatives, not the recommended starting point for this beginner curriculum. This course does not provide JetBrains installation or usage instructions.

Worked Example

Use the keyboard to open a project folder, create hello.js, move focus to the integrated terminal, and run node hello.js.

Expected Behavior or Output

The editor can open a JavaScript project, announce file names and diagnostics, and run the same file from its integrated terminal. The exact keyboard shortcuts may differ between VS Code and Theia.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming VS Code and Theia have identical extensions or keyboard shortcuts.
  • Installing extensions without checking compatibility with the chosen editor.
  • Relying on a mouse-only run button instead of terminal execution.

Activities

  1. Open the Command Palette using the keyboard.
  2. Install or verify JavaScript language support and Node.js tooling.
  3. Navigate between editor, terminal, and file explorer without a mouse.
  4. Confirm that the editor announces syntax errors and file names accessibly.

Accessibility Practice

Test the learner’s actual screen reader and braille display configuration. Do not claim universal accessibility; document editor, operating system, and access-technology versions used.

Skills Checklist

  • I can open and navigate a JavaScript workspace.
  • I can use the keyboard to move between editor and terminal.
  • I can locate diagnostics and read their messages.
  • I can verify the installed JavaScript language support.

Lesson 0.3: Your First JavaScript File

Reading References

  • MDN: JavaScript first steps.
  • Node.js: Running JavaScript files.

Learning Objectives

  • Create and save a JavaScript source file.
  • Run the file and distinguish script execution from the REPL.

Concept Explanation

A source file stores a repeatable program. The Node.js REPL evaluates individual expressions interactively; running a file executes its statements in sequence.

Hello World

Create hello.js:

console.log("Hello, World!");
console.log("Welcome to JavaScript!");

Run it:

node hello.js

Windows Powershell

node hello.js

The Node.js REPL

For quick experiments, open an interactive session:

node

Windows Powershell

node

Type JavaScript directly and press Enter to execute. Type .exit to quit.

Key Differences from Python

PythonJavaScript
print()console.log()
# for comments// for single-line, /* */ for multi-line
No semicolons requiredSemicolons optional but recommended
Indentation defines blocksCurly braces {} define blocks
def for functionsfunction or => for functions
True/Falsetrue/false (lowercase)
Nonenull and undefined
len(x)x.length

Worked Example

console.log("Hello, World!");
console.log("Welcome to JavaScript.");

Run the saved file with node hello.js.

Expected Behavior or Output

Running the saved file prints the exact greeting text in the terminal, in the order written in the file.

Common Mistakes

  • Saving source code with a hidden extra extension such as .js.txt.
  • Typing smart quotes instead of straight quotation marks.
  • Running the REPL command instead of executing the saved file.

Activities

  1. Create and save hello.js.
  2. Run the file from the terminal.
  3. Enter a short arithmetic expression in the Node.js REPL.
  4. Explain the difference between a saved script and an interactive REPL session.

Ensure the file name, extension, and terminal output are announced in sequence. Keep a terminal path available even when the editor provides a run command.

Common Mistakes

  • Saving source code with a hidden extra extension such as .js.txt.

Activities

  1. Create and save hello.js.
  2. Run the file from the terminal.
  3. Enter a short arithmetic expression in the Node.js REPL.
  4. Explain the difference between a saved script and an interactive REPL session.

Accessibility Practice

Ensure the file name, extension, and terminal output are announced in sequence. Keep a terminal path available even when the editor provides a run command.

Lesson 0.4: Node.js Projects, Terminal Execution, and Dependencies

Reading References

  • Node.js documentation: Getting Started and Command-Line API.
  • npm documentation: package.json and npm scripts.

Learning Objectives

  • Create a project directory and initialize a Node.js package.
  • Run a JavaScript file from a terminal and distinguish the working directory from the file location.
  • Explain what package.json records and when a dependency is needed.
  • Use npm scripts without relying on mouse-only editor controls.

Concept Explanation

A project is a directory containing source files and supporting configuration. Node.js executes a file with node filename.js. The terminal’s current working directory determines how relative paths such as ./data.json are resolved. The package.json file records project metadata, scripts, dependencies, and module mode. For this course, use one explicit module system per project: CommonJS with "type": "commonjs", or ECMAScript modules with "type": "module". Do not mix require() and import in the same instructional example.

Worked Example

From the terminal, create and enter a project directory:

mkdir js-foundations
cd js-foundations
npm init -y

Create hello.js:

"use strict";

const student = "Avery";
console.log(`Hello, ${student}! Your Node.js project is ready.`);

Run it:

node hello.js

Expected output:

Hello, Avery! Your Node.js project is ready.

Add a script to the scripts object in package.json:

{
  "type": "commonjs",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node hello.js"
  }
}

Run npm start. The script should print the same line.

Expected Behavior or Output

The project can be run with both node hello.js and npm start; both commands print the same greeting.

Common Mistakes

  • Running the command from the parent directory, so Node.js cannot find hello.js.
  • Naming the file hello.js.txt because file extensions are hidden.
  • Assuming a package must be installed for built-in Node.js modules such as node:fs or node:readline.
  • Mixing CommonJS and ES module syntax without configuring module mode.

Activities

  1. Use pwd (macOS/Linux) or Get-Location (PowerShell) to announce the current directory, then navigate into the project.
  2. Create profile.js and print the canonical student name Avery, age 16, and favorite subject Computer Science.
  3. Add a start npm script and run the same program with npm start.
  4. Deliberately run Node.js from the wrong directory; read the error, correct the working directory, and rerun.

Accessibility Practice

Use terminal commands and keyboard navigation throughout. Confirm the editor announces the file name and extension. Read the complete terminal error before acting on it. Keep output textual and sequential; do not make successful execution depend on a color change or visual notification.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create and enter a project directory from the terminal.
  • I can initialize and describe a package.json file.
  • I can run a JavaScript file with node and an npm script.
  • I can diagnose a wrong-working-directory error.
  • I can explain why a project should use one explicit module system.

Unit 1: Foundations — Getting Started with JavaScript

Overview

This unit covers JavaScript fundamentals: variables, data types, and basic output.

Lesson 1.1: Welcome to Computer Science

(See Python Unit 1.1 for conceptual content — hardware, software, algorithms, and problem-solving are language-agnostic.)

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 1, Lesson 1.1.
  • MDN: Introduction to JavaScript.

Learning Objectives

  • Define computer science as the study of computational problem-solving.
  • Distinguish hardware from software.
  • Describe JavaScript’s role in browser and server-side programming.

Concept Explanation

Computer science studies computational problem-solving: representing information, designing algorithms, and evaluating solutions. JavaScript is a programming language; Node.js and web browsers are different runtime environments that host JavaScript code.

JavaScript’s Role

JavaScript was created by Brendan Eich at Netscape in 1995. Originally just for web browsers, it now runs everywhere thanks to Node.js (2009).

Learning Objectives

  • Define computer science as the study of computational problem-solving.
  • Distinguish hardware from software.
  • Describe JavaScript’s role in browser and server-side programming.

Worked Example

A simple algorithm for preparing a school day can be written as ordered steps: check the schedule, pack required materials, travel to school, and attend the first class. A computer program expresses a precise algorithm so that a machine can execute it consistently.

Expected Behavior or Output

Students can explain the difference between a physical computer component and a program, and identify that JavaScript code can run in a browser or in Node.js.

Common Mistakes

  • Defining computer science as only learning a programming language.
  • Confusing a browser with JavaScript itself.
  • Assuming JavaScript running in Node.js has browser APIs such as document and window.

Activities

  1. Identify three hardware components and three software examples.
  2. Describe an everyday task as an ordered algorithm.
  3. Compare JavaScript in a browser with JavaScript in Node.js.
  4. Explain why this course starts with terminal programs.

Accessibility Practice

Describe hardware and software with textual examples. Do not require interpreting a diagram as the only way to understand system components.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define computer science.
  • I can distinguish hardware and software.
  • I can describe JavaScript’s browser and Node.js environments.
  • I can express a simple task as an algorithm.

A JavaScript program is a sequence of instructions. Node.js executes statements in order. The console.log() function writes text to standard output. JavaScript statements are commonly separated by line breaks and may optionally end with semicolons; this course uses semicolons consistently.

Run with node hello.js.

Hello, World!
Welcome to JavaScript.

Running node hello.js prints Hello, World! followed by Welcome to JavaScript. on the next line.

Common Mistakes

Lesson 1.3: Variables and Simple Data Types

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 1, Lesson 1.3.
  • MDN: JavaScript data types and structures.

Learning Objectives

  • Declare variables with const and let.
  • Store strings, numbers, and Booleans.
  • Explain JavaScript’s dynamic typing and primitive values.

Concept Explanation

A variable name refers to a value. Use const when the binding will not be reassigned and let when reassignment is required. JavaScript is dynamically typed: a variable can refer to values of different types over time.

console.log()

console.log("Hello, World!");
console.log(42);
console.log(true);
console.log("Value:", 42, "and", "text");

Declaring Variables

JavaScript has three ways to declare variables:

KeywordScopeReassignableUse When
constBlockNoValue won’t change (default choice)
letBlockYesValue will change
varFunctionYesLegacy — avoid in modern code
 
const PI = 3.14159;               // Cannot be reassigned
let score = 100;                  // Can change
score = 150;                      // OK

// var is function-scoped (legacy)
var oldWay = "avoid this";

Best practice: Use const by default; use let only when you need to reassign.

Template Literals

const name = "Alice";
const age = 15;

// Template literal (backticks — preferred)
console.log(`Hello, ${name}! You are ${age} years old.`);

// Concatenation (older style)
console.log("Hello, " + name + "! You are " + age + " years old.");

Additional Primitive Types and Type Conversion

Additional Primitive Types and Type Conversion

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 1, Lesson 1.3.
  • MDN: JavaScript data types and structures.

Learning Objectives

  • Declare variables with const and let.
  • Store strings, numbers, and Booleans.
  • Explain JavaScript’s dynamic typing and primitive values.

Concept Explanation

A variable name refers to a value. Use const when the binding will not be reassigned and let when reassignment is required. JavaScript is dynamically typed: a variable can refer to values of different types over time.

Primitive Types

// Number (integers and floats use the same type)
let integer = 42;
let decimal = 3.14;
let negative = -10;

// String
let name = "Alice";
let greeting = 'Hello';
let multiLine = `Line 1
Line 2`;

// Boolean
let isRaining = false;
let isLoggedIn = true;

// null (intentional absence of value)
let emptyValue = null;

// undefined (value not assigned)
let notAssigned;
console.log(notAssigned);  // undefined

// Check type
console.log(typeof 42);           // "number"
console.log(typeof "hello");      // "string"
console.log(typeof true);         // "boolean"
console.log(typeof null);         // "object" (known quirk!)
console.log(typeof undefined);    // "undefined"

Arithmetic Operators

console.log(5 + 3);   // 8
console.log(10 - 4);  // 6
console.log(7 * 6);   // 42
console.log(15 / 4);  // 3.75  (always decimal, unlike Python 2 or Java)
console.log(10 % 3);  // 1  (remainder)
console.log(2 ** 10); // 1024  (exponentiation)

// Math.floor for integer division equivalent
console.log(Math.floor(15 / 4));  // 3

Type Conversion

// String to Number
let str = "123";
let num = Number(str);          // 123
let numParsed = parseInt(str);  // 123
let floatParsed = parseFloat("3.14"); // 3.14

// Number to String
let n = 42;
let s = String(n);              // "42"
let s2 = n.toString();          // "42"
let s3 = `${n}`;               // "42" (template literal)

// Checking
console.log(isNaN("abc"));     // true — "not a number"
console.log(isNaN(42));        // false
console.log(Number("abc"));    // NaN

Constants

const MAX_SIZE = 100;
const APP_NAME = "My App";
const PI = Math.PI;  // Use Math.PI — already defined

Examples

Example 1.3.1: Personal Information

const myName = "Jamie";
const favoriteNumber = 7;
const heightInMeters = 1.75;
const likesPizza = true;

console.log(`Name: ${myName}`);
console.log(`Favorite number: ${favoriteNumber}`);
console.log(`Height: ${heightInMeters} meters`);
console.log(`Likes pizza: ${likesPizza}`);

Example 1.3.2: Simple Math

const num1 = 15;
const num2 = 7;

console.log(`Sum: ${num1 + num2}`);
console.log(`Difference: ${num1 - num2}`);
console.log(`Product: ${num1 * num2}`);
console.log(`Quotient: ${(num1 / num2).toFixed(2)}`);
console.log(`Remainder: ${num1 % num2}`);

Worked Example

const student = { name: "Avery", age: 16, heightM: 1.72, favoriteSubject: "Computer Science" };
console.log(`${student.name}, age ${student.age}`);
console.log(`Height: ${student.heightM} m`);

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints Avery’s name and age, then the height with the unit metres. The profile uses the shared canonical values.

Common Mistakes

  • Using var when const or let expresses the intended behavior more clearly.
  • Assuming JavaScript has separate integer and floating-point primitive types.
  • Confusing null with undefined.
  • Assuming a conversion such as Number("hello") throws instead of returning NaN.

Activities

Activity 1.3.1: Area Calculator

const length = 12;
const width = 5;
const height = 8;

const rectangleArea = length * width;
const boxVolume = length * width * height;
const circleArea = Math.PI * (length / 2) ** 2;

console.log(`Rectangle area: ${rectangleArea}`);
console.log(`Box volume: ${boxVolume}`);
console.log(`Circle area: ${circleArea.toFixed(2)}`);

  2. Print each property with a descriptive label.
  3. Compare typeof 16, typeof 1.72, typeof "Avery", and typeof true.
  4. Convert the text "16" to a number and test the invalid text "sixteen".

Accessibility Practice

Use meaningful variable names and explicit output labels. Explain punctuation such as braces, commas, quotation marks, and semicolons when reading code aloud.

Unit 2: Numeric Computations and Input/Output

Runtime baseline: Node.js 26.x. Examples use built-in ECMAScript and Node.js APIs; no third-party package is required for these lessons.

Overview

This unit follows the same design, expression, input/output, numeric-conversion, and mathematics sequence as the Python course. Use the shared bill of $24.50 and tip rate of 0.15, the student profile Avery (age 16, height 1.72 m), and the coordinates (3, 4). JavaScript is dynamically typed; input from a terminal arrives as text and must be converted and validated before arithmetic.

Lesson 2.1: The Software Development Process

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 2, Lesson 2.1.
  • MDN: JavaScript Guide, Grammar and Types.

Learning Objectives

  • Separate problem analysis, design, implementation, and testing.
  • Identify inputs, outputs, assumptions, and boundary cases before coding.
  • Write language-neutral pseudocode before JavaScript.

Concept Explanation

Use the same three-phase cycle for every language: design, implement, and test/debug. For a tip calculator, inputs are bill amount and tip rate; outputs are tip amount and total. State assumptions explicitly: the bill is nonnegative, the rate is a decimal fraction, and money is displayed to two decimal places. Pseudocode should describe the calculation without depending on JavaScript syntax.

Worked Example

Pseudocode:

GET bill amount
GET tip rate
CALCULATE tip = bill amount * tip rate
CALCULATE total = bill amount + tip
DISPLAY tip and total to two decimal places

JavaScript implementation using the canonical values:

const bill = 24.50;
const tipRate = 0.15;
const tip = bill * tipRate;
const total = bill + tip;

console.log(`Tip: $${tip.toFixed(2)}`);
console.log(`Total: $${total.toFixed(2)}`);

Expected output:

Tip: $3.67
Total: $28.18

Expected Behavior or Output

The canonical bill of $24.50 at a 0.15 rate produces a displayed tip of $3.67 and total of $28.18 with JavaScript’s binary floating-point and toFixed(2) behavior.

Common Mistakes

  • Coding before deciding what the program should accept and display.
  • Treating 15 as equivalent to 0.15 for a percentage rate.
  • Forgetting to test zero, negative, and unusually large inputs.
  • Rounding intermediate values when only the displayed result needs formatting.

Activities

  1. Write input/output tables for the tip calculator before coding.
  2. Add a test case for a $0.00 bill and explain its expected result.
  3. Change the tip rate to 0.20 and predict the output before running the program.
  4. Describe one invalid input and the validation rule that should reject it.

Accessibility Practice

Read the pseudocode and output in order. Use explicit labels for each displayed amount; do not rely on alignment, color, or visual placement to communicate which value is the tip and which is the total.

Skills Checklist

  • I can identify a program’s inputs, outputs, assumptions, and edge cases.
  • I can write pseudocode independently of JavaScript syntax.
  • I can distinguish design, implementation, and testing.
  • I can explain why expected results should be predicted before execution.

Lesson 2.2: Expressions and Assignment

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 2, Lesson 2.2.
  • MDN: Expressions and operators.

Learning Objectives

  • Evaluate arithmetic expressions using precedence and parentheses.
  • Assign and update variables with clear, predictable statements.
  • Explain the difference between =, ===, and arithmetic operators.

Concept Explanation

An expression produces a value. An assignment stores a value in a variable. JavaScript evaluates multiplication and division before addition and subtraction; parentheses make intended grouping explicit. Use === for strict equality in beginner examples so that JavaScript does not silently coerce unlike types during comparison.

Worked Example

let score = 10;
score = score + 5;
const subtotal = 3 * 4 + 2;
const grouped = 3 * (4 + 2);

console.log(`Score: ${score}`);
console.log(`Subtotal: ${subtotal}`);
console.log(`Grouped: ${grouped}`);
console.log(`Is score 15? ${score === 15}`);

Expected output:

Score: 15
Subtotal: 14
Grouped: 18
Is score 15? true

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints score 15, subtotal 14, grouped result 18, and strict comparison result true.

Common Mistakes

  • Using = when a comparison with === is intended.
  • Forgetting that const prevents reassignment of the binding.
  • Assuming arithmetic with a string will always behave like arithmetic with a number.
  • Omitting parentheses when they would make a multi-step expression easier to audit.

Activities

  1. Predict and then verify 8 + 4 * 2 and (8 + 4) * 2.
  2. Update a score from 82 by adding 9, then print the new value.
  3. Create a bill expression with a 15% tip using the canonical $24.50 bill.
  4. Explain why "15" === 15 evaluates to false.

Accessibility Practice

When reading code aloud, identify parentheses, operators, and assignment separately. Keep one calculation per line when that makes the sequence easier to navigate.

Skills Checklist

  • I can evaluate expressions using operator precedence.
  • I can use parentheses to control grouping.
  • I can update a variable with let.
  • I can explain assignment versus strict equality.

Lesson 2.3: Input and Output Revisited

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 2, Lesson 2.3.
  • Node.js documentation: readline.

Learning Objectives

  • Read terminal input with Node.js readline/promises.
  • Explain that terminal input is returned as a string.
  • Display a greeting and the sum of two validated numeric inputs.

Concept Explanation

Unlike Python’s built-in input(), Node.js uses an input API. The readline/promises module provides an asynchronous question() method. It returns text, so numeric input must be converted and checked. Always close the interface so the process can exit cleanly.

Worked Example

Save as sum-input.js and run with node sum-input.js:

const readline = require("node:readline/promises");
const { stdin, stdout } = require("node:process");

async function main() {
  const rl = readline.createInterface({ input: stdin, output: stdout });
  try {
    const name = await rl.question("What is your name? ");
    const firstText = await rl.question("Enter the first number: ");
    const secondText = await rl.question("Enter the second number: ");
    const first = Number(firstText);
    const second = Number(secondText);

    if (firstText.trim() === "" || secondText.trim() === ""
        || !Number.isFinite(first) || !Number.isFinite(second)) {
      console.log("Error: enter two valid numbers.");
      return;
    }

    console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);
    console.log(`Sum: ${first + second}`);
  } finally {
    rl.close();
  }
}

main();

Example interaction:

What is your name? Avery
Enter the first number: 12
Enter the second number: 8
Hello, Avery!
Sum: 20

Expected Behavior or Output

For inputs Avery, 12, and 8, the program prints Hello, Avery! and Sum: 20. Blank or nonnumeric input produces the validation message.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding two input strings and getting concatenation instead of numeric addition.
  • Treating Number("") as invalid even though it evaluates to zero; validate blank text explicitly.
  • Forgetting to await question().
  • Leaving the readline interface open.

Activities

  1. Run the example with the name Avery and numbers 12 and 8.
  2. Enter a blank value and confirm that the validation message appears.
  3. Enter a decimal and a negative number; explain why both are valid numeric values.
  4. Change the program to ask for the canonical age 16 and print the year of birth only after asking for a reference year.

Accessibility Practice

Use prompts that state exactly what input is expected. Announce the full error message and re-prompt when extending this example. Keep the interaction linear and keyboard-only.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create a Node.js readline interface.
  • I can read terminal input asynchronously.
  • I can convert and validate numeric text.
  • I can close the interface in a finally block.

Lesson 2.4: Computing with Numbers and Type Conversions

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 2, Lesson 2.4.
  • MDN: Number, Number.isFinite, and Number.isInteger.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish JavaScript numbers from numeric strings.
  • Convert text using Number() and parse integer text when appropriate.
  • Detect invalid numeric values, including NaN.

Concept Explanation

JavaScript has one ordinary Number type for integers and floating-point values. It uses IEEE 754 double-precision floating-point arithmetic. Number("16") returns 16; Number("sixteen") returns NaN. parseInt() parses an integer prefix, so it should not be used as a substitute for strict validation. Use Number.isFinite() to reject NaN and infinities.

Worked Example

const ageText = "16";
const heightText = "1.72";
const age = Number(ageText);
const height = Number(heightText);

console.log(`Age next year: ${age + 1}`);
console.log(`Height in centimeters: ${(height * 100).toFixed(0)}`);
console.log(`Is age valid? ${Number.isInteger(age) && age >= 0}`);
console.log(`Is 'sixteen' valid? ${Number.isFinite(Number("sixteen"))}`);

Expected output:

Age next year: 17
Height in centimeters: 172
Is age valid? true
Is 'sixteen' valid? false

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints age next year 17, height 172 centimetres, a valid age result of true, and an invalid numeric-text result of false.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming JavaScript separates integers and floats into different primitive types.
  • Forgetting that typeof NaN is "number".
  • Using parseInt("12abc") and accepting the partial result 12 without checking the entire input.
  • Comparing floating-point calculations for exact equality when a tolerance is needed.

Activities

  1. Convert the canonical age text "16" and height text "1.72" to numbers.
  2. Convert "abc" and ""; explain why blank input needs separate validation.
  3. Calculate the bill total from $24.50 and a 0.15 tip rate.
  4. Test whether 3.5 is an integer and whether Infinity is finite.

Accessibility Practice

Use textual labels that name the value and its unit. State why a conversion failed rather than only printing NaN.

Skills Checklist

  • I can convert numeric strings with Number().
  • I can detect invalid numeric values with Number.isFinite().
  • I can distinguish integers from non-integer numbers.
  • I can explain JavaScript’s single ordinary Number type.

Lesson 2.5: Using the Math Object

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 2, Lesson 2.5.
  • MDN: Math.

Learning Objectives

  • Use Math.PI, Math.sqrt(), Math.ceil(), and Math.floor().
  • Calculate circle area and circumference.
  • Calculate distance from the origin using the canonical coordinates (3, 4).

Concept Explanation

JavaScript’s built-in Math object provides mathematical constants and functions. It is used directly; it is not imported. Math.PI is the value of pi, Math.sqrt() calculates a square root, Math.ceil() rounds upward, and Math.floor() rounds downward.

Worked Example

const radius = 5;
const area = Math.PI * radius ** 2;
const circumference = 2 * Math.PI * radius;

const x = 3;
const y = 4;
const distance = Math.sqrt(x ** 2 + y ** 2);

console.log(`Area: ${area.toFixed(2)}`);
console.log(`Circumference: ${circumference.toFixed(2)}`);
console.log(`Distance from origin: ${distance.toFixed(2)}`);
console.log(`Ceiling of 4.2: ${Math.ceil(4.2)}`);
console.log(`Floor of 4.8: ${Math.floor(4.8)}`);

Expected output:

Area: 78.54
Circumference: 31.42
Distance from origin: 5.00
Ceiling of 4.2: 5
Floor of 4.8: 4

Expected Behavior or Output

For radius 5 and coordinates (3, 4), the program prints area 78.54, circumference 31.42, distance 5.00, ceiling 5, and floor 4.

Common Mistakes

  • Writing Math.pi instead of the case-sensitive Math.PI.
  • Calling Math.sqrt without parentheses.
  • Confusing Math.round() with ceiling or floor.
  • Forgetting that toFixed() returns a string for display.

Activities

  1. Calculate the area and circumference of a circle with radius 5.
  2. Calculate the distance from (3, 4) to the origin.
  3. Predict the results of Math.ceil(2.01) and Math.floor(2.99).
  4. Change the radius to 2.5 and report both results to two decimal places.

Accessibility Practice

Read each result with its label. Preserve units in prompts and output. Ensure mathematical notation is also explained in words when students are using a screen reader or braille display.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use Math.PI and Math.sqrt().
  • I can calculate circle area and circumference.
  • I can calculate distance from the origin.
  • I can distinguish ceiling, floor, and rounding.

Unit 3: Control Flow — Decisions, Lists, and Strings

Overview

This unit follows the Python sequence of Boolean reasoning, chained conditionals, arrays, iteration, and string operations. Use the shared grade thresholds and score list throughout.

Lesson 3.1: Boolean Expressions and if Statements

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 3, Lesson 3.1.
  • MDN: Expressions and operators.

Learning Objectives

  • Compare values with relational operators.
  • Combine conditions with &&, ||, and !.
  • Use an if statement to make a decision.

Concept Explanation

JavaScript Boolean values are true and false. Use strict equality (===) to avoid implicit type conversion during comparisons. Logical AND (&&) requires both conditions to be true; logical OR (||) requires at least one; logical NOT (!) reverses a Boolean value.

Worked Example

const score = 82;
const isPassing = score >= 60;
const isValid = score >= 0 && score <= 100;

if (isValid && isPassing) {
  console.log("Valid passing score.");
} else {
  console.log("Score is invalid or not passing.");
}

Expected output:

Valid passing score.

Expected Behavior or Output

With score 82, the program prints Valid passing score. because the score is between 0 and 100 and at least 60.

Common Mistakes

  • Using = instead of === in a comparison.
  • Confusing && with ||.
  • Forgetting that JavaScript conditions can use truthy/falsy values, not only Booleans.

Activities

  1. Test whether each canonical score is at least 60.
  2. Write a condition that accepts scores from 0 through 100.
  3. Compare 0, "0", "", and null using strict equality.
  4. Explain the result of true && false and true || false.

Accessibility Practice

Print the score and decision as a complete sentence. Do not use color alone to indicate pass/fail.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use relational operators.
  • I can combine conditions with logical operators.
  • I can write an if/else statement.
  • I can explain strict equality.

Lesson 3.2: Chained Conditionals (else if, else)

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 3, Lesson 3.2.
  • MDN: Conditional statements.

Learning Objectives

  • Use ordered conditional branches.
  • Apply the shared A–F grade thresholds.
  • Test branch boundaries.

Concept Explanation

A chained conditional evaluates branches in order and runs the first matching branch. JavaScript uses else if for intermediate alternatives. The shared thresholds are A at 90, B at 80, C at 70, D at 60, and F below 60.

Worked Example

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 3, Lesson 3.2.
  • MDN: Conditional statements.

Learning Objectives

  • Use ordered conditional branches.
  • Apply the shared A–F grade thresholds.
  • Test branch boundaries.

Worked Example

function getGrade(score) {
  if (score >= 90) {
    return "A";
  } else if (score >= 80) {
    return "B";
  } else if (score >= 70) {
    return "C";
  } else if (score >= 60) {
    return "D";
  } else {
    return "F";
  }
}

for (const score of [82, 91, 76, 88]) {
  console.log(`Score ${score}: ${getGrade(score)}`);
}

Expected output:

Score 82: B
Score 91: A
Score 76: C
Score 88: B

Expected Behavior or Output

The canonical scores are classified as 82:B, 91:A, 76:C, and 88:B.

Common Mistakes

  • Testing lower thresholds before higher ones.
  • Omitting the final fallback branch.
  • Failing to reject scores outside the valid range.

Activities

  1. Classify scores 82, 91, 76, and 88.
  2. Test 90, 89, 80, 79, 70, 69, 60, and 59.
  3. Add validation for scores below 0 or above 100.
  4. Explain why branch order matters.

Accessibility Practice

Print the numeric score and grade together, one record per line.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write chained conditionals.
  • I can implement the shared grade thresholds.
  • I can test boundary values.
  • I can validate a score range.

Lesson 3.3: Introduction to Arrays

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 3, Lesson 3.3.
  • MDN: Indexed collections — Arrays.

Learning Objectives

  • Create, access, and modify arrays.
  • Explain zero-based indexing and length.
  • Use the canonical scores [82, 91, 76, 88].

Concept Explanation

JavaScript arrays are ordered and zero-indexed. The first element is at index 0; the last is at array.length - 1. A const array can still have its elements changed because const prevents reassignment of the binding, not mutation of the array.

Worked Example

const scores = [82, 91, 76, 88];
console.log(`First score: ${scores[0]}`);
console.log(`Number of scores: ${scores.length}`);
scores[2] = 80;
console.log(`Updated third score: ${scores[2]}`);

Expected output:

First score: 82
Number of scores: 4
Updated third score: 80

Expected Behavior or Output

The initial array has four values. The first score is 82; after assigning index 2 to 80, the third score is 80.

Common Mistakes

  • Using index 1 for the first element.
  • Assuming const freezes array contents.
  • Reading beyond the array and receiving undefined.

Activities

  1. Read all four canonical scores by index.
  2. Change the third score from 76 to 80.
  3. Add a fifth score of 95 and report the new length.
  4. Explain the difference between an index and a one-based display number.

Accessibility Practice

Identify values by both position and meaning. Print one score per line.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create and access an array.
  • I can explain zero-based indexing.
  • I can update an array element.
  • I can use the length property.

Lesson 3.4: Iterating with for Loops

Concept Explanation

A for...of loop visits each value in an iterable collection. The loop variable holds the current score, not its array index.

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 3, Lesson 3.4.
  • MDN: Loops and iteration.

Learning Objectives

  • Iterate over arrays with for...of.
  • Calculate a total and average.
  • Compare indexed loops with value-based iteration.

Concept Explanation

A for...of loop visits each value in an iterable collection. The loop variable holds the current score, not its array index.

Worked Example

Worked Example

const scores = [82, 91, 76, 88];
let total = 0;

for (const score of scores) {
  total += score;
}

console.log(`Total: ${total}`);
console.log(`Average: ${(total / scores.length).toFixed(2)}`);

Expected output:

Total: 337
Average: 84.25

Expected Behavior or Output

The canonical score list totals 337 and has an average of 84.25.

Common Mistakes

  • Confusing an array index with an array value.
  • Modifying the collection while iterating without understanding the effect.
  • Using forEach() when early termination with break is required.

Activities

  1. Print each canonical score using for...of.
  2. Calculate the total and average.
  3. Print each score with a one-based display number.
  4. Compare for...of, indexed for, and forEach().

Accessibility Practice

Use one output line per score and include a meaningful label. Do not rely on visual alignment.

Skills Checklist

  • I can iterate over an array.
  • I can calculate a total and average.
  • I can use an indexed loop.
  • I can choose an appropriate loop form.

Lesson 3.5: Basic String Operations

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 3, Lesson 3.5.
  • MDN: String.

Learning Objectives

  • Concatenate strings and use template literals.
  • Normalize text and search within it.
  • Count string length and replace text.

Concept Explanation

JavaScript strings are immutable. Methods such as trim(), toUpperCase(), and toLowerCase() return new strings. Template literals use backticks and ${expression} interpolation.

Worked Example

Worked Example

const firstName = " Avery ";
const lastName = "Student";
const fullName = `${firstName.trim()} ${lastName}`;
const sample = "A student studies programming. Programming develops problem-solving skills.";

console.log(`Name: ${fullName}`);
console.log(`Uppercase: ${fullName.toUpperCase()}`);
console.log(`Contains programming: ${sample.toLowerCase().includes("programming")}`);
console.log(`Characters in name: ${fullName.length}`);

Expected output:

Name: Avery Student
Uppercase: AVERY STUDENT
Contains programming: true
Characters in name: 13

Expected Behavior or Output

The example prints Avery Student, its uppercase form, true for the programming search, and a character count of 13.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming string methods mutate the original string.
  • Forgetting to save the result of trim() or case conversion.
  • Treating UTF-16 code-unit length as the count of user-perceived characters in all Unicode text.

Activities

  1. Trim extra spaces from a name.
  2. Convert the canonical text sample to lowercase.
  3. Count the occurrences of the word “programming”.
  4. Replace “skills” with “abilities”.

Accessibility Practice

Use complete labels for string length and search results. Explain punctuation and whitespace explicitly.

Skills Checklist

  • I can concatenate strings and use template literals.
  • I can trim and change case.
  • I can search and replace text.
  • I can describe the Unicode caveat for string length.

Unit 4: Data Structures — Arrays, Fixed Sequences, and Objects

Overview

This unit maps Python lists, tuples, and dictionaries to idiomatic JavaScript. JavaScript arrays are mutable sequences; a frozen array can express fixed-sequence intent; plain objects represent records; and Map represents a dynamic key-value collection.

Lesson 4.1: More on Arrays

Concept Explanation

Array methods such as push(), pop(), and splice() mutate an array. Methods such as slice() return a new array. Numeric sorting requires a comparator because the default sort is lexicographic.

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 4, Lesson 4.1.
  • MDN: Array methods.

Learning Objectives

  • Add, insert, update, and remove array elements.
  • Distinguish mutating methods from methods that return a new array.
  • Preserve and process the canonical score data.

Concept Explanation

Array methods such as push(), pop(), and splice() mutate an array. Methods such as slice() return a new array. Numeric sorting requires a comparator because the default sort is lexicographic.

Worked Example

const scores = [82, 91, 76, 88];
scores.push(95);
scores.splice(1, 0, 85);
const removed = scores.pop();
console.log(`Removed: ${removed}`);
console.log(`Scores: ${scores.join(", ")}`);

Expected output:

Removed: 95
Scores: 82, 85, 91, 76, 88

Expected Behavior or Output

The example removes 95 and prints the remaining scores in the order 82, 85, 91, 76, 88.

Common Mistakes

  • Confusing splice() (mutates) with slice() (returns a copy).
  • Assuming pop() returns the updated array rather than the removed element.
  • Sorting numbers without a numeric comparator.

Activities

  1. Append 95 to the canonical scores.
  2. Insert 85 at index 1.
  3. Remove the final element and report the returned value.
  4. Sort a copy numerically with (a, b) => a - b.

Accessibility Practice

Announce whether an operation mutates the original array or returns a new one. Read resulting values sequentially.

Skills Checklist

  • I can add and remove array elements.
  • I can insert at an index.
  • I can distinguish mutating and non-mutating methods.
  • I can sort numeric arrays correctly.

Lesson 4.2: Organizing Arrays

Concept Explanation

Sorting and reversing can mutate their receiver. Spread syntax creates a shallow copy, allowing a separate primitive-value array to be sorted or reversed without changing the original.

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 4, Lesson 4.2.
  • MDN: Array sorting and iteration methods.

Learning Objectives

  • Sort and reverse arrays.
  • Create filtered and transformed arrays.
  • Explain mutation and copying.

Concept Explanation

Sorting and reversing can mutate their receiver. Spread syntax creates a shallow copy, allowing a separate primitive-value array to be sorted or reversed without changing the original.

Worked Example

const scores = [82, 91, 76, 88];
const sorted = [...scores].sort((a, b) => a - b);
const reversed = [...sorted].reverse();
console.log(`Original: ${scores.join(", ")}`);
console.log(`Sorted: ${sorted.join(", ")}`);
console.log(`Reversed: ${reversed.join(", ")}`);

Expected output:

Original: 82, 91, 76, 88
Sorted: 76, 82, 88, 91
Reversed: 91, 88, 82, 76

Expected Behavior or Output

The original order remains 82, 91, 76, 88; the sorted copy is 76, 82, 88, 91; the reversed copy is 91, 88, 82, 76.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling sort() without a comparator for numeric data.
  • Reversing the original array when a copy was intended.
  • Assuming spread syntax makes a deep copy of nested objects.

Activities

  1. Sort the canonical scores from lowest to highest.
  2. Reverse a copy and preserve the original order.
  3. Filter scores of 80 or higher.
  4. Explain why a shallow copy is sufficient for an array of primitive numbers but not necessarily for nested objects.

Accessibility Practice

Label each result as original, sorted, reversed, or filtered. Avoid presenting the distinction only through visual ordering.

Skills Checklist

  • I can sort numbers with a comparator.
  • I can reverse a copy of an array.
  • I can filter an array.
  • I can explain shallow copying.

Lesson 4.3: Tuples — Immutable Sequences in JavaScript

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 4, Lesson 4.3.
  • MDN: Object.freeze().

Learning Objectives

  • Explain that JavaScript has no built-in tuple type with Python tuple semantics.
  • Use a frozen array to express fixed-sequence intent.
  • Distinguish a constant binding from immutable object contents.

Concept Explanation

JavaScript has no native tuple type. For a short fixed sequence, a frozen array can communicate that the values should not be changed. Object.freeze() is shallow: nested objects are not automatically frozen. TypeScript has tuple types, but those are outside this JavaScript unit.

Worked Example

"use strict";
const coordinates = Object.freeze([3, 4]);
console.log(`x: ${coordinates[0]}`);
console.log(`y: ${coordinates[1]}`);
console.log(`Distance: ${Math.hypot(coordinates[0], coordinates[1])}`);

Expected Behavior or Output

x: 3
y: 4
Distance: 5

Attempting to change a frozen array element in strict mode throws a TypeError.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming const freezes array contents.
  • Assuming Object.freeze() is deep.
  • Describing a frozen array as a true language-level tuple.

Activities

  1. Create a frozen coordinate pair using the canonical values (3, 4).
  2. Read each coordinate by index and by a descriptive label.
  3. Attempt to change an element in strict mode and observe the error.
  4. Compare the frozen coordinates with a mutable scores array.

Accessibility Practice

Identify each position by semantic name (x or y), not only by index. Read the fixed-sequence contract aloud before attempting mutation.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain why JavaScript has no direct Python tuple equivalent.
  • I can use a frozen array for fixed-sequence intent.
  • I can distinguish const binding from object immutability.
  • I can explain the shallow behavior of Object.freeze().

Lesson 4.4: Introducing Dictionaries — JavaScript Objects and Map

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 4, Lesson 4.4.
  • MDN: Working with objects and Map.

Learning Objectives

  • Represent a record with an object literal.
  • Use Map for dynamic key-value storage.
  • Add, retrieve, update, and test entries.

Concept Explanation

A plain object is appropriate for a record with named fields such as name, quantity, and unit price. Map is appropriate for a dynamic key-value collection and supports keys of any value type. A missing object property or Map key returns undefined, not zero.

Worked Example

const inventory = [
  { name: "Notebook", quantity: 3, unitPrice: 2.50 },
  { name: "Pencil", quantity: 10, unitPrice: 0.50 },
  { name: "Folder", quantity: 4, unitPrice: 1.25 }
];

const quantities = new Map(inventory.map(item => [item.name, item.quantity]));
console.log(quantities.get("Notebook"));
console.log(quantities.has("Pencil"));
quantities.set("Pencil", 12);
console.log(quantities.get("Pencil"));

Expected Behavior or Output

3
true
12

The canonical inventory contains three records. Its total value is $17.50.

Common Mistakes

  • Confusing object properties with Map entries.
  • Using bracket notation on a Map instead of get() and set().
  • Assuming a missing key returns zero rather than undefined.

Activities

  1. Create the three canonical inventory records.
  2. Create a Map from item names to quantities.
  3. Update the Pencil quantity from 10 to 12.
  4. Calculate the total value of the original inventory and explain the effect of the quantity update.

Accessibility Practice

Print item names, quantities, and prices as labeled text. Use one inventory record per output line.

Skills Checklist

  • I can represent a record with a plain object.
  • I can create and use a Map.
  • I can add, retrieve, update, and test Map entries.
  • I can distinguish objects from Maps.

Lesson 4.5: Looping Through Objects and Maps

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 4, Lesson 4.5.
  • MDN: Object.entries() and Map iteration.

Learning Objectives

  • Traverse object keys, values, and key-value pairs.
  • Iterate over Map entries.
  • Produce readable reports from structured data.

Concept Explanation

Use Object.keys(), Object.values(), or Object.entries() to traverse an object. A Map is directly iterable and yields key-value pairs. Choose the method that matches the data structure rather than assuming the APIs are interchangeable.

Worked Example

const student = {
  name: "Avery",
  age: 16,
  heightM: 1.72,
  favoriteSubject: "Computer Science"
};

for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(student)) {
  console.log(`${key}: ${value}`);
}

Expected Behavior or Output

name: Avery
age: 16
heightM: 1.72
favoriteSubject: Computer Science

Common Mistakes

  • Iterating over object keys when key-value pairs are needed.
  • Modifying a collection during traversal without considering the effect.
  • Assuming Map and object iteration APIs are interchangeable.

Activities

  1. Print every field in Avery’s canonical student profile.
  2. Iterate over the inventory Map and print each item and quantity.
  3. Calculate the total number of inventory units.
  4. Compare Object.keys(), Object.values(), and Object.entries().

Accessibility Practice

Provide one key-value pair per line and announce when iteration begins and ends. Keep output order stable for instructional examples.

Skills Checklist

  • I can traverse object keys, values, and entries.
  • I can traverse Map entries.
  • I can choose the appropriate traversal API.
  • I can produce sequential textual reports.

Unit 5: User Input and while Loops

Overview

This unit builds on terminal input and introduces sentinel-controlled repetition, loop flags, break, and continue. The goal is to create predictable interactive programs with explicit stopping conditions.

Lesson 5.1: How Terminal Input Works

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 5, Lesson 5.1.
  • Node.js documentation: node:readline/promises.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why Node.js terminal input is asynchronous.
  • Read, trim, and validate a text response.
  • Close a readline interface reliably.

Concept Explanation

Node.js does not provide a built-in synchronous input() function. Use readline/promises and await question() to obtain a response. The result is a string; conversion and validation are separate steps.

Worked Example

const readline = require("node:readline/promises");
const { stdin, stdout } = require("node:process");

async function main() {
  const rl = readline.createInterface({ input: stdin, output: stdout });
  try {
    const response = (await rl.question("Enter your favorite subject: ")).trim();
    if (response === "") {
      console.log("Error: a subject is required.");
    } else {
      console.log(`Favorite subject: ${response}`);
    }
  } finally {
    rl.close();
  }
}
main();

Example interaction:

Enter your favorite subject: Computer Science
Favorite subject: Computer Science

Expected Behavior or Output

For the input Computer Science, the program prints Favorite subject: Computer Science. Blank input prints the required-field error.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting await before question().
  • Treating the response as a number without converting it.
  • Failing to close the interface.
  • Accepting an empty string when a nonempty response is required.

Activities

  1. Ask for the canonical student name Avery and print a greeting.
  2. Ask for age, convert it with Number(), and reject blank or non-finite input.
  3. Ask for a menu choice and normalize it with trim().
  4. Explain the purpose of try/finally around the readline interface.

Accessibility Practice

Use descriptive prompts, announce validation errors in text, and keep the prompt sequence linear. All steps must work from the terminal without mouse interaction.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create a readline interface.
  • I can await terminal input.
  • I can validate and normalize text input.
  • I can close the interface reliably.

Lesson 5.2: The while Loop in Action

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 5, Lesson 5.2.
  • MDN: while statement.

Learning Objectives

  • Write a condition-controlled loop.
  • Use a sentinel value to terminate repetition.
  • Explain the difference between a for loop and a while loop.

Concept Explanation

A while loop repeats as long as its condition is true. A sentinel is a special input value that signals completion. The loop must update state so its condition can eventually become false.

Worked Example

const scores = [82, 91, 76, 88];
let index = 0;
let total = 0;

while (index < scores.length) {
  total += scores[index];
  index += 1;
}

console.log(`Total: ${total}`);
console.log(`Average: ${(total / scores.length).toFixed(2)}`);

Expected output:

Total: 337
Average: 84.25

Expected Behavior or Output

The canonical score list produces total 337 and average 84.25.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting to increment the index.
  • Using a condition that is already false before the first iteration.
  • Updating the index after a branch that can skip the update.

Activities

  1. Count from 1 through 5 with a while loop.
  2. Sum the canonical scores and calculate their average.
  3. Design a sentinel-controlled menu that stops when the user enters “quit”.
  4. Trace the value of the loop index before and after each iteration.

Accessibility Practice

State the loop condition and termination rule before running the program. Provide a textual completion message.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write a condition-controlled loop.
  • I can use a sentinel to stop repetition.
  • I can update loop state correctly.
  • I can choose between for and while.

Lesson 5.3: Using Flags and break to Exit Loops

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 5, Lesson 5.3.
  • MDN: break statement.

Learning Objectives

  • Use a Boolean flag to record a condition.
  • Stop a loop early with break.
  • Distinguish normal loop completion from early termination.

Concept Explanation

A flag stores whether a condition has been found or satisfied. break exits the nearest loop immediately; code after the loop can then report the final result.

Worked Example

const scores = [82, 91, 76, 88];
let found = false;

for (const score of scores) {
  if (score > 90) {
    found = true;
    console.log(`First score above 90: ${score}`);
    break;
  }
}

if (!found) {
  console.log("No score above 90 was found.");
}

Expected output:

First score above 90: 91

Expected Behavior or Output

The canonical scores produce First score above 90: 91; if no value matches, the fallback message is printed.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a string such as “false” instead of the Boolean value false.
  • Forgetting to set the flag when the condition is met.
  • Placing break outside a loop or switch statement.

Activities

  1. Search the canonical scores for the first score greater than 90.
  2. Repeat the search for a score greater than 95 and report that none exists.
  3. Use a flag to validate that a required inventory item exists.
  4. Explain when break is clearer than changing the loop condition.

Accessibility Practice

Report both the search result and whether a match was found. Do not rely on color or a visual marker.

Skills Checklist

  • I can initialize and update a Boolean flag.
  • I can use break to stop a loop.
  • I can report successful and unsuccessful searches.
  • I can explain early termination.

Lesson 5.4: Using continue in Loops

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 5, Lesson 5.4.
  • MDN: continue statement.

Learning Objectives

  • Skip the current iteration with continue.
  • Validate data before processing it.
  • Explain the difference between continue and break.

Concept Explanation

The continue statement skips the remainder of the current iteration and starts the next one. It does not end the loop.

Worked Example

const entries = ["82", "", "91", "invalid", "76", "88"];
let total = 0;
let validCount = 0;

for (const entry of entries) {
  const score = Number(entry);
  if (entry.trim() === "" || !Number.isFinite(score)) {
    console.log("Skipping invalid score.");
    continue;
  }
  total += score;
  validCount += 1;
}

console.log(`Valid scores: ${validCount}`);
console.log(`Total: ${total}`);

Expected output:

Skipping invalid score.
Skipping invalid score.
Valid scores: 4
Total: 337

Expected Behavior or Output

The invalid blank and nonnumeric entries are skipped; four valid scores remain and their total is 337.

Common Mistakes

  • Using continue when the entire loop should end.
  • Skipping a loop-control update in a while loop.
  • Failing to explain why an entry was skipped.

Activities

  1. Process the canonical scores while skipping negative values.
  2. Add blank and nonnumeric entries and confirm they are rejected.
  3. Count accepted and rejected entries separately.
  4. Rewrite a short loop using if/else instead of continue; compare readability.

Accessibility Practice

Print a concise reason for each rejected entry. Keep accepted and rejected counts explicit.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use continue to skip an iteration.
  • I can validate data before processing.
  • I can distinguish continue from break.
  • I can report rejected input clearly.

Lesson 5.5: Avoiding Infinite Loops

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 5, Lesson 5.5.
  • MDN: Loops and iteration.

Learning Objectives

  • Identify loop conditions that never become false.
  • Trace and repair loop-control logic.
  • Test both normal and boundary termination.

Concept Explanation

An infinite loop occurs when the loop condition remains true indefinitely. Before execution, identify the variable that changes, the condition that ends the loop, and every path through the body. For interactive programs, include an explicit quit command.

Worked Example

let count = 1;
while (count <= 3) {
  console.log(`Count: ${count}`);
  count += 1;
}
console.log("Loop finished.");

Expected output:

Count: 1
Count: 2
Count: 3
Loop finished.

Expected Behavior or Output

The loop prints Count 1, Count 2, Count 3, then Loop finished. It terminates after exactly three iterations.

Common Mistakes

  • Never changing a variable used in the condition.
  • Incrementing in the wrong direction.
  • Creating a path through the loop that bypasses the update.
  • Testing only the normal path and not the stopping boundary.

Activities

  1. Trace the worked example by hand before running it.
  2. Diagnose a loop that decrements a counter while testing whether it is less than 10.
  3. Add a quit command to a menu loop.
  4. Test the loop with its initial value already at the boundary.

Accessibility Practice

Announce the expected maximum number of iterations for bounded examples. Stop runaway processes with the terminal interrupt command and describe the recovery procedure.

Skills Checklist

  • I can identify the termination condition.
  • I can trace loop state changes.
  • I can diagnose common infinite-loop causes.
  • I can test loop boundary cases.

Unit 6: Functions

Overview

Functions support decomposition, reuse, and testing. JavaScript supports declarations, expressions, arrow functions, default parameters, rest parameters, and closures. Unlike Python, JavaScript does not support Python-style keyword arguments; use an options object when named configuration is useful.

Lesson 6.1: Defining Functions

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 6, Lesson 6.1.
  • MDN: Functions.

Learning Objectives

  • Define and call a function.
  • Explain parameters and function bodies.
  • Choose a function declaration or expression.

Concept Explanation

A function is a reusable block of code. Parameters receive input values, and return sends a result back to the caller.

Worked Example

function calculateTip(bill, rate) {
  return bill * rate;
}

const tip = calculateTip(24.50, 0.15);
console.log(`Tip: $${tip.toFixed(2)}`);

Expected output:

Tip: $3.67

Expected Behavior or Output

The canonical bill and tip rate produce a displayed tip of $3.67.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling a function before understanding its parameter order.
  • Omitting return when the caller needs a result.
  • Confusing a function definition with a function call.

Activities

  1. Define calculateTip using the canonical bill and tip rate.
  2. Define a function that returns the average of the canonical scores.
  3. Call each function with at least two different inputs.
  4. Explain why returning a value is more reusable than printing inside the function.

Accessibility Practice

Use descriptive function and parameter names. Read the function declaration, call, and returned result as separate steps.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define and call a function.
  • I can identify parameters and arguments.
  • I can return a computed value.
  • I can use a function to reduce repeated code.

Lesson 6.2: Passing Arguments

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 6, Lesson 6.2.
  • MDN: Function parameters.

Learning Objectives

  • Pass positional arguments in the correct order.
  • Use default parameters.
  • Use an options object to model named configuration.

Concept Explanation

JavaScript arguments are positional. It does not have Python’s name=value call syntax. For functions with several optional settings, pass one object whose properties describe each setting.

Worked Example

function calculateTotal(bill, tipRate = 0.15) {
  return bill + bill * tipRate;
}

function describeStudent({ name, age, favoriteSubject }) {
  return `${name}, age ${age}, studies ${favoriteSubject}.`;
}

console.log(calculateTotal(24.50).toFixed(2));
console.log(calculateTotal(24.50, 0.20).toFixed(2));
console.log(describeStudent({
  name: "Avery",
  age: 16,
  favoriteSubject: "Computer Science"
}));

Expected output:

28.18
29.40
Avery, age 16, studies Computer Science.

Expected Behavior or Output

The default tip rate produces 28.18; the 0.20 rate produces 29.40; the student description names Avery and Computer Science.

Common Mistakes

  • Swapping positional arguments that have the same primitive type.
  • Assuming JavaScript supports Python keyword arguments.
  • Forgetting that a default parameter is used for an omitted or undefined argument, not for null.

Activities

  1. Call calculateTotal with the default rate and with a 0.20 rate.
  2. Create an options object for the canonical student profile.
  3. Omit one required property and decide how the function should validate it.
  4. Explain the difference between omitted, undefined, and null.

Accessibility Practice

Prefer clear property names over unexplained positional values when a function accepts several related settings.

Skills Checklist

  • I can pass positional arguments.
  • I can define default parameters.
  • I can use an options object.
  • I can explain JavaScript’s argument semantics.

Lesson 6.3: Return Values

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 6, Lesson 6.3.
  • MDN: return.

Learning Objectives

  • Return values from functions.
  • Distinguish returning from printing.
  • Handle early returns for invalid inputs.

Concept Explanation

A return value is data supplied to the caller. Printing is a side effect and does not substitute for returning a value.

Worked Example

function average(scores) {
  if (!Array.isArray(scores) || scores.length === 0) {
    return null;
  }
  const total = scores.reduce((sum, score) => sum + score, 0);
  return total / scores.length;
}

const result = average([82, 91, 76, 88]);
console.log(`Average: ${result.toFixed(2)}`);
console.log(`Empty input: ${average([])}`);

Expected output:

Average: 84.25
Empty input: null

Expected Behavior or Output

The canonical score average is 84.25 and an empty array returns null.

Common Mistakes

  • Expecting a function that only calls console.log() to return a useful value.
  • Forgetting that a function without an explicit return produces undefined.
  • Returning a formatted string when later calculations require a number.

Activities

  1. Write a function that returns the total of the canonical scores.
  2. Write a function that returns null for an empty list.
  3. Use the returned average in a second calculation.
  4. Compare a function that prints a result with one that returns it.

Accessibility Practice

Keep calculation results and explanatory output distinct. Use explicit labels when displaying a returned value.

Skills Checklist

  • I can return a value from a function.
  • I can use early returns for invalid cases.
  • I can distinguish undefined, null, and a computed value.
  • I can reuse returned values in later calculations.

Lesson 6.4: Functions with Arrays and Objects

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 6, Lesson 6.4.
  • MDN: Working with objects and arrays.

Learning Objectives

  • Pass arrays and objects to functions.
  • Process the canonical score and inventory data.
  • Explain that object and array values are passed by sharing their references.

Concept Explanation

Arrays and objects are passed as values that refer to the same underlying object. A function can therefore mutate caller-visible state unless it works on a copy.

Worked Example

function inventoryValue(items) {
  return items.reduce(
    (total, item) => total + item.quantity * item.unitPrice,
    0
  );
}

const inventory = [
  { name: "Notebook", quantity: 3, unitPrice: 2.50 },
  { name: "Pencil", quantity: 10, unitPrice: 0.50 },
  { name: "Folder", quantity: 4, unitPrice: 1.25 }
];

console.log(`Inventory value: $${inventoryValue(inventory).toFixed(2)}`);

Expected output:

Inventory value: $17.50

Expected Behavior or Output

The canonical inventory value is $17.50.

Common Mistakes

  • Mutating an array or object inside a function without documenting the side effect.
  • Assuming a new variable created with const makes the referenced object immutable.
  • Returning the wrong data shape for the caller.

Activities

  1. Write a function that returns the average of the canonical scores.
  2. Write a function that returns the total value of the canonical inventory.
  3. Add a new inventory item and verify the total changes by its line value.
  4. Write a non-mutating function that returns a filtered list of scores at least 80.

Accessibility Practice

Use named object properties and label each returned total. Explain whether a function changes the original collection.

Skills Checklist

  • I can pass arrays and objects to functions.
  • I can process a collection with reduce() or a loop.
  • I can explain reference sharing and mutation.
  • I can return a predictable result shape.

Lesson 6.5: Arbitrary Numbers of Arguments

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 6, Lesson 6.5.
  • MDN: Rest parameters.

Learning Objectives

  • Use rest parameters to collect arbitrary positional arguments.
  • Use spread syntax to pass array elements as arguments.
  • Explain the difference between rest and spread syntax.

Concept Explanation

A rest parameter gathers remaining positional arguments into an array. Spread syntax expands an iterable into individual arguments at a call site.

Worked Example

function sumScores(...scores) {
  return scores.reduce((total, score) => total + score, 0);
}

const values = [82, 91, 76, 88];
console.log(sumScores(...values));
console.log(sumScores(10, 20, 30));

Expected output:

337
60

Expected Behavior or Output

The four canonical scores sum to 337; the values 10, 20, and 30 sum to 60.

Common Mistakes

  • Confusing rest parameters in a function definition with spread syntax in a call.
  • Placing a rest parameter anywhere other than the final parameter position.
  • Passing a whole array when the function expects individual numeric arguments.

Activities

  1. Call sumScores with the four canonical scores.
  2. Call it with three different values.
  3. Pass an array using spread syntax.
  4. Explain why JavaScript rest parameters do not provide a direct equivalent to Python’s **kwargs.

Accessibility Practice

Use parameter names that communicate the expected value type. Keep the function’s input contract explicit.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define a rest parameter.
  • I can use spread syntax in a function call.
  • I can distinguish rest from spread.
  • I can explain the lack of Python-style keyword-argument collection.

Unit 7: Classes and Object-Oriented Programming

Overview

This unit uses the same student and inventory domains as the Python course. JavaScript classes use prototypes under the hood; private fields begin with #. Composition is often preferable to inheritance when one object contains another.

Lesson 7.1: Why Learn About Classes?

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 7, Lesson 7.1.
  • MDN: Classes.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain classes, objects, attributes, and methods.
  • Describe encapsulation and abstraction.
  • Identify an appropriate domain object.

Concept Explanation

A class defines the structure and behavior shared by its instances. An inventory item can store a name, quantity, and unit price and provide a method that calculates its line value.

Worked Example

class InventoryItem {
  constructor(name, quantity, unitPrice) {
    this.name = name;
    this.quantity = quantity;
    this.unitPrice = unitPrice;
  }

  lineValue() {
    return this.quantity * this.unitPrice;
  }
}

const notebook = new InventoryItem("Notebook", 3, 2.50);
console.log(`${notebook.name}: $${notebook.lineValue().toFixed(2)}`);

Expected output:

Notebook: $7.50

Expected Behavior or Output

An InventoryItem for three Notebooks at $2.50 each prints Notebook: $7.50.

Common Mistakes

  • Confusing the class with an instance.
  • Omitting this when accessing instance properties.
  • Defining behavior that belongs to an object as unrelated global variables.

Activities

  1. Create an InventoryItem for each canonical inventory record.
  2. Print each item’s line value.
  3. Create a Student class using Avery’s profile fields.
  4. Explain which data belongs in an instance and which behavior belongs in a method.

Accessibility Practice

Use descriptive property and method names. Announce object values by property name rather than relying on visual object inspection.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain a class and an instance.
  • I can define a constructor and method.
  • I can use this to access instance properties.
  • I can identify encapsulation in a small class.

Lesson 7.2: Creating and Using a Class

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 7, Lesson 7.2.
  • MDN: constructor.

Learning Objectives

  • Define a class with a constructor.
  • Instantiate multiple objects.
  • Validate constructor arguments.

Concept Explanation

A class constructor initializes each new instance. The new operator creates an object and calls the class constructor with the supplied arguments.

Worked Example

class Student {
  constructor(name, age, heightM, favoriteSubject) {
    if (typeof name !== "string" || name.trim() === "") {
      throw new TypeError("Student name is required.");
    }
    this.name = name;
    this.age = age;
    this.heightM = heightM;
    this.favoriteSubject = favoriteSubject;
  }
}

const student = new Student("Avery", 16, 1.72, "Computer Science");
console.log(`${student.name}, age ${student.age}`);

Expected output:

Avery, age 16

Expected Behavior or Output

The canonical Student instance prints Avery, age 16.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting the new keyword.
  • Using constructor parameters without assigning them to the instance.
  • Failing to validate required data.

Activities

  1. Create two Student instances with different values.
  2. Print each student’s name and favorite subject.
  3. Add validation that age is a nonnegative integer.
  4. Deliberately pass an invalid name and read the error.

Accessibility Practice

Make validation errors specific and textual. Keep constructor parameters in a consistent, documented order.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define a constructor.
  • I can instantiate multiple objects.
  • I can validate constructor inputs.
  • I can explain the role of new.

Lesson 7.3: Working with Attributes and Methods

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 7, Lesson 7.3.
  • MDN: Private class elements.

Learning Objectives

  • Read and update object properties.
  • Define methods that validate or transform state.
  • Use a private field for encapsulated state.

Concept Explanation

Methods define behavior associated with an instance. Private fields beginning with # can be accessed only from within the declaring class.

Worked Example

class InventoryItem {
  #quantity;

  constructor(name, quantity, unitPrice) {
    this.name = name;
    this.#quantity = quantity;
    this.unitPrice = unitPrice;
  }

  updateQuantity(newQuantity) {
    if (!Number.isInteger(newQuantity) || newQuantity < 0) {
      throw new RangeError("Quantity must be a nonnegative integer.");
    }
    this.#quantity = newQuantity;
  }

  describe() {
    return `${this.name}: quantity ${this.#quantity}`;
  }
}

const pencil = new InventoryItem("Pencil", 10, 0.50);
pencil.updateQuantity(12);
console.log(pencil.describe());

Expected output:

Pencil: quantity 12

Expected Behavior or Output

After updating the Pencil quantity to 12, the method prints Pencil: quantity 12.

Common Mistakes

  • Accessing a private field from outside its class.
  • Updating state without validating it.
  • Confusing a method call with a property read.

Activities

  1. Add a method that returns the item’s line value.
  2. Reject a negative quantity.
  3. Update the Notebook quantity from 3 to 5.
  4. Explain why a private field can protect an object’s invariants.

Accessibility Practice

Use methods that return clear text or values. State the validation rule before asking learners to test it.

Skills Checklist

  • I can read and update public properties.
  • I can define and call methods.
  • I can use a private class field.
  • I can validate state changes.

Lesson 7.4: Inheritance

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 7, Lesson 7.4.
  • MDN: Inheritance and the prototype chain.

Learning Objectives

  • Define a subclass with extends.
  • Call a parent constructor with super().
  • Override a method when specialized behavior is required.

Concept Explanation

Inheritance models an is-a relationship. A subclass uses extends and calls its parent constructor with super() before accessing this.

Worked Example

class InventoryItem {
  constructor(name, quantity) {
    this.name = name;
    this.quantity = quantity;
  }

  describe() {
    return `${this.name}: ${this.quantity} in stock`;
  }
}

class PerishableItem extends InventoryItem {
  constructor(name, quantity, expirationDate) {
    super(name, quantity);
    this.expirationDate = expirationDate;
  }

  describe() {
    return `${super.describe()}, expires ${this.expirationDate}`;
  }
}

const milk = new PerishableItem("Milk", 2, "2026-11-10");
console.log(milk.describe());

Expected output:

Milk: 2 in stock, expires 2026-11-10

Expected Behavior or Output

The PerishableItem example prints Milk: 2 in stock, expires 2026-11-10.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling this before super() in a derived constructor.
  • Forgetting to pass required parent arguments.
  • Using inheritance when composition would be simpler.

Activities

  1. Create a PerishableItem subclass with an expiration date.
  2. Override the description method.
  3. Test an instance with the canonical inventory quantity.
  4. Identify one situation where composition is preferable.

Accessibility Practice

Describe the parent/child relationship explicitly. Keep overridden method behavior predictable and document what changes.

Skills Checklist

  • I can extend a class.
  • I can call a parent constructor with super().
  • I can override a method.
  • I can explain when inheritance is appropriate.

Lesson 7.5: Instances as Attributes (Composition)

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 7, Lesson 7.5.
  • MDN: Working with objects.

Learning Objectives

  • Model a has-a relationship.
  • Store one object inside another object.
  • Explain composition as an alternative to inheritance.

Concept Explanation

Composition models a has-a relationship by storing one object as a property of another. It often provides a simpler alternative to inheritance.

Worked Example

class Student {
  constructor(name, age) {
    this.name = name;
    this.age = age;
  }
}

class StudentRecord {
  constructor(student, favoriteSubject) {
    this.student = student;
    this.favoriteSubject = favoriteSubject;
  }

  describe() {
    return `${this.student.name} studies ${this.favoriteSubject}.`;
  }
}

const record = new StudentRecord(
  new Student("Avery", 16),
  "Computer Science"
);
console.log(record.describe());

Expected output:

Avery studies Computer Science.

Expected Behavior or Output

The StudentRecord example prints Avery studies Computer Science..

Common Mistakes

  • Copying an object’s fields when a related object should be retained.
  • Confusing has-a composition with is-a inheritance.
  • Creating circular object references without a clear reason.

Activities

  1. Create a Student object for Avery.
  2. Place the Student object inside a StudentRecord.
  3. Add a second related object, such as a contact record.
  4. Explain why StudentRecord is not a subclass of Student.

Accessibility Practice
