Use explicit relationship names such as student and contact. Print nested values with labels.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model a has-a relationship.
  • I can store an object as another object’s property.
  • I can explain composition versus inheritance.
  • I can access nested object properties.

Unit 8: Files and Exceptions

Overview

This unit uses the same notes.txt and structured task/student records as the Python course. Node.js file APIs are asynchronous by default; use promises and try/catch/finally to make resource behavior explicit.

Lesson 8.1: Reading from a File

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 8, Lesson 8.1.
  • Node.js documentation: node:fs/promises.

Learning Objectives

  • Read a UTF-8 text file.
  • Distinguish whole-file reads from line-by-line processing.
  • Handle a missing file with a clear error.

Concept Explanation

The node:fs/promises API returns promises for file operations. UTF-8 decoding returns a string; omitting the encoding returns a Buffer.

Worked Example

Create notes.txt containing:

Practice JavaScript.
Review arrays and functions.

Read it:

const fs = require("node:fs/promises");

async function main() {
  try {
    const contents = await fs.readFile("notes.txt", "utf8");
    console.log("File contents:");
    console.log(contents.trimEnd());
  } catch (error) {
    if (error.code === "ENOENT") {
      console.log("Error: notes.txt was not found.");
    } else {
      throw error;
    }
  }
}

main();

Expected output:

File contents:
Practice JavaScript.
Review arrays and functions.

Expected Behavior or Output

With the sample notes.txt file present, both note lines are printed under the File contents label.

Common Mistakes

  • Omitting the encoding and receiving a Buffer.
  • Using the wrong working directory for a relative path.
  • Ignoring the rejected promise from file I/O.

Activities

  1. Create and read the canonical notes.txt file.
  2. Rename the file and verify the missing-file message.
  3. Read the file and count its lines.
  4. Explain the difference between a relative and absolute path.

Accessibility Practice

Report the file name and each line in reading order. Use textual errors that identify the missing path.

Skills Checklist

  • I can read a UTF-8 file with fs.readFile().
  • I can explain relative paths.
  • I can handle a missing file.
  • I can distinguish text from Buffer data.

Lesson 8.2: Writing to a File

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 8, Lesson 8.2.
  • Node.js documentation: writeFile() and appendFile().

Learning Objectives

  • Create or overwrite a text file.
  • Append content without replacing existing content.
  • Confirm successful file operations.

Concept Explanation

writeFile() creates or replaces file content; appendFile() adds content. Await each operation before relying on its result.

Worked Example

const fs = require("node:fs/promises");

async function main() {
  await fs.writeFile("notes.txt", "Practice JavaScript.\n", "utf8");
  await fs.appendFile("notes.txt", "Review arrays and functions.\n", "utf8");
  const saved = await fs.readFile("notes.txt", "utf8");
  console.log(saved.trimEnd());
  console.log("Notes saved.");
}

main().catch(error => {
  console.error(`File error: ${error.message}`);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Expected output:

Practice JavaScript.
Review arrays and functions.
Notes saved.

Expected Behavior or Output

The two note lines are printed, followed by Notes saved..

Common Mistakes

  • Using write mode when the intention is to append.
  • Forgetting to await a write before reading the file.
  • Assuming a successful call means the path is the intended one.

Activities

  1. Write a one-line note to notes.txt.
  2. Append a second line.
  3. Run the program twice and explain whether the content is overwritten or appended.
  4. Verify the saved text by reading it back programmatically.

Accessibility Practice

Print a confirmation that identifies the file and operation. Do not rely on a file icon or color to indicate success.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write a text file.
  • I can append to a text file.
  • I can await file operations.
  • I can verify saved content.

Lesson 8.3: Exceptions — Handling Errors

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 8, Lesson 8.3.
  • MDN: Error and try…catch.

Learning Objectives

  • Handle exceptions with try/catch.
  • Distinguish expected errors from unexpected errors.
  • Define a custom error class.

Concept Explanation

An exception interrupts normal control flow. try/catch handles expected failures, and custom Error subclasses can carry additional context.

Worked Example

class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(field, message) {
    super(message);
    this.name = "ValidationError";
    this.field = field;
  }
}

function validateAge(age) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(age) || age < 0) {
    throw new ValidationError("age", "Age must be a nonnegative integer.");
  }
  return age;
}

try {
  console.log(validateAge(16));
  validateAge(-1);
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof ValidationError) {
    console.log(`Validation failed for ${error.field}: ${error.message}`);
  } else {
    throw error;
  }
}

Expected output:

16
Validation failed for age: Age must be a nonnegative integer.

Expected Behavior or Output

The valid age 16 is printed; invalid age -1 produces the field-specific validation message.

Common Mistakes

  • Catching every error and silently ignoring it.
  • Throwing a string instead of an Error object.
  • Failing to rethrow unexpected errors.

Activities

  1. Validate that Avery’s age is 16.
  2. Test negative age, decimal age, and text input.
  3. Create a custom error for an invalid inventory quantity.
  4. Explain why unexpected errors should not be hidden.

Accessibility Practice

Error messages should identify the field, invalid value when safe, and correction expected. Keep error output textual.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use try/catch.
  • I can throw an Error object.
  • I can define a custom error class.
  • I can distinguish expected and unexpected errors.

Lesson 8.4: The else and finally Patterns

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 8, Lesson 8.4.
  • MDN: try…catch…finally.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain code that runs after success or regardless of success.
  • Use finally for cleanup.
  • Recognize that JavaScript does not have Python’s try/except/else syntax.

Concept Explanation

JavaScript has try, catch, and finally, but no direct else clause attached to a try statement. Put success-only work after the operation inside the try block. Put cleanup in finally.

Worked Example

async function loadNotes() {
  let contents;
  try {
    contents = await require("node:fs/promises").readFile("notes.txt", "utf8");
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(`Unable to read notes: ${error.message}`);
    return;
  } finally {
    console.log("Read attempt finished.");
  }

  console.log("Read succeeded.");
  console.log(contents.trimEnd());
}

loadNotes();

Expected Behavior or Output

The final status message is printed whether the read succeeds or fails. The success message and file contents appear only when the read succeeds.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming JavaScript supports Python’s try/except/else syntax.
  • Placing success-only code in finally.
  • Returning from finally and unintentionally overriding an earlier return or exception.

Activities

  1. Run the example with notes.txt present.
  2. Run it with notes.txt missing.
  3. Identify which messages appear in each case.
  4. Explain why cleanup belongs in finally.

Accessibility Practice

Use separate success and failure messages. Ensure the final status is announced regardless of outcome.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain JavaScript’s try/catch/finally structure.
  • I can identify success-only operations.
  • I can use finally for cleanup.
  • I can explain the absence of a direct try-else clause.

Lesson 8.5: Storing Data with JSON

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 8, Lesson 8.5.
  • MDN: JSON.

Learning Objectives

  • Convert JavaScript objects to JSON text.
  • Parse JSON text into JavaScript values.
  • Save and reload structured records.

Concept Explanation

JSON is a text representation of structured data. JSON.stringify() serializes supported JavaScript values; JSON.parse() reconstructs values from valid JSON text.

Worked Example

const fs = require("node:fs/promises");

async function main() {
  const tasks = [
    { id: 1, title: "Review arrays", done: false },
    { id: 2, title: "Practice functions", done: true }
  ];

  const jsonText = JSON.stringify(tasks, null, 2);
  await fs.writeFile("tasks.json", jsonText, "utf8");

  const loadedText = await fs.readFile("tasks.json", "utf8");
  const loadedTasks = JSON.parse(loadedText);
  console.log(`Loaded ${loadedTasks.length} tasks.`);
  console.log(`First task: ${loadedTasks[0].title}`);
}

main().catch(error => {
  console.error(`Storage error: ${error.message}`);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Expected output:

Loaded 2 tasks.
First task: Review arrays

Expected Behavior or Output

The example prints Loaded 2 tasks. and First task: Review arrays after saving and reloading the data.

Common Mistakes

  • Passing an already serialized string to JSON.stringify() and double-encoding it.
  • Parsing malformed JSON without catching SyntaxError.
  • Assuming JSON preserves functions, undefined values, or every JavaScript type.

Activities

  1. Save and reload the canonical task fields: id, title, description, done, created_at.
  2. Add a task and verify it survives a second program run.
  3. Deliberately corrupt the JSON and handle the parse error.
  4. Compare the in-memory object with the JSON text stored on disk.

Accessibility Practice

Use pretty-printed JSON for manual inspection and provide a textual confirmation after saving or loading.

Skills Checklist

  • I can serialize objects with JSON.stringify().
  • I can parse JSON with JSON.parse().
  • I can save and reload structured data.
  • I can handle malformed JSON.

Unit 9: Testing and Data Analysis

Overview

This unit follows the Python sequence: test a function, test a class, generate random values, analyze text, and process CSV data. Reuse the canonical score list, text sample, inventory, and CSV column names.

Lesson 9.1: Testing a Function

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 9, Lesson 9.1.
  • Node.js documentation: Test runner (node:test).

Learning Objectives

  • Write unit tests for deterministic functions.
  • Use assertions for expected and actual values.
  • Run tests from the terminal.

Concept Explanation

A unit test calls a deterministic function with known inputs and compares the returned value with an expected result. Tests should include ordinary inputs and boundary conditions.

Worked Example

Create math.js:

function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

function getGrade(score) {
  if (score >= 90) return "A";
  if (score >= 80) return "B";
  if (score >= 70) return "C";
  if (score >= 60) return "D";
  return "F";
}

module.exports = { add, getGrade };

Create math.test.js:

const test = require("node:test");
const assert = require("node:assert/strict");
const { add, getGrade } = require("./math");

test("add returns the sum", () => {
  assert.equal(add(5, 3), 8);
  assert.equal(add(-5, -3), -8);
  assert.equal(add(0, 7), 7);
});

test("getGrade follows shared thresholds", () => {
  assert.equal(getGrade(90), "A");
  assert.equal(getGrade(82), "B");
  assert.equal(getGrade(76), "C");
  assert.equal(getGrade(60), "D");
  assert.equal(getGrade(59), "F");
});

Run with node --test.

Expected result: two passing tests and zero failures.

Expected Behavior or Output

The Node.js test runner reports two passing tests and no failures when add() and getGrade() satisfy the stated contracts.

Common Mistakes

  • Testing only one typical value and ignoring boundaries.
  • Writing assertions that merely repeat the implementation.
  • Forgetting to export the function being tested.
  • Making tests depend on execution order or shared mutable state.

Activities

  1. Add tests for the canonical scores 82, 91, 76, and 88.
  2. Add boundary tests for every grade threshold.
  3. Add a test for invalid scores and decide what the function contract should be.
  4. Run the test file from the terminal and interpret the pass/fail summary.

Accessibility Practice

Read each test name and assertion result. Ensure failures identify the expected and actual values in text.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write a test with node:test.
  • I can assert expected values.
  • I can test normal and boundary cases.
  • I can run tests from the terminal.

Lesson 9.2: Testing a Class

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 9, Lesson 9.2.
  • Node.js documentation: Test runner and assert.

Learning Objectives

  • Test object construction, state changes, and methods.
  • Verify both valid and invalid operations.
  • Keep test cases independent.

Concept Explanation

A class test verifies observable behavior of an instance: construction, method results, valid state changes, and rejected invalid changes.

Worked Example

Assume InventoryItem exposes quantity, updateQuantity(), and lineValue(). A test file can verify its public behavior:

const test = require("node:test");
const assert = require("node:assert/strict");
const { InventoryItem } = require("./inventory-item");

test("inventory item updates quantity and calculates value", () => {
  const item = new InventoryItem("Notebook", 3, 2.50);
  assert.equal(item.lineValue(), 7.50);
  item.updateQuantity(5);
  assert.equal(item.lineValue(), 12.50);
});

test("inventory item rejects a negative quantity", () => {
  const item = new InventoryItem("Pencil", 10, 0.50);
  assert.throws(() => item.updateQuantity(-1), RangeError);
});

Expected result: both tests pass when the class enforces its stated contract.

Expected Behavior or Output

Both tests pass when the item value updates from $7.50 to $12.50 and a negative quantity throws RangeError.

Common Mistakes

  • Testing private implementation details instead of public behavior.
  • Reusing one mutated instance across unrelated tests.
  • Forgetting to test invalid state transitions.

Activities

  1. Test a Notebook item with quantity 3 and unit price 2.50.
  2. Verify its line value after changing quantity to 5.
  3. Verify that a negative quantity is rejected.
  4. Add a test for a zero quantity and explain whether it is valid.

Accessibility Practice

Give each test a descriptive name that states the behavior being verified. Avoid ambiguous test labels such as “test 1”.

Skills Checklist

  • I can instantiate an object in a test.
  • I can test a method’s return value.
  • I can test a state change.
  • I can assert that invalid operations throw.

Lesson 9.3: Introduction to Random Numbers

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 9, Lesson 9.3.
  • MDN: Math.random.

Learning Objectives

  • Generate random floating-point values and bounded integers.
  • Select a random element from an array.
  • Explain why random tests should not depend on a specific result.

Concept Explanation

Math.random() returns a pseudorandom floating-point value greater than or equal to zero and less than one. Transform it to a bounded integer with multiplication and Math.floor().

Worked Example

const randomDecimal = Math.random();
const randomInteger = Math.floor(Math.random() * 10) + 1;

const colors = ["red", "blue", "green"];
const randomChoice = colors[Math.floor(Math.random() * colors.length)];

console.log(`Decimal in [0, 1): ${randomDecimal >= 0 && randomDecimal < 1}`);
console.log(`Integer in 1..10: ${randomInteger >= 1 && randomInteger <= 10}`);
console.log(`Selected item is valid: ${colors.includes(randomChoice)}`);

Expected output: three lines containing true; the sampled values vary on each run.

Expected Behavior or Output

Each run prints true for all three range and membership checks; the sampled values may differ.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming Math.random() can return exactly 1.
  • Forgetting that Math.floor() is needed for an integer index.
  • Writing a test that expects one particular random result.

Activities

  1. Generate a random integer from 1 through 10.
  2. Select one of the canonical inventory item names.
  3. Run the program several times and observe that values vary.
  4. Explain why randomness makes exact-output tests unreliable without a controllable source.

Accessibility Practice

Label the range and meaning of each random value. Never require a visual animation to observe a random result.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use Math.random().
  • I can generate a bounded integer.
  • I can select a random array element.
  • I can test properties of random output rather than one exact sample.

Lesson 9.4: Analyzing Text Data

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 9, Lesson 9.4.
  • MDN: String and Map.

Learning Objectives

  • Normalize text before analysis.
  • Count words and character frequencies.
  • Use a Map to store frequency counts.

Concept Explanation

Text analysis requires explicit normalization and tokenization rules. A Map stores each token and its current frequency; the regular expression in this example treats hyphenated words as separate alphabetic tokens.

Worked Example

const sample = "A student studies programming. Programming develops problem-solving skills.";

function countWords(text) {
  const words = text.toLowerCase().match(/[a-z]+/g) ?? [];
  const counts = new Map();

  for (const word of words) {
    counts.set(word, (counts.get(word) ?? 0) + 1);
  }
  return counts;
}

const frequencies = countWords(sample);
for (const [word, count] of frequencies) {
  console.log(`${word}: ${count}`);
}

Expected output:

a: 1
student: 1
studies: 1
programming: 2
develops: 1
problem: 1
solving: 1
skills: 1

Expected Behavior or Output

The sample produces nine tokens and eight distinct token keys; programming has frequency 2 and every other displayed token has frequency 1.

Common Mistakes

  • Counting uppercase and lowercase forms as separate words.
  • Splitting on a single space and retaining punctuation.
  • Assuming a simple regular expression handles every language’s word boundaries.

Activities

  1. Count the words in the canonical text sample.
  2. Identify the most frequent word.
  3. Count characters after normalizing case.
  4. Explain how punctuation and hyphenation affect the result.

Accessibility Practice

Print each word and count as a labeled pair. State the normalization rules so learners can understand why the counts have those values.

Skills Checklist

  • I can normalize text before counting.
  • I can tokenize a simple English text sample.
  • I can store frequencies in a Map.
  • I can explain limitations of a simple tokenizer.

Lesson 9.5: Working with CSV Data

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 9, Lesson 9.5.
  • npm documentation: csv-parse.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain rows, columns, headers, and records.
  • Read CSV data with a standards-aware parser.
  • Compute a summary from the canonical column set.

Concept Explanation

CSV is a text format with quoting and escaping rules. Splitting every line on commas is not a correct general CSV parser because a quoted field may itself contain a comma or newline. Use a maintained parser for real CSV data. The canonical headers are student_id, first_name, last_name, score, and active.

Worked Example

Install the parser with npm install csv-parse. Save a small fixture as students.csv:

student_id,first_name,last_name,score,active
1,Avery,Student,91,true
2,Jordan,Lee,82,true
3,Casey,Smith,76,false

Read it with csv-parse:

const fs = require("node:fs");
const { parse } = require("csv-parse/sync");

const records = parse(fs.readFileSync("students.csv", "utf8"), {
  columns: true,
  skip_empty_lines: true,
  trim: true
});

const average = records.reduce((sum, row) => sum + Number(row.score), 0)
  / records.length;

console.log(`Loaded students: ${records.length}`);
console.log(`Average score: ${average.toFixed(2)}`);

Expected output:

Loaded students: 3
Average score: 83.00

Expected Behavior or Output

The sample CSV contains three records with scores 91, 82, and 76. The average is 83.00.

Common Mistakes

  • Splitting CSV lines on commas without handling quoted fields.
  • Forgetting that parsed field values are strings until converted.
  • Assuming every row contains every required column.
  • Failing to handle a missing or empty file.

Activities

  1. Create a CSV with the five canonical column names.
  2. Load the records and print each student’s name and score.
  3. Calculate the average score.
  4. Add a quoted field containing a comma and verify that the parser reads it as one field.

Accessibility Practice

Print one record per line with column names. Provide a textual summary of any malformed rows rather than relying on a spreadsheet’s visual highlighting.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain CSV headers and records.
  • I can parse CSV with a standards-aware library.
  • I can convert numeric fields before calculating.
  • I can summarize a dataset with labeled output.

Unit 10: Project-Based Learning — Text-Based Applications

Overview

The projects preserve the Python track’s requirements and user interaction. The text adventure uses the shared five-room graph (start_room, tunnel, clearing, locked_door_room, and treasure_room) and the shiny-key puzzle. The command-line to-do manager supports add, view, complete, delete, and JSON persistence.

Lesson 10.1: Designing Your Project

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 10, Lesson 10.1.
  • MDN: JavaScript modules and functions.

Learning Objectives

  • Apply top-down design to a multi-part program.
  • Identify inputs, outputs, data, and edge cases.
  • Write pseudocode and acceptance tests before implementation.

Concept Explanation

Top-down design breaks a large task into smaller responsibilities. The project should have separate functions for input, state changes, display, and persistence. Define command names and error behavior before writing code.

Worked Example

Text-adventure pseudocode:

CREATE rooms and exits
PLACE items in selected rooms
CREATE player at starting room
REPEAT
  DISPLAY current room and player status
  READ command
  VALIDATE command
  APPLY movement or inventory action
UNTIL player enters quit

Expected Behavior or Output

The learner produces pseudocode, a room/command specification, and acceptance tests before implementation.

Common Mistakes

  • Starting implementation before defining the project requirements.
  • Combining input, state changes, and display in one large function.
  • Omitting invalid-command and boundary cases.

Activities

  1. Draw or describe the five-room map in text.
  2. List every valid movement command and its destination.
  3. Define the to-do manager’s five menu operations.
  4. Write at least five acceptance tests before implementation.

Accessibility Practice

Use keyboard-operable commands, descriptive prompts, and predictable text output. Do not require maps, color, drag-and-drop, or mouse-only interaction.

Skills Checklist

  • I can decompose a project into functions or modules.
  • I can define inputs and outputs.
  • I can write pseudocode.
  • I can define acceptance tests and error cases.

Lesson 10.2: Building a Text-Based Adventure Game (Part 1)

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 10, Lesson 10.2.
  • Node.js documentation: readline/promises.

Learning Objectives

  • Model the five canonical rooms and their exits.
  • Move through connected rooms without changing state on invalid directions.
  • Explain the locked north exit from locked_door_room.

Shared Project Specification

Use the canonical five-room graph: start_room north to tunnel; tunnel south to start_room and east to clearing; clearing west to tunnel and north to locked_door_room; locked_door_room south to clearing and conditionally north to treasure_room after using shiny key. The player starts in start_room. Valid commands include north, south, east, west, take shiny key, use shiny key, and quit.

Concept Explanation

A room is represented by its identifier, description, and a map of valid exits. Movement looks up the requested direction and changes the player’s current room only when the exit exists.

Worked Example

const rooms = {
  start_room: { exits: { north: "tunnel" }, items: [] },
  tunnel: { exits: { south: "start_room", east: "clearing" }, items: [] },
  clearing: { exits: { west: "tunnel", north: "locked_door_room" }, items: [] },
  locked_door_room: { exits: { south: "clearing" }, items: [] },
  treasure_room: { exits: {}, items: [] }
};
function move(currentRoom, direction) {
  return rooms[currentRoom].exits[direction] ?? null;
}
console.log(move("start_room", "north"));
console.log(move("start_room", "west"));

Expected output:

tunnel
null

Expected Behavior or Output

Moving north from start_room returns tunnel. Moving west from start_room returns null; the locked-door north exit is added only after the key puzzle is solved.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding an exit in one direction but forgetting the reverse connection.
  • Accepting an exit that does not exist.
  • Confusing a room key with its display name.

Activities

  1. Build the five canonical rooms and their unconditional exits.
  2. Test north from start_room, east from tunnel, and north from clearing.
  3. Test an invalid movement without changing the current room.
  4. Add the conditional north exit from locked_door_room only after the key is used.

Accessibility Practice

Announce the current room, description, and available exits in a consistent order. Never make the map available only as a graphic.

Skills Checklist

  • I can represent rooms and exits as objects.
  • I can move between connected rooms.
  • I can reject invalid directions.
  • I can display room information sequentially.

Lesson 10.3: Building a Text-Based Adventure Game (Part 2)

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 10, Lesson 10.3.
  • MDN: Array methods and object methods.

Learning Objectives

  • Place shiny key in start_room and transfer it to inventory exactly once.
  • Require the key to be used in locked_door_room.
  • Unlock the conditional north exit to treasure_room.

Shared Project Specification

Place only the shiny key in start_room. The player uses take shiny key and use shiny key. The key must be used while in locked_door_room; this unlocks its north exit to treasure_room. Preserve these item names and rules across language tracks.

Concept Explanation

An item belongs either to a room or to the player’s inventory. Picking it up removes it from the room and adds it to inventory as one state transition.

Worked Example

const rooms = {
  start_room: { exits: { north: "tunnel" } },
  tunnel: { exits: { south: "start_room", east: "clearing" } },
  clearing: { exits: { west: "tunnel", north: "locked_door_room" } },
  locked_door_room: { exits: { south: "clearing" } },
  treasure_room: { exits: {} }
};
const roomItems = { start_room: ["shiny key"], tunnel: [], clearing: [], locked_door_room: [], treasure_room: [] };
const inventory = [];
let doorLocked = true;
function takeItem(room, requestedName) {
  const items = roomItems[room];
  const index = items.findIndex(item => item.toLowerCase() === requestedName.toLowerCase());
  if (index < 0) return false;
  inventory.push(items.splice(index, 1)[0]);
  return true;
}
function useKey(room, items) {
  if (room !== "locked_door_room") return "You must be at the locked door to use the key.";
  if (!items.includes("shiny key")) return "The door is locked.";
  doorLocked = false;
  rooms.locked_door_room.exits.north = "treasure_room";
  return "The door unlocks; north now leads to treasure_room.";
}
function runCommand(room, command) {
  if (command.startsWith("take ")) return takeItem(room, command.slice(5));
  if (command === "use shiny key") return useKey(room, inventory);
  return "I don't understand that command.";
}
console.log(runCommand("start_room", "take shiny key"));
console.log(runCommand("start_room", "take shiny key"));
console.log(inventory.join(", "));
console.log(runCommand("clearing", "use shiny key"));
console.log(runCommand("locked_door_room", "use shiny key"));
console.log(doorLocked);
console.log(rooms.locked_door_room.exits.north);

Expected output:

true
shiny key
You must be at the locked door to use the key.
The door unlocks; north now leads to treasure_room.
false
treasure_room

Expected Behavior or Output

The command dispatcher accepts the literal take shiny key and use shiny key commands. The second pickup is rejected without duplicating the inventory item. Key use is rejected outside locked_door_room; using it there unlocks the north exit.

true
false
shiny key
You must be at the locked door to use the key.
The door unlocks; north now leads to treasure_room.
false
treasure_room

Common Mistakes

  • Allowing an item to be picked up repeatedly after it has been removed.
  • Failing to normalize item names consistently.
  • Updating the room but not the inventory, or vice versa.

Activities

  1. Take shiny key from start_room.
  2. Attempt to take it a second time and verify inventory does not change.
  3. Attempt to use the key outside locked_door_room.
  4. Use the key in locked_door_room and verify the north exit leads to treasure_room.

Accessibility Practice

Confirm each successful pickup by item name. When pickup fails, explain whether the item is absent or the command is invalid.

Skills Checklist

  • I can store items in rooms.
  • I can transfer an item to inventory.
  • I can display inventory contents.
  • I can implement and test a puzzle condition.

Lesson 10.4: Developing a Command-Line To-Do Tool

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 10, Lesson 10.4.
  • Node.js documentation: File system and readline.

Learning Objectives

  • Implement add, view, complete, delete, and quit operations.
  • Validate a one-based task number.
  • Persist task data in JSON.

Concept Explanation

A command-line task manager separates data operations from prompts and display. Task numbers shown to users are one-based, while array indexes are zero-based.

Shared Project Specification

Each task has an identifier, description, completion state, and creation timestamp. The menu supports add task, view tasks, mark complete, delete, and quit. Save after every state-changing operation.

Worked Example

Core task operations:

function addTask(tasks, description, createdAt = new Date().toISOString()) {
  if (description.trim() === "") {
    throw new Error("Task description cannot be empty.");
  }
  tasks.push({
    id: tasks.length + 1,
    description: description.trim(),
    completed: false,
    createdAt
  });
}

function markComplete(tasks, taskNumber) {
  const index = taskNumber - 1;
  if (!Number.isInteger(taskNumber) || index < 0 || index >= tasks.length) {
    return false;
  }
  tasks[index].completed = true;
  return true;
}

Expected Behavior or Output

A valid task description is added with completed false and a timestamp; a valid task number marks the corresponding task complete.

Common Mistakes

  • Confusing the user’s one-based task number with a zero-based array index.
  • Allowing empty descriptions.
  • Saving only when the program exits, so an interrupted run loses changes.
  • Reusing task identifiers after deletion without a documented policy.

Activities

  1. Add two tasks and view them in numbered order.
  2. Mark the first task complete.
  3. Delete the second task.
  4. Save and reload the task list using JSON and verify the state persists.

Accessibility Practice

Number every task and include an explicit completion label such as “complete” or “not complete”. Confirm every add, update, and delete action in text.

Skills Checklist

  • I can add and display tasks.
  • I can mark a task complete.
  • I can delete a task by number.
  • I can persist tasks as JSON.
  • I can validate task descriptions and numbers.

Lesson 10.5: Refinement and User Experience

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 10, Lesson 10.5.
  • Node.js documentation: Process exit codes and error handling.

Learning Objectives

  • Improve prompt clarity and validation.
  • Test invalid commands and boundary cases.
  • Review output for predictable keyboard and screen-reader use.

Concept Explanation

A usable text program gives the same kind of response for the same kind of action. Prompts should state valid input, errors should explain the problem, and successful operations should confirm what changed. A help command should list every supported operation.

Expected Behavior or Output

The refined application handles blank input, unknown commands, invalid record numbers, empty lists, and malformed stored data with explicit text messages.

Worked Example

function validateMenuChoice(choice) {
  const validChoices = ["add", "view", "search", "edit", "delete", "help", "quit"];
  if (!validChoices.includes(choice.trim().toLowerCase())) {
    return "Invalid choice. Enter add, view, search, edit, delete, help, or quit.";
  }
  return "Command accepted.";
}
console.log(validateMenuChoice("unknown"));

Expected Behavior or Output

The refined application handles blank input, unknown commands, invalid record numbers, empty lists, and malformed stored data with explicit text messages.

Common Mistakes

  • Printing “Invalid input” without explaining valid choices.
  • Failing to confirm a successful action.
  • Letting malformed stored data crash the entire program.
  • Relying on visual formatting without textual labels.

Activities

  1. Add a help command to the to-do tool.
  2. Test blank input, unknown commands, invalid task numbers, and an empty task list.
  3. Review every prompt for a clear expected input format.
  4. Ask a partner to complete all tasks using keyboard navigation only and record obstacles.

Accessibility Practice

Use consistent separators, descriptive prompts, explicit errors, and sequential output. Do not claim a screen-reader test unless it has actually been performed.

Skills Checklist

  • I can validate user input.
  • I can provide specific error messages.
  • I can confirm successful operations.
  • I can review a CLI for keyboard and screen-reader usability.

Unit 11: Capstone Project — Accessible Personal Data Manager

Overview

Build a complete command-line personal data manager in JavaScript and Node.js. The implementation may choose a Contact Manager, Book Tracker, Recipe Collection, or Budget Tracker, but the data model, operations, persistence, accessibility, and acceptance tests must be equivalent across the language tracks. Unlike the Python implementation, which introduces NiceGUI, this JavaScript track uses a terminal interface so the core capstone remains independent of a browser UI.

Lesson 11.1: Project Introduction and Interface Design

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 11, Lesson 11.1.
  • Node.js documentation: readline/promises.

Learning Objectives

  • Select a capstone domain.
  • Translate requirements into a menu and command set.
  • Design a keyboard-first text interface.

Concept Explanation

The capstone is assessed on data operations and accessibility, not visual interface fluency. The terminal interface must support adding, viewing, searching, editing, deleting, and saving records. A help command must list all commands.

Worked Example

A minimal command menu might list: add, view, search, edit, delete, help, and quit. Each command maps to one named function.

Expected Behavior or Output

The project plan contains a selected domain, a record schema, command descriptions, and acceptance tests.

Common Mistakes

  • Choosing a domain before identifying required fields and operations.
  • Designing a visual-only interaction when the project requires an accessible text interface.
  • Omitting help and invalid-command behavior.

Activities

  1. Choose one project domain.
  2. List the fields each record requires.
  3. Design the menu and exact prompt wording.
  4. Write acceptance tests for all required operations.

Accessibility Practice

Every action must be possible from the keyboard. Prompts must name the expected field and format. Output must be sequential and understandable without visual layout.

Skills Checklist

  • I can select a project domain.
  • I can define a record schema.
  • I can design a text-only command interface.
  • I can write acceptance tests.

Lesson 11.2: Data Model and Storage

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 11, Lesson 11.2.
  • Node.js documentation: fs/promises and JSON.

Learning Objectives

  • Define a record model.
  • Persist records to JSON.
  • Handle missing, malformed, and inaccessible files.

Concept Explanation

The data model defines the fields and invariants of each record. JSON persistence stores the records between runs; load and save operations must handle file and parse failures.

Canonical Record Fields

Use these shared fields for the generic personal data manager: id, title, description, category, created_at, and updated_at. A selected domain may add fields, but must not remove the shared fields.

Worked Example

A record contains id, title, description, category, created_at, and updated_at. The id is unique; timestamps use ISO 8601 strings.

Expected Behavior or Output

After saving and reloading, all record fields and values are preserved. Missing files can initialize an empty collection; malformed JSON produces a clear error.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating parsed JSON as trusted data without validation.
  • Reusing record identifiers.
  • Overwriting valid data after a parse failure without informing the user.

Activities

  1. Define the record shape and document each field.
  2. Create a sample JSON file containing at least three records.
  3. Implement load and save functions.
  4. Test missing files, malformed JSON, and an empty data set.

Accessibility Practice

Use human-readable JSON during development. Provide explicit save/load confirmations and specific error messages.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define the record schema.
  • I can load and save JSON.
  • I can preserve timestamps and identifiers.
  • I can handle missing and malformed data.

Concept Explanation

The data model defines the fields and invariants of each record. JSON persistence stores the records between runs; load and save operations must handle file and parse failures.

Lesson 11.3: Displaying Items

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 11, Lesson 11.3.
  • Node.js documentation: console output and Array iteration.

Learning Objectives

  • Display every record with a one-based number.
  • Print each field with an explicit label.
  • Handle an empty collection.

Concept Explanation

Displaying records is a read operation. A one-based display number is a temporary selection aid; the stored identifier remains the stable record identity.

Worked Example

function displayItems(items) {
  if (items.length === 0) {
    console.log("No items have been saved.");
    return;
  }
  items.forEach((item, index) => {
    console.log(`Item ${index + 1}:`);
    console.log(`  Title: ${item.title}`);
    console.log(`  Category: ${item.category}`);
    console.log(`  Description: ${item.description}`);
  });
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Each record is announced with its number and labeled fields. An empty collection prints the no-items message.

Common Mistakes

  • Omitting field labels.
  • Using zero-based indexes as the displayed number.
  • Failing to handle an empty collection.

Activities

  1. Display three sample records in order.
  2. Display an empty list and confirm the message is clear.
  3. Include the record identifier and timestamps in the output.
  4. Review output using sequential screen-reader navigation.

Accessibility Practice

Use labels, stable ordering, and one record at a time. Do not rely on columns, color, or icons to convey record fields.

Skills Checklist

  • I can display all records.
  • I can number records for selection.
  • I can handle an empty collection.
  • I can label every displayed field.

Lesson 11.4: Searching, Adding, and Editing Items

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 11, Lessons 11.3–11.5.
  • Node.js documentation: Array methods and Date.

Learning Objectives

  • Add validated records with unique identifiers.
  • Search records by keyword.
  • Edit selected fields and update timestamps.

Concept Explanation

Searching filters records without changing the stored collection. Editing changes only permitted fields and updates the updated_at timestamp.

Worked Example

function searchItems(items, keyword) {
  const query = keyword.trim().toLowerCase();
  return items.filter(item =>
    item.title.toLowerCase().includes(query) ||
    item.description.toLowerCase().includes(query)
  );
}

function updateItem(item, changes) {
  const allowed = ["title", "description", "category"];
  for (const field of allowed) {
    if (Object.hasOwn(changes, field)) item[field] = changes[field];
  }
  item.updated_at = new Date().toISOString();
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Search returns matching titles or descriptions. A successful edit changes the requested field and refreshes updated_at.

Common Mistakes

  • Searching case-sensitively without documenting that behavior.
  • Allowing edits to immutable identifiers.
  • Failing to update the modification timestamp.

Activities

  1. Search records by a word in the title.
  2. Search by a word in the description.
  3. Edit a title and verify that updated_at changes.
  4. Reject an edit that contains only blank required fields.

Accessibility Practice

Report the number of matches and identify each result by its title and record number. Confirm every successful edit.

Skills Checklist

  • I can search records by keyword.
  • I can add a validated record.
  • I can update selected fields.
  • I can maintain the updated_at timestamp.

Lesson 11.5: Deleting Items, Persistence, and Final Verification

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 11, Lessons 11.3–11.5.
  • Node.js documentation: fs/promises and JSON.

Learning Objectives

  • Delete a record by its identifier or displayed number.
  • Save changes and reload them between program runs.
  • Verify the full CRUD workflow and error handling.

Concept Explanation

Deleting removes a selected record from the collection. Persistence must happen after the mutation so the deletion remains effective after the next program launch.

Worked Example

function deleteItem(items, id) {
  const index = items.findIndex(item => item.id === id);
  if (index < 0) return false;
  items.splice(index, 1);
  return true;
}

Expected Behavior or Output

After deleting and saving a record, reloading the JSON file confirms that the record is absent.

Common Mistakes

  • Deleting by a stale array index.
  • Failing to save after a deletion.
  • Omitting confirmation for an irreversible action.

Activities

  1. Delete one record and confirm the title of the deleted item.
  2. Save the remaining records to JSON.
  3. Restart the application and verify the deleted record is still absent.
  4. Run the full acceptance checklist: add, view, search, edit, delete, invalid input, missing file, malformed JSON, and help.

Accessibility Practice

Ask for confirmation before irreversible deletion. Announce success or failure in text and preserve predictable menu navigation.

Runnable Reference Implementation

The repository includes a tested JavaScript domain and JSON-storage reference core in capstone/README.md. Run node --test JAVASCRIPT/capstone/records.test.js from the repository root. The reference core does not replace the requirement to build and evaluate an accessible user interface.

Skills Checklist

  • I can delete a record safely.
  • I can persist and reload records.
  • I can verify the complete CRUD workflow.
  • I can test invalid input and storage failures.

Assessment Criteria

Functionality (60%)

  • All create, read, update, and delete operations work.
  • Data persists to JSON between program runs.
  • Search works by at least one field.
  • Invalid input is handled without crashing.

Code Quality (20%)

  • Functions have focused responsibilities.
  • Names are descriptive and consistent.
  • Code is organized into modules.
  • Key functions include JSDoc comments.

Accessibility and User Experience (15%)

  • Prompts are descriptive and clear.
  • Every state-changing operation has a confirmation.
  • Output is sequential and predictable.
  • A help system is available.
  • Keyboard-only operation is supported.

Documentation and Tests (5%)

  • README includes setup and usage instructions.
  • At least five unit tests cover key functions.
  • README includes screen-reader usage tips and a reflection.

Deliverables

  • Source files organized into modules.
  • A data folder with example JSON records.
  • A README with installation, run instructions, commands, screen-reader tips, and a reflection.
  • A test suite with at least five meaningful tests.

JavaScript Module Note

CommonJS and ECMAScript modules are both valid JavaScript module systems. For this curriculum, choose one mode explicitly in package.json and use it consistently. If using CommonJS, use require() and module.exports; if using ES modules, use import and export. Do not mix both systems in a single file.

AI Use Policy

AI may be used for personal conceptual explanations and reinforcement only. It may not write, autocomplete, repair, complete, or generate course code or assessment solutions. Students must be able to explain and independently produce their submitted work.

It explains the language-neutral vocabulary and concepts used in every language track, using non-visual examples.Julia is a high-level, dynamically typed, JIT-compiled language for numerical and scientific computing, simulation, optimization, statistics, and data-intensive research. Multiple dispatch, expressive types, array operations, and performance-oriented compilation support both interactive analysis and high-performance numerical kernels.

  • Use JSON3.jl for JSON and CSV.jl for standards-compliant CSV parsing; these are project dependencies, not Julia standard libraries.

Complete the shared IDE setup lesson and terminal prerequisite. The course supports keyboard-first work with screen readers, braille displays, magnification, and other access technology.

Unit 0: Accessible Environment and Toolchain

Course overview

Before you start: complete Unit P: Computing Foundations Primer. It explains the language-neutral vocabulary and concepts used in every language track, using non-visual examples.

Course Overview

Julia is a high-level, dynamically typed, JIT-compiled language for numerical and scientific computing, simulation, optimization, statistics, and data-intensive research. Multiple dispatch, expressive types, array operations, and performance-oriented compilation support interactive development and high-performance numerical kernels.

This course follows the Python curriculum’s unit sequence and shared problem contexts: Avery’s profile, calculator values, grade thresholds, scores, inventory, coordinates, text sample, CSV columns, task fields, text-adventure requirements, and personal-data-manager record model. Julia idioms are taught directly rather than mechanically translated.

Version baseline: Julia 1.12. Run project scripts with julia --project=. filename.jl. Examples use the language and standard libraries unless a dependency is identified.

Unit 0: Accessible Environment and Toolchain

Overview

Install Julia, configure an accessible editor and terminal workflow, create a reproducible project environment, and verify source files from the project root. Julia is JIT-compiled; learners run source files with the Julia executable or experiment in the REPL.

Lesson 0.1: Install and Verify Julia

Reading References

  • Official Julia downloads
  • Julia installation and getting started

Learning Objectives

  • Install Julia 1.12 and verify the executable.
  • Distinguish the Julia REPL from the operating-system shell.
  • Run a saved source file and interpret basic runtime output.

Concept Explanation

Install Julia from the official distribution or juliaup. Open a new terminal and run julia --version. Start the REPL with julia, enter an expression, and exit with exit() or Ctrl+D. Run a saved file with julia main.jl. Julia compiles functions just in time while executing source code; beginners do not create a separate executable for ordinary scripts.

Worked Example

println("Julia version: ", VERSION)
println("Hello, Julia!")

Expected Behavior or Output

The first line prints the installed Julia version; the second prints Hello, Julia!.

Common Mistakes

  • Using an existing terminal session whose PATH has not refreshed after installation.
  • Entering Julia REPL expressions at the operating-system shell prompt, or shell commands at the REPL prompt.
  • Running a filename that is not in the current working directory.

Activities

  1. Record the output of julia --version and the VERSION constant.
  2. Run Hello World once in the REPL and once from a saved .jl file.
  3. Deliberately use an incorrect filename and read the resulting diagnostic.
  4. Restart the terminal and verify that Julia remains available.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate installer controls and terminal output by keyboard. Confirm that the REPL prompt, punctuation, and error messages are announced by the learner’s screen reader or braille display.

Skills Checklist

  • I can install Julia and identify its version.
  • I can distinguish the REPL from the system shell.
  • I can run a saved .jl file from a terminal.
  • I can identify a missing-file or command-path error.
  • I can read prompts and diagnostics using my access technology.

Lesson 0.2: Workspace and First Run

Reading References

  • Julia command-line options
  • Julia file and I/O documentation

Learning Objectives

  • Create and identify a project root and source file.
  • Distinguish source files, generated files, and the process working directory.
  • Explain how Julia resolves relative paths.

Concept Explanation

Create a course directory and save main.jl in its root. Use pwd() in Julia (or pwd / Get-Location in the shell) to confirm the current directory. Julia resolves relative file paths from the process working directory, not automatically from the directory containing the source file. Keep source, test, data, and generated files in clearly named locations.

Worked Example

println("Project: Julia course workspace")
println("Working directory: ", pwd())

Expected Behavior or Output

The example prints a project label and the absolute path of the directory from which Julia is running.

Common Mistakes

  • Opening a parent directory instead of the actual project root.
  • Assuming relative paths are based on the source file’s location.
  • Saving the source file with an unintended extension such as .jl.txt.

Activities

  1. Create the project directory and verify its path with the terminal.
  2. Save and run main.jl from the project root.
  3. Change to a different working directory and observe how a relative path changes.
  4. Return to the project root and rerun the program successfully.

Accessibility Practice

Use terminal history and directory commands without drag-and-drop. Confirm that the editor exposes file names, indentation, and diagnostics in a linear reading order.

Skills Checklist

  • I can identify the project root and current working directory.
  • I can create and run main.jl.
  • I can explain how Julia resolves relative paths.
  • I can organize source and data files predictably.
  • I can navigate the workspace without mouse-only actions.

Lesson 0.3: Editor and Accessibility Workflow

Reading References

  • Julia extension for Visual Studio Code
  • Shared IDE setup lesson

Learning Objectives

  • Configure VS Code, VSCodium, or Theia for Julia development.
  • Navigate source, diagnostics, terminal, and project files by keyboard.
  • Verify that the editor and terminal use the same Julia installation.

Concept Explanation

Install the Julia extension available in the chosen editor, select the same Julia executable used in the terminal, and open the project root. Verify syntax diagnostics, symbol navigation, terminal focus, and file navigation. Marketplace extensions are not automatically available in VSCodium or Theia; check the extension registry for the selected editor. An editor’s syntax coloring alone does not establish that the language server is working.

Worked Example

function greet(name::AbstractString)
    return "Hello, $(name)!"
end
println(greet("Avery"))

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints Hello, Avery!. The function accepts an abstract string argument and returns a string.

Common Mistakes

  • Selecting a different Julia installation in the editor than the one used by the terminal.
  • Treating syntax coloring as proof that language-server diagnostics and navigation work.
  • Depending on mouse-only controls or unannounced inline diagnostics.

Activities

  1. Open the course project root in the selected editor.
  2. Navigate the worked example by line, word, and character.
  3. Introduce a syntax error, locate the diagnostic, and correct it.
  4. Run the file from both the integrated terminal and the system terminal.

Accessibility Practice

Test punctuation verbosity, indentation announcements, completion popups, diagnostics, terminal focus, and editor panels with the learner’s access technology. Keep a terminal-first workflow available if an extension is inaccessible.

Skills Checklist

  • I can open the project root and identify the Julia executable.
  • I can navigate and edit Julia source by keyboard.
  • I can locate and correct a language-server diagnostic.
  • I can run a source file without relying on a mouse.
  • I can describe any editor accessibility limitation and use a workable alternative.

Lesson 0.4: Project Environments, Dependencies, and Terminal Usage

Reading References

  • Julia package manager
  • Project environments

Learning Objectives

  • Activate a project-local Julia environment.
  • Explain the roles of Project.toml and Manifest.toml.
  • Add and instantiate dependencies in the intended project.
  • Run scripts and tests with the project environment active.

Concept Explanation

Run julia --project=. from the project root. At the REPL use using Pkg; Pkg.activate("."). Add a dependency with Pkg.add("JSON3"); direct dependencies are recorded in Project.toml and the resolved dependency graph in Manifest.toml. Reproduce an environment with Pkg.instantiate(). Run scripts with julia --project=. main.jl and tests with julia --project=. test/runtests.jl. Use a project environment rather than adding course dependencies to the global environment.

Worked Example

using Pkg
Pkg.activate(".")
println("Active project: ", Base.active_project())

Expected Behavior or Output

The package manager activates the current directory as the project and prints the active project file path. When no project exists yet, Julia may create the project metadata as part of activation or package operations.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding a package before activating the intended project.
  • Omitting --project=. when running a script that imports project dependencies.
  • Deleting or ignoring the manifest when exact dependency reproducibility is required.

Activities

  1. Activate the course directory and confirm the active project path.
  2. Add JSON3 and inspect the resulting TOML project and manifest files.
  3. Start a fresh Julia process and run Pkg.instantiate().
  4. Run a dependency-using script with and without the project flag and explain the difference.

Accessibility Practice

Inspect TOML files as text and read package-manager output sequentially. Keep installation and test commands in documented terminal steps rather than relying on transient editor notifications.

Skills Checklist

  • I can activate a project-local environment.
  • I can explain the purpose of Project.toml and Manifest.toml.
  • I can add and instantiate a dependency in the correct project.
  • I can run scripts and tests from the terminal with the project active.
  • I can inspect dependency metadata using keyboard-accessible tools.

Lesson 1.1: Computer science and problem solving

Reading References

  • Julia Documentation
  • Julia Base and standard-library reference.
  • Corresponding Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem and data.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain computer science and problem solving using Julia terminology.
  • Apply the relevant syntax and standard-library facilities.
  • Test normal, boundary, and invalid cases using shared course data.

Concept Explanation

Julia is a high-level, dynamically typed, JIT-compiled language. Values have concrete types and variables are bindings. Define inputs and outputs, choose a finite algorithm, and test ordinary and boundary cases.

Lesson focus: Computer science and problem solving. The worked example is self-contained unless a standard-library import is shown.

Worked Example

println("Computer science turns a problem into a finite sequence of precise steps.")

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints a result based on the stated inputs. Predict the result before running it, then compare the observed output. File examples use temporary paths and close resources within the callback.

Common Mistakes

  • Inspect values with typeof rather than assuming a static declaration.
  • Do not confuse a variable binding with a const binding.
  • Read UndefVarError and MethodError diagnostics before changing code.

Activities

  1. Run the example and explain each expression in execution order.
  2. Change a canonical profile value and predict the output.
  3. Inspect each value with typeof and explain the result.
  4. Introduce and correct an undefined-name error.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate source by line, word, and character. Inspect operators, punctuation, mutation markers, and block-ending end keywords. Run from the terminal and read output and diagnostics sequentially. Do not rely on syntax color or mouse-only controls.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain computer science and problem solving in Julia terminology.
  • I can trace the example and predict its output.
  • I can adapt the example to canonical shared data.
  • I can identify and correct a Julia-specific error or edge case.
  • I can run and inspect the program using keyboard-accessible tools.

Unit 2: Numeric Computations

Overview

This unit covers development process, expressions, assignment, input/output, conversions, arithmetic, math library. Follow the same problem progression as Python so that the main comparison is language syntax and semantics. Use the worked examples as starting points, then complete the activities independently.

Lesson 2.1: Design and tracing

Reading References

  • Julia Documentation
  • Julia Base and standard-library reference.
  • Corresponding Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem and data.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain design and tracing using Julia terminology.
  • Apply the relevant syntax and standard-library facilities.
  • Test normal, boundary, and invalid cases using shared course data.

Concept Explanation

Julia evaluates expressions and binds names with =. Numeric text must be converted before arithmetic; use parse for trusted input and tryparse when conversion may fail. π, hypot, exponentiation with ^, and round(...; digits=...) support common calculations.

Lesson focus: Design and tracing. The worked example is self-contained unless a standard-library import is shown.

Worked Example

bill = 24.50; rate = 0.15
println("Tip: ", bill * rate, "; total: ", bill * (1 + rate))

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints a result based on the stated inputs. Predict the result before running it, then compare the observed output. File examples use temporary paths and close resources within the callback.

Common Mistakes

  • Use == for equality; = binds a value.
  • Validate uncertain text with tryparse before arithmetic.
  • Avoid rounding intermediate values before the final result.

Activities

  1. Trace each expression and record intermediate values.
  2. Calculate the canonical $24.50 bill with a 15% tip.
  3. Test a boundary and invalid input; state the intended behavior.
  4. Refactor the calculation into a function without changing its result.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate source by line, word, and character. Inspect operators, punctuation, mutation markers, and block-ending end keywords. Run from the terminal and read output and diagnostics sequentially. Do not rely on syntax color or mouse-only controls.

Skills Checklist

Concept Explanation

Julia evaluates expressions and binds names with =. Numeric text must be converted before arithmetic; use parse for trusted input and tryparse when conversion may fail. π, hypot, exponentiation with ^, and round(...; digits=...) support common calculations.

Lesson focus: Using the Math Library. The worked example is self-contained unless a standard-library import is shown.

Worked Example

radius = 3.0
println("Area: ", π * radius^2, "; circumference: ", 2π * radius, "; distance: ", hypot(3,4))

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints a result based on the stated inputs. Predict the result before running it, then compare the observed output. File examples use temporary paths and close resources within the callback.

Common Mistakes

  • Use == for equality; = binds a value.
  • Validate uncertain text with tryparse before arithmetic.
  • Avoid rounding intermediate values before the final result.

Activities

  1. Trace each expression and record intermediate values.
  2. Calculate the canonical $24.50 bill with a 15% tip.

Julia uses if/elseif/else/end, short-circuit Boolean operators, and one-based indexing. for iterates over values, enumerate supplies indices, and dotted operators broadcast. Strings are UTF-8, so character count and byte indexing differ.

Common Mistakes

Lesson 4.1: Mutable sequences

Reading References

  • Julia Documentation

Learning Objectives

  • Explain mutable sequences using Julia terminology.
  • Apply the relevant syntax and standard-library facilities.
  • Test normal, boundary, and invalid cases using shared course data.

Concept Explanation

Julia provides mutable arrays, immutable tuples and named tuples, and dictionaries for key-value data. Mutating functions conventionally end in !. Sort keys or entries when deterministic report order matters.

Lesson focus: Mutable sequences. The worked example is self-contained unless a standard-library import is shown.

Worked Example

scores = [82, 91, 76, 88]
push!(scores, 95); insert!(scores, 2, 85)
println(scores)

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints a result based on the stated inputs. Predict the result before running it, then compare the observed output. File examples use temporary paths and close resources within the callback.

Common Mistakes

  • Tuples and named tuples are immutable; arrays and dictionaries are mutable.
  • Use get or haskey for possibly absent dictionary keys.
  • A shallow copy does not duplicate nested mutable values.

Activities

  1. Represent the canonical inventory using a dictionary.
  2. Add, update, and remove an entry, checking each state.
  3. Compare tuple, named tuple, vector, and dictionary semantics.

Concept Explanation

Lesson focus: While loops. The worked example is self-contained unless a standard-library import is shown.

Worked Example

function run_commands()
    commands = ["list", "help", "quit"]
    index = 1
    while index <= length(commands)
        println(commands[index])
        commands[index] == "quit" && break
        index += 1
    end
end
run_commands()

  • Julia Base and standard-library reference.
  • Corresponding Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem and data.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain infinite-loop prevention using Julia terminology.
  • Apply the relevant syntax and standard-library facilities.
  • Test normal, boundary, and invalid cases using shared course data.

Concept Explanation

Interactive input arrives as text through readline; validate and convert it before use. A while loop repeats while its condition is true, break exits the nearest loop, and continue skips to the next iteration.

Lesson focus: Infinite-loop prevention. The worked example is self-contained unless a standard-library import is shown.

Worked Example

for attempt in 1:3
    println("Attempt $attempt")
end

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints a result based on the stated inputs. Predict the result before running it, then compare the observed output. File examples use temporary paths and close resources within the callback.

Common Mistakes

  • Convert and validate readline() input before numeric operations.
  • Every while loop needs progress or an explicit exit.
  • Place break and continue at the intended loop nesting level.

Activities

  1. Test valid, invalid, and sentinel command input.
  2. Trace loop state and condition on each iteration.
  3. Stop a search at the first matching score.
  4. Prove termination for empty and no-match inputs.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate source by line, word, and character. Inspect operators, punctuation, mutation markers, and block-ending end keywords. Run from the terminal and read output and diagnostics sequentially. Do not rely on syntax color or mouse-only controls.

  • I can explain infinite-loop prevention in Julia terminology.
  • I can trace the example and predict its output.
  • I can adapt the example to canonical shared data.
  • I can identify and correct a Julia-specific error or edge case.

Lesson 6.1: Defining functions

Reading References

  • Julia Documentation
  • Julia Base and standard-library reference.
  • Corresponding Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem and data.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain defining functions using Julia terminology.
  • Apply the relevant syntax and standard-library facilities.
  • Test normal, boundary, and invalid cases using shared course data.

Concept Explanation

Functions are first-class values. Julia supports positional and keyword arguments, optional defaults, multiple dispatch, and variadic positional arguments with .... The final expression is returned implicitly.

Lesson focus: Defining functions. The worked example is self-contained unless a standard-library import is shown.

Worked Example

tip(bill, rate=0.15) = bill * rate
println(tip(24.50))

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints a result based on the stated inputs. Predict the result before running it, then compare the observed output. File examples use temporary paths and close resources within the callback.

Common Mistakes

  • Printing a value is not the same as returning it.
  • Distinguish positional arguments from keyword arguments after the semicolon.
  • Use ... deliberately when collecting variadic arguments.

Activities

  1. Call a function and inspect its return value independently of printing.
  2. Add boundary and invalid-argument tests.
  3. Use keyword or variadic arguments where appropriate.
  4. Compose two functions without duplicating calculations.

Accessibility Practice

Unit 7: Object-Oriented Programming

Overview

Lesson 7.1: Types and object models

Reading References

  • Julia Documentation
  • Julia Base and standard-library reference.
  • Corresponding Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem and data.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain types and object models using Julia terminology.
  • Apply the relevant syntax and standard-library facilities.
  • Test normal, boundary, and invalid cases using shared course data.

Concept Explanation

Declare composite types with struct or mutable struct. Concrete types do not inherit from other concrete types; abstract types define dispatch hierarchies, and methods specialize on argument types. Composition models related data.

Lesson focus: Types and object models. The worked example is self-contained unless a standard-library import is shown.

Worked Example

struct Student
    name::String
    age::Int
end
println(Student("Avery",16))

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints a result based on the stated inputs. Predict the result before running it, then compare the observed output. File examples use temporary paths and close resources within the callback.

Common Mistakes

  • Concrete Julia structs do not inherit from other concrete structs.
  • An immutable struct cannot have its fields reassigned.
  • Use abstract supertypes and multiple dispatch for polymorphic behavior.

Activities

  1. Model Avery or an inventory item with a Julia composite type.
  2. Create multiple instances and inspect their fields.
  3. Add a validation or display method using multiple dispatch.
  4. Explain whether composition, immutability, or mutability fits the model.

Unit 8: Files and Exceptions

Overview

Follow the same problem progression as Python so that the main comparison is language syntax and semantics. Use the worked examples as starting points, then complete the activities independently.

Lesson 8.1: Reading text files

Reading References

  • Julia Documentation
  • Julia Base and standard-library reference.
  • Corresponding Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem and data.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain reading text files using Julia terminology.
  • Apply the relevant syntax and standard-library facilities.
  • Test normal, boundary, and invalid cases using shared course data.

Concept Explanation

Use open(path) do io ... end to close files even when operations fail. eachline supports line processing. Julia has TOML in its standard library but no general JSON parser; use JSON3.jl for JSON.

Lesson focus: Reading text files. The worked example is self-contained unless a standard-library import is shown.

Worked Example

mktemp() do path, io
    write(io,"Avery studies Julia.\n"); close(io)
    open(path,"r") do file
        foreach(println, eachline(file))
    end
end

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints a result based on the stated inputs. Predict the result before running it, then compare the observed output. File examples use temporary paths and close resources within the callback.

Common Mistakes

  • Relative paths are resolved from the process working directory.
  • Use open(path) do io to guarantee resource cleanup.
  • Catch expected exceptions specifically rather than hiding all failures.

Activities

  1. Create a temporary file fixture and read it line by line.
  2. Test empty, missing, and malformed files.
  3. Verify resources close after successful and exceptional paths.
  4. Document the file format and parser limitations.

Accessibility Practice
