Lesson 10.2: Text adventure: five rooms and movement

Reading References

  • Julia dictionaries
  • Julia input and output
  • Canonical shared project specification: Python Unit 10, Lesson 10.3.

Learning Objectives

  • Represent all five canonical rooms and exits with Julia dictionaries.
  • Validate movement before changing the current room.
  • Explain why treasure_room is not reachable until the key puzzle is implemented.

Concept Explanation

The shared graph has five rooms: start_room, tunnel, clearing, locked_door_room, and treasure_room. Each room stores a description and an exits dictionary. The player starts in start_room. Part 1 leaves the north exit from locked_door_room unavailable. The get function returns nothing for an absent direction, so an invalid command does not change state.

Worked Example

function main()
rooms = Dict(
    "start_room" => (description = "A dimly lit cave. A narrow passage leads north.",
                     exits = Dict("north" => "tunnel")),
    "tunnel" => (description = "A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.",
                 exits = Dict("south" => "start_room", "east" => "clearing")),
    "clearing" => (description = "A quiet clearing. An antechamber lies to the north.",
                   exits = Dict("west" => "tunnel", "north" => "locked_door_room")),
    "locked_door_room" => (description = "A chamber with a heavy door to the north.",
                           exits = Dict("south" => "clearing")),
    "treasure_room" => (description = "You found the treasure. You win!",
                        exits = Dict())
)

current_room = "start_room"
while true
    room = rooms[current_room]
    println("---")
    println(room.description)
    println("What do you want to do?")
    command = eof(stdin) ? "quit" : lowercase(strip(readline()))
    if command == "quit"
        println("Exiting game. Goodbye!")
        break
    end
    destination = get(room.exits, command, nothing)
    if destination === nothing
        println("You cannot go that way. Enter a listed direction or quit.")
    else
        current_room = destination
    end
end
end

main()

Expected Behavior or Output

Enter north, east, north, north, quit. The player reaches tunnel, clearing, and locked_door_room. The second north is rejected and the current room does not change. The treasure room exists but has no incoming exit in Part 1.

Common Mistakes

  • Indexing a dictionary with an unvalidated direction.

  • Updating current_room before checking whether get returned nothing.

  • Defining a destination that is not one of the five room identifiers.

  • Adding the treasure exit before implementing the key puzzle.

  • In Julia, place the interactive loop inside a function such as main() so assignments update the function-local current_room rather than triggering top-level soft-scope ambiguity.

Activities

  1. Trace north, east, north, north and record the current room.
  2. Try west from start_room and verify that the room does not change.
  3. Check every exit destination against the room dictionary.
  4. Explain why treasure_room cannot yet be reached.

Accessibility Practice

Announce the room description and prompt in a consistent order. The invalid-movement response explains what happened and how to continue. Run from the terminal and inspect output sequentially with the learner’s access technology.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model all five canonical rooms.
  • I can represent exits with dictionaries.
  • I can reject invalid movement without changing state.
  • I can explain why the treasure room is not yet reachable.

Lesson 10.3: Text adventure: shiny key and locked door

Reading References

  • Julia arrays
  • Julia dictionaries
  • Canonical shared project specification: Python Unit 10, Lesson 10.3.

Learning Objectives

  • Place the shiny key in start_room and transfer it to inventory exactly once.
  • Require key use in locked_door_room.
  • Unlock the north exit only after the puzzle succeeds.
  • End the game when the player reaches treasure_room.

Concept Explanation

Keep the same five-room graph. Each room has a mutable items vector. Taking the shiny key removes it from start_room and adds it to inventory. Using the key succeeds only in locked_door_room when inventory contains it. The north exit remains blocked until the key is used.

Worked Example

function main()
rooms = Dict(
    "start_room" => (description = "A dimly lit cave.",
                     exits = Dict("north" => "tunnel"), items = ["shiny key"]),
    "tunnel" => (description = "A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.",
                 exits = Dict("south" => "start_room", "east" => "clearing"), items = String[]),
    "clearing" => (description = "A quiet clearing. Antechamber lies to the north.",
                   exits = Dict("west" => "tunnel", "north" => "locked_door_room"), items = String[]),
    "locked_door_room" => (description = "A chamber with a heavy door to the north.",
                           exits = Dict("south" => "clearing", "north" => "treasure_room"), items = String[]),
    "treasure_room" => (description = "You found the treasure. You win!",
                        exits = Dict(), items = String[])
)

current_room = "start_room"
inventory = String[]
door_locked = true

while true
    room = rooms[current_room]
    println()
    println(room.description)
    current_room == "treasure_room" && break
    !isempty(room.items) && println("You see: ", join(room.items, ", "))
    println("Your inventory: ", isempty(inventory) ? "empty" : join(inventory, ", "))
    println("What do you want to do?")
    command = eof(stdin) ? "quit" : lowercase(strip(readline()))

    if command == "quit"
        println("You quit the adventure.")
        break
    elseif command == "take shiny key"
        index = findfirst(==("shiny key"), room.items)
        if index === nothing
            println("There is no shiny key here to take.")
        else
            deleteat!(room.items, index)
            push!(inventory, "shiny key")
            println("You picked up the shiny key.")
        end
    elseif command == "use shiny key"
        if current_room != "locked_door_room"
            println("You must be at the locked door to use the key.")
        elseif !("shiny key" in inventory)
            println("You do not have the shiny key.")
        else
            door_locked = false
            println("You unlocked the door!")
        end
    elseif current_room == "locked_door_room" && command == "north" && door_locked
        println("The door is locked! You need to use the shiny key here.")
    elseif haskey(room.exits, command)
        current_room = room.exits[command]
    else
        println("Invalid command. Enter north, south, east, west, take shiny key, use shiny key, or quit.")
    end
end
end

main()

Expected Behavior or Output

Enter north, east, north, north, south, west, south, take shiny key, north, east, north, use shiny key, north. The first north from locked_door_room is rejected. Taking the key removes it from the room and adds it to inventory. Using it outside locked_door_room is rejected. Using it there unlocks the door; the final north reaches treasure_room and prints the win description.

Common Mistakes

  • Deleting the key from the room without adding it to inventory.

  • Unlocking the door outside locked_door_room.

  • Unlocking the door without checking inventory.

  • Allowing north movement before door_locked becomes false.

  • Mutating a copied room collection instead of the stored mutable vector.

  • In Julia, place the interactive loop inside a function such as main() so assignments update the function-local current_room rather than triggering top-level soft-scope ambiguity.

Activities

  1. Run the complete puzzle sequence and record room, items, inventory, and door state.
  2. Attempt to take the key twice; the second attempt must be rejected.
  3. Try to use the key outside locked_door_room.
  4. Try north before and after unlocking.
  5. Add a help command listing every supported command.

Accessibility Practice

Announce the room, visible items, inventory, and prompt as separate text lines. Error messages explain the failed action. Test the complete interaction with keyboard-only input and sequential screen-reader output.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model the five canonical rooms.
  • I can transfer the key from a room to inventory.
  • I can prevent duplicate pickup.
  • I can require key use in locked_door_room.
  • I can block and unlock the north exit.
  • I can end the game in treasure_room.

Navigate source by line, word, and character. Inspect operators, punctuation, mutation markers, and block-ending end keywords. Run from the terminal and read output and diagnostics sequentially. Do not rely on syntax color or mouse-only controls.

Julia-specific package and data-format notes

  • The standard library includes Test, Random, and TOML.
  • Julia does not include a general JSON parser in its standard library. Use JSON3.jl for JSON serialization and parsing, and record it in the active Project.toml.
  • Use CSV.jl for quoted delimiters, escaped quotes, or embedded newlines. The introductory split approach is limited to simple sample data.
  • Use DataFrames.jl only when tabular analysis justifies the dependency; begin with arrays, tuples, named tuples, and dictionaries.
  • Standard Julia arrays are one-based. Use eachindex or enumerate when iteration needs indices.

AI Policy

AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, or generate course code or assessment solutions.

Introduction to Kotlin

Before you start: complete Unit P: Computing Foundations Primer. It explains the language-neutral vocabulary and concepts used in every language track, using non-visual examples.

Standardized beginner curriculum

This course is a Kotlin/JVM parallel track aligned to the shared 12-unit, 57-lesson sequence. It assumes no prior Java experience. Kotlin is statically typed, supports nullable and non-nullable types, and interoperates with Java libraries on the JVM.

Toolchain

  • Use a supported JDK; the course Java pathway baseline is JDK 25 LTS.
  • Use Kotlin compiler and Gradle plugin 1.9.24 (the version used by the example-validation workflow) for the documented course baseline; check the Kotlin release process before changing versions.
  • Verify the compiler with kotlinc -version and the runtime with java -version.
  • For a single file: kotlinc Hello.kt -include-runtime -d hello.jar, then java -jar hello.jar.
  • For multi-file work, use the Gradle wrapper and Kotlin/JVM plugin. Commit the wrapper so the build version is reproducible.

Course files

  • Unit 0: accessible development environment
  • Unit 1: foundations of computing
  • Unit 2: numeric computations
  • Unit 3: control flow, decisions, and loops
  • Unit 4: data structures, lists, and dictionaries
  • Unit 5: user input and while loops
  • Unit 6: functions
  • Unit 7: classes and object-oriented programming
  • Unit 8: files and exceptions
  • Unit 9: testing and data analysis
  • Unit 10: project-based text applications
  • Unit 11: accessible personal data manager capstone
  • Complete standalone Kotlin reference lessons
  • 57-topic index
  • Teacher guide
  • Expected output fixtures for all 57 examples
  • Standardization audit

Kotlin semantics emphasized

Teach val versus var, static typing and inference, explicit numeric conversions, nullable types, safe calls (?.), Elvis expressions (?:), and the risk of not-null assertions (!!). Kotlin has no general tuple syntax; use named data classes, Pair, or Triple as appropriate. Distinguish read-only collection interfaces from mutable collections. Kotlin classes are final by default; inheritance requires deliberate open declarations. Use use for resource-safe operations and maintained libraries for JSON and CSV.

Accessibility baseline

Use keyboard-first editor and terminal workflows. Verify the selected Kotlin language server, diagnostics, Gradle tasks, and screen-reader announcements with the learner’s actual access technology. Explain punctuation and indentation explicitly. Prefer named intermediate values and short functions over deeply nested expressions. The default capstone interface is text-first; a GUI is not required to demonstrate the shared data operations.

Assessment and AI-use policy

Assess conceptual understanding, independent tracing, testing, explanation, and accessible tool use. AI may support conceptual understanding and reinforcement only; it must not generate, complete, repair, refactor, or write course code or assessment solutions for students or instructors.

The lesson files provide the aligned instructional structure. The audit records what has and has not been verified; structural completeness is not a claim that every example or full application has passed runtime tests.

GUI, visualization, and workbench accessibility

See the shared GUI, visualization, and workbench accessibility reference for screen-reader support by toolkit, platform-specific activation settings, recommended alternatives, and interfaces that must not be required without an equivalent accessible route.

AI Policy

AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, or generate course code or assessment solutions.

Verification status

Every lesson has one Kotlin example that uses the shared datasets. All 57 examples compile together with kotlinc 1.9.24, run independently with empty standard input, and match the exact output in examples_expected.json (scripts/check_kotlin_examples.py; checked on JDK 21). The “Expected Behavior or Output” blocks in the lessons are captured from runs of the same examples, with the standard input shown where a program reads input. This has not been tested with screen readers or braille displays.

Recommended introductory books

  • Griffiths, Dawn, and David Griffiths. Head First Kotlin: A Brain-Friendly Guide. O’Reilly Media, 2019. A hands-on introduction to Kotlin syntax and programming concepts. Publisher catalog.
  • Eckel, Bruce, and Svetlana Isakova. Atomic Kotlin. Mindview, 2021. Presents Kotlin concepts in small, focused lessons with exercises; intended for both beginning and experienced programmers. Author-maintained learning resources.
  • Aigner, Sebastian, Roman Elizarov, Svetlana Isakova, and Dmitry Jemerov. Kotlin in Action, 2nd edition. Manning, 2024. A comprehensive treatment aimed primarily at readers familiar with Java or another object-oriented language. Kotlin documentation’s book recommendations.

Suggested use: Head First Kotlin or Atomic Kotlin is the more suitable first companion. Treat Kotlin in Action as a follow-on reference, not a prerequisite. Check current Kotlin documentation when book examples differ from the course baseline.

Unit 0: Accessible Development Environment

Overview

Set up the language toolchain, a project folder, and a keyboard-first editor workflow that can be read with speech or braille, and learn how projects and dependencies are organized.

Lesson 0.1: Installing the Kotlin Compiler and JDK

Reading References

  • Kotlin command-line compiler
  • Get started with Kotlin
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 0.1: Installing Python and uv

Learning Objectives

  • Install a JDK and the Kotlin command-line compiler from trusted sources.
  • Verify both tools from the terminal.
  • Compile and run a first program.

Concept Explanation

Kotlin/JVM programs are compiled to Java bytecode and run on a Java Virtual Machine, so two tools are needed: a JDK (Java Development Kit) and the Kotlin compiler, kotlinc. This course’s documented baseline is Kotlin 1.9.24 (the example checks in this repository use it) running on a supported JDK; check the Kotlin release page before changing versions.

Choose one installation route and write down which one you used: a JDK from your operating system’s package manager or a vendor build, and the compiler from the official Kotlin release archive, from a version manager such as SDKMAN, or from your package manager. Package managers often install the newest Kotlin rather than 1.9.24, so always verify the version.

Verify both tools from the terminal:

java -version
kotlinc -version

The second command prints a line of the form info: kotlinc-jvm 1.9.24 (JRE 21...). The numbers depend on what you installed; the point is that both commands run and report a version.

To compile and run the example below, save it as hello.kt, then:

kotlinc hello.kt -include-runtime -d hello.jar
java -jar hello.jar

-include-runtime packs the Kotlin library into the jar so that java -jar can run it, and -d names the output. The first compile of a session can take several seconds.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    println("Kotlin toolchain ready.")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Kotlin toolchain ready.

Common Mistakes

  1. Installing a JDK but not the Kotlin compiler (or the reverse) and concluding that nothing works.
  2. Assuming the newest Kotlin is the course version. Check kotlinc -version.
  3. Running kotlinc without -include-runtime and then being unable to start the jar with java -jar.

Activities

  1. Install both tools and record the exact output of the two version commands.
  2. Compile and run the example from the keyboard and note how long the first compile takes.
  3. Rename the file hello.kt to hello.txt, try to compile it, and write down the error.
  4. Explain in two sentences why Kotlin needs a JDK.

Accessibility Practice

Run each command from the keyboard only and read the output line by line with your screen reader. Confirm that the version numbers are announced clearly. Compiler warnings appear before the result, so jump to the last line of output to find whether the compile succeeded.

Skills Checklist

  • I can install a JDK and the Kotlin compiler.
  • I can verify both versions.
  • I can compile and run a first program.
  • I know what -include-runtime does.
  • I can say which route I used.

Lesson 0.2: Workspace and First Run

Reading References

  • Kotlin command-line compiler
  • Basic syntax
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 0.2: Configuring Your Screen Reader for VS Code or Theia IDE

Learning Objectives

  • Create a project folder with a first source file.
  • Compile and run it from the terminal.
  • Read a compiler error and find the file, line, and column.

Concept Explanation

A project folder keeps one program’s files together. Create a folder named kotlin-course, save a file named main.kt inside it, and use a terminal opened in that folder. The folder you are working in is the working directory; commands look for relative file names there.

Every Kotlin program starts at a function named main. A source file may contain fun main() with no parameters, or fun main(args: Array<String>) to receive command-line arguments. Statements run in order, and Kotlin does not require semicolons at the ends of lines.

Compile and run from the working directory:

kotlinc main.kt -include-runtime -d main.jar
java -jar main.jar

If the file contains a mistake, kotlinc prints messages of the form main.kt:3:5: error: .... Read each as file name, line, column, then the description. Always go to that line first, and fix the first error before the others, because later errors are often caused by it.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    println("Hello, Avery!")
    println("Welcome to Kotlin programming!")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Hello, Avery!
Welcome to Kotlin programming!

Common Mistakes

  1. Running the commands from a different folder, so the compiler cannot find main.kt.
  2. Fixing the last error message first. Start with the first one.
  3. Saving the file with a different extension or name than the one in the command.

Activities

  1. Create the folder and file from the keyboard and run the program. Record the working directory.
  2. Delete the closing quotation mark on line 2, compile, and write down the file, line, column, and description in the message. Then restore it.
  3. Add a third println with your own name and predict the output before running.
  4. Explain in your own words what the working directory is.

Accessibility Practice

Create the folder and file with terminal commands or your editor’s keyboard commands. When the compiler reports an error, use your screen reader’s line-by-line review to read the file name, line, and column first, then jump to that line in the editor.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create a project folder and source file.
  • I can compile and run from the terminal.
  • I can read the file, line, and column of an error.
  • I know that Kotlin does not need semicolons.
  • I know what the working directory is.

Lesson 0.3: Editor Extensions and Reading Kotlin Aloud

Reading References

  • Null safety
  • Basic syntax
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 0.3: Setting Up Your VS Code or Theia IDE Workspace

Learning Objectives

  • Configure an editor so Kotlin source is readable by speech or braille.
  • Choose a punctuation level that announces the symbols that carry meaning in Kotlin.
  • Read nullable types, safe calls, and the Elvis operator aloud.

Concept Explanation

Complete the shared IDE setup lesson first. Then adapt the editor for Kotlin. A Kotlin language extension is optional; the course works with a plain editor and the terminal. If you install one, take it only from a source you trust and read the permissions it requests.

Kotlin code uses several symbols that a screen reader may skip at low punctuation settings. Learn to say them: ? after a type means nullable, ?. is a safe call, ?: is the Elvis operator that supplies a default, !! is a not-null assertion that crashes if the value is null, -> separates a condition from its result in when, { } hold blocks, and $name or ${expression} insert a value into a string.

Unlike Python, Kotlin does not use indentation to decide structure. Braces do, and indentation is for people; count the closing braces when you read a nested block.

Read the example aloud: “val name colon String question mark equals null. println open parenthesis name question-dot length question-colon minus one close parenthesis.” Then say what it prints.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    val name: String? = null
    println(name?.length ?: -1)
    val title: String? = "Kotlin"
    println(title?.length ?: -1)
    println("name is $name and title has ${title?.length} characters")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

-1
6
name is null and title has 6 characters

Common Mistakes

  1. Setting punctuation so low that ?, ?., and ?: are never spoken, then misreading nullable code.
  2. Relying on indentation alone to see where a block ends. Count the closing braces.
  3. Installing several overlapping extensions and getting duplicate diagnostics.

Activities

  1. Test your editor with the example and record the punctuation level at which every symbol is announced.
  2. Navigate the file by line, word, and character and note the commands you used.
  3. Remove a closing brace, save, and find how your editor reports it. Then restore it.
  4. Write a half-page note of your edit, compile, and run steps using only the keyboard.

Accessibility Practice

This whole lesson is accessibility practice. Verify that you can open the file, move to a given line, read a line character by character, compile in the terminal, and read the output. Record the operating system, editor, and access technology you actually tested; do not describe the setup as verified for other combinations.

Skills Checklist

  • I can configure my editor for keyboard-only use.
  • I can hear every symbol in a nullable expression.
  • I can read ?. and ?: aloud.
  • I know Kotlin structure comes from braces.
  • I can compile and read the output from the keyboard.

Lesson 0.4: Kotlin Toolchain, Terminal, and Command-Line Arguments

Reading References

  • Kotlin command-line compiler
  • Basic syntax
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 0.4: Python Environments, Terminal Usage, and Accessibility Tools

Learning Objectives

  • Run a program with command-line arguments.
  • Describe the project root and where compiled files go.
  • Explain when Gradle is needed.

Concept Explanation

A command-line argument is an extra word typed after the program name. A main function declared as fun main(args: Array<String>) receives them in args. This is the simplest way to pass input without a prompt, and it is easy to test.

Keep each project in its own folder and run commands from the project root, the folder that holds the sources. For a single file the compile-and-run commands from Lesson 0.2 are enough. For several files, or when you need a library, use Gradle with the Kotlin/JVM plugin and commit the Gradle wrapper so every machine builds with the same version. Do not add Gradle to a one-file exercise.

kotlinc accepts several source files in one command and one -d output jar. The program in this lesson can be run with:

kotlinc args.kt -include-runtime -d args.jar
java -jar args.jar red blue

Worked Example

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    println("Argument count: ${args.size}")
    for ((index, arg) in args.withIndex()) {
        println("Argument ${index + 1}: $arg")
    }
    if (args.isEmpty()) {
        println("No arguments were given.")
    }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Run with the command-line arguments red blue.

The program prints:

Argument count: 2
Argument 1: red
Argument 2: blue

Common Mistakes

  1. Forgetting that args is empty when no arguments are typed, then reading args[0] and crashing.
  2. Counting arguments from 1. The first argument is at index 0.
  3. Using Gradle for a single-file exercise, which adds files and steps that are not needed.

Activities

  1. Run the program with red blue and then with no arguments. Compare the output.
  2. Pass three words and a number and print the number plus one.
  3. Change the program to print the arguments in reverse order.
  4. Explain when a project needs Gradle and when it does not.

Accessibility Practice

Arguments let you test a program without answering prompts, so every run produces plain text that is read in order. Read the output of the two runs aloud and compare them line by line.

Skills Checklist

  • I can run a program with arguments.
  • I know args starts at index 0.
  • I can say where the project root is.
  • I know when Gradle is needed.
  • I can compile several files in one command.

Unit 1: Foundations of Computing

Overview

Connect problem solving and algorithms to a first program, then learn variables, values, and types using the shared student profile.

Lesson 1.1: Welcome to Computer Science

Reading References

  • Basic syntax
  • Control flow
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 1.1: Welcome to Computer Science

Learning Objectives

  • Explain hardware, software, and algorithm in your own words.
  • Turn a written algorithm into a short Kotlin program.
  • Predict a program’s output by hand before running it.

Concept Explanation

Computers follow instructions exactly. Hardware is the machine, software is the set of instructions it follows, and an algorithm is an ordered, finite list of clear steps that solves a problem. Unit P of this repository covers these ideas in detail.

A reliable way to solve a problem is to understand it, break it into steps, write the steps in plain language, translate them into code, and test the result.

The plan here is: set a total to zero; for each score, add it to the total; divide the total by the number of scores; report both. In Kotlin, val makes a read-only name and var makes a name that can be reassigned, for (score in scores) visits a list in order, and scores.size is the number of items.

The shared scores are 82, 91, 76, and 88. Their total is 337 and their average is 84.25. A hand trace should reach the same numbers: 82, 173, 249, then 337.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    val scores = listOf(82, 91, 76, 88)
    var total = 0
    for (score in scores) {
        total += score
    }
    val average = total.toDouble() / scores.size
    println("Total: $total")
    println("Average: $average")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Total: 337
Average: 84.25

Common Mistakes

  1. Writing code before writing the steps, then forgetting to divide by the number of scores.
  2. Dividing two integers and expecting a decimal. 337 / 4 is 84; convert one side with toDouble().
  3. Declaring total with val and then trying to add to it, which is a compile error.

Activities

  1. Trace the loop by hand and write the running total after each score.
  2. Change the list to 90 and 80 and predict the total and average before running.
  3. Add a loop that finds the highest score and prints it.
  4. Explain the difference between the algorithm and the program in two sentences.

Accessibility Practice

Write the hand trace as numbered sentences, one for each loop pass, and read it back with your screen reader. Compare it with the two printed lines in order.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define hardware, software, and algorithm.
  • I can describe an algorithm as ordered steps.
  • I can trace a loop by hand.
  • I can explain val versus var.
  • I can run the program and compare it with my trace.

Lesson 1.2: Your First Kotlin Program

Reading References

  • Basic syntax
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 1.2: Your First Python Program - Hello World

Learning Objectives

  • Write and run a program that prints text.
  • Use comments and string templates.
  • Explain that statements run in order.

Concept Explanation

A Kotlin program is a list of statements that run in order inside main. println writes its argument and ends the line; print writes without ending the line. Text in double quotation marks is a string.

A string template inserts a value into text: $name inserts a variable, and ${expression} inserts the result of any expression. A line comment starts with // and a block comment is written between /* and */. Triple quotation marks, """...""", make a raw string that can span lines.

Because Kotlin is a compiled language, a mistake such as a missing quotation mark is reported at compile time and no program is produced.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    // This program greets the shared student.
    val name = "Avery"
    println("Hello, $name!")
    print("No new line here, ")
    println("then one here.")
    println("Name has ${name.length} letters.")
    println("""Two lines
in one raw string.""")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Hello, Avery!
No new line here, then one here.
Name has 5 letters.
Two lines
in one raw string.

Common Mistakes

  1. Using a curly quotation mark pasted from a document instead of a straight one, which is a syntax error.
  2. Writing $name where a longer expression needs ${...}, such as $name.length, which inserts the name and then the text .length.
  3. Forgetting that print does not end the line.

Activities

  1. Run the program and describe how the second and third lines differ from the others.
  2. Change the greeting to use your own name and predict the output.
  3. Print three lines: your name, the course name, and today’s task.
  4. Add a comment above every line and read the file aloud with the comments.

Accessibility Practice

Run from the terminal and read the output line by line. Check that your screen reader announces the dollar sign and the braces in a string template, since they decide what the program prints.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write and run a program that prints text.
  • I can use string templates.
  • I can write comments.
  • I know how print and println differ.
  • I can read a first compile error.

Lesson 1.3: Variables and Simple Data Types

Reading References

  • Basic types
  • Basic syntax
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 1.3: Variables and Simple Data Types

Learning Objectives

  • Declare read-only and changeable variables.
  • Name Kotlin’s basic types and check a value’s type.
  • Explain type inference.

Concept Explanation

Kotlin is statically typed: every value has a type that the compiler knows. You may write the type, as in val age: Int = 16, or let the compiler infer it from the value, as in val age = 16. The type is still fixed after inference; Kotlin is not dynamically typed.

val declares a read-only name that cannot be reassigned. var declares a name that can. Prefer val, and use var only when a value must change.

The basic types are Int and Long (whole numbers), Double and Float (decimals), Boolean, Char, and String. A whole-number literal such as 16 is an Int, and a literal with a decimal point such as 1.72 is a Double. value::class.simpleName reports a value’s type name.

The shared student profile is name Avery, age 16, height 1.72 meters, and favorite subject Computer Science. The shared Notebook item has quantity 3 and unit price 2.50, so three notebooks cost 7.5.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    val name = "Avery"
    val age = 16
    val height = 1.72
    val favoriteSubject = "Computer Science"
    println("$name, $age, $height, $favoriteSubject")
    println("${name::class.simpleName} ${age::class.simpleName} ${height::class.simpleName}")

    val notebookPrice = 2.50
    val notebookQuantity = 3
    println("Notebook total: ${notebookPrice * notebookQuantity}")

    var visits = 1
    visits += 1
    println("Visits: $visits")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Avery, 16, 1.72, Computer Science
String Int Double
Notebook total: 7.5
Visits: 2

Common Mistakes

  1. Declaring with val and then reassigning, which is a compile error.
  2. Assuming inference makes Kotlin dynamic. val x = 16 can never hold text later.
  3. Mixing Int and Double without conversion in a declaration that names the type, such as val d: Double = 16, which does not compile.

Activities

  1. Run the example and write each type name in the order printed.
  2. Change age to 16L and predict the type name.
  3. Add a Boolean likesCs and print its type.
  4. Explain, without code, when to choose var over val.

Accessibility Practice

Say names with their capital letters aloud (favoriteSubject), and print each value inside a labelled sentence so that the screen reader announces the name and value together.

Skills Checklist

  • I can declare val and var.
  • I can name Kotlin’s basic types.
  • I can explain type inference.
  • I can check a value’s type name.
  • I can explain why val is preferred.

Unit 2: Numeric Computations

Overview

Plan and build the tip calculator, learn the language’s numeric operators and conversions, read typed input safely, and use the math library.

Lesson 2.1: The Software Development Process

Reading References

  • Basic syntax
  • Basic types
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 2.1: The Software Development Process

Learning Objectives

  • Describe the design, implement, and test cycle.
  • Write pseudocode for the tip calculator and implement it.
  • Explain why money is formatted to two decimals.

Concept Explanation

Software is built in a cycle: understand the problem, design a solution, implement it, test it, and refine it. Design comes first. For the tip calculator the plan is: get the bill, calculate 15 percent of it as the tip, add the tip to the bill for the total, and print the tip and the total.

With the shared values (bill 24.50, tip rate 0.15) the exact tip is 3.675 and the total is 28.175. "%.2f".format(x) formats a number with two decimals. On the JVM, formatting rounds half up using the decimal digits of the Double, so Kotlin and Java display the tip as 3.68; Python, C, Go, and several other languages display 3.67 for the same stored number. Both are correct displays of the same value.

Formatting uses the default locale. In a locale that writes decimals with a comma, "%.2f".format(x) prints a comma. Pass java.util.Locale.US as the first argument for fixed output.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    val bill = 24.5
    val tipRate = 0.15

    val tip = bill * tipRate
    val total = bill + tip

    println("Bill: " + "%.2f".format(bill))
    println("Tip: " + "%.2f".format(tip))
    println("Total: " + "%.2f".format(total))
    println("Tip with an explicit locale: " + "%.2f".format(java.util.Locale.US, tip))
    println("Unformatted tip: $tip")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Bill: 24.50
Tip: 3.68
Total: 28.18
Tip with an explicit locale: 3.68
Unformatted tip: 3.675

Common Mistakes

  1. Writing the rate as 15 instead of 0.15, which makes the tip fifteen times too large.
  2. Rounding the tip first and then adding it, which can change the total by a cent.
  3. Assuming every language prints the same two-decimal text for 3.675.

Activities

  1. Trace the plan with the shared values and write each result as a sentence.
  2. Change the rate to 0.20 and predict the tip and total (4.90 and 29.40).
  3. Add a test for a bill of 100 with a written expected result before running.
  4. Explain in two sentences why the program prints 3.68 even though the stored value is just below 3.675.

Accessibility Practice

Print each result on its own labelled line (Tip: 3.68) so a screen reader announces one clear unit per line. Never use alignment or spacing to carry meaning.

Skills Checklist

  • I can name the stages of the development cycle.
  • I can write pseudocode for a calculation.
  • I can format a number with format.
  • I know formatting depends on the locale.
  • I can explain why displays can differ between languages.

Lesson 2.2: Expressions and Assignment

Reading References

  • Basic types
  • Basic syntax
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 2.2: Elements of Programs - Expressions and Assignment

Learning Objectives

  • Evaluate expressions using operator precedence.
  • Use integer division, remainder, and compound assignment.
  • Join strings with templates and +.

Concept Explanation

An expression produces a value. The arithmetic operators are +, -, *, /, and % (remainder). Multiplication, division, and remainder happen before addition and subtraction, and parentheses change the order, so 8 + 4 * 2 is 16 and (8 + 4) * 2 is 24.

Division depends on the types. Two Int values give an Int, so 7 / 2 is 3. If either side is a Double, the result is a Double, so 7 / 2.0 is 3.5. The remainder 7 % 2 is 1.

Assignment stores a value: score = score + 9, shortened to score += 9. Only a var can be assigned again. Comparison uses ==, !=, <, <=, >, and >=. In Kotlin == compares values, not identities.

Kotlin does not convert numbers automatically: you cannot add an Int variable to a Long variable without a conversion. This catches mistakes at compile time.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    println(8 + 4 * 2)
    println((8 + 4) * 2)

    var score = 82
    score += 9
    println("New score: $score")

    println(7 / 2)
    println(7 / 2.0)
    println(7 % 2)
    println(-7 / 2)
    println(5 != 6)
    println("Avery" + " " + "Student")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

16
24
New score: 91
3
3.5
1
-3
true
Avery Student

Common Mistakes

  1. Expecting 7 / 2 to be 3.5. With two Int values the fraction is dropped.
  2. Reassigning a val, which is a compile error.
  3. Writing score =+ 9 and storing positive nine instead of adding.

Activities

  1. Predict the ten output lines before running, then compare.
  2. Write an expression for the area and the perimeter of a 12 by 8 rectangle.
  3. Explain why -7 / 2 prints -3 rather than -4.
  4. Join your name, a space, and your age into one string in two different ways.

Accessibility Practice

Say operators by name when reading code aloud (‘slash’, ‘percent’, ‘plus equals’). Raise your punctuation level while checking expressions so that parentheses and operators are all announced.

Skills Checklist

  • I can apply operator precedence.
  • I can predict Int and Double division.
  • I can use += and %.
  • I know only var can be reassigned.
  • I can join strings.

Lesson 2.3: Console Input and Output

Reading References

  • Basic syntax
  • Null safety
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 2.3: Input and Output Revisited

Learning Objectives

  • Read a line with readlnOrNull.
  • Convert text with toIntOrNull.
  • Handle missing and invalid input.

Concept Explanation

readlnOrNull() reads one line from standard input and returns a String?: the text without the line ending, or null at the end of input. readln() is similar but throws an exception at the end of input, so this course prefers readlnOrNull().

Typed text is always a string. toIntOrNull() returns an Int?: the number, or null when the text is not a valid whole number. The safe-call operator ?. stops a chain at null, so readlnOrNull()?.trim()?.toIntOrNull() reads, trims, and converts, and gives null if any step has nothing to work on.

After a null check on a val, Kotlin treats the value as non-null: this is a smart cast. The example reads a name and two numbers and prints a greeting and their sum. With Avery, 12, and 8 the sum is 20. Prompts are printed on their own lines so the screen reader reads each cleanly.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    println("Enter your name:")
    val name = readlnOrNull()
    println("Enter the first number:")
    val first = readlnOrNull()?.trim()?.toIntOrNull()
    println("Enter the second number:")
    val second = readlnOrNull()?.trim()?.toIntOrNull()

    if (name != null && first != null && second != null) {
        println("Hello, $name!")
        println("The sum of $first and $second is ${first + second}.")
    } else {
        println("Input was missing or not a number.")
    }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

With the following lines typed as standard input (piped input is not echoed, so it does not appear in the output):

Avery
12
8

the program prints:

Enter your name:
Enter the first number:
Enter the second number:
Hello, Avery!
The sum of 12 and 8 is 20.

With no standard input at all, the program ends cleanly and prints:

Enter your name:
Enter the first number:
Enter the second number:
Input was missing or not a number.

Common Mistakes

  1. Using readln() and crashing at the end of input.
  2. Doing arithmetic on a String read from input without converting it.
  3. Using !! to silence the null check, which crashes on exactly the input the program should handle.

Activities

  1. Run with Avery, 12, and 8 and confirm the output.
  2. Type twelve for the first number and explain the result.
  3. Run with no input and describe the output.
  4. Change the program to subtract the second number from the first.

Accessibility Practice

Every prompt is a complete sentence on its own line and every result is a complete sentence. When you test, listen for whether the prompt is read in full before you begin to type.

Skills Checklist

  • I can read a line with readlnOrNull.
  • I can convert text with toIntOrNull.
  • I understand String? and ?..
  • I can write clear prompts.
  • I handle missing and invalid input.

Lesson 2.4: Numbers and Type Conversions

Reading References

  • Basic types
  • Basic syntax
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 2.4: Computing with Numbers and Type Conversions

Learning Objectives

  • Convert explicitly between numbers and text.
  • Explain truncation and rounding.
  • Explain why decimal arithmetic is approximate.

Concept Explanation

Kotlin never converts numeric types for you. Use the conversion functions: toInt(), toLong(), toDouble(), and toString(). "16".toInt() converts text and throws an exception if the text is invalid, so for typed input prefer toIntOrNull() and toDoubleOrNull(), which return null instead.

toInt() on a Double truncates toward zero: 3.9.toInt() is 3. To round, use kotlin.math.roundToInt(), which rounds halves up: 3.5.roundToInt() is 4.

A Double is a binary approximation. 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3; this is correct behavior. Compare decimals with a tolerance and format them for display.

The shared student has age 16 and height 1.72 meters; the example converts text to those values and computes the height in centimeters.

Worked Example

import kotlin.math.roundToInt

fun main() {
    val age = "16".toInt()
    val height = "1.72".toDouble()
    println("$age ${age::class.simpleName}")
    println("$height ${height::class.simpleName}")

    println("abc".toIntOrNull())
    println("".toIntOrNull())
    println(42.toString() + " is now text")

    println(3.9.toInt())
    println(3.5.roundToInt())
    println(0.1 + 0.2)

    val heightCm = height * 100
    println("Height in centimeters: " + "%.1f".format(heightCm))
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

16 Int
1.72 Double
null
null
42 is now text
3
4
0.30000000000000004
Height in centimeters: 172.0

Common Mistakes

  1. Using toInt() on untrusted text and crashing with NumberFormatException.
  2. Expecting toInt() to round. It truncates.
  3. Comparing decimals with == after arithmetic.

Activities

  1. Predict each of the ten lines before running, then compare.
  2. Check what " 16 ".toIntOrNull() and "1e3".toDoubleOrNull() return and explain each.
  3. Write code that reads a line and prints a clear message when the conversion fails.
  4. Explain the difference between 3.5.toInt() and 3.5.roundToInt().

Accessibility Practice

Format floating-point results so that the screen reader reads short numbers. Read the type names aloud and note that Int and Double are announced as words, not symbols.

Skills Checklist

  • I can convert between text and numbers.
  • I know toInt() truncates.
  • I can use roundToInt().
  • I can use toIntOrNull().
  • I can explain why decimals are approximate.

Lesson 2.5: Using the Math Library

Reading References

  • Basic types
  • Kotlin standard library: kotlin.math
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 2.5: Using the Math Library

Learning Objectives

  • Use PI, sqrt, pow, and hypot from kotlin.math.
  • Compute circle area and circumference.
  • Compute the distance from the origin.

Concept Explanation

The kotlin.math package supplies PI, sqrt, abs, max, min, floor, ceil, hypot, and the pow extension function. Import what you use: import kotlin.math.PI, or import kotlin.math.* for everything.

For a circle of radius 5 the area is PI * radius.pow(2) (about 78.54) and the circumference is 2 * PI * radius (about 31.42). Kotlin has a built-in hypotenuse function, so the distance from the origin to the shared point (3, 4) is hypot(3.0, 4.0), which is 5.0.

The math functions take Double values. sqrt(81.0) returns 9.0, a Double, so it prints with a decimal point.

Worked Example

import kotlin.math.PI
import kotlin.math.abs
import kotlin.math.hypot
import kotlin.math.max
import kotlin.math.min
import kotlin.math.pow
import kotlin.math.sqrt

fun main() {
    val radius = 5.0
    val area = PI * radius.pow(2)
    val circumference = 2 * PI * radius
    println("Area: " + "%.2f".format(area))
    println("Circumference: " + "%.2f".format(circumference))

    println(sqrt(81.0))
    println("Distance from origin: " + "%.2f".format(hypot(3.0, 4.0)))
    println("${max(82, 91)} ${min(76, 88)} ${abs(-5)}")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Area: 78.54
Circumference: 31.42
9.0
Distance from origin: 5.00
91 76 5

Common Mistakes

  1. Forgetting the import, so sqrt is an unresolved reference.
  2. Passing an Int to sqrt, which needs a Double.
  3. Writing the area as PI * radius * 2; the radius must be squared.

Activities

  1. Predict each printed line and then run the program.
  2. Compute the area for radius 2.5 by hand and with the program.
  3. Change the point to (6, 8) and predict the distance before running.
  4. Print the larger of two shared scores using max.

Accessibility Practice

Round results with format so that the screen reader announces 78.54 rather than fifteen digits. Say ‘dot’ aloud in kotlin.math and radius.pow.

Skills Checklist

  • I can import and use kotlin.math.
  • I can compute circle area and circumference.
  • I can compute distance with hypot.
  • I can format results to two decimals.
  • I know math functions take Double.

Unit 3: Control Flow — Decisions and Loops

Overview

Make decisions, classify the shared scores with the shared grade thresholds, and learn collections, loops, and strings.

Lesson 3.1: Boolean Expressions and if

Reading References

  • Control flow
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 3.1: Boolean Expressions and if Statements

Learning Objectives

  • Write comparisons and combine them with &&, ||, and !.
  • Use if as a statement and as an expression.
  • Test a range with in.

Concept Explanation

A Boolean expression is true or false. Comparisons use ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=, and conditions combine with && (and), || (or), and ! (not). A condition must be a real Boolean: Kotlin never treats 0, an empty string, or null as false.

if can be a statement that chooses what to run, or an expression that produces a value: val label = if (score >= 90) "high" else "not high". When if is used as an expression, else is required. in 80..89 tests whether a value is inside a range, both ends included.

The shared score is 82. It passes (at least 60), it is in the 80 to 89 range, and it is not at least 90.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    val score = 82

    if (score >= 60) {
        println("Avery passed.")
    } else {
        println("Avery did not pass.")
    }

    println(score >= 80 && score < 90)
    println(score < 60 || score > 100)
    println(!(score >= 90))
    println(score in 80..89)

    val label = if (score >= 90) "high" else "not high"
    println(label)
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Avery passed.
true
false
true
true
not high

Common Mistakes

  1. Writing = where == is meant, which does not compile as a condition.
  2. Leaving out else when if is used as an expression.
  3. Expecting a number or text to act as a condition. It must be a Boolean.

Activities

  1. Change the score to 59 and predict which lines change.
  2. Write a condition that is true only for scores from 70 to 79 inclusive, in two ways.
  3. Rewrite the label line as an if statement.
  4. Explain why if (score) is not allowed in Kotlin.

Accessibility Practice

Read each condition aloud with ‘greater than or equal to’, ‘and’, ‘or’, and ‘not’. Check that your screen reader announces && and || so you do not confuse them with single symbols.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write comparisons and combine them.
  • I can write if and else.
  • I can use if as an expression.
  • I can test a range with in.
  • I know conditions must be Boolean.

Lesson 3.2: Chained Conditions with when

Reading References

  • Control flow: when
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 3.2: Chained Conditionals (elif, else)

Learning Objectives

  • Use when to choose among several conditions.
  • Classify the shared grade thresholds.
  • Test boundary scores.

Concept Explanation

Kotlin has no elif. Use else if for a short chain, or when, which tests conditions from top to bottom and runs the first branch that is true. when without an argument takes a Boolean condition for each branch, and it is an expression when you use its value; then an else branch is required.

The shared grade thresholds are 90 or more for A, 80 or more for B, 70 or more for C, 60 or more for D, and anything lower for F. Because branches are tested in order, each later test needs only a lower bound.

Boundary scores sit exactly on or just below a threshold. The scores 90, 89, 80, 79, 70, 69, 60, and 59 check every boundary.

Worked Example

fun classify(score: Int): String = when {
    score >= 90 -> "A"
    score >= 80 -> "B"
    score >= 70 -> "C"
    score >= 60 -> "D"
    else -> "F"
}

fun main() {
    for (score in listOf(90, 89, 80, 79, 70, 69, 60, 59)) {
        println("$score ${classify(score)}")
    }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

90 A
89 B
80 B
79 C
70 C
69 D
60 D
59 F

Common Mistakes

  1. Putting the branches in the wrong order, such as testing score >= 60 first so every passing score is a D.
  2. Using > instead of >=, so exactly 90 receives a B.
  3. Forgetting the else branch in a when expression, which does not compile.

Activities

  1. Trace the score 82 through each branch and say which one runs.
  2. Add the scores 100 and 0 to the list and predict their grades.
  3. Reorder the branches so score >= 60 is first, run it, and explain the wrong output.
  4. Write isPassing(score) that returns a Boolean using when.

Accessibility Practice

Read the eight output lines in order. Each is a number, a space, and a letter, so they are easy to follow by ear and in braille.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write a when chain.
  • I know branch order matters.
  • I can classify with the shared thresholds.
  • I can choose boundary tests.
  • I know a when expression needs else.

Lesson 3.3: Lists

Reading References

  • Collections overview
  • List-specific operations
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 3.3: Introduction to Lists

Learning Objectives

  • Create read-only and mutable lists.
  • Index from 0 and use size, last(), and getOrNull.
  • Explain the difference between a read-only view and a copy.

Concept Explanation

listOf(...) creates a read-only list and mutableListOf(...) creates a list you can change. Indexes start at 0, so scores[0] is the first item, scores.last() is the last, and scores.size is the length. Reading outside the list with [] throws an IndexOutOfBoundsException; getOrNull(index) returns null instead.

Read-only is a property of the type, not of the data. A List<Int> variable cannot change the list, but if it refers to the same list as a MutableList<Int>, the other reference can still change it. To protect a list, make a copy with toList().

The shared list is 82, 91, 76, 88. Python uses the same 0-based indexes.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    val scores = mutableListOf(82, 91, 76, 88)
    println(scores[0])
    println(scores.last())
    println(scores.size)

    scores[2] = 80
    println(scores)

    val readOnlyView: List<Int> = scores
    val copy = scores.toList()
    scores[0] = 100
    println("view: ${readOnlyView[0]}, copy: ${copy[0]}")
    println(scores.getOrNull(10))
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

82
88
4
[82, 91, 80, 88]
view: 100, copy: 82
null

Common Mistakes

  1. Using index 1 for the first item. The first item is at index 0.
  2. Using [10] on a short list and crashing instead of using getOrNull.
  3. Assuming a List variable guarantees the data cannot change.

Activities

  1. Predict each of the seven outputs before running.
  2. Replace the second score with 95 and print the list.
  3. Make a copy of the list and show that changing the original does not change the copy.
  4. Explain, in two sentences, why List is called read-only rather than immutable.

Accessibility Practice

Print a whole list on one line and its size on another, so the screen reader announces a complete state in one pass. When reading scores[0] aloud, say ‘scores, open bracket, zero, close bracket’.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create List and MutableList values.
  • I can index from 0.
  • I can use getOrNull.
  • I can make a copy with toList().
  • I can explain read-only versus immutable.

Lesson 3.4: Loops

Reading References

  • Control flow: for loops
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 3.4: Iterating with for Loops

Learning Objectives

  • Use for with ranges, until, downTo, and step.
  • Visit a list by value and with its index.
  • Compute the total and average of the shared scores.

Concept Explanation

for (x in collection) visits every element. A range 1..3 includes both ends, 1 until 3 excludes the end, 10 downTo 1 counts down, and step 3 skips values: for (i in 10 downTo 1 step 3). withIndex() gives each element with its position: for ((index, value) in scores.withIndex()).

The standard library can do common work without a loop: sum() adds a list of numbers and average() returns the mean as a Double. A loop is still the way to learn what those functions do.

The shared scores 82, 91, 76, 88 total 337 and average 84.25.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    val scores = listOf(82, 91, 76, 88)
    var total = 0
    for ((index, score) in scores.withIndex()) {
        println("Adding score ${index + 1}: $score")
        total += score
    }
    println("Total: $total")
    println("Average: ${total.toDouble() / scores.size}")
    println("Same results: ${scores.sum()} and ${scores.average()}")

    for (i in 1..3) println("Count: $i")
    for (i in 1 until 3) println("Until: $i")
    for (i in 10 downTo 1 step 3) println("Step: $i")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Adding score 1: 82
Adding score 2: 91
Adding score 3: 76
Adding score 4: 88
Total: 337
Average: 84.25
Same results: 337 and 84.25
Count: 1
Count: 2
Count: 3
Until: 1
Until: 2
Step: 10
Step: 7
Step: 4
Step: 1

Common Mistakes

  1. Using 1..scores.size as indexes, which reads one position past the end of a 0-based list.
  2. Forgetting that .. includes the end while until excludes it.
  3. Dividing the Int total by the size and getting a truncated result.

Activities

  1. Predict the last seven output lines before running.
  2. Change the loop to print only the scores above 80.
  3. Write a loop that counts from 20 down to 0 by 5.
  4. Explain why scores.average() prints 84.25 and not 84.

Accessibility Practice

Each output line starts with a label and a number, so the running total is read step by step. Count the lines to confirm that the loop ran four times.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use ranges, until, downTo, and step.
  • I can visit a list with its index.
  • I can total and average a list.
  • I know .. includes its end.
  • I can use sum() and average().

Lesson 3.5: Strings

Reading References

  • Strings
  • Basic types
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 3.5: Basic String Operations

Learning Objectives

  • Use length, lowercase, contains, indexOf, and trim.
  • Normalize a name and search the shared text sample.
  • Explain that strings are immutable.

Concept Explanation

A Kotlin String is an immutable sequence of characters. length is its size, and text[0] is the first character. Functions such as lowercase() and uppercase() return a new string; they never change the original.

Useful functions: trim(), contains(text), indexOf(text) (which returns -1 when the text is missing), replace, startsWith, and replaceFirstChar { it.uppercase() } to capitalize. Regex("programming").findAll(text).count() counts non-overlapping matches.

The shared text sample is “A student studies programming. Programming develops problem-solving skills.” It has 75 characters and contains programming twice (once in each case), found at index 18 after lowercasing.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    val rawName = "  avery  "
    val cleanName = rawName.trim().replaceFirstChar { it.uppercase() }
    println("Name: '$cleanName'")

    val text = "A student studies programming. Programming develops problem-solving skills."
    val lowered = text.lowercase()
    println("Characters: ${text.length}")
    println("Contains 'programming': ${lowered.contains("programming")}")
    println("First index of 'programming': ${lowered.indexOf("programming")}")
    println("Times 'programming' appears: ${Regex("programming").findAll(lowered).count()}")
    println("Missing word index: ${lowered.indexOf("kotlin")}")
    println(text.uppercase().take(9))
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Name: 'Avery'
Characters: 75
Contains 'programming': true
First index of 'programming': 18
Times 'programming' appears: 2
Missing word index: -1
A STUDENT

Common Mistakes

  1. Expecting text.uppercase() to change text. Assign or print the result.
  2. Treating indexOf as an error when it returns -1.
  3. Counting positions from 1. The first character is at index 0.

Activities

  1. Predict the printed values, then run and compare.
  2. Find the index of the word student in the sample text.
  3. Replace every programming with coding and print the result.
  4. Write code that trims and capitalizes " riley ".

Accessibility Practice

Strings with many quotation marks are hard to read by ear. Say ‘single quote’ and ‘double quote’ aloud when checking a line, and print results inside labelled sentences so values are not run together.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use common String functions.
  • I can search text and find positions.
  • I can trim and capitalize a name.
  • I know strings are immutable.
  • I can count matches with Regex.

Unit 4: Data Structures — Lists and Dictionaries

Overview

Work with lists, sorting, fixed records, dictionaries, and stable traversal of the shared inventory.

Lesson 4.1: More on Mutable Lists

Reading References

  • Collections overview
  • Adding and removing elements
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 4.1: More on Lists

Learning Objectives

  • Add, insert, replace, and remove list items.
  • Remove by value and by position without confusing them.
  • Search a list with in and indexOf.

Concept Explanation

A MutableList changes with add(value) (append), add(index, value) (insert and shift), set or list[i] = value (replace), remove(value) (remove the first matching value), and removeAt(index) (remove by position). For a list of Int, remove(76) removes the number 76, while removeAt(76) would try to remove position 76. removeAt returns the removed item.

value in list tests membership, and indexOf(value) returns the position or -1. These searches look at each item in turn, so they take longer for longer lists.

Avoid removeLast() in code that must run on several JDK versions: newer JDKs add a method with the same name to List, and the behavior depends on the JDK. removeAt(lastIndex) is portable.

The example applies the same operations as the Python course to the shared scores, from [82, 91, 76, 88] to [82, 85, 93, 88].

Worked Example

fun main() {
    val scores = mutableListOf(82, 91, 76, 88)

    scores.add(95)
    scores.add(1, 85)
    scores[2] = 93
    scores.remove(76)
    val last = scores.removeAt(scores.lastIndex)

    println(scores)
    println("${scores.size} items; removed $last")
    println(88 in scores)
    println(scores.indexOf(88))
    println(scores.indexOf(100))
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

[82, 85, 93, 88]
4 items; removed 95
true
3
-1

Common Mistakes

  1. Confusing remove(76) (by value) with removeAt(76) (by position).
  2. Removing items inside a for loop over the same list, which throws ConcurrentModificationException.
  3. Calling removeLast() and getting different behavior on different JDKs.

Activities

  1. Trace the list after every operation and write each version as a sentence.
  2. Remove the first score with removeAt(0) and describe what happens to the others.
  3. Remove every score below 80 safely, using removeAll { ... }.
  4. Print the position of the first score above 90 with indexOfFirst.

Accessibility Practice

After every change, print the whole list on one line so the screen reader reads a complete state in one pass. Say the method names aloud, and notice how remove and removeAt sound different.

Skills Checklist

  • I can add, insert, replace, and remove items.
  • I can tell remove from removeAt.
  • I can search with in and indexOf.
  • I know why removeLast() is avoided.
  • I can show a list in one line.

Lesson 4.2: Sorting and Organizing Lists

Reading References

  • Ordering
  • Collections overview
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 4.2: Organizing Lists

Learning Objectives

  • Sort a list ascending and descending.
  • Tell sorted() (a new list) from sort() (in place).
  • Sort by a computed key.

Concept Explanation

Kotlin offers two families. Returning functions leave the original alone and give a new list: sorted(), sortedDescending(), sortedBy { ... }, and reversed(). In-place functions change a MutableList: sort(), sortDescending(), and reverse(). A read-only List has only the returning kind.

sortedBy { it.length } sorts by a computed key, here the length of each word, and keeps the original order of items with equal keys because the sort is stable.

The shared scores sort to 76, 82, 88, 91 in ascending order and 91, 88, 82, 76 in descending order.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    val scores = mutableListOf(82, 91, 76, 88)

    println("Original: $scores")
    println("Ascending: ${scores.sorted()}")
    println("Descending: ${scores.sortedDescending()}")
    println("Still original: $scores")

    scores.sort()
    println("Sorted in place: $scores")
    scores.reverse()
    println("Reversed in place: $scores")

    val words = listOf("pencil", "folder", "notebook")
    println(words.sorted())
    println(words.sortedBy { it.length })
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Original: [82, 91, 76, 88]
Ascending: [76, 82, 88, 91]
Descending: [91, 88, 82, 76]
Still original: [82, 91, 76, 88]
Sorted in place: [76, 82, 88, 91]
Reversed in place: [91, 88, 82, 76]
[folder, notebook, pencil]
[pencil, folder, notebook]

Common Mistakes

  1. Expecting sorted() to change the list. It returns a new list.
  2. Calling sort() on a read-only List, which does not compile.
  3. Expecting reverse() to sort. It only flips the current order.

Activities

  1. Predict each printed line before running.
  2. Print the scores in descending order without changing the original.
  3. Sort the words by their last letter with sortedBy.
  4. Explain the difference between sorted() and sort() in two sentences.

Accessibility Practice

Print each result on its own labelled line (Ascending:, Descending:). The first and last numbers are the quickest to check by ear.

Skills Checklist

  • I can sort ascending and descending.
  • I know which functions change the list.
  • I can use sortedBy.
  • I can reverse a list.
  • I can keep the original order.

Lesson 4.3: Pairs, Triples, and Data Classes

Reading References

  • Data classes
  • Destructuring declarations
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 4.3: Tuples - Immutable Lists

Learning Objectives

  • Use Pair and Triple for small fixed groups.
  • Declare a data class with val properties.
  • Unpack values with destructuring.

Concept Explanation

Kotlin has no general tuple type. For two or three values, use Pair(a, b) and Triple(a, b, c), whose parts are first, second, and third. For anything you will use more than briefly, a data class with named properties is clearer: data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int).

A data class automatically provides toString(), equals() (so two points with the same values are equal), copy() (a new object with some values changed), and destructuring: val (x, y) = point. With val properties, the object cannot change after it is created, so use copy(y = 10) to get a changed version.

The shared coordinates are x = 3 and y = 4.

Worked Example

data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int)

fun minMax(values: List<Int>): Pair<Int, Int> = Pair(values.min(), values.max())

fun main() {
    val (x, y) = Pair(3, 4)
    println("x=$x y=$y")

    val point = Point(3, 4)
    println(point)
    val moved = point.copy(y = 10)
    println("$point -> $moved")
    println(point == Point(3, 4))

    val (low, high) = minMax(listOf(82, 91, 76, 88))
    println("low=$low high=$high")

    val profile = Triple("Avery", 16, 1.72)
    println("${profile.first} ${profile.second} ${profile.third}")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

x=3 y=4
Point(x=3, y=4)
Point(x=3, y=4) -> Point(x=3, y=10)
true
low=76 high=91
Avery 16 1.72

Common Mistakes

  1. Using var properties in a data class and then being surprised when values change.
  2. Expecting copy() to change the original. It returns a new object.
  3. Using Pair with unclear meanings (first, second) in code that others must read.

Activities

  1. Predict the output, then run.
  2. Create a Student data class for the shared profile and print it.
  3. Use copy to make a student one year older and print both.
  4. Explain when a data class is a better choice than a Pair.

Accessibility Practice

Named properties read better aloud than first and second. Printing a data class shows its name and every property, so the screen reader announces Point(x=3, y=4) as a complete sentence.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use Pair and Triple.
  • I can declare a data class.
  • I can destructure values.
  • I can use copy().
  • I can choose between a pair and a data class.

Lesson 4.4: Maps

Reading References

  • Map-specific operations
  • Collections overview
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 4.4: Introducing Dictionaries

Learning Objectives

  • Create a map and read, add, change, and remove entries.
  • Handle a missing key with ?:.
  • Model the shared inventory item with a data class.

Concept Explanation

A Map pairs keys with values. mapOf(...) is read-only and mutableMapOf(...) can change. Read with map[key], which returns a nullable value: it is null when the key is missing. Combine it with the Elvis operator to supply a default: map[key] ?: "unknown".

map[key] = value adds or replaces an entry, remove(key) deletes one, containsKey(key) tests for a key, and size counts the entries. mutableMapOf keeps insertion order.

A map with values of different types, such as MutableMap<String, Any>, is flexible but loses type checking. When the fields are known, a data class is safer, so the shared Notebook item is a data class.

Worked Example

data class Item(val name: String, var quantity: Int, val unitPrice: Double)

fun main() {
    val profile = mutableMapOf<String, Any>(
        "name" to "Avery",
        "age" to 16,
        "heightM" to 1.72,
        "favoriteSubject" to "Computer Science",
    )
    println(profile["name"])
    profile["age"] = 17
    profile["gradeLevel"] = 11
    profile.remove("heightM")
    println(profile)
    println(profile["heightM"])
    println(profile["heightM"] ?: "unknown")
    println(profile.containsKey("gradeLevel"))

    val item = Item("Notebook", 3, 2.50)
    item.quantity += 2
    println(item)
    println("Stock value: ${item.quantity * item.unitPrice}")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Avery
{name=Avery, age=17, favoriteSubject=Computer Science, gradeLevel=11}
null
unknown
true
Item(name=Notebook, quantity=5, unitPrice=2.5)
Stock value: 12.5

Common Mistakes

  1. Using a missing key and expecting an error. The result is null.
  2. Using !! on a map lookup, which crashes when the key is missing.
  3. Storing mixed types in Map<String, Any> and then needing casts everywhere.

Activities

  1. Predict the printed lines before running.
  2. Add a discount key to the item as a data class property and print the discounted value.
  3. Remove favoriteSubject and show what the lookup returns.
  4. Explain why a data class is safer than Map<String, Any> for a record.

Accessibility Practice

Print one entry per line when you need to read a map, because a one-line {a=1, b=2} is hard to navigate. Choose key names that read well aloud, such as unitPrice.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create and change a map.
  • I know a lookup returns a nullable value.
  • I can supply a default with ?:.
  • I can model an item with a data class.
  • I can test for a key.

Lesson 4.5: Traversing Maps

Reading References

  • Map-specific operations
  • Collections overview
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 4.5: Looping Through Dictionaries

Learning Objectives

  • Visit keys, values, and key-value pairs.
  • Explain which maps keep insertion order.
  • Produce sorted output and total the shared inventory.

Concept Explanation

for (key in map.keys) visits keys, for (value in map.values) visits values, and for ((key, value) in map) visits pairs with destructuring.

Order matters for readable output. mutableMapOf, linkedMapOf, and mapOf keep insertion order, so output is stable. hashMapOf makes no promise about order. To list keys alphabetically, use toSortedMap().

sumOf { ... } adds a computed number for every element, which is the compact way to total the shared inventory: Notebook (3 at 2.50), Pencil (10 at 0.50), and Folder (4 at 1.25) are worth 7.50 + 5.00 + 5.00 = 17.50.

Worked Example

data class Stock(val quantity: Int, val unitPrice: Double)

fun main() {
    val inventory = linkedMapOf(
        "Notebook" to Stock(3, 2.50),
        "Pencil" to Stock(10, 0.50),
        "Folder" to Stock(4, 1.25),
    )

    println("Keys:")
    for (name in inventory.keys) println(name)

    println("Quantities:")
    for (stock in inventory.values) println(stock.quantity)

    var totalValue = 0.0
    for ((name, stock) in inventory) {
        val lineValue = stock.quantity * stock.unitPrice
        println("$name: ${stock.quantity} in stock, value ${"%.2f".format(lineValue)}")
        totalValue += lineValue
    }
    println("Total inventory value: ${"%.2f".format(totalValue)}")

    println(inventory.toSortedMap().keys)
    println(inventory.values.sumOf { it.quantity * it.unitPrice })
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Keys:
Notebook
Pencil
Folder
Quantities:
3
10
4
Notebook: 3 in stock, value 7.50
Pencil: 10 in stock, value 5.00
Folder: 4 in stock, value 5.00
Total inventory value: 17.50
[Folder, Notebook, Pencil]
17.5

Common Mistakes

  1. Using a HashMap and expecting the same order every run.
  2. Adding or removing entries while looping over the map, which throws ConcurrentModificationException.
  3. Forgetting the parentheses in for ((name, stock) in inventory) and iterating over entries without unpacking them.

Activities

  1. Run the example and write the three key-value lines in order.
  2. Print only the items with a quantity below 5.
  3. Print the items from the highest line value to the lowest.
  4. Explain how toSortedMap() differs from the default order.

Accessibility Practice

Printing each inventory line as one sentence lets the screen reader announce the name, quantity, and value together. Because the order is stable, you can learn it and compare runs by ear.

Skills Checklist

  • I can visit keys, values, and pairs.
  • I know which maps keep insertion order.
  • I can sort keys.
  • I can total with sumOf.
  • I can total the shared inventory.

Unit 5: User Input and while Loops

Overview

Read and validate input, write sentinel and flag loops, skip entries, and prevent endless loops.

Lesson 5.1: How Console Input Works

Reading References

  • Basic syntax
  • Null safety
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 5.1: How the input() Function Works

Learning Objectives

  • Read a line and recognize it as text.
  • Convert it safely and handle failure.
  • Handle the end of input.

Concept Explanation

readlnOrNull() returns the next line as a String?, or null when the input has ended. It never returns a number: typed digits are text until you convert them. toIntOrNull() returns an Int?, and a null result means the text was not a whole number.

A program that reads input must plan for three cases: a valid value, an invalid value, and no value at all. The example reads an age and then a second value, so you can see the valid, invalid, and missing cases. With the typed value 16 the age five years later is 21; the second value, abc, is rejected.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    println("How old are you?")
    val text = readlnOrNull()
    println("Read: ${if (text == null) "nothing" else text::class.simpleName}")

    val age = text?.trim()?.toIntOrNull()
    if (age != null) {
        println("In 5 years: ${age + 5}")
    } else {
        println("That was not a whole number.")
    }

    println("Enter another value:")
    val second = readlnOrNull()?.trim()?.toIntOrNull()
    if (second != null) {
        println("Number: $second")
    } else {
        println("Not a number; toIntOrNull returned null.")
    }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

With the following lines typed as standard input (piped input is not echoed, so it does not appear in the output):

16
abc

the program prints:

How old are you?
Read: String
In 5 years: 21
Enter another value:
Not a number; toIntOrNull returned null.

With no standard input at all, the program ends cleanly and prints:

How old are you?
Read: nothing
That was not a whole number.
Enter another value:
Not a number; toIntOrNull returned null.

Common Mistakes

  1. Adding to the text without converting it, which does not compile or gives joined text.
  2. Using toInt() on user input and crashing on abc.
  3. Forgetting that an empty answer is not a number, so toIntOrNull() is null.

Activities

  1. Run with 16 and then abc and compare with the shown output.
  2. Run with no input and explain every line printed.
  3. Accept an age only from 0 to 120.
  4. Rewrite the program using readln() and describe what happens at the end of input.

Accessibility Practice

Each prompt is a complete sentence on its own line. Run the program twice, once typing and once with piped input, and compare what your screen reader announces.

Skills Checklist

  • I can read a line of input.
  • I can convert and validate it.
  • I handle null at the end of input.
  • I know typed input is text.
  • I can write a clear prompt.

Lesson 5.2: The while Loop in Action

Reading References

  • Control flow: while loops
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 5.2: The while Loop in Action

Learning Objectives

  • Write a counting while loop.
  • Write a sentinel loop that ends on a command.
  • Stop at the end of input.

Concept Explanation

while (condition) { ... } repeats while the condition is true, testing before each pass. A loop needs a way to make its condition false, normally by changing a variable inside the body: count++ adds one.

A sentinel is a special input that tells the loop to stop. Here it is the word quit. The standard pattern reads once before the loop and again at the end of each pass, and tests for null as well, so the loop ends when input runs out even without quit.

The example counts from 1 to 5, then repeats a message prompt until the user types quit.

Worked Example

fun main() {
    var count = 1
    while (count <= 5) {
        println(count)
        count++
    }
    println("Counting finished!")

    println("Enter a message, or type quit to exit:")
    var message = readlnOrNull()
    while (message != null && message != "quit") {
        println("You said: $message")
        println("Enter a message, or type quit to exit:")
        message = readlnOrNull()
    }
    println("Goodbye!")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

With the following lines typed as standard input (piped input is not echoed, so it does not appear in the output):

hello
scores
quit

the program prints:

1
2
3
4
5
Counting finished!
Enter a message, or type quit to exit:
You said: hello
Enter a message, or type quit to exit:
You said: scores
Enter a message, or type quit to exit:
Goodbye!

With no standard input at all, the program ends cleanly and prints:

1
2
3
4
5
Counting finished!
Enter a message, or type quit to exit:
Goodbye!

Common Mistakes

  1. Forgetting to change the loop variable, which creates an endless loop.
  2. Testing for quit but not for null, so the loop reads forever after input ends.
  3. Reading input only before the loop and never again inside it.

Activities

  1. Predict the output for the typed lines hello, scores, and quit.
  2. Change the sentinel to exit and update the prompt.
  3. Count the messages entered and print the count at the end.
  4. Rewrite the counting loop with for (count in 1..5) and compare.

Accessibility Practice

Each prompt is on its own line and each response begins with You said:, so the conversation can be followed in order by ear. If a loop floods the screen reader, stop it with Ctrl+C.
