Room descriptions do not claim that an item is still present. Room items and inventory are announced on separate lines.

Worked Example

class Room(
    val description: String,
    val exits: Map<String, String>,
    val items: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf(),
)

fun main() {
    val rooms = mapOf(
        "start_room" to Room("A dimly lit cave.", mapOf("north" to "tunnel"), mutableListOf("shiny key")),
        "tunnel" to Room("A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.", mapOf("south" to "start_room", "east" to "clearing")),
        "clearing" to Room("A quiet clearing. An antechamber lies to the north.", mapOf("west" to "tunnel", "north" to "locked_door_room")),
        "locked_door_room" to Room("A chamber with a heavy door to the north.", mapOf("south" to "clearing", "north" to "treasure_room")),
        "treasure_room" to Room("You found the treasure. You win!", emptyMap()),
    )
    var currentRoom = "start_room"
    val inventory = mutableListOf<String>()
    var doorLocked = true

    while (true) {
        val room = rooms.getValue(currentRoom)
        println()
        println(room.description)
        if (currentRoom == "treasure_room") break
        if (room.items.isNotEmpty()) println("You see: " + room.items.joinToString(", "))
        println("Your inventory: " + if (inventory.isEmpty()) "empty" else inventory.joinToString(", "))
        println("What do you want to do?")
        val command = (readlnOrNull() ?: "quit").trim().lowercase()

        when {
            command == "quit" -> {
                println("You quit the adventure.")
                break
            }
            command == "take shiny key" -> {
                if (room.items.remove("shiny key")) {
                    inventory.add("shiny key")
                    println("You picked up the shiny key.")
                } else println("There is no shiny key here to take.")
            }
            command == "use shiny key" -> when {
                currentRoom != "locked_door_room" -> println("You must be at the locked door to use the key.")
                "shiny key" !in inventory -> println("You do not have the shiny key.")
                else -> {
                    doorLocked = false
                    println("You unlocked the door!")
                }
            }
            currentRoom == "locked_door_room" && command == "north" && doorLocked ->
                println("The door is locked! You need to use the shiny key here.")
            command in room.exits -> currentRoom = room.exits.getValue(command)
            else -> println("Invalid command. Enter north, south, east, west, take shiny key, use shiny key, or quit.")
        }
    }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Use this sequence to verify the puzzle: north, east, north, north, south, west, south, take shiny key, north, east, north, use shiny key, north.

The first north attempt from locked_door_room must be rejected. Taking the key removes it from start_room and adds it to inventory. Using it outside locked_door_room must be rejected. Using it there prints You unlocked the door!; the next north reaches treasure_room and prints You found the treasure. You win!. End-of-file is treated as quit.

Common Mistakes

  1. Leaving the shiny key in the room after adding it to inventory.
  2. Unlocking the door outside locked_door_room.
  3. Unlocking the door without checking inventory.
  4. Allowing north movement before doorLocked becomes false.
  5. Describing the key as still on the floor after it has been collected.

Activities

  1. Run the full sequence and record room, room items, inventory, and door state after every command.
  2. Try take shiny key twice; the second attempt must not duplicate the item.
  3. Try use shiny key in start_room and clearing; both attempts must be rejected.
  4. Try north from locked_door_room before and after unlocking.
  5. Add a look command that announces room, visible items, inventory, and exits in a consistent order.

Accessibility Practice

Announce room description, visible items, inventory, and prompt as separate text lines. Every failed action explains why it failed. Listen to the full puzzle sequence and verify that key location and door state are unambiguous.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model the five canonical rooms.
  • I can transfer the shiny key from a room to inventory.
  • I can prevent duplicate pickup.
  • I can require key use in the locked-door room.
  • I can block and unlock the north exit.
  • I can end the game when the treasure room is reached.

Lesson 10.4: Command-Line To-Do List

Reading References

  • Collections overview
  • Exceptions
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 10.4: Building a Command-Line To-Do List

Learning Objectives

  • Keep records with the shared fields.
  • Save and load them as JSON.
  • Offer add, view, mark-done, save, load, and quit commands.

Concept Explanation

A to-do list ties together records, loops, functions, and files. Each task has the shared fields id, title, description, done, and created_at. The program keeps a list of tasks in memory, shows a numbered menu, and saves the list to todos.json when asked and on exit.

Saving uses the teaching JSON helper from Lesson 8.5, included here so the example runs on its own. At start-up the program loads the file if it exists. A missing file is normal on first use, and a damaged file must not crash the program: it prints a message and starts with an empty list.

New ids are one more than the highest existing id. The status is shown as the words done and not done, never with a symbol or color alone.

In the sample session the user adds two tasks, views the list, marks task 2 done, views it again, tries an invalid menu choice, views the list, and quits.

Worked Example

object Json {
    fun encode(value: Any?): String = when (value) {
        null -> "null"
        is String -> quote(value)
        is Boolean, is Int, is Long, is Double -> value.toString()
        is Map<*, *> -> value.entries.sortedBy { it.key.toString() }
            .joinToString(",", "{", "}") { quote(it.key.toString()) + ":" + encode(it.value) }
        is List<*> -> value.joinToString(",", "[", "]") { encode(it) }
        else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("cannot encode ${value::class.simpleName}")
    }

    private fun quote(text: String): String {
        val out = StringBuilder("\"")
        for (c in text) {
            when {
                c == '"' -> out.append("\\\"")
                c == '\\' -> out.append("\\\\")
                c == '\n' -> out.append("\\n")
                c == '\r' -> out.append("\\r")
                c == '\t' -> out.append("\\t")
                c < ' ' -> out.append("\\u%04x".format(c.code))
                else -> out.append(c)
            }
        }
        return out.append('"').toString()
    }

    fun decode(text: String): Any? = Parser(text).parse()

    private class Parser(private val text: String) {
        private var pos = 0

        private fun fail(message: String): Nothing =
            throw IllegalArgumentException("$message at position $pos")

        private fun skip() {
            while (pos < text.length && text[pos].isWhitespace()) pos++
        }

        fun parse(): Any? {
            val result = value()
            skip()
            if (pos < text.length) fail("unexpected extra text")
            return result
        }

        private fun value(): Any? {
            skip()
            if (pos >= text.length) fail("unexpected end of text")
            val c = text[pos]
            return when {
                c == '{' -> obj()
                c == '[' -> list()
                c == '"' -> str()
                text.startsWith("true", pos) -> { pos += 4; true }
                text.startsWith("false", pos) -> { pos += 5; false }
                text.startsWith("null", pos) -> { pos += 4; null }
                c == '-' || c.isDigit() -> number()
                else -> fail("unexpected character")
            }
        }

        private fun number(): Any {
            val start = pos
            if (text[pos] == '-') pos++
            while (pos < text.length && (text[pos].isDigit() || text[pos] in ".eE+-")) pos++
            val token = text.substring(start, pos)
            return token.toLongOrNull() ?: token.toDoubleOrNull() ?: fail("bad number")
        }

        private fun str(): String {
            pos++
            val out = StringBuilder()
            while (true) {
                if (pos >= text.length) fail("unterminated string")
                val c = text[pos++]
                if (c == '"') return out.toString()
                if (c != '\\') { out.append(c); continue }
                if (pos >= text.length) fail("bad escape")
                when (text[pos++]) {
                    'n' -> out.append('\n')
                    't' -> out.append('\t')
                    'r' -> out.append('\r')
                    '"' -> out.append('"')
                    '\\' -> out.append('\\')
                    '/' -> out.append('/')
                    'u' -> {
                        if (pos + 4 > text.length) fail("bad escape")
                        out.append(text.substring(pos, pos + 4).toInt(16).toChar())
                        pos += 4
                    }
                    else -> fail("bad escape")
                }
            }
        }

        private fun obj(): Map<String, Any?> {
            pos++
            val map = LinkedHashMap<String, Any?>()
            skip()
            if (pos < text.length && text[pos] == '}') { pos++; return map }
            while (true) {
                skip()
                if (pos >= text.length || text[pos] != '"') fail("expected a key")
                val key = str()
                skip()
                if (pos >= text.length || text[pos] != ':') fail("expected ':'")
                pos++
                map[key] = value()
                skip()
                if (pos >= text.length) fail("unterminated object")
                val d = text[pos++]
                if (d == '}') return map
                if (d != ',') { pos--; fail("expected ',' or '}'") }
            }
        }

        private fun list(): List<Any?> {
            pos++
            val items = ArrayList<Any?>()
            skip()
            if (pos < text.length && text[pos] == ']') { pos++; return items }
            while (true) {
                items.add(value())
                skip()
                if (pos >= text.length) fail("unterminated list")
                val d = text[pos++]
                if (d == ']') return items
                if (d != ',') { pos--; fail("expected ',' or ']'") }
            }
        }
    }
}

val todoFile = java.io.File("todos.json")
var todos = mutableListOf<MutableMap<String, Any?>>()

fun loadTodos() {
    if (!todoFile.exists()) {
        println("No existing tasks found.")
        todos = mutableListOf()
        return
    }
    try {
        val data = Json.decode(todoFile.readText()) as List<*>
        todos = data.map { (it as Map<*, *>).entries.associate { e -> e.key.toString() to e.value }.toMutableMap() }.toMutableList()
        println("Tasks loaded.")
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        println("Error: todos.json is not valid JSON. Starting with an empty list.")
        todos = mutableListOf()
    }
}

fun saveTodos() {
    todoFile.writeText(Json.encode(todos))
    println("Tasks saved.")
}

fun nextId(): Long = (todos.maxOfOrNull { it["id"] as Long } ?: 0L) + 1

fun addTask(title: String, description: String) {
    if (title.isBlank()) {
        println("A title is required.")
        return
    }
    val stamp = java.time.LocalDateTime.now().format(java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss"))
    todos.add(mutableMapOf("id" to nextId(), "title" to title.trim(), "description" to description.trim(), "done" to false, "created_at" to stamp))
    println("Task '${title.trim()}' added.")
}

fun viewTasks() {
    if (todos.isEmpty()) {
        println("No tasks in your list.")
        return
    }
    println("--- Your To-Do List ---")
    for (task in todos) {
        val status = if (task["done"] == true) "done" else "not done"
        println("${task["id"]}. ${task["title"]} ($status)")
    }
    println("-----------------------")
}

fun markDone(text: String?) {
    val id = text?.trim()?.toLongOrNull()
    if (id == null) {
        println("Please enter a whole number.")
        return
    }
    val task = todos.firstOrNull { it["id"] == id }
    if (task == null) {
        println("No task has that number.")
        return
    }
    task["done"] = true
    println("Task '${task["title"]}' marked as done.")
}

fun showMenu() {
    println()
    println("--- To-Do List Menu ---")
    println("1. Add Task")
    println("2. View Tasks")
    println("3. Mark Task Done")
    println("4. Save Tasks")
    println("5. Load Tasks")
    println("6. Quit")
    println("-----------------------")
}

fun main() {
    loadTodos()
    while (true) {
        showMenu()
        println("Enter your choice (1-6):")
        val choice = readlnOrNull() ?: "6"
        when (choice) {
            "1" -> {
                println("Enter task title:")
                val title = readlnOrNull() ?: ""
                println("Enter task description:")
                val description = readlnOrNull() ?: ""
                addTask(title, description)
            }
            "2" -> viewTasks()
            "3" -> {
                viewTasks()
                println("Enter task number to mark done:")
                markDone(readlnOrNull())
            }
            "4" -> saveTodos()
            "5" -> loadTodos()
            "6" -> {
                saveTodos()
                println("Goodbye!")
                return
            }
            else -> println("Invalid choice. Please try again.")
        }
    }
}

Lesson 10.5: User Experience and Input Validation

Reading References

  • Functions
  • Null safety
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 10.5: Refining User Experience and Validation

Learning Objectives

  • Write reusable validation functions.
  • Limit retries and handle the end of input.
  • Write clear, accessible messages.

Concept Explanation

Reusable validation functions make every menu and form consistent. askNumber(prompt, low, high, attempts) prints a prompt, reads a line, converts it, checks the range, and either returns the number or explains the problem and asks again. After the allowed attempts, or at the end of input, it returns null. askYesNo(prompt) accepts y, yes, n, and no in any letter case.

Good messages say what was wrong and what to do: “Enter a whole number from 0 to 100,” not “Invalid.” They never depend on color, position, or symbols alone, and they use the same wording every time. The return type Int? makes the caller deal with the failure case.

The example reads a score with the typed lines abc, 105, and 88, then asks a yes or no question with the lines maybe and y.

Worked Example

fun askNumber(prompt: String, low: Int, high: Int, attempts: Int): Int? {
    for (attempt in 1..attempts) {
        println(prompt)
        val text = readlnOrNull() ?: return null
        val number = text.trim().toIntOrNull()
        if (number != null && number in low..high) return number
        println("Enter a whole number from $low to $high. You have ${attempts - attempt} attempt(s) left.")
    }
    return null
}

fun askYesNo(prompt: String): Boolean? {
    while (true) {
        println("$prompt (yes or no)")
        val text = readlnOrNull()?.trim()?.lowercase() ?: return null
        if (text == "y" || text == "yes") return true
        if (text == "n" || text == "no") return false
        println("Please answer yes or no.")
    }
}

fun main() {
    val score = askNumber("Enter a score from 0 to 100:", 0, 100, 3)
    if (score != null) {
        println("Accepted score: $score")
    } else {
        println("No valid score was entered.")
    }

    val keep = askYesNo("Save this score?")
    println("Save answer: $keep")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

With the following lines typed as standard input (piped input is not echoed, so it does not appear in the output):

abc
105
88
maybe
y

the program prints:

Enter a score from 0 to 100:
Enter a whole number from 0 to 100. You have 2 attempt(s) left.
Enter a score from 0 to 100:
Enter a whole number from 0 to 100. You have 1 attempt(s) left.
Enter a score from 0 to 100:
Accepted score: 88
Save this score? (yes or no)
Please answer yes or no.
Save this score? (yes or no)
Save answer: true

With no standard input at all, the program ends cleanly and prints:

Enter a score from 0 to 100:
No valid score was entered.
Save this score? (yes or no)
Save answer: null

Common Mistakes

  1. Writing the message “Invalid” without saying what is valid.
  2. Accepting a decimal such as 88.5 for a field that requires a whole number.
  3. Looping forever on bad input instead of limiting attempts.

Activities

  1. Run the sample input and read each message aloud.
  2. Run with three invalid numbers and read the final message.
  3. Add askText(prompt) that rejects empty answers.
  4. Rewrite two messages from earlier lessons so they say what to do next.

Accessibility Practice

Check that every error message ends with an action the user can take, and that the same situation always produces the same words.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write reusable validation functions.
  • I limit retries.
  • I handle the end of input.
  • I write messages that say what to do.
  • I keep wording consistent.

Unit 11: Capstone — Accessible Personal Data Manager

Overview

Build a personal data manager with the shared record schema, storage, search and completion, acceptance tests, and a documentation and accessibility check.

Lesson 11.1: Capstone: Requirements and Design

Reading References

  • Data classes
  • Collections overview
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 11.1: Introduction to NiceGUI (capstone planning)

Learning Objectives

  • Write requirements for a personal data manager.
  • Define the shared record schema as a data class.
  • Check records against the validation rules before building features.

Concept Explanation

The capstone is a personal data manager: a program that keeps a list of records, lets the user add, view, search, change, complete, and delete them, and saves them to a file. In the Kotlin track it is a text program, so it runs from the terminal and is fully usable with a screen reader or braille display.

Shared record schema (all general-purpose language tracks). Every record has id (unique whole number), title, description, category, created_at, and updated_at (ISO 8601 text). A project may add fields, such as an optional done flag, but must not remove these. Kotlin property names use camel case (createdAt), and the stored JSON uses the shared names.

Validation rules. A record must have a non-empty title and a non-empty category. Timestamps are ISO 8601 text such as 2026-01-15T09:00:00.

Design before coding: list the operations, then the data, then the messages. The example checks the three shared sample records against the rules and prints them as a plain-text list.

Worked Example

data class Record(
    val id: Int,
    val title: String,
    val description: String,
    val category: String,
    val createdAt: String,
    val updatedAt: String,
)

fun validate(title: String?, category: String?): String? = when {
    title == null || title.isBlank() -> "A title is required."
    category == null || category.isBlank() -> "A category is required."
    else -> null
}

fun main() {
    val sample = listOf(
        Record(1, "Notebook", "Course notes", "supplies", "2026-01-15T09:00:00", "2026-01-15T09:00:00"),
        Record(2, "Pencil", "Box of 10", "supplies", "2026-01-15T09:05:00", "2026-01-15T09:05:00"),
        Record(3, "Study plan", "Weekly schedule", "planning", "2026-01-15T09:10:00", "2026-01-15T09:10:00"),
    )

    for (record in sample) {
        val problem = validate(record.title, record.category)
        println("${record.id}. ${record.title} [${record.category}] - ${problem ?: "valid"}")
    }

    println(validate("  ", "supplies"))
    println(validate("Ruler", ""))
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

1. Notebook [supplies] - valid
2. Pencil [supplies] - valid
3. Study plan [planning] - valid
A title is required.
A category is required.

Common Mistakes

  1. Starting to build features before agreeing on the record fields.
  2. Allowing a record with an empty title because the check was left for later.
  3. Storing timestamps in different formats in different places.

Activities

  1. Write the seven operations as a numbered list of requirements.
  2. Add one project-specific property and say how it is validated.
  3. Write three sample records for your own project.
  4. Describe in plain sentences what each shared field means.

Accessibility Practice

Design the screen output as lines of plain text: one record per line, with the same field order each time. Decide the wording of every message now so that it can be tested.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write requirements.
  • I know the shared record fields.
  • I can write validation rules.
  • I can describe sample data.
  • I can plan messages before coding.

Lesson 11.2: Capstone: Data Model and Storage

Reading References

  • Data classes
  • Exceptions
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 11.2: Data Model and Storage

Learning Objectives

  • Store records as data class objects.
  • Save and load them as JSON.
  • Confirm that every field survives a round trip.

Concept Explanation

Records are stored as a list of data class objects in memory and as a JSON array on disk. The storage layer has two functions: saveRecords(path, records) and loadRecords(path). Loading returns a pair of the records and a message, so the caller decides what to do when the file is missing or damaged.

A Record is converted to a map for saving (toMap) and rebuilt from a decoded map when loading (toRecord), which checks that each field is present and has the right type. The optional done field defaults to false.

The example uses the teaching JSON helper from Lesson 8.5 (included so the program runs on its own). After saving and reloading it compares the lists; data classes compare by value, so this round-trip test checks every field of every record. It is the first acceptance test for storage.

Worked Example

object Json {
    fun encode(value: Any?): String = when (value) {
        null -> "null"
        is String -> quote(value)
        is Boolean, is Int, is Long, is Double -> value.toString()
        is Map<*, *> -> value.entries.sortedBy { it.key.toString() }
            .joinToString(",", "{", "}") { quote(it.key.toString()) + ":" + encode(it.value) }
        is List<*> -> value.joinToString(",", "[", "]") { encode(it) }
        else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("cannot encode ${value::class.simpleName}")
    }

    private fun quote(text: String): String {
        val out = StringBuilder("\"")
        for (c in text) {
            when {
                c == '"' -> out.append("\\\"")
                c == '\\' -> out.append("\\\\")
                c == '\n' -> out.append("\\n")
                c == '\r' -> out.append("\\r")
                c == '\t' -> out.append("\\t")
                c < ' ' -> out.append("\\u%04x".format(c.code))
                else -> out.append(c)
            }
        }
        return out.append('"').toString()
    }

    fun decode(text: String): Any? = Parser(text).parse()

    private class Parser(private val text: String) {
        private var pos = 0

        private fun fail(message: String): Nothing =
            throw IllegalArgumentException("$message at position $pos")

        private fun skip() {
            while (pos < text.length && text[pos].isWhitespace()) pos++
        }

        fun parse(): Any? {
            val result = value()
            skip()
            if (pos < text.length) fail("unexpected extra text")
            return result
        }

        private fun value(): Any? {
            skip()
            if (pos >= text.length) fail("unexpected end of text")
            val c = text[pos]
            return when {
                c == '{' -> obj()
                c == '[' -> list()
                c == '"' -> str()
                text.startsWith("true", pos) -> { pos += 4; true }
                text.startsWith("false", pos) -> { pos += 5; false }
                text.startsWith("null", pos) -> { pos += 4; null }
                c == '-' || c.isDigit() -> number()
                else -> fail("unexpected character")
            }
        }

        private fun number(): Any {
            val start = pos
            if (text[pos] == '-') pos++
            while (pos < text.length && (text[pos].isDigit() || text[pos] in ".eE+-")) pos++
            val token = text.substring(start, pos)
            return token.toLongOrNull() ?: token.toDoubleOrNull() ?: fail("bad number")
        }

        private fun str(): String {
            pos++
            val out = StringBuilder()
            while (true) {
                if (pos >= text.length) fail("unterminated string")
                val c = text[pos++]
                if (c == '"') return out.toString()
                if (c != '\\') { out.append(c); continue }
                if (pos >= text.length) fail("bad escape")
                when (text[pos++]) {
                    'n' -> out.append('\n')
                    't' -> out.append('\t')
                    'r' -> out.append('\r')
                    '"' -> out.append('"')
                    '\\' -> out.append('\\')
                    '/' -> out.append('/')
                    'u' -> {
                        if (pos + 4 > text.length) fail("bad escape")
                        out.append(text.substring(pos, pos + 4).toInt(16).toChar())
                        pos += 4
                    }
                    else -> fail("bad escape")
                }
            }
        }

        private fun obj(): Map<String, Any?> {
            pos++
            val map = LinkedHashMap<String, Any?>()
            skip()
            if (pos < text.length && text[pos] == '}') { pos++; return map }
            while (true) {
                skip()
                if (pos >= text.length || text[pos] != '"') fail("expected a key")
                val key = str()
                skip()
                if (pos >= text.length || text[pos] != ':') fail("expected ':'")
                pos++
                map[key] = value()
                skip()
                if (pos >= text.length) fail("unterminated object")
                val d = text[pos++]
                if (d == '}') return map
                if (d != ',') { pos--; fail("expected ',' or '}'") }
            }
        }

        private fun list(): List<Any?> {
            pos++
            val items = ArrayList<Any?>()
            skip()
            if (pos < text.length && text[pos] == ']') { pos++; return items }
            while (true) {
                items.add(value())
                skip()
                if (pos >= text.length) fail("unterminated list")
                val d = text[pos++]
                if (d == ']') return items
                if (d != ',') { pos--; fail("expected ',' or ']'") }
            }
        }
    }
}

data class Record(
    val id: Int,
    val title: String,
    val description: String,
    val category: String,
    val createdAt: String,
    val updatedAt: String,
    val done: Boolean = false,
)

fun Record.toMap(): Map<String, Any?> = mapOf(
    "id" to id, "title" to title, "description" to description, "category" to category,
    "created_at" to createdAt, "updated_at" to updatedAt, "done" to done,
)

fun toRecord(entry: Any?): Record {
    val map = entry as? Map<*, *> ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("a record must be an object")
    fun text(key: String) = map[key] as? String ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("missing field $key")
    val id = (map["id"] as? Long)?.toInt() ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("missing field id")
    return Record(id, text("title"), text("description"), text("category"),
        text("created_at"), text("updated_at"), map["done"] as? Boolean ?: false)
}

fun saveRecords(path: String, records: List<Record>) {
    java.io.File(path).writeText(Json.encode(records.map { it.toMap() }))
}

fun loadRecords(path: String): Pair<List<Record>, String?> {
    val file = java.io.File(path)
    if (!file.exists()) return Pair(emptyList(), "Could not open $path: file not found.")
    return try {
        Pair((Json.decode(file.readText()) as List<*>).map { toRecord(it) }, null)
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        Pair(emptyList(), "The data file is not valid: ${e.message}")
    }
}

fun main() {
    val sample = listOf(
        Record(1, "Notebook", "Course notes", "supplies", "2026-01-15T09:00:00", "2026-01-15T09:00:00"),
        Record(2, "Pencil", "Box of 10", "supplies", "2026-01-15T09:05:00", "2026-01-15T09:05:00"),
        Record(3, "Study plan", "Weekly schedule", "planning", "2026-01-15T09:10:00", "2026-01-15T09:10:00"),
    )

    saveRecords("records.json", sample)
    val (loaded, problem) = loadRecords("records.json")
    println("Round trip preserved all fields: ${loaded == sample}")
    println("Records loaded: ${loaded.size}")
    println(problem)

    println(loadRecords("missing.json").second)

    java.io.File("broken.json").writeText("[{\"id\": 1,")
    println(loadRecords("broken.json").second)
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Round trip preserved all fields: true
Records loaded: 3
null
Could not open missing.json: file not found.
The data file is not valid: expected a key at position 10

Common Mistakes

  1. Overwriting the data file with an empty list after a failed load.
  2. Saving only some of the fields.
  3. Assuming a loaded record has every field without checking.

Activities

  1. Run the program and open records.json to read the saved text.
  2. Add a field to Record, save it, and confirm that it survives the round trip.
  3. Make toRecord reject a record whose title is blank.
  4. Explain why loadRecords returns a message and does not throw.

Accessibility Practice

Messages that name the file and the problem read clearly in speech. After saving, read the file in the terminal to confirm it contains what you expect.

Skills Checklist

  • I can store records in data class objects.
  • I can save and load JSON.
  • I can run a round-trip test.
  • I handle missing and damaged files.
  • I do not overwrite good data after a failed load.

Lesson 11.3: Capstone: Core Operations

Reading References

  • Classes
  • Collections overview
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 11.3: Displaying and Managing Items

Learning Objectives

  • Add, list, search, change, complete, and delete records.
  • Assign new ids and update timestamps correctly.
  • Return a message when an operation cannot be done.

Concept Explanation

A Manager class holds the records and offers one function per operation. Each function that can fail returns a pair of the result and a message, so the user interface can show the message and decide what to do. New ids are one more than the highest id, so ids are never reused while higher ids exist. Updating a record sets updatedAt but never changes createdAt, which is a val. Completing a record sets the optional done field to true and counts as an update.

For repeatable output the example passes in a fake clock that returns a new fixed time on each call. A real program passes a function that reads the real time.

The example adds the three shared sample records, lists them, searches for “note”, changes one description, completes one record, deletes one, and tries to delete a record that does not exist.

Worked Example

data class Record(
    val id: Int,
    var title: String,
    var description: String,
    var category: String,
    val createdAt: String,
    var updatedAt: String,
    var done: Boolean = false,
)

fun validate(title: String?, category: String?): String? = when {
    title == null || title.isBlank() -> "A title is required."
    category == null || category.isBlank() -> "A category is required."
    else -> null
}

class Manager(private val clock: () -> String) {
    val records = mutableListOf<Record>()

    private fun nextId(): Int = (records.maxOfOrNull { it.id } ?: 0) + 1

    fun find(id: Int): Record? = records.firstOrNull { it.id == id }

    fun add(title: String, description: String, category: String): Pair<Record?, String?> {
        val problem = validate(title, category)
        if (problem != null) return Pair(null, problem)
        val stamp = clock()
        val record = Record(nextId(), title.trim(), description.trim(), category.trim(), stamp, stamp)
        records.add(record)
        return Pair(record, null)
    }

    fun update(
        id: Int,
        title: String? = null,
        description: String? = null,
        category: String? = null,
        done: Boolean? = null,
    ): Pair<Record?, String?> {
        val record = find(id) ?: return Pair(null, "No record has that id.")
        val problem = validate(title ?: record.title, category ?: record.category)
        if (problem != null) return Pair(null, problem)
        if (title != null) record.title = title.trim()
        if (description != null) record.description = description.trim()
        if (category != null) record.category = category.trim()
        if (done != null) record.done = done
        record.updatedAt = clock()
        return Pair(record, null)
    }

    fun complete(id: Int) = update(id, done = true)

    fun delete(id: Int): Pair<Boolean, String?> {
        val record = find(id) ?: return Pair(false, "No record has that id.")
        records.remove(record)
        return Pair(true, null)
    }

    fun search(text: String): List<Record> {
        val needle = text.trim().lowercase()
        return records.filter { it.title.lowercase().contains(needle) || it.description.lowercase().contains(needle) }
    }
}

fun describe(record: Record): String =
    "${record.id}. ${record.title} [${record.category}] (${if (record.done) "done" else "not done"})"

fun makeClock(): () -> String {
    var ticks = 0
    return {
        ticks++
        "2026-01-15T10:00:%02d".format(ticks)
    }
}

fun show(manager: Manager) {
    for (record in manager.records) println(describe(record))
}

fun main() {
    val manager = Manager(makeClock())
    manager.add("Notebook", "Course notes", "supplies")
    manager.add("Pencil", "Box of 10", "supplies")
    manager.add("Study plan", "Weekly schedule", "planning")
    show(manager)

    println("Search for 'note':")
    for (record in manager.search("note")) println(record.title)

    manager.update(2, description = "Box of 12")
    manager.complete(3)
    println("${manager.find(2)?.description} ${manager.find(2)?.updatedAt}")
    println(manager.delete(1))
    println(manager.delete(99))
    show(manager)
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

1. Notebook [supplies] (not done)
2. Pencil [supplies] (not done)
3. Study plan [planning] (not done)
Search for 'note':
Notebook
Box of 12 2026-01-15T10:00:04
(true, null)
(false, No record has that id.)
2. Pencil [supplies] (not done)
3. Study plan [planning] (done)

Common Mistakes

  1. Reusing a deleted record’s id by counting the list size instead of using the highest id.
  2. Changing createdAt when updating a record (the property is a val to prevent this).
  3. Throwing an exception for a missing record where a message to display is more helpful.

Activities

  1. Predict the output before running.
  2. Add listByCategory(category) to Manager.
  3. Add a rule that blocks completing a record that is already complete, with a message.
  4. Explain how the fake clock makes the output repeatable.

Accessibility Practice

List output uses the same fixed format for every record and the words done and not done. Search results print only titles, so each line is short.

Skills Checklist

  • I can implement add, list, search, change, complete, and delete.
  • I assign unique ids.
  • I update timestamps correctly.
  • I return clear messages for failures.
  • I can make output repeatable with a fake clock.

Lesson 11.4: Capstone: Validation and Acceptance Tests

Reading References

  • Exceptions
  • Functions
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 11.4: Testing and Refinement

Learning Objectives

  • Run the shared acceptance tests.
  • Verify that validation rejects bad data.
  • Read and interpret test results.

Concept Explanation

The shared acceptance tests describe behavior that every language track’s capstone must show:

  1. Adding a record with an empty title is rejected with a clear message.
  2. A new record receives an unused id.
  3. Updating a record changes updated_at but not created_at.
  4. Deleting a record removes only that record.
  5. Saving and reloading preserves all fields and values (shown in Lesson 11.2).
  6. Every message and control can be used without color or a mouse (checked by hand in Lesson 11.5).

This lesson automates tests 1 to 4 and also tests completion and the rejection of a blank title in an update. Each test builds a new Manager, so tests cannot affect each other. The fake clock keeps timestamps predictable so a test can check that updatedAt changed while createdAt did not.

Worked Example

data class Record(
    val id: Int,
    var title: String,
    var description: String,
    var category: String,
    val createdAt: String,
    var updatedAt: String,
    var done: Boolean = false,
)

fun validate(title: String?, category: String?): String? = when {
    title == null || title.isBlank() -> "A title is required."
    category == null || category.isBlank() -> "A category is required."
    else -> null
}

class Manager(private val clock: () -> String) {
    val records = mutableListOf<Record>()

    private fun nextId(): Int = (records.maxOfOrNull { it.id } ?: 0) + 1

    fun find(id: Int): Record? = records.firstOrNull { it.id == id }

    fun add(title: String, description: String, category: String): Pair<Record?, String?> {
        val problem = validate(title, category)
        if (problem != null) return Pair(null, problem)
        val stamp = clock()
        val record = Record(nextId(), title.trim(), description.trim(), category.trim(), stamp, stamp)
        records.add(record)
        return Pair(record, null)
    }

    fun update(
        id: Int,
        title: String? = null,
        description: String? = null,
        category: String? = null,
        done: Boolean? = null,
    ): Pair<Record?, String?> {
        val record = find(id) ?: return Pair(null, "No record has that id.")
        val problem = validate(title ?: record.title, category ?: record.category)
        if (problem != null) return Pair(null, problem)
        if (title != null) record.title = title.trim()
        if (description != null) record.description = description.trim()
        if (category != null) record.category = category.trim()
        if (done != null) record.done = done
        record.updatedAt = clock()
        return Pair(record, null)
    }

    fun complete(id: Int) = update(id, done = true)

    fun delete(id: Int): Pair<Boolean, String?> {
        val record = find(id) ?: return Pair(false, "No record has that id.")
        records.remove(record)
        return Pair(true, null)
    }

    fun search(text: String): List<Record> {
        val needle = text.trim().lowercase()
        return records.filter { it.title.lowercase().contains(needle) || it.description.lowercase().contains(needle) }
    }
}

fun describe(record: Record): String =
    "${record.id}. ${record.title} [${record.category}] (${if (record.done) "done" else "not done"})"

fun makeClock(): () -> String {
    var ticks = 0
    return {
        ticks++
        "2026-01-15T10:00:%02d".format(ticks)
    }
}

var failures = 0

fun test(name: String, body: () -> Unit) {
    val result = runCatching(body)
    if (result.isSuccess) {
        println("PASS $name")
    } else {
        failures++
        println("FAIL $name: ${result.exceptionOrNull()?.message}")
    }
}

fun assertThat(condition: Boolean, message: String) {
    if (!condition) throw AssertionError(message)
}

fun fresh(): Manager {
    val manager = Manager(makeClock())
    manager.add("Notebook", "Course notes", "supplies")
    manager.add("Pencil", "Box of 10", "supplies")
    manager.add("Study plan", "Weekly schedule", "planning")
    return manager
}

fun main() {
    test("1. an empty title is rejected") {
        val manager = fresh()
        val (record, message) = manager.add("   ", "x", "supplies")
        assertThat(record == null && message == "A title is required.", "expected the title message")
        assertThat(manager.records.size == 3, "the list should be unchanged")
    }

    test("2. a new record gets an unused id") {
        val manager = fresh()
        manager.delete(2)
        val (record, _) = manager.add("Ruler", "30 cm", "supplies")
        assertThat(record?.id == 4, "expected id 4 but got ${record?.id}")
    }

    test("3. update changes updatedAt but not createdAt") {
        val manager = fresh()
        val before = manager.find(1)!!.copy()
        manager.update(1, description = "Lecture notes")
        val after = manager.find(1)!!
        assertThat(after.createdAt == before.createdAt, "createdAt changed")
        assertThat(after.updatedAt != before.updatedAt, "updatedAt did not change")
    }

    test("4. delete removes only that record") {
        val manager = fresh()
        manager.delete(2)
        val ids = manager.records.map { it.id }
        assertThat(ids == listOf(1, 3), "wrong records remain: $ids")
    }

    test("5. complete marks done and updates the record") {
        val manager = fresh()
        val (record, _) = manager.complete(3)
        assertThat(record?.done == true && record.updatedAt != record.createdAt, "completion not recorded")
    }

    test("6. a blank title cannot be saved by update") {
        val manager = fresh()
        val (record, message) = manager.update(1, title = "")
        assertThat(record == null && message == "A title is required.", "update accepted a blank title")
    }

    println(if (failures == 0) "All acceptance tests passed." else "$failures test(s) failed.")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

PASS 1. an empty title is rejected
PASS 2. a new record gets an unused id
PASS 3. update changes updatedAt but not createdAt
PASS 4. delete removes only that record
PASS 5. complete marks done and updates the record
PASS 6. a blank title cannot be saved by update
All acceptance tests passed.

Common Mistakes

  1. Sharing one manager between tests, so one test’s deletions change the next test.
  2. Checking only that no exception occurred, and not checking the result.
  3. Writing the expected message differently from the program, so a correct program fails the test.

Activities

  1. Break Manager.update so it also changes createdAt (make the property a var) and watch test 3 fail. Restore it.
  2. Add a test that searching ignores case.
  3. Add a test that deleting an unknown id returns false and a message.
  4. Explain why test 2 deletes record 2 before adding the new one.

Accessibility Practice

The test names begin with the acceptance-test number, so PASS and FAIL lines can be matched to the specification. Read only the first word of each line to hear the overall result quickly.

Skills Checklist

  • I can run the shared acceptance tests.
  • I can test validation failures.
  • I can test timestamps with a fake clock.
  • I can read PASS and FAIL lines.
  • I use a fresh manager for every test.

Lesson 11.5: Capstone: Documentation and Presentation

Reading References

  • Basic syntax
  • Unit P, Lesson P.6: files, data formats, and the shared accessible workflow
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 11.5: Final Submission

Learning Objectives

  • Write a plain-text project summary.
  • Report a count of records by category.
  • Complete a manual accessibility check.

Concept Explanation

Documentation tells a future reader what the program does and how to run it. Write it as plain text or Markdown with short headings, numbered steps, and complete sentences. Include: the purpose of the program, the compile and run commands, the shared record fields, the commands a user can give, the accessibility checks you carried out, and what you would improve next.

The example generates a summary from the shared sample data. It counts records by category and prints the categories in alphabetical order so the output is stable. It then prints the manual accessibility checklist. The unchecked boxes [ ] are for you to complete by hand with your own access technology; the program cannot verify them.

Acceptance test 6 is a manual check: every message and control can be used without color or a mouse. Test it with the keyboard only, and with the screen reader or braille display you actually use. Record what you tested and its version; do not claim compatibility with software you did not test.

Worked Example

data class Record(val id: Int, val title: String, val category: String)

fun main() {
    val sample = listOf(
        Record(1, "Notebook", "supplies"),
        Record(2, "Pencil", "supplies"),
        Record(3, "Study plan", "planning"),
    )

    val counts = sample.groupingBy { it.category }.eachCount().toSortedMap()

    println("Personal Data Manager - Summary")
    println("Records: ${sample.size}")
    println("Categories:")
    for ((category, count) in counts) {
        println("- $category: $count")
    }

    println()
    println("Manual accessibility checklist (complete this by hand):")
    val checks = listOf(
        "[ ] Every command can be used with the keyboard only.",
        "[ ] Every message is a complete sentence that says what to do next.",
        "[ ] No meaning depends on color, position, or symbols alone.",
        "[ ] The output was read with my own screen reader or braille display.",
        "[ ] I recorded the operating system, program, and version I tested.",
    )
    for (check in checks) println(check)
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Personal Data Manager - Summary
Records: 3
Categories:
- planning: 1
- supplies: 2

Manual accessibility checklist (complete this by hand):
[ ] Every command can be used with the keyboard only.
[ ] Every message is a complete sentence that says what to do next.
[ ] No meaning depends on color, position, or symbols alone.
[ ] The output was read with my own screen reader or braille display.
[ ] I recorded the operating system, program, and version I tested.

Common Mistakes

  1. Writing documentation that only the author can follow.
  2. Claiming that a program is accessible without recording what was tested and how.
  3. Letting the documentation drift from the program after later changes.

Activities

  1. Write the project summary for your own capstone using the headings above.
  2. Run the keyboard-only check and record each problem you find.
  3. Ask a classmate to follow your run instructions from a fresh folder and note where they get stuck.
  4. Write three improvements for the next version, ordered by user benefit.

Accessibility Practice

This is the final accessibility lesson. Read your own documentation aloud from start to finish. Anything you have to look at the screen to understand needs rewriting.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write a plain-text project summary.
  • I can report counts by category.
  • I can run a manual accessibility check.
  • I record what I tested.
  • I do not claim untested compatibility.

AI Policy

AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, or generate course code or assessment solutions.

Lua Curriculum

Lua is a lightweight, embeddable scripting language used in game scripting, application extension, configuration, automation, and embedded environments. This track teaches general programming concepts while making Lua’s table-centric data model and compact runtime explicit.

Before you start

Complete the Computing Foundations Primer and the Terminal Skills prerequisite. The course is designed for beginners and does not assume prior programming experience.

Course sequence

  • Unit 0: interpreter and toolchain concepts, workspace, accessible editor workflow, and project dependencies.
  • Unit 1: computing foundations and first Lua programs.
  • Units 2–4: values, numeric computation, input/output, control flow, and tables.
  • Units 5–8: iteration, functions, modularity, object patterns, files, and errors.
  • Units 9–11: testing, data processing, projects, and capstone work.

See the complete Lua lessons, the Lua topic index, and the existing Lua course overview and toolchain notes.

Lua language concepts

Lua is dynamically typed. Tables can represent sequences, maps, records, and objects. Sequence indexing conventionally begins at 1. ipairs iterates sequence entries; pairs iterates key/value pairs without guaranteeing traversal order. Only nil and false are falsey. Functions are values and can return multiple results. Metatables support customized lookup and operator behavior.

File operations return values that should be checked. JSON and CSV support are provided through external packages rather than the core standard library. The course identifies external dependencies where used.

Toolchain baseline

The examples target Lua 5.4 and the standard library. LuaRocks is introduced as an optional package manager, not a prerequisite for the core course. Refer to the Lua overview for the validation command and current verification notes.

Accessibility

Use keyboard-first editing and terminal workflows. Verify screen-reader output for punctuation, nesting, diagnostics, paths, and program output. The core course should not depend on visual-only game editors or graphical tools.

Recommended introductory books

  • Burton, Brian. Learning Lua: A Guide for Getting Started. Burtons Media Group, 2023. A beginner-oriented introduction to Lua scripting, with examples relevant to embedded applications and game scripting. Publisher page.
  • Ierusalimschy, Roberto. Programming in Lua, 4th edition. Lua.org, 2016. The authoritative book by Lua’s chief architect, covering the language and its C API. It assumes general programming experience, though it does not assume prior Lua knowledge. Official book page.

Suggested use: Learning Lua is the more direct first book for this track. Use Programming in Lua as the detailed language reference once basic programming concepts are familiar. Its fourth edition targets Lua 5.3; consult the current Lua 5.4 reference manual for version-specific differences.

LUA Lessons

The curriculum is organized as one Markdown file per unit.

  • accessible environment and toolchain
  • foundations of computing
  • numeric computations
  • control flow decisions and loops
  • data structures lists and dictionaries
  • user input and while loops
  • functions
  • classes and object oriented programming
  • files and exceptions
  • testing and data analysis
  • project based learning text based applications
  • capstone accessible personal data manager

Unit 0: Accessible Environment and Toolchain

Course overview

Course alignment and implementation notes

This course follows the Python canonical sequence in lesson_standardization.json. The shared problem contexts, inputs, records, boundaries, and expected results are preserved; Lua syntax and idioms are taught directly rather than transliterated from Python. Lua tables represent sequences, maps, and records; sequences are one-indexed; only false and nil are false; pairs does not guarantee order; ipairs traverses a consecutive sequence. Lua has no built-in class, tuple, continue statement, or JSON library. These differences are taught explicitly.

Runtime: Lua 5.4. Run a file with lua5.4 filename.lua; syntax-check with luac5.4 -p filename.lua. Use local variables by default. The Lua standard library does not include a JSON or general CSV parser; capstone persistence must declare and document an approved dependency (for example, dkjson), and CSV parsing must use a tested parser when quoted fields are in scope.

Accessibility and lesson conventions

Use the terminal and keyboard for every exercise. Read code and output sequentially; describe braces, brackets, quotes, punctuation, and indentation in prose. Do not communicate status through color alone. Provide explicit prompts, errors, confirmations, and textual equivalents for any visual output. The course does not claim screen-reader or braille verification until those workflows have been tested on named platforms.

Each lesson includes a focused explanation, runnable worked example, expected behavior, common mistakes, practice, accessibility practice, and a skills check. Save each fenced example to a separate file or copy it into the Lua REPL.

Overview

Install Lua 5.4, create a project folder, set up a keyboard-first editor workflow, and learn how Lua finds modules. No programming experience is needed beyond Unit P.

Lesson 0.1: Install and Verify Lua

Reading References

  • Programming in Lua, 4th edition (Roberto Ierusalimschy): Chapter 1 (Getting Started)
  • Lua 5.4 Reference Manual: Section 7 (Lua Standalone)
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 0.1 Installing Python and uv

Learning Objectives

  • Install Lua 5.4 using a trusted source for your operating system.
  • Verify the installed version from the terminal.
  • Run a one-line program with the interpreter before creating any file.

Concept Explanation

Lua is a small interpreted language. The program that reads and runs Lua source is called the interpreter. Installing Lua therefore means installing one command-line program. This course targets Lua 5.4; features such as integer and float number subtypes, // integer division, and <close> variables belong to Lua 5.3 and 5.4, so an older 5.1 or 5.2 interpreter will not run every example.

Choose one installation route and write down which one you used:

  • Debian or Ubuntu Linux: the package manager provides lua5.4, and the command is lua5.4.
  • macOS: a package manager such as Homebrew provides a lua formula. After installing, check the version, because the command is usually named lua.
  • Windows: use a Lua 5.4 binary distribution or a package manager you already trust, then confirm the command name and that it is on your PATH.
  • Any system: Lua can be built from the source archive at lua.org if you prefer.

The command name differs by system (lua5.4 or lua). This course writes lua5.4; substitute your own command everywhere. Always confirm the version with -v rather than assuming, because a computer can have an old Lua installed alongside a new one.

The -e option runs a statement given on the command line, which proves the interpreter works before you create a project.

Worked Example

lua5.4 -v
lua5.4 -e "print('Hello from Lua')"

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output (the patch number and year depend on the version you installed; this was observed with Lua 5.4.6):

Lua 5.4.6  Copyright (C) 1994-2023 Lua.org, PUC-Rio
Hello from Lua

Common Mistakes

  1. Installing a package named lua and assuming it is Lua 5.4. Run the version command to confirm.
  2. Mixing up the command name: typing lua when the installed command is lua5.4, then concluding the install failed.
  3. Running a Lua statement in a shell without noticing that the shell’s own quoting rules changed the quotation marks.

Activities

  1. Install Lua and record the exact output of the version command.
  2. Run lua5.4 -e "print(1 + 1)" and explain each part of the command in your own words.
  3. Find out which command name your system uses and write it on the first line of your course notes file.
  4. Explain the difference between the interpreter and the source file it reads.

Accessibility Practice

Run each command from the keyboard only. After pressing Enter, use your screen reader’s review commands to read the output line by line, and confirm that the version number is announced. If you use a braille display, check that the quotation marks in the second command are shown.

Skills Checklist

  • I can install Lua 5.4 and say which route I used.
  • I can run the version command and read the result.
  • I know which command name my computer uses.
  • I can run a one-line Lua statement from the terminal.
  • I can say what the interpreter does.

Lesson 0.2: Workspace and First Run

Reading References

  • Programming in Lua, 4th edition (Roberto Ierusalimschy): Chapter 1 (Getting Started)
  • Lua 5.4 Reference Manual: Section 7 (Lua Standalone)
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 0.2 Installing and configuring VS Code or Theia IDE

Learning Objectives

  • Create a course folder with a first source file.
  • Run the file from the terminal and read the result.
  • Read a Lua error message and find the file name and line number.

Concept Explanation

A project folder keeps one program’s files together. Create a folder named lua-course, and inside it save a file named main.lua. Lua source files conventionally end in .lua. From the terminal, change into the folder (this is your working directory) and run the file by giving its name to the interpreter: lua5.4 main.lua.

Lua runs the file from top to bottom as one unit called a chunk. print writes its arguments to the terminal and ends with a new line. The global variable _VERSION holds the language version as text, which is a quick way to confirm that the file ran under Lua 5.4.

If a file contains a mistake, the interpreter prints a message of the form lua5.4: main.lua:3: .... Read it in three parts: the program name, the file name and line number (main.lua:3), and a description of the problem. Always go to that line first.

To check syntax without running a program, use the compiler front end: luac5.4 -p main.lua. It prints nothing when the file is syntactically valid.

Worked Example

-- main.lua: the first program in the course project folder
print("Hello, Lua!")
print(_VERSION)

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Hello, Lua!
Lua 5.4

Common Mistakes

  1. Running the command from the wrong folder, so the interpreter reports that it cannot open main.lua.
  2. Saving the file with a hidden extra extension such as main.lua.txt, so the file name does not match.
  3. Ignoring the line number in an error message and re-reading the whole file instead.

Activities

  1. Create the folder and file, then run them. Record the working directory shown by pwd (macOS and Linux) or cd (Windows).
  2. Remove the closing quotation mark on line 2, run the file, and write down the file name, line number, and description in the error message. Then restore the file.
  3. Run luac5.4 -p main.lua before and after the mistake and compare what is printed.
  4. Add a third line that prints your own name, and predict the output before running it.

Accessibility Practice

Use a keyboard-only route to create the folder and file (terminal commands or your editor’s keyboard commands). Read your error message with the screen reader’s line-by-line review, and find the line number without relying on a mouse or on color.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create a project folder and a .lua file.
  • I can run the file from the terminal.
  • I can say what the working directory is.
  • I can read the file name and line number in an error.
  • I can check syntax with luac5.4 -p.

Lesson 0.3: Editor and Accessibility Workflow

Reading References

  • Programming in Lua, 4th edition (Roberto Ierusalimschy): Chapter 1 (Getting Started)
  • This repository: IDE setup lesson
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 0.3 Editor extensions and project workspace

Learning Objectives

  • Configure an editor so Lua source can be read by speech or braille.
  • Choose a punctuation announcement level that distinguishes brackets, braces, and quotation marks.
  • Practice navigating a Lua file by line, word, and character.

Concept Explanation

Complete the shared IDE setup lesson first. Then adapt the editor for Lua:

  • Install only a Lua language extension from a source you trust, such as a Lua language server, and read what permissions it requests. An extension is optional; the course works with a plain text editor and the terminal.
  • Set your screen reader’s punctuation level high enough to hear the symbols that carry meaning in Lua: braces { } that surround tables, square brackets [ ] for indexing, the length operator #, the concatenation operator .., the not-equal operator ~=, and the comment marker --.
  • Lua does not use indentation to decide structure. Blocks end with the keyword end, so each if, for, while, and function needs a matching end. Indentation is for people, and your editor’s indentation guides or announcements still help you count nesting levels.

Practise reading the example below aloud, saying each symbol: “local scores equals open brace eighty-two comma ninety-one comma seventy-six comma eighty-eight close brace.” Then say what #scores and scores[1] mean.

Worked Example

local scores = {82, 91, 76, 88}
print(string.format("count=%d first=%d last=%d", #scores, scores[1], scores[#scores]))

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

count=4 first=82 last=88

Common Mistakes

  1. Setting punctuation announcement so low that {, }, and .. are never spoken, then misreading a table or a string join.
  2. Forgetting that a Lua block closes with end, and relying on indentation alone.
  3. Installing several overlapping extensions and getting duplicate, confusing diagnostics.

Activities

  1. Test your editor with the example. Record the punctuation level at which every symbol in line 1 is announced.
  2. Navigate the file by line, then by word, then by character, and note the keyboard commands you used.
  3. Introduce a missing end in a small if block, save, and find how your editor reports the problem. Then fix it.
  4. Write a half-page note describing your edit, run, and fix cycle using only the keyboard.

Accessibility Practice

This whole lesson is accessibility practice. Verify that you can open the file, move to a given line number, read a line character by character, run the program in the terminal, and read the output. Do not describe this workflow as screen-reader tested for others; record only what you tested yourself, with the names of your operating system, editor, and access technology.

Skills Checklist

  • I can configure my editor for keyboard-only use.
  • I can hear or feel every symbol in a Lua table and string join.
  • I can explain why Lua blocks end with end.
  • I can navigate a file by line, word, and character.
  • I can run and read a program entirely from the keyboard.

Lesson 0.4: Project Environments, Dependencies, and Terminal Usage

Reading References

  • Programming in Lua, 4th edition (Roberto Ierusalimschy): Chapter 17 (Modules and Packages)
  • Lua 5.4 Reference Manual: Section 6.3 (Modules)
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 0.4 Python environments and terminal usage

Learning Objectives

  • Keep each project in its own folder and run commands from its root.
  • Load code from a second file with require and explain package.path.
  • Explain what LuaRocks is and when it is needed.

Concept Explanation

Run commands from the project root, the folder that holds your main file. Keep different projects in different folders so their files never mix.

A Lua module is a file that returns a value, usually a table of functions. The function require("name") finds the file name.lua, runs it once, and returns what it returned. Lua searches the places listed in package.path, a text value where each template uses ? as a stand-in for the module name. Adding ./?.lua; to the front tells Lua to look in the current folder first.

The standard library is enough for this course. LuaRocks is Lua’s package manager for external packages; it records a package in a rockspec file and can install either system-wide or into a local tree. Use it only when a project needs an external package, and prefer a local tree so a project does not change the whole computer.

The example below is self-contained: it writes a tiny module file, then loads it with require, so the same lesson works in an empty folder.

Worked Example

-- Create a small module file, then load it with require.
local file = assert(io.open("pricing.lua", "w"))
file:write([[
local M = {}
function M.line_total(quantity, unit_price)
  return quantity * unit_price
end
return M
]])
file:close()

package.path = "./?.lua;" .. package.path
local pricing = require("pricing")
print(pricing.line_total(3, 2.50))

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

7.5

Common Mistakes

  1. Running a program from a different folder, so require cannot find a module in the current folder.
  2. Forgetting that a module file must return its table; without it require returns true and calls such as pricing.line_total fail.
  3. Installing every package system-wide instead of keeping dependencies with the project.

Activities

  1. Run the example, then open the new pricing.lua file and read it aloud, line by line.
  2. Add a second function, line_value_with_discount, to the module and call it from the main file.
  3. Run the program from a different folder and record the error message. Explain why it happened.
  4. Print package.path and write down, in your own words, what the first template means.

Accessibility Practice

Keep one project per folder and begin every session by confirming your working directory with a command and reading the result. Read the long text in package.path with character navigation, noting where each semicolon separates one template from the next.

Skills Checklist

  • I can identify the project root and run commands from it.
  • I can load a module with require.
  • I can explain what package.path contains.
  • I can say when LuaRocks is needed.
  • I can run a program from the terminal and read its output.

Unit 1: Foundations of Computing

Overview

Turn a written algorithm into Lua, run a first program, and learn variables, values, and Lua’s dynamic types. The shared student profile appears here for the first time.

Lesson 1.1: Computer Science and Problem Solving

Reading References

  • Programming in Lua, 4th edition (Roberto Ierusalimschy): Chapter 1 (Getting Started)
  • Zelle: Chapter 1, pages 1-7 (shared with the Python track)
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 1.1 Welcome to Computer Science

Learning Objectives

  • Explain hardware, software, and algorithms in your own words.
  • Turn a written algorithm into a short Lua program.
  • Predict a program’s output by hand before running it.

Concept Explanation

Computers follow instructions exactly. Hardware is the physical machine; software is the set of instructions it follows; an algorithm is an ordered, finite list of clear steps that solves a problem. The foundations unit of this repository (Unit P) covers these ideas in detail.

Computer science is mainly about solving problems, and programming is how a solution is carried out. A reliable approach is to understand the problem, break it into small steps, write the algorithm in plain language, translate it into code, and test it.

Here the algorithm is: “set a total to zero; for each score, add it to the total; divide the total by the number of scores; report both.” Lua’s local keyword creates a variable that exists only in its block, for ... in ipairs(...) visits a list in order, and # gives the length of a list.

The scores 82, 91, 76, and 88 are the course’s shared data. Their total is 337 and their average is 84.25. A hand trace should reach the same numbers before the program is run.

Worked Example

-- Algorithm: total and average of the shared scores.
local scores = {82, 91, 76, 88}
local total = 0
for _, score in ipairs(scores) do
  total = total + score
end
local average = total / #scores
print(string.format("Total: %d", total))
print(string.format("Average: %.2f", average))

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Total: 337
Average: 84.25

Common Mistakes

  1. Starting to code before writing the steps, then forgetting the step that divides by the number of scores.
  2. Writing local total without giving it a value, so the first addition fails on nil.
  3. Using / and expecting a whole number. In Lua 5.4, / always produces a float.

Activities

  1. Trace the program by hand, writing the running total after each score: 82, 173, 249, 337.
  2. Change the list to {90, 80} and predict the total and average before running.
  3. Add a line that reports the highest score using a second loop.
  4. Explain, in two sentences, the difference between the algorithm and the Lua program.

Accessibility Practice

Write your hand trace as numbered sentences, one per loop step, rather than as a table, and read it back with your screen reader. Compare it with the program’s printed lines in order.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define hardware, software, and algorithm.
  • I can describe an algorithm as ordered steps.
  • I can trace a loop by hand.
  • I can read a short Lua program aloud.
  • I can run it and compare the output with my trace.

Lesson 1.2: Your First Lua Program

Reading References

  • Programming in Lua, 4th edition (Roberto Ierusalimschy): Chapter 1 (Getting Started)
  • Lua 5.4 Reference Manual: Section 3.1 (Blocks) and Section 3.3.5 (For Statement)
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 1.2 Your First Python Program - Hello World

Learning Objectives

  • Write and run a program that prints text.
  • Use comments to document code.
  • Explain that Lua executes statements in order, top to bottom.

Concept Explanation

A Lua program is a sequence of statements that run in order. print is a built-in function that writes its arguments to the terminal. Text in quotation marks is a string. Single or double quotes both work, and a string written with double square brackets, [[ ... ]], can span several lines.

A line comment starts with -- and runs to the end of the line; Lua ignores it. A long comment starts with --[[ and ends with ]].

print separates multiple arguments with a tab character. io.write writes exactly what you give it with nothing added, so a new line must be written as the escape sequence \n. Knowing the difference matters because a screen reader may read a tab as a pause, and because exact output is easier to test.

Worked Example

-- This program prints a greeting for the shared student.
print("Hello, Avery!")
print("Welcome to Lua programming!")
io.write("No new line here, ")
io.write("then one here.\n")
print("a", "b", "c")

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Hello, Avery!
Welcome to Lua programming!
No new line here, then one here.
a	b	c

Common Mistakes

  1. Using a curly quotation mark pasted from a document instead of a straight quotation mark, which causes a syntax error.
  2. Expecting io.write to add a new line the way print does.
  3. Writing print 'Hello' with a missing space or quotation mark and misreading the resulting error.

Activities

  1. Run the program and describe in words how the last line differs from the line before it.
  2. Change the greeting to use your own name and predict the output.
  3. Write a program that prints three lines: your name, the course name, and today’s task.
  4. Add a comment above each line and read the file aloud with comments included.

Accessibility Practice

Run the file from the terminal and read the output in order. Note that a, b, and c on the last line are separated by tab characters; check whether your screen reader announces them.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write and run a program that prints text.
  • I can write a line comment.
  • I can explain how print and io.write differ.
  • I can say that statements run in order.
  • I can read a first error message.

Lesson 1.3: Variables, Values, and Dynamic Types

Reading References

  • Programming in Lua, 4th edition (Roberto Ierusalimschy): Chapter 3 (Numbers), Chapter 4 (Strings)
  • Lua 5.4 Reference Manual: Section 2.1 (Values and Types)
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 1.3 Variables and Simple Data Types

Learning Objectives

  • Create local variables and assign values.
  • Name the basic Lua types and check a value’s type.
  • Explain nil and the difference between local and global variables.

Concept Explanation

A variable is a name that refers to a value. In Lua, variables do not have types; values do. The same variable may refer to a number now and a string later. The basic types are nil, boolean, number, string, table, and function. The function type(value) returns the type name as a string.

Lua 5.4 numbers have two subtypes: integer (whole numbers such as 16) and float (numbers with a decimal point such as 1.72). math.type(value) reports integer or float.

Always declare variables with local. A variable assigned without local becomes a global variable visible to the whole program, which is a common source of hard-to-find bugs. A variable that has never been assigned has the value nil, which means “no value.”

The shared student profile is name Avery, age 16, height 1.72 meters, and favorite subject Computer Science. The shared inventory item Notebook has quantity 3 and unit price 2.50, so three notebooks cost 7.5.

Worked Example

local name = "Avery"
local age = 16
local height = 1.72
local favorite_subject = "Computer Science"

print(name, age, height, favorite_subject)
print(type(name), type(age), type(height), type(favorite_subject))
print(math.type(age), math.type(height))

local notebook_price = 2.50
local notebook_quantity = 3
print("Notebook total:", notebook_price * notebook_quantity)

local missing
print(missing, type(missing))

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Avery	16	1.72	Computer Science
string	number	number	string
integer	float
Notebook total:	7.5
nil	nil

Common Mistakes

  1. Forgetting local, which silently creates a global variable that other code can change.
  2. Expecting Lua to report an error for an unassigned variable. It simply has the value nil.
  3. Confusing = (assignment) with == (comparison).

Activities

  1. Run the example and write down each type name in the order it was printed.
  2. Change age to 16.0 and predict what math.type(age) prints.
  3. Add a boolean variable likes_cs set to true and print its type.
  4. Explain, without code, why type(nil) is the string nil while a missing variable’s value is the value nil.

Accessibility Practice

Read the variable names aloud as part of each line, for example ‘local favorite underscore subject’. Check that your screen reader pauses at the underscore so you can tell favorite_subject from two words.

Skills Checklist

  • I can declare local variables and assign values.
  • I can name Lua’s basic types.
  • I can use type and math.type.
  • I can explain nil.
  • I can explain why local matters.

Concept Explanation

Plan, implement, and test the same tip-calculator problem. Separate input values from the calculation and presentation.

Worked Example

local bill_cents = 2450
local tip_rate_percent = 15
-- Integer arithmetic avoids binary floating-point rounding errors.
local tip_cents = (bill_cents * tip_rate_percent + 50) // 100
local total_cents = bill_cents + tip_cents
print(string.format("Tip: $%.2f", tip_cents / 100))
print(string.format("Total: $%.2f", total_cents / 100))

Expected Behavior or Output

Tip: $3.68
Total: $28.18
```8.18

Common Mistakes

  • Using binary floating-point display rounding as a substitute for a currency-rounding policy.
  • Skipping parentheses when operator precedence is not obvious.
  • Assuming tonumber succeeds for every string.
