Learning Objectives

  • Explain the concept using Lua terminology.
  • Trace the worked example and predict its behavior.
  • Modify and test the example while preserving the shared data contract.

Concept Explanation

A command-line application needs explicit help, validation, confirmations, and readable errors. Keep all critical information in text.

Worked Example

local function validate_title(title)
  if title == nil or title:match("^%s*$") then
    return false, "Title is required; enter at least one non-space character."
  end
  return true, "Title accepted."
end
local ok, message = validate_title("   ")
print(message)

Expected Behavior or Output

Title is required; enter at least one non-space character.

Common Mistakes

  • Copying a Python assumption into Lua without checking the Lua 5.4 semantics.
  • Changing the canonical input values and then comparing output against the shared fixture.
  • Skipping a negative or boundary case for the lesson’s main operation.

Activities

  1. Trace the 10.5 Refinement and Accessibility worked example and explain each statement in Lua terms.
  2. Change one noncanonical test value while keeping the shared fixture intact; predict the result before execution.
  3. Add a boundary or invalid-input test for the main operation in this lesson.
  4. Explain one semantic difference between Lua and Python that affects 10.5 refinement and accessibility.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate by line, word, and character; identify delimiters and nesting verbally; execute from the terminal; and read the output and any error messages sequentially. Do not rely on syntax highlighting or color to understand the example.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain the concept in Lua terminology.
  • I can trace and predict the example’s behavior.
  • I can run and modify the example from the terminal.
  • I can test a boundary or invalid case.
  • I can explain the relevant Lua-specific semantic difference.

Overview

Plan a text project, build the shared text adventure in two parts, build the command-line to-do manager, and refine input validation.

Lesson 10.1: Planning a Text-Based Project

Reading References

  • Programming in Lua, 4th edition (Roberto Ierusalimschy): Chapter 6 (Functions) and Chapter 5 (Tables)
  • Lua 5.4 Reference Manual: Section 3.3 (Statements)
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 10.1 Project Planning and Design

Learning Objectives

  • Write a short requirements list.
  • Design a command loop with a table of handlers.
  • Plan in small steps and test each one.

Concept Explanation

A project is easier to finish when you plan it in small steps. Write down what the program must do (requirements), what information it keeps (data), and the commands a person can give (interface). Build one small piece, test it, and then add the next.

Text-based projects share a command loop: show a prompt, read a line, find the matching action, and repeat until the user quits. A good Lua design stores actions in a table whose keys are command names and whose values are functions. A new command is then one new entry, and an unknown command is a failed lookup that prints a helpful message.

The loop must stop when the input ends (nil) as well as on quit.

The example is a skeleton with three commands. Typing help, look, an unknown word, and quit shows each path.

Worked Example

local commands = {
  help = function() print("Commands: help, look, quit") end,
  look = function() print("You are in a dark cave.") end,
}

print("Type a command:")
local line = io.read()
while line ~= nil and line ~= "quit" do
  local handler = commands[line]
  if handler then
    handler()
  else
    print("I don't understand that command. Type help for a list.")
  end
  print("Type a command:")
  line = io.read()
end
print("Goodbye!")

Expected Behavior or Output

When the standard input is the following lines (the program’s own prompts and results are shown separately because piped input is not echoed):

help
look
dance
quit

the program prints:

Type a command:
Commands: help, look, quit
Type a command:
You are in a dark cave.
Type a command:
I don't understand that command. Type help for a list.
Type a command:
Goodbye!

Common Mistakes

  1. Starting to code before listing the requirements.
  2. Using a long chain of if statements for commands instead of a table of handlers.
  3. Forgetting that an unknown command should explain what to do next.

Activities

  1. Write five requirements for the text adventure and the to-do list.
  2. Add a score command that prints the shared scores.
  3. Add the command aliases h and l without copying the functions.
  4. Describe the data for the capstone in three sentences.

Accessibility Practice

Prompts and responses are on separate lines and every response is a complete sentence. Test the prompts by listening to them before you add features.

Skills Checklist

  • I can list requirements.
  • I can design a command loop.
  • I can use a table of handlers.
  • I handle unknown commands.
  • I handle the end of input.

Lesson 10.2: Text Adventure, Part 1: Rooms and Movement

Reading References

  • Programming in Lua, 4th edition (Roberto Ierusalimschy): Chapter 5 (Tables)
  • Lua 5.4 Reference Manual: Section 3.4.9 (Table Constructors)
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 10.2 Building a Text-Based Adventure Game (Part 1)

Learning Objectives

  • Represent rooms and exits with tables.
  • Move the player by command.
  • Handle impossible moves and the end of input.

Concept Explanation

A room is a table with a description and an exits table that maps a direction to the name of another room. The program remembers the player’s location in one variable, current_room. A move looks up the command in the current room’s exits; if it is found, current_room changes, otherwise the program explains that the move is impossible.

This is the same three-room layout as the Python course: a cave, a tunnel, and a clearing. Part 2 adds items and a locked door.

The example is played with the commands north, east, west, up, south, and quit. The command up is not an exit anywhere, so it prints the help message.

Worked Example

local rooms = {
  start_room = {
    description = "You are in a dimly lit cave. There's a narrow passage to the NORTH.",
    exits = {north = "tunnel"},
  },
  tunnel = {
    description = "The tunnel is damp and cold. You can go SOUTH back to the cave or EAST to a clearing.",
    exits = {south = "start_room", east = "clearing"},
  },
  clearing = {
    description = "You've reached a small, sunny clearing. A faint path leads WEST.",
    exits = {west = "tunnel"},
  },
}

local current_room = "start_room"

while true do
  print("---")
  print(rooms[current_room].description)
  print("What do you want to do?")
  local command = io.read()
  if command == nil then command = "quit" end
  command = command:lower()

  if rooms[current_room].exits[command] then
    current_room = rooms[current_room].exits[command]
  elseif command == "quit" then
    print("Exiting game. Goodbye!")
    break
  else
    print("I don't understand that command or you can't go that way.")
  end
end

Expected Behavior or Output

When the standard input is the following lines (the program’s own prompts and results are shown separately because piped input is not echoed):

north
east
west
up
south
quit

the program prints:

---
You are in a dimly lit cave. There's a narrow passage to the NORTH.
What do you want to do?
---
The tunnel is damp and cold. You can go SOUTH back to the cave or EAST to a clearing.
What do you want to do?
---
You've reached a small, sunny clearing. A faint path leads WEST.
What do you want to do?
---
The tunnel is damp and cold. You can go SOUTH back to the cave or EAST to a clearing.
What do you want to do?
I don't understand that command or you can't go that way.
---
The tunnel is damp and cold. You can go SOUTH back to the cave or EAST to a clearing.
What do you want to do?
---
You are in a dimly lit cave. There's a narrow passage to the NORTH.
What do you want to do?
Exiting game. Goodbye!

Common Mistakes

  1. Looking up a direction that is not in exits and expecting an error. The lookup returns nil, which is the signal to explain the move is impossible.
  2. Forgetting to treat the end of input as quit, so the program loops forever when input is piped in.
  3. Misspelling a room name in exits, so the move leads to a room that does not exist.

Activities

  1. Trace the six commands by hand and write the room after each one.
  2. Add a fourth room reached from the clearing and test it.
  3. Add the aliases n, s, e, and w.
  4. Check that every exit names a real room by writing a loop that tests the whole table.

Accessibility Practice

Each turn prints a separator line, the description, and the prompt on its own line. Listen to a whole turn to confirm that a player could follow it without seeing the screen.

Skills Checklist

  • I can represent rooms with tables.
  • I can move the player by command.
  • I can handle an impossible move.
  • I treat end of input as quit.
  • I can trace a game by hand.

Lesson 10.3: Text Adventure, Part 2: Items and a Locked Door

Reading References

  • Programming in Lua, 4th edition (Roberto Ierusalimschy): Chapter 5 (Tables) and Chapter 6 (Functions)
  • Lua 5.4 Reference Manual: Section 6.6 (Table Manipulation)
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 10.3 Building a Text-Based Adventure Game (Part 2)

Learning Objectives

  • Keep items in rooms and in an inventory.
  • Implement take and use commands.
  • Block and then allow a move with a locked door.

Concept Explanation

Part 2 adds state: items in rooms, an inventory, and a door that is locked until the player uses the key. This is the shared specification used by every language track: three rooms (start, locked_door_room, treasure_room); the commands north, south, east, west, take shiny key, use shiny key, and quit; the door between the chamber and the treasure room stays locked until the key is used there; reaching the treasure room ends the game.

Items are lists of names. Taking an item removes it from the room’s list and appends it to the inventory. The locked door is a Boolean variable, door_locked. A move through the door checks it first.

The program is played with: north (into the chamber), north (the locked door refuses), south, take shiny key, north, use shiny key, north (the treasure room).

Worked Example

local rooms = {
  start = {
    description = "A dark cave.",
    exits = {north = "locked_door_room"},
    items = {"shiny key"},
  },
  locked_door_room = {
    description = "A small chamber with a heavy door to the NORTH.",
    exits = {south = "start", north = "treasure_room"},
    items = {},
  },
  treasure_room = {
    description = "A glittering room full of treasure. You win!",
    exits = {south = "locked_door_room"},
    items = {},
  },
}

local function index_of(list, value)
  for index, item in ipairs(list) do
    if item == value then return index end
  end
  return nil
end

local current_room = "start"
local inventory = {}
local door_locked = true

while true do
  local room = rooms[current_room]
  print("")
  print(room.description)
  if current_room == "treasure_room" then break end
  if #room.items > 0 then print("You see: " .. table.concat(room.items, ", ")) end
  print("Your inventory: " .. (#inventory > 0 and table.concat(inventory, ", ") or "empty"))
  print("What do you want to do?")

  local command = io.read()
  if command == nil then command = "quit" end
  command = command:lower()

  if command == "take shiny key" and index_of(room.items, "shiny key") then
    table.remove(room.items, index_of(room.items, "shiny key"))
    inventory[#inventory + 1] = "shiny key"
    print("You picked up the shiny key.")
  elseif command == "use shiny key" and current_room == "locked_door_room" and index_of(inventory, "shiny key") then
    door_locked = false
    print("You unlocked the door!")
  elseif room.exits[command] then
    if current_room == "locked_door_room" and command == "north" and door_locked then
      print("The door is locked! You need a key.")
    else
      current_room = room.exits[command]
    end
  elseif command == "quit" then
    print("Exiting game. Goodbye!")
    break
  else
    print("I don't understand that command.")
  end
end

Expected Behavior or Output

When the standard input is the following lines (the program’s own prompts and results are shown separately because piped input is not echoed):

north
north
south
take shiny key
north
use shiny key
north

the program prints:


A dark cave.
You see: shiny key
Your inventory: empty
What do you want to do?

A small chamber with a heavy door to the NORTH.
Your inventory: empty
What do you want to do?
The door is locked! You need a key.

A small chamber with a heavy door to the NORTH.
Your inventory: empty
What do you want to do?

A dark cave.
You see: shiny key
Your inventory: empty
What do you want to do?
You picked up the shiny key.

A dark cave.
Your inventory: shiny key
What do you want to do?

A small chamber with a heavy door to the NORTH.
Your inventory: shiny key
What do you want to do?
You unlocked the door!

A small chamber with a heavy door to the NORTH.
Your inventory: shiny key
What do you want to do?

A glittering room full of treasure. You win!

Common Mistakes

  1. Making the door’s locked state part of the exits so that the “locked” message can never be reached.
  2. Defining an exit to a room that is missing from the rooms table, which crashes when the player arrives.
  3. Printing a fixed room description that still mentions an item after the player has taken it.

Activities

  1. Play the program with the shown commands and follow each turn on paper.
  2. Try use shiny key in the cave and describe what happens.
  3. Add a second item and require both to open the door.
  4. Write a short list of the game’s states (location, inventory, door) and say which command changes each.

Accessibility Practice

The room description never mentions the key. The separate line ‘You see:’ lists items, so the description stays true after the key is taken and the screen reader announces the current state.

Skills Checklist

  • I can store items in rooms and an inventory.
  • I can implement take and use commands.
  • I can block and allow a move.
  • I can list the game’s state variables.
  • I can keep descriptions true after state changes.

Lesson 10.4: Command-Line To-Do List

Reading References

  • Programming in Lua, 4th edition (Roberto Ierusalimschy): Chapter 15 (Data Files and Serialization)
  • Lua 5.4 Reference Manual: Section 6.8 (Input and Output Facilities)
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 10.4 Building a Command-Line To-Do List

Learning Objectives

  • Keep records with the shared fields.
  • Save and load them as JSON.
  • Offer add, view, mark-done, save, load, and quit commands.

Concept Explanation

A to-do list ties together records, loops, functions, and files. Each task has the shared fields id, title, description, done, and created_at. The program keeps a list of tasks in memory, shows a numbered menu, and saves the list to todos.json when asked and on exit.

Saving uses the teaching JSON helper from Lesson 8.5 (included here so the example runs on its own). On start-up the program loads the file if it exists. A missing file is normal on first use, and a damaged file must not crash the program: it prints a message and starts with an empty list.

New ids are one more than the highest existing id, so ids stay unique even after a task is removed. The status is shown as the words done and not done, never with a symbol or color alone.

In the sample session the user adds two tasks, views the list, marks task 2 as done, views it again, tries an invalid menu choice, views the list, and quits.

Worked Example

local json = {}

local escapes = {['"'] = '\\"', ['\\'] = '\\\\', ['\n'] = '\\n', ['\r'] = '\\r', ['\t'] = '\\t'}

function json.encode(value)
  local kind = type(value)
  if kind == "string" then
    return '"' .. value:gsub('[%c"\\]', function(c)
      return escapes[c] or string.format("\\u%04x", c:byte())
    end) .. '"'
  elseif kind == "number" then
    return math.type(value) == "integer" and tostring(value) or string.format("%.14g", value)
  elseif kind == "boolean" then
    return tostring(value)
  elseif kind == "nil" then
    return "null"
  elseif kind == "table" then
    local parts = {}
    if value[1] ~= nil or next(value) == nil then
      for _, item in ipairs(value) do parts[#parts + 1] = json.encode(item) end
      return "[" .. table.concat(parts, ",") .. "]"
    end
    local keys = {}
    for key in pairs(value) do keys[#keys + 1] = key end
    table.sort(keys)
    for _, key in ipairs(keys) do
      parts[#parts + 1] = json.encode(tostring(key)) .. ":" .. json.encode(value[key])
    end
    return "{" .. table.concat(parts, ",") .. "}"
  end
  error("cannot encode a value of type " .. kind, 0)
end

function json.decode(text)
  local position = 1
  local read_value

  local function skip()
    position = text:find("%S", position) or #text + 1
  end

  local function fail(message)
    error(message .. " at position " .. position, 0)
  end

  local function read_string()
    local pieces = {}
    position = position + 1
    while true do
      local c = text:sub(position, position)
      if c == "" then fail("unterminated string") end
      if c == '"' then
        position = position + 1
        return table.concat(pieces)
      elseif c == "\\" then
        local n = text:sub(position + 1, position + 1)
        local simple = {n = "\n", t = "\t", r = "\r", ['"'] = '"', ["\\"] = "\\", ["/"] = "/"}
        if n == "u" then
          pieces[#pieces + 1] = utf8.char(tonumber(text:sub(position + 2, position + 5), 16))
          position = position + 6
        elseif simple[n] then
          pieces[#pieces + 1] = simple[n]
          position = position + 2
        else
          fail("bad escape")
        end
      else
        pieces[#pieces + 1] = c
        position = position + 1
      end
    end
  end

  function read_value()
    skip()
    local c = text:sub(position, position)
    if c == "{" then
      local object = {}
      position = position + 1
      skip()
      if text:sub(position, position) == "}" then position = position + 1; return object end
      while true do
        skip()
        if text:sub(position, position) ~= '"' then fail("expected a key") end
        local key = read_string()
        skip()
        if text:sub(position, position) ~= ":" then fail("expected ':'") end
        position = position + 1
        object[key] = read_value()
        skip()
        local d = text:sub(position, position)
        position = position + 1
        if d == "}" then return object end
        if d ~= "," then position = position - 1; fail("expected ',' or '}'") end
      end
    elseif c == "[" then
      local list = {}
      position = position + 1
      skip()
      if text:sub(position, position) == "]" then position = position + 1; return list end
      while true do
        list[#list + 1] = read_value()
        skip()
        local d = text:sub(position, position)
        position = position + 1
        if d == "]" then return list end
        if d ~= "," then position = position - 1; fail("expected ',' or ']'") end
      end
    elseif c == '"' then
      return read_string()
    elseif text:find("^true", position) then
      position = position + 4; return true
    elseif text:find("^false", position) then
      position = position + 5; return false
    elseif text:find("^null", position) then
      position = position + 4; return nil
    end
    local number = text:match("^-?%d+%.?%d*[eE]?[+-]?%d*", position)
    if not number or number == "" then fail("unexpected character") end
    position = position + #number
    return tonumber(number)
  end

  local result = read_value()
  skip()
  if position <= #text then fail("unexpected extra text") end
  return result
end

local TODO_FILE = "todos.json"
local todos = {}

local function load_todos()
  local file = io.open(TODO_FILE, "r")
  if not file then
    print("No existing tasks found.")
    todos = {}
    return
  end
  local text = file:read("a")
  file:close()
  local ok, data = pcall(json.decode, text)
  if ok and type(data) == "table" then
    todos = data
    print("Tasks loaded.")
  else
    print("Error: todos.json is not valid JSON. Starting with an empty list.")
    todos = {}
  end
end

local function save_todos()
  local file = assert(io.open(TODO_FILE, "w"))
  file:write(json.encode(todos))
  file:close()
  print("Tasks saved.")
end

local function next_id()
  local highest = 0
  for _, task in ipairs(todos) do
    if task.id > highest then highest = task.id end
  end
  return highest + 1
end

local function add_task(title, description)
  title = (title or ""):match("^%s*(.-)%s*$")
  if title == "" then
    print("A title is required.")
    return
  end
  todos[#todos + 1] = {
    id = next_id(),
    title = title,
    description = (description or ""):match("^%s*(.-)%s*$"),
    done = false,
    created_at = os.date("!%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S"),
  }
  print("Task '" .. title .. "' added.")
end

local function view_tasks()
  if #todos == 0 then
    print("No tasks in your list.")
    return
  end
  print("--- Your To-Do List ---")
  for _, task in ipairs(todos) do
    print(string.format("%d. %s (%s)", task.id, task.title, task.done and "done" or "not done"))
  end
  print("-----------------------")
end

local function mark_done(text)
  local id = tonumber(text)
  if not id then
    print("Please enter a whole number.")
    return
  end
  for _, task in ipairs(todos) do
    if task.id == id then
      task.done = true
      print("Task '" .. task.title .. "' marked as done.")
      return
    end
  end
  print("No task has that number.")
end

local function show_menu()
  print("")
  print("--- To-Do List Menu ---")
  print("1. Add Task")
  print("2. View Tasks")
  print("3. Mark Task Done")
  print("4. Save Tasks")
  print("5. Load Tasks")
  print("6. Quit")
  print("-----------------------")
end

load_todos()
while true do
  show_menu()
  print("Enter your choice (1-6):")
  local choice = io.read()
  if choice == nil then choice = "6" end

  if choice == "1" then
    print("Enter task title:")
    local title = io.read()
    print("Enter task description:")
    local description = io.read()
    add_task(title, description)
  elseif choice == "2" then
    view_tasks()
  elseif choice == "3" then
    view_tasks()
    print("Enter task number to mark done:")
    mark_done(io.read())
  elseif choice == "4" then
    save_todos()
  elseif choice == "5" then
    load_todos()
  elseif choice == "6" then
    save_todos()
    print("Goodbye!")
    break
  else
    print("Invalid choice. Please try again.")
  end
end

Common Mistakes

  1. Saving the file but never loading it, so tasks disappear between runs.
  2. Reusing a deleted task’s id, which can confuse saved references.
  3. Letting a damaged todos.json crash the program instead of printing a message.

Activities

  1. Run the sample session and then run the program again with the input 2 then 6 to see the saved tasks.
  2. Add a command to delete a task by number.
  3. Open todos.json and read the saved text. Edit it to remove a bracket and rerun.
  4. Add a description display to the view command.

Accessibility Practice

Every menu is printed as numbered lines and each prompt is on its own line. The status words are done and not done, not symbols, so the list reads clearly in speech and braille.

Lesson 10.5: User Experience and Input Validation

Reading References

  • Programming in Lua, 4th edition (Roberto Ierusalimschy): Chapter 6 (Functions) and Chapter 16 (Compilation, Execution, and Errors)
  • Lua 5.4 Reference Manual: Section 6.8 (io.read)
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 10.5 Refining User Experience and Validation

Learning Objectives

  • Write reusable validation functions.
  • Limit retries and handle the end of input.
  • Write clear, accessible messages.

Concept Explanation

Reusable validation functions make every menu and form consistent. ask_number(prompt, low, high, attempts) prints a prompt, reads a line, converts it, checks the range, and either returns the number or explains the problem and asks again. After the allowed attempts, or at the end of input, it returns nil and a reason. ask_yes_no(prompt) accepts y, yes, n, and no, in any letter case.

Good messages say what was wrong and what to do: “Enter a whole number from 0 to 100,” not “Invalid.” They never depend on color, position, or symbols alone, and they use the same wording every time.

The example reads a score with the typed lines abc, 105, and 88, then asks a yes or no question with the lines maybe and y.

Worked Example

local function ask_number(prompt, low, high, attempts)
  for attempt = 1, attempts do
    print(prompt)
    local text = io.read()
    if text == nil then return nil, "No more input." end
    local number = tonumber(text)
    if number and number == math.floor(number) and number >= low and number <= high then
      return math.tointeger(number)
    end
    print(string.format("Enter a whole number from %d to %d. You have %d attempt(s) left.", low, high, attempts - attempt))
  end
  return nil, "Too many invalid attempts."
end

local function ask_yes_no(prompt)
  while true do
    print(prompt .. " (yes or no)")
    local text = io.read()
    if text == nil then return nil end
    text = text:lower()
    if text == "y" or text == "yes" then return true end
    if text == "n" or text == "no" then return false end
    print("Please answer yes or no.")
  end
end

local score, reason = ask_number("Enter a score from 0 to 100:", 0, 100, 3)
if score then
  print("Accepted score: " .. score)
else
  print("No score: " .. reason)
end

local keep = ask_yes_no("Save this score?")
print("Save answer:", keep)

Expected Behavior or Output

When the standard input is the following lines (the program’s own prompts and results are shown separately because piped input is not echoed):

abc
105
88
maybe
y

the program prints:

Enter a score from 0 to 100:
Enter a whole number from 0 to 100. You have 2 attempt(s) left.
Enter a score from 0 to 100:
Enter a whole number from 0 to 100. You have 1 attempt(s) left.
Enter a score from 0 to 100:
Accepted score: 88
Save this score? (yes or no)
Please answer yes or no.
Save this score? (yes or no)
Save answer:	true

Common Mistakes

  1. Writing the message “Invalid” without saying what is valid.
  2. Accepting a decimal such as 88.5 for a field that requires a whole number.
  3. Looping forever on bad input instead of limiting attempts.

Activities

  1. Run the sample input and read each message aloud.
  2. Run with three invalid numbers and read the final message.
  3. Add a function ask_text(prompt) that rejects empty answers.
  4. Rewrite two messages from earlier lessons so they say what to do next.

Accessibility Practice

Check that every error message ends with an action the user can take, and that the same situation always produces the same words.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write reusable validation functions.
  • I limit retries.
  • I handle the end of input.
  • I write messages that say what to do.
  • I keep wording consistent.

Lesson 11.3 Create, Read, Update, Delete

Reading References

  • Lua 5.4 Reference Manual: https://www.lua.org/manual/5.4/
  • Programming in Lua: https://www.lua.org/pil/
  • Corresponding Python lesson in the canonical course map.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the concept using Lua terminology.
  • Trace the worked example and predict its behavior.
  • Modify and test the example while preserving the shared data contract.

Concept Explanation

Implement CRUD as separate functions. Updating a record should also update updated_at; deleting a missing ID should return a clear status.

Worked Example

local records = {{
  id = 1,
  title = "Programming notes",
  description = "Review lists and dictionaries",
  category = "Study",
  created_at = "2025-01-15T09:00:00Z",
  updated_at = "2025-01-15T09:00:00Z"
}}
local function find_record(id)
  for _, record in ipairs(records) do
    if record.id == id then return record end
  end
  return nil
end
local function update_title(id, title, updated_at)
  local record = find_record(id)
  if not record then return false end
  record.title = title
  record.updated_at = updated_at
  return true
end
local function delete_record(id)
  for index, record in ipairs(records) do
    if record.id == id then
      table.remove(records, index)
      return true
    end
  end
  return false
end
local found = find_record(1)
print("Found:", found.title, found.category)
print("Updated:", update_title(1, "Revised notes", "2025-01-16T09:00:00Z"))
print("Updated title:", records[1].title)
print("Deleted:", delete_record(1))
print("Missing delete:", delete_record(9))

Expected Behavior or Output

Found:	Programming notes	Study
Updated:	true
Updated title:	Revised notes
Deleted:	true
Missing delete:	false

Common Mistakes

  • Copying a Python assumption into Lua without checking the Lua 5.4 semantics.
  • Changing the canonical input values and then comparing output against the shared fixture.
  • Skipping a negative or boundary case for the lesson’s main operation.

Activities

  1. Trace the 11.3 Create, Read, Update, Delete worked example and explain each statement in Lua terms.
  2. Change one noncanonical test value while keeping the shared fixture intact; predict the result before execution.
  3. Add a boundary or invalid-input test for the main operation in this lesson.
  4. Explain one semantic difference between Lua and Python that affects 11.3 create, read, update, delete.

Lesson 11.4 Validation and Tests

Reading References

  • Lua 5.4 Reference Manual: https://www.lua.org/manual/5.4/

Concept Explanation

Test required fields, duplicate identifiers, not-found behavior, and persistence failures. Assertions should verify results, not merely execute examples.

Worked Example

local function valid_record(record)
  return type(record.id) == "number"
    and type(record.title) == "string" and record.title ~= ""
    and type(record.description) == "string"
    and type(record.category) == "string"
    and type(record.created_at) == "string"
    and type(record.updated_at) == "string"
end
assert(valid_record({id=1,title="A",description="B",category="C",created_at="now",updated_at="now"}))
print("record validation passed")

Canonical shared data contract

The following values must remain identical to the Python source and the other general-purpose tracks:

  • Student: Avery, age 16, height 1.72 meters, favorite subject Computer Science.
  • Calculator: bill 24.50, tip rate 0.15; round half-up to the nearest cent; tip displays as $3.68 and total as $28.18.
  • Grade thresholds: A ≥ 90, B ≥ 80, C ≥ 70, D ≥ 60, otherwise F. Scores: 82, 91, 76, 88; total 337; average 84.25.
  • Inventory: Notebook (3 at $2.50), Pencil (10 at $0.50), Folder (4 at $1.25); total $17.50.
  • Coordinates: (3, 4); distance from origin 5.
  • Text: A student studies programming. Programming develops problem-solving skills.
  • CSV fields: student_id, first_name, last_name, score, active.
  • To-do fields: id, title, description, done, created_at.
  • Capstone fields: id, title, description, category, created_at, updated_at.

Course projects and acceptance criteria

The text adventure uses the shared five-room graph: start_room (north → tunnel, shiny key), tunnel (south → start_room, east → clearing), clearing (west → tunnel, north → locked_door_room), locked_door_room (south → clearing, north → treasure_room only after unlocking), and terminal treasure_room. The player takes the shiny key in start_room, travels to locked_door_room, uses the key there, and enters treasure_room to win. Commands are north, south, east, west, take shiny key, use shiny key, and quit. The command-line to-do manager must implement create, list, update/complete, delete, save, and load with all five canonical fields. The capstone must implement list/display, add, search, update, delete, and persistence for the six-field record. A terminal interface is acceptable for Lua, but the data model, operations, acceptance tests, and keyboard/text accessibility requirements remain equivalent.

AI and assessment integrity

AI must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, or generate course code or assessment solutions. Students may use only instructor-authorized conceptual explanations that do not produce deliverable code. Do not recommend AI-generated code as a workflow or as a first draft.

Validation status

The earlier smoke-execution result applies only to the previous version of this file. The current checker now compares exact stdout for all 53 lesson examples; run the updated Lua 5.4 workflow and complete end-to-end project/persistence tests before marking the projects verified.

Introduction to Computer Science with Python

Before you start: complete Unit P: Computing Foundations Primer. It explains the language-neutral vocabulary and concepts used in every language track, using non-visual examples.

Accessible beginner curriculum

The Python curriculum is a complete introductory pathway in programming and core computer science. It is designed to be usable by blind and visually impaired learners who use screen readers, braille displays, magnification, keyboard navigation, or combinations of access technologies. It is also suitable for sighted beginners and mixed-vision classrooms.

Python is a practical first language for many learners because it has compact syntax, an interactive interpreter, and a broad standard library. The course uses those strengths to teach problem-solving rather than treating programming as memorizing commands.

Recommended sequence: complete Units 0–11 in order. The unit files group related units for navigation; use the headings and lesson numbers within each file.

Course outcomes

By the end of the curriculum, learners should be able to:

  • Explain basic computer science concepts and the iterative software-development process.
  • Configure a Python environment and use an editor, terminal, and interactive interpreter.
  • Write, run, read, and modify programs using variables, built-in types, expressions, and input/output.
  • Use Boolean expressions, conditionals, and loops to control program behavior.
  • Work with strings, lists, tuples, dictionaries, and common collection operations.
  • Design and call functions with parameters and return values.
  • Explain and implement introductory classes, objects, attributes, methods, and inheritance.
  • Read and write files, handle exceptions, and organize program behavior.
  • Apply introductory testing and data-analysis techniques.
  • Plan, implement, test, and explain text-based projects and a capstone application.
  • Evaluate prompts, messages, and output for clarity when consumed sequentially with assistive technology.

These outcomes represent introductory proficiency, not mastery of every part of Python.

Prerequisites and intended learners

No previous programming experience is required. Learners need access to a computer on which Python can be installed or provided, a keyboard-accessible development environment, and a way to run terminal commands. Basic file management and keyboard navigation are helpful.

Screen-reader fluency and programming readiness are separate skills. A student who needs additional time to navigate an editor may still understand algorithms and programming concepts. Teachers can teach access workflows alongside programming; see the Python teacher’s guide.

Learning sequence

UnitMain topicsEvidence of progress
0. Accessible setupPython installation, Visual Studio Code, screen-reader configuration, workspace, terminal, and environmentsOpen a project, create a file, run a program, and locate output
1. FoundationsComputer science, hardware and software, problem solving, first program, variables, and basic typesExplain a simple program and identify its values and statements
2. Numeric programsSoftware-development cycle, expressions, assignment, input/output, conversion, math operations, and formatted outputDesign and run a small interactive calculation
3. Control flowBoolean expressions, conditionals, lists, loops, and string operationsExpress decisions and repetition and predict execution
4. Data structuresList operations, tuples, dictionaries, and organizing informationSelect and manipulate a suitable collection
5. Input and iterationValidating user input and using while loops for repeated interactionBuild a robust text-based interaction loop
6. FunctionsDecomposition, parameters, return values, scope, and reusable logicDivide a problem into named, testable operations
7. Object-oriented programmingClasses, objects, attributes, methods, and inheritanceModel a simple domain with related objects
8. Files and exceptionsPersistent data, file operations, exceptions, and safe resource handlingRead/write data and respond to common failures
9. Testing and data analysisTesting program behavior and analyzing structured dataValidate behavior with repeatable checks
10. Project-based learningRequirements, top-down design, text-based applications, and incremental implementationPlan and build a multi-feature program
11. CapstoneIntegration, testing, documentation, and presentationDemonstrate and explain an independent solution

Materials and navigation

  • Unit 0: Setting Up Your Accessible Python Development Environment
  • Unit 1: Foundations of Computing and Getting Started with Python
  • Unit 2: Writing Simple Programs and Numeric Computations
  • Unit 3: Control Flow — Decisions and Loops
  • Units 4–6: Data Structures and Functions
  • Units 7–9: Object-Oriented Programming and Files
  • Units 10–11: Projects and Capstone
  • Teacher’s guide: instructor planning, accessible instruction, assessment, and AI guidance

Return to the curriculum overview to compare the three language pathways.

Recommended environment

The setup unit contains the Python-specific runtime and project instructions. For a cross-language comparison and detailed installation steps for Visual Studio Code, VSCodium, and Theia IDE, see the standalone IDE setup lesson. In general, learners need:

  • A currently supported Python 3 release compatible with the course examples.
  • Visual Studio Code or Theia IDE, or another keyboard-accessible editor that supports Python and the learner’s screen reader.
  • Python language tooling for the selected editor.
  • A screen reader such as NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, or Narrator, a braille display, magnification, or the access technology used by the learner.
  • A terminal for running programs and reading text output.

Use a project-specific virtual environment for packages. Keep dependencies limited in the introductory sequence; when a third-party package is necessary, explain why it is needed, how it is installed, and how to verify it.

Install uv using its official installation instructions. In a new project folder, use the same project workflow on macOS, Linux, and Windows:

uv init --python 3.12
uv add requests
uv run python main.py
uv tree

Windows Powershell

uv init --python 3.12
uv add requests
uv run python main.py
uv tree

uv creates and manages the project-local .venv, records dependencies in pyproject.toml and uv.lock, and runs commands in that environment. Students do not need to activate the environment manually. Use uv add package rather than global pip install package.

Python version and coding conventions

All examples target Python 3.12+. The course uses syntax and standard-library APIs available in Python 3.12; learners may use a newer stable interpreter without changing the lessons. Do not assume that a feature available in the newest Python release is available to every learner.

Use current, readable Python conventions:

  • Follow PEP 8 for naming, four-space indentation, whitespace, imports, and readable line length. Use snake_case for variables and functions, PascalCase for classes, and UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants.
  • Prefer descriptive names, f-strings, and explicit intermediate steps over dense one-liners.
  • Use pathlib.Path for filesystem paths, with statements for files and other managed resources, and if name == “main” for runnable module entry points.
  • Add type annotations to function parameters and return values as concepts become appropriate. Built-in generics such as list[str], dict[str, int], and tuple[float, float] are supported by the 3.12 baseline; avoid legacy typing.List/typing.Dict forms in new examples.
  • Catch specific exceptions, keep try blocks narrow, and do not silently ignore errors. Use None for an intentional absence of a value and compare it with is None.
  • Use uv to manage project dependencies: uv add package records a dependency in pyproject.toml; uv run executes in the managed project environment. Do not use global pip installs.
  • Keep dependencies minimal. Optional quality tools such as Ruff and pytest can be introduced after learners understand the standard-library workflow.

The curriculum favors clarity and compatibility over novelty. It does not require Python 3.13–3.15-only syntax or APIs.

Accessibility and instructional design

Python uses indentation to define code blocks. Consistent indentation, whitespace navigation, and screen-reader announcement settings are especially important. Learners should practice reading a block’s start and end, identifying which statements belong to a condition or loop, and moving between indentation levels.

The curriculum emphasizes keyboard-first editor and terminal workflows, explicit reading of punctuation and operators, text-based exercises, clear prompts and errors, debugging, descriptive names, and manageable line lengths.

Do not assume all learners use the same screen reader or prefer speech. Braille, magnification, speech, switch access, and other configurations may require different pacing and navigation strategies. Ask learners what works for them and adapt without changing the learning objective.

How to study each lesson

  1. Read the overview and identify the new concepts.
  2. Trace each example line by line; describe the role of indentation and punctuation.
  3. Predict the output before running the program.
  4. Run the example and compare actual output with the prediction.
  5. Change one value or statement and observe the effect.
  6. Complete the activities independently before consulting a worked solution.
  7. When an error occurs, read the traceback, identify the exception type and line, inspect nearby code, and test one correction at a time.
  8. Explain the solution in plain language and record unresolved questions.

Keep a portfolio. Save small experiments as well as completed projects; revision is evidence of learning.

Assessment and project work

A useful portfolio includes short programs, input/output examples, debugging notes, tests, and project milestones. Instructors can assess algorithmic reasoning, code correctness, use of appropriate data structures, testing, clarity, accessibility of interaction, and the learner’s ability to explain and modify the program.

The capstone should have a clear problem statement, user needs, a manageable feature list, text-based interaction, a test plan, and a short explanation or demonstration. Success means the learner can explain the design and limitations, not merely that the code runs.

Teaching with AI

AI assistants can explain a Python traceback, suggest test cases, compare alternatives, or provide a second explanation. They can also hallucinate APIs, invent package names, produce insecure file handling, or generate dense code that is difficult to navigate with speech or braille.

Students should follow the instructor’s activity-specific policy, disclose assistance where required, and explain and modify every submitted line. Do not enter student records, credentials, private code, or sensitive data into public AI services. AI must not replace independent work in assessments designed to measure individual skills. The teacher’s guide contains a fuller protocol.

Recommended introductory books

  • Matthes, Eric. Python Crash Course: A Hands-On, Project-Based Introduction to Programming, 3rd edition. No Starch Press, 2023. A practical introduction organized around core language concepts and substantial projects. Publisher page.
  • Zelle, John M. Python Programming: An Introduction to Computer Science, 4th edition. Franklin, Beedle & Associates, 2024. A first-course computer science textbook that develops problem solving and programming through Python. Book information.
  • Zinoviev, Dmitry, Paul Gries, Jennifer Campbell, and Jason Montojo. Practical Programming: An Introduction to Computer Science Using Python, 4th edition. Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2026. A current, no-prior-experience introduction to computer science and programming, with emphasis on design, algorithms, testing, and debugging. Publisher page.
  • Downey, Allen B. Think Python: How to Think Like a Computer Scientist, 3rd edition. Green Tea Press, 2024. A free, concept-oriented introduction emphasizing computational thinking, functions, data structures, and problem solving. Author’s book site.
  • Sweigart, Al. Automate the Boring Stuff with Python: Practical Programming for Total Beginners, 3rd edition. No Starch Press, 2025. A task-oriented introduction that teaches programming through useful automation projects. Publisher page.

Suggested use: select one primary text rather than attempting all three at once. Think Python is useful for conceptual reinforcement; Python Crash Course offers a project-based sequence; Automate the Boring Stuff connects fundamentals to practical tasks. The curriculum’s own examples and exercises remain authoritative for course requirements.

Further learning

Use the official Python documentation as the reference for language behavior and standard-library APIs. The curriculum also draws on Python Crash Course by Eric Matthes and Python Programming: An Introduction to Computer Science by John Zelle. See the unit materials and teacher’s guide for additional references.

The objective is to develop a repeatable approach to understanding problems, writing clear programs, testing behavior, and learning new tools independently.

GUI, visualization, and workbench accessibility

See the shared GUI, visualization, and workbench accessibility reference for screen-reader support by toolkit, platform-specific activation settings, recommended alternatives, and interfaces that must not be required without an equivalent accessible route.

AI Policy

AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, or generate course code or assessment solutions.

Capstone code

The verified Unit 11 code (logic module, NiceGUI pages, and tests) is in capstone/.

PYTHON Lessons

The curriculum is organized as one Markdown file per unit.

  • setting up your accessible python development environme
  • foundations of computing and getting started with pytho
  • writing simple programs and numeric computations
  • control flow decisions and loops
  • data structures lists and dictionaries
  • user input and while loops
  • functions
  • classes and object oriented programming
  • files and exceptions
  • testing and data analysis
  • project based learning building text based applications
  • capstone project accessible personal data manager

Unit 0: Setting Up Your Accessible Python Development Environment

Before you start: complete Unit P: Computing Foundations Primer. It explains the language-neutral vocabulary and concepts used in every language track, using non-visual examples.

Overview

A detailed environment setup is not merely a technical prerequisite; it empowers students and reduces dependency on external assistance. For visually impaired students, relying on external help for every setup or environment issue can be disempowering and slow down the learning process. This unit provides extremely detailed, screen-reader-friendly instructions for environment setup.

Target Audience: Students with no prior programming experience, relying on screen readers for all computer interactions.

Lesson 0.1: Installing Python and uv

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 1, pages 3–14
  • Matthes: Appendix A, pages 463–468

Learning Objectives

  • Successfully download the Python 3 installer for my operating system.
  • Run the Python installer and correctly select the “Add Python to PATH” option.
  • Successfully download the VS Code installer for my operating system.
  • Run the VS Code installer and correctly select the “Add to PATH” option.
  • Open my computer’s system terminal.
  • Verify Python’s installation by running python3 --version in the terminal.
  • Verify VS Code’s installation by running code --version in the terminal.

Concept Explanation

Installing Python 3

Python is not always installed on a computer by default. You may install Python 3.12 or newer from the official Python downloads page, or let uv install and manage the course interpreter after you install uv. All course examples remain compatible with Python 3.12.

Windows

  1. Locate the downloaded .exe file (usually in your Downloads folder). Activate it.
  2. CRUCIAL STEP: When the installer window appears, check the “Add Python to PATH” checkbox. Use Tab to navigate to this checkbox and press Spacebar to check it.
  3. Navigate to “Install Now” and activate it.
  4. Follow any further prompts. Activate “Close” when finished.

macOS

  1. Locate the downloaded .pkg file. Activate it.
  2. Activate “Continue” through the steps.
  3. Agree to the license terms. Choose the installation location (default is fine).
  4. Enter your administrator password when prompted.
  5. Activate “Install” and then “Close” when finished.

Linux

Python 3 is often pre-installed. Verify in a terminal:

python3 --version

Windows PowerShell (Windows 11):

py -3 --version

If not installed (Debian/Ubuntu):

sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3 curl
python3 --version  # Confirm this is 3.12 or newer

Windows PowerShell (Windows 11):

# Windows uses winget; no apt package-index update is needed.
winget install --id Python.Python.3.12 -e
py -3 --version  # Confirm this is 3.12 or newer

Installing uv and a managed Python interpreter

uv is the recommended Python project and environment manager. It installs and manages Python interpreters, creates a project-local .venv, records dependencies, and runs commands in the correct environment. Install uv using the official standalone installer; this does not require Python or pip to be installed first.

macOS and Linux:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
uv --version
uv python install 3.12
uv python list

Windows PowerShell (Windows 11):

powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
uv --version
uv python install 3.12
uv python list

If the uv command is not found immediately after installation, open a new terminal as instructed by the installer. The managed interpreter must be Python 3.12 or newer for this course.

Installing Visual Studio Code or Theia IDE

  1. Install Visual Studio Code or Theia IDE. Theia supports many VS Code extensions through Open VSX, but check that the required extensions are available and test them with the learner’s screen reader.

Windows

  • CRUCIAL STEP: On the “Select Additional Tasks” screen, check “Add to PATH”.
  • Activate “Next” and then “Install”.

macOS

  • Drag the “Visual Studio Code” application to your “Applications” folder.

Linux (Debian/Ubuntu)

cd Downloads
sudo dpkg -i code_*.deb

Windows PowerShell (Windows 11):

Set-Location "$HOME\Downloads"
winget install --id Microsoft.VisualStudioCode -e

Verify VS Code

code --version

Windows PowerShell (Windows 11):

code --version

Editor alternative: Theia IDE

Theia IDE is another option instead of Visual Studio Code. It supports the keyboard- and screen-reader-oriented accessibility workflows used in this course. Its interface is similar in many respects and it supports many VS Code extensions through the Open VSX registry, but not every extension or shortcut is identical. Install the Python and language-support extensions available for Theia, then test navigation, diagnostics, terminal access, and screen-reader announcements with the learner’s access technology.

Worked Example

Run these commands in a terminal after installing Python and uv. On Windows, py replaces python3 if that is how your installation was set up.

python3 --version
uv --version
python3 -c "print('Hello from Python')"

Expected Behavior or Output

The first two commands print version numbers, and the third prints one line. The numbers depend on what you installed; this was observed with Python 3.12.3 and uv 0.11.7 on Linux:

Python 3.12.3
uv 0.11.7
Hello from Python

If a command is not found, the installation or the PATH setting is incomplete; reopen the terminal and try again before changing anything else.

Common Mistakes

  1. Installing Python but not opening a new terminal, so the old PATH is still in use and the command is reported as not found.
  2. Using the system Python for everything instead of a project environment, which later causes version and package conflicts.
  3. Copying an installer command from an unknown website. Use the official download pages and read what a command does before running it.

Activities

  1. Run the three verification commands and record the exact output in your notes file.
  2. Find which command name your system uses for Python (python, python3, or py) and write it down.
  3. Explain in two sentences what uv is used for in this course.
  4. Close and reopen the terminal and repeat the commands; note whether anything changed.

Accessibility Practice

Run every command from the keyboard and read the output with your screen reader’s line-by-line review. Confirm that the version numbers are announced clearly, digit by digit. Prefer the terminal route to any graphical installer step that is hard to operate with your access technology, and ask a sighted or experienced helper only for steps you cannot perform yourself.

Skills Checklist

  • I can successfully download the Python 3 installer for my operating system.
  • I can run the Python installer and correctly select the “Add Python to PATH” option.
  • I can successfully download the VS Code installer for my operating system.
  • I can run the VS Code installer and correctly select the “Add to PATH” option.
  • I can open my computer’s system terminal.
  • I can verify Python’s installation by running python3 --version in the terminal.
  • I can verify VS Code’s installation by running code --version in the terminal.

Lesson 0.2: Configuring Your Screen Reader for VS Code or Theia IDE

Reading References

  • Matthes: Appendix B, pages 469–476
  • Matthes: Appendix C, pages 477–482

Learning Objectives

  • Identify and toggle VS Code’s “Screen Reader Optimized Mode”.
  • Open and close the “Accessible View”.
  • Navigate between VS Code panes using Tab and Shift+Tab.
  • Navigate line by line and character by character within the editor.
  • Locate and listen to information in the VS Code Status Bar.
  • Configure my screen reader to announce indentation changes.

Concept Explanation

General Screen Reader Tips for VS Code

1. Use Screen Reader Mode

  • Press Ctrl + Shift + P to open the Command Palette.
  • Type “Toggle Screen Reader Optimized” and press Enter.

2. Accessible View

  • Press Shift + Alt + F2 (Windows/Linux) or Shift + Option + F2 (macOS).
  • Opens a flat, text-based representation of complex UI elements.
  • Press Esc to close.

3. Keyboard-First Navigation

  • Tab and Shift+Tab: Move focus between UI elements.
  • Arrow Keys: Navigate within active panes.

4. Status Bar The status bar at the bottom provides current line/column number, file type, active Python environment, and error/warning counts.

Screen Reader Indentation Configuration

Python relies heavily on indentation. Configure your screen reader to announce indentation changes.

NVDA (Windows)

  1. Press NVDA Key + N → Preferences → Settings.
  2. Find “Document Formatting”.
  3. Locate “Indentation” and set it to “Say all” or “Beeps”.
  4. Activate “OK”.

JAWS (Windows)

  1. Press JAWS Key + J → Alt+O for Options → B for Basics.
  2. Find “Text Processing” settings.
  3. Configure indentation announcement.

VoiceOver (macOS)

VoiceOver generally handles indentation well by default, announcing “4 spaces” or “tab” as you navigate.

Worked Example

Create a file named indent_test.py with exactly these lines, using four spaces for each indentation level:

score = 82
if score >= 60:
    print("Passed")
    if score >= 80:
        print("Strong pass")
print("Done")

Move through it line by line and have your screen reader announce the indentation of lines 3 to 5.

Expected Behavior or Output

When the file is read line by line, line 3 and line 5 are announced one indentation level in, line 4 two levels in, and the last line at the left margin. Running python3 indent_test.py prints:

Passed
Strong pass
Done

If the screen reader does not report indentation, adjust the settings described above until it does; Python uses indentation to decide which lines belong together.

Common Mistakes

  1. Leaving the indentation announcement turned off and then misreading which lines belong to an if block.
  2. Mixing tabs and spaces in one file, which Python rejects with an IndentationError.
  3. Changing several screen reader settings at once, so it is impossible to tell which change helped.

Activities

  1. Change one setting at a time and record how the reading of indent_test.py changes.
  2. Add a fifth indented line inside the inner if and predict the output before running.
  3. Read the file once by character and once by word; note which is faster for checking indentation.
  4. Write the keyboard commands you use to jump to the next line with the same indentation as the current line, if your editor has one.

Accessibility Practice

This lesson is the accessibility foundation for the course. Record, in your own notes, the operating system, editor, screen reader, and version you tested with. Do not describe a setup as verified for other users; it is verified only for the combination you actually ran.

Skills Checklist

  • I can identify and toggle VS Code’s “Screen Reader Optimized Mode”.
  • I can open and close the “Accessible View”.
  • I can navigate between VS Code panes using Tab and Shift+Tab.
  • I can navigate line by line and character by character within the editor.
  • I can locate and listen to information in the VS Code Status Bar.
  • I can configure my screen reader to announce indentation changes.

Lesson 0.3: Setting Up Your VS Code or Theia IDE Workspace

Reading References

  • Matthes: Appendix B, pages 469–476
  • Matthes: Chapter 8, pages 149–152

Learning Objectives

  • Open the Extensions view in my selected editor.
  • Verify that Python language support and its language server are installed and enabled.
  • Create a new folder for Python projects.
  • Open the project folder as the editor workspace.
  • Navigate the editor, file explorer, terminal, and diagnostics using the keyboard.
  • Use the Command Palette or equivalent command interface.

Concept Explanation

Install and verify Python language extensions

Choose the extension instructions for the editor you are using. The Python interpreter and project environment are separate from the editor extensions; installing an extension does not install Python or project dependencies.

Visual Studio Code

  1. Open the Extensions view with Ctrl + Shift + X (Windows/Linux) or Command + Shift + X (macOS).
  2. Install Python by Microsoft. This provides Python environment discovery, run/debug integration, and interpreter selection.
  3. Install Pylance for language intelligence, completion, navigation, and type diagnostics.
  4. Confirm both extensions are enabled for this workspace. Do not use Code Runner for course projects: it can run a file outside the project’s managed environment and bypass the standard uv run workflow.

Theia IDE

  1. Open View → Extensions (or the Extensions view available in your Theia distribution).
  2. Search the configured Open VSX registry for a Python language extension and a compatible Python language server.
  3. Check the extension publisher, supported Theia version, and extension documentation. Do not assume that Microsoft’s Python or Pylance extensions are available or interchangeable in Theia.
  4. Confirm that completion, go-to-definition, diagnostics, interpreter discovery, terminal access, and debugging work with the selected Python installation. If a required capability is unavailable, use a verified supported extension or choose VS Code for this course.

In either editor, install only extensions needed for the course, keep them enabled for the project workspace, and test their announcements and keyboard navigation with the learner’s screen reader before relying on them.

Creating Your First Workspace Folder

Windows: Open File Explorer (Windows Key + E). Navigate to Documents. Press Ctrl + Shift + N to create a new folder named PythonProjects.

macOS: Open Finder. Navigate to Documents. Press Command + Shift + N to create PythonProjects.

Opening the Folder in VS Code

Method 1 (Recommended): Open terminal, navigate to the folder, then:

code .

Windows PowerShell (Windows 11):

code .

Method 2 (VS Code): Press Ctrl + K, Ctrl + O to open a folder.

Theia IDE: Use the File → Open Folder command (or the equivalent workspace-opening command in your Theia distribution) and select the project folder. Confirm that the folder containing pyproject.toml is the workspace root; opening only hello.py can prevent the editor from discovering the project’s .venv and configuration.

VS Code Navigation Shortcuts

AreaShortcut
ExplorerCtrl + Shift + E
SearchCtrl + Shift + F
ExtensionsCtrl + Shift + X
Toggle SidebarCtrl + B
Command PaletteCtrl + Shift + P
Problems ViewCtrl + Shift + M
Next ErrorF8
Previous ErrorShift + F8
Integrated Terminal`Ctrl + ``

Advanced editor options

Experienced coders may prefer JetBrains IDEs such as PyCharm. These are advanced alternatives, not the recommended starting point for this beginner curriculum. This course does not provide JetBrains installation or usage instructions.

Worked Example

Create a project folder and a first file, then run it from the terminal as well as from the editor:

mkdir python-course
cd python-course
code .

In the editor, create hello.py containing print("Hello, Avery!"), save it, and then run it from the terminal with python3 hello.py.

Expected Behavior or Output

The terminal prints one line:

Hello, Avery!

The editor’s Run command should produce the same line in its integrated terminal. If the two differ, the editor is using a different Python interpreter from the terminal; check which interpreter is selected.

Common Mistakes

  1. Opening a single file instead of the project folder, so the editor does not know the project’s interpreter or files.
  2. Selecting a different Python interpreter in the editor from the one used in the terminal, so the same program behaves differently.
  3. Depending only on the editor’s Run button, which hides the exact command being run.

Activities

  1. Create the folder and file from the keyboard only and write down each keyboard command you used.
  2. Open the folder in the editor and list the files using the keyboard.
  3. Run hello.py from the editor and from the terminal, and compare the output.
  4. Change the greeting to use your own name and rerun it.

Accessibility Practice

Use the keyboard to open the folder, move between the file list, the editor, and the terminal, and return. Note which shortcuts your screen reader announces and which you must learn by heart. Always keep one terminal route available, since it does not depend on any editor feature.

Skills Checklist

  • I can open the Extensions view in my selected editor.
  • I can verify that Python language support and its language server are installed and enabled.
  • I can create a new folder for Python projects.
  • I can open the project folder as the editor workspace.
  • I can navigate the editor, file explorer, terminal, and diagnostics using the keyboard.
  • I can use the Command Palette or equivalent command interface.

Lesson 0.4: Python Environments, Terminal Usage, and Accessibility Tools

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 1, pages 3–14
  • Matthes: Chapter 8, pages 149–152
  • Matthes: Chapter 11, pages 210–211

Learning Objectives

  • Create a new Python file (.py) in VS Code.
  • Write a simple print() statement.
  • Run a Python script from the system terminal.
  • Run a Python script from the integrated terminal in VS Code.
  • Understand why virtual environments are useful.
  • Initialize a Python project with uv init.
  • Add a project dependency with uv add and inspect it with uv tree.
  • Run a program with uv run and select the project’s .venv interpreter in my editor.

Concept Explanation

Creating Your First Python File

  1. Ensure Explorer is focused: Ctrl + Shift + E.
  2. Create new file: Ctrl + N.
  3. Save: Ctrl + S. Name it hello.py.
  4. Type:
print("Hello from VS Code!")

Running Python Scripts

From System Terminal:

cd ~/Documents/PythonProjects
python3 hello.py

Windows PowerShell (Windows 11):

Set-Location "$HOME\Documents\PythonProjects"
py -3 hello.py

From VS Code Integrated Terminal:

  1. Open terminal: `Ctrl + ``
  2. The terminal opens in your project folder automatically.
  3. Run: python3 hello.py

Project environments and dependencies with uv

Use one isolated environment per Python project. The recommended course workflow uses uv; it creates and manages the project’s .venv automatically, so learners do not need to activate it manually. Run these commands from the project folder. If the folder does not yet contain a project, initialize it first.

Create the project environment, add a dependency, and run the program:

uv init --python 3.12
uv add requests
uv run python hello.py
uv tree

Windows PowerShell (Windows 11):

uv init --python 3.12
uv add requests
uv run python hello.py
uv tree
  • uv init creates the project configuration.
  • uv add requests installs the package into the project environment and records it in pyproject.toml and uv.lock.
  • uv run python hello.py runs the program with the project’s managed interpreter and dependencies.
  • uv tree lists the dependency tree.

Run without installing a project dependency: for a one-off tool or script dependency, use uv run --with package command or uvx tool-name. Do not use bare/global pip install or python -m pip install for course packages.

Select and verify the project interpreter in VS Code or Theia IDE: open the project folder (the folder containing pyproject.toml) as the workspace, then choose the interpreter inside that project’s .venv directory: .venv/bin/python on macOS/Linux or .venv\\Scripts\\python.exe on Windows. In VS Code, use Python: Select Interpreter and select the workspace environment. In Theia, use the Python extension’s interpreter-selection command or setting. If the environment is not listed, create it with uv init --python 3.12, reopen the project folder, and select it again.

Build the habit of checking the active environment before running or debugging code. The editor’s selected interpreter, its integrated terminal, and the command-line workflow must all point to the same project. Run course programs with uv run python filename.py; add packages with uv add package-name. Do not install course dependencies globally. If an editor’s Run or Debug action does not use the project interpreter, correct its interpreter/launch configuration or use the terminal command rather than accepting a run from the wrong environment.

Optional venv concepts: uv uses the standard .venv directory. Students may inspect it and learn that it isolates project dependencies, but routine manual activation is not required when commands are run with uv run.

VS Code and Theia IDE Accessibility Features

The following shortcuts are VS Code defaults. Theia provides comparable keyboard and screen-reader workflows, but verify command names and keybindings in the installed version.

  • Accessible View (Shift+Alt+F2): Reveals hover information and error details.
  • Focus on Errors (F8 / Shift+F8): Jump between errors without visual scanning.
  • Go to Definition (F12): Navigate to where a function or variable is defined.
  • Go to Reference (Shift+F12): Find all usages of a symbol.
  • Go to Line/Column (Ctrl+G): Jump to a specific line number.

Python Documentation

The official Python documentation is well-structured and accessible: https://docs.python.org/3/

Unit 0 Completion Checklist

  • uv is installed and uv run python --version reports Python 3.12 or newer.
  • VS Code or Theia IDE is installed and I can open the course project.
  • Your screen reader is configured to announce indentation changes in your chosen editor.
  • You can open your PythonProjects folder in VS Code or Theia IDE.
  • You have installed Python language support in your chosen editor (the Python extension in VS Code or its compatible Theia alternative).
  • You can create a new .py file, write print("Hello!"), and save it.
  • You can run your hello.py file from both terminals.
  • You can create a project environment with uv init and add dependencies with uv add.
  • You can run project code with uv run and select the project’s .venv interpreter in your editor.
  • You know how to use Ctrl + Shift + P (Command Palette) and F8 (Go to next error).

Congratulations! You now have a powerful and accessible development environment ready for your Python journey.

Worked Example

Create a project environment with uv, add nothing, and run a script inside it:

mkdir env-demo
cd env-demo
uv init
uv run python -c "print('Running inside the project environment')"

Expected Behavior or Output

uv init creates project files and the last command prints:

Running inside the project environment

Use uv run (or activate the environment) every time you run the project, so the same Python and the same packages are used.

Common Mistakes

  1. Installing packages into the system Python instead of the project environment.
  2. Running a script from the wrong working directory, so relative file names are not found.
  3. Forgetting which environment is active and getting different results for the same code.

Activities

  1. Run pwd (macOS and Linux) or cd (Windows) and write down the working directory.
  2. List the files that uv init created and say what each one is for.
  3. Create a second project folder and confirm that its environment is separate.
  4. Write the three terminal commands you need to start work on a project each day.

Accessibility Practice

Terminal output is plain text and works well with a screen reader or braille display. Learn the keys that jump to the start and end of the last command’s output, and confirm the working directory before every run. Avoid long one-line commands you cannot navigate; break them with line continuation or run them in steps.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create a new Python file (.py) in VS Code.
  • I can write a simple print() statement.
  • I can run a Python script from the system terminal.
  • I can run a Python script from the integrated terminal in VS Code.
  • I understand why virtual environments are useful.
  • I can initialize a Python project with uv init.
  • I can add a project dependency with uv add and inspect it with uv tree.
  • I can run a program with uv run and select the project’s .venv interpreter in my editor.

Unit 1: Foundations of Computing and Getting Started with Python

Overview

Compatibility: All code examples in this curriculum target Python 3.12 and newer. The course avoids syntax and APIs introduced after Python 3.12.

This unit covers basic computer science concepts, setting up the Python environment, and writing and executing simple Python programs.

Objectives:

  • Understand what computer science is and how hardware relates to software.
  • Write and run your first Python program.
  • Use variables to store and manipulate simple data types.

Lesson 1.1: Welcome to Computer Science

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 1, pages 1–7
  • Matthes: Chapter 1, pages 3–14

Learning Objectives

  • Define what computer science is.
  • Distinguish between computer hardware and software.
  • Explain what a computer program is.
  • Identify Python as a programming language.

Concept Explanation

What Is Computer Science?

A computer is a universal machine — it can be programmed to solve any problem that can be broken down into a series of precise, logical steps. The true power of a computer doesn’t come from its hardware but from the software we create.

Computer science is the study of problem-solving, not just programming. It’s an interdisciplinary field involving breaking down complex problems, designing algorithms, and implementing efficient solutions.

Hardware vs. Software

ComponentDescription
HardwarePhysical components you can touch: keyboard, screen, processor, memory
SoftwareInstructions that direct hardware: programs, operating systems, apps
CPUThe processor that executes instructions
Memory (RAM)Temporary storage for active programs and data
StoragePermanent storage for files

Analogy: Think of a kitchen. The stove, refrigerator, and pots are hardware. A cookie recipe is software — it provides precise steps for the “hardware” (the cook) to follow.

Why Python?

Python is an ideal language for beginners because of its:

  • Readability — English-like syntax makes code easy to understand.
  • Simplicity — Less “boilerplate” code than other languages.
  • Versatility — Used in web development, data science, AI, and more.

The Problem-Solving Approach

  1. Understand the problem.
  2. Break it down into smaller pieces.
  3. Design a step-by-step solution (an algorithm).
  4. Implement the solution in Python.
  5. Test and refine your code.

Worked Example

The problem-solving approach applied to a small task: find the total and average of the shared scores 82, 91, 76, and 88.

Algorithm in plain steps: set the total to 0; for each score, add it to the total; divide the total by the number of scores; report both.

scores = [82, 91, 76, 88]
total = 0
for score in scores:
    total = total + score
average = total / len(scores)
print("Total:", total)
print("Average:", average)

Expected Behavior or Output

Output of example 1:

Total: 337
Average: 84.25

Common Mistakes

  1. Writing code before writing the steps, then forgetting to divide by the number of scores.
  2. Confusing the program with the algorithm. The algorithm is the plan; the program is one way of carrying it out.
  3. Expecting a computer to fill in a step you did not state.

Activities

Activity 1.1.1: “Human Computer” Role-Play

  • In pairs, one student is the “computer” and the other is the “programmer.”
  • The programmer provides simple, precise instructions for a common task (e.g., “make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich”).
  • The “computer” follows only what is literally said.
  • Purpose: Illustrate the need for precise, unambiguous instructions.

Activity 1.1.2: Identify Hardware and Software

  • List five items you use daily.
  • For each, identify whether it is hardware or software and explain your choice.

Accessibility Practice

Write the plain-language steps as a numbered list and read it back with your screen reader before coding. Trace the loop by hand as numbered sentences (82, then 173, then 249, then 337) rather than as a table, so every state is read in order.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define what computer science is.
  • I can distinguish between computer hardware and software.
  • I can explain what a computer program is.
  • I can identify Python as a programming language.

Lesson 1.2: Your First Python Program — “Hello World!”

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 1, pages 7–13
  • Matthes: Chapter 1, pages 3–14

Learning Objectives

  • Write a print() statement in Python.
  • Save a Python file with the .py extension.
  • Execute a Python script from the terminal.
  • Understand that the output of print() appears in the terminal.

Concept Explanation

The print() Function

The print() function is Python’s primary method for displaying output to the user.

print("Hello, World!")

Expected output:

Hello, World!

Key Concepts

  • Strings are text data enclosed in quotation marks (single or double).
  • Comments start with # and are ignored by Python.
  • Python executes code line by line, from top to bottom.

Worked Example

Example 1.2.1: Simple Greeting

# This program prints a classic greeting.
print("Hello, World!")

Example 1.2.2: Personalized Message

# This program prints a message with your name.
print("Hello, Avery!")
print("Welcome to Python programming!")

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Hello, Avery!
Welcome to Python programming!

Common Mistakes

print("Hello, World"        # Missing closing parenthesis — SyntaxError
print "Hello"               # Python 2 style — SyntaxError in Python 3
Print("Hello")              # Capital P — NameError

Activities

Activity 1.2.1: My First Message

  1. Open VS Code and confirm the PythonProjects folder is open.
  2. Create a new file as my_message.py.
  3. Type: 
    print("My favorite color is blue.")
print("My favorite animal is a dog.")
  4. Save and run the file.

Activity 1.2.2: Exploring Print Statements

  1. Experiment with:
    • Printing numbers: print(123)
    • Printing sentences with punctuation.
    • Omitting quotes: print(Hello) — expect a NameError.

Accessibility Practice

Run the file from the terminal and read the output line by line. Check that your screen reader announces the quotation marks and parentheses in print("Hello, Avery!"), because a missing closing quotation mark is the most common first error. If the error message is long, jump to its last line, which names the problem.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write a print() statement in Python.
  • I can save a Python file with the .py extension.
  • I can execute a Python script from the terminal.
  • I understand that the output of print() appears in the terminal.

Lesson 1.3: Variables and Simple Data Types

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 2, pages 24–26
  • Matthes: Chapter 2, pages 15–32

Learning Objectives

  • Define what a variable is in programming.
  • Create a valid variable name in Python.
  • Assign string, integer, and float values to variables.
  • Use print() to display the value of a variable.
  • Perform basic arithmetic operations with numbers in Python.

Concept Explanation

What Is a Variable?

A variable is a name that refers to a value stored in the computer’s memory. The assignment operator = creates a connection between a name and a value.

name = "Avery"
age = 16
height = 1.72
favorite_subject = "Computer Science"

Rules for variable names:

  • Must start with a letter or underscore
  • Can only contain letters, digits, and underscores
  • Are case-sensitive (age is different from Age)
  • Cannot be a Python keyword (if, for, while, etc.)

Best practices:

  • Use descriptive names: student_count, not sc
  • Use lowercase with underscores: first_name

Essential Data Types

TypeDescriptionExamples
str (String)Text data"hello", "Python"
int (Integer)Whole numbers10, -5, 0
float (Float)Numbers with decimals3.14, 9.99
