bool (Boolean)True or FalseTrue, False

Key Table: Python Data Types and Operations

Data TypeDescriptionExample ValueCommon Operations
strText, words, sentences"Hello", "Python"+ (concatenation), len(), .upper()
intWhole numbers10, -5, 0+, -, *, /, %
floatNumbers with decimals3.14, 9.99, 0.0+, -, *, /

Worked Example

Example 1.3.1: Storing and Printing a String

student_name = "Avery"
print("Hello, " + student_name + "!")

Example 1.3.2: The Shared Student Profile and Notebook Cost The same student profile and inventory item are used in every language track, so you can compare how each language declares the same data.

name = "Avery"
age = 16
height = 1.72
favorite_subject = "Computer Science"

print("Name:", name)
print("Age:", age)
print("Height in meters:", height)
print("Favorite subject:", favorite_subject)
print(type(name), type(age), type(height), type(favorite_subject))

notebook_price = 2.50
notebook_quantity = 3
notebook_total = notebook_price * notebook_quantity
print("Notebook total:", notebook_total)

Python decides each variable’s type from the value you assign (dynamic typing). type() reports it: str, int, float, str.

Expected Behavior or Output

Output:

Hello, Avery!

Expected output:

Name: Avery
Age: 16
Height in meters: 1.72
Favorite subject: Computer Science
<class 'str'> <class 'int'> <class 'float'> <class 'str'>
Notebook total: 7.5

Common Mistakes

2nd_number = 10         # Invalid variable name — starts with digit
print("Result: " + 42)  # TypeError — can't concatenate str and int

Activities

Activity 1.3.1: Personal Information Variables

my_name = "Avery"
favorite_number = 7
height_in_meters = 1.72
favorite_food = "pizza"

print("My name is:", my_name)
print("My favorite number is:", favorite_number)
print("My height is:", height_in_meters, "meters")
print("My favorite food is:", favorite_food)

Activity 1.3.2: Simple Math Challenge

num1 = 15
num2 = 7
sum_result = num1 + num2
difference = num1 - num2
product = num1 * num2
quotient = num1 / num2

print("Sum:", sum_result)
print("Difference:", difference)
print("Product:", product)
print("Quotient:", quotient)

Accessibility Practice

Say variable names aloud with their underscores (favorite_subject) and listen for the pause so you can tell one name from two words. Print each value on its own labelled line so the screen reader announces the name and the value together, and avoid relying on the spacing between printed items.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define what a variable is in programming.
  • I can create a valid variable name in Python.
  • I can assign string, integer, and float values to variables.
  • I can use print() to display the value of a variable.
  • I can perform basic arithmetic operations with numbers in Python.

Canonical Shared Dataset — Student Profile

The parallel-language courses use the same student record. Keep these values unchanged when translating the example into another language.

student_profile = {
    "name": "Avery",
    "age": 16,
    "height_m": 1.72,
    "favorite_subject": "Computer Science",
}
print(student_profile["name"])
print(student_profile["age"])
print(student_profile["height_m"])
print(student_profile["favorite_subject"])

Expected output:

Avery
16
1.72
Computer Science

Use this record in place of unrelated personal-profile values in parallel-track comparison exercises. The earlier Hello World example remains a minimal first-program demonstration.

Unit 2: Writing Simple Programs and Numeric Computations

Overview

Compatibility: All code examples in this curriculum target Python 3.12 and newer. The course avoids syntax and APIs introduced after Python 3.12.

This unit explores the software development process, more complex numeric operations, and how to obtain and use input from users.

Objectives:

  • Understand the phases of software development.
  • Work with different numeric data types (integers, floats).
  • Perform type conversions.
  • Use mathematical operators and the math library.
  • Get user input with input().

Lesson 2.1: The Software Development Process

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 2, pages 21–22 and pages 35–36

Learning Objectives

  • Describe the purpose of the software development process.
  • List and briefly explain the main phases of software development.
  • Understand that problem-solving and design happen before writing code.

Concept Explanation

The Three-Phase Development Process

1. Design (Plan first) Before writing any code, fully understand the problem:

  • Identify inputs (information the program needs) and outputs (results it must produce).
  • Write an algorithm — a step-by-step plan in plain English (pseudocode).
  • Consider edge cases — unusual inputs that might break your program.

2. Implement (Write the code)

  • Translate your design into Python syntax.
  • Code incrementally — build in small pieces and test as you go.
  • Follow coding standards and use descriptive variable names.

3. Test and Debug (Verify it works)

  • Run with a variety of inputs, including normal values and edge cases.
  • Read error messages carefully — they tell you the type of error and the line number.
  • Use print() statements to check variable values during debugging.

Why This Process Matters

  • Reduces frustration — Having a plan prevents getting stuck.
  • Improves code quality — A thoughtful design leads to cleaner code.
  • Simplifies debugging — Test each component in isolation.
  • Saves time — Good design prevents time-consuming rewrites.

Worked Example

Implement the pseudocode from the activity below with the shared values (bill 24.50, tip rate 0.15):

bill = 24.5
tip_rate = 0.15

tip = bill * tip_rate
total = bill + tip

print(f"Bill: {bill:.2f}")
print(f"Tip: {tip:.2f}")
print(f"Total: {total:.2f}")

Expected Behavior or Output

Output of example 1:

Bill: 24.50
Tip: 3.67
Total: 28.18

Common Mistakes

  1. Writing the rate as 15 instead of 0.15, which makes the tip fifteen times too large.
  2. Rounding the tip before adding it to the bill, which can change the total by a cent.
  3. Skipping tests for a zero bill or a negative bill.

Activities

Activity 2.1.1: Planning a Tip Calculator Write pseudocode before coding:

1. GET bill amount from user
2. CALCULATE tip as 15% of bill amount
3. CALCULATE total amount (bill + tip)
4. PRINT tip amount
5. PRINT total amount

Trace this plan with the shared calculator values: the bill is 24.50 and the tip rate is 0.15. The tip is 24.50 × 0.15 = 3.675 and the total is 24.50 + 3.675 = 28.175. Shown with two decimal places, Python displays the tip as 3.67 and the total as 28.18, because 3.675 cannot be stored exactly in binary floating point. You will implement this plan in Lesson 2.4.

Activity 2.1.2: Tracing a Simple Program Without running the code, trace the execution and predict output:

a = 10
b = 5
c = a * b
a = a + 2
print(c)
print(a)

Accessibility Practice

Write the design steps as a numbered list and print every result on its own labelled line (Tip: 3.67), so a screen reader reads each result as one clear unit. Do not use alignment or spacing to convey meaning.

Skills Checklist

  • I can describe the purpose of the software development process.
  • I can list and briefly explain the main phases of software development.
  • I understand that problem-solving and design happen before writing code.

Lesson 2.2: Elements of Programs — Expressions and Assignment

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 2, pages 24–26

Learning Objectives

  • Identify an expression in Python code.
  • Predict the result of simple Python expressions.
  • Explain how the assignment operator = works.
  • Demonstrate how to update a variable’s value.

Concept Explanation

Expressions and Assignment

An expression is any combination of values, variables, and operators that evaluates to a single result. Python follows the standard mathematical order of operations (PEMDAS).

result1 = 10 / 2 + 3  # 10/2 is 5, then 5+3 = 8.0
message = "Python" + " " + "is fun!"

Assignment:

score = 82
score = score + 9  # score is now 91

Worked Example

Example 2.2.1: Expression Evaluation

result1 = 10 / 2 + 3
print("Result 1:", result1)   # Output: Result 1: 8.0
print("Precedence:", 8 + 4 * 2)   # Output: Precedence: 16
print("Grouped:", (8 + 4) * 2)    # Output: Grouped: 24

message = "Python" + " " + "is fun!"
print("Message:", message)    # Output: Message: Python is fun!

Example 2.2.2: Reassigning Variables

score = 82
print("Initial score:", score)
score = score + 9
print("New score:", score)     # Output: New score: 91

Expected Behavior or Output

Output of example 1:

Result 1: 8.0
Precedence: 16
Grouped: 24
Message: Python is fun!

Output of example 2:

Initial score: 82
New score: 91

Common Mistakes

  1. Reading = as “equals”. In an assignment it means “store the value on the right in the name on the left.”
  2. Forgetting that / always gives a float, so 10 / 2 is 5.0, not 5.
  3. Expecting 8 + 4 * 2 to be 24. Multiplication happens first, so it is 16; use parentheses to change the order.

Activities

  1. Predict the value of 8 + 4 * 2, (8 + 4) * 2, 7 // 2, 7 % 2, and 2 ** 3, then check each in Python.
  2. Start with score = 82 and write two statements that raise it by 9 and then double it. Predict the result.
  3. Join the strings "Avery" and "Student" with a space between them using +.
  4. Explain, in two sentences, why score = score + 9 is valid even though it looks like an impossible equation.

Accessibility Practice

Say operators by name when reading code aloud: ‘double star’ for **, ‘double slash’ for //, ‘percent’ for %. Raise your screen reader’s punctuation level while reading expressions so that parentheses and operators are all announced.

Skills Checklist

  • I can identify an expression in Python code.
  • I can predict the result of simple Python expressions.
  • I can explain how the assignment operator = works.
  • I can demonstrate how to update a variable’s value.

Lesson 2.3: Input and Output Revisited

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 2, pages 27–33
  • Matthes: Chapter 7, pages 114–116

Learning Objectives

  • Use the input() function to ask the user for information.
  • Provide a clear prompt message when using input().
  • Remember that input() returns a string, even for numbers.
  • Combine text and variable values in a print() statement using f-strings.

Concept Explanation

The input() Function

The input() function pauses program execution and waits for the user to type something and press Enter. It always returns a string.

user_name = input("What is your name? ")
print(f"Hello, {user_name}! Nice to meet you.")

F-Strings (Formatted String Literals)

F-strings provide a clean way to embed variable values directly into a string:

name = "Avery"
age = 16
print(f"Hello, {name}! You are {age} years old.")

Converting Input for Calculations

Since input() always returns a string, you must convert it for math:

age_str = input("How old are you? ")
age_int = int(age_str)
print(f"Next year you will be {age_int + 1} years old.")

Worked Example

Example 2.3.1: Basic Input

user_name = input("What is your name? ")
print(f"Hello, {user_name}! Nice to meet you.")

Example 2.3.2: Numeric Input and Calculation

user_name = input("Enter your name: ")

num1_str = input("Enter the first number: ")
num1 = int(num1_str)

num2_str = input("Enter the second number: ")
num2 = int(num2_str)

sum_result = num1 + num2
print(f"Hello, {user_name}!")
print(f"The sum of {num1} and {num2} is {sum_result}.")

If the user types text that is not a whole number, int() raises a ValueError. Lesson 8.3 shows how to handle that.

Expected Behavior or Output

Sample run (typed input shown after each prompt):

What is your name? Avery
Hello, Avery! Nice to meet you.

Sample run (typed input shown after each prompt):

Enter your name: Avery
Enter the first number: 12
Enter the second number: 8
Hello, Avery!
The sum of 12 and 8 is 20.

Common Mistakes

  1. Forgetting that input() always returns text. "12" + "8" joins the text to make "128", and does not add.
  2. Calling int() on text that is not a whole number, which raises a ValueError.
  3. Writing a prompt that does not say what to type, such as input("> ").

Activities

Activity 2.3.1: Temperature Converter

fahrenheit_str = input("Enter temperature in Fahrenheit: ")
fahrenheit = float(fahrenheit_str)
celsius = (fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9
print(f"{fahrenheit}°F is {celsius:.2f}°C")

Accessibility Practice

Write each prompt as a complete sentence that says what to enter, such as Enter the first number: , and end it with a space so the answer starts after it. Test the program with your screen reader to confirm the prompt is read before you start typing.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use the input() function to ask the user for information.
  • I can provide a clear prompt message when using input().
  • I remember that input() returns a string, even for numbers.
  • I can combine text and variable values in a print() statement using f-strings.

Lesson 2.4: Computing with Numbers and Type Conversions

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 3, pages 41–48
  • Matthes: Chapter 2, pages 26–28

Learning Objectives

  • Identify when to use an integer versus a float.
  • Convert a string to an integer using int().
  • Convert a string to a float using float().
  • Convert a number to a string using str().
  • Apply type conversions to perform calculations on user input.
  • Understand and can apply the order of operations.

Concept Explanation

Integers and Floats

TypeDescriptionExample
intWhole numbers (exact)5, -20, 1000000
floatNumbers with decimals3.14, -2.5, 6.0

Key behaviors:

  • Division / always returns a float: 10 / 2 → 5.0
  • Floor division // returns the integer part: 10 // 3 → 3
  • Mixed operations promote to float: 10 + 3.5 → 13.5

Type Conversion Functions

int("123")      # → 123  (truncates: int(3.9) → 3)
float("3.14")   # → 3.14
str(42)         # → "42"

Worked Example

Example 2.4.1: Type Conversion

num_str = "123"
num_int = int(num_str)
print(f"String '{num_str}' as integer: {num_int}, type: {type(num_int)}")

num_float = float(num_str)
print(f"String '{num_str}' as float: {num_float}, type: {type(num_float)}")

my_number = 42
my_text = str(my_number)
print(f"Integer {my_number} as string: '{my_text}', type: {type(my_text)}")

Common Type Error:

# This will cause a TypeError:
# print("My age is " + 14)
# Fix: print("My age is " + str(14))
# Or: print(f"My age is {14}")

Example 2.4.2: Tip Calculator (shared calculator values)

bill = 24.5
tip_rate = 0.15

tip = bill * tip_rate
total = bill + tip

print(f"Bill: {bill:.2f}")
print(f"Tip: {tip:.2f}")
print(f"Total: {total:.2f}")

The unrounded values are 3.675 and 28.175. Python’s :.2f formatting displays 3.67 and 28.18. This is binary floating-point behavior, not a mistake in the program; other languages may round the tip to 3.68.

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Bill: 24.50
Tip: 3.67
Total: 28.18

Common Mistakes

  1. Converting with int() and expecting rounding. int(3.9) is 3 because it removes the fraction.
  2. Expecting 0.1 + 0.2 to equal exactly 0.3. Floating-point numbers are approximations.
  3. Forgetting to convert typed text before arithmetic, then seeing TypeError or joined text instead of a sum.

Activities

Activity 2.4.1: Mixed Bag Calculator

age_str = input("Enter your age: ")
age = int(age_str)

height_str = input("Enter your height in meters: ")
height = float(height_str)

phrase = input("Enter a short phrase: ")

print(f"Age doubled: {age * 2}")
print(f"Height in centimeters: {height * 100:.1f}")
print(f"Phrase length: {len(phrase)} characters")

Sample run (typed input shown after each prompt):

Enter your age: 16
Enter your height in meters: 1.72
Enter a short phrase: Computer Science
Age doubled: 32
Height in centimeters: 172.0
Phrase length: 16 characters

Accessibility Practice

When printing floating-point results, format them (:.2f) so the screen reader reads a short number instead of a long unrounded one. Read the type names printed by type() aloud, and note that <class 'int'> is announced with its angle brackets.

Skills Checklist

  • I can identify when to use an integer versus a float.
  • I can convert a string to an integer using int().
  • I can convert a string to a float using float().
  • I can convert a number to a string using str().
  • I can apply type conversions to perform calculations on user input.
  • I understand and can apply the order of operations.

Lesson 2.5: Using the Math Library

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 3, pages 49–51

Learning Objectives

  • Explain what a Python module is.
  • Import the math module into my program.
  • Use math.pi and math.sqrt().
  • Use math.ceil() to round up and math.floor() to round down.

Concept Explanation

Importing the Math Module

import math

Key Math Functions and Constants

Function/ConstantDescriptionExample
math.piπ ≈ 3.14159math.pi
math.ee ≈ 2.71828math.e
math.sqrt(x)Square root of xmath.sqrt(25) → 5.0
math.pow(x, y)x raised to power ymath.pow(2, 4) → 16.0
math.ceil(x)Round upmath.ceil(4.2) → 5
math.floor(x)Round downmath.floor(4.8) → 4
math.log(x, base)Logarithmmath.log(100, 10) → 2.0
math.sin(x)Sine (in radians)math.sin(math.pi/2) → 1.0
math.radians(deg)Convert degrees to radiansmath.radians(90)

Worked Example

Example 2.5.1: Circle Calculations

import math

radius = 5
area = math.pi * radius ** 2
circumference = 2 * math.pi * radius

print(f"Area of circle with radius {radius}: {area:.2f}")
print(f"Circumference: {circumference:.2f}")

number = 81
square_root = math.sqrt(number)
print(f"Square root of {number}: {square_root}")

Expected Behavior or Output

Output of example 1:

Area of circle with radius 5: 78.54
Circumference: 31.42
Square root of 81: 9.0

Common Mistakes

  1. Forgetting import math, so math.sqrt raises a NameError.
  2. Writing math.pi * radius * 2 for the area. The radius must be squared: math.pi * radius ** 2.
  3. Expecting math.sqrt(81) to print 9. It prints 9.0 because square roots are floats.

Activities

Activity 2.5.1: Circle Calculator

import math

radius_str = input("Enter the radius: ")
radius = float(radius_str)

area = math.pi * radius ** 2
circumference = 2 * math.pi * radius

print(f"Area: {area:.2f}")
print(f"Circumference: {circumference:.2f}")

Activity 2.5.2: Distance Finder

import math

x = float(input("Enter x coordinate: "))
y = float(input("Enter y coordinate: "))
distance = math.sqrt(x**2 + y**2)
print(f"Distance from origin: {distance:.2f}")

Sample run with the shared coordinates x = 3 and y = 4 (typed input shown after each prompt):

Enter x coordinate: 3
Enter y coordinate: 4
Distance from origin: 5.00

Accessibility Practice

Round results with :.2f so the screen reader announces 78.54 rather than fifteen digits. Say the dotted names aloud (‘math dot sqrt’) and listen for the dot, since a missing dot is a common transcription mistake when reading code by ear.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain what a Python module is.
  • I can import the math module into my program.
  • I can use math.pi and math.sqrt().
  • I can use math.ceil() to round up and math.floor() to round down.

Canonical Shared Dataset — Calculator and Coordinates

Use the canonical bill and tip rate in every parallel-language implementation.

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

bill = Decimal("24.50")
tip_rate = Decimal("0.15")
tip = (bill * tip_rate).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)
total = bill + tip
print(f"Tip: ${tip:.2f}")
print(f"Total: ${total:.2f}")

Expected output:

Tip: $3.68
Total: $28.18

Use the same coordinate values for the math-library example:

import math
x, y = 3, 4
distance = math.sqrt(x**2 + y**2)
print(distance)

Expected output: 5.0. The shared monetary contract rounds the tip to cents using decimal half-up rounding before adding it to the bill. Use decimal arithmetic rather than binary floating-point formatting for currency.

Unit 3: Control Flow — Decisions and Loops

Overview

Compatibility: All examples target Python 3.12 and newer; they avoid syntax and standard-library APIs introduced after Python 3.12.

This unit introduces how programs make decisions using if statements and perform repetitive tasks with for loops, along with fundamental string manipulation techniques.

Objectives:

  • Control program flow with if, elif, and else.
  • Iterate over sequences using for loops.
  • Understand and manipulate strings.

Lesson 3.1: Boolean Expressions and if Statements

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 7, pages 165–173
  • Matthes: Chapter 5, pages 71–78

Learning Objectives

  • Identify True and False as Boolean values.
  • Use comparison operators to create Boolean expressions.
  • Write a basic if statement.
  • Correctly indent the code block belonging to an if statement.

Concept Explanation

Comparison and Boolean Operators

OperatorMeaningExampleResult
==Equal to5 == 5True
!=Not equal to5 != 10True
<Less than5 < 10True
>Greater than10 > 5True
<=Less than or equal to5 <= 5True
>=Greater than or equal10 >= 5True
Boolean OperatorDescriptionExampleResult
andTrue if both are trueTrue and FalseFalse
orTrue if at least one is trueTrue or FalseTrue
notInverts the truth valuenot TrueFalse

The if Statement

score = 59
if score >= 60:
    print("Passing score.")
print("Program finished.")  # This runs regardless

Indentation defines which lines belong to the if block.

Worked Example

Example 3.1.1: Comparing a Score

score = 82

if score >= 60:
    print("Avery passed.")
else:
    print("Avery did not pass.")

print(score >= 80 and score < 90)   # both conditions must be true
print(score < 60 or score > 100)    # at least one condition must be true
print(not score >= 90)              # reverses True and False

Example 3.1.2: Password Length Check

password = "mysecret"
if len(password) < 8:
    print("Weak password: Must be at least 8 characters.")

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Avery passed.
True
False
True

Common Mistakes

  1. Writing = where == is needed in a condition, which is a syntax error in Python.
  2. Forgetting the colon at the end of the if line or the indentation of its block.
  3. Writing score >= 80 and < 90 instead of repeating the variable in each comparison.

Activities

Activity 3.1.1: Number Comparison Game

num1 = int(input("Enter the first number: "))
num2 = int(input("Enter the second number: "))

if num1 > num2:
    print(f"{num1} is greater than {num2}.")
if num1 == num2:
    print("The numbers are equal.")
if num1 < num2:
    print(f"{num1} is less than {num2}.")

Accessibility Practice

Read each condition aloud using the words ‘greater than or equal to’, ‘and’, ‘or’, and ‘not’. Confirm that your screen reader announces the colon at the end of the if line and the indentation of the next line, because these decide which statements run.

Skills Checklist

  • I can identify True and False as Boolean values.
  • I can use comparison operators to create Boolean expressions.
  • I can write a basic if statement.
  • I can correctly indent the code block belonging to an if statement.

Lesson 3.2: Chained Conditionals (elif, else)

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 7, pages 173–176
  • Matthes: Chapter 5, pages 79–84

Learning Objectives

  • Use an else statement to provide an alternative path.
  • Use elif to check multiple conditions in order.
  • Use and, or, and not operators to combine conditions.

Concept Explanation

if-elif-else Structure

Python checks each condition in sequential order. As soon as a condition is True, it runs that block and skips the rest.

score = 82

if score >= 90:
    print("Grade: A")
elif score >= 80:
    print("Grade: B")
elif score >= 70:
    print("Grade: C")
elif score >= 60:
    print("Grade: D")
else:
    print("Grade: F")

Output: Grade: B

Worked Example

Example 3.2.1: Grade Classification and Boundary Scores Every language track uses these same thresholds: A at 90, B at 80, C at 70, D at 60, otherwise F. The test scores sit exactly on and just below each boundary. (The def and return lines are explained fully in Unit 6; for now read classify(score) as “the grade for this score.”)

def classify(score):
    if score >= 90:
        return "A"
    elif score >= 80:
        return "B"
    elif score >= 70:
        return "C"
    elif score >= 60:
        return "D"
    else:
        return "F"

for score in [90, 89, 80, 79, 70, 69, 60, 59]:
    print(score, classify(score))

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

90 A
89 B
80 B
79 C
70 C
69 D
60 D
59 F

Common Mistakes

  1. Putting the conditions in the wrong order, such as testing score >= 60 first so every passing score is reported as a D.
  2. Using > instead of >=, so exactly 90 receives a B.
  3. Using a separate if for each grade instead of elif, so more than one message can print.

Activities

Activity 3.2.1: Grade Checker

score = int(input("Enter a score from 0 to 100: "))

if score >= 90:
    print("Grade: A")
elif score >= 80:
    print("Grade: B")
elif score >= 70:
    print("Grade: C")
elif score >= 60:
    print("Grade: D")
else:
    print("Grade: F")

Sample run (typed input shown after each prompt):

Enter a score from 0 to 100: 88
Grade: B

Run it again with 90, 89, 60, and 59 and confirm the grades A, B, D, and F.

Accessibility Practice

Read the boundary results aloud in order (90 A, 89 B, 80 B, 79 C…). Each line is a number, a space, and a letter, so it is easy to follow by ear and in braille. Do not rely on indentation alone to see which elif belongs to which if; count the lines that start at the left margin.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use an else statement to provide an alternative path.
  • I can use elif to check multiple conditions in order.
  • I can use and, or, and not operators to combine conditions.

Lesson 3.3: Introduction to Lists

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 5, pages 105–106
  • Matthes: Chapter 3, pages 33–47

Learning Objectives

  • Create a list in Python.
  • Access individual items in a list using their index.
  • Access list items from the end using negative indices.
  • Change the value of an item at a specific index.

Concept Explanation

A list is an ordered collection of values written between square brackets. Each value has a position called an index, and Python starts counting at 0. Negative indexes count from the end, so -1 is the last item. Lists are mutable: you can replace an item without creating a new list.

Creating and Accessing Lists

scores = [82, 91, 76, 88]

print(scores[0])   # 82  (first item)
print(scores[-1])  # 88  (last item)
print(len(scores)) # 4

Zero-based indexing: The first item is at index 0.

Modifying Lists

Worked Example

scores = [82, 91, 76, 88]
scores[2] = 80  # Change the third score (index 2) from 76 to 80
print(scores)   # [82, 91, 80, 88]

Expected Behavior or Output

Output of example 1:

[82, 91, 80, 88]

Common Mistakes

  1. Using scores[1] for the first item. The first item is at index 0.
  2. Using an index that is too large, which raises an IndexError. The last valid index is len(scores) - 1.
  3. Assuming copy = scores makes a separate list. Both names refer to the same list.

Activities

Activity 3.3.1: My Top 3 Hobbies

hobbies = ["reading", "coding", "hiking"]
print("My hobbies:", hobbies)
print("My second hobby:", hobbies[1])
hobbies[2] = "swimming"
print("Updated hobbies:", hobbies)

Accessibility Practice

When reading scores[-1] aloud, say ‘scores, open bracket, minus one, close bracket’ so the sign is not lost. Print a whole list on one line, and read its length separately, so the screen reader announces the state of the list in a single pass.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create a list in Python.
  • I can access individual items in a list using their index.
  • I can access list items from the end using negative indices.
  • I can change the value of an item at a specific index.

Lesson 3.4: Iterating with for Loops

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 2, pages 34–36
  • Matthes: Chapter 4, pages 49–60

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the purpose of a for loop.
  • Write a for loop to iterate over items in a list.
  • Write a for loop to iterate over characters in a string.
  • Use the range() function to control how many times a loop runs.

Concept Explanation

The for Loop Structure

for item in sequence:
    # code that runs for each item

Worked Example

Example 3.4.1: Total and Average of the Shared Scores

scores = [82, 91, 76, 88]
total = 0

for score in scores:
    print(f"Adding {score}")
    total = total + score

average = total / len(scores)
print(f"Total: {total}")
print(f"Average: {average}")

Example 3.4.2: Looping Through a String

word = "Python"
for char in word:
    print(char)

Example 3.4.3: Using range()

for i in range(5):      # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
    print(i)

for i in range(2, 8):   # 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7
    print(i)

for i in range(0, 10, 2):  # 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
    print(i)

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Adding 82
Adding 91
Adding 76
Adding 88
Total: 337
Average: 84.25

Common Mistakes

  1. Forgetting the colon after the for line or indenting the loop body inconsistently.
  2. Changing a list while looping over it, which can skip items.
  3. Using range(1, 4) and expecting it to include 4. The stop value is not included.

Activities

Activity 3.4.1: My Favorite Things

favorite_things = ["sunshine", "coffee", "books", "music", "mountains"]
for thing in favorite_things:
    print(f"I love {thing}!")

Activity 3.4.2: Countdown Timer

start = int(input("Enter a starting number: "))
for i in range(start, 0, -1):
    print(i)
print("Blast off!")

Accessibility Practice

Print one labelled line per loop pass (Adding 82), so your screen reader reads each step. Count the lines to confirm the loop ran the expected number of times, since the loop’s structure is carried by indentation and not by visible braces.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain the purpose of a for loop.
  • I can write a for loop to iterate over items in a list.
  • I can write a for loop to iterate over characters in a string.
  • I can use the range() function to control how many times a loop runs.

Lesson 3.5: Basic String Operations

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 5, pages 99–115
  • Matthes: Chapter 2, pages 19–25

Learning Objectives

  • Combine strings using concatenation.
  • Find the length of a string using len().
  • Convert a string to uppercase/lowercase.
  • Remove extra spaces using .strip().
  • Replace parts of a string using .replace().

Concept Explanation

Common String Methods

message = "  Hello Python!  "

message.strip()          # "Hello Python!"   — removes whitespace
message.upper()          # "  HELLO PYTHON!  "
message.lower()          # "  hello python!  "
message.replace("Hello", "Hi")  # "  Hi Python!  "
len(message)             # 17

Important: String methods return a new string — they do not modify the original.

Worked Example

Example 3.5.1: String Manipulation

message = "  Hello Python  "
print(f"Original: '{message}'")
print(f"Length: {len(message)}")
print(f"Uppercase: '{message.upper()}'")
print(f"Stripped: '{message.strip()}'")

Example 3.5.2: Normalizing a Name and Searching the Shared Text Sample

raw_name = "  avery  "
clean_name = raw_name.strip().title()
print(f"Name: '{clean_name}'")

text = "A student studies programming. Programming develops problem-solving skills."
lowered = text.lower()
print("Characters:", len(text))
print("Contains 'programming':", "programming" in lowered)
print("First position of 'programming':", lowered.find("programming"))
print("Times 'programming' appears:", lowered.count("programming"))

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Name: 'Avery'
Characters: 75
Contains 'programming': True
First position of 'programming': 18
Times 'programming' appears: 2

Common Mistakes

  1. Expecting text.upper() to change text. Strings are immutable; assign the result: text = text.upper().
  2. Forgetting that find returns -1, not an error, when the text is missing.
  3. Counting positions from 1. The first character is at index 0.

Activities

Activity 3.5.1: Name Formatter

first_name = input("Enter your first name: ")
last_name = input("Enter your last name: ")
full_name = first_name + " " + last_name
print(f"Full name: {full_name}")
print(f"Uppercase: {full_name.upper()}")
print(f"Total characters: {len(full_name)}")

Accessibility Practice

Strings with many quotation marks are hard to read by ear. Say ‘single quote’ and ‘double quote’ aloud when checking a line, and print results inside labelled sentences such as Characters: 75 so the screen reader does not run values together.

Skills Checklist

  • I can combine strings using concatenation.
  • I can find the length of a string using len().
  • I can convert a string to uppercase/lowercase.
  • I can remove extra spaces using .strip().
  • I can replace parts of a string using .replace().

Canonical Shared Dataset — Grade Thresholds and Scores

All tracks must classify scores using A ≥ 90, B ≥ 80, C ≥ 70, D ≥ 60, and F otherwise. Use the same score sequence.

scores = [82, 91, 76, 88]

def grade_for(score):
    if score >= 90:
        return "A"
    if score >= 80:
        return "B"
    if score >= 70:
        return "C"
    if score >= 60:
        return "D"
    return "F"

for score in scores:
    print(score, grade_for(score))

total = sum(scores)
average = total / len(scores)
print("Total:", total)
print("Average:", average)

Expected output:

82 B
91 A
76 C
88 B
Total: 337
Average: 84.25

Boundary tests must include 90, 80, 70, 60, and 59. Do not silently change a threshold or replace the shared scores with a different set in a parallel example.

Unit 4: Data Structures — Lists and Dictionaries

Overview

Compatibility: All examples target Python 3.12 and newer; they avoid syntax and standard-library APIs introduced after Python 3.12.

This unit deepens understanding of lists and introduces dictionaries as powerful mechanisms for organizing data.

Objectives:

  • Add, remove, and organize list elements.
  • Work with tuples (immutable lists).
  • Use dictionaries for key-value pair storage.
  • Loop through dictionaries.

Lesson 4.1: More on Lists

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 3 (Introducing Lists) and Chapter 4 (Working with Lists)

Learning Objectives

  • Add an item to the end of a list using .append().
  • Insert an item at a specific position using .insert().
  • Remove an item by index using del.
  • Remove an item and retrieve its value using .pop().
  • Remove the first occurrence of a value using .remove().

Concept Explanation

Adding and Removing Elements

my_list = [10, 20, 30]

my_list.append(40)          # Add to end → [10, 20, 30, 40]
my_list.insert(1, 15)       # Insert at index 1 → [10, 15, 20, 30, 40]
del my_list[0]              # Delete by index → [15, 20, 30, 40]
removed = my_list.pop()     # Remove and return last → removed=40, list=[15, 20, 30]
my_list.remove(20)          # Remove by value → [15, 30]

Worked Example

scores = [82, 91, 76, 88]

scores.append(95)        # [82, 91, 76, 88, 95]
scores.insert(1, 85)     # [82, 85, 91, 76, 88, 95]
scores[2] = 93           # [82, 85, 93, 76, 88, 95]
scores.remove(76)        # [82, 85, 93, 88, 95]
last_score = scores.pop()  # last_score is 95

print(scores)
print(len(scores))
print(88 in scores)

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

[82, 85, 93, 88]
4
True

Common Mistakes

  1. Using list.insert(value, position). The position comes first: scores.insert(1, 85).
  2. Calling remove() with a value that is not in the list, which raises a ValueError; check with in first.
  3. Removing items from a list while looping over it, which skips the item after each removal.

Activities

  1. Trace the list after each operation in the example and write each version as one sentence.
  2. Remove the first score with pop(0) and explain what happens to the other scores.
  3. Write code that removes every score below 80 safely.
  4. Print the position of the first score above 90 with index(), and explain what happens if none exists.

Accessibility Practice

After every change, print the whole list on one line so a screen reader reads a complete state in one pass. Say the comments aloud as part of each line, since they hold the expected value after the change.

Skills Checklist

  • I can add an item to the end of a list using .append().
  • I can insert an item at a specific position using .insert().
  • I can remove an item by index using del.
  • I can remove an item and retrieve its value using .pop().
  • I can remove the first occurrence of a value using .remove().

Lesson 4.2: Organizing Lists

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 3 (Introducing Lists) and Chapter 4 (Working with Lists)

Learning Objectives

  • Sort a list permanently using .sort().
  • Get a temporarily sorted version using sorted().
  • Reverse a list using .reverse().
  • Find how many items are in a list using len().

Concept Explanation

Lists can be reordered in two ways. sort() changes the list in place and returns nothing. sorted() returns a new sorted list and leaves the original unchanged. Both accept reverse=True for descending order.

Sorting and Reversing

Worked Example

scores = [82, 91, 76, 88]
scores.sort()                           # Permanent sort in-place
print(scores)                           # [76, 82, 88, 91]

fruits = ["orange", "apple", "banana"]
sorted_fruits = sorted(fruits)          # Temporary sort — original unchanged
print(fruits)                           # ['orange', 'apple', 'banana']
print(sorted_fruits)                    # ['apple', 'banana', 'orange']

scores.reverse()                        # Reverse in-place -> [91, 88, 82, 76]
scores.sort(reverse=True)               # Sort descending -> [91, 88, 82, 76]
print(scores)                           # [91, 88, 82, 76]
print(len(scores))                      # Length: 4

Expected Behavior or Output

Output of example 1:

[76, 82, 88, 91]
['orange', 'apple', 'banana']
['apple', 'banana', 'orange']
[91, 88, 82, 76]
4

Common Mistakes

  1. Writing scores = scores.sort(). sort() returns None, so the list is lost.
  2. Sorting a list that mixes numbers and text, which raises a TypeError.
  3. Expecting reverse() to sort. It only flips the current order.

Activities

  1. Predict the result of scores.sort() and scores.sort(reverse=True) on the shared scores, then check.
  2. Use sorted(scores) and show that the original list is unchanged.
  3. Sort the words ["pencil", "folder", "notebook"] and print them.
  4. Explain the difference between sort() and sorted() in two sentences.

Accessibility Practice

Print each sorted version on its own labelled line (Ascending:, Descending:). The first and last numbers are the quickest to check by ear.

Skills Checklist

  • I can sort a list permanently using .sort().
  • I can get a temporarily sorted version using sorted().
  • I can reverse a list using .reverse().
  • I can find how many items are in a list using len().

Lesson 4.3: Tuples — Immutable Lists

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 4 (Working with Lists), the section on tuples

Learning Objectives

  • Create a tuple in Python.
  • Explain the main difference between a list and a tuple (mutability).
  • Access items in a tuple by their index.

Concept Explanation

A tuple is an ordered collection like a list, written with parentheses, but it cannot be changed after it is created. Use a tuple for a fixed group of values such as the shared coordinates (3, 4). Because it cannot change, a tuple can also be used where Python needs a value that never changes, such as a dictionary key.

Tuples

Tuples are defined with parentheses and cannot be changed after creation.

When to use tuples: For data that should remain constant (coordinates, RGB values, fixed settings).

Worked Example

coordinates = (3, 4)
x, y = coordinates        # tuple unpacking
print(coordinates[0])     # 3
print(coordinates[-1])    # 4
print(x, y)               # 3 4

# This would cause a TypeError:
# coordinates[1] = 5

Expected Behavior or Output

Output of example 1:

3
4
3 4

Common Mistakes

  1. Writing (5) for a one-item tuple. A one-item tuple needs a comma: (5,).
  2. Trying to assign to an item (coordinates[1] = 5), which raises a TypeError.
  3. Using a list when the data should never change, so an accidental change goes unnoticed.

Activities

  1. Create the tuple (3, 4), unpack it into x and y, and print both.
  2. Write a function that returns a name, an age, and a height as a tuple and unpack all three.
  3. Try to change one item of a tuple and read the error message aloud.
  4. Explain, in two sentences, when a tuple is a better choice than a list.

Accessibility Practice

Say the parentheses and the commas aloud when reading a tuple, because a one-item tuple differs from a plain value only by its trailing comma. Read error messages from the last line upward to find the problem quickly.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create a tuple in Python.
  • I can explain the main difference between a list and a tuple (mutability).
  • I can access items in a tuple by their index.

Lesson 4.4: Introducing Dictionaries

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 11, pages 307–309
  • Matthes: Chapter 6, pages 91–98

Learning Objectives

  • Create a dictionary in Python.
  • Explain what a key-value pair is.
  • Access a value in a dictionary using its key.
  • Add, modify, and remove key-value pairs.

Concept Explanation

Dictionary Basics

A dictionary stores key-value pairs. Keys must be unique and immutable (strings, numbers, tuples). Values can be anything.

student_profile = {
    "name": "Avery",
    "age": 16,
    "height_m": 1.72,
    "favorite_subject": "Computer Science",
}

print(student_profile["name"])
print(student_profile["favorite_subject"])

# Demonstrate adding and removing a temporary key without changing
# the four-field canonical student record.
student_profile["temporary_note"] = "Dictionary example"
del student_profile["temporary_note"]
print(sorted(student_profile))

Expected output:

Avery
Computer Science
['age', 'favorite_subject', 'height_m', 'name']

Worked Example

Example 4.4.1: Inventory Item Dictionary

item = {
    "name": "Notebook",
    "quantity": 3,
    "unit_price": 2.50
}

print(f"Item: {item['name']}")
print(f"Quantity: {item['quantity']}")

item["quantity"] = item["quantity"] + 2    # restock two more
item["location"] = "Shelf A"               # add a new key
print(item)
print("Stock value:", item["quantity"] * item["unit_price"])

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Item: Notebook
Quantity: 3
{'name': 'Notebook', 'quantity': 5, 'unit_price': 2.5, 'location': 'Shelf A'}
Stock value: 12.5

Common Mistakes

  1. Using a key that does not exist (profile["grade"]), which raises a KeyError; use profile.get("grade") to receive None instead.
  2. Forgetting the quotation marks around a text key, so Python looks for a variable.
  3. Expecting dictionary order to be sorted. Dictionaries keep insertion order, not alphabetical order.

Activities

  1. Predict the printed values before running the example, then run it.
  2. Add a "discount" key to the item and print the discounted line value.
  3. Remove "favorite_subject" from the profile with del and show what get returns afterward.
  4. Write a check that tells whether an item has all of the keys name, quantity, and unit_price.

Accessibility Practice

Choose key names that read well aloud, such as unit_price. Print one key and value per line, so the screen reader announces each pair separately, and avoid relying on curly braces alone to see where a dictionary ends.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create a dictionary in Python.
  • I can explain what a key-value pair is.
  • I can access a value in a dictionary using its key.
  • I can add, modify, and remove key-value pairs.

Lesson 4.5: Looping Through Dictionaries

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 6 (Dictionaries), the sections on looping through a dictionary

Learning Objectives

  • Loop through all the keys in a dictionary.
  • Loop through all the values in a dictionary.
  • Loop through both keys and values at the same time.

Concept Explanation

Dictionary Iteration Methods

Worked Example

inventory = {
    "Notebook": {"quantity": 3, "unit_price": 2.50},
    "Pencil": {"quantity": 10, "unit_price": 0.50},
    "Folder": {"quantity": 4, "unit_price": 1.25},
}

# Loop through keys (default)
for item_name in inventory:
    print(item_name)

# Loop through values only
for details in inventory.values():
    print(details["quantity"])

# Loop through key-value pairs
total_value = 0
for item_name, details in inventory.items():
    line_value = details["quantity"] * details["unit_price"]
    print(f"{item_name}: {details['quantity']} in stock, value {line_value:.2f}")
    total_value += line_value
print(f"Total inventory value: {total_value:.2f}")

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Notebook
Pencil
Folder
3
10
4
Notebook: 3 in stock, value 7.50
Pencil: 10 in stock, value 5.00
Folder: 4 in stock, value 5.00
Total inventory value: 17.50

Common Mistakes

  1. Looping with for item in inventory and expecting the values. The default loop gives the keys.
  2. Changing the dictionary’s size while looping over it, which raises a RuntimeError.
  3. Forgetting .items() when both the key and the value are needed.

Activities

  1. Run the example and write the three key-value lines in order.
  2. Print only the items with a quantity below 5.
  3. Print the inventory sorted by the line value, highest first.
  4. Explain why .items() returns pairs and how the loop unpacks them.

Accessibility Practice

Print each inventory item as one complete sentence so the screen reader reads the name, quantity, and value together. Python dictionaries keep insertion order, so the order is stable and can be learned by ear.

Skills Checklist

  • I can loop through all the keys in a dictionary.
  • I can loop through all the values in a dictionary.
  • I can loop through both keys and values at the same time.

Unit 5: User Input and while Loops

Overview

This unit focuses on obtaining diverse input from users and controlling program execution through indefinite loops.

Objectives:

  • Implement indefinite loops using while statements.
  • Control while loop execution with break and continue.
  • Avoid infinite loops.

Lesson 5.1: How the input() Function Works

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 7 (User Input and while Loops), the section on how the input() function works
  • Zelle: Chapter 2 (Writing Simple Programs), the section on input

Learning Objectives

  • Effectively use input() to get user data.
  • Confirm that input()’s return value is always a string.
  • Convert user input to a numeric type when necessary.

Concept Explanation

input(prompt) shows the prompt, waits for the user to press Enter, and returns what was typed as a string, even when the user typed digits. To use the value as a number, convert it with int() or float(). Checking first with isdigit() avoids an error for text that is not a whole number; Lesson 8.3 shows the general solution, exceptions.

Key Reminder

input() always returns a string. Convert to numeric types as needed.

age_input = input("How old are you? ")
print(f"Type: {type(age_input)}")    # <class 'str'>

age_int = int(age_input)
print(f"In 5 years: {age_int + 5}")

Worked Example

text = input("How old are you? ")
print("Type:", type(text).__name__)
if text.isdigit():
    age = int(text)
    print("In 5 years:", age + 5)
else:
    print("That was not a whole number.")

Expected Behavior or Output

Sample run typing 16:

How old are you? 16
Type: str
In 5 years: 21

Sample run typing abc:

How old are you? abc
Type: str
That was not a whole number.

Common Mistakes

  1. Adding to the value returned by input() without converting it. "16" + 5 raises a TypeError.
  2. Calling int() on text such as "abc" or an empty answer, which raises a ValueError.
  3. Using isdigit() for numbers with a minus sign or a decimal point, which it rejects.

Activities

  1. Run the program typing 16, then abc, then just Enter. Compare the three outputs.
  2. Change the program so that it accepts an age only from 0 to 120.
  3. Write a program that asks for a name and a number and prints one sentence using both.
  4. Explain why type(text) is str even when you typed 16.

Accessibility Practice

Each prompt ends with a space and says what to type. When you test, listen to whether your screen reader reads the prompt in full before you start typing, and write the prompt text so it still makes sense when read on its own.

Skills Checklist

  • I can effectively use input() to get user data.
  • I can confirm that input()’s return value is always a string.
  • I can convert user input to a numeric type when necessary.

Lesson 5.2: The while Loop in Action

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 7 (User Input and while Loops)
  • Zelle: Chapter 8 (Loop Structures and Booleans)

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the difference between a for loop and a while loop.
  • Write a basic while loop.
  • Make sure my while loop has a way to stop.

Concept Explanation

for vs. while Loop Comparison

Featurefor Loopwhile Loop
PurposeDefinite iteration (known count)Indefinite iteration (condition-based)
When to UseIterating over lists, rangesRepeating until a condition is met
Control VariableAutomatically updatedMust be manually updated
RiskLess prone to infinite loopsHigh risk if condition never becomes false

Worked Example

count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)
    count += 1
print("Counting finished!")

message = input("Enter a message, or type quit to exit: ")
while message != "quit":
    print("You said: " + message)
    message = input("Enter a message, or type quit to exit: ")
print("Goodbye!")

Expected Behavior or Output

Sample run typing hello, scores, and quit:

1
2
3
4
5
Counting finished!
Enter a message, or type quit to exit: hello
You said: hello
Enter a message, or type quit to exit: scores
You said: scores
Enter a message, or type quit to exit: quit
Goodbye!

Common Mistakes

  1. Forgetting to change the loop variable, which creates an endless loop.
  2. Reading input only before the loop and never again inside it, so the same message repeats forever.
  3. Comparing the sentinel with different capitalization (Quit and quit) and never stopping.

Activities

  1. Predict the output for the typed lines hello, scores, and quit.
  2. Change the sentinel to exit and update the prompt.
  3. Count how many messages were entered and print the count at the end.
  4. Rewrite the counting loop as a for loop with range and compare the two.

Accessibility Practice

Each prompt is a full sentence that names the way to stop. The response begins with the label You said: so the conversation can be followed in order by ear. If a loop floods the screen reader with output, stop it with Ctrl+C.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain the difference between a for loop and a while loop.
  • I can write a basic while loop.
  • I can make sure my while loop has a way to stop.

Lesson 5.3: Using Flags and break to Exit Loops

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 7 (User Input and while Loops)

Learning Objectives

  • Use a Boolean “flag” variable to control a while loop.
  • Use the break statement to exit a loop early.

Concept Explanation

Flag Variable

active = True
while active:
    message = input("Say something (or 'quit' to stop): ")
    if message == 'quit':
        active = False
    else:
        print(f"You said: {message}")

break Statement

while True:
    city = input("Enter a city (or 'done' to finish): ")
    if city == 'done':
        break
    print(f"I've heard {city} is a great place!")

Worked Example

Example: Stopping a Search with a Flag and break (shared scores)

scores = [82, 91, 76, 88]
found = False
index = 0

while index < len(scores):
    if scores[index] >= 90:
        found = True
        break
    index += 1

if found:
    print(f"First score of 90 or higher: {scores[index]} at index {index}")
else:
    print("No score of 90 or higher.")

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

First score of 90 or higher: 91 at index 1

Common Mistakes

  1. Setting the flag but running more code in the same pass that should have been skipped.
  2. Forgetting to set the result variable before the loop and misreading an old value afterward.
  3. Using break in an inner loop and expecting it to leave the outer loop. It leaves only the innermost loop.

Activities

  1. Change the search to find the first score below 80 and predict the index.
  2. Rewrite a flag-controlled loop so that it uses break and compare the two versions.
  3. Write a loop that stops when the user types quit and also stops after 5 attempts.
  4. Explain in two sentences when a flag is clearer than break.

Accessibility Practice

Report search results as complete sentences that include both the value and its position, so the sentence is understood without any layout. Remember that Python indexes start at 0, and say ‘index 1’ aloud rather than ‘second’ to avoid confusion.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use a Boolean “flag” variable to control a while loop.
  • I can use the break statement to exit a loop early.

Lesson 5.4: Using continue in Loops

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 7 (User Input and while Loops), the section on using continue

Learning Objectives

  • Use continue to skip the rest of the current loop iteration.
  • Identify scenarios where continue would be useful.

Concept Explanation

continue — Skip the Current Iteration

number = 0
while number < 10:
    number += 1
    if number % 2 == 0:
        continue        # Skip even numbers
    print(number)       # Prints 1, 3, 5, 7, 9

continue vs. break

  • break — exits the loop entirely
  • continue — skips only the current iteration, loop continues

Worked Example

Example: Skipping Invalid Entries with continue

raw_scores = [82, -5, 91, 105, 76, 88]
valid_total = 0
valid_count = 0

for raw in raw_scores:
    if raw < 0 or raw > 100:
        print(f"Skipping invalid score: {raw}")
        continue
    valid_total += raw
    valid_count += 1

print(f"Valid scores: {valid_count}, total: {valid_total}")

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Skipping invalid score: -5
Skipping invalid score: 105
Valid scores: 4, total: 337

Common Mistakes

  1. Placing statements that must always run after continue, so they are skipped.
  2. Using continue in a while loop before changing the loop variable, which creates an endless loop.
  3. Confusing continue (skip this pass) with break (leave the loop).

Activities

  1. Predict the printed lines and the final total of the invalid-scores example.
  2. Skip scores below 80 instead.
  3. Rewrite the invalid-scores loop with an if/else and no continue, and compare the readability.
  4. Write a loop over range(1, 10) that prints only odd numbers using continue.

Accessibility Practice

Print a line for every skipped entry, so the screen reader announces what was ignored. Never skip silently when a user needs to know what the program did with their data.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use continue to skip the rest of the current loop iteration.
  • I can identify scenarios where continue would be useful.

Lesson 5.5: Avoiding Infinite Loops

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 7 (User Input and while Loops), the sections on avoiding infinite loops
  • Zelle: Chapter 8 (Loop Structures and Booleans)

Learning Objectives

  • Define what an infinite loop is.
  • Identify common causes of infinite loops.
  • Stop a running program in an infinite loop.

Concept Explanation

An infinite loop never ends because its condition always remains True.

Common causes:

  1. Forgetting to update the loop variable.
  2. Updating the variable in the wrong direction.
  3. Using an incorrect logical condition.
# INFINITE LOOP — Don't run!
count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)
    # Missing: count += 1

# CORRECT
count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)
    count += 1

To stop a running infinite loop: Press Ctrl + C in the terminal.

Worked Example

MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3
attempts = 0
score = None

while attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS:
    attempts += 1
    text = input(f"Enter a score from 0 to 100 (attempt {attempts} of {MAX_ATTEMPTS}): ")
    if text.isdigit() and 0 <= int(text) <= 100:
        score = int(text)
        break
    print("Invalid score: " + text)

if score is not None:
    print("Accepted score:", score)
else:
    print("No valid score was entered.")

Expected Behavior or Output

Sample run typing abc, 105, and 88:

Enter a score from 0 to 100 (attempt 1 of 3): abc
Invalid score: abc
Enter a score from 0 to 100 (attempt 2 of 3): 105
Invalid score: 105
Enter a score from 0 to 100 (attempt 3 of 3): 88
Accepted score: 88

Sample run typing three invalid lines (x, y, z):

Enter a score from 0 to 100 (attempt 1 of 3): x
Invalid score: x
Enter a score from 0 to 100 (attempt 2 of 3): y
Invalid score: y
Enter a score from 0 to 100 (attempt 3 of 3): z
Invalid score: z
No valid score was entered.

Common Mistakes

  1. Forgetting to increase attempts, so the limit is never reached.
  2. Testing the wrong variable in the loop condition, so it never becomes false.
  3. Not knowing the interrupt key. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop a program that will not end.

Activities

  1. Run the sample with abc, 105, and 88 and confirm the accepted score.
  2. Run it with three invalid lines and read the final message.
  3. Change the limit to 5 and test it.
  4. For each loop you have written so far, write down what makes it stop.

Accessibility Practice

A loop that cannot be stopped is an accessibility problem as well as a bug, because it can flood a screen reader with output. Learn Ctrl+C before running loops, give every input loop a limit, and write error messages that say what is valid.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define what an infinite loop is.
  • I can identify common causes of infinite loops.
  • I know how to stop a running program in an infinite loop.

Unit 6: Functions

Overview

This unit introduces functions, enabling organization of code into reusable blocks, passing arguments, and returning values.

Objectives:

  • Define and call functions.
  • Pass arguments to functions.
  • Return values from functions.
  • Understand the concept of scope.

Lesson 6.1: Defining Functions

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 6, pages 137–142
  • Matthes: Chapter 8, pages 129–130

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why functions are useful.
  • Define a simple function in Python.
  • Use parameters to specify function inputs.
  • Call a function by its name.

Concept Explanation

Function Syntax

def function_name(parameter1, parameter2):
    """Docstring describing what the function does."""
    # Function body
    print(f"Hello, {parameter1}!")

Worked Example

Example 6.1.1: Simple Greeting Function

def greet_user():
    """Prints a simple greeting message."""
    print("Hello, Python programmer!")

greet_user()   # Call the function
greet_user()   # Call it again

Example 6.1.2: Function with a Parameter

def greet_name(name):
    """Prints a personalized greeting."""
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

greet_name("Avery")
greet_name("Riley")

Example 6.1.3: A Reusable Tip Calculator (shared calculator values)

def show_tip(bill, tip_rate):
    """Print the tip and the total for a bill."""
    tip = bill * tip_rate
    print(f"Tip: {tip:.2f}")
    print(f"Total: {bill + tip:.2f}")

show_tip(24.5, 0.15)

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Tip: 3.67
Total: 28.18

Common Mistakes

  1. Writing greet_user without parentheses and expecting the function to run.
  2. Forgetting the colon after the def line, or the indentation of the body.
  3. Passing arguments in the wrong order, such as show_tip(0.15, 24.5).

Activities

  1. Call show_tip(100, 0.2) and predict both printed lines.
  2. Write a function describe_student(name, age) that prints one sentence.
  3. Call greet_name() with no argument and read the error message.
  4. Explain the difference between a parameter and an argument using the example.

Accessibility Practice

Choose function names that read as actions when spoken, such as show_tip. Print complete sentences from a function so the screen reader announces the result of each call separately, and say ‘open parenthesis, close parenthesis’ for an empty parameter list.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain why functions are useful.
  • I can define a simple function in Python.
  • I can use parameters to specify function inputs.
  • I can call a function by its name.

Lesson 6.2: Passing Arguments

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 8 (Functions), the sections on passing arguments
  • Zelle: Chapter 6 (Defining Functions)

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate between a parameter and an argument.
  • Pass arguments using positional order.
  • Pass arguments using keyword arguments.

Concept Explanation

Positional vs. Keyword Arguments

def describe_animal(animal_type, animal_name):
    print(f"I have a {animal_type} named {animal_name}.")

# Positional arguments (order matters)
describe_animal("dog", "Buddy")

# Keyword arguments (order doesn't matter)
describe_animal(animal_name="Max", animal_type="cat")

Default Values

def make_shirt(size, message="I love Python"):
    print(f"Making a {size}-sized shirt: '{message}'")

make_shirt("large")                       # Uses default message
make_shirt("medium", "Hello World")       # Custom message

Worked Example

Example: Default, Positional, and Keyword Arguments (shared calculator values)

def calculate_total(bill, tip_rate=0.15):
    return bill + bill * tip_rate

print(f"{calculate_total(24.5):.2f}")                       # default rate
print(f"{calculate_total(24.5, 0.20):.2f}")                 # positional
print(f"{calculate_total(tip_rate=0.10, bill=24.5):.2f}")   # keyword

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

28.18
29.40
26.95

Common Mistakes

  1. Putting a parameter with a default before a parameter without one in the definition, which is a syntax error.
  2. Mixing positional and keyword arguments in an order Python does not allow (positional first).
  3. Using a mutable default such as [], which is shared between calls.

Activities

  1. Predict the three totals in the example before running it.
  2. Add a third parameter round_total with the default False and use it.
  3. Call the function with the arguments in a different order using keywords.
  4. Explain why tip_rate=0.15 is called a default value.

Accessibility Practice

Keyword arguments make a call read as a sentence: ‘calculate total, bill equals 24.5, tip rate equals 0.10’. Say the equals signs aloud and check that your screen reader announces them.

Skills Checklist

  • I can differentiate between a parameter and an argument.
  • I can pass arguments using positional order.
  • I can pass arguments using keyword arguments.

Lesson 6.3: Return Values

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 8 (Functions), the section on return values
  • Zelle: Chapter 6 (Defining Functions)

Learning Objectives

  • Use return to send a value back from a function.
  • Explain the difference between print() and return.
  • Store the returned value of a function in a variable.

Concept Explanation

The return Statement

def add_numbers(num1, num2):
    """Adds two numbers and returns the result."""
    total = num1 + num2
    return total

result = add_numbers(5, 3)
print(f"The sum is: {result}")   # 8

Key difference: print() displays a value; return sends a value back to the caller for further use.

Worked Example

Example: Returning Computed Results (shared scores)

def average(scores):
    """Return the average of a list of scores."""
    return sum(scores) / len(scores)

def classify(score):
    if score >= 90:
        return "A"
    elif score >= 80:
        return "B"
    elif score >= 70:
        return "C"
    elif score >= 60:
        return "D"
    return "F"

avg = average([82, 91, 76, 88])   # returned, not just printed
print(f"Average: {avg}")
print(f"Grade for the average: {classify(avg)}")

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Average: 84.25
Grade for the average: B

Common Mistakes

  1. Printing inside a function and then trying to use the result in a calculation. The function returned None.
  2. Writing statements after return in the same block. They never run.
  3. Ignoring a returned value, so the work of the function is lost.

Activities

  1. Predict the two printed results of the example before running.
  2. Write total(list) that returns the sum of a list of numbers.
  3. Write is_passing(score) that returns True or False using the shared thresholds.
  4. Explain the difference between print and return in two sentences.

Accessibility Practice

Return values from functions and print them in one place. A function that prints and returns at the same time can announce a result twice. Read the single printed line aloud and check it matches the returned value.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use return to send a value back from a function.
  • I can explain the difference between print() and return.
  • I can store the returned value of a function in a variable.

Lesson 6.4: Functions with Lists and Dictionaries

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 8 (Functions), the section on passing a list to a function

Learning Objectives

  • Pass a list or dictionary as an argument to a function.
  • Understand that modifying a list inside a function affects the original.
  • Create a copy of a list to avoid unintended modifications.

Concept Explanation

Since lists are mutable, modifying them inside a function changes the original:

def add_score(score_list, new_score):
    score_list.append(new_score)

scores = [82, 91, 76, 88]
add_score(scores, 95)
print(scores)   # [82, 91, 76, 88, 95]  - the original list changed

Expected output:

[82, 91, 76, 88, 95]

To prevent modification, pass a copy:

add_score(scores[:], 100)   # Original unchanged

Worked Example

Example: Processing the Shared Inventory with a Function

def inventory_value(inventory):
    total = 0
    for details in inventory.values():
        total += details["quantity"] * details["unit_price"]
    return total

inventory = {
    "Notebook": {"quantity": 3, "unit_price": 2.50},
    "Pencil": {"quantity": 10, "unit_price": 0.50},
    "Folder": {"quantity": 4, "unit_price": 1.25},
}
print(f"Total inventory value: {inventory_value(inventory):.2f}")

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Total inventory value: 17.50

Common Mistakes

  1. Expecting a function to receive its own copy of a list. It receives the same list and can change it.
  2. Changing a list inside a function that is meant only to read it.
  3. Making a copy with copy = original instead of original[:] or list(original).

Activities

  1. Predict the printed lists in the example before running it.
  2. Write scale_prices(inventory, factor) that changes the prices in place and show the effect.
  3. Rewrite it so it returns a new inventory and leaves the original unchanged.
  4. Explain the difference between passing a number and passing a list to a function.

Accessibility Practice

State aloud before each call whether the function changes its argument. Print the list before and after the call so a screen reader user hears the effect, and use names such as add_score that say a change will happen.

Skills Checklist

  • I can pass a list or dictionary as an argument to a function.
  • I understand that modifying a list inside a function affects the original.
  • I can create a copy of a list to avoid unintended modifications.

Lesson 6.5: Arbitrary Number of Arguments

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 8 (Functions), the section on passing an arbitrary number of arguments

Learning Objectives

  • Define a function using *args for arbitrary positional arguments.
  • Define a function using **kwargs for arbitrary keyword arguments.

Concept Explanation

*args — Arbitrary Positional Arguments

def make_pizza(size, *toppings):
    print(f"Making a {size}-inch pizza with:")
    for topping in toppings:
        print(f"  - {topping}")

make_pizza(12, 'pepperoni')
make_pizza(16, 'mushrooms', 'green peppers', 'extra cheese')

Example: Variable Number of Scores

def average(*scores):
    return sum(scores) / len(scores)

print(average(82, 91, 76, 88))   # any number of arguments
print(average(90, 80))

Expected output:

84.25
85.0

**kwargs — Arbitrary Keyword Arguments

Worked Example

def build_profile(first, last, **user_info):
    user_info['first_name'] = first
    user_info['last_name'] = last
    return user_info

profile = build_profile('albert', 'einstein',
                        location='princeton',
                        field='physics')
print(profile)

Expected Behavior or Output

Output of example 1:

{'location': 'princeton', 'field': 'physics', 'first_name': 'albert', 'last_name': 'einstein'}

Common Mistakes

  1. Calling average() with no arguments, which divides by zero. Check the count first.
  2. Putting *args before a normal parameter and being unable to pass the normal one by position.
  3. Forgetting that *args is a tuple, not a list, so it cannot be changed.

Activities

  1. Predict the result of average(82, 91, 76, 88) and average(90, 80).
  2. Write maximum(*numbers) that returns the largest argument.
  3. Write join_words(separator, *words) that joins any number of words.
  4. Explain what the * does in a call such as average(*scores).

Accessibility Practice

Read variadic signatures aloud: ‘define average, open parenthesis, star scores, close parenthesis’. Make sure your screen reader announces the star, since it changes the meaning of the parameter.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define a function using *args for arbitrary positional arguments.
  • I can define a function using **kwargs for arbitrary keyword arguments.

Canonical Shared Dataset — Inventory, Collections, and Functions

Use the same inventory records for list, dictionary, iteration, and function examples.

inventory = [
    {"name": "Notebook", "quantity": 3, "unit_price": 2.50},
    {"name": "Pencil", "quantity": 10, "unit_price": 0.50},
    {"name": "Folder", "quantity": 4, "unit_price": 1.25},
]

def item_value(item):
    return item["quantity"] * item["unit_price"]

for item in inventory:
    print(item["name"], item["quantity"], f"${item['unit_price']:.2f}",
          f"${item_value(item):.2f}")

grand_total = sum(item_value(item) for item in inventory)
print(f"Inventory total: ${grand_total:.2f}")

Expected output:

Notebook 3 $2.50 $7.50
Pencil 10 $0.50 $5.00
Folder 4 $1.25 $5.00
Inventory total: $17.50

For sequence exercises, use the canonical scores [82, 91, 76, 88]. For immutable-sequence exercises, use coordinates (3, 4). Keep language-specific collection types idiomatic while preserving record values and calculation results.

Unit 7: Classes and Object-Oriented Programming

Overview

Compatibility: All examples target Python 3.12 and newer; they avoid syntax and standard-library APIs introduced after Python 3.12.

This unit introduces the fundamental concepts of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) in Python, focusing on defining and using classes, attributes, methods, and inheritance.

Objectives:

  • Define and instantiate classes.
  • Work with attributes and methods.
  • Understand inheritance and composition.

Lesson 7.1: Why Learn About Classes?

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 4, pages 65–67; Chapter 10, pages 247–248
  • Matthes: Chapter 9, page 157

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the basic idea of Object-Oriented Programming.
  • Describe a class as a blueprint and an object as an instance.

Concept Explanation

A class describes what a kind of thing knows (its attributes) and what it can do (its methods). An object is one actual thing made from a class. Bundling data with the functions that work on it is called encapsulation, and it keeps related code together so a change in one place does not break unrelated code.

Classes as Blueprints

A class is a blueprint or template for creating objects. An object is a concrete instance created from that blueprint.

Analogy: An “Item” class defines that every inventory item has a name, a quantity, and a unit_price (attributes) and can report its total_value() (a method). A Notebook and a Pencil are two separate objects of the same “Item” class. This course models the same inventory item in every language.

Key OOP Concepts

  • Encapsulation — Bundling data and methods into a single unit.
  • Abstraction — Hiding complexity from the outside.
  • Inheritance — New class reuses functionality of existing class.
  • Polymorphism — Same method name behaves differently for different classes.

Worked Example

A student profile kept as loose variables is easy to mix up. As an object, the same data and the operations on it travel together:

class Item:
    def __init__(self, name, quantity, unit_price):
        self.name = name
        self.quantity = quantity
        self.unit_price = unit_price

    def total_value(self):
        return self.quantity * self.unit_price


notebook = Item("Notebook", 3, 2.50)
print(notebook.name, notebook.total_value())

Expected Behavior or Output

Output of example 1:

Notebook 7.5

Common Mistakes

  1. Treating a class as one single thing. A class is a blueprint, and each call such as Item(...) makes a separate object.
  2. Putting unrelated data into one class so that it has no clear purpose.
  3. Skipping the design step and creating classes before knowing what data and operations are needed.

Activities

  1. List the attributes and methods of a Student class for the shared profile (Avery, 16, 1.72, Computer Science).
  2. Describe in two sentences how a class differs from an object, using Item and notebook.
  3. Name three real things and for each write one attribute and one method.
  4. Explain what encapsulation means and why it helps when a program grows.

Accessibility Practice

Describe a class as a list read in order: its name, then its attributes, then its methods. Reading a class definition aloud works best by saying ‘class Item, colon, define init, open parenthesis, self, comma, name…’ and listening for the colons and indentation that show structure.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain the basic idea of Object-Oriented Programming.
  • I can describe a class as a blueprint and an object as an instance.

Lesson 7.2: Creating and Using a Class

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 10, pages 248–254
  • Matthes: Chapter 9, pages 158–162

Learning Objectives

  • Define a basic Python class.
  • Define the __init__ method within a class.
  • Understand the purpose of the self parameter.
  • Create an instance (object) of a class.

Concept Explanation

Class Syntax

The __init__() method runs automatically when a new object is created. self refers to the specific instance being created. Each of the three objects above has the same fields (name, quantity, unit_price) with different values. Keeping the attributes inside the object, and changing them only through methods, is called encapsulation.

Worked Example

class Item:
    """An inventory item with a name, a quantity, and a unit price."""

    def __init__(self, name, quantity, unit_price):
        """Initialize the item's attributes."""
        self.name = name
        self.quantity = quantity
        self.unit_price = unit_price


notebook = Item("Notebook", 3, 2.50)
pencil = Item("Pencil", 10, 0.50)
folder = Item("Folder", 4, 1.25)

print(f"{notebook.name}: {notebook.quantity} at {notebook.unit_price}")
print(f"{pencil.name}: {pencil.quantity} at {pencil.unit_price}")
print(f"{folder.name}: {folder.quantity} at {folder.unit_price}")

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Notebook: 3 at 2.5
Pencil: 10 at 0.5
Folder: 4 at 1.25

Common Mistakes

  1. Forgetting self as the first parameter of __init__, which raises a TypeError when an object is created.
  2. Writing name = name instead of self.name = name, so the value is lost when __init__ ends.
  3. Writing __init__ with one underscore on each side, so it is not recognized.

Activities

  1. Create a fourth item with your own values and print its fields.
  2. Add a check in __init__ that rejects a negative quantity by printing a message.
  3. Create two items with the same name and different quantities and show that changing one does not change the other.
  4. Explain what self refers to in your own words.

Accessibility Practice

Say the double underscores aloud (‘dunder init’) and confirm that your screen reader announces them, because _init_ with a single underscore fails silently. Print each object on its own line with its name, so the output can be matched to the objects by ear.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define a basic Python class.
  • I can define the __init__ method within a class.
  • I understand the purpose of the self parameter.
  • I can create an instance (object) of a class.

Lesson 7.3: Working with Attributes and Methods

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 9, pages 162–166

Learning Objectives

  • Access an object’s attributes using dot notation.
  • Define and call methods within a class.
  • Use a method to change an object’s attribute.

Concept Explanation

Calling Methods

Worked Example

class Item:
    """An inventory item with a name, a quantity, and a unit price."""

    def __init__(self, name, quantity, unit_price):
        """Initialize the item's attributes."""
        self.name = name
        self.quantity = quantity
        self.unit_price = unit_price

    def total_value(self):
        """Return quantity multiplied by unit price."""
        return self.quantity * self.unit_price

    def is_valid(self):
        """An item is valid if it has a name and non-negative numbers."""
        return bool(self.name) and self.quantity >= 0 and self.unit_price >= 0

    def restock(self, amount):
        """Add stock; reject a negative amount."""
        if amount < 0:
            print("Cannot restock a negative amount.")
            return
        self.quantity += amount

    def describe(self):
        print(f"{self.name}: {self.quantity} at {self.unit_price:.2f} each, "
              f"value {self.total_value():.2f}")


notebook = Item("Notebook", 3, 2.50)
notebook.describe()
notebook.restock(2)          # method-based modification
notebook.describe()
notebook.quantity = 4        # direct attribute modification
notebook.describe()
notebook.restock(-1)         # validation message
print(notebook.is_valid())

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Notebook: 3 at 2.50 each, value 7.50
Notebook: 5 at 2.50 each, value 12.50
Notebook: 4 at 2.50 each, value 10.00
Cannot restock a negative amount.
True

Common Mistakes

  1. Calling a method without parentheses (notebook.describe), which refers to the method but does not run it.
  2. Changing an attribute directly and skipping the validation that a method would have performed.
  3. Forgetting self. when a method uses an attribute, which raises a NameError.

Activities

  1. Predict the output of each call in the example before running it.
  2. Add a method discount(rate) that returns the value after a discount without changing the item.
  3. Call restock(-1) and read the message. Then change the method to reject zero as well.
  4. Explain the difference between changing quantity directly and calling restock.

Accessibility Practice
