Name methods after actions (restock, describe) so the call reads as a sentence. Print one line per method call, so a screen reader announces the effect of every step in order.

Skills Checklist

  • I can access an object’s attributes using dot notation.
  • I can define and call methods within a class.
  • I can use a method to change an object’s attribute.

Lesson 7.4: Inheritance

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 12, pages 351–352
  • Matthes: Chapter 9, pages 167–170

Learning Objectives

  • Define a child class that inherits from a parent class.
  • Use super().__init__() to properly initialize inherited attributes.
  • Add new attributes and methods to a child class.
  • Override a parent method in a child class.

Concept Explanation

Creating a Child Class

super() Function

super().__init__() calls the parent class’s __init__() method, ensuring inherited attributes are properly initialized. In the example, DiscountedItem overrides total_value(); the inherited describe() automatically uses the new version. This is polymorphism: the same method name behaves differently for different classes.

Worked Example

class Item:
    """An inventory item with a name, a quantity, and a unit price."""

    def __init__(self, name, quantity, unit_price):
        """Initialize the item's attributes."""
        self.name = name
        self.quantity = quantity
        self.unit_price = unit_price

    def total_value(self):
        return self.quantity * self.unit_price

    def describe(self):
        print(f"{self.name}: {self.quantity} at {self.unit_price:.2f} each, "
              f"value {self.total_value():.2f}")


class DiscountedItem(Item):
    """An item sold at a discount; inherits from Item."""

    def __init__(self, name, quantity, unit_price, discount_rate):
        super().__init__(name, quantity, unit_price)   # Call parent's __init__
        self.discount_rate = discount_rate

    def total_value(self):                              # Override
        return super().total_value() * (1 - self.discount_rate)


folder = DiscountedItem("Folder", 4, 1.25, 0.20)
folder.describe()        # inherited describe() calls the overridden total_value()
print(isinstance(folder, Item))

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Folder: 4 at 1.25 each, value 4.00
True

Common Mistakes

  1. Forgetting to call super().__init__(), so the parent’s attributes are never created.
  2. Overriding a method but changing what it returns, so code that uses the parent version breaks.
  3. Using inheritance for a “has a” relationship; use composition (Lesson 7.5) instead.

Activities

  1. Predict the printed value and the final True of the example before running it.
  2. Add a subclass PerishableItem with an expires attribute and override describe.
  3. Explain why describe prints the discounted value without being redefined.
  4. List the lookup order Python uses to find describe for a DiscountedItem.

Accessibility Practice

Describe inheritance as an ordered list: the object’s own class first, then its parent. Speaking the chain aloud (‘DiscountedItem, then Item’) is clearer than a diagram.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define a child class that inherits from a parent class.
  • I can use super().__init__() to properly initialize inherited attributes.
  • I can add new attributes and methods to a child class.
  • I can override a parent method in a child class.

Lesson 7.5: Instances as Attributes (Composition)

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 9 (Classes), the section on instances as attributes
  • Zelle: Chapter 10 (Defining Classes)

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the concept of composition in OOP.
  • Create an instance of one class and assign it as an attribute of another.
  • Access attributes and methods of a nested object.

Concept Explanation

Composition — “Has-A” Relationship

Instead of inheriting, a class contains an instance of another class as an attribute.

Worked Example

class Item:
    """An inventory item with a name, a quantity, and a unit price."""

    def __init__(self, name, quantity, unit_price):
        """Initialize the item's attributes."""
        self.name = name
        self.quantity = quantity
        self.unit_price = unit_price

    def total_value(self):
        return self.quantity * self.unit_price


class Inventory:
    """An Inventory HAS-A list of Item objects (composition)."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []

    def add(self, item):
        self.items.append(item)

    def total_value(self):
        return sum(item.total_value() for item in self.items)

    def report(self):
        for item in self.items:
            print(f"{item.name}: {item.quantity}")
        print(f"Total value: {self.total_value():.2f}")


inventory = Inventory()
inventory.add(Item("Notebook", 3, 2.50))
inventory.add(Item("Pencil", 10, 0.50))
inventory.add(Item("Folder", 4, 1.25))
inventory.report()

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Notebook: 3
Pencil: 10
Folder: 4
Total value: 17.50

Common Mistakes

  1. Using inheritance where a “has a” relationship is meant.
  2. Letting the container reach into each item’s attributes instead of calling the item’s own methods.
  3. Creating the list in a default argument or at class level, so every Inventory shares one list.

Activities

  1. Predict the output of the example.
  2. Add Inventory.find(name) that returns the item with that name or None.
  3. Add Inventory.remove(name) and test it.
  4. Explain the difference between “is a” and “has a” with two examples.

Accessibility Practice

Report the inventory as one labelled line per item and a final total line, so a screen reader reads a complete summary in order.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain the concept of composition in OOP.
  • I can create an instance of one class and assign it as an attribute of another.
  • I can access attributes and methods of a nested object.

Unit 8: Files and Exceptions

Overview

This unit covers interacting with text files for reading and writing data, handling common errors gracefully using exceptions, and storing data using JSON.

Objectives:

  • Read from and write to files.
  • Handle exceptions with try-except blocks.

Lesson 8.1: Reading from a File

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 5, pages 125–127
  • Matthes: Chapter 10, pages 184–189

Learning Objectives

  • Open a file for reading using with open().
  • Read the entire content of a file into a string.
  • Read a file line by line using a for loop.
  • Remove whitespace/newlines using .strip().

Concept Explanation

Reading Files

Create a file named notes.txt in your project folder containing exactly these two lines:

Practice Python.
Review lists and functions.

The with statement automatically closes the file even if an error occurs.

File Modes

ModeDescription
'r'Read (default)
'w'Write (creates new or overwrites)
'a'Append (adds to end)

Worked Example

# Reading entire file
with open('notes.txt', 'r') as file_object:
    contents = file_object.read()
print(contents)

# Reading line by line
with open('notes.txt', 'r') as file_object:
    for line in file_object:
        print(line.strip())

# Reading all lines into a list
with open('notes.txt', 'r') as file_object:
    lines = file_object.readlines()
print(len(lines))

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Practice Python.
Review lists and functions.

Practice Python.
Review lists and functions.
2

Common Mistakes

  1. Opening a file that does not exist without handling the FileNotFoundError.
  2. Forgetting that a relative path starts from the working directory, not from the program’s folder.
  3. Forgetting that readlines() keeps the newline at the end of each line.

Activities

  1. Run the example and describe each block of output.
  2. Add a third line to notes.txt and predict the new line count.
  3. Print each line with its line number.
  4. Open a file that does not exist and print a friendly message that includes the file name.

Accessibility Practice

Read the output aloud in order. Make any error message a complete sentence that includes the file name, so it is clear without seeing the screen.

Skills Checklist

  • I can open a file for reading using with open().
  • I can read the entire content of a file into a string.

Lesson 8.2: Writing to a File

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 5, pages 127–128
  • Matthes: Chapter 10, pages 190–192

Learning Objectives

  • Open a file for writing using "w" mode.
  • Open a file for appending using "a" mode.
  • Write a string to a file.
  • Add newlines to a file using \n.

Concept Explanation

Important: The .write() method does not add newlines automatically. Use \n.

Worked Example

# Write mode (overwrites existing content)
with open('notes.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write("Practice Python.\n")

# Append mode (adds to end)
with open('notes.txt', 'a') as f:
    f.write("Review lists and functions.\n")

with open('notes.txt', 'r') as f:
    print(f.read())

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Practice Python.
Review lists and functions.

Common Mistakes

  1. Using mode 'w' when 'a' was intended, which erases earlier content.
  2. Forgetting \n, so all written lines run together.
  3. Not using with, so the file may stay open if an error occurs.

Activities

  1. Predict the output, then run.
  2. Change the second open to mode 'w' and explain the difference.
  3. Append a third line with the current number of lines.
  4. Write the shared scores, one per line, then read them back and total them.

Accessibility Practice

Always read a written file back in the terminal to confirm it, using line navigation, so you do not depend on assumptions about what was saved.

Skills Checklist

  • I can open a file for writing using "w" mode.
  • I can open a file for appending using "a" mode.
  • I can write a string to a file.
  • I can add newlines to a file using \n.

Lesson 8.3: Exceptions — Handling Errors

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 7, pages 177–179
  • Matthes: Chapter 10, pages 192–199

Learning Objectives

  • Use a try-except block to handle errors.
  • Name common exception types and what causes them.
  • Catch specific exception types.

Concept Explanation

try-except Block

try:
    result = 10 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("Error: You cannot divide by zero!")
print("Program continues after error handling.")

Common Exception Types

ExceptionWhen it occurs
ValueErrorInvalid value (e.g., int("abc"))
ZeroDivisionErrorDivision by zero
FileNotFoundErrorFile doesn’t exist
IndexErrorList index out of range
KeyErrorDictionary key doesn’t exist
TypeErrorWrong type (e.g., "5" + 5)

Worked Example

Example 8.3.1: Handling ZeroDivisionError

try:
    result = 10 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("Error: Cannot divide by zero!")

Example 8.3.3: Missing File and Malformed Data

try:
    with open("missing_notes.txt", "r") as f:
        print(f.read())
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("Error: missing_notes.txt was not found.")

try:
    score = int("abc")
except ValueError:
    print("Error: 'abc' is not a valid score.")

Example 8.3.2: Handling ValueError

try:
    num = int(input("Enter a number: "))
    print(f"You entered: {num}")
except ValueError:
    print("Error: That was not a valid number.")

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Error: missing_notes.txt was not found.
Error: 'abc' is not a valid score.

Common Mistakes

  1. Using a bare except: that hides every error, including mistakes in your own code.
  2. Putting too much code inside try, so it is unclear which line failed.
  3. Catching an error and printing nothing, so the user does not know what happened.

Activities

  1. Predict each printed line of the missing-file example before running it.
  2. Wrap int(input(...)) so that invalid input prints a clear message and asks again.
  3. Catch ZeroDivisionError in a function that computes an average of an empty list.
  4. Explain when to catch an exception and when to let it stop the program.

Accessibility Practice

Write error messages as complete sentences that name the problem and the next step, such as ‘Enter a whole number from 0 to 100.’ Read the exception name aloud when you see it in a traceback, then jump to the last line of the traceback.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use a try-except block to handle errors.
  • I can name common exception types and what causes them.
  • I can catch specific exception types.

Lesson 8.4: The else and finally Blocks

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 10 (Files and Exceptions), the sections on the else block
  • Zelle: Chapter 5 (Sequences: Strings, Lists, and Files)

Learning Objectives

  • Use an else block for code that runs only on success.
  • Use a finally block for code that always runs.

Concept Explanation

else Block — Runs only on success

try:
    num = int(input("Enter a number: "))
except ValueError:
    print("That's not a number.")
else:
    print(f"You entered {num}.")   # Only runs if no exception

finally Block — Always runs (cleanup)

Worked Example

# For file I/O, prefer a with statement. This example demonstrates
# finally for cleanup of a resource managed manually.
file_handle = None
try:
    file_handle = open('cleanup_demo.txt', 'w')
    file_handle.write("Some data.")
except TypeError:
    print("A type error occurred.")
finally:
    if file_handle:
        file_handle.close()     # Always closes the file
        print("File closed.")

Expected Behavior or Output

Output of example 1:

File closed.

Common Mistakes

  1. Putting code in else that can itself fail, so its errors are not handled.
  2. Relying on finally to return a value, which can hide an earlier error.
  3. Closing a file manually and forgetting to do so when an error occurs; prefer with.

Activities

  1. Predict the output of both runs of the example.
  2. Add a finally block that prints a message even when an error occurs.
  3. Rewrite the example with with and explain why it is shorter and safer.
  4. Explain in two sentences what else adds to try and except.

Accessibility Practice

Print a status line in each block (try, except, else, finally), so a screen reader announces which path ran. Short, labelled lines make the control flow audible.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use an else block for code that runs only on success.
  • I can use a finally block for code that always runs.

Lesson 8.5: Storing Data with JSON

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 10, pages 200–204

Learning Objectives

  • Explain what JSON is and why it’s used.
  • Use json.dump() to save Python data to a JSON file.
  • Use json.load() to load JSON data from a file.
  • Save and load lists of dictionaries using JSON.

Concept Explanation

The json Module

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight format for storing and exchanging data. Python’s json module converts between Python objects and JSON.

import json

# Save data
task = {
    "id": 1,
    "title": "Practice Python",
    "description": "Complete the shared dataset exercises",
    "done": False,
    "created_at": "2025-01-15T09:00:00Z",
}

with open("tasks.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    json.dump([task], file, indent=4)

# Load and verify all five canonical fields.
try:
    with open("tasks.json", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        loaded_tasks = json.load(file)
    loaded_task = loaded_tasks[0]
    required_fields = {"id", "title", "description", "done", "created_at"}
    if set(loaded_task) != required_fields:
        raise ValueError("Task record does not match the five-field schema")
    print(loaded_task["id"], loaded_task["title"], loaded_task["done"])
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("Task file not found.")
except (json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError) as error:
    print(f"Invalid task data: {error}")

JSON ↔ Python Mapping

JSONPython
Object {}Dictionary {}
Array []List []
Stringstr
Numberint or float
Booleanbool
nullNone

Worked Example

import json

tasks = [
    {"id": 1, "title": "Study programming", "description": "Finish Unit 8",
     "done": False, "created_at": "2026-01-15T09:00:00"},
    {"id": 2, "title": "Review scores", "description": "Check the four scores",
     "done": True, "created_at": "2026-01-15T09:30:00"},
]

with open('tasks.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(tasks, f, indent=4)

try:
    with open('tasks.json', 'r') as f:
        loaded = json.load(f)
    for task in loaded:
        status = "done" if task["done"] else "not done"
        print(f"{task['id']}: {task['title']} ({status})")
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("Tasks file not found.")
except json.JSONDecodeError:
    print("Error: Could not decode tasks file.")

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

1: Study programming (not done)
2: Review scores (done)

Common Mistakes

  1. Calling json.dump with a file opened in read mode.
  2. Trying to save an object that JSON cannot represent, such as a custom class instance.
  3. Not handling json.JSONDecodeError, so a damaged file crashes the program.

Activities

  1. Run the example and read the saved JSON text from tasks.json.
  2. Edit tasks.json by hand to remove a closing bracket and run the program again.
  3. Add a third task and confirm that it is saved and loaded.
  4. Explain why True in Python becomes true in the JSON file.

Accessibility Practice

Open tasks.json in the terminal and read it as text. Because indent=4 puts one field per line, the file reads line by line with a screen reader. Practise moving through it by word or character.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain what JSON is and why it’s used.
  • I can use json.dump() to save Python data to a JSON file.
  • I can use json.load() to load JSON data from a file.
  • I can save and load lists of dictionaries using JSON.

Unit 9: Testing and Data Analysis

Overview

This unit introduces testing code for correctness and explores basic text-based data analysis.

Lesson 9.1: Testing a Function

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 11, pages 209–217

Learning Objectives

  • Create a basic test class using unittest.TestCase.
  • Define test methods within a test class.
  • Use assertEqual() to check for expected results.
  • Run unit tests from the terminal.

Concept Explanation

Unit Testing with unittest

# my_functions.py
def add(a, b):
    return a + b


def calculate_tip(bill, rate):
    return bill * rate


def classify(score):
    if score >= 90:
        return "A"
    elif score >= 80:
        return "B"
    elif score >= 70:
        return "C"
    elif score >= 60:
        return "D"
    return "F"

# test_my_functions.py
import unittest
from my_functions import add, calculate_tip, classify


class TestFunctions(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_add(self):
        self.assertEqual(add(5, 3), 8)
        self.assertEqual(add(-5, -3), -8)
        self.assertEqual(add(10, -4), 6)

    def test_tip(self):
        # Decimal results are compared with a tolerance, not exact equality.
        self.assertAlmostEqual(calculate_tip(24.5, 0.15), 3.675)
        self.assertEqual(calculate_tip(0, 0.15), 0)

    def test_classify_boundaries(self):
        self.assertEqual(classify(90), "A")
        self.assertEqual(classify(89), "B")
        self.assertEqual(classify(60), "D")
        self.assertEqual(classify(59), "F")


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()

Run the tests from the terminal with python test_my_functions.py or python -m unittest. Expected output (the timing line will differ):

...
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 3 tests in 0.001s

OK

The three tests check the same inputs and expected results in every language track: add(5, 3) is 8, the tip for a bill of 24.50 at 0.15 is 3.675, and the grade boundaries 90, 89, 60, and 59 give A, B, D, and F.

Worked Example

# my_functions.py
def add(a, b):
    return a + b


def calculate_tip(bill, rate):
    return bill * rate


def classify(score):
    if score >= 90:
        return "A"
    elif score >= 80:
        return "B"
    elif score >= 70:
        return "C"
    elif score >= 60:
        return "D"
    return "F"

# test_my_functions.py
import unittest
from my_functions import add, calculate_tip, classify


class TestFunctions(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_add(self):
        self.assertEqual(add(5, 3), 8)
        self.assertEqual(add(-5, -3), -8)
        self.assertEqual(add(10, -4), 6)

    def test_tip(self):
        # Decimal results are compared with a tolerance, not exact equality.
        self.assertAlmostEqual(calculate_tip(24.5, 0.15), 3.675)
        self.assertEqual(calculate_tip(0, 0.15), 0)

    def test_classify_boundaries(self):
        self.assertEqual(classify(90), "A")
        self.assertEqual(classify(89), "B")
        self.assertEqual(classify(60), "D")
        self.assertEqual(classify(59), "F")


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()

Run the tests from the terminal with python test_my_functions.py or python -m unittest.

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output (the timing line differs from run to run):

...
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 3 tests in 0.001s

OK

The three tests check the same inputs and expected results in every language track: add(5, 3) is 8, the tip for a bill of 24.50 at 0.15 is 3.675, and the grade boundaries 90, 89, 60, and 59 give A, B, D, and F.

Common Mistakes

  1. Comparing decimal results with assertEqual. Use assertAlmostEqual, because floating-point results are approximations.
  2. Naming a test method without the test_ prefix, so unittest never runs it.
  3. Testing only typical values and skipping the boundaries 90, 89, 60, and 59.

Activities

  1. Change one expected value so a test fails, read the failure message, and then restore it.
  2. Add tests for the grades at 80, 79, 70, and 69.
  3. Write the tests for is_passing(score) before you write the function.
  4. Explain why the tip test uses a tolerance.

Accessibility Practice

A passing run prints a short summary (Ran 3 tests ... OK) that is quick to read. A failing run prints the test name and the expected and actual values on separate lines; jump to those lines first. Name each test as a sentence that completes ‘This test checks that…’.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create a basic test class using unittest.TestCase.
  • I can define test methods within a test class.
  • I can use assertEqual() to check for expected results.
  • I can run unit tests from the terminal.

Lesson 9.2: Testing a Class

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 11 (Testing Your Code), the sections on testing a class

Learning Objectives

  • Write tests for a Python class.
  • Use setUp() to prepare my tests.

Concept Explanation

The setUp() Method

setUp() runs before every test method, providing a fresh instance each time:

# item.py  (the Item class from Unit 7, with a restock method)
class Item:
    def __init__(self, name, quantity, unit_price):
        self.name = name
        self.quantity = quantity
        self.unit_price = unit_price

    def total_value(self):
        return self.quantity * self.unit_price

    def restock(self, amount):
        if amount < 0:
            raise ValueError("amount must not be negative")
        self.quantity += amount

# test_item.py
import unittest
from item import Item


class TestItem(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        """Create a fresh Notebook for every test method."""
        self.item = Item("Notebook", 3, 2.50)

    def test_total_value(self):
        self.assertAlmostEqual(self.item.total_value(), 7.5)

    def test_restock(self):
        self.item.restock(2)
        self.assertEqual(self.item.quantity, 5)

    def test_restock_rejects_negative_amount(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            self.item.restock(-1)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()

Expected output (the timing line will differ):

...
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 3 tests in 0.001s

OK

Because setUp() runs before each test, test_restock changing the quantity to 5 does not affect test_total_value, which still sees 3 notebooks.

Worked Example

# item.py  (the Item class from Unit 7, with a restock method)
class Item:
    def __init__(self, name, quantity, unit_price):
        self.name = name
        self.quantity = quantity
        self.unit_price = unit_price

    def total_value(self):
        return self.quantity * self.unit_price

    def restock(self, amount):
        if amount < 0:
            raise ValueError("amount must not be negative")
        self.quantity += amount

# test_item.py
import unittest
from item import Item


class TestItem(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        """Create a fresh Notebook for every test method."""
        self.item = Item("Notebook", 3, 2.50)

    def test_total_value(self):
        self.assertAlmostEqual(self.item.total_value(), 7.5)

    def test_restock(self):
        self.item.restock(2)
        self.assertEqual(self.item.quantity, 5)

    def test_restock_rejects_negative_amount(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            self.item.restock(-1)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output (the timing line differs):

...
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 3 tests in 0.001s

OK

Because setUp() runs before each test, test_restock changing the quantity to 5 does not affect test_total_value, which still sees 3 notebooks.

Common Mistakes

  1. Sharing one object between tests so that an earlier test changes the later ones; use setUp.
  2. Testing only the successful path and never the error path.
  3. Forgetting self. inside a test method, so the fixture object is not found.

Activities

  1. Add a test that restock(0) leaves the quantity unchanged.
  2. Add a test for the is_valid method from Unit 7.
  3. Break restock on purpose and read the failure report.
  4. Explain why setUp creates a new item for each test.

Accessibility Practice

Name each test as a short sentence that says what behavior it checks, so the PASS or FAIL report reads as a clear statement. Read the summary line first, and open the failure details only when it says FAILED.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write tests for a Python class.
  • I can use setUp() to prepare my tests.

Lesson 9.3: Introduction to Random Numbers

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 9 (Classes), the section on the random module
  • Zelle: Chapter 9 (Simulation and Design)

Learning Objectives

  • Import the random module.
  • Generate a random integer within a range.
  • Select a random item from a list.

Concept Explanation

Without the random.seed(...) line the values change on every run. Use a seed when you need to test or reproduce a result.

Worked Example

import random

random.seed(42)   # a fixed seed makes the "random" results repeatable

die_roll = random.randint(1, 6)          # random integer (inclusive)
print(f"You rolled: {die_roll}")

rand_float = random.random()             # random float from 0.0 up to 1.0
print(f"Random decimal: {rand_float:.4f}")

scores = [82, 91, 76, 88]
chosen = random.choice(scores)           # random choice from a list
print(f"Chosen score: {chosen}")

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output with random.seed(42) on Python 3.12:

You rolled: 6
Random decimal: 0.1113
Chosen score: 76

Common Mistakes

  1. Testing for specific random values that change between Python versions; test properties such as the range instead.
  2. Calling random.seed() in every loop pass, which repeats the same value.
  3. Forgetting that randint(1, 6) includes both ends, while randrange(1, 6) does not include 6.

Activities

  1. Run the example three times with the seed line and then three times without it; compare.
  2. Change the seed and check that the ranges still hold.
  3. Simulate 600 rolls and count how many of each face appeared (the counts will differ).
  4. Explain why a test should check a property rather than a specific random number.

Accessibility Practice

When output is random, print yes or no results about properties (All rolls between 1 and 6: True) so the screen reader announces the same result on every run and does not read unpredictable values.

Skills Checklist

  • I can import the random module.
  • I can generate a random integer within a range.
  • I can select a random item from a list.

Lesson 9.4: Analyzing Text Data

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 6 (Dictionaries), the section on counting with dictionaries
  • Zelle: Chapter 5 (Sequences: Strings, Lists, and Files)

Learning Objectives

  • Read text content from a file.
  • Split a string of text into individual words.
  • Use a dictionary to count the frequency of words.

Concept Explanation

Worked Example

sentence = "A student studies programming. Programming develops problem-solving skills."
words = sentence.lower().replace(".", "").split()

word_frequencies = {}
for word in words:
    word_frequencies[word] = word_frequencies.get(word, 0) + 1

print("Word count:", len(words))
print("Word Frequencies:")
for word, count in word_frequencies.items():
    print(f"'{word}': {count}")

letter_counts = {}
for ch in text.lower():
    if ch.isalpha():
        letter_counts[ch] = letter_counts.get(ch, 0) + 1

top_three = sorted(letter_counts.items(), key=lambda pair: (-pair[1], pair[0]))[:3]
print("Most common letters:", top_three)

Expected Behavior or Output

Expected output:

Word count: 8
Word Frequencies:
'a': 1
'student': 1
'studies': 1
'programming': 2
'develops': 1
'problem-solving': 1
'skills': 1
Most common letters: [('s', 7), ('e', 5), ('g', 5)]

Common Mistakes

  1. Counting punctuation as part of a word, so programming. and programming become different words.
  2. Forgetting to convert text to lower case before counting, so Programming and programming are counted separately.
  3. Sorting a dictionary by key when the count was intended.

Activities

  1. Predict the word count and the count for programming before running.
  2. Count the words longer than 8 letters.
  3. Print the longest word.
  4. Change the sort so ties are listed in reverse alphabetical order.

Accessibility Practice

Read the frequency list in its fixed order. Because the order is stable, you can learn it and compare runs by ear. Print each pair as a short sentence ('programming': 2) with the same wording every time.

Skills Checklist

  • I can read text content from a file.
  • I can split a string of text into individual words.
  • I can use a dictionary to count the frequency of words.

Lesson 9.5: Working with CSV Data

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 10 (Files and Exceptions), the section on CSV files
  • Zelle: Chapter 5 (Sequences: Strings, Lists, and Files)

Learning Objectives

  • Explain what CSV data is.
  • Read a CSV file line by line.
  • Split a line of CSV data into individual values.

Concept Explanation

Save this as students.csv (the same file is used in every language track):

student_id,first_name,last_name,score,active
1,Avery,Student,91,true
2,Jordan,Lee,82,true
3,Casey,Smith,76,false

The csv module handles quoted fields and embedded commas correctly. Splitting each line on commas with line.split(',') works only for simple files where no value contains a comma.

Worked Example

import csv

filename = 'students.csv'
try:
    with open(filename, 'r', newline='') as file_object:
        reader = csv.DictReader(file_object)
        print(f"Columns: {reader.fieldnames}")
        scores = []
        active_count = 0
        for row in reader:
            scores.append(int(row["score"]))
            if row["active"] == "true":
                active_count += 1
            print(f"{row['student_id']}: {row['first_name']} {row['last_name']} scored {row['score']}")
    print(f"Students: {len(scores)}")
    print(f"Average score: {sum(scores) / len(scores):.2f}")
    print(f"Active students: {active_count}")
except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"Error: The file {filename} was not found.")

Reading the Canonical CSV Schema

Use the standard csv module rather than splitting rows on commas. A quoted field may itself contain a comma.

import csv
from io import StringIO

csv_text = """student_id,first_name,last_name,score,active
1001,Avery,Jordan,82,true
1002,Riley,Chen,91,true
1003,Sam,Patel,76,false
1004,Morgan,Diaz,88,true
"""

reader = csv.DictReader(StringIO(csv_text))
for row in reader:
    print(row["student_id"], row["first_name"], row["last_name"],
          row["score"], row["active"])

Expected output:

1001 Avery Jordan 82 true
1002 Riley Chen 91 true
1003 Sam Patel 76 false
1004 Morgan Diaz 88 true

Common Mistakes

  1. Splitting a CSV line at every comma when a value itself contains a quoted comma; use the csv module.
  2. Forgetting to convert the text in the score column to a number.
  3. Opening a CSV file without newline='', which can produce blank rows on some systems.

Activities

  1. Predict the printed lines before running.
  2. Add a fourth student and check the new average.
  3. Print only the active students.
  4. Explain, with an example, why "Smith, Jr." breaks line.split(',').

Accessibility Practice

Print one student per line with the same wording each time, so the screen reader announces a repeating pattern that is easy to compare line by line. Read the column names aloud once at the start so the values that follow have meaning.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain what CSV data is.
  • I can read a CSV file line by line.
  • I can split a line of CSV data into individual values.

Canonical Shared Dataset — Text, CSV, Tasks, and Tests

Text analysis

Use this exact sentence for word-count and character-processing exercises:

text_sample = "A student studies programming. Programming develops problem-solving skills."
words = text_sample.lower().replace(".", "").split()
print("Words:", len(words))
print("Programming:", words.count("programming"))

Expected output:

Words: 8
Programming: 2

CSV schema

The shared CSV header is exactly student_id,first_name,last_name,score,active. Example rows:

student_id,first_name,last_name,score,active
1001,Avery,Jordan,82,true
1002,Riley,Chen,91,true
1003,Sam,Patel,76,false
1004,Morgan,Diaz,88,true

Use the csv module and named column positions; do not substitute a different three-column name/age/grade schema.

import csv
from io import StringIO

csv_text = """student_id,first_name,last_name,score,active
1001,Avery,Jordan,82,true
1002,Riley,Chen,91,true
1003,Sam,Patel,76,false
1004,Morgan,Diaz,88,true
"""
for row in csv.DictReader(StringIO(csv_text)):
    print(row["student_id"], row["first_name"], row["last_name"],
          row["score"], row["active"])

Expected output:

1001 Avery Jordan 82 true
1002 Riley Chen 91 true
1003 Sam Patel 76 false
1004 Morgan Diaz 88 true

To-do record schema

Use all five fields in every serialized task record: id, title, description, done, and created_at.

task = {
    "id": 1,
    "title": "Practice Python",
    "description": "Complete the shared dataset exercises",
    "done": False,
    "created_at": "2025-01-15T09:00:00Z",
}

import json

task = {
    "id": 1,
    "title": "Practice Python",
    "description": "Complete the shared dataset exercises",
    "done": False,
    "created_at": "2025-01-15T09:00:00Z",
}
serialized = json.dumps([task])
loaded_tasks = json.loads(serialized)
loaded_task = loaded_tasks[0]
required_fields = {"id", "title", "description", "done", "created_at"}
assert set(loaded_task) == required_fields
print(loaded_task["id"], loaded_task["title"], loaded_task["done"])

Expected output:

1 Practice Python False

Tests should assert deterministic results for the shared tip calculator, grade classifier, inventory total, and text sample. Random-number lessons must seed the generator when an exact result is asserted.

Unit 10: Project-Based Learning — Building Text-Based Applications

Overview

Compatibility: All examples target Python 3.12 and newer; they avoid syntax and standard-library APIs introduced after Python 3.12.

This unit guides students through designing and building larger, interactive text-based applications, integrating all previously learned concepts.

Objectives:

  • Practice modular programming and code organization.
  • Develop a text-based interactive program.
  • Apply top-down design principles.

Lesson 10.1: Designing Your Project

Reading References

  • Zelle: Chapter 9, pages 225–235
  • Matthes: Part II: Projects, pages 225–226

Learning Objectives

  • Break down a larger problem into smaller, manageable parts.
  • Identify the key features required for a project.
  • Plan which data structures will be most suitable for my project’s data.
  • Outline the main steps or flow of my program.

Concept Explanation

Top-Down Design

Top-down design (stepwise refinement) breaks a complex problem into smaller, more manageable subproblems.

The Design Process:

1. Analyze the Problem

  • Identify inputs (information the program needs).
  • Identify outputs (results it must produce).
  • Define the scope of the project.

2. Determine the Major Components Write a high-level algorithm in plain English:

show_greeting()
get_user_input()
calculate_cost()
print_ticket()

3. Refine Each Component Repeat the design process for each component, adding detail until simple enough to code.

Benefits of Top-Down Design

  • Reduces Complexity — Focus on one piece at a time.
  • Encourages Reusability — Functions written for one part may be useful elsewhere.
  • Simplifies Debugging — Test each component in isolation.
  • Improves Collaboration — Clear plan for assigning work.

Accessibility Considerations for I/O Design

  • Provide clear, descriptive prompts for all input.
  • Provide explicit, labeled output — avoid relying on visual formatting.
  • Print confirmation messages after every action.
  • Use consistent output separators like --- to group information.

Worked Example

Top-down design applied to the command-line to-do tool. The top-level plan names the major components, and the first runnable version contains only the first component:

show_menu()
get_choice()
add_task() / view_tasks() / mark_done() / save_tasks()
repeat until the user chooses to quit

def show_menu():
    print("1. Add task")
    print("2. View tasks")
    print("3. Quit")


def run():
    show_menu()
    print("(The choices are not implemented yet.)")


run()

Expected Behavior or Output

Output of example 1:

1. Add task
2. View tasks
3. Quit
(The choices are not implemented yet.)

Common Mistakes

  1. Starting to code the whole program at once instead of building and testing one component at a time.
  2. Writing a design that names steps too vague to turn into code, such as “handle the data”.
  3. Forgetting the messages: a design that lists operations but not what the user sees after each one.

Activities

  1. Write the top-level design for the text adventure as a numbered list of components.
  2. Refine one component of your design into three smaller steps.
  3. Write the exact wording of five prompts and messages that your project will use.
  4. Explain in two sentences how the design lets you test one function in isolation.

Accessibility Practice

Write the design as a numbered list and read it aloud before coding. Decide the wording of every prompt and message now, and check that none depends on color, layout, or symbols alone.

Skills Checklist

  • I can break down a larger problem into smaller, manageable parts.
  • I can identify the key features required for a project.
  • I can plan which data structures will be most suitable for my project’s data.
  • I can outline the main steps or flow of my program.

Lesson 10.2: Building a Text-Based Adventure Game (Part 1)

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 6, pages 105–111

Learning Objectives

  • Design a way to represent different locations in a text-based game.
  • Implement player movement based on user commands.
  • Update and track the player’s current location.
  • Parse simple commands from user input.

Concept Explanation

Room Definition and Movement

Worked Example

room_descriptions = {
    "start_room": {
        "description": "A dimly lit cave. A narrow passage leads north.",
        "exits": {"north": "tunnel"},
        "items": [],
    },
    "tunnel": {
        "description": "A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.",
        "exits": {"south": "start_room", "east": "clearing"},
        "items": [],
    },
    "clearing": {
        "description": "A quiet clearing. A small antechamber lies to the north.",
        "exits": {"west": "tunnel", "north": "locked_door_room"},
        "items": [],
    },
    "locked_door_room": {
        "description": "A chamber with a heavy locked door to the north.",
        "exits": {"south": "clearing"},
        "items": [],
    },
    "treasure_room": {
        "description": "You found the treasure. You win!",
        "exits": {},
        "items": [],
    },
}

current_room = "start_room"

while True:
    print("---")
    print(room_descriptions[current_room]["description"])
    command = input("What do you want to do? ").lower()

    if command in room_descriptions[current_room]["exits"]:
        current_room = room_descriptions[current_room]["exits"][command]
    elif command == "quit":
        print("Exiting game. Goodbye!")
        break
    else:
        print("I don't understand that command or you can't go that way.")

Expected Behavior or Output

Sample run typing north, east, north, north, quit (typed input shown after each prompt):

---
A dimly lit cave. A narrow passage leads north.
What do you want to do? north
---
A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.
What do you want to do? east
---
A quiet clearing. A small antechamber lies to the north.
What do you want to do? north
---
A chamber with a heavy locked door to the north.
What do you want to do? north
I don't understand that command or you can't go that way.
---
A chamber with a heavy locked door to the north.
What do you want to do? quit
Exiting game. Goodbye!

Common Mistakes

  1. Looking up a direction that is not in exits with square brackets, which raises a KeyError. Use in to test first.
  2. Forgetting that input() raises EOFError at the end of piped input; scripted tests should end with quit.
  3. Misspelling a room name in exits, so a move leads to a room that does not exist.

Activities

  1. Trace north, east, north, north, quit and record the room after each command.
  2. Try west from start_room and verify that the location does not change.
  3. Verify that north from locked_door_room is rejected and leaves the player in that room.
  4. Write a loop that checks that every exit names a real room.

Accessibility Practice

Each turn prints a separator line, the description, and the prompt, so a whole turn can be read in order. Listen to one turn from start to finish to confirm that a player could follow it without seeing the screen.

Skills Checklist

  • I can design a way to represent different locations in a text-based game.
  • I can implement player movement based on user commands.
  • I can update and track the player’s current location.
  • I can parse simple commands from user input.

Lesson 10.3: Building a Text-Based Adventure Game (Part 2)

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 6 (Dictionaries) and Chapter 8 (Functions)

Learning Objectives

  • Add items to locations and manage a player’s inventory.
  • Implement commands for picking up and dropping items.
  • Design and implement a simple puzzle.
  • Define win/lose conditions for the game.

Concept Explanation

Adding Items, Inventory, and Puzzles

These rules are the shared text-adventure specification for every language track: five rooms (start_room, tunnel, clearing, locked_door_room, and treasure_room). The player starts in start_room; its north exit leads to tunnel. From tunnel, south returns to start_room and east leads to clearing. From clearing, west returns to tunnel and north leads to locked_door_room. From locked_door_room, south returns to clearing; north leads to treasure_room only after the player has taken the shiny key from start_room and used it in locked_door_room. The supported commands are north, south, east, west, take shiny key, use shiny key, and quit. Reaching treasure_room ends the game.

Worked Example

rooms = {
    "start_room": {
        "description": "A dimly lit cave. A shiny key rests on the ground.",
        "exits": {"north": "tunnel"},
        "items": ["shiny key"],
    },
    "tunnel": {
        "description": "A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.",
        "exits": {"south": "start_room", "east": "clearing"},
        "items": [],
    },
    "clearing": {
        "description": "A quiet clearing. A small antechamber lies to the north.",
        "exits": {"west": "tunnel", "north": "locked_door_room"},
        "items": [],
    },
    "locked_door_room": {
        "description": "A chamber with a heavy locked door to the north.",
        "exits": {"south": "clearing", "north": "treasure_room"},
        "items": [],
    },
    "treasure_room": {
        "description": "You found the treasure. You win!",
        "exits": {},
        "items": [],
    },
}

current_room = "start_room"
player_inventory = []
door_locked = True

while True:
    print("\n" + rooms[current_room]["description"])
    if current_room == "treasure_room":
        break
    if rooms[current_room]["items"]:
        print(f"You see: {', '.join(rooms[current_room]['items'])}")
    print(f"Your inventory: {', '.join(player_inventory) if player_inventory else 'empty'}")

    if current_room == "treasure_room":
        break

    command = input("What do you want to do? ").strip().lower()

    if command == "take shiny key" and "shiny key" in rooms[current_room]["items"]:
        player_inventory.append("shiny key")
        rooms[current_room]["items"].remove("shiny key")
        print("You picked up the shiny key.")
    elif command == "use shiny key" and current_room == "locked_door_room" and "shiny key" in player_inventory:
        door_locked = False
        print("You unlocked the door!")
    elif command in rooms[current_room]["exits"]:
        if current_room == "locked_door_room" and command == "north" and door_locked:
            print("The door is locked! You need a key.")
        else:
            current_room = rooms[current_room]["exits"][command]
    elif command == "quit":
        print("You quit the adventure.")
        break
    else:
        print("Invalid command. Use a direction, 'take shiny key', 'use shiny key', or 'quit'.")

Expected Behavior or Output

Sample play (typed input shown after each prompt). The player reaches the chamber, finds the door locked, returns to take the key, then unlocks the door and wins:


A dark cave.
You see: shiny key
Your inventory: empty
What do you want to do? north

A small chamber with a heavy door to the NORTH.
Your inventory: empty
What do you want to do? north
The door is locked! You need a key.

A small chamber with a heavy door to the NORTH.
Your inventory: empty
What do you want to do? south

A dark cave.
You see: shiny key
Your inventory: empty
What do you want to do? take shiny key
You picked up the shiny key.

A dark cave.
Your inventory: shiny key
What do you want to do? north

A small chamber with a heavy door to the NORTH.
Your inventory: shiny key
What do you want to do? use shiny key
You unlocked the door!

A small chamber with a heavy door to the NORTH.
Your inventory: shiny key
What do you want to do? north

A glittering room full of treasure. You win!

Common Mistakes

  1. Making the door’s locked state part of the exits so the “locked” message can never be reached.
  2. Defining an exit to a room that is missing from the rooms dictionary, which crashes when the player arrives.
  3. Printing a fixed room description that still mentions an item after the player has taken it.

Activities

  1. Play the program with the sample commands and follow each turn on paper.
  2. Try use shiny key in the cave and describe what happens.
  3. Add a second item and require both to open the door.
  4. List the game’s state (location, inventory, door) and say which command changes each part.

Accessibility Practice

The room description never mentions the key. A separate ‘You see:’ line lists items, so the description stays true after the key is taken and the screen reader announces the current state.

Skills Checklist

  • I can add items to locations and manage a player’s inventory.
  • I can implement commands for picking up and dropping items.
  • I can design and implement a simple puzzle.
  • I can define win/lose conditions for the game.

Lesson 10.4: Developing a Command-Line Tool

Canonical To-Do Record and Required Operations

Every task must preserve exactly these fields:

task = {
    "id": 1,
    "title": "Practice Python",
    "description": "Complete the shared dataset exercises",
    "done": False,
    "created_at": "2025-01-15T09:00:00Z",
}

Design the command-line interface around these operations:

OperationRequired behavior
AddReject a blank title; assign a unique integer ID; initialize done to False; preserve all five fields
ListDisplay tasks in ID order and state whether each is complete
Complete/updateFind by ID, update done, and report a missing or invalid ID
DeleteRemove by ID and report a missing or invalid ID
SaveSerialize the complete list as JSON
LoadValidate that the top level is a list and every task has exactly the five required fields and appropriate value types

Use the following function boundaries as a design scaffold. Implement and test each function as a separate exercise; this outline intentionally does not provide the project solution.

def add_task(tasks, title, description, created_at):
    # TODO: validate title, allocate a unique ID, and append a five-field record
    raise NotImplementedError


def list_tasks(tasks):
    # TODO: display records in a stable order
    raise NotImplementedError


def update_task(tasks, task_id, *, done=None, title=None, description=None):
    # TODO: locate by ID, validate updates, and report a missing ID
    raise NotImplementedError


def delete_task(tasks, task_id):
    # TODO: remove by ID and report a missing ID
    raise NotImplementedError


def save_tasks(tasks, path):
    # TODO: write all five fields as JSON
    raise NotImplementedError


def load_tasks(path):
    # TODO: handle missing/malformed JSON and validate every record
    raise NotImplementedError

Do not substitute list positions for IDs. Deleting or sorting a task must not change the identity of any remaining task. Use a deterministic timestamp fixture in tests; do not call the wall clock in expected-output tests.

Skills Checklist

  • I can design an interactive menu system for a tool.
  • I can use a while loop to maintain continuous user interaction.
  • I can break down the tool’s functionality into separate functions.
  • I can implement file I/O to save and load data.

Lesson 10.5: Refinement and User Experience

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 10 (Files and Exceptions), the sections on exceptions
  • Zelle: Chapter 8 (Loop Structures and Booleans)

Learning Objectives

  • Write clear, descriptive prompts for user input.
  • Handle invalid input gracefully using try-except.
  • Provide helpful error messages.

Concept Explanation

Principles for Accessible Text Programs

  1. Clear prompts — Tell the user exactly what to enter and in what format.
  2. Consistent output — Use the same format for similar information.
  3. Graceful error handling — Never let the program crash on bad input.
  4. Helpful error messages — Tell the user what went wrong and how to fix it.
  5. “Help” commands — Provide a way to list available commands.
  6. Confirmation messages — Confirm every action taken.

Robust Input Validation

Worked Example

def get_positive_number(prompt):
    """Prompts user until a positive integer is entered."""
    while True:
        try:
            num = int(input(prompt))
            if num > 0:
                return num
            else:
                print("Please enter a positive number.")
        except ValueError:
            print("Invalid input. Please enter a whole number.")


age = get_positive_number("Enter your age: ")
print(f"You entered age: {age}")

Expected Behavior or Output

Sample run typing abc, -4, 0, 16 (typed input shown after each prompt):

Enter your age: abc
Invalid input. Please enter a whole number.
Enter your age: -4
Please enter a positive number.
Enter your age: 0
Please enter a positive number.
Enter your age: 16
You entered age: 16

Common Mistakes

  1. Writing the message “Invalid” without saying what is valid.
  2. Accepting a decimal such as 88.5 for a field that requires a whole number.
  3. Looping forever on bad input instead of limiting attempts or providing a way to quit.

Activities

  1. Run the example typing abc, -4, 0, and 16, and read each message aloud.
  2. Add an upper limit of 120 and a message that names it.
  3. Write get_yes_no(prompt) that accepts only yes or no in any letter case.
  4. Rewrite two messages from earlier lessons so they say what to do next.

Accessibility Practice

Check that every error message ends with an action the user can take, and that the same situation always produces the same words. Test with your screen reader that a message is announced before the next prompt appears.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write clear, descriptive prompts for user input.
  • I can handle invalid input gracefully using try-except.
  • I can provide helpful error messages.

Unit 11: Capstone Project — Accessible Personal Data Manager

Overview

Students develop a fully functional personal data manager that is built to work with a screen reader and keyboard. The program keeps a list of structured records, lets the user add, view, search, change, complete, and delete them, and saves them to a JSON file. The Python track builds it as a small local web application with NiceGUI. The other language tracks build a text-based version with the same records, rules, and tests.

Project Goal: Build an application to manage structured records with list, add, search, update, delete, and JSON persistence operations. The interface may be GUI-based in Python; the same data contract and operation semantics apply to the Lua terminal implementation.

Project Options:

  • Contact Manager
  • Book/Movie Tracker
  • Study Notes Manager
  • Personal Inventory

Every option uses the same six-field record schema (id, title, description, category, created_at, updated_at). The selected project domain changes the meaning of the field values, not the record shape or required operations.

Lesson 11.1: Introduction to NiceGUI

  1. Add New Item — A form to input details for a new item.
  2. View All Items — Display items in a clear, accessible list format.
  3. Edit Item — Select an existing item and modify its details.
  4. Search Items — Find records by ID and case-insensitive text in title, description, or category; report no matches explicitly.
  5. Delete Item — Remove an item from the collection and confirm the result.
  6. Save/Load Data — Persist the data to a JSON file and validate the complete six-field schema on load.

Learning Objectives

  • Install NiceGUI with uv and start a page from the terminal.
  • Explain that each ui. call creates an element and that an event handler runs when the user acts.
  • Give every input a label and report results in a plain text status line.

Concept Explanation

NiceGUI lets you build a web page in Python. When the program runs it starts a small web server on your own computer and prints an address, normally http://localhost:8080. You open that address in a browser. Nothing is sent to other people; the page is served only from your computer unless you choose otherwise.

Setup. Install the package into the project environment:

uv add nicegui

Windows PowerShell uses the same command:

uv add nicegui

Elements and handlers. Each call such as ui.label(...), ui.input(...), or ui.button(...) creates an element on the page. A button takes an on_click function, called a handler, that runs when the user presses it. The code inside @ui.page("/") builds the page each time someone opens it.

Starting the server. ui.run(...) starts the server. Guard it with if __name__ in {"__main__", "__mp_main__"}: as NiceGUI requires. Pass show=False so that no browser is opened automatically, and reload=False while learning.

Accessibility. NiceGUI pages are ordinary web pages, so a screen reader reads them as any other page. Three habits make them usable: give every input a clear label, because the label text is what a screen reader announces for the field; report every result in a plain text label as well as in a pop-up, because a pop-up message disappears; and never use color as the only signal. The status label below uses the standard attributes role="status" and aria-live="polite", which ask assistive technology to announce changes. Whether your screen reader announces them as intended must be tested with your own setup.

Worked Example

Save this as hello_app.py:

from nicegui import ui


@ui.page("/")
def main_page():
    ui.page_title("Personal Data Manager")
    ui.label("Personal Data Manager")
    name = ui.input(label="Your name")
    greeting = ui.label("Type a name and press the button.").props('role="status" aria-live="polite"')

    def greet():
        if name.value.strip():
            greeting.set_text(f"Hello, {name.value.strip()}!")
        else:
            greeting.set_text("Please enter a name.")

    ui.button("Greet", on_click=greet)


if __name__ in {"__main__", "__mp_main__"}:
    ui.run(title="Personal Data Manager", reload=False, show=False)

Start it from the terminal and open the address that it prints:

uv run python hello_app.py

The repository also includes a user-level test, test_hello_ui.py, which needs uv add --dev pytest pytest-asyncio:

from nicegui.testing import User

pytest_plugins = ["nicegui.testing.user_plugin"]


async def test_greeting(user: User) -> None:
    await user.open("/")
    await user.should_see("Personal Data Manager")
    user.find("Greet").click()
    await user.should_see("Please enter a name.")
    user.find("Your name").type("Avery")
    user.find("Greet").click()
    await user.should_see("Hello, Avery!")

# pytest.ini
[pytest]
asyncio_mode = auto
asyncio_default_fixture_loop_scope = function
main_file = hello_app.py

Expected Behavior or Output

When the program starts, the terminal prints a line like this one (the address and port depend on your computer; the default port is 8080):

NiceGUI ready to go on http://localhost:8080, and http://192.0.2.2:8080

The page title is Personal Data Manager. Pressing Greet with an empty field sets the status line to Please enter a name.; after typing Avery it says Hello, Avery!. Running the test with python -m pytest -q test_hello_ui.py prints:

1 passed

Common Mistakes

  1. Calling ui.run() without the __name__ guard, which can start the server twice.
  2. Relying only on ui.notify, whose message disappears, instead of also updating a text status line.
  3. Leaving an input without a label, so the screen reader announces only “edit text”.
  4. Starting a second copy of the program while the first still holds the port.

Activities

  1. Start hello_app.py and read the page title and the status line with your screen reader.
  2. Change the greeting to include the time of day using a second input.
  3. Run the test file and then break the greeting text on purpose to watch the test fail.
  4. Add a second button that clears the name and sets the status line to Name cleared.

Accessibility Practice

Open the page with the keyboard only: press Tab to move between the input and the button and read each stop. Check that the input’s label is announced and that the status line is read after you press the button. Record the browser, screen reader, and version you tested, and do not claim the page is accessible to other setups.

Skills Checklist

  • I can install NiceGUI and start a page from the terminal.
  • I can explain elements and event handlers.
  • I can give every input a label.
  • I can report results in a plain text status line.
  • I can run a user-level test.

Lesson 11.2: Data Model and Storage

Reading References

  • Matthes: Chapter 6 (Dictionaries) and Chapter 10 (Files and Exceptions)
  • Python documentation: the json and datetime modules

Learning Objectives

  • Represent each record as a dictionary with the shared fields.
  • Validate input and return a clear message when it is invalid.
  • Save to and load from a JSON file, and handle a missing or damaged file.

Concept Explanation

The data and the rules live in one module, records.py, that contains no user-interface code. Keeping logic separate from the page has two benefits: the rules can be tested without a browser, and the same logic can serve a different front end later.

Each record is a dictionary with the shared fields (id, title, description, category, created_at, updated_at) and the optional done field. Dictionaries convert directly to JSON.

Rules. A title and a category are required. A new record gets an id one higher than the highest in use. created_at is set once and never changes. updated_at changes whenever a record is updated, completed, or edited. Every function that can fail returns a clear message instead of raising an error that the user must interpret; functions return a pair (result, message).

Storage. save_records writes the list as JSON. load_records treats a missing file as an empty list (this is normal on first use), and returns a message when the file is damaged or does not contain valid records, so the program never overwrites good data with an empty list without telling the user.

Testable time. Functions that stamp a record take a clock argument that defaults to the real time. Tests pass a fake clock so that timestamps are predictable.

Worked Example

Save this as records.py:

"""Logic for the Personal Data Manager. No user-interface code lives here."""
import json
from datetime import datetime

REQUIRED_FIELDS = ("id", "title", "description", "category", "created_at", "updated_at")


def now():
    """Return the current time as ISO 8601 text, for example 2026-01-15T09:00:00."""
    return datetime.now().isoformat(timespec="seconds")


def validate(title, category):
    """Return an error message for invalid input, or None when it is valid."""
    if not title or not title.strip():
        return "A title is required."
    if not category or not category.strip():
        return "A category is required."
    return None


def next_id(records):
    """Return one more than the highest id in use (1 for an empty list)."""
    return max((record["id"] for record in records), default=0) + 1


def find(records, record_id):
    """Return the record with this id, or None."""
    for record in records:
        if record["id"] == record_id:
            return record
    return None


def add_record(records, title, description, category, clock=now):
    """Add a record. Return (record, None) on success or (None, message) on failure."""
    problem = validate(title, category)
    if problem:
        return None, problem
    stamp = clock()
    record = {
        "id": next_id(records),
        "title": title.strip(),
        "description": (description or "").strip(),
        "category": category.strip(),
        "created_at": stamp,
        "updated_at": stamp,
        "done": False,
    }
    records.append(record)
    return record, None


def update_record(records, record_id, changes, clock=now):
    """Change fields of a record. created_at and id never change."""
    record = find(records, record_id)
    if record is None:
        return None, "No record has that id."
    problem = validate(changes.get("title", record["title"]), changes.get("category", record["category"]))
    if problem:
        return None, problem
    for key, value in changes.items():
        if key not in ("id", "created_at"):
            record[key] = value.strip() if isinstance(value, str) else value
    record["updated_at"] = clock()
    return record, None


def complete_record(records, record_id, clock=now):
    """Mark a record done; this counts as an update."""
    return update_record(records, record_id, {"done": True}, clock)


def delete_record(records, record_id):
    """Remove one record. Return (True, None) or (False, message)."""
    record = find(records, record_id)
    if record is None:
        return False, "No record has that id."
    records.remove(record)
    return True, None


def search(records, text):
    """Return records whose title or description contains the text (ignoring case)."""
    needle = text.strip().lower()
    return [r for r in records if needle in r["title"].lower() or needle in r["description"].lower()]


def describe(record):
    """One line of plain text for a record; status is shown in words, never by color."""
    status = "done" if record.get("done") else "not done"
    return f"{record['id']}. {record['title']} [{record['category']}] ({status})"


def save_records(path, records):
    """Write records to a JSON file."""
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        json.dump(records, file, indent=4)


def load_records(path):
    """Return (records, None) or ([], message). A missing file is not an error."""
    try:
        with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
            data = json.load(file)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return [], None
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return [], f"{path} is not valid JSON, so the list starts empty."
    if not isinstance(data, list) or not all(isinstance(r, dict) and all(f in r for f in REQUIRED_FIELDS) for r in data):
        return [], f"{path} does not contain valid records, so the list starts empty."
    return data, None

Try it with this short script, demo.py, in the same folder:

import records

ticks = iter(range(1, 100))


def clock():
    return f"2026-01-15T10:00:{next(ticks):02d}"


items = []
records.add_record(items, "Notebook", "Course notes", "supplies", clock)
records.add_record(items, "Pencil", "Box of 10", "supplies", clock)
print(records.add_record(items, "  ", "x", "supplies", clock))
for item in items:
    print(records.describe(item))

records.save_records("data.json", items)
loaded, problem = records.load_records("data.json")
print(loaded == items, problem)
print(records.load_records("missing.json"))

Expected Behavior or Output

Running python demo.py prints:

(None, 'A title is required.')
1. Notebook [supplies] (not done)
2. Pencil [supplies] (not done)
True None
([], None)

The invalid record is rejected with (None, 'A title is required.'). The saved and reloaded list equals the original (True None), and a missing file gives an empty list with no message.

Common Mistakes

  1. Letting the user interface and the rules share the same code, so neither can be tested alone.
  2. Overwriting data.json with an empty list after a failed load.
  3. Changing created_at when a record is edited.
  4. Reusing an old id by counting the list length instead of using the highest id.

Activities

  1. Run demo.py and open the saved data.json. Read the text aloud.
  2. Add a rule that a title may not be longer than 60 characters, with a clear message.
  3. Add an is_done filter function that returns only completed records.
  4. Damage data.json by deleting a bracket and run load_records again; read the message it returns.

Accessibility Practice

Messages are complete sentences that say what is wrong (A title is required.) so they read clearly in speech and braille. After saving, read data.json in the terminal; indent=4 puts one field per line, which reads well line by line.

Skills Checklist

  • I can represent records as dictionaries.
  • I can validate input and return clear messages.
  • I can save and load JSON.
  • I can handle a missing or damaged file.
  • I can keep logic separate from the user interface.

Lesson 11.3: Displaying and Searching Items

Reading References

  • NiceGUI documentation (official site, nicegui.io); check the documentation for the version you installed

Learning Objectives

  • Build a page that adds a record and lists all records.
  • Filter the list as the user types in a search box.
  • Show errors in a status line that is also announced.

Concept Explanation

The page uses the functions from records.py. It builds a form for a new record, a search box, and a list. The list is rebuilt by one function, refresh(), that clears the list column and then creates one label per record. Calling refresh() after every change keeps the page and the data in step.

Each record is shown as one plain sentence produced by describe(), for example 1. Notebook [supplies] (not done). The status is the words done and not done, never a color or an icon alone. The description appears on its own line prefixed Details:.

The search box filters as the user types: search_text.on_value_change(...) calls refresh(), which uses search() when the box is not empty.

Every input has a unique label (Record title, Record description, Record category, Search title or description). Unique labels let a screen reader user tell the fields apart and let the tests find them.

Worked Example

Save this as app_v1.py (it uses records.py from Lesson 11.2):

"""Personal Data Manager, version for Lesson 11.3: add, list, and search."""
import os
from pathlib import Path

from nicegui import ui

import records as store

DATA_FILE = Path(os.environ.get("PDM_DATA_FILE", "data.json"))
items, load_problem = store.load_records(DATA_FILE)


@ui.page("/")
def main_page():
    ui.page_title("Personal Data Manager")
    ui.label("Personal Data Manager").classes("text-2xl")

    # A plain-text status line. aria-live asks assistive technology to announce changes.
    status = ui.label(load_problem or "Ready.").props('role="status" aria-live="polite"')

    def say(message, ok=True):
        status.set_text(message)
        ui.notify(message, type="positive" if ok else "negative")

    ui.label("Add a record")
    title = ui.input(label="Record title")
    description = ui.input(label="Record description")
    category = ui.input(label="Record category")

    ui.label("Find records")
    search_text = ui.input(label="Search title or description")

    ui.label("Records")
    list_column = ui.column()

    def refresh():
        shown = store.search(items, search_text.value) if search_text.value else items
        list_column.clear()
        with list_column:
            if not shown:
                ui.label("No records to show.")
            for record in shown:
                ui.label(store.describe(record))
                if record["description"]:
                    ui.label("Details: " + record["description"])

    def add_clicked():
        record, problem = store.add_record(items, title.value, description.value, category.value)
        if problem:
            say(problem, ok=False)
            return
        store.save_records(DATA_FILE, items)
        title.set_value("")
        description.set_value("")
        category.set_value("")
        refresh()
        say(f"Added record {record['id']}: {record['title']}.")

    ui.button("Add record", on_click=add_clicked)
    search_text.on_value_change(lambda _: refresh())
    refresh()


if __name__ in {"__main__", "__mp_main__"}:
    ui.run(title="Personal Data Manager", reload=False, show=False)

The user-level test test_app_v1_ui.py:

import os
import tempfile

from nicegui.testing import User

pytest_plugins = ["nicegui.testing.user_plugin"]
os.environ["PDM_DATA_FILE"] = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "data.json")


async def test_add_and_search(user: User) -> None:
    await user.open("/")
    await user.should_see("No records to show.")
    for title, description, category in [("Notebook", "Course notes", "supplies"), ("Pencil", "Box of 10", "supplies")]:
        user.find("Record title").type(title)
        user.find("Record description").type(description)
        user.find("Record category").type(category)
        user.find("Add record").click()
    await user.should_see("2. Pencil [supplies] (not done)")
    user.find("Search title or description").type("note")
    await user.should_see("1. Notebook [supplies] (not done)")
    await user.should_not_see("2. Pencil [supplies] (not done)")
    user.find("Add record").click()
    await user.should_see("A title is required.")

Notebook [supplies] (not done) and 2. Pencil [supplies] (not done). Typing note in the search box leaves only the Notebook line. Pressing Add record with an empty title sets the status line to A title is required. Running the test prints:

1 passed

Common Mistakes

  1. Building the list outside refresh(), so it is not updated when the data changes.
  2. Using the same label text for two inputs, so the screen reader cannot tell them apart.
  3. Showing a record’s status only by color.
  4. Forgetting to clear the form after a successful add, so the next record starts with old text.

Activities

  1. Add the three shared sample records through the page and compare the list with the sample data.
  2. Add a category filter next to the search box.
  3. Show the number of records after the list, for example 3 records.
  4. Break the describe() text on purpose and see which test fails.

Accessibility Practice

Tab through the form and confirm that each field is announced with its label. After pressing Add record, listen for the status line. If your screen reader does not announce it, note the browser and screen reader you used, then add a visible sentence under the button as a fallback.

Skills Checklist

  • I can build a form and a list in NiceGUI.
  • I can refresh the list after every change.
  • I can filter the list with a search box.
  • I can show status in words.
  • I can give each input a unique label.

Lesson 11.4: Changing, Completing, and Deleting Items

Reading References

  • NiceGUI documentation (official site, nicegui.io); check the documentation for the version you installed

Learning Objectives

  • Select a record from a list and change its title or category.
  • Mark a record done and delete a record.
  • Save after every successful change and report each result.

Concept Explanation

The finished page adds a chooser (ui.select) that lists every record by its descriptive sentence, plus buttons to change, complete, or delete the chosen record. All three handlers follow the same pattern: check that a record is chosen, call the matching function in records.py, show the message if it failed, and otherwise save the file, refresh the list, and report what happened.

update_record changes only the fields that are supplied and always updates updated_at. complete_record is an update that sets done to True. delete_record removes exactly one record. After a delete the chooser is cleared so a stale choice cannot be used.

Notice that the handlers contain no rules. A rule such as “a title is required” exists once, in records.py, and applies the same way no matter which control triggers it.

Worked Example

The finished app.py (it uses records.py from Lesson 11.2):

"""Personal Data Manager: a NiceGUI front end for records.py."""
import os
from pathlib import Path

from nicegui import ui

import records as store

DATA_FILE = Path(os.environ.get("PDM_DATA_FILE", "data.json"))
items, load_problem = store.load_records(DATA_FILE)


@ui.page("/")
def main_page():
    ui.page_title("Personal Data Manager")
    ui.label("Personal Data Manager").classes("text-2xl")

    # A plain-text status line. aria-live asks assistive technology to announce changes.
    status = ui.label(load_problem or "Ready.").props('role="status" aria-live="polite"')

    def say(message, ok=True):
        status.set_text(message)
        ui.notify(message, type="positive" if ok else "negative")

    ui.label("Add a record")
    title = ui.input(label="Record title")
    description = ui.input(label="Record description")
    category = ui.input(label="Record category")

    ui.label("Find records")
    search_text = ui.input(label="Search title or description")

    ui.label("Records")
    list_column = ui.column()

    ui.label("Change one record")
    chooser = ui.select(options={}, label="Choose a record")
    new_title = ui.input(label="New title (leave blank to keep)")
    new_category = ui.input(label="New category (leave blank to keep)")

    def refresh():
        shown = store.search(items, search_text.value) if search_text.value else items
        list_column.clear()
        with list_column:
            if not shown:
                ui.label("No records to show.")
            for record in shown:
                ui.label(store.describe(record))
                if record["description"]:
                    ui.label("Details: " + record["description"])
        chooser.set_options({r["id"]: store.describe(r) for r in items})

    def add_clicked():
        record, problem = store.add_record(items, title.value, description.value, category.value)
        if problem:
            say(problem, ok=False)
            return
        store.save_records(DATA_FILE, items)
        title.set_value("")
        description.set_value("")
        category.set_value("")
        refresh()
        say(f"Added record {record['id']}: {record['title']}.")

    def change_clicked():
        if chooser.value is None:
            say("Choose a record first.", ok=False)
            return
        changes = {}
        if new_title.value.strip():
            changes["title"] = new_title.value
        if new_category.value.strip():
            changes["category"] = new_category.value
        if not changes:
            say("Enter a new title or a new category.", ok=False)
            return
        record, problem = store.update_record(items, chooser.value, changes)
        if problem:
            say(problem, ok=False)
            return
        store.save_records(DATA_FILE, items)
        new_title.set_value("")
        new_category.set_value("")
        refresh()
        say(f"Updated record {record['id']}.")

    def complete_clicked():
        if chooser.value is None:
            say("Choose a record first.", ok=False)
            return
        record, problem = store.complete_record(items, chooser.value)
        if problem:
            say(problem, ok=False)
            return
        store.save_records(DATA_FILE, items)
        refresh()
        say(f"Marked record {record['id']} as done.")

    def delete_clicked():
        if chooser.value is None:
            say("Choose a record first.", ok=False)
            return
        record_id = chooser.value
        ok, problem = store.delete_record(items, record_id)
        if not ok:
            say(problem, ok=False)
            return
        store.save_records(DATA_FILE, items)
        chooser.set_value(None)
        refresh()
        say(f"Deleted record {record_id}.")

    ui.button("Add record", on_click=add_clicked)
    search_text.on_value_change(lambda _: refresh())
    ui.button("Change selected record", on_click=change_clicked)
    ui.button("Mark selected record done", on_click=complete_clicked)
    ui.button("Delete selected record", on_click=delete_clicked)
    refresh()


if __name__ in {"__main__", "__mp_main__"}:
    ui.run(title="Personal Data Manager", reload=False, show=False)

The user-level test test_app_ui.py:

"""User-level tests for app.py. They need: pip install nicegui pytest pytest-asyncio"""

async def test_add_search_complete_delete(user: User) -> None:

    user.find("1. Notebook [supplies] (not done)").click()
