Skills Checklist

  • I can write reusable validation functions.
  • I limit retries.
  • I handle the end of input.
  • I write messages that say what to do.
  • I keep wording consistent.

Unit 11: Capstone

Overview

This unit develops capstone through Rust’s type system and standard library. Prerequisites: prior units, a working Cargo project, and the ability to read compiler diagnostics. Preserve shared course datasets and test boundary conditions explicitly.

Lesson 11.1: Requirements and design

Reading References

  • The Rust Programming Language: Structs
  • The Rust Programming Language: Result
  • Rust standard library documentation
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 11.1: Introduction to NiceGUI

Learning Objectives

  • Write requirements for a personal data manager.
  • Define the shared record schema as a struct.
  • Check records against the validation rules before building features.

Concept Explanation

The capstone is a personal data manager: a program that keeps a list of records, lets the user add, view, search, change, complete, and delete them, and saves them to a file. In the Rust track it is a text program, so it runs from the terminal and is fully usable with a screen reader or braille display.

Shared record schema (all general-purpose language tracks). Every record has id (unique whole number), title, description, category, created_at, and updated_at (ISO 8601 text). A project may add fields, such as an optional done flag, but must not remove these. Rust field names use snake_case, the same as the stored JSON.

Validation rules. A record must have a non-empty title and a non-empty category. Timestamps are ISO 8601 text such as 2026-01-15T09:00:00. A Result<(), String> return type states in the signature that validation can fail with a message.

Design before coding: list the operations, then the data, then the messages. The example checks the three shared sample records against the rules and prints them as a plain-text list.

Worked Example

struct Entry {
    id: i32,
    title: String,
    description: String,
    category: String,
    created_at: String,
    updated_at: String,
}

fn validate(title: &str, category: &str) -> Result<(), String> {
    if title.trim().is_empty() {
        return Err("A title is required.".to_string());
    }
    if category.trim().is_empty() {
        return Err("A category is required.".to_string());
    }
    Ok(())
}

fn entry(id: i32, title: &str, description: &str, category: &str, created_at: &str) -> Entry {
    Entry {
        id,
        title: title.to_string(),
        description: description.to_string(),
        category: category.to_string(),
        created_at: created_at.to_string(),
        updated_at: created_at.to_string(),
    }
}

fn main() {
    let sample = vec![
        entry(1, "Notebook", "Course notes", "supplies", "2026-01-15T09:00:00"),
        entry(2, "Pencil", "Box of 10", "supplies", "2026-01-15T09:05:00"),
        entry(3, "Study plan", "Weekly schedule", "planning", "2026-01-15T09:10:00"),
    ];

    for record in &sample {
        let outcome = match validate(&record.title, &record.category) {
            Ok(()) => "valid".to_string(),
            Err(message) => message,
        };
        println!("{}. {} [{}] - {}", record.id, record.title, record.category, outcome);
    }
    println!("{} | {} | {}", sample[0].description, sample[0].created_at, sample[0].updated_at);

    println!("{:?}", validate("  ", "supplies"));
    println!("{:?}", validate("Ruler", ""));
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

1. Notebook [supplies] - valid
2. Pencil [supplies] - valid
3. Study plan [planning] - valid
Course notes | 2026-01-15T09:00:00 | 2026-01-15T09:00:00
Err("A title is required.")
Err("A category is required.")

Common Mistakes

  1. Starting to build features before agreeing on the record fields.
  2. Allowing a record with an empty title because the check was left for later.
  3. Storing timestamps in different formats in different places.

Activities

  1. Write the seven operations as a numbered list of requirements.
  2. Add one project-specific field and say how it is validated.
  3. Write three sample records for your own project.
  4. Describe in plain sentences what each shared field means.

Accessibility Practice

Design the screen output as lines of plain text: one record per line, with the same field order each time. Decide the wording of every message now so that it can be tested.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write requirements.
  • I know the shared record fields.
  • I can write validation rules.
  • I can describe sample data.
  • I can plan messages before coding.

Lesson 11.2: Data model and storage

Reading References

  • The Rust Programming Language: Result
  • The Rust Programming Language: Reading a File
  • Rust standard library documentation
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 11.2: Data Model and Storage

Learning Objectives

  • Store records as structs.
  • Save and load them as JSON.
  • Confirm that every field survives a round trip.

Concept Explanation

Records are stored as a Vec<Entry> in memory and as a JSON array on disk. The storage layer has two functions: save_entries(path, entries) and load_entries(path), which returns Result<Vec<Entry>, String> so the caller decides what to do when the file is missing or damaged.

An Entry is converted to a Json::Object for saving (to_json) and rebuilt from one when loading (from_json), which checks that each field is present and has the right type. The optional done field defaults to false.

The example uses the teaching JSON helper from Lesson 8.5 (included so the program runs on its own). After saving and reloading it compares the lists; deriving PartialEq lets Rust compare structs field by field, so this round-trip test checks every field of every entry. It is the first acceptance test for storage.

Worked Example

#![allow(dead_code)]
use std::collections::BTreeMap;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum Json {
    Null,
    Bool(bool),
    Int(i64),
    Float(f64),
    Str(String),
    List(Vec<Json>),
    Object(BTreeMap<String, Json>),
}

fn quote(text: &str) -> String {
    let mut out = String::from("\"");
    for c in text.chars() {
        match c {
            '"' => out.push_str("\\\""),
            '\\' => out.push_str("\\\\"),
            '\n' => out.push_str("\\n"),
            '\r' => out.push_str("\\r"),
            '\t' => out.push_str("\\t"),
            c if (c as u32) < 0x20 => out.push_str(&format!("\\u{:04x}", c as u32)),
            c => out.push(c),
        }
    }
    out.push('"');
    out
}

fn encode(value: &Json) -> String {
    match value {
        Json::Null => "null".to_string(),
        Json::Bool(flag) => flag.to_string(),
        Json::Int(number) => number.to_string(),
        Json::Float(number) => number.to_string(),
        Json::Str(text) => quote(text),
        Json::List(items) => {
            let parts: Vec<String> = items.iter().map(encode).collect();
            format!("[{}]", parts.join(","))
        }
        Json::Object(map) => {
            let parts: Vec<String> = map.iter().map(|(key, item)| format!("{}:{}", quote(key), encode(item))).collect();
            format!("{{{}}}", parts.join(","))
        }
    }
}

struct Parser {
    chars: Vec<char>,
    pos: usize,
}

impl Parser {
    fn fail<T>(&self, message: &str) -> Result<T, String> {
        Err(format!("{message} at position {}", self.pos))
    }

    fn skip(&mut self) {
        while self.pos < self.chars.len() && self.chars[self.pos].is_whitespace() {
            self.pos += 1;
        }
    }

    fn peek(&self) -> Option<char> {
        self.chars.get(self.pos).copied()
    }

    fn starts_with(&self, word: &str) -> bool {
        word.chars().enumerate().all(|(i, c)| self.chars.get(self.pos + i) == Some(&c))
    }

    fn value(&mut self) -> Result<Json, String> {
        self.skip();
        match self.peek() {
            None => self.fail("unexpected end of text"),
            Some('{') => self.object(),
            Some('[') => self.list(),
            Some('"') => Ok(Json::Str(self.string()?)),
            Some(c) if c == '-' || c.is_ascii_digit() => self.number(),
            Some(_) if self.starts_with("true") => {
                self.pos += 4;
                Ok(Json::Bool(true))
            }
            Some(_) if self.starts_with("false") => {
                self.pos += 5;
                Ok(Json::Bool(false))
            }
            Some(_) if self.starts_with("null") => {
                self.pos += 4;
                Ok(Json::Null)
            }
            Some(_) => self.fail("unexpected character"),
        }
    }

    fn number(&mut self) -> Result<Json, String> {
        let start = self.pos;
        if self.peek() == Some('-') {
            self.pos += 1;
        }
        while let Some(c) = self.peek() {
            if c.is_ascii_digit() || ".eE+-".contains(c) {
                self.pos += 1;
            } else {
                break;
            }
        }
        let token: String = self.chars[start..self.pos].iter().collect();
        if let Ok(number) = token.parse::<i64>() {
            return Ok(Json::Int(number));
        }
        match token.parse::<f64>() {
            Ok(number) => Ok(Json::Float(number)),
            Err(_) => self.fail("bad number"),
        }
    }

    fn string(&mut self) -> Result<String, String> {
        self.pos += 1;
        let mut out = String::new();
        loop {
            let Some(c) = self.peek() else {
                return self.fail("unterminated string");
            };
            self.pos += 1;
            match c {
                '"' => return Ok(out),
                '\\' => {
                    let Some(escape) = self.peek() else {
                        return self.fail("bad escape");
                    };
                    self.pos += 1;
                    match escape {
                        'n' => out.push('\n'),
                        't' => out.push('\t'),
                        'r' => out.push('\r'),
                        '"' => out.push('"'),
                        '\\' => out.push('\\'),
                        '/' => out.push('/'),
                        'u' => {
                            if self.pos + 4 > self.chars.len() {
                                return self.fail("bad escape");
                            }
                            let hex: String = self.chars[self.pos..self.pos + 4].iter().collect();
                            let code = u32::from_str_radix(&hex, 16).map_err(|_| "bad escape".to_string())?;
                            out.push(char::from_u32(code).unwrap_or('?'));
                            self.pos += 4;
                        }
                        _ => return self.fail("bad escape"),
                    }
                }
                other => out.push(other),
            }
        }
    }

    fn object(&mut self) -> Result<Json, String> {
        self.pos += 1;
        let mut map = BTreeMap::new();
        self.skip();
        if self.peek() == Some('}') {
            self.pos += 1;
            return Ok(Json::Object(map));
        }
        loop {
            self.skip();
            if self.peek() != Some('"') {
                return self.fail("expected a key");
            }
            let key = self.string()?;
            self.skip();
            if self.peek() != Some(':') {
                return self.fail("expected ':'");
            }
            self.pos += 1;
            let item = self.value()?;
            map.insert(key, item);
            self.skip();
            match self.peek() {
                None => return self.fail("unterminated object"),
                Some('}') => {
                    self.pos += 1;
                    return Ok(Json::Object(map));
                }
                Some(',') => self.pos += 1,
                Some(_) => return self.fail("expected ',' or '}'"),
            }
        }
    }

    fn list(&mut self) -> Result<Json, String> {
        self.pos += 1;
        let mut items = Vec::new();
        self.skip();
        if self.peek() == Some(']') {
            self.pos += 1;
            return Ok(Json::List(items));
        }
        loop {
            items.push(self.value()?);
            self.skip();
            match self.peek() {
                None => return self.fail("unterminated list"),
                Some(']') => {
                    self.pos += 1;
                    return Ok(Json::List(items));
                }
                Some(',') => self.pos += 1,
                Some(_) => return self.fail("expected ',' or ']'"),
            }
        }
    }
}

fn decode(text: &str) -> Result<Json, String> {
    let mut parser = Parser { chars: text.chars().collect(), pos: 0 };
    let value = parser.value()?;
    parser.skip();
    if parser.pos < parser.chars.len() {
        return parser.fail("unexpected extra text");
    }
    Ok(value)
}

use std::fs;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct Entry {
    id: i64,
    title: String,
    description: String,
    category: String,
    created_at: String,
    updated_at: String,
    done: bool,
}

fn to_json(entry: &Entry) -> Json {
    let mut map = BTreeMap::new();
    map.insert("id".to_string(), Json::Int(entry.id));
    map.insert("title".to_string(), Json::Str(entry.title.clone()));
    map.insert("description".to_string(), Json::Str(entry.description.clone()));
    map.insert("category".to_string(), Json::Str(entry.category.clone()));
    map.insert("created_at".to_string(), Json::Str(entry.created_at.clone()));
    map.insert("updated_at".to_string(), Json::Str(entry.updated_at.clone()));
    map.insert("done".to_string(), Json::Bool(entry.done));
    Json::Object(map)
}

fn text_field(map: &BTreeMap<String, Json>, key: &str) -> Result<String, String> {
    match map.get(key) {
        Some(Json::Str(text)) => Ok(text.clone()),
        _ => Err(format!("missing field {key}")),
    }
}

fn from_json(value: &Json) -> Result<Entry, String> {
    let Json::Object(map) = value else {
        return Err("a record must be an object".to_string());
    };
    let id = match map.get("id") {
        Some(Json::Int(number)) => *number,
        _ => return Err("missing field id".to_string()),
    };
    Ok(Entry {
        id,
        title: text_field(map, "title")?,
        description: text_field(map, "description")?,
        category: text_field(map, "category")?,
        created_at: text_field(map, "created_at")?,
        updated_at: text_field(map, "updated_at")?,
        done: map.get("done") == Some(&Json::Bool(true)),
    })
}

fn save_entries(path: &str, entries: &[Entry]) -> Result<(), String> {
    let list = Json::List(entries.iter().map(to_json).collect());
    fs::write(path, encode(&list)).map_err(|_| format!("Could not write {path}."))
}

fn load_entries(path: &str) -> Result<Vec<Entry>, String> {
    let text = fs::read_to_string(path).map_err(|_| format!("Could not open {path}: file not found."))?;
    match decode(&text) {
        Ok(Json::List(items)) => items.iter().map(from_json).collect::<Result<Vec<Entry>, String>>().map_err(|e| format!("The data file is not valid: {e}")),
        Ok(_) => Err("The data file is not valid: expected a list".to_string()),
        Err(message) => Err(format!("The data file is not valid: {message}")),
    }
}

fn entry(id: i64, title: &str, description: &str, category: &str, stamp: &str) -> Entry {
    Entry {
        id,
        title: title.to_string(),
        description: description.to_string(),
        category: category.to_string(),
        created_at: stamp.to_string(),
        updated_at: stamp.to_string(),
        done: false,
    }
}

fn main() {
    let sample = vec![
        entry(1, "Notebook", "Course notes", "supplies", "2026-01-15T09:00:00"),
        entry(2, "Pencil", "Box of 10", "supplies", "2026-01-15T09:05:00"),
        entry(3, "Study plan", "Weekly schedule", "planning", "2026-01-15T09:10:00"),
    ];

    println!("{:?}", save_entries("records.json", &sample));
    match load_entries("records.json") {
        Ok(loaded) => {
            println!("Round trip preserved all fields: {}", loaded == sample);
            println!("Records loaded: {}", loaded.len());
        }
        Err(message) => println!("{message}"),
    }

    if let Err(message) = load_entries("missing.json") {
        println!("{message}");
    }

    fs::write("broken.json", "[{\"id\": 1,").expect("could not write the broken file");
    if let Err(message) = load_entries("broken.json") {
        println!("{message}");
    }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Ok(())
Round trip preserved all fields: true
Records loaded: 3
Could not open missing.json: file not found.
The data file is not valid: expected a key at position 10

Common Mistakes

  1. Overwriting the data file with an empty list after a failed load.
  2. Saving only some of the fields.
  3. Assuming a loaded record has every field without checking.

Activities

  1. Run the program and open records.json to read the saved text.
  2. Add a field to Entry, save it, and confirm that it survives the round trip.
  3. Make from_json reject a record whose title is blank.
  4. Explain why load_entries returns a Result and does not panic.

Accessibility Practice

Messages that name the file and the problem read clearly in speech. After saving, read the file in the terminal to confirm it contains what you expect.

Skills Checklist

  • I can store records in structs.
  • I can save and load JSON.
  • I can run a round-trip test.
  • I handle missing and damaged files.
  • I do not overwrite good data after a failed load.

Lesson 11.3: Create, read, update, delete

Reading References

  • The Rust Programming Language: Method Syntax
  • The Rust Programming Language: Result
  • Rust standard library documentation
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 11.3: Displaying and Managing Items

Learning Objectives

  • Add, list, search, change, complete, and delete records.
  • Assign new ids and update timestamps correctly.
  • Return a Result with a message when an operation cannot be done.

Concept Explanation

A Manager struct owns the entries and offers one method per operation. Each method that can fail returns a Result<_, String> whose Err holds the message to show. New ids are one more than the highest id, so ids are never reused while higher ids exist. Updating an entry sets updated_at but never changes created_at. A Changes struct with Option fields says which fields to change, so Changes { done: Some(true), ..Default::default() } changes only done. Completing an entry counts as an update.

For repeatable output the example passes in a fake clock: a boxed closure that returns a new fixed time on each call. A real program passes a closure that reads the real time.

The example adds the three shared sample records, lists them, searches for “note”, changes one description, completes one entry, deletes one, and tries to delete an entry that does not exist.

Worked Example

#![allow(dead_code)]
struct Entry {
    id: i32,
    title: String,
    description: String,
    category: String,
    created_at: String,
    updated_at: String,
    done: bool,
}

impl Entry {
    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        format!("{}. {} [{}] ({})", self.id, self.title, self.category, if self.done { "done" } else { "not done" })
    }
}

#[derive(Default)]
struct Changes {
    title: Option<String>,
    description: Option<String>,
    category: Option<String>,
    done: Option<bool>,
}

fn validate(title: &str, category: &str) -> Result<(), String> {
    if title.trim().is_empty() {
        return Err("A title is required.".to_string());
    }
    if category.trim().is_empty() {
        return Err("A category is required.".to_string());
    }
    Ok(())
}

struct Manager {
    entries: Vec<Entry>,
    clock: Box<dyn FnMut() -> String>,
}

impl Manager {
    fn new(clock: Box<dyn FnMut() -> String>) -> Manager {
        Manager { entries: Vec::new(), clock }
    }

    fn next_id(&self) -> i32 {
        self.entries.iter().map(|entry| entry.id).max().unwrap_or(0) + 1
    }

    fn find(&self, id: i32) -> Option<&Entry> {
        self.entries.iter().find(|entry| entry.id == id)
    }

    fn add(&mut self, title: &str, description: &str, category: &str) -> Result<i32, String> {
        validate(title, category)?;
        let stamp = (self.clock)();
        let id = self.next_id();
        self.entries.push(Entry {
            id,
            title: title.trim().to_string(),
            description: description.trim().to_string(),
            category: category.trim().to_string(),
            created_at: stamp.clone(),
            updated_at: stamp,
            done: false,
        });
        Ok(id)
    }

    fn update(&mut self, id: i32, changes: Changes) -> Result<(), String> {
        let (title, category) = match self.find(id) {
            Some(entry) => (
                changes.title.clone().unwrap_or_else(|| entry.title.clone()),
                changes.category.clone().unwrap_or_else(|| entry.category.clone()),
            ),
            None => return Err("No record has that id.".to_string()),
        };
        validate(&title, &category)?;
        let stamp = (self.clock)();
        let entry = self.entries.iter_mut().find(|entry| entry.id == id).ok_or("No record has that id.")?;
        if let Some(value) = changes.title {
            entry.title = value.trim().to_string();
        }
        if let Some(value) = changes.description {
            entry.description = value.trim().to_string();
        }
        if let Some(value) = changes.category {
            entry.category = value.trim().to_string();
        }
        if let Some(value) = changes.done {
            entry.done = value;
        }
        entry.updated_at = stamp;
        Ok(())
    }

    fn complete(&mut self, id: i32) -> Result<(), String> {
        self.update(id, Changes { done: Some(true), ..Default::default() })
    }

    fn delete(&mut self, id: i32) -> Result<(), String> {
        let position = self.entries.iter().position(|entry| entry.id == id).ok_or("No record has that id.")?;
        self.entries.remove(position);
        Ok(())
    }

    fn search(&self, text: &str) -> Vec<&Entry> {
        let needle = text.trim().to_lowercase();
        self.entries
            .iter()
            .filter(|entry| entry.title.to_lowercase().contains(&needle) || entry.description.to_lowercase().contains(&needle))
            .collect()
    }
}

fn fake_clock() -> Box<dyn FnMut() -> String> {
    let mut ticks = 0;
    Box::new(move || {
        ticks += 1;
        format!("2026-01-15T10:00:{ticks:02}")
    })
}

fn show(manager: &Manager) {
    for entry in &manager.entries {
        println!("{}", entry.describe());
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut manager = Manager::new(fake_clock());
    manager.add("Notebook", "Course notes", "supplies").unwrap();
    manager.add("Pencil", "Box of 10", "supplies").unwrap();
    manager.add("Study plan", "Weekly schedule", "planning").unwrap();
    show(&manager);

    println!("Search for 'note':");
    for entry in manager.search("note") {
        println!("{}", entry.title);
    }

    manager.update(2, Changes { description: Some("Box of 12".to_string()), ..Default::default() }).unwrap();
    manager.complete(3).unwrap();
    if let Some(entry) = manager.find(2) {
        println!("{} {} {}", entry.description, entry.created_at, entry.updated_at);
    }

    println!("{:?}", manager.delete(1));
    println!("{:?}", manager.delete(99));
    show(&manager);
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

1. Notebook [supplies] (not done)
2. Pencil [supplies] (not done)
3. Study plan [planning] (not done)
Search for 'note':
Notebook
Box of 12 2026-01-15T10:00:02 2026-01-15T10:00:04
Ok(())
Err("No record has that id.")
2. Pencil [supplies] (not done)
3. Study plan [planning] (done)

Common Mistakes

  1. Reusing a deleted entry’s id by counting the vector length instead of using the highest id.
  2. Changing created_at when updating a record.
  3. Calling unwrap() on every Result in a real program instead of showing the message to the user.

Activities

  1. Predict the output before running.
  2. Add list_by_category(category) to Manager.
  3. Add a rule that blocks completing an entry that is already complete, with a message.
  4. Explain how the fake clock makes the output repeatable.

Accessibility Practice

List output uses the same fixed format for every record and the words done and not done. Search results print only titles, so each line is short.

Skills Checklist

  • I can implement add, list, search, change, complete, and delete.
  • I assign unique ids.
  • I update timestamps correctly.
  • I return clear messages for failures.
  • I can make output repeatable with a fake clock.

Lesson 11.4: Validation and tests

Reading References

  • The Rust Programming Language: How to Write Tests
  • The Rust Programming Language: Test Organization
  • Rust standard library documentation
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 11.4: Testing and Refinement

Learning Objectives

  • Run the shared acceptance tests.
  • Verify that validation rejects bad data.
  • Read and interpret test results.

Concept Explanation

The shared acceptance tests describe behavior that every language track’s capstone must show:

  1. Adding a record with an empty title is rejected with a clear message.
  2. A new record receives an unused id.
  3. Updating a record changes updated_at but not created_at.
  4. Deleting a record removes only that record.
  5. Saving and reloading preserves all fields and values (shown in Lesson 11.2).
  6. Every message and control can be used without color or a mouse (checked by hand in Lesson 11.5).

This lesson automates tests 1 to 4 and also tests completion and the rejection of a blank title in an update. Each test builds a new Manager, so tests cannot affect each other. The fake clock keeps timestamps predictable so a test can check that updated_at changed while created_at did not. Each test is a function returning Result<(), String>, run by a small loop that prints PASS or FAIL.

Worked Example

#![allow(dead_code)]
struct Entry {
    id: i32,
    title: String,
    description: String,
    category: String,
    created_at: String,
    updated_at: String,
    done: bool,
}

impl Entry {
    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        format!("{}. {} [{}] ({})", self.id, self.title, self.category, if self.done { "done" } else { "not done" })
    }
}

#[derive(Default)]
struct Changes {
    title: Option<String>,
    description: Option<String>,
    category: Option<String>,
    done: Option<bool>,
}

fn validate(title: &str, category: &str) -> Result<(), String> {
    if title.trim().is_empty() {
        return Err("A title is required.".to_string());
    }
    if category.trim().is_empty() {
        return Err("A category is required.".to_string());
    }
    Ok(())
}

struct Manager {
    entries: Vec<Entry>,
    clock: Box<dyn FnMut() -> String>,
}

impl Manager {
    fn new(clock: Box<dyn FnMut() -> String>) -> Manager {
        Manager { entries: Vec::new(), clock }
    }

    fn next_id(&self) -> i32 {
        self.entries.iter().map(|entry| entry.id).max().unwrap_or(0) + 1
    }

    fn find(&self, id: i32) -> Option<&Entry> {
        self.entries.iter().find(|entry| entry.id == id)
    }

    fn add(&mut self, title: &str, description: &str, category: &str) -> Result<i32, String> {
        validate(title, category)?;
        let stamp = (self.clock)();
        let id = self.next_id();
        self.entries.push(Entry {
            id,
            title: title.trim().to_string(),
            description: description.trim().to_string(),
            category: category.trim().to_string(),
            created_at: stamp.clone(),
            updated_at: stamp,
            done: false,
        });
        Ok(id)
    }

    fn update(&mut self, id: i32, changes: Changes) -> Result<(), String> {
        let (title, category) = match self.find(id) {
            Some(entry) => (
                changes.title.clone().unwrap_or_else(|| entry.title.clone()),
                changes.category.clone().unwrap_or_else(|| entry.category.clone()),
            ),
            None => return Err("No record has that id.".to_string()),
        };
        validate(&title, &category)?;
        let stamp = (self.clock)();
        let entry = self.entries.iter_mut().find(|entry| entry.id == id).ok_or("No record has that id.")?;
        if let Some(value) = changes.title {
            entry.title = value.trim().to_string();
        }
        if let Some(value) = changes.description {
            entry.description = value.trim().to_string();
        }
        if let Some(value) = changes.category {
            entry.category = value.trim().to_string();
        }
        if let Some(value) = changes.done {
            entry.done = value;
        }
        entry.updated_at = stamp;
        Ok(())
    }

    fn complete(&mut self, id: i32) -> Result<(), String> {
        self.update(id, Changes { done: Some(true), ..Default::default() })
    }

    fn delete(&mut self, id: i32) -> Result<(), String> {
        let position = self.entries.iter().position(|entry| entry.id == id).ok_or("No record has that id.")?;
        self.entries.remove(position);
        Ok(())
    }

    fn search(&self, text: &str) -> Vec<&Entry> {
        let needle = text.trim().to_lowercase();
        self.entries
            .iter()
            .filter(|entry| entry.title.to_lowercase().contains(&needle) || entry.description.to_lowercase().contains(&needle))
            .collect()
    }
}

fn fake_clock() -> Box<dyn FnMut() -> String> {
    let mut ticks = 0;
    Box::new(move || {
        ticks += 1;
        format!("2026-01-15T10:00:{ticks:02}")
    })
}

fn expect(condition: bool, message: &str) -> Result<(), String> {
    if condition {
        Ok(())
    } else {
        Err(message.to_string())
    }
}

fn fresh() -> Manager {
    let mut manager = Manager::new(fake_clock());
    manager.add("Notebook", "Course notes", "supplies").unwrap();
    manager.add("Pencil", "Box of 10", "supplies").unwrap();
    manager.add("Study plan", "Weekly schedule", "planning").unwrap();
    manager
}

fn empty_title_is_rejected() -> Result<(), String> {
    let mut manager = fresh();
    expect(manager.add("   ", "x", "supplies") == Err("A title is required.".to_string()), "expected the title message")?;
    expect(manager.entries.len() == 3, "the list should be unchanged")
}

fn new_record_gets_an_unused_id() -> Result<(), String> {
    let mut manager = fresh();
    manager.delete(2)?;
    let id = manager.add("Ruler", "30 cm", "supplies")?;
    expect(id == 4, "expected id 4")
}

fn update_changes_updated_at_but_not_created_at() -> Result<(), String> {
    let mut manager = fresh();
    let (created, updated) = {
        let entry = manager.find(1).ok_or("record 1 missing")?;
        (entry.created_at.clone(), entry.updated_at.clone())
    };
    manager.update(1, Changes { description: Some("Lecture notes".to_string()), ..Default::default() })?;
    let entry = manager.find(1).ok_or("record 1 missing")?;
    expect(entry.created_at == created, "created_at changed")?;
    expect(entry.updated_at != updated, "updated_at did not change")
}

fn delete_removes_only_that_record() -> Result<(), String> {
    let mut manager = fresh();
    manager.delete(2)?;
    let ids: Vec<i32> = manager.entries.iter().map(|entry| entry.id).collect();
    expect(ids == vec![1, 3], "wrong records remain")
}

fn complete_marks_done_and_updates_the_record() -> Result<(), String> {
    let mut manager = fresh();
    manager.complete(3)?;
    let entry = manager.find(3).ok_or("record 3 missing")?;
    expect(entry.done && entry.updated_at != entry.created_at, "completion not recorded")
}

fn blank_title_cannot_be_saved_by_update() -> Result<(), String> {
    let mut manager = fresh();
    let result = manager.update(1, Changes { title: Some(String::new()), ..Default::default() });
    expect(result == Err("A title is required.".to_string()), "update accepted a blank title")
}

fn main() {
    let tests: [(&str, fn() -> Result<(), String>); 6] = [
        ("1. an empty title is rejected", empty_title_is_rejected),
        ("2. a new record gets an unused id", new_record_gets_an_unused_id),
        ("3. update changes updated_at but not created_at", update_changes_updated_at_but_not_created_at),
        ("4. delete removes only that record", delete_removes_only_that_record),
        ("5. complete marks done and updates the record", complete_marks_done_and_updates_the_record),
        ("6. a blank title cannot be saved by update", blank_title_cannot_be_saved_by_update),
    ];

    let mut failures = 0;
    for (name, test) in tests {
        match test() {
            Ok(()) => println!("PASS {name}"),
            Err(message) => {
                failures += 1;
                println!("FAIL {name}: {message}");
            }
        }
    }
    if failures == 0 {
        println!("All acceptance tests passed.");
    } else {
        println!("{failures} test(s) failed.");
    }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

PASS 1. an empty title is rejected
PASS 2. a new record gets an unused id
PASS 3. update changes updated_at but not created_at
PASS 4. delete removes only that record
PASS 5. complete marks done and updates the record
PASS 6. a blank title cannot be saved by update
All acceptance tests passed.

Common Mistakes

  1. Sharing one manager between tests, so one test’s deletions change the next test.
  2. Checking only that no error occurred, and not checking the result.
  3. Writing the expected message differently from the program, so a correct program fails the test.

Activities

  1. Break Manager::update so it also changes created_at and watch test 3 fail. Restore it.
  2. Add a test that searching ignores case.
  3. Add a test that deleting an unknown id returns a message.
  4. Explain why test 2 deletes record 2 before adding the new one.

Accessibility Practice

The test names begin with the acceptance-test number, so PASS and FAIL lines can be matched to the specification. Read only the first word of each line to hear the overall result quickly.

Skills Checklist

  • I can run the shared acceptance tests.
  • I can test validation failures.
  • I can test timestamps with a fake clock.
  • I can read PASS and FAIL lines.
  • I use a fresh manager for every test.

Lesson 11.5: Documentation and presentation

Reading References

  • Rust standard library documentation
  • Unit P, Lesson P.6: files, data formats, and the shared accessible workflow
  • Matching Python lesson: Lesson 11.5: Final Submission

Learning Objectives

  • Write a plain-text project summary.
  • Report a count of records by category.
  • Complete a manual accessibility check.

Concept Explanation

Documentation tells a future reader what the program does and how to run it. Write it as plain text or Markdown with short headings, numbered steps, and complete sentences. Include: the purpose of the program, the cargo commands to build and run it, the shared record fields, the commands a user can give, the accessibility checks you carried out, and what you would improve next.

The example generates a summary from the shared sample data. It counts records by category in a BTreeMap, which keeps its keys sorted, so the output is stable. It then prints the manual accessibility checklist. The unchecked boxes [ ] are for you to complete by hand with your own access technology; the program cannot verify them.

Acceptance test 6 is a manual check: every message and control can be used without color or a mouse. Test it with the keyboard only, and with the screen reader or braille display you actually use. Record what you tested and its version; do not claim compatibility with software you did not test.

Worked Example

use std::collections::BTreeMap;

struct Entry {
    id: i32,
    title: String,
    category: String,
}

fn main() {
    let sample = vec![
        Entry { id: 1, title: "Notebook".to_string(), category: "supplies".to_string() },
        Entry { id: 2, title: "Pencil".to_string(), category: "supplies".to_string() },
        Entry { id: 3, title: "Study plan".to_string(), category: "planning".to_string() },
    ];

    let mut counts: BTreeMap<&str, u32> = BTreeMap::new();
    for entry in &sample {
        *counts.entry(entry.category.as_str()).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }

    println!("Personal Data Manager - Summary");
    println!("Records: {}", sample.len());
    println!("Categories:");
    for (category, count) in &counts {
        println!("- {category}: {count}");
    }
    let titles: Vec<String> = sample.iter().map(|entry| format!("{} ({})", entry.title, entry.id)).collect();
    println!("Titles: {}", titles.join(", "));

    println!();
    println!("Manual accessibility checklist (complete this by hand):");
    let checks = [
        "[ ] Every command can be used with the keyboard only.",
        "[ ] Every message is a complete sentence that says what to do next.",
        "[ ] No meaning depends on color, position, or symbols alone.",
        "[ ] The output was read with my own screen reader or braille display.",
        "[ ] I recorded the operating system, program, and version I tested.",
    ];
    for check in checks {
        println!("{check}");
    }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints:

Personal Data Manager - Summary
Records: 3
Categories:
- planning: 1
- supplies: 2
Titles: Notebook (1), Pencil (2), Study plan (3)

Manual accessibility checklist (complete this by hand):
[ ] Every command can be used with the keyboard only.
[ ] Every message is a complete sentence that says what to do next.
[ ] No meaning depends on color, position, or symbols alone.
[ ] The output was read with my own screen reader or braille display.
[ ] I recorded the operating system, program, and version I tested.

Common Mistakes

  1. Writing documentation that only the author can follow.
  2. Claiming that a program is accessible without recording what was tested and how.
  3. Letting the documentation drift from the program after later changes.

Activities

  1. Write the project summary for your own capstone using the headings above.
  2. Run the keyboard-only check and record each problem you find.
  3. Ask a classmate to follow your run instructions from a fresh folder and note where they get stuck.
  4. Write three improvements for the next version, ordered by user benefit.

Accessibility Practice

This is the final accessibility lesson. Read your own documentation aloud from start to finish. Anything you have to look at the screen to understand needs rewriting.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write a plain-text project summary.
  • I can report counts by category.
  • I can run a manual accessibility check.
  • I record what I tested.
  • I do not claim untested compatibility.

Course-Wide Assessment and Portfolio

Submit a Cargo project that compiles with the Rust 2024 edition, passes cargo fmt –check, cargo check, and cargo test, and documents its data model, input validation, error handling, persistence format, and keyboard/screen-reader workflow. Include a README with exact build, test, and run commands.

AI Policy

AI tools may explain compiler diagnostics, compare ownership strategies, and suggest tests. Learners must explain every ownership transfer, borrow, trait bound, error path, and dependency. Compile and test generated code, review dependency provenance, and do not expose private data or credentials. AI output is a draft, not evidence of correctness.

Rust-Specific Verification Notes

The JSON example demonstrates the serialized record shape only; production code should use serde_json. The deterministic pseudo-random example is not cryptographically secure and is not a substitute for a maintained random-number generator.

Swift Curriculum

Before you start: complete Unit P: Computing Foundations Primer. It explains the language-neutral vocabulary and concepts used in every language track, using non-visual examples.

Swift is used for iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, server applications, and systems components. Its static type system, optionals, value semantics, protocols, structured error handling, Codable, and concurrency support robust application development.

Course structure

A complete course aligned to the Python curriculum’s Units 0–11, including four environment/toolchain lessons and 53 numbered lessons. The worked examples reuse shared course contexts: Avery’s profile, calculator and tip values, grades, scores, inventory, coordinates, text samples, CSV fields, task records, text-adventure requirements, and personal-record management.

Environment

  • Baseline: Swift 6 language mode and a current Swift 6 toolchain.
  • Verify with swift --version and swiftc --version.
  • Run a single source file with swift main.swift.
  • Initialize a package with swift package init --type executable; build, run, and test with swift build, swift run, and swift test.
  • Xcode and Apple platform SDKs are required for iOS simulator and Apple-platform application development.
  • Use Foundation for file operations and Codable JSON encoding. Use a standards-aware CSV library for quoted fields and embedded newlines.

Complete the shared IDE setup lesson and terminal prerequisite. The course supports keyboard-first work with screen readers, braille displays, magnification, and other access technology.

  • Complete lessons
  • Topic index
  • Example validation instructions

GUI, visualization, and workbench accessibility

See the shared GUI, visualization, and workbench accessibility reference for screen-reader support by toolkit, platform-specific activation settings, recommended alternatives, and interfaces that must not be required without an equivalent accessible route.

AI Policy

AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, or generate course code or assessment solutions.

A structured introduction to Swift fundamentals, collections, functions, protocols, error handling, memory management, and application development. Publisher page.

Suggested use: use the Big Nerd Ranch guide for language concepts and Apple’s materials for platform-specific context. The book predates Swift 6 language mode; follow the curriculum’s Swift 6 baseline and current Swift documentation where concurrency or compiler diagnostics differ.

Course Overview

Swift is used for iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, server applications, and systems components. Unit 0: Accessible Environment and Toolchain

Overview

Install and verify the Swift toolchain, create a predictable workspace, configure an accessible editor, and understand Swift Package Manager. On macOS, Xcode provides the integrated toolchain and simulator; supported Linux and Windows distributions can use the Swift toolchain for command-line development. iOS application development requires macOS and Xcode.

Lesson 0.1: Install and Verify Swift

Reading References

  • Swift.org downloads
  • The Swift Programming Language

Learning Objectives

  • Install Swift 6 or Xcode with the Swift 6 toolchain.
  • Verify compiler and interpreter availability.
  • Distinguish the Swift REPL, script execution, and compilation.

Concept Explanation

On macOS, install Xcode or the official Swift toolchain. On supported Linux or Windows systems, follow the official Swift installation instructions for the platform. Open a new terminal and run swift --version and swiftc --version. Run a source file with swift main.swift; compile an executable with swiftc main.swift -o main and run it with ./main. Xcode is required for Apple-platform SDKs and iOS simulators.

Worked Example

print("Swift toolchain is available.")
print("Run swift --version to inspect the installed version.")

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints two lines confirming that the source file executes. The terminal version command reports the installed compiler version.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a terminal session whose PATH has not refreshed after installation.
  • Assuming the Swift REPL, script interpreter, compiler, and Xcode are interchangeable tools.
  • Expecting iOS simulator tooling on a non-macOS host.

Activities

  1. Install Swift or Xcode using the official platform instructions.
  2. Record the output of swift --version and swiftc --version.
  3. Run the worked example as a script and compile it as an executable.
  4. Deliberately use an incorrect filename and read the compiler or runtime diagnostic.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate the installer and terminal by keyboard. Confirm that prompts, compiler messages, punctuation, and build output are announced by the learner’s screen reader or braille display.

Skills Checklist

  • I can install and identify a supported Swift toolchain.
  • I can report the installed Swift version.
  • I can run a Swift script from the terminal.
  • I can compile and execute a standalone Swift program.
  • I can read terminal output and diagnostics using my access technology.

Lesson 0.2: Workspace and First Run

Reading References

  • Swift command-line usage
  • Swift Package Manager

Learning Objectives

  • Create and identify a project root and Swift source file.
  • Distinguish source files from generated build artifacts.
  • Explain how the process working directory affects relative file paths.

Concept Explanation

Create a course directory and save main.swift in its root. Use pwd in the terminal to confirm the current directory. Swift resolves relative file paths from the process working directory, not automatically from the source file’s directory. Keep source, test, data, and generated files in predictable locations. Package builds create a .build directory.

Worked Example

import Foundation
print("Project: Swift course workspace")
print("Working directory: \(FileManager.default.currentDirectoryPath)")

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints a project label and the absolute path of the directory from which it is running.

Common Mistakes

  • Opening a parent directory instead of the intended project root.
  • Assuming relative file paths are based on the source file’s location.
  • Editing or deleting generated files under .build instead of source files.

Activities

  1. Create the project directory and verify it with pwd.
  2. Save and run main.swift from the project root.
  3. Change to a different working directory and observe how a relative path resolves.
  4. Create a Swift package and identify its source and build directories.

Accessibility Practice

Use terminal history and directory commands without drag-and-drop. Verify that editor file navigation, indentation, build output, and diagnostics are exposed in a linear reading order.

Skills Checklist

  • I can identify the project root and current working directory.
  • I can create and run main.swift.
  • I can explain how relative paths are resolved.
  • I can distinguish source files from generated build artifacts.
  • I can navigate the workspace without mouse-only actions.

Lesson 0.3: Editor and Accessibility Workflow

Reading References

  • Swift tools and editors
  • Shared IDE setup lesson

Learning Objectives

  • Configure VS Code, VSCodium, Theia, or Xcode for Swift development.
  • Navigate source, diagnostics, terminal, and project files by keyboard.
  • Verify that editor language tooling uses the intended Swift toolchain.

Concept Explanation

Open the project root in the chosen editor and install compatible Swift language support. On macOS, Xcode provides integrated Swift editing and debugging. In VS Code or VSCodium, configure the Swift extension and sourcekit-lsp using the selected toolchain; extension availability differs across marketplaces. Theia may require a compatible extension distribution. Verify diagnostics and symbol navigation rather than relying on syntax coloring alone.

Worked Example

func greet(_ name: String) -> String {
    return "Hello, \(name)!"
}
print(greet("Avery"))

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints Hello, Avery!. The editor should identify the function and its parameter type.

Common Mistakes

  • Selecting a different Swift toolchain in the editor than in the terminal.
  • Treating syntax coloring as proof that SourceKit-LSP diagnostics work.
  • Depending on mouse-only navigation or inaccessible inline diagnostic panels.

Activities

  1. Open the course project root in the selected editor.
  2. Navigate the worked example by line, word, and character.
  3. Introduce a type error, locate the diagnostic, and correct it.
  4. Run the file from the integrated terminal and system terminal.

Accessibility Practice

Test punctuation verbosity, indentation announcements, completion popups, diagnostic navigation, terminal focus, and editor panels with the learner’s access technology. Keep a terminal-first workflow available.

Skills Checklist

  • I can open the project root and select the intended Swift toolchain.
  • I can navigate and edit Swift source by keyboard.
  • I can locate and correct a compiler or language-server diagnostic.
  • I can run source code without mouse-dependent actions.
  • I can describe editor accessibility limitations and use a workable alternative.

Lesson 0.4: Project Environments, Dependencies, and Terminal Usage

Reading References

  • Swift Package Manager
  • PackageDescription API

Learning Objectives

  • Create and inspect a Swift package.
  • Explain the roles of Package.swift, source targets, and test targets.
  • Add and resolve dependencies with Swift Package Manager.
  • Build, test, and run a package from the terminal.

Concept Explanation

Use Swift Package Manager for multi-file applications and dependencies. Run swift package init --type executable from the project root. The package manifest Package.swift declares products, targets, and dependencies. Run swift package resolve, swift build, swift test, and swift run. Package artifacts are generated under .build; do not edit them directly. For Apple platform applications, Xcode projects and platform SDK configuration may also be required.

Worked Example

let manifestResponsibilities = ["package name", "products", "targets", "dependencies"]
print("Package.swift declares: \(manifestResponsibilities.joined(separator: ", "))")

Expected Behavior or Output

This manifest declares an executable package target named CourseDemo. Swift Package Manager uses it to determine how to build the package.

Common Mistakes

  • Running package commands from a directory that does not contain Package.swift.
  • Editing generated files in .build instead of the package sources or manifest.
  • Adding a dependency without declaring the product in the appropriate target.

Activities

  1. Initialize an executable package and inspect its directory structure.
  2. Run swift build and swift run.
  3. Add a test target and run swift test.
  4. Add a small external dependency in a practice package and inspect the manifest and resolved package graph.

Accessibility Practice

Read Package.swift as source text and inspect build/test output sequentially. Document commands and error messages; do not rely on transient editor notifications or mouse-only build controls.

Skills Checklist

  • I can initialize a Swift package.
  • I can explain the purpose of Package.swift and its targets.
  • I can resolve declared package dependencies.
  • I can build, run, and test from the terminal.
  • I can inspect package output using keyboard-accessible tools.

Unit 1: Foundations of Computing

Overview

Computer science expresses problems as precise inputs, transformations, and outputs. A program executes statements in order unless control flow changes that order. Swift is statically typed with type inference; let creates an immutable binding and var a mutable binding.

Lesson 1.1: Computer science and problem solving

Reading References

  • The Swift Programming Language
  • Swift Standard Library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain computer science and problem solving using Swift terminology.
  • Apply the relevant language and standard-library features correctly.
  • Test normal, boundary, and invalid cases using the shared course data.

Concept Explanation

Computer science expresses problems as precise inputs, transformations, and outputs. A program executes statements in order unless control flow changes that order. Swift is statically typed with type inference; let creates an immutable binding and var a mutable binding.

Lesson focus: Computer science and problem solving. The example uses Swift-native semantics and a canonical course context rather than mechanically translating Python.

Worked Example

let problem = "Calculate a class average"
let inputs = ["82", "91", "76", "88"]
let steps = ["collect scores", "validate each score", "calculate the mean", "report the result"]
for (index, step) in steps.enumerated() {
    print("\(index + 1). \(step)")
}
print("Problem: \(problem); inputs: \(inputs.count)\n")

Expected Behavior or Output

The example is a self-contained Swift program. Predict the output from the stated values before running it, then compare the actual result. Examples that read input accept a line from standard input; file examples use temporary paths.

Common Mistakes

  • Prefer let for bindings that never change; use var only when mutation is required.
  • Swift uses static typing with inference; a binding’s type is fixed after initialization.
  • Do not assume Python indexing, collection, or string semantics carry over.

Activities

  1. Trace the algorithm and state the input, process, and output.
  2. Change the canonical learner data and predict the printed result.
  3. Write a short sequence of steps for calculating a class average.
  4. Run the example and explain its output without syntax highlighting.

Accessibility Practice

Navigate source by line, word, and character. Inspect punctuation, braces, optionals, argument labels, and compiler diagnostics. Run from the terminal and read prompts and output sequentially. Do not rely on syntax coloring, color-only status, or mouse-only actions.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain computer science and problem solving in Swift terminology.
  • I can trace the example and predict its behavior.
  • I can adapt the example to the shared canonical data.
  • I can identify and correct a Swift-specific error or edge case.
  • I can run and inspect the program using keyboard-accessible tools.

Unit 3: Control Flow

Overview

Swift uses Bool conditions, if/else if/else, switch, zero-based arrays, and for-in loops. Array subscripting requires a valid index. Strings are collections of extended grapheme clusters; use String APIs rather than assuming integer offsets are byte offsets.

Lesson 3.1: Boolean expressions and if statements

Reading References

  • The Swift Programming Language
  • Swift Standard Library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain boolean expressions and if statements using Swift terminology.
  • Apply the relevant language and standard-library features correctly.
  • Test normal, boundary, and invalid cases using the shared course data.

Concept Explanation

Swift uses Bool conditions, if/else if/else, switch, zero-based arrays, and for-in loops. Array subscripting requires a valid index. Strings are collections of extended grapheme clusters; use String APIs rather than assuming integer offsets are byte offsets.

Lesson focus: Boolean expressions and if statements. The example uses Swift-native semantics and a canonical course context rather than mechanically translating Python.

Worked Example

let score = 82
let isPassing = score >= 60 && score <= 100
let hasPerfectScore = score == 100
if isPassing {
    print("Passing: \(score)")
} else {
    print("Needs review")
}
print("Perfect: \(hasPerfectScore)")

Expected Behavior or Output

The example is a self-contained Swift program. Predict the output from the stated values before running it, then compare the actual result. Examples that read input accept a line from standard input; file examples use temporary paths.

Common Mistakes

  • Swift Boolean conditions must be Bool; integers are not truthy or falsy.
  • Array indices are zero-based and valid indices stop before count.
  • Handle optional lookups and user input instead of force-unwrapping.

Unit 4: Data Structures

Overview

Swift’s Array, Dictionary, and Set are value types. Tuples group fixed related values; dictionaries map unique keys to values and return optionals on lookup. Collection methods such as map, filter, sorted, and reduce express transformations.

Lesson 4.4: Dictionaries and key-value data

Reading References

  • The Swift Programming Language
  • Swift Standard Library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain dictionaries and key-value data using Swift terminology.
  • Apply the relevant language and standard-library features correctly.
  • Test normal, boundary, and invalid cases using the shared course data.

Concept Explanation

Swift’s Array, Dictionary, and Set are value types. Tuples group fixed related values; dictionaries map unique keys to values and return optionals on lookup. Collection methods such as map, filter, sorted, and reduce express transformations.

Lesson focus: Dictionaries and key-value data. The example uses Swift-native semantics and a canonical course context rather than mechanically translating Python.

Worked Example

var inventory: [String: Int] = ["Notebook": 3, "Pencil": 10]
inventory["Folder"] = 4
inventory["Pencil"] = nil
print("notebooks=\(inventory["Notebook"] ?? 0)")
print("keys=\(inventory.keys.sorted())")

Expected Behavior or Output

The example is a self-contained Swift program. Predict the output from the stated values before running it, then compare the actual result. Examples that read input accept a line from standard input; file examples use temporary paths.

Common Mistakes

  • Arrays and dictionaries are value types with copy-on-write behavior.
  • Dictionary iteration order is not a stable presentation order; sort keys for deterministic output.
  • A dictionary subscript returns an optional because the key may be absent.

Activities

  2. Sort inventory keys and explain why output order matters.
  3. Represent a coordinate and learner record with tuples.

Lesson 10.2: Text adventure: five rooms and movement

Reading References

  • The Swift Programming Language
  • Swift Dictionary
  • Canonical shared project specification: Python Unit 10, Lesson 10.3.

Learning Objectives

  • Represent all five canonical rooms and exits with Swift dictionaries and structs.
  • Validate movement before changing the current room.
  • Explain why treasure_room is not reachable until the key puzzle is implemented.

Concept Explanation

The shared graph has five rooms: start_room, tunnel, clearing, locked_door_room, and treasure_room. A Room value stores a description and its exits. The player begins in start_room. Part 1 leaves the north exit from locked_door_room unavailable. Optional dictionary lookup makes a missing direction explicit, so invalid movement cannot change state.

Worked Example

import Foundation

struct Room {
    let description: String
    let exits: [String: String]
}

let rooms: [String: Room] = [
    "start_room": Room(description: "A dimly lit cave. A narrow passage leads north.", exits: ["north": "tunnel"]),
    "tunnel": Room(description: "A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.", exits: ["south": "start_room", "east": "clearing"]),
    "clearing": Room(description: "A quiet clearing. An antechamber lies to the north.", exits: ["west": "tunnel", "north": "locked_door_room"]),
    "locked_door_room": Room(description: "A chamber with a heavy door to the north.", exits: ["south": "clearing"]),
    "treasure_room": Room(description: "You found the treasure. You win!", exits: [:])
]

var currentRoom = "start_room"
while true {
    let room = rooms[currentRoom]!
    print("---")
    print(room.description)
    print("What do you want to do?")
    let command = readLine()?.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines).lowercased() ?? "quit"
    if command == "quit" {
        print("Exiting game. Goodbye!")
        break
    }
    if let destination = room.exits[command] {
        currentRoom = destination
    } else {
        print("You cannot go that way. Enter a listed direction or quit.")
    }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Enter north, east, north, north, quit. The player reaches tunnel, clearing, and locked_door_room. The second north is rejected and the current room does not change. The treasure room exists but has no incoming exit in Part 1.

Common Mistakes

  • Force-unwrapping a direction lookup that may be nil.
  • Updating currentRoom before validating the exit.
  • Defining a destination that is not one of the five room identifiers.
  • Adding the treasure exit before implementing the key puzzle.

Activities

  1. Trace north, east, north, north and record the current room.
  2. Try west from start_room and verify that the room does not change.
  3. Check every exit destination against the room dictionary.
  4. Explain why treasure_room cannot yet be reached.

Accessibility Practice

Announce the room description and prompt in a consistent order. The invalid-movement response explains what happened and how to continue. Run from the terminal and inspect output sequentially with the learner’s access technology.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model all five canonical rooms.
  • I can represent exits with dictionaries.
  • I can reject invalid movement without changing state.
  • I can explain why the treasure room is not yet reachable.

Lesson 10.3: Text adventure: shiny key and locked door

Reading References

  • The Swift Programming Language: Collections
  • Swift Array
  • Canonical shared project specification: Python Unit 10, Lesson 10.3.

Learning Objectives

  • Place the shiny key in start_room and transfer it to inventory exactly once.
  • Require key use in locked_door_room.
  • Unlock the north exit only after the puzzle succeeds.
  • End the game when the player reaches treasure_room.

Concept Explanation

Keep the same five-room graph. Each Room reference stores a mutable item array and exit dictionary. Picking up the shiny key removes it from start_room and adds it to inventory. Using the key succeeds only in locked_door_room when inventory contains it. The north exit remains blocked until the key is used.

Worked Example

import Foundation

final class Room {
    let description: String
    var exits: [String: String]
    var items: [String]

    init(_ description: String, exits: [String: String], items: [String] = []) {
        self.description = description
        self.exits = exits
        self.items = items
    }
}

let rooms: [String: Room] = [
    "start_room": Room("A dimly lit cave.", exits: ["north": "tunnel"], items: ["shiny key"]),
    "tunnel": Room("A damp tunnel. Passages lead south and east.", exits: ["south": "start_room", "east": "clearing"]),
    "clearing": Room("A quiet clearing. An antechamber lies to the north.", exits: ["west": "tunnel", "north": "locked_door_room"]),
    "locked_door_room": Room("A chamber with a heavy door to the north.", exits: ["south": "clearing", "north": "treasure_room"]),
    "treasure_room": Room("You found the treasure. You win!", exits: [:])
]

var currentRoom = "start_room"
var inventory: [String] = []
var doorLocked = true

while true {
    let room = rooms[currentRoom]!
    print()
    print(room.description)
    if currentRoom == "treasure_room" { break }
    if !room.items.isEmpty { print("You see: " + room.items.joined(separator: ", ")) }
    print("Your inventory: " + (inventory.isEmpty ? "empty" : inventory.joined(separator: ", ")))
    print("What do you want to do?")
    let command = readLine()?.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines).lowercased() ?? "quit"

    if command == "quit" {
        print("You quit the adventure.")
        break
    } else if command == "take shiny key" {
        if let index = room.items.firstIndex(of: "shiny key") {
            room.items.remove(at: index)
            inventory.append("shiny key")
            print("You picked up the shiny key.")
        } else {
            print("There is no shiny key here to take.")
        }
    } else if command == "use shiny key" {
        if currentRoom != "locked_door_room" {
            print("You must be at the locked door to use the key.")
        } else if !inventory.contains("shiny key") {
            print("You do not have the shiny key.")
        } else {
            doorLocked = false
            print("You unlocked the door!")
        }
    } else if currentRoom == "locked_door_room" && command == "north" && doorLocked {
        print("The door is locked! You need to use the shiny key here.")
    } else if let destination = room.exits[command] {
        currentRoom = destination
    } else {
        print("Invalid command. Enter north, south, east, west, take shiny key, use shiny key, or quit.")
    }
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Enter north, east, north, north, south, west, south, take shiny key, north, east, north, use shiny key, north. The first north from locked_door_room is rejected. Taking the key removes it from the room and adds it to inventory. Using it outside locked_door_room is rejected. Using it there unlocks the door; the final north reaches treasure_room and prints the win description.

Common Mistakes

  • Removing the key from the room without adding it to inventory.
  • Unlocking the door outside locked_door_room.
  • Unlocking the door without checking inventory.
  • Allowing north movement before doorLocked becomes false.
  • Treating an invalid optional lookup as a destination.

Activities

  1. Run the complete puzzle sequence and record room, items, inventory, and door state.
  2. Attempt to take the key twice; the second attempt must be rejected.
  3. Try to use the key outside locked_door_room.
  4. Try north before and after unlocking.
  5. Add a help command listing every supported command.

Accessibility Practice

Announce the room, visible items, inventory, and prompt as separate text lines. Error messages explain the failed action. Test the complete interaction with keyboard-only input and sequential screen-reader output.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model the five canonical rooms.
  • I can transfer the key from a room to inventory.
  • I can prevent duplicate pickup.
  • I can require key use in locked_door_room.
  • I can block and unlock the north exit.
  • I can end the game in treasure_room.

enum TitleError: Error { case blank }
import Foundation
func cleanTitle(_ raw: String) -> Result<String, TitleError> {

}
for raw in ["  Study Swift  ", "   "] {

    case .success(let title): print("Accepted: \(title)")
    case .failure: print("Error: title cannot be blank")
    }
}

Lesson 11.2: Data model and storage

Reading References

  • The Swift Programming Language
  • Swift Standard Library
  • Matching Python curriculum lesson for the shared problem context.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain data model and storage using Swift terminology.
  • Apply the relevant language and standard-library features correctly.

Concept Explanation

The capstone is a personal-record manager with stable identifiers, validated create/read/update/delete operations, and Codable persistence. Separate the data model, validation, storage, and command-line interface; verify save/reload and document limitations.

Lesson focus: Data model and storage. The example uses Swift-native semantics and a canonical course context rather than mechanically translating Python.

Worked Example

import Foundation
struct PersonalRecord: Codable, Identifiable {
    let id: Int
    var title: String
    var description: String
    var category: String
    let createdAt: String
    var updatedAt: String
}
let record = PersonalRecord(id: 1, title: "Study Swift", description: "Review Codable",
                            category: "learning", createdAt: "2026-11-01", updatedAt: "2026-11-01")
do {
    let encoder = JSONEncoder()
    encoder.keyEncodingStrategy = .convertToSnakeCase
    encoder.outputFormatting = [.sortedKeys]
    let json = try encoder.encode(record)
    print(String(decoding: json, as: UTF8.self))
    let decoder = JSONDecoder()
    decoder.keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase
    let restored = try decoder.decode(PersonalRecord.self, from: json)
    print("Decoded record: \(restored.id), \(restored.title), \(restored.category)")
} catch {
    print("JSON round trip failed: \(error)")
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The example is a self-contained Swift program. Predict the output from the stated values before running it, then compare the actual result. Examples that read input accept a line from standard input; file examples use temporary paths.

  • Foundation provides file handling, JSONEncoder/JSONDecoder, date and URL facilities, and string formatting.
  • Use XCTest in a Swift package for a full test suite; the standalone examples use precondition for dependency-free smoke checks.
  • The introductory CSV example handles simple unquoted rows only. Use a maintained CSV library for quoted commas, escaped quotes, and embedded newlines.
  • Swift concurrency uses structured tasks and actors; add concurrency only when the problem requires it and test isolation and cancellation explicitly.

AI Policy

AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, or generate course code or assessment solutions.

Introduction to Computer Science with TypeScript

Before you start: complete Unit P: Computing Foundations Primer. It explains the language-neutral vocabulary and concepts used in every language track, using non-visual examples.

Accessible beginner curriculum using Node.js

This curriculum teaches introductory programming and computer science through TypeScript, using Node.js for program execution and text-based input/output. It is designed for blind and visually impaired learners who use screen readers, braille displays, magnification, keyboard navigation, or combinations of access technologies. It is also suitable for sighted beginners and mixed-vision classrooms.

TypeScript is widely used in browser applications, server-side systems, and developer tools. This course deliberately starts with Node.js and terminal programs so learners can master programming concepts without needing to interpret a visual web page or graphical interface. Browser-based development can be a later extension.

Course outcomes

By the end of this curriculum, learners should be able to:

  • Explain introductory computer science concepts and the software-development cycle.
  • Install and verify Node.js and use an editor, terminal, and Node.js REPL.
  • Write TypeScript programs using variables, primitive values, expressions, and output.
  • Explain TypeScript’s compile-time type checking and JavaScript’s runtime coercion, truthy/falsy values, undefined, null, and NaN.
  • Accept and validate terminal input using Node.js input mechanisms.
  • Use decisions, loops, arrays, readonly tuples, typed objects, interfaces, Maps, and common collection operations.
  • Use union types, generic types, discriminated unions, and type guards to model and validate data.
  • Design functions and use parameters, return values, scope, and closures.
  • Explain classes and object-oriented programming at an introductory level.
  • Work with files, modules, errors, and asynchronous operations introduced by the curriculum.
  • Use Maps, Sets, data processing, and automated tests.
  • Design, implement, test, and explain text-based projects and a capstone.
  • Evaluate prompts, output order, error messages, and interaction for screen-reader usability.

The goal is a strong introductory foundation, not mastery of the entire TypeScript language or ecosystem.

Prerequisites and intended learners

No previous programming experience is required. Learners need a computer on which a supported Node.js release can be installed, a keyboard-accessible editor, and a terminal. Basic keyboard and file-management skills are useful. Screen-reader proficiency can develop alongside programming.

The course is intended primarily for beginning learners, including students using NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, Narrator, braille displays, or magnification. The TypeScript teacher’s guide includes strategies for pacing, asynchronous concepts, accessible debugging, and differentiated instruction.

Why TypeScript and Node.js?

TypeScript connects foundational programming concepts to a large software ecosystem. The compiler checks TypeScript and emits JavaScript; Node.js executes that output, supporting a text-first course.

  • Programs can run in a terminal and provide text output.
  • The Node.js REPL supports short JavaScript runtime experiments; use the TypeScript compiler, editor, or playground to check TypeScript annotations.
  • The same language can later be used for accessible web applications and server-side programs.
  • Learners can encounter real-world concepts such as asynchronous operations and modules in a controlled sequence.

TypeScript adds static checking, but its emitted JavaScript still has JavaScript’s runtime behavior. Coercion can produce surprising results when values enter through untrusted boundaries or types are bypassed; undefined, null, and NaN are distinct; arrays and objects have different semantics; and asynchronous code introduces ordering and error-handling questions.

Learning sequence

UnitMain topicsEvidence of progress
0. Environment setupNode.js, editor setup, terminal, first file, REPLVerify Node.js and run a script
1. FoundationsComputer science, TypeScript role, variables, output, values and typesExplain a simple script and its values
2. Numbers and inputMath operations, Node.js input, conversion, and validationBuild an interactive terminal calculation
3. Control flowBoolean logic, grade classification, arrays, iteration, and string operationsPredict and control program paths
4. Arrays and objectsCollections, indexed data, properties, and iterationOrganize and process related data
5. User input and loopsTyped terminal input, validation, while loops, flags, break, and continueBuild a robust interactive loop
6. FunctionsFunction forms, parameters, return values, scope, and closuresDecompose a problem into reusable functions
7. Classes and OOPClasses, instances, fields, methods, and object-oriented designModel a simple problem domain
8. Files and errorsFile operations, modules where introduced, and error handlingPersist data and handle expected failures
9. Testing and data analysisnode:test, class tests, random values, text frequency, and CSV parsingVerify behavior and summarize structured data
10. Project-based learningText-based applications and incremental designImplement a multi-feature project
