The course contains 57 mapped lesson sections across Units 0–11. Each substantive lesson includes references, objectives, a concept explanation, a TypeScript worked example, expected behavior, common mistakes, activities, accessibility practice, and a skills checklist.

Materials and navigation

  • Units 0–1: Setup and Foundations
  • Units 2–4: Numbers, Input, Control Flow, and Data
  • Units 5–8: Strings, Functions, OOP, and Files
  • Units 9–11: Modules, Collections, Testing, and Projects
  • Teacher’s guide: instructor planning, accessible instruction, assessment, and AI guidance
  • Topic index
  • Standardization audit and validation status

Return to the curriculum overview to compare Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, and Java.

Runtime version and modern TypeScript conventions

Use Node.js 26.13.0 LTS (the current LTS release as of October 30, 2026) for the course. Node.js 24 is also in LTS maintenance, but new installations should use the current 26.x LTS line. Keep examples compatible with the Node.js 26 LTS runtime and use the latest security/maintenance patch in that line. Check the official Node.js release schedule before installing or upgrading.

The course follows modern TypeScript practices:

  • Use const by default and let only when reassignment is required; avoid var in new code.
  • Use === and !== for comparisons; convert user input explicitly with Number, String, or other deliberate parsing.
  • Prefer descriptive names, small functions, template literals, array methods where they improve clarity, and async/await for asynchronous work.
  • Use node: specifiers for built-in modules (for example, node:fs and node:readline/promises).
  • Declare module format explicitly in package.json. Use type: commonjs for CommonJS examples and type: module for ES module examples; do not mix require/module.exports with import/export in the same module.
  • Handle rejected promises and file-system errors explicitly. Do not assume parsed JSON or external input has the expected shape.
  • Use the built-in node:test and node:assert/strict modules for dependency-free introductory tests; Jest is an optional extension, not a course prerequisite.
  • Keep dependencies local to a project, review package provenance, and commit a lockfile for reproducible installations.

Why TypeScript is emerging

TypeScript is an increasingly common choice for application-scale JavaScript projects. It keeps JavaScript’s ecosystem and runtime model while adding a static type system, so many mistakes can be found by the editor or compiler before a program runs. This is particularly useful as projects grow: function contracts, object shapes, nullability, and module boundaries become more explicit, and refactoring tools can reason about those declarations.

TypeScript is safer in important ways, but it is not a proof of correctness. Types are erased when TypeScript is compiled to JavaScript; they do not validate JSON, user input, network responses, database records, or other runtime data. A type assertion can also silence the checker without making a value safe. Teach strict checking, runtime validation at trust boundaries, and tests together.

Recommended environment

Use Node.js 26.13.0 LTS (current LTS as of October 30, 2026) and the current stable TypeScript compiler, 7.0.2. TypeScript is a compile-time language layer: Node.js runs the JavaScript output, not TypeScript source in the ordinary compiled workflow.

Follow Unit 0 for detailed installation and verification. Use the latest security/maintenance patch in the Node.js 26 LTS line. Check the official Node.js download page before installing or upgrading.

Recommended tools include Node.js and npm, Visual Studio Code or Theia IDE, a terminal, and the learner’s preferred access technology. Theia is an alternative with similar keyboard- and screen-reader-oriented workflows; verify language extensions through Open VSX and test the learner’s screen reader. Use project-local npm dependencies and npx/npm scripts; avoid global installs. Explain each third-party dependency and review its provenance and maintenance before adding it.

Typical verification commands:

node --version
npx tsc --version
npm --version
node

Windows Powershell

node --version
npx tsc --version
npm --version
node

At the Node.js prompt, enter a short JavaScript expression and read the returned value. This does not type-check TypeScript annotations. Use a TypeScript-aware editor, the TypeScript playground, or npx tsc to check TypeScript code. Use .exit or the documented keyboard command to leave the REPL.

TypeScript conventions

  • Enable strict type checking in tsconfig.json; do not use any as a routine escape hatch.
  • Prefer inference for obvious local values and explicit annotations for function parameters, public APIs, object shapes, and values whose intent is not obvious.
  • Use interfaces or type aliases to describe object contracts, discriminated unions for state variants, and unknown rather than any for untrusted values.
  • Keep strictNullChecks enabled. Check nullable values explicitly and narrow union types before using them.
  • Treat type assertions as a last resort; they do not perform runtime conversion or validation.
  • Compile with tsc before running the emitted JavaScript. Keep Node.js module mode explicit and use matching TypeScript module settings.

Accessibility and instructional design

TypeScript uses braces to delimit blocks and semicolons may be optional in many contexts. Teach one consistent style and explain punctuation explicitly. Screen-reader users benefit from short functions, descriptive identifiers, predictable formatting, and output that is meaningful when read linearly.

The curriculum emphasizes keyboard-first editor, terminal, and REPL workflows; explicit reading of braces, parentheses, brackets, commas, operators, and template literals; terminal-based core activities; clear prompts and errors; and step-by-step debugging of coercion and asynchronous behavior.

Accessibility is not guaranteed merely because an application prints text. Consider output order, repeated announcements, asynchronous messages, and whether a learner can review the result after it appears. Adapt to the student’s actual technology and preferences.

How to study each lesson

  1. Read the lesson overview and identify the new language features.
  2. Read each example structurally. Identify blocks, expressions, function calls, and data values.
  3. Predict output and note assumptions about types or coercion.
  4. Run the example in Node.js and compare actual and expected results.
  5. Change one variable or expression and observe behavior.
  6. Complete the exercises and record questions.
  7. When a result is unexpected, inspect the value and its type, then trace the relevant control flow.
  8. For asynchronous examples, identify when an operation begins, what is awaited, and when its result becomes available.
  9. Explain the program in your own words and save the work in a portfolio.

Use the REPL for short experiments and files for complete programs. Keep experiments small enough that output can be reviewed without losing context.

Assessment and projects

Assessment can include predicting output, explaining type behavior, tracing a loop, writing a function, refactoring a program, identifying a bug, creating tests, and building a text-based application. Evaluate reasoning, correctness, testing, clarity, and the learner’s ability to explain and change their code.

The capstone should include a written problem statement, requirements, input/output design, data representation, implementation milestones, test cases, and a short demonstration or explanation. The learner should be able to discuss known limitations and how to improve the program.

Teaching with AI

Teaching with AI

For student coursework and assessments, AI may be used only to support personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It may explain a language concept, clarify terminology, or help a learner understand a compiler diagnostic at a conceptual level. It must not write, autocomplete, repair, complete, refactor, or generate course code, project code, test solutions, or assessment answers. It must not provide a ready-to-submit algorithm or implementation.

The learner must write and debug all course code independently. Accessibility tools that provide keyboard navigation, screen-reader output, braille access, magnification, or speech input are not prohibited answer-generation tools. Instructors remain responsible for following institutional policy and protecting student information. See the teacher’s guide for implementation guidance.

Repeatable curriculum validation

The repository includes a strict TypeScript checker and GitHub Actions workflow. From the repository root, install the documented checker dependencies and run:

node scripts/check_typescript_curriculum.mjs

The checker verifies all 57 lesson structures and type-checks isolated TypeScript examples in strict mode. It does not execute examples or assert their expected output; runtime and end-to-end testing remain separate verification tasks.

Recommended introductory books

  • Goldberg, Josh. Learning TypeScript. O’Reilly Media, 2022. A practical guide to TypeScript’s type system, inference, unions, narrowing, generics, and integration with JavaScript. Publisher page.

Prerequisite note: this book is most useful after learners understand basic JavaScript syntax, values, functions, arrays, objects, and modules. Complete the JavaScript foundations first or use the JavaScript curriculum as a companion. TypeScript’s types are primarily checked at compile time; pair the book with this curriculum’s explanations of runtime validation and JavaScript execution.

Further learning

Use MDN’s TypeScript Guide for language concepts and the Node.js documentation for runtime APIs. Eloquent TypeScript is a further introductory text. Check version-specific documentation when examples depend on newer features.

The course uses TypeScript to teach transferable problem-solving skills. Learners who can reason about values, control flow, data, functions, errors, and tests are prepared to explore browser programming and other parts of the ecosystem.

GUI, visualization, and workbench accessibility

See the shared GUI, visualization, and workbench accessibility reference for screen-reader support by toolkit, platform-specific activation settings, recommended alternatives, and interfaces that must not be required without an equivalent accessible route.

Unit 0: Accessible Development Environment

Before you start: complete Unit P: Computing Foundations Primer. It explains the language-neutral vocabulary and concepts used in every language track, using non-visual examples.

Overview

Set up Node.js, TypeScript, an editor, workspace, and terminal workflow. The TypeScript adaptation preserves the shared Python curriculum’s learning objectives, datasets, expected results, and assessment criteria while teaching TypeScript’s compile-time type system and JavaScript runtime behavior.

Lesson 0.1: Installing Node.js, npm, and TypeScript

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 0 lesson 0.1 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Install and verify the Node.js runtime, npm, and a project-local TypeScript compiler.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

Node.js executes JavaScript. TypeScript is checked and compiled before execution in this course. npm installs project-local tools so learners use a reproducible compiler version.

Worked Example

const runtime = "Node.js 26 LTS";
const compiler = "TypeScript 7.x";
console.log(`Runtime: ${runtime}`);
console.log(`Compiler: ${compiler}`);

Expected Behavior or Output

The two lines identify the runtime and compiler separately. node --version, npm --version, and npx tsc --version verify the actual installations.

Common Mistakes

  • Confusing the TypeScript compiler with the Node.js runtime.
  • Installing tools globally and losing project reproducibility.
  • Assuming a Node.js REPL type-checks TypeScript annotations.

Activities

  1. Verify Node.js and npm versions in a terminal.
  2. Create a project folder and initialize npm.
  3. Install TypeScript as a development dependency and verify it with npx.

Accessibility Practice

Read each command and its purpose before running it. Keep terminal output in a sequential log. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can distinguish Node.js from TypeScript.
  • I can verify the runtime, npm, and compiler.
  • I can install a project-local compiler.

Lesson 0.2: Configuring VS Code or Theia for accessible TypeScript work

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 0 lesson 0.2 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Configure an editor, TypeScript language service, terminal, and keyboard-first navigation.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

The editor provides navigation, diagnostics, and refactoring support; the compiler remains the authoritative type checker. VS Code and Theia may differ in shortcuts and extension availability.

Worked Example

const editor = "VS Code or Theia";
const languageService = "TypeScript";
console.log(`${editor}: ${languageService} support enabled`);

Expected Behavior or Output

The message confirms the intended editor and language support; verify actual navigation and diagnostic announcements with the learner’s access technology.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming the editor’s visual layout is required for completing tasks.
  • Using mouse-only instructions or undocumented shortcuts.
  • Treating a language-service suggestion as proof that a program is correct.

Activities

  1. Open a workspace using the keyboard.
  2. Navigate to a diagnostic by keyboard and read its full message.
  3. Run a TypeScript build from the integrated terminal.

Accessibility Practice

Test line, word, character, symbol, and diagnostic navigation with the learner’s screen reader or braille display. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can navigate the editor by keyboard.
  • I can locate and understand a TypeScript diagnostic.
  • I can run a build without relying on mouse-only controls.

Lesson 0.3: Creating the course workspace and editor extensions

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 0 lesson 0.3 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Create a consistent workspace and configure TypeScript formatting and project navigation.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A workspace groups source files and configuration. TypeScript projects use package.json for scripts and dependencies and tsconfig.json for compiler behavior.

Worked Example

const project = { name: "typescript-course", source: "src", output: "dist" };
console.log(`${project.name}: ${project.source} -> ${project.output}`);

Expected Behavior or Output

The project name and source/output folders are announced as text. A standard project keeps editable TypeScript in src and emitted JavaScript in dist.

Common Mistakes

  • Editing generated JavaScript instead of TypeScript source.
  • Placing course files in an unknown working directory.
  • Installing editor extensions without checking publisher and availability.

Activities

  1. Create src and dist folders.
  2. Open the project folder rather than an individual file.
  3. Enable TypeScript language support and verify its version.

Accessibility Practice

Use descriptive folder and file names. Announce the current working directory before running project commands. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create and open a project workspace.
  • I can identify source and generated-output folders.
  • I can verify TypeScript editor support.

Project configuration and module mode

Use a project-local TypeScript compiler and strict checking. A representative tsconfig.json is:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmitOnError": true,
    "outDir": "dist",
    "rootDir": "src"
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"]
}

For the compiled Node.js workflow, set "type": "module" in package.json and use ES module imports consistently. If a project uses CommonJS instead, set "type": "commonjs" and use matching compiler settings. Do not mix require() and import in one module.

A typical script is "build": "tsc" and "start": "node dist/hello.js". Run npm run build before npm start.

Lesson 0.4: Your first TypeScript file and terminal workflow

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 0 lesson 0.4 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Write, compile, and execute a small TypeScript program from the terminal.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

The compiler checks .ts source and emits .js. Node.js runs the emitted JavaScript. A package script makes the workflow repeatable.

Worked Example

const greeting: string = "Hello, World!";
console.log(greeting);
console.log("Welcome to TypeScript.");

Expected Behavior or Output

Compilation succeeds and Node.js prints Hello, World! and Welcome to TypeScript. on separate lines.

Common Mistakes

  • Trying to run a TypeScript file as though it were ordinary JavaScript.
  • Running Node.js from the wrong working directory.
  • Ignoring compiler errors and executing stale output.

Activities

  1. Save the example as src/hello.ts.
  2. Compile with the project tsconfig.
  3. Run the emitted JavaScript with Node.js.

Accessibility Practice

Read compiler diagnostics before running the program. Keep source and output paths explicit. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write a .ts file.
  • I can compile it with tsc.
  • I can run emitted JavaScript with Node.js.

Unit 1: Foundations of Computing

Overview

Introduce computer science, first programs, variables, and primitive types. The TypeScript adaptation preserves the shared Python curriculum’s learning objectives, datasets, expected results, and assessment criteria while teaching TypeScript’s compile-time type system and JavaScript runtime behavior.

Lesson 1.1: Welcome to computer science

Concept Explanation

Computer science studies computation and information. An algorithm is a finite, ordered set of steps for solving a problem; TypeScript is one language used to express algorithms.

Worked Example

const steps = ["understand the problem", "design steps", "implement", "test"];
for (const [index, step] of steps.entries()) {
  console.log(`${index + 1}. ${step}`);
}

Expected Behavior or Output

Four ordered steps are printed, from understanding the problem through testing.

Common Mistakes

  • Equating computer science with learning syntax only.
  • Beginning implementation before defining the problem.
  • Treating one programming language as the only way to express an algorithm.

Activities

  1. Describe an everyday algorithm in plain language.
  2. Identify input, processing, and output for a tip calculator.
  3. Explain how testing provides evidence about a solution.

Accessibility Practice

Present algorithms as numbered text steps. Do not rely on flowchart colors or spatial layout alone. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define computer science and an algorithm.
  • I can identify input, processing, and output.
  • I can describe a testable solution plan.

Lesson 1.2: Your first TypeScript program: Hello World

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 1 lesson 1.2 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Create a source file, compile it, and explain sequential execution and output.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

Statements execute in sequence unless control flow changes that order. console.log writes a line of text to standard output.

Worked Example

console.log("Hello, World!");
console.log("Welcome to TypeScript.");

Expected Behavior or Output

The terminal prints the two messages in source order, one per line.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting to save the source file before compiling.
  • Expecting TypeScript annotations to appear in runtime output.
  • Changing capitalization or punctuation in an exact-output exercise.

Activities

  1. Change the second message and compile again.
  2. Add a third line and predict its position.
  3. Explain the difference between source code and terminal output.

Accessibility Practice

Read one statement at a time and compare source order with output order. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can create and run a first program.
  • I can predict sequential output.
  • I can distinguish source text from program output.

Lesson 1.3: Variables and simple data types

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 1 lesson 1.3 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Declare typed variables and represent the canonical student profile.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

TypeScript can infer many local types, but annotations make contracts explicit. const prevents reassignment of a binding; it does not deeply freeze an object.

Worked Example

const student: { name: string; age: number; heightM: number; favoriteSubject: string } = {
  name: "Avery", age: 16, heightM: 1.72, favoriteSubject: "Computer Science"
};
console.log(`${student.name}, age ${student.age}`);
console.log(`Height: ${student.heightM} m`);
console.log(student.favoriteSubject);

Expected Behavior or Output

The output identifies Avery, age 16, height 1.72 m, and Computer Science.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a string where a number is required.
  • Assuming const makes object properties immutable.
  • Using any to bypass a type error rather than correcting the type.

Activities

  1. Declare string, number, and boolean values.
  2. Add a field to the student profile and update its type.
  3. Explain type inference versus an explicit annotation.

Accessibility Practice

Read property names and types aloud. Use one property per line for structured output. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can declare typed variables.
  • I can explain const and type inference.
  • I can model the canonical student profile.

Unit 2: Numeric Computations

Overview

Translate requirements into programs, expressions, input, conversions, and mathematical calculations. The TypeScript adaptation preserves the shared Python curriculum’s learning objectives, datasets, expected results, and assessment criteria while teaching TypeScript’s compile-time type system and JavaScript runtime behavior.

Overview

Translate requirements into programs, expressions, input, conversions, and mathematical calculations. The TypeScript adaptation preserves the shared Python curriculum’s learning objectives, datasets, expected results, and assessment criteria while teaching TypeScript’s compile-time type system and JavaScript runtime behavior.

Lesson 2.1: The software development process

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 2 lesson 2.1 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Apply the design, implementation, and testing cycle to the canonical tip calculator.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A problem statement becomes requirements, an algorithm, an implementation, and tests. The shared calculator uses a $24.50 bill and a 15% tip rate.

Worked Example

const bill = 24.50;
const tipRate = 0.15;
const tip = bill * tipRate;
const total = bill + tip;
console.log(`Tip: $${tip.toFixed(2)}`);
console.log(`Total: $${total.toFixed(2)}`);

Expected Behavior or Output

The tip is $3.67 and the total is $28.18 when rounded with toFixed(2). The exact product 3.675 is stored as 3.67499999999999982, so toFixed(2) rounds the tip down.

Common Mistakes

  • Coding before identifying inputs and expected results.
  • Confusing the tip amount with the final total.
  • Assuming binary floating-point represents every decimal exactly.

Activities

  1. Write requirements for the tip calculator.
  2. Predict the result before running the example.
  3. Test a zero tip rate and a different bill amount.

Accessibility Practice

State the input values and output labels explicitly. Explain rounding rather than relying on visual currency formatting. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can describe the development cycle.
  • I can translate requirements into an algorithm.
  • I can compare expected and actual results.

Lesson 2.2: Expressions and assignment

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 2 lesson 2.2 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Evaluate arithmetic expressions and update a score using typed variables.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

An expression produces a value. Assignment stores a value in a variable. Parentheses make grouping explicit and TypeScript checks the declared value types.

Worked Example

let score: number = 10;
score = score + 5;
const subtotal = 2 + 3 * 4;
const grouped = (2 + 3) * 4;
console.log(score, subtotal, grouped);

Expected Behavior or Output

The output values are 15, 14, and 20.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming multiplication and addition have equal precedence.
  • Using const for a variable that must be reassigned.
  • Confusing equality comparison with assignment.

Activities

  1. Predict the value of expressions with and without parentheses.
  2. Update a score by adding 5.

Lesson 2.3: Input and output in Node.js

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 2 lesson 2.3 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Prompt for a name and two numbers using asynchronous terminal input.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

Node.js readline/promises returns Promises. await pauses the async function until the user responds. Input arrives as text and must be converted and validated.

Worked Example

import { createInterface } from "node:readline/promises";
import { stdin, stdout } from "node:process";

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const rl = createInterface({ input: stdin, output: stdout });
  try {
    const name = await rl.question("Enter your name: ");
    const first = Number(await rl.question("First number: "));
    const second = Number(await rl.question("Second number: "));
    if (!Number.isFinite(first) || !Number.isFinite(second)) {
      console.log("Enter valid numbers.");
      return;
    }
    console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);
    console.log(`Sum: ${first + second}`);
  } finally {
    rl.close();
  }
}
void main();

Expected Behavior or Output

For name Avery and numbers 12 and 8, output is Hello, Avery! and Sum: 20. The interface closes on both success and early return.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting that terminal input is text.
  • Using a number without checking whether conversion succeeded.
  • Leaving the readline interface open so the process does not exit.

Activities

  1. Prompt for a name and two numbers.
  2. Try blank and nonnumeric input.
  3. Explain why await and finally are used.

Accessibility Practice

Use clear prompts with trailing spaces and one question at a time. Announce validation errors in plain text. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can collect terminal input asynchronously.
  • I can convert and validate numeric text.
  • I can close the input interface reliably.

Lesson 2.4: Computing with numbers and type conversions

Reading References

Concept Explanation

TypeScript’s static types do not change runtime parsing. Number converts text; Number.isFinite rejects NaN and infinities. The source type must reflect values after validation.

Worked Example

const ageText: string = "16";
const age = Number(ageText);
const heightM = 1.72;
const heightCm = heightM * 100;
console.log(`Age next year: ${age + 1}`);
console.log(`Height: ${heightCm} cm`);
console.log(Number.isFinite(age));
console.log(Number.isFinite(Number("sixteen")));

Expected Behavior or Output

Output: age next year 17, height 172 cm, true, false.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming a type annotation validates text received at runtime.
  • Treating Number(“”) as invalid even though it becomes zero.
  • Failing to check NaN after conversion.

Activities

  1. Convert the string 16 to a number.
  2. Compare Number(“16”), Number(“”), and Number(“sixteen”).
  3. Validate a user-entered age within a reasonable range.

Accessibility Practice

Lesson 3.2: Chained conditionals and grade classification

function getGrade(score: number): string {

  else return "F";
}

}

Lesson 4.2: Organizing arrays: sorting and reversing

Reading References

Concept Explanation

The default sort compares values as strings. Numeric sorting needs a comparator. toSorted returns a sorted copy on supported modern runtimes; spread plus sort is a compatible alternative.

Worked Example

const scores = [82, 91, 76, 88];
const ascending = [...scores].sort((a, b) => a - b);
const descending = [...ascending].reverse();

console.log(ascending.join(", "));
console.log(descending.join(", "));

Original: 82, 91, 76, 88. Ascending: 76, 82, 88, 91. Descending: 91, 88, 82, 76.

Common Mistakes

  • Using default lexicographic sort for numbers.
  • Sorting the original when it must be preserved.
  • Reversing a copy before it has been sorted.

Activities

  2. Create a descending copy.
  3. Explain why the original array remains unchanged.

Concept Explanation

TypeScript supports tuple types for fixed-length sequences with known positions. readonly prevents element reassignment during type checking; it does not create a runtime security boundary.

Worked Example

const coordinates: readonly [number, number] = [3, 4];
const [x, y] = coordinates;
console.log(`x: ${x}`);
console.log(`y: ${y}`);

The output is x 3, y 4, and distance 5.

  • Assuming readonly adds deep runtime immutability.
  • Reversing the semantic order of x and y.

Activities

  2. Destructure x and y into named variables.

Lesson 4.4: Introducing dictionaries: typed objects and records

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 4 lesson 4.4 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Represent inventory items with interfaces and look up quantities with Map.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

An interface describes the shape of an object. A Map stores dynamic key-value pairs and supports keys of different types. These structures serve different purposes.

Worked Example

interface InventoryItem { name: string; quantity: number; unitPrice: number }
const inventory: InventoryItem[] = [
  { name: "Notebook", quantity: 3, unitPrice: 2.5 },
  { name: "Pencil", quantity: 10, unitPrice: 0.5 },
  { name: "Folder", quantity: 4, unitPrice: 1.25 }
];
const quantities = new Map<string, number>(inventory.map(item => [item.name, item.quantity]));
console.log(quantities.get("Notebook"));
console.log(quantities.has("Pencil"));

Expected Behavior or Output

The Notebook quantity is 3 and the Map contains Pencil.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a plain object when Map key semantics are needed.
  • Using Map bracket notation instead of get and set.
  • Forgetting to define a type for structured records.

Activities

  1. Create the three canonical inventory items.
  2. Create a Map from item names to quantities.
  3. Calculate the total inventory value of $17.50.

Accessibility Practice

Print each inventory item as a labeled record rather than a visual table only. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can describe an object with an interface.
  • I can create and query a Map.
  • I can distinguish record types from dynamic key-value collections.

TypeScript type-system extension

Interfaces describe object shapes; generic types let a function or collection preserve the type of the values it handles. A discriminated union represents a value that can be one of several known states.

type Result<T> =
  | { ok: true; value: T }
  | { ok: false; error: string };

function first<T>(values: readonly T[]): T | undefined {
  return values[0];
}

function describeResult<T>(result: Result<T>): string {
  if (result.ok) return `Success: ${String(result.value)}`;
  return `Failure: ${result.error}`;
}

console.log(first<number>([82, 91, 76, 88]));
console.log(describeResult<number>({ ok: false, error: "No score" }));

The ok property narrows the union to its success or failure shape. Generic T preserves the element type rather than discarding it as any.

Lesson 5.1: How terminal input works

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 5 lesson 5.1 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html

Concept Explanation

Worked Example

import { createInterface } from "node:readline/promises";
import { stdin, stdout } from "node:process";
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const rl = createInterface({ input: stdin, output: stdout });
  try {
    const subject = await rl.question("Favorite subject: ");
    if (subject.trim() === "") console.log("A subject is required.");
    else console.log(`Favorite subject: ${subject.trim()}`);
  } finally { rl.close(); }
}
void main();

Expected Behavior or Output

A valid answer prints Favorite subject: Computer Science; blank input prints the required-field message.

Common Mistakes

  • Declaring the input as number before parsing it.
  • Forgetting to trim whitespace before checking blank input.

  2. Test blank input and surrounding spaces.
  3. Explain why the input variable has type string.

Skills Checklist

  • I can close the readline interface.

Overview

Lesson 5.1: How terminal input works

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 5 lesson 5.1 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Collect text from the user and validate it before using it.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A while loop repeats while its condition is true. The loop body must eventually change the state used by the condition or exit explicitly.

Worked Example

const commands = ["view", "help", "quit"];
let index = 0;
while (commands[index] !== "quit") {
  console.log(`Command: ${commands[index]}`);
  index += 1;
}
console.log("Session ended.");

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints view, help, and Session ended. It does not print quit as an ordinary command.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting to update the loop index.
  • Checking the wrong sentinel value.
  • Accessing an array element without accounting for the end of the array.

Activities

  1. Trace each loop iteration on paper.
  2. Change the sentinel command and predict termination.
  3. Write a menu loop that ends on quit.

Accessibility Practice

Show the loop condition and state update as separate lines. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can identify a while-loop condition.
  • I can update state to ensure progress.
  • I can use a sentinel to end a loop.

Lesson 5.3: Using flags and break to exit loops

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 5 lesson 5.3 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Use a boolean flag and break to stop a search at the first match.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A flag records whether a condition has been met. break exits the nearest loop immediately. TypeScript can infer a boolean flag or use an explicit annotation.

Worked Example

const scores = [82, 91, 76, 88];
let found = false;
for (const score of scores) {
  if (score > 90) {
    console.log(`First score above 90: ${score}`);
    found = true;
    break;
  }
}
if (!found) console.log("No score above 90.");

Expected Behavior or Output

The first score above 90 is 91.

Common Mistakes

  • Setting the flag after a break that can never be reached.
  • Using break outside a loop or switch.
  • Failing to report the no-match case.

Activities

  1. Search for a score above 90.
  2. Search for a score above 95 and test the fallback.
  3. Compare flag-controlled termination with a return from a function.

Accessibility Practice

Report the match or no-match result in text, not by color or sound alone. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use a boolean flag.
  • I can stop a loop with break.
  • I can handle a search with no result.

Lesson 5.4: Using continue in loops

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 5 lesson 5.4 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Skip invalid values while continuing to process later entries.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

continue skips the rest of the current iteration and begins the next one. It does not terminate the loop. A typed array can still contain invalid values when values come from runtime sources.

Worked Example

const entries: string[] = ["82", "", "91", "not a score", "76", "88"];
let total = 0;
for (const entry of entries) {
  const score = Number(entry);
  if (!Number.isFinite(score)) continue;
  total += score;
}
console.log(total);

Expected Behavior or Output

The valid entries total 337; the blank entry converts to zero with Number, so a stronger version should reject blank strings explicitly before conversion.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming Number on blank text is an error.
  • Using break when later values still need processing.
  • Placing the update after continue so it is skipped.

Activities

  1. Add an explicit blank-string check.
  2. Skip nonnumeric entries and count accepted values.
  3. Compare continue and break with a traced example.

Accessibility Practice

Print the number of accepted and skipped entries so outcomes are clear. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use continue to skip an iteration.
  • I can validate before conversion.
  • I can distinguish continue from break.

Lesson 5.5: Avoiding infinite loops

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 5 lesson 5.5 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Diagnose loop termination by tracing the control variable and condition.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

An infinite loop occurs when its continuation condition never becomes false. TypeScript cannot prove that a loop will terminate; test the control variable and every branch that updates it.

Worked Example

let count = 1;
while (count <= 3) {
  console.log(`Count ${count}`);
  count += 1;
}
console.log("Loop finished.");

Expected Behavior or Output

The output is Count 1, Count 2, Count 3, then Loop finished.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting to increment or otherwise update the control variable.
  • Using continue before the update statement.
  • Using a boundary condition that never becomes false.

Activities

  1. Trace the value of count on each iteration.
  2. Identify a continue path that skips an update.
  3. Describe a safe way to stop a runaway terminal process.

Accessibility Practice

Provide a keyboard-only recovery procedure and explicit termination message. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can trace loop state.
  • I can identify non-terminating paths.
  • I can design a loop with a clear exit.

Unit 6: Functions

Overview

Define typed functions, arguments, return values, and collection-processing functions. The TypeScript adaptation preserves the shared Python curriculum’s learning objectives, datasets, expected results, and assessment criteria while teaching TypeScript’s compile-time type system and JavaScript runtime behavior. The readline/promises interface returns a string for each answer. TypeScript’s annotation does not convert or validate that string.

Worked Example

import { createInterface } from "node:readline/promises";
import { stdin, stdout } from "node:process";
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const rl = createInterface({ input: stdin, output: stdout });
  try {
    const subject = await rl.question("Favorite subject: ");
    if (subject.trim() === "") console.log("A subject is required.");
    else console.log(`Favorite subject: ${subject.trim()}`);
  } finally { rl.close(); }
}
void main();

Expected Behavior or Output

A valid answer prints Favorite subject: Computer Science; blank input prints the required-field message.

Common Mistakes

  • Declaring the input as number before parsing it.
  • Forgetting to trim whitespace before checking blank input.
  • Not closing the readline interface.

Activities

  1. Prompt for a favorite subject.
  2. Test blank input and surrounding spaces.
  3. Explain why the input variable has type string.

Accessibility Practice

Use one prompt and one response at a time. State validation failures explicitly. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can collect a string from terminal input.
  • I can reject blank input.
  • I can close the readline interface.

Lesson 5.2: The while loop in action

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 5 lesson 5.2 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Repeat a prompt until a sentinel command is entered.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A while loop repeats while its condition is true. The loop body must eventually change the state used by the condition or exit explicitly.

Worked Example

const commands = ["view", "help", "quit"];
let index = 0;
while (commands[index] !== "quit") {
  console.log(`Command: ${commands[index]}`);
  index += 1;
}
console.log("Session ended.");

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints view, help, and Session ended. It does not print quit as an ordinary command.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting to update the loop index.
  • Checking the wrong sentinel value.
  • Accessing an array element without accounting for the end of the array.

Activities

  1. Trace each loop iteration on paper.
  2. Change the sentinel command and predict termination.
  3. Write a menu loop that ends on quit.

Accessibility Practice

Show the loop condition and state update as separate lines. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can identify a while-loop condition.
  • I can update state to ensure progress.
  • I can use a sentinel to end a loop.

Lesson 5.3: Using flags and break to exit loops

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 5 lesson 5.3 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Use a boolean flag and break to stop a search at the first match.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A flag records whether a condition has been met. break exits the nearest loop immediately. TypeScript can infer a boolean flag or use an explicit annotation.

Worked Example

const scores = [82, 91, 76, 88];
let found = false;
for (const score of scores) {
  if (score > 90) {
    console.log(`First score above 90: ${score}`);
    found = true;
    break;
  }
}
if (!found) console.log("No score above 90.");

Expected Behavior or Output

The first score above 90 is 91.

Common Mistakes

  • Setting the flag after a break that can never be reached.
  • Using break outside a loop or switch.
  • Failing to report the no-match case.

Activities

  1. Search for a score above 90.
  2. Search for a score above 95 and test the fallback.
  3. Compare flag-controlled termination with a return from a function.

Accessibility Practice

Report the match or no-match result in text, not by color or sound alone. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can use a boolean flag.
  • I can stop a loop with break.
  • I can handle a search with no result.

Overview

Define typed functions, arguments, return values, and collection-processing functions. The TypeScript adaptation preserves the shared Python curriculum’s learning objectives, datasets, expected results, and assessment criteria while teaching TypeScript’s compile-time type system and JavaScript runtime behavior.

Lesson 6.1: Defining functions

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 6 lesson 6.1 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Define a typed function that calculates a tip and total.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A function packages reusable behavior. Parameter types describe accepted inputs and a return type describes the result. A function can return a value without printing it.

Worked Example

function calculateTip(bill: number, rate: number): number {
  return bill * rate;
}
console.log(calculateTip(24.5, 0.15).toFixed(2));

Expected Behavior or Output

The tip amount is 3.68 when formatted to two decimal places.

Common Mistakes

  • Omitting a return on one branch of a typed function.
  • Printing instead of returning a result needed by the caller.
  • Using overly broad any types.

Activities

  1. Write a function that returns a tip amount.
  2. Add a function that returns bill plus tip.
  3. Test the canonical bill and rate.

Accessibility Practice

Keep the signature on one line and read parameter and return types explicitly. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can declare a function.
  • I can type parameters and return values.
  • I can distinguish returning from printing.

Lesson 6.2: Passing arguments

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 6 lesson 6.2 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Use positional, optional, and default parameters in typed function calls.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

TypeScript supports positional arguments and default values. It does not have Python-style named keyword arguments; use an options object when callers need named configuration.

Worked Example

interface TipOptions { rate?: number; includeTotal?: boolean }
function describeTip(bill: number, options: TipOptions = {}): string {
  const rate = options.rate ?? 0.15;
  const tip = bill * rate;
  return options.includeTotal ? `Tip ${tip.toFixed(2)}, total ${(bill + tip).toFixed(2)}` : `Tip ${tip.toFixed(2)}`;
}
console.log(describeTip(24.5, { rate: 0.2, includeTotal: true }));

Expected Behavior or Output

The output is Tip 4.90, total 29.40.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming TypeScript supports named keyword arguments.
  • Using || when zero is a meaningful option value.
  • Making an options field required when a default is intended.

Activities

  1. Call a function with positional arguments.
  2. Add a default tip rate.
  3. Use an options object to request the total.

Accessibility Practice

Read option names and values explicitly. Avoid deeply nested option objects in beginner examples. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can pass positional arguments.
  • I can use default and optional parameters.
  • I can model named options with an interface.

Lesson 6.3: Return values

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 6 lesson 6.3 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Return computed values and handle empty collections explicitly.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A return value is data supplied to the caller. A return type can include null to represent an absent result; strictNullChecks requires the caller to handle that possibility.

Worked Example

function average(values: number[]): number | null {
  if (values.length === 0) return null;
  return values.reduce((sum, value) => sum + value, 0) / values.length;
}
console.log(average([82, 91, 76, 88]));
console.log(average([]));

Expected Behavior or Output

The averages are 84.25 and null.

Common Mistakes

  • Returning undefined accidentally on an empty path.
  • Ignoring a nullable return value.
  • Confusing a side effect with a computed result.

Activities

  1. Calculate the canonical score average.
  2. Call the function with an empty array.
  3. Use a null check before formatting the result.

Accessibility Practice

Explain every possible return value before showing the caller. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can return a computed value.
  • I can express an absent result with null.
  • I can handle a union return type.

Lesson 6.4: Functions with arrays and objects

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 6 lesson 6.4 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Pass typed arrays and inventory records to reusable processing functions.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

Arrays and objects are reference values. A function can mutate caller-visible data. Use readonly parameters or copy inputs when mutation is not part of the contract.

Worked Example

interface Item { name: string; quantity: number; unitPrice: number }
function inventoryValue(items: readonly Item[]): number {
  return items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.quantity * item.unitPrice, 0);
}
const items: Item[] = [
  { name: "Notebook", quantity: 3, unitPrice: 2.5 },
  { name: "Pencil", quantity: 10, unitPrice: 0.5 },
  { name: "Folder", quantity: 4, unitPrice: 1.25 }
];
console.log(inventoryValue(items).toFixed(2));

Expected Behavior or Output

The inventory value is 17.50.

Common Mistakes

  • Mutating an input collection unexpectedly.
  • Using an object shape inconsistent with the interface.
  • Forgetting that readonly is a compile-time constraint, not deep freezing.

Activities

  1. Write a function that totals inventory value.
  2. Write a function that returns scores above 80.
  3. Explain whether each function mutates its input.

Accessibility Practice

Use named fields and one output line per record. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can type an object interface.
  • I can accept readonly arrays.
  • I can write a collection-processing function.

Lesson 6.5: Arbitrary numbers of arguments

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 6 lesson 6.5 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Use typed rest parameters and options objects to handle variable inputs.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A rest parameter gathers remaining positional arguments into an array. TypeScript requires the rest parameter’s element type. An options object is a clear alternative to Python-style keyword arguments.

Worked Example

function sum(...values: number[]): number {
  return values.reduce((total, value) => total + value, 0);
}
console.log(sum(10, 20, 30));
console.log(sum(82, 91, 76, 88));

Expected Behavior or Output

The results are 60 and 337.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating the rest parameter as a single number.
  • Placing parameters after a rest parameter.
  • Using any[] instead of a meaningful element type.

Activities

  1. Call sum with three values.
  2. Call sum with the canonical scores.
  3. Compare a rest parameter with an options object.

Accessibility Practice

Describe the collected values as an ordered list. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can declare a typed rest parameter.
  • I can pass a variable number of values.
  • I can explain the difference between rest parameters and options objects.

Unit 7: Classes and Object-Oriented Programming

Overview

Model state and behavior using classes, inheritance, and composition. The TypeScript adaptation preserves the shared Python curriculum’s learning objectives, datasets, expected results, and assessment criteria while teaching TypeScript’s compile-time type system and JavaScript runtime behavior.

Lesson 7.1: Why learn about classes?

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 7 lesson 7.1 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain classes, instances, encapsulation, and object state with an inventory example.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A class describes the state and behavior of objects. TypeScript classes add static type checking, access modifiers, and optional private fields; types are erased from emitted JavaScript.

Worked Example

class InventoryItem {
  constructor(public name: string, public quantity: number, public unitPrice: number) {}
  value(): number { return this.quantity * this.unitPrice; }
}
const notebook = new InventoryItem("Notebook", 3, 2.5);
console.log(`${notebook.name}: ${notebook.value().toFixed(2)}`);

Expected Behavior or Output

The output is Notebook: 7.50.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating a class as only a data container without behavior.
  • Confusing a class with an instance.
  • Assuming TypeScript access modifiers create runtime security.

Activities

  1. Identify the fields and behavior of an inventory item.
  2. Create two instances with different values.
  3. Explain what the class and each instance represent.

Accessibility Practice

Use meaningful instance names and print a labeled summary. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain class and instance.
  • I can identify state and behavior.
  • I can create a simple class.

Lesson 7.2: Creating and using a class

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 7 lesson 7.2 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Create a Student class and instantiate the canonical learner profile.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A constructor initializes an instance. Parameter properties can declare and initialize fields in one place. Explicit types make the class contract readable.

Worked Example

class Student {
  constructor(public name: string, public age: number, public favoriteSubject: string) {}
  describe(): string { return `${this.name}, age ${this.age}, studies ${this.favoriteSubject}`; }
}
const learner = new Student("Avery", 16, "Computer Science");
console.log(learner.describe());

Expected Behavior or Output

The output is Avery, age 16, studies Computer Science.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting new when constructing an instance.
  • Using a parameter type that conflicts with the property type.
  • Writing a method that refers to a variable instead of this.

Activities

  1. Create Avery’s Student instance.
  2. Create a second student instance.
  3. Call describe on both instances.

Accessibility Practice

Read constructor parameters in order and label each property. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define a constructor.
  • I can instantiate a class.
  • I can call an instance method.

Lesson 7.3: Working with attributes and methods

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 7 lesson 7.3 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Add validation and update behavior to a class.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

Methods define operations over an instance’s state. Encapsulation keeps validation close to the state it protects. Private fields and access modifiers guide compile-time access.

Worked Example

class StockItem {
  #quantity: number;
  constructor(public name: string, quantity: number) { this.#quantity = quantity; }
  get quantity(): number { return this.#quantity; }
  setQuantity(value: number): void {
    if (!Number.isInteger(value) || value < 0) throw new RangeError("Quantity must be a nonnegative integer.");
    this.#quantity = value;
  }
}
const pencil = new StockItem("Pencil", 10);
pencil.setQuantity(12);
console.log(pencil.quantity);

Expected Behavior or Output

The output is 12. A negative or fractional quantity throws RangeError.

Common Mistakes

  • Changing state without validation.
  • Assuming a private field is accessible outside its class.
  • Allowing negative quantities.

Activities

  1. Update Pencil quantity to 12.
  2. Try a negative quantity and inspect the error.
  3. Explain the difference between a property and a method.

Accessibility Practice

Use explicit validation messages and one state change per operation. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define methods and fields.
  • I can protect state with private fields.
  • I can validate state updates.

Lesson 7.4: Inheritance

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 7 lesson 7.4 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Create a specialized item class that extends a base class.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

Inheritance models an is-a relationship. A subclass uses extends and calls super before accessing this. Use inheritance only when the subtype genuinely satisfies the base contract.

Worked Example

class Item {
  constructor(public name: string, public quantity: number) {}
}
class PerishableItem extends Item {
  constructor(name: string, quantity: number, public expiresOn: string) {
    super(name, quantity);
  }
  describe(): string { return `${this.name}: ${this.quantity} in stock, expires ${this.expiresOn}`; }
}
console.log(new PerishableItem("Milk", 2, "2026-11-10").describe());

Expected Behavior or Output

The output is Milk: 2 in stock, expires 2026-11-10.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting to call super before using this.
  • Extending a class only to reuse unrelated code.
  • Changing a subclass method so it violates the base contract.

Activities

  1. Create a PerishableItem.
  2. Override or add a method with a clear contract.
  3. Compare inheritance with composition.

Accessibility Practice

Use a descriptive sentence for the specialized instance. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can extend a base class.
  • I can call super in a constructor.
  • I can explain when inheritance is appropriate.

Lesson 7.5: Composition: instances as attributes

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 7 lesson 7.5 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Build a record from related objects using composition.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

Composition models a has-a relationship. A class stores another object as a property rather than inheriting its behavior. This often keeps responsibilities smaller.

Worked Example

class Student {
  constructor(public name: string, public age: number, public favoriteSubject: string) {}
}
class Course {
  constructor(public title: string) {}
}
class StudentRecord {
  constructor(public student: Student, public course: Course) {}
  describe(): string { return `${this.student.name} studies ${this.course.title}.`; }
}
const record = new StudentRecord(new Student("Avery", 16, "Computer Science"), new Course("Computer Science"));
console.log(record.describe());

Expected Behavior or Output

The output is Avery studies Computer Science.

Common Mistakes

  • Using inheritance for a has-a relationship.
  • Creating tightly coupled classes with unclear responsibilities.
  • Duplicating data already stored in a related object.

Activities

  1. Create a StudentRecord containing a Student and Course.
  2. Add a method that describes the relationship.
  3. Draw a text outline of the object relationships.

Accessibility Practice

Explain object relationships in words before reading nested property access. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model a has-a relationship.
  • I can compose objects from instances.
  • I can distinguish composition from inheritance.
