Overview

Read and write files, handle errors, and persist validated JSON. The TypeScript adaptation preserves the shared Python curriculum’s learning objectives, datasets, expected results, and assessment criteria while teaching TypeScript’s compile-time type system and JavaScript runtime behavior.

Lesson 8.1: Reading from a file

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 8 lesson 8.1 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Read a line-oriented notes file with the promise-based file system API.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

The node:fs/promises API returns Promises. readFile with UTF-8 encoding returns a string. Await file operations and handle missing-file errors explicitly.

Worked Example

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const content = await readFile("notes.txt", "utf8");
  console.log("File contents:");
  console.log(content);
}
void main();

Expected Behavior or Output

With the sample file containing two notes, both lines appear after File contents:.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading from the wrong working directory.
  • Forgetting await and logging a Promise.
  • Assuming a file exists without handling ENOENT.

Activities

  1. Create notes.txt with two lines.
  2. Read and print the file contents.
  3. Run from a different working directory and diagnose the path.

Accessibility Practice

Print a label before file contents and explain the working directory. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can read a UTF-8 text file.
  • I can await an asynchronous operation.
  • I can identify the current working directory.

Lesson 8.2: Writing to a file

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 8 lesson 8.2 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Create and append to the same notes file using promise-based file operations.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

writeFile creates or replaces content; appendFile adds content. Await each operation so writes happen in the intended order.

Worked Example

import { writeFile, appendFile, readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  await writeFile("notes.txt", "Review arrays\n", "utf8");
  await appendFile("notes.txt", "Practice typed functions\n", "utf8");
  console.log(await readFile("notes.txt", "utf8"));
}
void main();

Expected Behavior or Output

The file contains Review arrays followed by Practice typed functions, each on its own line.

Common Mistakes

  • Using writeFile when existing content must be preserved.
  • Not awaiting a write before reading the file.
  • Writing to an unexpected path.

Activities

  1. Create a new notes file.
  2. Append a second line.
  3. Read the file and verify both lines and their order.

Accessibility Practice

Announce whether an operation creates, replaces, appends, or reads data. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write a UTF-8 file.
  • I can append without replacing existing text.
  • I can sequence asynchronous file operations.

Lesson 8.3: Exceptions and error handling

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 8 lesson 8.3 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Handle expected file and validation errors with try/catch.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

An exception interrupts normal control flow. Catch expected failures and inspect unknown error values safely; do not assume every thrown value is an Error instance.

Worked Example

function validateAge(age: number): void {
  if (!Number.isInteger(age) || age < 0 || age > 120) {
    throw new RangeError("Age must be a whole number from 0 to 120.");
  }
}
try {
  validateAge(16);
  console.log("Age accepted.");
  validateAge(-1);
} catch (error: unknown) {
  if (error instanceof Error) console.log(error.message);
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints Age accepted. followed by the validation message.

Common Mistakes

  • Catching every error and silently ignoring it.
  • Typing catch values as any.
  • Using exceptions for ordinary expected branching.

Activities

  1. Test a valid age.
  2. Test -1 and 121.
  3. Handle a missing file separately from malformed file contents.

Accessibility Practice

Use explicit error messages that identify the invalid field and recovery action. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can throw a validation error.
  • I can catch unknown errors safely.
  • I can distinguish expected failures.

Lesson 8.4: The else and finally patterns

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 8 lesson 8.4 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Separate successful operations from cleanup that must always occur.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

JavaScript has no try-else clause. Put success-only work after a successful try operation and use finally for cleanup. A finally block runs whether the try succeeds or fails.

Worked Example

async function loadMessage(): Promise<void> {
  let loaded = false;
  try {
    const message = "Notes loaded.";
    console.log(message);
    loaded = true;
  } catch (error: unknown) {
    console.log("Unable to load notes.");
  } finally {
    console.log("Load attempt finished.");
  }
  if (loaded) console.log("Ready to continue.");
}
void loadMessage();

Expected Behavior or Output

On success, the program prints Notes loaded, Load attempt finished, and Ready to continue. On failure, the final status still prints.

Common Mistakes

  • Putting success-only code in finally.
  • Assuming TypeScript has Python’s try-else syntax.
  • Returning from finally and accidentally overriding an earlier result.

Activities

  1. Trace success and failure paths.
  2. Move the success message outside the try block.
  3. Explain which cleanup must always run.

Accessibility Practice

Label success, failure, and finalization messages distinctly. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model success and failure paths.
  • I can use finally for cleanup.
  • I can explain the absence of a try-else clause.

Lesson 8.5: Storing structured data with JSON

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 8 lesson 8.5 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Serialize typed records and validate parsed JSON before use.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

JSON.parse returns untrusted runtime data. A TypeScript assertion does not validate its shape. Parse into unknown and use a type guard before treating it as a record.

Worked Example

interface Task { id: number; title: string; done: boolean }
function isTask(value: unknown): value is Task {
  return typeof value === "object" && value !== null &&
    "id" in value && typeof value.id === "number" &&
    "title" in value && typeof value.title === "string" &&
    "done" in value && typeof value.done === "boolean";
}
const encoded = JSON.stringify({ id: 1, title: "Review arrays", done: false });
const parsed: unknown = JSON.parse(encoded);
if (isTask(parsed)) console.log(`${parsed.id}: ${parsed.title}`);

Expected Behavior or Output

The program prints 1: Review arrays only after validating the parsed object.

Common Mistakes

  • Using as Task as if it checked runtime data.
  • Assuming JSON.parse cannot fail.
  • Failing to validate each required field.

Activities

  1. Serialize a task object.
  2. Parse it as unknown and validate it.
  3. Test missing fields and wrong field types.

Accessibility Practice

Print field names and validation errors as text. Never rely on color-only success indicators. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can serialize an object to JSON.
  • I can parse JSON as unknown.
  • I can validate external data with a type guard.

Unit 9: Testing and Data Analysis

Overview

Test functions and classes, generate random values, analyze text, and parse CSV. The TypeScript adaptation preserves the shared Python curriculum’s learning objectives, datasets, expected results, and assessment criteria while teaching TypeScript’s compile-time type system and JavaScript runtime behavior.

Lesson 9.1: Testing a function

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 9 lesson 9.1 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Write built-in Node.js tests for arithmetic and grade classification functions.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

Unit tests verify a function’s contract with known inputs and expected outputs. Node’s built-in node:test and node:assert/strict avoid a third-party test framework for introductory work.

Worked Example

import test from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
function add(a: number, b: number): number { return a + b; }
function getGrade(score: number): string { return score >= 90 ? "A" : score >= 80 ? "B" : score >= 70 ? "C" : score >= 60 ? "D" : "F"; }
test("add returns the sum", () => assert.equal(add(5, 3), 8));
test("82 receives grade B", () => assert.equal(getGrade(82), "B"));

Expected Behavior or Output

The test runner reports two passing tests and no failures.

Common Mistakes

  • Testing only one ordinary value.
  • Using an incorrect expected value copied from the implementation.
  • Failing to run tests after changing a function.

Activities

  1. Test add with positive, negative, and zero values.
  2. Test every grade threshold and its lower neighbor.
  3. Run tests with node –test after compiling the TypeScript test file.

Accessibility Practice

Use descriptive test names that read as complete sentences. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can write a unit test.
  • I can assert an expected result.
  • I can test normal and boundary inputs.

Lesson 9.2: Testing a class

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 9 lesson 9.2 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Test class construction, state changes, and invalid operations.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A class test checks observable behavior: constructor values, method results, state updates, and rejected invalid states. Keep tests independent and deterministic.

Worked Example

import test from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
class StockItem {
  constructor(public name: string, public quantity: number) {}
  setQuantity(value: number): void { if (value < 0) throw new RangeError("Invalid quantity"); this.quantity = value; }
}
test("quantity can be updated", () => {
  const item = new StockItem("Pencil", 10);
  item.setQuantity(12);
  assert.equal(item.quantity, 12);
});

Expected Behavior or Output

The test passes when the quantity changes from 10 to 12.

Common Mistakes

  • Sharing mutable state between tests.
  • Testing private implementation details rather than behavior.
  • Failing to test invalid state changes.

Activities

  1. Test a valid quantity update.
  2. Assert that a negative quantity throws RangeError.
  3. Create a fresh instance in each test.

Accessibility Practice

Keep test names and failure output specific to the state being checked. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can test class behavior.
  • I can test state changes.
  • I can assert that invalid operations throw.

Lesson 9.3: Introduction to random numbers

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 9 lesson 9.3 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Generate bounded integers, decimals, and selections with Math.random.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

Math.random returns a pseudorandom number in the range zero inclusive to one exclusive. Scale and floor it to produce a bounded integer; do not use it for security tokens.

Worked Example

const integer = Math.floor(Math.random() * 10) + 1;
const decimal = Math.random();
const choices = ["red", "blue", "green"];
const choice = choices[Math.floor(Math.random() * choices.length)];
console.log(integer >= 1 && integer <= 10);
console.log(decimal >= 0 && decimal < 1);
console.log(choices.includes(choice));

Expected Behavior or Output

All three checks print true; sampled values can differ on each run.

Common Mistakes

  • Using Math.round and creating uneven endpoint probabilities.
  • Forgetting that the upper bound is exclusive.
  • Using Math.random for passwords or cryptographic secrets.

Activities

  1. Generate an integer from 1 to 10.
  2. Generate a decimal in [0,1).
  3. Choose one item from a typed array.

Accessibility Practice

Report range checks as text; explain that the actual sample changes between runs. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can describe Math.random’s range.
  • I can generate a bounded integer.
  • I can select a random array element.

Lesson 9.4: Analyzing text data

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 9 lesson 9.4 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Count words in the canonical text using normalization and a typed Map.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

Text analysis requires explicit normalization and tokenization rules. A Map stores each token and its frequency. The regular expression below splits on non-letter characters.

Worked Example

const text = "A student studies programming. Programming develops problem-solving skills.";
const words = text.toLowerCase().match(/[a-z]+/g) ?? [];
const counts = new Map<string, number>();
for (const word of words) counts.set(word, (counts.get(word) ?? 0) + 1);
console.log(`Tokens: ${words.length}`);
console.log(`Programming: ${counts.get("programming")}`);

Expected Behavior or Output

The sample produces 10 alphabetic tokens under this tokenization rule; programming appears twice.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming punctuation and hyphens are words.
  • Using a plain object without considering inherited property names.
  • Failing to define how case and punctuation are normalized.

Activities

  1. Count all tokens in the canonical text.
  2. Report the frequency of programming.
  3. Compare token counts with a rule that treats problem-solving as one token.

Accessibility Practice

State the tokenization rule before reporting counts. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can normalize text.
  • I can count tokens with a Map.
  • I can explain how tokenization affects results.

Lesson 9.5: Working with CSV data

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 9 lesson 9.5 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Read the shared CSV columns using a standards-aware parser.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

CSV supports quoted fields, commas inside quotes, and escaped quotation marks. Use a maintained parser rather than splitting lines on commas. Parsed records still need validation.

Worked Example

import { parse } from "csv-parse/sync";
const csv = "student_id,first_name,last_name,score,active\n1,Avery,Stone,91,true\n2,Jordan,Lee,82,false";
const records = parse(csv, { columns: true, skip_empty_lines: true }) as Array<Record<string, string>>;
const average = records.reduce((sum, row) => sum + Number(row.score), 0) / records.length;
console.log(`Records: ${records.length}`);
console.log(`Average: ${average.toFixed(2)}`);

Expected Behavior or Output

The two sample records have scores 91 and 82; the average is 86.50.

Common Mistakes

  • Splitting CSV lines and fields manually.
  • Assuming every parsed field is already a number or boolean.
  • Ignoring malformed rows and missing columns.

Activities

  1. Parse the shared CSV columns.
  2. Calculate the score average for the sample records.
  3. Test a quoted name containing a comma.

Accessibility Practice

Print record count and summary labels rather than a visual-only chart. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can parse CSV with a dedicated parser.
  • I can validate parsed field values.
  • I can calculate a summary from CSV records.

Lesson 10.1: Designing a text-based project

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 10 lesson 10.1 in the canonical Python curriculum.

  • Plan requirements, data structures, commands, and acceptance tests before implementation.

Concept Explanation

Top-down design decomposes a project into smaller responsibilities. For an accessible terminal project, define prompts, commands, textual feedback, invalid-input behavior, and a quit path before coding.

Worked Example

const requirements = ["list rooms", "move by direction", "take item", "view inventory", "quit"];
for (const requirement of requirements) console.log(`Requirement: ${requirement}`);

Expected Behavior or Output

Five requirements are printed in a stable order.

Common Mistakes

  • Designing a visual-only interaction for a text-based project.
  • Omitting error and quit behavior.

Activities

  1. Write the project requirements in plain language.
  2. Identify input, state, and output for each command.
  3. Write at least five acceptance tests before implementation.

Lesson 10.2: Text adventure part 1: rooms and movement

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 10 lesson 10.2 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Model the five canonical rooms with typed exits and movement.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A room has an identifier, description, and exits. A movement operation changes the current room only when the requested exit exists. A Record type can model a fixed set of room identifiers.

Worked Example

type RoomId = "start_room" | "tunnel" | "clearing" | "locked_door_room" | "treasure_room";
const exits: Record<RoomId, Partial<Record<string, RoomId>>> = {
  start_room: { north: "tunnel" },
  tunnel: { south: "start_room", east: "clearing" },
  clearing: { west: "tunnel", north: "locked_door_room" },
  locked_door_room: { south: "clearing" },
  treasure_room: {}
};
function move(room: RoomId, direction: string): RoomId | null {
  return exits[room][direction.toLowerCase()] ?? null;
}
console.log(move("start_room", "north"));
console.log(move("start_room", "west"));

Expected Behavior or Output

Moving north from start_room returns tunnel; moving west returns null. The north exit from locked_door_room is conditional on using shiny key.

Common Mistakes

  • Allowing movement through an exit that is not defined.
  • Changing the room before validating the direction.
  • Using arbitrary strings where a RoomId union is safer.

Activities

  1. Create all five canonical rooms and unconditional exits.
  2. Move north from start_room and east from tunnel.
  3. Attempt an invalid direction and report the result.
  4. Add the conditional locked_door_room north exit only after the key is used.

Accessibility Practice

Announce current room and available exits as labeled text. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model rooms and exits.
  • I can use a union type for room identifiers.
  • I can validate movement.

Lesson 10.3: Text adventure part 2: items, inventory, and puzzle

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 10 lesson 10.3 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Implement pickup of shiny key from start_room and the conditional locked-door puzzle.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

An item moves from one room to inventory as one state transition. The shiny key moves from start_room to inventory as one state transition. The player must use it in locked_door_room to unlock the north exit to treasure_room.

Worked Example

type RoomId = "start_room" | "tunnel" | "clearing" | "locked_door_room" | "treasure_room";
type Direction = "north" | "south" | "east" | "west";
const exits: Record<RoomId, Partial<Record<Direction, RoomId>>> = {
  start_room: { north: "tunnel" },
  tunnel: { south: "start_room", east: "clearing" },
  clearing: { west: "tunnel", north: "locked_door_room" },
  locked_door_room: { south: "clearing" },
  treasure_room: {}
};
const roomItems: Record<RoomId, string[]> = {
  start_room: ["shiny key"], tunnel: [], clearing: [], locked_door_room: [], treasure_room: []
};
const inventory: string[] = [];
let doorLocked = true;
function takeItem(room: RoomId, item: string): boolean {
  const items = roomItems[room];
  const index = items.findIndex(value => value.toLowerCase() === item.toLowerCase());
  if (index < 0) return false;
  inventory.push(items.splice(index, 1)[0]);
  return true;
}
function useKey(room: RoomId): string {
  if (room !== "locked_door_room") return "You must be at the locked door to use the key.";
  if (!inventory.includes("shiny key")) return "The door is locked.";
  doorLocked = false;
  exits.locked_door_room.north = "treasure_room";
  return "The door unlocks; north now leads to treasure_room.";
}
function runCommand(room: RoomId, command: string): boolean | string {
  if (command.startsWith("take ")) return takeItem(room, command.slice(5));
  if (command === "use shiny key") return useKey(room);
  return "I don't understand that command.";
}
console.log(runCommand("start_room", "take shiny key"));
console.log(runCommand("start_room", "take shiny key"));
console.log(inventory.join(", "));
console.log(runCommand("clearing", "use shiny key"));
console.log(runCommand("locked_door_room", "use shiny key"));
console.log(doorLocked);
console.log(exits.locked_door_room.north);

Expected Behavior or Output

The command dispatcher accepts the literal take shiny key and use shiny key commands. The second pickup is rejected without duplicating the inventory item. Key use is rejected outside locked_door_room; using it there unlocks the north exit.

true
false
shiny key
You must be at the locked door to use the key.
The door unlocks; north now leads to treasure_room.
false
treasure_room

Common Mistakes

  • Allowing the same item to be collected repeatedly.
  • Updating inventory without removing the room item.
  • Checking for the wrong key name or case.

Activities

  1. Take shiny key from start_room.
  2. Attempt to take it twice and verify duplicate pickup is rejected.
  3. Attempt to use the key outside locked_door_room.
  4. Use the key in locked_door_room and verify the north exit is unlocked.

Accessibility Practice

Confirm each pickup by item name and state whether the puzzle is locked or open. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can transfer an item into inventory.
  • I can prevent duplicate pickup.
  • I can implement the shiny-key puzzle: move the key from start_room to inventory, require its use in locked_door_room, and unlock the north exit to treasure_room.

Lesson 10.4: Developing a command-line to-do tool

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 10 lesson 10.4 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Implement add, view, complete, delete, and quit operations with typed tasks.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A task has an id, title, description, done state, and creation timestamp. User-facing task numbers are one-based; array indexes are zero-based. Persist after every state-changing operation.

Worked Example

interface Todo { id: number; title: string; description: string; done: boolean; created_at: string }
const tasks: Todo[] = [];
function addTask(title: string, description: string): Todo {
  const task: Todo = { id: tasks.length + 1, title, description, done: false, created_at: new Date().toISOString() };
  tasks.push(task);
  return task;
}
console.log(addTask("Review arrays", "Practice typed collection methods").done);

Expected Behavior or Output

A new task is added with done false and an ISO timestamp.

Common Mistakes

  • Using an array index as a permanent identifier.
  • Failing to save after a state change.
  • Accepting a blank task title.

Activities

  1. Add a task and view it.
  2. Mark a task complete and delete another.
  3. Persist and reload the task array as JSON.

Accessibility Practice

Use one task per output block with field labels and a clear confirmation. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can model a typed task.
  • I can implement task creation.
  • I can identify persistence points.

Lesson 10.5: Refinement and accessible text user experience

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 10 lesson 10.5 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Improve validation, prompts, error messages, and recovery paths.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

A usable terminal interface has explicit prompts, predictable output, help text, and recoverable errors. A robust program validates untrusted values before changing state.

Worked Example

function normalizeCommand(input: string): string {
  return input.trim().toLowerCase();
}
function validateTitle(input: string): string | null {
  const title = input.trim();
  return title.length === 0 ? "Title cannot be blank." : null;
}
console.log(normalizeCommand("  VIEW "));
console.log(validateTitle("   "));

Expected Behavior or Output

The output is view and Title cannot be blank.

Common Mistakes

  • Providing vague messages such as invalid input without a recovery hint.
  • Using color as the only status indicator.
  • Failing to test blank input, unknown commands, and empty collections.

Activities

  1. Add a help command.
  2. Test blank, malformed, and unknown commands.
  3. Review every message in sequential screen-reader output.

Accessibility Practice

Provide text equivalents for every status and avoid cursor-position-dependent instructions. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can normalize command input.
  • I can validate required fields.
  • I can review a text interface for accessibility.

Unit 11: Capstone — Accessible Personal Data Manager

Overview

Integrate typed records, terminal interaction, persistence, CRUD, testing, and accessibility. The TypeScript adaptation preserves the shared Python curriculum’s learning objectives, datasets, expected results, and assessment criteria while teaching TypeScript’s compile-time type system and JavaScript runtime behavior.

Lesson 11.1: Capstone interface and requirements

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 11 lesson 11.1 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Plan an accessible terminal interface for the personal data manager.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

The Python source uses NiceGUI, but the TypeScript track uses a terminal interface to preserve the same user-facing requirements without requiring browser UI. Commands include list, add, search, update, delete, help, and quit.

Worked Example

const commands = ["list", "add", "search", "update", "delete", "help", "quit"];
console.log(commands.join(", "));

Expected Behavior or Output

The command list contains all seven required operations.

Common Mistakes

  • Copying a GUI-specific implementation when the language track requires an accessible alternative.
  • Omitting a help or quit command.
  • Designing commands without defining expected output.

Activities

  1. Choose a terminal command syntax.
  2. Write a help response for every command.
  3. Define keyboard-only acceptance tests.

Accessibility Practice

Specify prompt order and output as linear text. Do not require mouse use. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can explain the language-specific interface adaptation.
  • I can define the required commands.
  • I can create accessibility acceptance tests.

Lesson 11.2: Capstone data model and JSON storage

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 11 lesson 11.2 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Define the shared record schema and save/load records safely.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

Each record has id, title, description, category, created_at, and updated_at. TypeScript interfaces describe the expected shape, but JSON input must be validated at runtime.

Worked Example

interface DataRecord { id: number; title: string; description: string; category: string; created_at: string; updated_at: string }
const record: DataRecord = { id: 1, title: "Course notes", description: "Review arrays", category: "Study", created_at: "2026-11-01T10:00:00.000Z", updated_at: "2026-11-01T10:00:00.000Z" };
const serialized = JSON.stringify([record], null, 2);
console.log(serialized.includes("Course notes"));

Expected Behavior or Output

The check prints true and the JSON contains all six fields.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a type assertion instead of validating loaded JSON.
  • Reusing record identifiers.
  • Overwriting valid data after a parse failure without reporting it.

Activities

  1. Define the six-field interface.
  2. Serialize one record and inspect the JSON.
  3. Load and validate records before using them.

Accessibility Practice

Read the schema field by field and keep timestamps in a consistent ISO format. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can define the capstone record interface.
  • I can serialize structured data.
  • I can explain runtime validation of stored JSON.

Lesson 11.3: Capstone list and display operations

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 11 lesson 11.3 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Display records in a stable, labeled, sequential format.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

Listing is a read operation and should not mutate data. Stable identifiers are distinct from temporary one-based display positions.

Worked Example

const records = [{ id: 7, title: "Course notes", category: "Study", done: false }];
for (const [index, record] of records.entries()) {
  console.log(`Item ${index + 1}`);
  console.log(`ID: ${record.id}`);
  console.log(`Title: ${record.title}`);
  console.log(`Category: ${record.category}`);
  console.log(`Done: ${record.done}`);
}

Expected Behavior or Output

The record is displayed as Item 1 with ID 7 and its labeled fields.

Common Mistakes

  • Using the displayed list number as the permanent ID.
  • Omitting labels and making output ambiguous.
  • Failing to handle an empty collection.

Activities

  1. Display one record.
  2. Display multiple records.
  3. Display an empty list with a clear message.

Accessibility Practice

Use stable labels and one field per line for sequential reading. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can display records with labels.
  • I can distinguish display position from record ID.
  • I can handle an empty collection.

Lesson 11.4: Capstone add, search, and update operations

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 11 lesson 11.4 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Implement creation, case-insensitive search, and safe record updates.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

Create, search, and update are separate operations. Update only permitted fields and refresh updated_at. Search should not change stored records.

Worked Example

interface Entry { id: number; title: string; description: string; updated_at: string }
function search(entries: readonly Entry[], query: string): Entry[] {
  const term = query.trim().toLowerCase();
  return entries.filter(entry => `${entry.title} ${entry.description}`.toLowerCase().includes(term));
}
const entries: Entry[] = [{ id: 1, title: "Course notes", description: "Review arrays", updated_at: "2026-11-01T10:00:00.000Z" }];
console.log(search(entries, "ARRAYS").length);

Expected Behavior or Output

The search returns one matching record.

Common Mistakes

  • Searching case-sensitively without documenting that choice.
  • Allowing edits to immutable identifiers.
  • Forgetting to refresh updated_at after an edit.

Activities

  1. Add a record with all required fields.
  2. Search by title and description.
  3. Update a title and verify the timestamp changes.

Accessibility Practice

Confirm each successful action by record ID and field name. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Skills Checklist

  • I can add a valid record.
  • I can search without mutating records.
  • I can update permitted fields and timestamps.

Lesson 11.5: Capstone delete, completion, and final verification

Reading References

  • Python source counterpart: Unit 11 lesson 11.5 in the canonical Python curriculum.
  • TypeScript Handbook: https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html
  • Node.js documentation where terminal, file, or runtime APIs are used.

Learning Objectives

  • Implement delete and completion behavior and verify persistence and accessibility.
  • Explain the TypeScript-specific language or runtime behavior used in the lesson.
  • Predict the example’s behavior and test a boundary or invalid case.

Concept Explanation

Deletion removes a selected record by stable ID. Completion updates the record state. The capstone should have tests for CRUD behavior, JSON persistence, invalid input, and empty data.

Worked Example

interface TaskRecord { id: number; title: string; done: boolean }
function markDone(records: TaskRecord[], id: number): boolean {
  const record = records.find(item => item.id === id);
  if (!record) return false;
  record.done = true;
  return true;
}
const records: TaskRecord[] = [{ id: 4, title: "Test persistence", done: false }];
console.log(markDone(records, 4));
console.log(records[0].done);

Expected Behavior or Output

The function returns true and the record’s done field becomes true.

Common Mistakes

  • Deleting by a stale array index.
  • Failing to save after a mutation.
  • Testing only the successful path.

Activities

  1. Delete a record by ID and verify it remains absent after reload.
  2. Mark a record complete and test missing IDs.
  3. Run at least five tests covering CRUD, persistence, and validation.

Accessibility Practice

Verify keyboard-only use, help text, confirmations, errors, and sequential output with the intended access technology. All prompts, errors, and status messages must have meaningful text equivalents; keyboard operation is required.

Runnable Reference Implementation

The repository includes a tested TypeScript domain and JSON-storage reference core in capstone/README.md. Run tsc -p TYPESCRIPT/capstone/tsconfig.json, then node --test TYPESCRIPT/capstone/records.test.js from the repository root. The reference core does not replace the requirement to build and evaluate an accessible user interface.

Skills Checklist

  • I can delete by stable identifier.
  • I can update completion state.
  • I can plan end-to-end and accessibility tests.

Standalone Topics and Focused Language Modules

This section contains focused introductions to important areas of computing that complement the full programming-language curricula. These topics are useful in their own right and are frequently used alongside one or more general-purpose programming languages.

The standalone modules are intentionally narrower than the full language courses. Each introduces a specific technology or discipline, explains its core concepts and common workflows, and provides practice activities and further reading. They are not arranged as a sequence of increasingly difficult languages, and they do not replace the shared computing foundations or terminal prerequisite.

Modules in this section

Git: Version Control

Git is the distributed version control system used by nearly all modern software development. It records the history of a project as a series of snapshots and lets multiple people work concurrently.

This module introduces repositories, commits and commit messages, the staging area, reading git status, git log, and git diff output, branching and merging, conflict resolution, remotes, and collaboration through pull requests, including review from the command line. It builds the commit-graph mental model through textual history rather than diagrams.

HTML and CSS: Structure and Presentation for the Web

HTML and CSS are the foundational technologies for structuring and presenting web content.

  • HTML describes the meaning and structure of a document: headings, paragraphs, links, lists, forms, tables, and other content.
  • CSS controls presentation and layout, including typography, spacing, responsive design, and visual states.
  • Together, they form the foundation for browser-based user interfaces and are used with JavaScript or TypeScript in interactive web applications.

This module emphasizes semantic HTML, separation of structure from presentation, and accessibility as part of document design. It is a useful starting point for web development regardless of which scripting language or framework is introduced later.

Markdown: Technical Documentation

Markdown is a lightweight plain-text markup language used for documentation, README files, technical notes, and web content. It is the default documentation format of GitHub, package registries, static site generators, and developer communication tools.

This module introduces headings, lists, links, images, code blocks, tables, and blockquotes; reference-style links; dialect differences between CommonMark and GitHub Flavored Markdown; and a screen-reader authoring workflow that verifies structure by heading navigation and linting rather than visual preview.

R: Statistical Computing

R is a language and environment for statistical computing, data analysis, and graphics. It is widely used in research, public health, economics, social science, government, and business analytics.

This module introduces R’s core data types and structures, vectorized operations, functions, data frames, data import, descriptive statistics, and reproducible analysis. It is focused on understanding and working with data rather than covering every part of the R ecosystem.

Regular Expressions: Pattern-Based Text Processing

A regular expression is a compact pattern language for finding, extracting, validating, and replacing text that shares a structure. Regex is supported in every mainstream language, in editors, and in command-line tools such as grep and sed.

This module introduces literals, character classes, quantifiers and greediness, anchors, groups and backreferences, flags, and dialect differences (PCRE, POSIX, RE2, JavaScript). It emphasizes verbose-mode patterns with comments, interactive testing, and the classic pitfalls, including catastrophic backtracking and applying regex to nested structured formats.

SQL: Relational Databases

SQL (Structured Query Language) is used to define, query, and manipulate data in relational database systems. It is declarative: a query describes the information to retrieve or the change to make, while the database engine determines how to execute it.

This module introduces tables, rows, columns, keys, filtering, sorting, aggregation, joins, data definition and manipulation, transactions, and safe query practices. SQL is commonly used from applications written in other languages, as well as in database administration and analytics tools.

Structured Data Formats: JSON, YAML, and TOML

Modern software exchanges configuration and data through a small set of text formats: JSON for APIs and data interchange, YAML for infrastructure and pipeline configuration, and TOML for application and tool configuration.

This module introduces the syntax and data model of each format, multi-line strings and block scalars in YAML, tables and arrays of tables in TOML, validation tooling such as jq, yq, and schema validators, and guidance on choosing the appropriate format for a task. It pays particular attention to YAML’s indentation sensitivity in non-visual workflows.

Web Accessibility: ARIA, WCAG, and Accessible Design

Web accessibility is the practice of building websites and applications usable by people with disabilities, including screen-reader users, keyboard-only users, and users with cognitive or motor disabilities.

This module extends the HTML and CSS module. It introduces the accessibility tree, the WCAG principles and levels, semantic HTML that requires no ARIA, correct use of ARIA roles, states, and properties, keyboard interaction and focus management, accessible forms and error reporting, and a testing workflow covering keyboard, screen reader, and automated scans. It also outlines accessibility as a professional specialization.

How to use these modules

  1. Complete the shared Computing Foundations Primer.
  2. Complete the Terminal Skills prerequisite, using Bash on macOS/Linux or PowerShell on Windows.
  3. Review the development environment guide and environment isolation guide when you need an editor, runtime, database, or project environment.
  4. Choose the module that matches the task or domain you want to understand. The modules can be studied independently; there is no required order among them. Two light recommendations apply: complete the Git module before modules that assume repository workflows, and complete the Markdown module before modules that ask for written documentation.
  5. Work through each module’s learning objectives, examples, practice sequence, and recommended reading. Type and modify the examples rather than only reading them.

These modules can also be used alongside the full curricula:

  • Git complements every curriculum in this textbook: all project work, collaboration, and capstone submission assumes version control.
  • HTML and CSS pair naturally with the JavaScript and TypeScript curricula, but the markup and style-sheet concepts are language-independent.
  • Markdown is the writing medium of every repository and pairs with any curriculum; its documentation workflows are language-independent.
  • R can complement Python and other languages used for data analysis. It also provides a separate statistical-computing workflow.
  • Regular expressions are used across all the language curricula for searching, validation, and text transformation, and are a daily tool in shell and editor workflows.
  • SQL complements nearly every language that reads from or writes to relational databases. The SQL module focuses on the query language and relational concepts, not on a specific database vendor or application framework.
  • Structured data formats appear throughout the full curricula: JSON in APIs and data files, YAML in CI and deployment configuration, and TOML in Python and Rust project files.
  • Web accessibility extends the HTML and CSS module and pairs with the JavaScript and TypeScript curricula; it is also a professional specialization in its own right.

Accessibility and learning approach

The modules follow the same accessibility-first approach as the rest of the textbook:

  • Examples are presented as text and are intended to be usable with a keyboard and screen reader.
  • Concepts are explained in prose as well as code; learners should not have to infer essential information from color, layout, or an image.
  • Web examples emphasize semantic HTML, meaningful labels, logical headings, keyboard access, and visible focus.
  • Data and visualization examples should provide text summaries or structured tables as alternatives to graphics.
  • Database examples explain query results through column names, row counts, and values rather than relying on a visual result grid alone.

No technology or editor is automatically accessible in every configuration. See the screen-reader-accessible GUI libraries and implementation guide for framework selection and testing guidance.

Scope and prerequisites

These are focused modules, not complete reference manuals. They introduce foundational ideas and direct learners to maintained documentation and additional reading. They do not attempt to teach every framework, database product, statistical method, or deployment workflow.

The modules assume basic computer use, file and folder navigation, and familiarity with the shared foundations material. They do not require prior experience with Git, HTML, CSS, Markdown, R, regular expressions, SQL, structured data formats, or web accessibility.

Section index

Use the Standalone Topics Index for a compact topic-by-topic reference.

Git and Version Control

Purpose

Git is the distributed version control system used by nearly all modern software development. It records the history of a project as a series of snapshots, lets multiple people work concurrently, and provides the mechanism for reviewing and reverting changes. This module introduces Git as a command-line workflow: repositories, commits, branches, remotes, and collaboration through pull requests, with attention to how each step reads in a non-visual environment.

Git is almost entirely text-based, which makes it unusually accessible — but its output can be verbose, and its mental model (a directed graph of commits) is usually taught visually. This module builds the model through linear history and textual output rather than diagrams.

Learning objectives

By the end of this module, learners should be able to explain what version control is and why it matters; initialize a repository and make commits with meaningful messages; read git status, git log, and git diff output; create, switch, and merge branches; resolve a simple merge conflict; connect a local repository to a remote and push and pull; open and review a pull request; and describe what HEAD, the staging area, and the working tree are.

The mental model

Git manages three areas:

  • Working tree: the files as they currently exist on disk.
  • Staging area (index): the set of changes selected to go into the next commit.
  • Repository history: the chain of committed snapshots.

A commit is a named snapshot of the staging area, linked to its parent commit. The history is a graph, but in ordinary work it behaves like a line: each new commit points back to the one before it. HEAD is a pointer to the commit currently checked out — usually the tip of the current branch.

Basic workflow

git init                     # create a repository in the current directory
git status                   # what is modified, staged, or untracked
git add README.md            # stage one file
git add -p                   # stage interactively, hunk by hunk
git commit -m "Add README"   # record a snapshot
git log --oneline            # compact history, one line per commit

Write commit messages as complete, imperative sentences: “Add input validation to the parser”, not “stuff”. The first line should stand alone; larger explanations go after a blank line. Good messages are how future readers — including screen reader users skimming history — understand the project.

Reading changes

git diff is the most important accessibility surface in Git. It prints changes as unified diff hunks: lines beginning with - were removed, lines beginning with + were added, and context lines are unchanged. Learn to read diffs linearly before relying on any visual diff tool.

git diff              # unstaged changes
git diff --staged     # what the next commit will contain
git diff main..task   # differences between two branches

Useful reading options:

  • git diff --word-diff shows changes within a line, which is often easier to follow by ear than whole-line replacement.
  • git log --stat summarizes which files each commit touched.
  • git show prints the full diff of a single commit.

Branching and merging

A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. Creating one is instant and cheap.

git switch -c fix-typo      # create and switch to a new branch
# ... edit and commit ...
git switch main             # return to main
git merge fix-typo          # bring the work in
git branch -d fix-typo      # delete the merged branch

A fast-forward merge simply moves the branch pointer. When both branches have diverged, Git creates a merge commit; when the same lines changed in both, it reports a conflict. Conflicts are marked in the file itself with <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers. Resolve by editing the file to the intended final text, removing the markers, staging the file, and committing. git status lists conflicted files; git diff shows the markers in context.

Remotes and collaboration

git clone https://github.com/example/project.git
git remote -v               # list configured remotes
git push origin main        # upload commits
git pull                    # fetch and merge others' commits
git fetch                   # download without merging

The standard hosted workflow (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) is:

  1. Fork or clone the repository.
  2. Create a topic branch.
  3. Commit changes with clear messages.
  4. Push the branch and open a pull request (PR).
  5. Respond to review comments, push follow-up commits, and merge after approval.

PR review is text-based: the diff, the comments, and the checks are all readable in a browser with a screen reader, or via the gh command-line tool (gh pr view, gh pr diff, gh pr checks), which many screen reader users prefer because everything stays in the terminal.

Undoing things

  • git restore file — discard unstaged changes to a file.
  • git restore --staged file — unstage without discarding.
  • git commit --amend — fix the most recent commit (before it has been pushed).
  • git revert <commit> — create a new commit that undoes an old one. Safe on shared branches.
  • git reset — move a branch pointer; prefer revert on pushed history.

Accessibility notes

  • Terminal-based Git is fully screen-reader compatible; prefer --oneline and --stat flags to keep output compact.
  • git add -p and interactive rebase are prompt-driven and work well with a linear reading flow.
  • Web-based review interfaces change frequently; the gh CLI provides a stable, textual alternative for PR workflows.
  • Never rely on color alone to interpret diffs — read the -/+ prefixes.

Practice sequence

  1. Initialize a repository, create three files, and make three separate commits, each touching one file.
  2. Read git log --oneline and git show HEAD aloud-in-your-head: confirm you can tell what each commit did.
  3. Edit two files, stage only one, and verify with git diff --staged versus git diff.
  4. Create a branch, make a commit, switch back, make a conflicting change on main, and resolve the merge conflict.
  5. Push a branch to a hosted remote and open a pull request; review it with gh pr diff.
  6. Use git revert to undo a commit and inspect the resulting history.

Recommended introductory books

  • Chacon, Scott, and Ben Straub. Pro Git, 2nd edition. Apress, 2014. The canonical, freely licensed reference; chapters 1–3 cover everything in this module. Free online book.
  • Withee, Sarah. Git For Dummies. Wiley, 2023. A gentler first pass if Pro Git feels dense on a first read.

Suggested use: work through Pro Git chapters 1–3 sequentially, then keep the rest as reference. Skim chapter 7 (Git tools) only after the practice sequence.

Further learning

  • Official Git documentation
  • GitHub CLI (gh) manual
  • Conventional Commits — a commit-message convention widely used in open source
  • Oh Shit, Git!?! — plain-language recipes for recovering from common mistakes

HTML and CSS: Structure and Presentation for the Web

Purpose

This introductory module explains how web documents are structured with HTML and presented with CSS. It is designed for learners who already understand basic files, folders, and text editing. It does not assume prior web-development experience.

Learning objectives

By the end of this module, learners should be able to explain the roles of HTML and CSS; create a semantic HTML document with a meaningful title, headings, paragraphs, links, lists, and form controls; distinguish semantic structure from visual presentation; associate labels with form controls; apply basic CSS selectors and box-model properties; and explain why accessibility belongs in document structure.

HTML: semantic document structure

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes the meaning and structure of web content. Elements are represented by tags and may contain text, attributes, and nested elements. Browsers construct a document object model from the markup.

Semantic elements communicate purpose. Use headings in a logical hierarchy, paragraphs for prose, lists for grouped items, links for navigation, buttons for actions, and labels for form controls. Prefer native HTML semantics over generic containers with improvised behavior.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Course Notes</title>
</head>
<body>
  <header>
    <h1>Course Notes</h1>
  </header>
  <main>
    <h2>Current topic</h2>
    <p>Semantic HTML describes the meaning of content.</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Structure content with meaningful elements.</li>
      <li>Use links for navigation.</li>
    </ul>
  </main>
</body>
</html>

The heading hierarchy should reflect the document outline. A heading is not simply a larger font. A screen-reader user may navigate directly by headings, links, landmarks, or form controls, so each must have a clear purpose.

CSS: presentation rules

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) describes how elements are presented. A rule consists of a selector and declarations. A declaration contains a property and value.

body {
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  line-height: 1.5;
  margin: 2rem;
}

main {
  max-width: 70ch;
}

a {
  text-decoration: underline;
}

Selectors identify elements. Properties describe presentation. The cascade resolves competing declarations based on origin, importance, specificity, and source order. The box model describes content, padding, border, and margin. Layout systems such as Flexbox and Grid support responsive page structure.

Accessibility principles

  • Use semantic HTML before adding ARIA attributes.
  • Preserve a logical heading hierarchy.
  • Provide descriptive link text and labels for all form controls.
  • Ensure keyboard access and visible focus.
  • Do not use color alone to communicate state or meaning.
  • Maintain sufficient text and interface contrast.
  • Avoid removing browser zoom or text-resizing capabilities.
  • Use alternative text for informative images; use empty alternative text for decorative images.
  • Ensure dynamic content changes are perceivable and do not unexpectedly move focus.
  • Test with keyboard navigation and screen readers, not only visual inspection.

Accessible HTML does not guarantee an accessible page. The complete interaction, browser behavior, CSS, and any JavaScript must be tested.

Practice sequence

  1. Identify the semantic elements in a supplied page and explain their roles.
  2. Create a page with one main heading, two subheadings, paragraphs, a list, and descriptive links.
  3. Add CSS for readable line length, spacing, and link distinction without relying on color alone.
  4. Inspect the page using keyboard navigation and a screen reader.
  5. Explain one difference between a semantic HTML element and a generic div.

Recommended introductory books

  • Robbins, Jennifer. Learning Web Design: A Beginner’s Guide to HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Web Graphics, 5th edition. O’Reilly Media, 2018. A broad introduction to web fundamentals, semantic HTML, CSS, responsive layouts, and web design tools. Publisher page.

Accessibility note: this is a visual-design-oriented book and may use diagrams, screenshots, and visual examples. Use it selectively for terminology and reference; this module’s semantic, keyboard-first, and screen-reader-oriented explanations remain the required learning path. Validate examples against current HTML and CSS standards.

Further learning

  • MDN HTML documentation
  • MDN CSS documentation
  • W3C Web Accessibility Initiative

Web Accessibility: ARIA, WCAG, and Accessible Design

Purpose

Web accessibility is the practice of building websites and applications that people can use regardless of disability — including blind and low-vision users who rely on screen readers, keyboard-only users, and users with cognitive or motor disabilities. This module introduces accessibility as an engineering discipline: the standards (WCAG), the technologies (semantic HTML, ARIA, CSS, and the accessibility tree), the testing workflow (keyboard first, then screen reader), and the legal and professional context.

This module extends the HTML and CSS module. It assumes learners can write semantic HTML and basic stylesheets, and builds the accessibility layer on top. For a curriculum aimed at visually impaired learners, accessibility is not merely a compliance topic: it is a domain in which blind developers are, with proper training, among the most credible experts in the industry.

Learning objectives

By the end of this module, learners should be able to explain how the accessibility tree connects the DOM to assistive technology; state the four WCAG principles (POUR) and give an example conformance technique for each; write semantic HTML that needs no ARIA; apply ARIA roles, states, and properties correctly and explain the first rule of ARIA; implement accessible forms, tables, and dialogs; design and test keyboard interaction, focus order, and visible focus; write text alternatives for images, charts, and controls; and conduct a basic screen-reader and keyboard audit of a web page.

How assistive technology sees the web

A screen reader does not read the rendered pixels; it reads the accessibility tree, a parallel structure derived from the DOM. Each element exposes a name (its accessible label), a role (what it is), a value (its current state, where applicable), and its state and properties (expanded, checked, disabled, required). Browsers compute this tree from native HTML semantics first, then from ARIA attributes where authors supply them.

This is why semantic HTML is the foundation: a native <button> automatically has role button, is focusable, responds to Enter and Space, and announces itself correctly. A <div onclick=...> has none of that, and no amount of styling will add it.

WCAG: the standard

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), published by the W3C, organize success criteria under four principles — POUR:

  • Perceivable: information must be available to sight, hearing, or touch. Examples: text alternatives for images, captions for video, sufficient contrast.
  • Operable: every function must be usable without requiring specific physical abilities. Examples: full keyboard operability, no time limits without a way to extend, no seizure-inducing content.
  • Understandable: content and controls must be predictable. Examples: consistent navigation, labeled inputs, clear error messages.
  • Robust: content must work with current and future assistive technology. Examples: valid markup, correct name/role/value.

WCAG 2.1 and 2.2 define levels A, AA, and AAA. Level AA is the common legal and contractual target (including under the ADA, Section 508, and the European Accessibility Act). Learn the AA criteria relevant to your work; do not try to memorize all of them at once.

Semantic HTML first

The most effective accessibility technique is choosing the right element:

  • <button> for actions, <a href> for navigation — never a clickable <div>.
  • <nav>, <main>, <header>, <footer>, <section>, <article> for landmarks, which screen readers expose for direct navigation.
  • One <h1> per page and a heading hierarchy without gaps.
  • <label for="id"> bound to every form control.
  • <table> with <th scope="col|row"> for genuine data tables — never for layout.
  • Native <details>/<summary> for disclosure widgets when possible.

ARIA: when HTML is not enough

ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) supplies semantics the platform does not. Its first rule: do not use ARIA if a native element would work — incorrect ARIA is worse than none.

<!-- Bad: a div with a click handler has no role, no focus, no keyboard support -->
<div class="btn" onclick="save()">Save</div>

<!-- Good: native semantics -->
<button type="button" onclick="save()">Save</button>

<!-- Necessary ARIA: a tabbed interface has no single native element -->
<div role="tablist">
  <button role="tab" aria-selected="true" aria-controls="panel-1" id="tab-1">Details</button>
  ...
</div>
<div role="tabpanel" id="panel-1" aria-labelledby="tab-1">...</div>

Key attribute families:

  • Roles: tab, dialog, alert, switch, progressbar, grid.
  • States: aria-expanded, aria-checked, aria-disabled, aria-current.
  • Properties: aria-label and aria-labelledby (naming), aria-describedby (description), aria-live (announcing dynamic updates).

aria-live regions are how a page reports changes without a page load: form validation results, status messages, new chat lines. Use role="status" (polite) or role="alert" (assertive) rather than raw aria-live values where possible.

Keyboard and focus

  • Everything clickable must be reachable with Tab and operable with Enter, Space, and arrow keys as appropriate.
  • Manage focus in scripts: when a dialog opens, move focus into it; when it closes, restore focus to the trigger; trap focus inside while it is open (use the native <dialog> element, which does much of this for you).
  • Never remove the focus outline without providing an equally visible replacement style.
  • Respect prefers-reduced-motion in animations.
  • Provide a “skip to main content” link as the first focusable element on pages with long navigation.

Forms and errors

<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input id="email" type="email" autocomplete="email"
       aria-describedby="email-hint email-error">
<p id="email-hint">We send one confirmation message.</p>
<p id="email-error" role="alert">Enter an address in the name@example.com format.</p>

Errors must be text, associated with the field, and announced. Do not report errors by color or icon alone, and do not rely on placeholder text as the only label.

Testing workflow

  1. Unplug the mouse (figuratively): navigate the page with Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, and arrow keys only.
  2. Screen-reader pass: test with at least NVDA (free, Windows) and VoiceOver (built into macOS and iOS); JAWS on Windows is also common. Learn the headings list, links list, and form-controls list commands — those are how real users audit a page.
  3. Automated scan: axe DevTools, Lighthouse, or WAVE catch roughly a third of issues (missing alt text, contrast, unlabeled controls). Automation finds violations, not usability.
  4. Zoom and reflow: at 200% zoom and 320px width, no content may be lost or require two-dimensional scrolling (WCAG 1.4.10).
  5. Manual judgment: the remaining two-thirds of accessibility problems — focus order, announcement timing, meaningful alt text — require a human, and this is where trained screen-reader users have a professional edge.

Accessibility as a career path

Digital accessibility is a growing, undersupplied specialty: auditors, remediation engineers, accessibility QA, and inclusive-design consultants. Professional credentials include the IAAP Certified Professional in Accessibility Core Competencies (CPACC) and Web Accessibility Specialist (WAS). Blind professionals are well represented — and highly sought after — in this field.

Practice sequence

  1. Take a page built with <div> buttons and rebuild it with semantic elements; verify the tab order and announcements improve with no JavaScript changes.
  2. Add a complete ARIA tabbed interface with correct roving tabindex and arrow-key navigation, testing entirely by keyboard.
  3. Build a form with labeled fields, hint text, and an aria-live error region; trigger each error and confirm it is announced.
  4. Run an axe or Lighthouse scan on a real page, fix every reported issue, and list two issues the scan missed that you found by keyboard testing.
  5. Write alt text for five images of increasing complexity, including one chart, using a short description plus a data table for the chart.
  6. Audit one public website with NVDA’s headings and links lists and write a one-page findings memo.

Recommended introductory books

  • W3C Web Accessibility Initiative. Web Accessibility Perspectives and the WCAG quick reference. Free, and the authoritative mapping of requirements to techniques. WCAG 2 quick reference.
  • Gilbert, Regine. Inclusive Design for a Digital World. Apress, 2019. A practitioner-oriented introduction covering design and code.
  • Kalbag, Laura. Accessibility for Everyone. A Book Apart, 2017. A short, plain-language orientation to the whole discipline, useful before diving into standards.

Suggested use: start with Accessibility for Everyone for the framing, then work directly from the WCAG quick reference while coding — it is the reference you will actually use professionally. Use the Perspectives videos to understand user impact.

Further learning

  • W3C WAI: Introduction to Web Accessibility
  • ARIA Authoring Practices Guide — tested interaction patterns for widgets
  • MDN Accessibility documentation
  • Deque axe DevTools and WebAIM — testing tools and articles
  • NVDA screen reader — free, open source, and scriptable

Markdown: Technical Documentation

Purpose

Markdown is a lightweight plain-text markup language used to write documentation, README files, technical notes, and web content. It is the default documentation format of GitHub, most package registries, static site generators, and developer communication tools. This module introduces Markdown as a practical documentation skill, with emphasis on writing documents that are both easy to maintain and easy to navigate with a screen reader.

Markdown is particularly well suited to non-visual workflows. Its source is plain text, its syntax is a small set of punctuation conventions, and its structure is expressed linearly rather than spatially. A screen reader user can both author and verify Markdown without any visual rendering.

Learning objectives

By the end of this module, learners should be able to explain where Markdown is used and why it dominates technical documentation; write headings, paragraphs, lists, links, images, code blocks, tables, and blockquotes; distinguish inline from reference-style links; write documents with a single top-level heading and a logical heading hierarchy; use semantic alternatives (descriptive link text, alt text, tables with headers); explain the differences between CommonMark, GitHub Flavored Markdown, and MultiMarkdown; and choose and use a linting or preview tool appropriate to a screen-reader workflow.

Why Markdown for documentation

  • Plain text: version-controllable with Git, diffable line by line, and readable in any editor or terminal.
  • Portable: renders on GitHub, GitLab, npm, PyPI, Read the Docs, Discourse, Slack, and hundreds of other tools.
  • Convertable: Pandoc and static site generators transform Markdown into HTML, PDF, EPUB, and Word formats.
  • Low syntax cost: the punctuation marks carry meaning, so documents remain readable even as raw text.

Core syntax

Headings

Headings are written with leading hash marks. The number of hash marks is the heading level.

# Document title (h1)
## Section (h2)
### Subsection (h3)

Use exactly one h1 per document and never skip levels (for example, h2 directly to h4). Screen readers navigate by heading level, so a clean hierarchy is an accessibility feature of the document itself.

Paragraphs and emphasis

Paragraphs are separated by blank lines. Within a line, wrap text in single asterisks for emphasis and double asterisks for strong importance.

This is a paragraph with *emphasis* and **strong importance**.

Lists

Unordered lists use hyphens; ordered lists use numbers followed by periods. Nested items are indented by two to four spaces.

- First item
- Second item
  - Nested item

1. Install the runtime
2. Configure the environment
3. Run the test suite

Links and images

Inline links place the text in square brackets and the target in parentheses. Reference-style links move targets to the bottom of the document, which keeps prose readable when read aloud.

See the [installation guide](https://example.com/install) for details.

See the [installation guide][install] for details.

[install]: https://example.com/install

Images use the same syntax with a leading exclamation mark. The alt text is what a screen reader announces, so describe the image’s content or purpose.

![Bar chart of test coverage rising from 40 to 90 percent](coverage.png)

Write link text that makes sense out of context. Avoid bare URLs and phrases like “click here” or “this link”; screen reader users often pull up a list of links and read it in isolation.

Code

Inline code uses backticks; fenced code blocks use triple backticks, with a language identifier that enables syntax highlighting on renderers that support it.

Run `npm install` before building.

```python
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}"
```

Blockquotes and horizontal rules

> Quoted material goes here.

---

Tables (GitHub Flavored Markdown)

Tables use pipes and a separator row. Include a header row; screen readers announce column headers as the reader moves between cells.

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `git status` | Show working tree state |
| `git log` | Show commit history |

Tables are the least screen-reader-friendly Markdown structure. For anything beyond a few rows, consider a definition list or a sequence of short headings and paragraphs instead.

Escaping

Prefix a literal punctuation character with a backslash to prevent it from being interpreted as syntax: \*not emphasis\*.

Dialects and specifications

  • CommonMark is the baseline specification most renderers implement.
  • GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM) extends CommonMark with tables, task lists, strikethrough, and automatic linking. It is the practical standard for repository documentation.
  • MultiMarkdown and Pandoc Markdown add footnotes, citations, and definition lists, and are common in academic and publishing workflows.

When writing for an unknown renderer, stay within CommonMark plus tables.

Screen-reader workflow

  • Read documents by heading navigation to check structure before checking content.
  • Use reference-style links in long documents so prose reads cleanly.
  • Verify that every image has alt text and every link has descriptive text.
  • Prefer lists and headings over ASCII layout, aligned columns, and horizontal spacing, which do not survive linear reading.
  • A linter such as markdownlint catches broken nesting, missing alt text, and inconsistent heading levels without requiring visual preview.

Practice sequence

  1. Write a README for a small script with one h1, three h2 sections, and a bulleted requirements list.
  2. Add a fenced code block with a language identifier, then a table of three commands.
  3. Convert three inline links to reference-style links and re-read the document by headings and links list.
  4. Add an image with descriptive alt text, then temporarily rename the image file to confirm the alt text is what carries the meaning.
  5. Run markdownlint (or an equivalent) on the document and fix every warning.
  6. Use Pandoc to convert the document to HTML and inspect the heading structure.

Recommended introductory books

  • MacFarlane, John. Pandoc User’s Guide. Freely available and the definitive reference for Markdown’s extensions and conversion workflows. Free online manual.
  • LeBlanc, David. The Markdown Guide. 2020. A free, syntax-focused reference organized by element, useful as a lookup companion. Free online book.

Suggested use: keep the Markdown Guide open as a syntax reference while writing; consult the Pandoc manual when converting documents to other formats.

Further learning

  • CommonMark specification
  • GitHub Flavored Markdown spec
  • markdownlint
  • Semantic line breaks — a convention that makes Markdown diffs and screen-reader line navigation more meaningful

R: Statistical Computing

Purpose

R is a programming language and environment designed for statistical computing, data analysis, and graphics. It is widely used in research, public health, economics, social science, government, and industry analytics. This module introduces R as a programming language for reproducible data work.

Learning objectives

By the end of this module, learners should be able to describe the role of R in statistical computing; assign values and recognize common data types; create and inspect vectors, lists, matrices, and data frames; use indexing and basic functions; summarize a small dataset; read a delimited data file; and explain reproducible scripts and documented analysis.

R as a language and environment

R provides an interactive console, a language runtime, a large package ecosystem, and tools for statistical analysis and visualization. The R Project maintains the language and core environment. Posit develops widely used products such as RStudio, but R and RStudio are distinct: R is the language and runtime; RStudio is an IDE that can support R workflows.

Core values and objects

R has numeric, integer, character, logical, complex, and other specialized data types. Assignment is commonly written with the left-arrow operator, though equals is also accepted in many contexts.

student_name <- "Avery"
scores <- c(82, 91, 76, 88)
