mean_score <- mean(scores)
score_count <- length(scores)

print(mean_score)
print(score_count)

The c() function combines values into a vector. Vectors are central to R’s model of data. Many operations are vectorized, meaning an operation can apply across a vector without writing an explicit loop.

Data structures

  • Vector: one-dimensional collection whose elements share a common type.
  • List: collection that can contain elements of different types and structures.
  • Matrix: two-dimensional homogeneous data structure.
  • Array: multidimensional homogeneous data structure.
  • Data frame: tabular structure whose columns may have different types.
  • Factor: categorical data with defined levels.

Indexing in R commonly begins at 1. Square brackets select elements or subsets. The dollar-sign operator is often used to access a named data-frame column or list element.

Functions and analysis

Functions accept arguments and return values. R includes built-in functions for summary statistics, sorting, aggregation, and modeling. Packages extend the language for specialized methods. Package versions and data sources should be recorded so analyses can be reproduced.

scores <- c(82, 91, 76, 88)

summary(scores)
median(scores)
sd(scores)

Statistical summaries should be interpreted in context. A numerical result is not automatically evidence of a meaningful effect or causal relationship.

Data import and reproducibility

Delimited files are common sources of tabular data. Learners should inspect column names, data types, missing values, and row counts before analysis. Base R includes read.csv() for common CSV files. Larger workflows may use maintained packages such as readr or data.table.

Keep analysis steps in scripts or documented notebooks rather than relying only on a sequence of commands entered interactively. Record package versions, data provenance, assumptions, and transformations. Protect confidential or personally identifying data.

Accessibility and visualization

R’s text console and printed summaries support text-first analysis. Graphics and IDE data viewers may require additional accessibility evaluation. A chart should not be the only representation of a result: provide a textual description, table, or statistical summary where appropriate. Do not require learners to infer exact values from color or spatial position alone.

Practice sequence

  1. Create a numeric vector and calculate its mean, median, minimum, and maximum.
  2. Build a data frame with names and scores.
  3. Select one column and identify the number of observations.
  4. Read a CSV file and inspect its dimensions and column names.
  5. Write a short paragraph interpreting the summary without overstating what the data establish.

Recommended introductory books

  • Grolemund, Garrett. Hands-On Programming with R. O’Reilly Media, 2014. Written for readers without programming experience; introduces R through small projects, data objects, functions, scripts, and practical analysis. The full text is freely available online. Free book and publisher page.
  • Wickham, Hadley, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund. R for Data Science, 2nd edition. O’Reilly Media, 2023. A free guide to importing, transforming, visualizing, and communicating data with the tidyverse. Free online book.

Suggested use: start with Hands-On Programming with R if programming itself is new. Use R for Data Science as a follow-on for data analysis workflows. The second book focuses on the tidyverse ecosystem and is not a substitute for learning base R fundamentals.

Further learning

  • The R Project
  • An Introduction to R
  • RStudio / Posit documentation

Regular Expressions

Purpose

A regular expression (regex) is a compact pattern language for describing sets of text: finding, extracting, validating, and replacing strings that share a structure. Regex is supported in every mainstream language (Python re, JavaScript, Java, .NET, Go, Rust), in editors, in command-line tools such as grep and sed, and in many screen-reader and text-processing workflows. This module introduces the core pattern syntax, the main dialect differences, and the discipline of writing patterns that are readable and testable.

Regex is a high-leverage skill for non-visual computing: a single well-written pattern can accomplish text restructuring that would otherwise require visually scanning a document.

Learning objectives

By the end of this module, learners should be able to explain what a regex matches and where regex is and is not appropriate; use literals, character classes, quantifiers, anchors, groups, and alternation; use capture groups and backreferences to extract and restructure text; read and apply common flags such as case-insensitive and multiline matching; distinguish the major dialects (PCRE, POSIX, and language-specific variants); use an online tester and command-line tools to develop patterns; and recognize the classic pitfalls, including catastrophic backtracking and using regex on nested structures.

Literals, metacharacters, and escapes

Most characters match themselves. A small set are metacharacters: . ^ $ * + ? ( ) [ ] { } | \ . Prefix a metacharacter with a backslash to match it literally — for example, \. matches a period.

Character classes

[abc]        one of the characters a, b, or c
[a-z0-9]     any lowercase letter or digit
[^abc]       any character except a, b, or c
\d           a digit (same as [0-9] in most dialects)
\w           a word character (letter, digit, underscore)
\s           whitespace
.            any character except newline

Negated classes and [^...] are the workhorses of “match until” patterns. \b is a word boundary: \bcat\b matches the word “cat” but not “category”.

Quantifiers and greediness

*        zero or more
+        one or more
?        zero or one
{3}      exactly three
{2,5}    between two and five

Quantifiers are greedy by default: they consume as much as possible. Adding ? makes them lazy: .*? stops at the first possible match. Greediness is the single most common source of surprising matches — <.*> against <a> <b> matches the whole string, while <.*?> matches <a>.

Anchors, alternation, and grouping

^cat$        the entire line is exactly "cat" (with multiline flag)
cat|dog      "cat" or "dog"
(colou?r)    group: matches "color" or "colour"
(?:cat)      non-capturing group

Parentheses create capture groups, which number from 1 in order of opening parenthesis. Group 0 is the whole match. Backreferences (\1) and, in some dialects, named groups ((?P<year>\d{4})) make patterns self-documenting and replacements precise.

Extraction and replacement

The classic restructuring pattern: capture the pieces, then rebuild them.

import re

text = "Published 2026-03-14; revised 2026-09-02."
pattern = r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})"
matches = re.findall(pattern, text)          # [('2026','03','14'), ...]
swapped = re.sub(pattern, r"\2/\3/\1", text) # 03/14/2026

Flags

  • i — case-insensitive matching.
  • m — ^ and $ match at line boundaries, not just string boundaries.
  • s — . also matches newlines.
  • x — verbose mode: whitespace and # comments in the pattern are ignored. Verbose mode is the most effective accessibility feature regex has; use it for any nontrivial pattern.
pattern = re.compile(r"""
    (\d{4})   # year
    -         # separator
    (\d{2})   # month
    -         # separator
    (\d{2})   # day
""", re.VERBOSE)

Dialects and tooling

  • PCRE (Perl-compatible) is the most feature-rich dialect and the de facto reference; Python, PHP, and most editors are close to it.
  • POSIX regex (as in basic grep) is more limited; use grep -E for extended syntax.
  • RE2 (Go, and optional elsewhere) forbids backreferences in exchange for guaranteed linear-time matching.
  • JavaScript regex lacks lookbehind in older engines and uses /pattern/flags literals.

Develop patterns interactively in an online tester such as regex101 (which explains each token in plain language — a genuinely screen-reader-friendly explanation mode), then confirm behavior in the target language, because dialects differ. On the command line, grep -E, sed -E, and rg (ripgrep) are the daily tools.

Pitfalls and discipline

  • Regex is the wrong tool for nested or structured formats such as HTML, JSON, or XML. Use a parser.
  • Catastrophic backtracking: nested quantifiers like (a+)+ can make matching time explode. Prefer explicit, anchored patterns.
  • Validation: a regex can confirm shape, not correctness. \d{5} matches a five-digit string; it does not confirm it is a real postal code.
  • Readability: prefer verbose mode, named groups, and comments. A pattern no one can read is a bug waiting to happen.

Practice sequence

  1. Use grep -E to find every line in a text file containing a four-digit year.
  2. Write a pattern that matches US phone numbers in both 555-1234 and (555) 555-1234 formats; test it in regex101.
  3. Extract all email-shaped strings from a document and print only the domain parts, using a capture group.
  4. Use sed -E to convert YYYY-MM-DD dates in a file to MM/DD/YYYY.
  5. Rewrite one dense one-line pattern in verbose mode with comments, and confirm it still matches the same strings.
  6. Deliberately construct a nested-quantifier pattern, observe the slowdown on a long input, then fix it.

Recommended introductory books

  • Goyvaerts, Jan, and Steven Levithan. Regular Expressions Cookbook, 2nd edition. O’Reilly Media, 2012. Task-oriented recipes (dates, URLs, identifiers) with dialect-specific variants; ideal as a lookup reference after the fundamentals.
  • Friedl, Jeffrey E. F. Mastering Regular Expressions, 3rd edition. O’Reilly Media, 2006. The deep treatment of how regex engines work, including backtracking and efficiency.

Suggested use: learn the syntax from any tutorial or the regex101 explanation panel, then use the Cookbook as your day-to-day reference. Read Mastering Regular Expressions only if you need to debug performance or engine behavior.

Further learning

  • regex101 — interactive tester with plain-language token explanations
  • Regular-Expressions.info — comprehensive syntax reference
  • Python re module documentation
  • MDN: Regular Expressions (JavaScript)

SQL: Relational Databases

Purpose

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language used to define, query, and manipulate data in relational database systems. This module introduces relational concepts and the core query patterns used to retrieve and maintain structured data.

Learning objectives

By the end of this module, learners should be able to explain tables, rows, columns, primary keys, and foreign keys; write a basic SELECT query with filtering and sorting; use aggregate functions and GROUP BY; combine related tables with joins; explain data definition and manipulation; describe transactions and integrity constraints; and recognize parameterized queries and least-privilege access.

Relational database concepts

A relational database organizes information into tables. Each table has columns that define attributes and rows that represent records. A primary key identifies a row. A foreign key expresses a relationship to a key in another table.

A database schema defines tables, columns, types, constraints, and relationships. Normalization is a design discipline that reduces unnecessary duplication and update anomalies. The appropriate degree of normalization depends on the application and its performance requirements.

Querying data

The SELECT statement retrieves data. WHERE filters rows, ORDER BY sorts results, and LIMIT restricts the number of rows returned in systems that support that syntax.

SELECT student_name, score
FROM student_scores
WHERE score >= 80
ORDER BY score DESC;

SQL is declarative: a query describes the result to retrieve, while the database engine chooses an execution plan. Result order is not guaranteed unless an explicit ORDER BY is included.

Aggregation

Aggregate functions summarize groups of rows. Common functions include COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX.

SELECT course_id, AVG(score) AS average_score
FROM student_scores
GROUP BY course_id
ORDER BY course_id;

GROUP BY forms groups for aggregation. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, while WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. NULL represents missing or unknown information and requires careful handling; ordinary equality comparisons do not test for null values.

Joining tables

Joins combine rows from related tables. An inner join returns matching rows. A left join preserves all rows from the left table and supplies nulls for unmatched right-side columns. Join conditions should use the intended keys; incorrect joins can multiply rows or silently omit records.

SELECT students.student_name, enrollments.course_id
FROM students
INNER JOIN enrollments
  ON students.student_id = enrollments.student_id;

Data definition and manipulation

  • CREATE TABLE defines a table.
  • ALTER TABLE changes a table definition.
  • INSERT adds rows.
  • UPDATE modifies rows.
  • DELETE removes rows.
  • DROP removes database objects.

Data-changing statements should be tested carefully, especially when they lack a restrictive WHERE clause. Use transactions when a group of changes must succeed or fail together. Understand the database’s transaction and isolation behavior before relying on assumptions.

Security and responsible use

Use parameterized queries rather than constructing SQL by concatenating untrusted input. Grant applications only the database permissions they require. Avoid storing plaintext passwords or exposing confidential records in logs and examples. Do not run destructive queries against production data during practice. Use an isolated training database with synthetic data.

Accessibility

A database client should expose query editors, result grids, errors, and schema navigation through keyboard and assistive technology. A visual result grid should not be the only way to inspect results; learners should be able to retrieve rows as text or another accessible representation. Explain query output in terms of column names, row counts, and values.

Practice sequence

  1. Create or inspect a table with a primary key.
  2. Select chosen columns and filter rows.
  3. Sort results explicitly.
  4. Calculate a group average with GROUP BY.
  5. Join two tables using a foreign-key relationship.
  6. Explain how a parameterized query protects user-supplied values.

Recommended introductory books

  • Beaulieu, Alan. Learning SQL, 3rd edition. O’Reilly Media, 2020. A beginner-oriented introduction to relational database concepts, schema creation, data manipulation, joins, and querying. Publisher page.
  • Viescas, John L. SQL Queries for Mere Mortals: A Hands-On Guide to Data Manipulation in SQL, 4th edition. Addison-Wesley Professional, 2018. A step-by-step treatment of relational thinking and query construction. Publisher page.

Suggested use: Learning SQL is a suitable primary companion for the module. SQL Queries for Mere Mortals provides additional practice in reasoning about queries and relational structures. Both books discuss particular database implementations; SQL dialects differ, so check syntax against the database engine used in a project.

Further learning

  • PostgreSQL documentation
  • SQLite documentation
  • SQL language reference in Microsoft Learn

Structured Data Formats: JSON, YAML, and TOML

Purpose

Modern software exchanges configuration and data through a small set of text formats: JSON for APIs and data interchange, YAML for infrastructure and pipeline configuration, and TOML for application and tool configuration. None of these is a programming language, but fluency in them is a daily professional requirement. This module introduces the syntax, data model, and appropriate use of each format, and the errors that most commonly occur when writing them.

All three formats are plain text and therefore fully workable with a screen reader. The module pays particular attention to indentation-sensitive syntax (YAML), which is the main accessibility pitfall, and to validation tooling that catches mistakes without visual inspection.

Learning objectives

By the end of this module, learners should be able to read and write valid JSON, including nested objects and arrays; read and write YAML, including lists, mappings, and multi-line strings; read and write TOML, including tables and arrays of tables; choose the appropriate format for a given task and justify the choice; validate files with the appropriate schema or linting tool; and recognize the characteristic failure modes of each format (trailing commas in JSON, indentation errors in YAML, mis-nested tables in TOML).

JSON

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) has exactly six value types: string, number, boolean (true/false), null, object, and array. Strings use double quotes; object keys must be strings; no comments, no trailing commas.

{
  "name": "avery",
  "roles": ["student", "tutor"],
  "active": true,
  "score": 91.5,
  "address": {
    "city": "Denver",
    "state": "CO"
  },
  "courses": [
    { "title": "Algorithms", "grade": "A" },
    { "title": "Databases", "grade": "B+" }
  ]
}

Reading rules of thumb:

  • Objects {} are unordered key→value mappings; arrays [] are ordered lists.
  • Nesting is unlimited, but deeply nested JSON is hard to navigate by ear — flatten structures where you control the schema.
  • JSON has no date type; dates are strings, conventionally ISO 8601 (2026-11-11T09:30:00Z).

Tooling: jq for querying and transforming JSON in the terminal (jq '.courses[].title' file.json), and JSON Schema for validating structure. Most editors and linters detect trailing commas and unquoted keys.

YAML

YAML is indentation-based: nesting is expressed with spaces (never tabs). It is a superset of JSON in most implementations, and is the standard format for GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, Docker Compose, Ansible, and countless CI systems.

name: curriculum-build
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
schedule:
  - day: monday
    topic: git
  - day: wednesday
    topic: testing
notes: >
  Folded scalar: newlines become spaces.
raw: |
  Literal block: newlines are preserved.

Key syntax:

  • Mappings: key: value, one per line; nested keys are indented (commonly two spaces).
  • Sequences: - item lines, or inline [a, b].
  • Scalars: usually unquoted; quote when the value could be misread (for example, "on", "no", "3.10" — YAML 1.1 treats some unquoted words and version-like strings as booleans or numbers).
  • Block scalars: > folds newlines into spaces; | preserves them.
  • Anchors and aliases (&base, *base) reuse blocks; merge keys (<<: *base) combine mappings.

YAML’s indentation sensitivity is its main hazard in a non-visual workflow: a one-space error silently changes the structure. Mitigate it by (1) using an editor that shows indentation levels audibly or via status information, (2) running a YAML parser (yq, or python -c "import yaml, sys; yaml.safe_load(sys.stdin)") after every edit, and (3) validating against the tool’s schema (for example, actionlint for GitHub Actions). Where a choice exists, JSON or TOML is often the safer authoring format.

TOML

TOML (Tom’s Obvious, Minimal Language) is designed for application configuration: explicit, section-based, and insensitive to indentation. It is the format of Cargo.toml (Rust), pyproject.toml (Python), and Go modules.

title = "Curriculum settings"

[author]
name = "Avery"
roles = ["student", "tutor"]

[build]
target = "web"
flags = ["--verbose", "--watch"]

[[courses]]
title = "Algorithms"
grade = "A"

[[courses]]
title = "Databases"
grade = "B+"

Key syntax:

  • Key/value pairs at the top level or inside [table] sections.
  • Sub-tables use dotted names: [build.options] nests under [build].
  • Arrays of tables use [[name]]; each occurrence appends one element.
  • Types: strings (double quotes, or single quotes for literal strings), integers, floats, booleans, arrays, inline tables ({ x = 1 }), and a native date/time type — a genuine advantage over JSON.
  • Multiline strings use triple quotes; comments start with #.

TOML’s error messages from standard parsers are precise and line-numbered, which makes it the most screen-reader-friendly of the three formats to debug.

Choosing a format

  • JSON: machine-to-machine interchange, API payloads, data files consumed by code. No comments makes it poor for hand-edited configuration.
  • YAML: configuration written and read by humans in DevOps/CI contexts, especially where a tool mandates it. Powerful but indentation-fragile.
  • TOML: application configuration with a schema the author controls; explicit and robust, but less common in interchange.

Practice sequence

  1. Write a JSON file describing a course catalog (three courses, each with topics and a reading list), then query it with jq to print only course titles.
  2. Introduce a trailing comma and an unquoted key; run a JSON validator and read the error messages.
  3. Rewrite the same data in YAML, then deliberately break the indentation of one nested list and observe what the parser reports.
  4. Rewrite the data a third time in TOML using arrays of tables, and add comments explaining each section.
  5. Validate a GitHub Actions workflow with actionlint (or any schema validator) and fix every reported problem.
  6. Write a short paragraph arguing which of the three formats you would choose for a new tool’s configuration file, and why.

Recommended introductory books

  • Tom Preston-Werner, Pradyun Gedam, et al. TOML v1.0.0 specification. Short, free, and readable end to end. Specification.
  • YAML and JSON are best learned from their official specifications and tutorials rather than books: the YAML specification and Learn YAML in Y Minutes, plus MDN on JSON.
  • Hiltgen, Sam. jq in Action. Manning (forthcoming/current editions). For learners who want terminal-side JSON querying as a daily skill; the jq manual is free and comprehensive.

Suggested use: the specifications are short enough to be the primary texts. Use a cookbook-style resource (Learn X in Y Minutes) for a first pass, then keep the TOML and jq references at hand.

Further learning

  • JSON specification (ECMA-404)
  • JSON Schema
  • yq — command-line YAML/JSON/TOML processor
  • actionlint — GitHub Actions workflow validator

Teacher’s Guides for Each Course

Use these guides to plan instruction, adapt the course for learners who use assistive technology, teach language-specific concepts, assess learning, and prepare the development environment. Each guide supplements the corresponding curriculum overview and lessons.

Full language curricula

  • C Teacher’s Guide
  • C# Teacher’s Guide
  • C++ Teacher’s Guide
  • Go Teacher’s Guide
  • Java Teacher’s Guide
  • JavaScript Teacher’s Guide
  • Julia Teacher’s Guide
  • Kotlin Teacher’s Guide
  • Lua Teacher’s Guide
  • Python Teacher’s Guide
  • Rust Teacher’s Guide
  • Swift Teacher’s Guide
