The guides are ordered alphabetically by language name. The standalone HTML/CSS, R, and SQL modules are focused technology resources rather than full language curricula, so they are not included in this language-guide set.

C Teacher’s Guide

Purpose and course context

This guide supports instructors teaching the C curriculum to beginning programmers, including blind and visually impaired learners using screen readers, braille displays, magnification, keyboard navigation, or combinations of access technology. It supplements the C curriculum overview, complete lessons, and topic index.

The course targets C17 and a GCC or Clang workflow. C is a compiled procedural language in which learners work directly with explicit types, arrays, structs, pointers, memory lifetimes, and return-code-based error handling. Do not treat C as merely Python with different punctuation: its model of memory and program execution is a central learning objective.

Outcomes and sequence

Follow Units 0–11 in order, after the shared Computing Foundations Primer and Terminal Skills prerequisite. Learners should be able to create and compile a project, interpret compiler diagnostics, use scalar types and expressions, implement decisions and loops, work with arrays and strings, define functions and structs, reason about pointers and object lifetimes, process files, check return values, test behavior, and complete the capstone.

Use the same lesson rhythm throughout: state the objective; define vocabulary; explain the code’s structure and punctuation; ask for a prediction; compile and run; inspect output and diagnostics; modify one feature; and ask the learner to explain the result.

Toolchain and compilation

Use a C17-capable GCC or Clang compiler. The curriculum’s representative command is:

cc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -g main.c -o main
./main

Explain each compiler option: language standard, warnings, debug information, source input, and output executable. Compile after small changes rather than accumulating many errors. Teach the learner to read the first diagnostic, identify its file and line, navigate directly to that location, and distinguish a warning from an error. Warnings are instructional feedback; do not normalize ignoring them.

Teaching C’s distinctive concepts

Types, expressions, and input

C does not provide Python-style automatic conversion for every operation. Teach integer division, signed and unsigned values, floating-point representation, integer promotions, and explicit conversions with small examples. Use format specifiers carefully and explain that a mismatch between a format string and the corresponding argument can cause undefined behavior. Validate input results; never assume a conversion succeeded merely because a prompt was displayed.

Arrays, strings, and bounds

An array is a fixed-size contiguous sequence; it does not carry a runtime length that can safely be recovered from an arbitrary pointer. A C string is a character sequence terminated by a null character. Teach the distinction between array capacity, current string length, and the terminating null byte. Make bounds checks explicit and use size-aware library operations. Do not teach unsafe input functions or imply that a buffer automatically expands.

Pointers, structs, and lifetime

Introduce addresses and indirection with a stable verbal model: a pointer stores an address, and dereferencing accesses the object at that address. Distinguish a pointer from the object it points to. Teach null pointers, initialization, pointer arithmetic limits, and the lifetime of automatic, static, and dynamically allocated objects. Every allocation needs a clear ownership and release plan; pair allocation and deallocation in the same documented responsibility. Do not present a pointer as an integer or suggest that every pointer is safe to dereference.

Use structs to model named records. Prefer named fields over parallel arrays when they improve the learner’s ability to inspect and explain a record. Explain that passing a struct by value copies it, while passing a pointer permits access to the original object.

Errors and files

C has no built-in exception mechanism. Teach functions’ return values, status codes, output parameters, and relevant library error indicators. Check the result of file opening, reading, writing, and closing operations. Make failure paths explicit and ensure resources are released on every path. JSON persistence in the course uses a documented external library; distinguish library functionality from the C standard library and explain its build/link requirements.

Accessibility and classroom delivery

  • Keep demonstrations and assessments text-first; make terminal output and compiler diagnostics available as selectable text.
  • Describe braces, parentheses, brackets, pointer operators, ampersands, semicolons, and nesting explicitly when first introduced.
  • Teach editor navigation by line, symbol, diagnostic, and file; provide keyboard equivalents for every essential action.
  • Let learners configure punctuation verbosity and braille output to match their needs.
  • Avoid visual memory diagrams as the only explanation. Describe memory regions, addresses, array positions, and ownership verbally or with structured text.
  • Do not require a visual debugger, graphical IDE feature, or GUI-only workflow without an equivalent accessible route.
  • Allow time for navigating compiler output and reviewing punctuation; assess conceptual understanding separately from navigation speed.

A text interface is not automatically accessible. Test the actual compiler, terminal, editor, and assistive-technology combination used in class.

Assessment and common misconceptions

Assess compilation, runtime behavior, reasoning, and safety separately. Ask learners to explain array bounds, string termination, pointer validity, object lifetime, and the consequences of unchecked input. Include normal, boundary, and invalid-input tests. Useful debugging tasks include a format-specifier mismatch, an off-by-one loop, a failed file open, and a pointer that is not initialized.

Do not equate a successful compile with correctness or memory safety. The repository’s example checks, where available, establish only their documented scope; they do not replace behavioral tests or hands-on accessibility validation.

Differentiation and pacing

Some learners will need additional practice with punctuation, nested blocks, compiler invocation, or terminal navigation. Others may be ready for deeper work on const-correctness, allocation strategies, or API contracts. Keep the learning objective constant while varying the amount of scaffolding, number of examples, and time allowed. Offer a short trace table in text for loops and pointer changes; never require a visual memory diagram.

AI-use policy

Follow the repository’s course policy: AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, refactor, or generate course code or assessment solutions. Apply the same rule to instructor demonstrations and student submissions.

Instructor preparation and maintenance

Before teaching, verify the installed compiler and its C17 support, run the repository’s current example-validation procedure if provided, and confirm the terminal/editor workflow with the learner’s assistive technology. Record compiler version, platform, command, and validation scope. When changing examples, update related expected output and validation materials together. Consult the shared accessibility guidance before selecting any graphical tool.

C# Teacher’s Guide

Purpose and course context

This guide supports the C# curriculum, designed for beginning programmers including blind and visually impaired learners who use screen readers, braille displays, magnification, or keyboard navigation. It supplements the complete lessons and topic index.

The course uses the .NET 10 SDK and C# 14 toolchain. C# is a statically typed, managed language with a broad .NET library ecosystem. Teach the language and the .NET runtime as related but distinct ideas: C# is the source language; the SDK builds projects; the runtime executes applications; and libraries provide APIs.

Outcomes and course sequence

Complete the shared Computing Foundations Primer and Terminal Skills prerequisite, then follow Units 0–11. Learners should be able to create and run a console project, read compiler diagnostics, use types and expressions, implement control flow, work with collections, write methods and classes, handle files and exceptions, test programs, and complete the capstone. They should understand nullable reference types and the role of the .NET project system.

Use a repeatable lesson structure: objective and vocabulary; explicit code walkthrough; prediction; build/run; output and diagnostic review; independent modification; explanation. Require learners to explain what the program does, not merely repeat the compiler’s response.

Toolchain and build workflow

Use the .NET 10 SDK and create a console project with:

dotnet new console
dotnet run
dotnet build
dotnet test

Explain the project file, target framework, SDK, compiler, runtime, NuGet dependency, and build artifacts. Run commands from the project directory and teach learners to identify the current working directory. Use repository-defined commands and dependencies; avoid global, undocumented tooling. The curriculum’s automated checker builds and smoke-executes each fenced C# example with nullable analysis and warnings treated as errors. This is a useful baseline check, not proof of expected-output correctness or complete capstone behavior.

Teaching C# concepts

Types, conversions, and nullability

C# is statically typed. Explain type inference with var without implying dynamic typing. Teach numeric conversions, integer division, overflow behavior, and the difference between value types and reference types at an introductory level. Nullable reference types provide compiler analysis; they do not make runtime null values impossible. Use nullable annotations and flow analysis to reason about possible absence. Avoid suppressing warnings with the null-forgiving operator as a routine fix.

Collections and data modeling

Compare arrays, List, Dictionary<TKey,TValue>, and other collections by ordering, key lookup, mutability, and intended use. Teach generic type parameters as constraints on the values a collection accepts. Use named record or class models when they make domain data easier to inspect and explain. Avoid opaque tuples for long-lived records.

Methods, classes, and object-oriented design

Teach method signatures as contracts: name, parameters, return type, and observable behavior. Explain constructors, properties, access modifiers, static members, interfaces, and composition. Inheritance should solve a clear substitutability problem rather than serve as the default reuse technique. Distinguish reference identity from value equality and teach equality deliberately when learners use records or custom types.

Exceptions, files, and tests

Teach exceptions for exceptional failures and validation for expected invalid input. Use explicit paths, predictable fixtures, and deterministic output. Explain working directories and dispose resources reliably, using using declarations or statements where appropriate. Tests should cover normal, boundary, and invalid cases. Learners should read assertion failures and compiler diagnostics as structured text.

Accessibility and delivery

  • Keep essential instruction, code, diagnostics, and output in selectable text.
  • State braces, angle brackets, nullable markers, question marks, lambda arrows, and generic type syntax explicitly when introduced.
  • Teach keyboard-first editor, terminal, build, and test workflows.
  • Ensure diagnostics can be navigated by file, line, and severity; explain the difference between build warnings and errors.
  • Do not make a visual debugger, GUI designer, or IDE-only feature the sole route to completing an objective.
  • Use text descriptions for object relationships and collection contents; do not rely on diagrams or syntax color.
  • Allow time for screen-reader verbosity and braille review. Assess reasoning independently of navigation speed.

Test the actual .NET SDK, editor, and assistive technology used by the learner. A successful build does not establish that the workflow is accessible.

Assessment and differentiation

Ask learners to explain type choices, nullable-flow assumptions, collection selection, method contracts, object responsibilities, and exception paths. Require tests for empty collections, missing keys, null values, malformed input, and unavailable files. Evaluate correctness, reasoning, test quality, and communication separately.

Provide scaffolded starter projects and short diagnostics for learners who need additional practice. Extend advanced learners with LINQ, asynchronous methods, interfaces, or dependency design only when these topics reinforce the stated outcomes; do not overload the beginner sequence.

AI-use policy

AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, refactor, or generate course code or assessment solutions. Keep this rule consistent across demonstrations, homework, and assessment.

Instructor preparation and maintenance

Before the course, verify the .NET 10 SDK and C# 14 compiler baseline, run the repository’s C# example checker, and separately test expected behavior and accessibility. The published smoke check is not a substitute for complete behavioral testing. Record exact SDK versions and validation scope. Consult the shared GUI and workbench accessibility guidance before requiring graphical tools.

C++ Teacher’s Guide

Purpose and course context

This guide supports instruction in the C++ curriculum for beginning programmers, including blind and visually impaired learners using screen readers, braille displays, magnification, or keyboard-first workflows. It supplements the complete lessons and topic index.

The course targets C++20 and GCC, Clang, or MSVC. C++ combines procedural, object-oriented, and generic programming with a large standard library. Instruction should make abstraction useful without hiding object lifetime, value semantics, resource ownership, or the behavior of the compiled program.

Outcomes and instructional sequence

Complete the shared Computing Foundations Primer and Terminal Skills prerequisite, then teach Units 0–11 in order. Learners should be able to build and run a project, interpret compiler diagnostics, use types and expressions, control flow, standard containers, functions, classes, files, exceptions, tests, and an integrated capstone. They should also explain the difference between copying a value, borrowing through a reference, and transferring or sharing ownership.

Use a consistent cycle: objective and vocabulary; code-structure preview; learner prediction; compilation and execution; diagnostic/output review; one deliberate modification; learner explanation. Keep examples small enough that a screen-reader user can navigate the complete construct without losing context.

Toolchain and project workflow

Use a C++20-capable GCC, Clang, or MSVC toolchain. The representative GCC/Clang command is:

c++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror main.cpp -o main
./main

Explain compiler, linker, source file, executable, standard-library headers, and build configuration. Teach project builds consistently and explain when a lesson uses a fragment that is wrapped by a validation harness. Treat warnings as feedback. The course’s published example check compiles and links fenced examples; compilation is not equivalent to full behavioral testing or accessibility certification.

Teaching C++ concepts deliberately

Values, references, and object lifetime

Start with values and ordinary function calls, then introduce references and pointers as different forms of access to objects. Teach const references for read-only access where appropriate. Explain scope, lifetime, temporary objects, and the consequences of returning a reference to an object that no longer exists. Learners should be able to state which function or object owns a resource and how long it remains valid.

Standard containers and algorithms

Prefer standard containers such as std::vector, std::array, std::string, and std::map over raw arrays for ordinary application-level tasks. Explain container size, indexing, iteration, and invalidation rules at the level needed by each lesson. Teach iterators as positions in a sequence and algorithms as operations over ranges. Do not imply that every container has constant-time indexing or that modifying a container can never invalidate an iterator or reference.

Classes, RAII, and resource management

Teach classes as contracts around state and behavior, not as a requirement to model every noun. Introduce constructors, access control, invariants, and member functions. RAII is a core C++ design principle: resource acquisition and release should be tied to object lifetime. Use standard library resource-managing types before introducing manual new/delete. Explain copying and moving as distinct operations, and introduce smart pointers only when ownership relationships justify them. Avoid teaching raw owning pointers as the default.

Exceptions, files, and generic code

Explain exceptions as a control-flow mechanism for exceptional failure, not as a substitute for validating ordinary user input. Teach file streams and check their state. Introduce templates and generic algorithms through concrete use cases, emphasizing type requirements and compiler diagnostics. When diagnostics are long, teach learners to locate the first meaningful error rather than reading every cascading message as an independent failure.

Accessibility and delivery

  • Use selectable text for source, build output, test results, and diagnostics.
  • Explicitly name punctuation and delimiters, including angle brackets, scope resolution, ampersands, asterisks, braces, and template syntax.
  • Teach keyboard navigation by symbol, line, file, and diagnostic; provide non-mouse build and run commands.
  • Avoid relying on syntax colors, indentation guides, object inspectors, or graphical debugger panes to communicate program structure.
  • Describe container contents, iterator positions, object lifetimes, and ownership in ordered text.
  • Provide a text alternative for diagrams and ensure any GUI or game-engine work has an accessible nonvisual route.
  • Allow additional time for verbose compiler diagnostics and template errors without reducing the conceptual objective.

Validate the actual compiler/editor/screen-reader combination in the classroom. Accessibility support varies by platform and version.

Assessment

Assess both code behavior and explanation. Ask learners to justify a container choice, trace a function call, identify an object’s lifetime, explain a resource’s owner, and distinguish an exception from an ordinary validation result. Include tests for empty and non-empty collections, boundary indexes, failed file operations, and invalid input. A compile-only example check is useful but does not establish correct output, resource safety, or complete project behavior.

Differentiation

For learners who need more structure, use short programs, explicit build commands, and one new abstraction at a time. For learners ready to extend the material, compare vector and map tradeoffs, exception guarantees, move semantics, interfaces, and algorithmic complexity. Keep visual memory models optional; use text traces and named states as the shared representation.

AI-use policy

AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, refactor, or generate course code or assessment solutions. Apply this consistently to instructor and learner work.

Instructor preparation

Verify a C++20 compiler, run the current repository validation script, and separately execute representative examples with expected input and output. Check that build commands and diagnostics are accessible through the learner’s tools. Record compiler versions and distinguish compilation/linking evidence from behavioral and assistive-technology testing. See the shared GUI and workbench accessibility guidance before requiring a graphical environment.

Go Teacher’s Guide

Purpose and course context

This guide supports instructors using the Go curriculum with beginning programmers, including blind and visually impaired learners using screen readers, braille displays, magnification, or keyboard navigation. It supplements the complete lessons and topic index.

Go is a compiled, statically typed language used for command-line tools, network services, infrastructure, and concurrent systems. Its package model, slices, maps, structs, interfaces, explicit error returns, and goroutines shape the course. The curriculum uses a current stable Go toolchain; check the repository’s stated baseline before each term.

Outcomes and sequence

Complete the shared Computing Foundations Primer and Terminal Skills prerequisite, then follow Units 0–11. Learners should create a module, build and run programs, interpret compiler diagnostics, use static types and control flow, work with slices and maps, define functions and structs, use interfaces, handle errors, process files and data, test code, and complete the capstone. They should understand Go’s concurrency model conceptually even when concurrency is not required for every task.

Use a consistent cycle: objective and vocabulary; code walkthrough; prediction; gofmt/build/run; output and diagnostic review; modification; learner explanation. Keep examples small and avoid introducing concurrency, interfaces, and error handling all at once.

Toolchain and modules

Verify the installed version with go version. Create a project with:

mkdir courseapp
cd courseapp
go mod init example.com/courseapp
go run .
go test ./...

Explain package declarations, imports, module paths, the go.mod file, and the difference between go run and go build. Use gofmt consistently; formatting is part of the standard Go workflow, not a cosmetic optional step. Teach learners to run commands from the module root and interpret package-qualified diagnostics.

Teaching Go’s language model

Types, zero values, and conversions

Go is statically typed and uses explicit conversions between many numeric types. Explain zero values and initialization, and contrast a declared variable with an inferred short declaration. Teach that short declarations have scope rules and are not interchangeable with assignment. Do not imply that Go performs arbitrary implicit numeric conversion.

Slices, maps, structs, and interfaces

A slice is a descriptor over an underlying array; its length and capacity are different. Appending may allocate a new backing array, so explain when two slices may share storage. Maps provide key/value lookup but do not promise iteration order. Use structs for named records and interfaces to describe behavior at the point where abstraction is useful. Explain that Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly; avoid teaching interfaces as mandatory ceremony for every type.

Errors and concurrency

Errors are values returned by functions. Teach the pattern of checking an error before using the accompanying result. Do not normalize ignored errors or use panic/recover for ordinary input validation. Introduce goroutines and channels with a clear model of independent execution and communication; discuss cancellation, blocking, and synchronization before assigning multi-goroutine projects. Race freedom cannot be inferred from a successful build or test run without an appropriate race check.

Files and tests

Use explicit paths and deterministic fixtures. Explain the process working directory, os package operations, and error checks. Teach table-driven tests after learners understand functions and assertions. Include normal, boundary, and invalid cases; use temporary directories for file exercises where appropriate.

Accessibility and instructional delivery

  • Present source, gofmt output, compiler messages, test output, and command results as text.
  • Explicitly describe braces, short declarations, pointers, channel operators, and interface method sets.
  • Teach keyboard-first editor navigation and terminal commands; no mouse-only run controls.
  • Explain goroutine and channel traces as ordered text events rather than relying on animation or diagrams.
  • Ensure learners can navigate test failures by package, file, line, and test name.
  • Avoid color-only status indicators and graphical workbenches without an equivalent text workflow.
  • Allow additional time for punctuation verbosity and diagnostic navigation.

Verify accessibility with the actual OS, editor, terminal, screen reader, and braille display used in class.

Assessment and differentiation

Assess whether the learner can explain types, slice length versus capacity, map ordering, interface satisfaction, explicit error handling, and concurrency risks. Require tests for empty collections, missing keys, file errors, and malformed input. For concurrency, ask learners to identify possible blocking and shared-state access before execution. Distinguish compilation, smoke execution, expected-output validation, race testing, and accessibility testing; they are different forms of evidence.

Scaffold with single-package programs and sequential code first. Extend learners with additional packages, interfaces, context cancellation, or concurrent workers only after the core data and error models are stable.

AI-use policy

AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, refactor, or generate course code or assessment solutions.

Instructor preparation

Verify the Go toolchain, run the repository’s gofmt/build/smoke-check workflow, and separately inspect expected behavior and accessibility. The current example check does not establish exact output, capstone correctness, race freedom, or assistive-technology certification. Record toolchain versions and validation scope. See the shared accessibility guidance.

Teacher’s Guide: Introduction to Computer Science with Java

For Students with Visual Impairments — Complete Instructor Edition

How to use this teacher’s guide

This guide is a companion for instructors, not a script that must be followed word for word. Read the philosophy, learner-context, and technology sections before the first lesson; use the unit notes while planning; and return to the assessment, differentiation, AI, and quick-reference sections throughout the course. Adapt procedures to the learner’s actual assistive technology, operating system, course goals, and prior experience. Confirm tool-specific instructions in current official documentation because editor, screen-reader, and runtime behavior changes over time.

Plan for both programming learning and access to the programming environment. Establish what the student can already do independently, what access skills need instruction, what supports are already in place, and how the learner prefers to receive feedback. Never assume a diagnosis predicts a student’s preferred tools or level of independence.

JDK 25 LTS baseline and current Java conventions

Use JDK 25 LTS for the learner materials. JDK 25 is the current LTS release as of October 30, 2026; install its latest security update. JDK 27 is newer but is not the LTS baseline. Teach and assess against standard Java 25, not preview features or vendor-specific extensions. Keep classic class-based program structure in the early lessons even though newer Java releases offer more concise launch forms; this keeps the progression explicit and transferable.

Model current Java conventions consistently: PascalCase types; camelCase fields, methods, parameters, and local variables; UPPER_SNAKE_CASE constants; explicit imports; generics instead of raw types; interfaces such as List/Map in declarations; braces for all control-flow blocks; and meaningful method boundaries. Use String.equals for content equality, never ==. Prefer try-with-resources for files and scanners that own resources. Use var only for local variables when the initializer makes the type obvious; keep explicit types in beginner code. Use descriptive exception handling and avoid swallowing exceptions. Avoid preview features unless a lesson explicitly identifies them.

Table of Contents

  1. Philosophy and Why Java
  2. Java-Specific Accessibility Challenges
  3. Classroom Setup and Configuration
  4. Spoken Java Conventions
  5. Unit 0–1: Setup and Foundations
  6. Unit 2: I/O and the Math Class
  7. Unit 3: Control Flow
  8. Unit 4: Arrays and ArrayLists
  9. Unit 5: Strings and String Processing
  10. Unit 6: Methods
  11. Unit 7: Classes and OOP
  12. Unit 8: Files and Exception Handling
  13. Unit 9: Collections, Analysis, and Testing
  14. Units 10–11: Projects and Capstone
  15. Bridging from Python to Java
  16. Assessment Strategies
  17. Supporting Diverse Needs
  18. Alternative and Supplementary Resources
  19. Quick Reference Sheets
  20. Teaching AI Tools Responsibly
  21. Comprehensive Instructional Planning and Course Implementation

1. Philosophy and Why Java

The Case for Teaching Java to Blind Students

Java is not the easiest language for beginners, and its verbosity creates overhead that requires specific pedagogical attention. Despite this, Java has genuine advantages for visually impaired learners that are often overlooked:

Compile-time error detection. Java’s compiler catches type errors, name errors, and structural mistakes before any code runs. A blind student does not need to search through runtime output for subtle type mismatches — the compiler announces them precisely and immediately with file name, line number, and error description.

Strong, static typing is auditorily informative. When IntelliSense in VS Code suggests methods, it includes the return type: “double getBalance() — returns a double.” This type information helps a screen reader user understand what a method does without having to navigate to its definition.

Enforced code structure. Every Java program requires a class; every executable program requires a main method with a specific signature. This structure is more overhead to type but less ambiguity about how programs are organized. For a student who cannot visually scan a file for structure, predictable structural conventions reduce cognitive load.

Exception specification. Java’s checked exceptions force programmers to declare which exceptions a method can throw. This means a screen reader user reading a method signature gets information about failure modes that Python provides only through documentation.

Enterprise relevance. Java remains a dominant language in enterprise software, Android development, and many backend systems. A student who learns Java learns patterns that transfer directly to professional employment.

2. Java-Specific Accessibility Challenges

The Verbosity Problem

Java requires significantly more text than Python to accomplish the same task:

// Java: Hello, World
public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, World!");
    }
}

# Python: Hello, World
print("Hello, World!")

For a sighted student, extra text is a visual annoyance. For a blind student, it is additional audio before they reach the meaningful code. Mitigation strategies:

  1. Code templates. Provide a starter file the student copies for every new program. They modify only the method body for early lessons. This reduces the typing burden and prevents structural errors while the student is learning concepts.

  2. JShell (Java REPL). Java includes an interactive shell since Java 9: run jshell in the terminal. JShell strips away class and method boilerplate. For exploration and experimentation, JShell is far more accessible than creating files:

    jshell> int x = 5;
x ==> 5
jshell> System.out.println(x * 2);
10

  3. Progressive disclosure. In early lessons, treat public static void main(String[] args) { as a formula, not something to understand. Students learn to recognize it by ear. Explain each word only when the concept it relates to (access modifiers, static methods, arrays) is being taught.

Integer Division Surprises

Java’s / operator performs integer division when both operands are integers:

  • 15 / 4 = 3 (not 3.75)
  • 15.0 / 4 = 3.75
  • (double) 15 / 4 = 3.75

This is silent — there is no error or warning. A blind student may not catch a calculation that silently discards its decimal portion. Teach the rule explicitly: if you want a decimal result, at least one operand must be a double.

The String Equality Trap

== on Strings compares memory addresses, not content. Two strings with identical characters in different memory locations are == false but .equals() true. This never appears in Python; blind students coming from Python are not conditioned to suspect == as a source of String bugs.

Teaching approach: Show the broken behavior explicitly. Use new String("hello") == new String("hello") which is guaranteed to be false even though the strings are identical. Then show .equals() which is true. Make .equals() for Strings a non-negotiable rule from day one.

Null Pointer Exceptions

NullPointerException is the most common Java runtime error. It occurs when you call a method or access a field on a variable that holds null (no object reference). Unlike Python’s AttributeError which gives useful context, Java’s NPE message is often terse. Teaching students to recognize and debug NPEs is essential.

3. Classroom Setup and Configuration

IDE Configuration

Visual Studio Code with Extension Pack for Java: This is the primary documented setup. The Extension Pack includes Language Support for Java (Red Hat), Debugger for Java, Java Test Runner, Maven for Java, and Project Manager for Java.

Theia IDE: Theia IDE is an alternative with the keyboard- and screen-reader-oriented accessibility workflows expected in this course. Check the Open VSX registry for compatible Java language support, debugging, and test extensions. Not every VS Code extension is available or behaves identically, so verify the student’s actual workflow.

Other tools: BlueJ, DrJava, and Eclipse may be considered only when their accessibility and feature set fit the learner and the lesson. JetBrains IDEs (including IntelliJ IDEA) are intentionally not recommended for this introductory course. They are capable products, but their extensive feature set and complexity add unnecessary overhead for beginning programmers.

VS Code Java Specific Settings:

{
  "java.completion.enabled": true,
  "java.format.enabled": true,
  "editor.formatOnSave": true,
  "java.saveActions.organizeImports": true,
  "java.completion.importOrder": ["java", "javax", "com", ""],
  "editor.suggestOnTriggerCharacters": true
}

Key accessibility setting: Enable “Trigger suggestions” on . so that typing myObject. causes IntelliSense to announce available methods. This allows audio exploration of an object’s API.

JDK Installation Verification

java --version      # Runtime version
javac --version     # Compiler version
jshell              # Start REPL (Ctrl+D or /exit to quit)

Windows Powershell

java --version      # Runtime version
javac --version     # Compiler version
jshell              # Start REPL (Ctrl+D or /exit to quit)

All three must work before proceeding. If jshell is not found, the student may have installed only the JRE (runtime), not the full JDK. The JDK must be installed.

4. Spoken Java Conventions

Extend the Python symbol conventions with Java-specific additions:

Symbol/PatternSpoken Form
public“public”
private“private”
static“static”
void“void” (returns nothing)
new“new”
this.“this dot”
super.“super dot”
@Override“at-override annotation”
// comment“double-slash comment”
/* ... */“block comment”
/** ... */“JavaDoc comment”
String[]“String array”
ArrayList<String>“ArrayList of String”
HashMap<String, Integer>“HashMap from String to Integer”
throws IOException“throws IOException”
System.out.println()“sysout” or “system-out-println”
System.out.printf()“system-out-printf”
Integer.parseInt()“Integer-parse-int”
(int) x“cast to int”
null“null”
NullPointerException“null pointer exception”
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException“array index out of bounds”

Reading a method signature:

public double calculateArea(double radius) throws IllegalArgumentException

“public double method calculateArea, takes a double called radius, may throw IllegalArgumentException”

5. Unit 0–1: Setup and Foundations

Lesson 0.1: Installing the JDK

Instructional Cues

  • Use Adoptium (Eclipse Temurin) rather than Oracle JDK. The Oracle JDK requires account creation and license agreement navigation. Adoptium is fully open-source and simpler to download.
  • Verify the download before running. Adoptium provides SHA checksums. Teaching students to verify downloads is a security habit worth establishing.
  • Windows installer tip: The Adoptium .msi installer includes a checkbox for “Set JAVA_HOME variable.” Ensure this is checked. Many Java tools (Maven, Gradle, some IDEs) require JAVA_HOME to be set.

JShell as the First Environment

Before any file-based Java, spend time in JShell:

$ jshell
|  Welcome to JShell -- Version 17.0.x
|  For an introduction type: /help intro

jshell> 5 + 3
$1 ==> 8

jshell> "Hello " + "World"
$2 ==> "Hello World"

jshell> int x = 42;
x ==> 42

jshell> System.out.println("Value: " + x);
Value: 42

JShell gives immediate auditory feedback — type an expression, hear the result. This is much more accessible for early exploration than the compile-run-read cycle.

JShell commands to teach:

  • /list — show all code entered so far
  • /edit — open in editor
  • /vars — show all variables
  • /methods — show all methods defined
  • /exit — quit JShell

Thought Experiments

  1. “Python is interpreted — each line runs immediately. Java compiles to bytecode first, then runs. What does this mean for the kind of errors you encounter, and when? If you have a SyntaxError on line 50, in Python you might not discover it until the program reaches line 50. In Java, when do you discover it?”

  2. “The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) allows the same Java bytecode to run on Windows, macOS, and Linux. The JVM is different on each platform, but the bytecode is the same. What does this tell you about how Java achieves portability? What alternative approaches could a language designer take?”

  3. “JShell is a Read-Eval-Print Loop (REPL). Python has one; JavaScript has one; many languages have one. But Java didn’t have one until 2016. Why might a language’s designers add a REPL 20 years after the language was created? What did programmers do without it?”

  4. “Java was originally designed for embedded systems (like televisions), then became dominant for web servers, then for Android apps. Each time it succeeded in a new domain, it required extending the language. What does this history suggest about the relationship between a language’s design and the problems it eventually solves?”

Lesson 1.2: Your First Java Program

Instructional Cues

Anatomy reading exercise — before typing any code: Read the Hello World program aloud, symbol by symbol, using the pronunciation table:

public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, World!");
    }
}

“public class HelloWorld open-brace newline four-spaces public static void main open-paren String array args close-paren open-brace newline eight-spaces System dot out dot println open-paren quote Hello comma World! close-quote close-paren semicolon newline four-spaces close-brace newline close-brace”

This exercise establishes pattern recognition for the boilerplate that the student will type hundreds of times. Making it auditorily familiar early reduces cognitive load later.

Three System.out methods:

System.out.println("With newline at end");     // Most common
System.out.print("No newline at end");          // For prompts
System.out.printf("Pi is %.2f%n", Math.PI);    // Formatted

For accessible programs, printf is extremely valuable — it produces consistent, predictable output formatting that reads cleanly with a screen reader.

Thought Experiments

  1. “Every Java program requires a public class whose name matches the file name. Why does Java enforce this one-to-one correspondence? What would break if you could put multiple public classes in one file?”

  2. “The main method signature is exactly public static void main(String[] args). It cannot be public void main() or static void main(String[] args). Why is this signature fixed? What does each word contribute?”

  3. “Java uses curly braces {} to delimit code blocks; Python uses indentation. From an accessibility perspective — for a blind programmer — which approach provides better information about structure when read aloud? Consider that braces can be read as ‘open block’ and ‘close block,’ while indentation changes require screen reader configuration.”

  4. “System.out.println() is long to type but descriptively named. Python’s print() is short. What naming philosophy does each represent? When does conciseness become ambiguity?”

Lesson 1.3: Variables and Primitive Data Types

Instructional Cues

Type declaration as specification: Frame Java’s type declarations positively: “When you write int score = 85, you’re telling Java: this variable will always hold a whole number. Java then protects you — if you accidentally try to put a name or a decimal into it, the compiler tells you immediately.”

The eight primitive types — prioritize four: In this curriculum, students need: int, double, boolean, char. The others (byte, short, long, float) exist but are rarely needed in beginner programs. Introduce the four primary types fully before acknowledging the others exist.

Type casting demonstration:

// Widening (automatic)
int i = 100;
double d = i;   // 100 -> 100.0, automatic

// Narrowing (explicit, may lose data)
double pi = 3.14159;
int truncated = (int) pi;  // 3.14159 -> 3, data LOST

System.out.println("Truncated: " + truncated);  // 3, not 4!

The truncation behavior (not rounding) is consistently surprising. Demonstrate it with (int) 3.9 producing 3, and ask: “Is this rounding or truncating? What is the difference? When would truncation cause a bug?”

Non-Obvious Accessibility Strategies

  • System.out.printf() for consistent numeric output: printf("Balance: $%.2f%n", balance) always produces exactly 2 decimal places. Without formatting, double values may produce varying numbers of decimal places (3.0, 3.14, 3.1415926535...) that read differently each time. Consistent formatting makes output more predictable.

  • Scanner.hasNext___() methods: Before calling scanner.nextInt(), check scanner.hasNextInt(). If the user typed a non-integer, this returns false and prevents the exception, allowing graceful re-prompting. For a blind student who may not immediately catch an exception in terminal output, this is defensive programming with real accessibility value.

Thought Experiments

  1. “Java’s int holds values from about -2.1 billion to +2.1 billion. What happens if you exceed this limit (integer overflow)? The value silently wraps around to the opposite extreme. Name a real-world system where integer overflow has caused a documented failure.”

  2. “Java has int (primitive) and Integer (object). They hold the same values but behave differently. int cannot be null; Integer can. int cannot be used in a List<int> — you need List<Integer>. Why would a language designer make this distinction? What does it cost? What does it protect against?”

  3. “Java’s char holds a single Unicode character. char c = 'A' stores the letter A. But char is also a numeric type — (int) 'A' is 65. What does this dual nature (character and number) tell you about how computers store text internally?”

6. Unit 2: I/O and the Math Class

Lesson 2.2: Scanner for User Input

Instructional Cues

The Scanner as a wrapper — explain the layers:

Keyboard
  V produces bytes
System.in (InputStream)
  V raw byte stream
new Scanner(System.in)
  V wraps with text-reading methods
scanner.nextLine(), scanner.nextInt(), etc.

This layered model explains why Scanner is needed rather than reading from System.in directly. It also foreshadows file reading where new Scanner(new File(...)) replaces new Scanner(System.in).

nextInt() / nextLine() pitfall — mandatory demonstration:

Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);
System.out.print("Enter your age: ");
int age = scanner.nextInt();          // Reads "25", leaves "\n" in buffer
System.out.print("Enter your name: ");
String name = scanner.nextLine();     // Reads the leftover "\n" --- gets EMPTY string!
System.out.println("Hello " + name + ", age " + age);
// Output: "Hello , age 25" --- name is empty!

The fix:

int age = scanner.nextInt();
scanner.nextLine();          // Consume the leftover newline
String name = scanner.nextLine();   // Now reads properly

Run the broken version first. The student should hear the incorrect output and understand why before seeing the fix.

Thought Experiments

  1. “The Scanner reads from a ‘stream’ of input. A stream is a sequence of data that flows from a source to a destination. System.in is the keyboard stream. What other streams exist in a typical program? (Think about file streams, network streams, the output stream.)”

  2. “After scanner.nextInt(), there’s a leftover newline in the buffer. What IS a buffer? Why does the operating system buffer keyboard input rather than delivering each character the moment a key is pressed?”

  3. “In GUI (graphical) programs, users fill out forms with text fields and click buttons. There’s no scanner.nextLine(). What mechanism do GUI programs use to collect user input? How does event-driven GUI input differ from sequential console input?”

7. Unit 3: Control Flow

Lessons 3.1–3.3

Instructional Cues

String comparison — immediate practice:

String day = "Wednesday";

// Wrong --- compares memory addresses
if (day == "Wednesday") {
    System.out.println("Middle of the week");  // May or may not print
}

// Correct --- compares content
if (day.equals("Wednesday")) {
    System.out.println("Middle of the week");  // Always correct
}

// Case-insensitive
if (day.equalsIgnoreCase("wednesday")) {
    System.out.println("This works too");
}

Create a practice file with 10 comparisons, half using == and half using .equals(). Ask the student to predict which ones will work correctly before running.

Switch expressions (Java 14+):

Modern Java supports switch expressions that return a value:

String dayType = switch (day) {
    case "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday" -> "Weekday";
    case "Saturday", "Sunday" -> "Weekend";
    default -> "Unknown";
};
System.out.println(day + " is a " + dayType);

This eliminates the fallthrough problem and is more concise. Teach both traditional switch (for reading legacy code) and switch expressions (for writing new code).

Thought Experiments

  1. “Java uses && for AND, || for OR, ! for NOT. Python uses the words and, or, not. Which approach is more readable when heard aloud by a screen reader? Is there a meaningful accessibility argument for one over the other?”

  2. “The enhanced for loop for (String item : list) is simpler to write than the traditional for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++). But sometimes you need the index. Name three operations you can do with the traditional loop that you cannot do (directly) with the enhanced loop.”

  3. “Java’s switch statement traditionally falls through from one case to the next unless you write break. This ‘feature’ has caused countless bugs. Modern Java (14+) has switch expressions that don’t fall through. What does this change tell you about how programming language design evolves in response to real-world usage patterns?”

  4. “Short-circuit evaluation: if (obj != null && obj.getValue() > 0) — if obj is null, the second condition is never evaluated. This prevents a NullPointerException. How does this behavior make certain coding patterns possible that would otherwise crash?”

8. Unit 4: Arrays and ArrayLists

Lesson 4.1: Arrays

Instructional Cues

The fixed-size limitation — demonstrate, don’t just describe:

String[] fruits = new String[3];
fruits[0] = "apple";
fruits[1] = "banana";
fruits[2] = "cherry";
fruits[3] = "date";   // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException!

Let the student hear the exception and analyze the message: Index 3 out of bounds for length 3. Ask: “The message gives you two numbers. What are they? What does each tell you?”

Arrays.toString() as mandatory print method:

The first time print(fruits) produces [Ljava.lang.String;@7a5d012b, stop and explain: “This is the memory address of the array, not its contents. Java arrays don’t have a built-in ‘print nicely’ behavior. Always use Arrays.toString(fruits) or loop through manually.”

The for vs for-each tradeoff — make it concrete:

// for-each: simple, clear, but no index
for (String fruit : fruits) {
    System.out.println(fruit);
}

// traditional: more complex, but gives index
for (int i = 0; i < fruits.length; i++) {
    System.out.println(i + ": " + fruits[i]);
}

// The numbered version is more accessible!

For blind students, numbered output (showing both index and value) is generally more useful than unnumbered output. Teach the traditional for loop for array printing specifically because it enables indexed output.

Thought Experiments

  1. “Arrays are stored in contiguous memory — all elements in a row, one after another. This is why accessing by index is fast: the address of element i is just the start address plus i × element size. Why does this contiguous storage make inserting into the middle of an array slow? What must happen to all the elements after the insertion point?”

  2. “If you create String[] arr = new String[5], what are the initial values of arr[0] through arr[4]? Now create int[] nums = new int[5] — what are the initial values? Why are the defaults different between String arrays and int arrays?”

  3. “Two-dimensional arrays in Java are ‘arrays of arrays.’ This means each row can have a different length — a ‘jagged array.’ When would a jagged array be more appropriate than a rectangular 2D array? Give a real-world data example.”

Lesson 4.2: ArrayLists

Instructional Cues

Autoboxing — explain the invisibility:

ArrayList<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
numbers.add(42);        // 42 (int) is auto-boxed to Integer(42)
int first = numbers.get(0);  // Integer(42) is auto-unboxed to 42

This happens invisibly but has a performance cost. For the course, tell students: “Use ArrayList<Integer> when you need a flexible list of integers. The boxing/unboxing is automatic but slightly less efficient than an array of int.”

Removal by index vs. by value:

ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("a", "b", "c", "b", "d"));
list.remove(1);            // Removes by INDEX --- removes "b" at position 1
list.remove("b");          // Removes by VALUE --- removes first "b" found
list.removeAll(Arrays.asList("b", "c"));  // Removes all matching values

Ask the student: “If I call list.remove(0) on a list of integers [10, 20, 30], does this remove the element at index 0 (which is 10) or remove the value 0 (which doesn’t exist)? How does Java decide?” (Answer: removes index 0, because 0 is an int, not an Integer.)

Thought Experiments

  1. “An ArrayList doubles its internal capacity when it runs out of space. If you start with capacity 16 and keep adding elements, when does reallocation occur? Trace the capacity: 16 -> 32 -> 64 -> 128… What is the total cost (in element moves) of adding 1000 elements to an initially empty ArrayList this way? Is this efficient?”

  2. “Java generics ArrayList<String> enforce type safety at compile time. Python lists can hold any types mixed together. When is a typed list (Java style) better? When is a mixed list (Python style) more flexible? Which approach produces more reliable programs?”

9. Unit 5: Strings and String Processing

Instructional Cues

String immutability — the Java version:

In Java, Strings are immutable for the same reason as Python. But Java’s String object is also interned — the JVM may reuse the same String object for two variables holding the same literal value. This is why == sometimes works for String comparison (when both refer to the same interned object) but is not reliable.

StringBuilder motivation:

// Inefficient --- creates 100,000 String objects
String result = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
    result += "x";
}

// Efficient --- modifies a single buffer
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
    sb.append("x");
}
String result = sb.toString();

The + in a loop creates a new String object on every iteration, then discards the old one. For small loops this is fine; for large loops it’s a significant performance problem. StringBuilder maintains a mutable buffer.

Thought Experiments

  1. “String concatenation with + is convenient but expensive in loops. In Python, the equivalent is also discouraged — use ''.join(list) instead. What does this common advice across two languages tell you about how immutable strings interact with loops?”

  2. “Java’s String.format() and printf() use format specifiers like %s, %d, %f. Python uses f-strings with {}. What are the accessibility tradeoffs of each approach? Which reads more naturally when heard aloud? Which is easier to type?”

  3. “Regular expressions are a tiny language inside a programming language. \\d+ matches one or more digits. [a-zA-Z]+ matches one or more letters. Why do programmers use regular expressions despite their difficult-to-read syntax? What would the alternative be for complex pattern matching?”

10. Unit 6: Methods

Instructional Cues

Method overloading — auditory navigation:

public static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
public static double add(double a, double b) { return a + b; }
public static int add(int a, int b, int c) { return a + b + c; }

When IntelliSense shows overloads in VS Code, pressing Shift+Alt+F2 (Accessible View) lists them all. Teach students to use this to discover available overloads.

void vs. return type — make the distinction tangible:

// void: for side effects only
public static void printGreeting(String name) {
    System.out.println("Hello, " + name + "!");
}

// Return type: for computation
public static double calculateTip(double billAmount, double rate) {
    return billAmount * rate;
}

// Using them:
printGreeting("Alice");                      // Standalone call
double tip = calculateTip(50.00, 0.18);      // Must capture return value
System.out.printf("Tip: $%.2f%n", tip);

“void methods exist to DO something. Return-type methods exist to CALCULATE something and give you the result. Ask: ‘Do I need to use the output later in my code?’ If yes, it needs a return type.”

Thought Experiments

  1. “Java methods can throw exceptions: public double sqrt(double n) throws IllegalArgumentException. This signature tells callers that the method might fail in a specific way. Python has no equivalent syntax. What is the programmer’s obligation when they see throws in a method signature?”

  2. “Static methods belong to the class, not to any instance: Math.sqrt(25) — you don’t need a Math object. Instance methods belong to an object: myString.length(). What is the conceptual difference? When should a method be static vs. instance?”

  3. “Method parameters in Java are ‘pass by value’ for primitives and ‘pass by reference’ for objects. For primitives: the method gets a copy, and modifying the parameter doesn’t affect the original. For objects: the method gets the reference, and modifications to the object’s fields DO affect the original. Design a test to confirm this behavior for both cases.”

  4. _“Recursion: a method that calls itself. int factorial(int n) { return n == 0 ? 1 : n _ factorial(n-1); }. Every recursive solution has an iterative equivalent. When is the recursive version clearer? What is the risk of deep recursion (many nested calls)?”*

11. Unit 7: Classes and OOP

Extended Instructional Cues

The mandatory __str__ equivalent in Java — toString():

Every student-defined class must override toString(). Without it, System.out.println(myObject) produces an unreadable string. The @Override annotation makes this explicit:

@Override
public String toString() {
    return String.format("Dog[name=%s, age=%d]", name, age);
}

Require this in every class from Unit 7 onward. Explain: “When your screen reader reads System.out.println(myDog), it reads whatever toString() returns. If you don’t define toString(), you’ll hear a memory address. That’s useless.”

JavaDoc comments as accessible documentation:

Teach this format for every method:

/**
 * Calculates the area of this circle.
 *
 * @return the area as a double, in square units
 * @throws IllegalArgumentException if radius is negative
 */
public double getArea() {
    if (radius < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Radius cannot be negative");
    return Math.PI * radius * radius;
}

When IntelliSense shows this method in VS Code, pressing Shift+Alt+F2 reads the JavaDoc aloud. This makes the student’s own code navigable via audio — a profound accessibility benefit.

The VS Code symbol navigator: Ctrl+Shift+O opens a dropdown listing all methods in the current file. Type a few letters to filter. This allows jumping to any method by name — much more efficient than arrow-key navigation through a long file.

Access modifiers — enforce from day one:

ModifierRuleReason
private on fieldsAlwaysEncapsulation; prevents direct manipulation
public on getters/settersWhen neededControlled access
private on helper methodsYesInternal implementation detail
public on methods the user callsYesInterface to the class

Establish this as a non-negotiable habit, not a preference. “Private fields, public interface. Every time.”

Thought Experiments

  1. “Encapsulation means the internal state of an object is private. Only its public methods can access or modify it. Why would you want to prevent direct access to account.balance? What bugs could occur if balance were public?”

  2. “Inheritance creates a hierarchy. A SavingsAccount extends BankAccount. Every SavingsAccount is-a BankAccount, but not every BankAccount is-a SavingsAccount. What are the type-safety implications of this? If you have a BankAccount variable, can it hold a SavingsAccount object?”

  3. “Java interfaces define contracts — a list of methods that any implementing class must provide. A class can implement multiple interfaces but can only extend one class. Why this asymmetry? What problem does single inheritance solve? What does it prevent?”

  4. “Design Pattern: the Factory Method creates objects without specifying the exact class. Instead of new Dog(), you’d call AnimalFactory.create("dog"). What is the advantage of this indirection? When would it be useful?”

  5. “Object-oriented programming was supposed to model the real world. A Dog is-a Animal. But real-world relationships are complex — a FlyingFish is both a Fish and can fly like a Bird. How does Java’s single-inheritance model handle this situation? What alternatives exist?”

  6. “Polymorphism means one interface, many implementations. Animal[] animals = {new Dog(), new Cat(), new Bird()}; for (Animal a : animals) { a.speak(); } — each animal speaks differently. Why is this more flexible than checking instanceof and calling different methods explicitly?”

Alternative Resources

  • “Head First Design Patterns” by Freeman, Robson et al.: Visual book, but audio-describable concepts. Covers fundamental OOP design patterns. For advanced students.
  • “Effective Java” by Joshua Bloch: The definitive book on Java best practices. Dense but invaluable for understanding WHY Java is designed the way it is.
  • Oracle Java Tutorials (docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/): Comprehensive, plain HTML, fully accessible. Covers OOP concepts with extensive examples.

12. Unit 8: Files and Exception Handling

Instructional Cues

Checked vs. unchecked exceptions — the core distinction:

TypeExamplesMust Handle?Why?
CheckedIOException, FileNotFoundException, SQLExceptionYes — compiler enforcesThese are recoverable; programmer should handle them
Unchecked (RuntimeException)NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, IllegalArgumentExceptionNo — optionalUsually indicate programming errors; may not be recoverable

“Checked exceptions are like warning labels: ‘This operation can fail. You must decide what to do if it does.’ Unchecked exceptions are usually bugs — the program did something wrong.”

Try-with-resources — teach first, manual close second:

// Modern: try-with-resources (always teach this first)
try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"))) {
    String line;
    while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
        System.out.println(line);
    }
} catch (IOException e) {
    System.out.println("Error reading file: " + e.getMessage());
}
// reader is automatically closed here, even if an exception occurred

// Legacy: manual close (show this so students understand what try-with-resources does)
BufferedReader reader = null;
try {
    reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"));
    // ... use reader
} catch (IOException e) {
    System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());
} finally {
    if (reader != null) {
        try { reader.close(); } catch (IOException e) { /* ignore */ }
    }
}

Show the legacy version to explain why try-with-resources exists and what it simplifies.

Thought Experiments

  1. “Checked exceptions force you to handle failures at compile time. Critics argue this creates ‘exception chaining hell’ — every method signature becomes littered with throws clauses. Defenders argue it makes failure modes explicit and programs more reliable. Which side do you find more persuasive? Why?”

  2. “Java’s Path and Files classes (java.nio.file) are a modern replacement for the older File class. The older File class’s delete() method returns a boolean (true/false) instead of throwing an exception. What is the danger of reporting failure via a return value? What might a programmer accidentally do wrong?”

  3. “A NullPointerException is called ‘The Billion Dollar Mistake’ by its inventor Tony Hoare. Explain why null references cause so many bugs. Newer languages (Kotlin, Swift) have built-in null safety. What would Java code look like if null didn’t exist?”

13. Unit 9: Collections, Analysis, and Testing

JUnit Testing Deep Dive

Instructional Cues

Test output is inherently accessible: JUnit produces plain text output: . for each passing test, F for failures, with descriptive failure messages. This is one of the most screen-reader-friendly outputs in the entire course. Let students experience testing by running a test suite and listening to the results before writing their own tests.

Test naming convention — sentence style:

@Test
public void calculateArea_withPositiveRadius_returnsCorrectValue() { }

@Test
public void calculateArea_withZeroRadius_returnsZero() { }

@Test
public void calculateArea_withNegativeRadius_throwsException() { }

The naming convention methodName_condition_expectedBehavior makes test names read as complete sentences when the test runner announces them. This is both good practice and an accessibility benefit — each test announcement tells you exactly what was tested.

assertThrows — test that exceptions work correctly:

@Test
public void withdraw_withInsufficientFunds_throwsException() {
    BankAccount account = new BankAccount(100.0);
    assertThrows(InsufficientFundsException.class, () -> account.withdraw(200.0));
}

Testing for exceptions is as important as testing for correct outputs. Many beginners only test the “happy path.”

Thought Experiments

  1. “Test-driven development (TDD) says: write the test first, then write the implementation. How does writing a test first change the way you think about a method? What is forced to be clear before you write a line of implementation?”

  2. “Mocking means replacing real dependencies (like a database or file system) with fake versions for testing. Why would you want to test a method that reads from a database without using a real database? What complexity does mocking introduce?”

  3. “A project has 100% test coverage — tests execute every line. Is the software correct? Name a bug that 100% coverage would not catch. (Hint: think about a bug that only appears with certain combinations of inputs.)”

14. Units 10–11: Projects and Capstone

Java Project Architecture

For the capstone, encourage a clean package structure:

src/
|--- com/
|   +--- student/
|       +--- datamanager/
|           |--- model/
|           |   +--- Contact.java
|           |--- storage/
|           |   |--- DataManager.java
|           |   +--- JsonStorage.java
|           |--- ui/
|           |   +--- ConsoleUI.java
|           +--- Main.java
test/
+--- com/
    +--- student/
        +--- datamanager/
            |--- model/
            |   +--- ContactTest.java
            +--- storage/
                +--- DataManagerTest.java

Navigating packages in VS Code: Ctrl+Shift+E for Explorer (shows package tree), Ctrl+P to open any file by name, Ctrl+Shift+O for symbols within the current file.

IDE-Generated Code Accessibility

VS Code and compatible Java IDE extensions can generate getters, setters, constructors, and toString. Teach these as time-savers, but require students to read and understand all generated code:

  • Ctrl+Shift+P -> “Java: Generate Getters and Setters”
  • Ctrl+Shift+P -> “Java: Override/Implement Methods”
  • Ctrl+Shift+P -> “Java: Generate toString”

Generated code is correct but often not styled for accessibility (missing JavaDoc, generic names). Require students to add JavaDoc and verify toString() output is meaningful when heard.

Thought Experiments

  1. “Java in enterprise software is often criticized for having too much ‘boilerplate’ — code that exists for structural reasons rather than to express logic. How does this boilerplate affect the experience of maintaining a large Java codebase? What tools and patterns does the Java ecosystem provide to reduce it?”

  2. “Your capstone application stores data in a file. If your team adds a new field to the data class, existing saved files no longer match the new format. This is a ‘schema migration’ problem. How would you design your storage layer to handle this gracefully?”

15. Bridging from Python to Java

For courses that teach Python before Java, use these comparison thought experiments to bridge the languages:

Syntax bridge table:

PythonJavaNotes

x = 5int x = 5;Java requires type declaration and semicolon
if condition:if (condition) {Parens around condition; brace instead of colon
elifelse ifTwo words in Java
for item in list:for (Type item : list) {Java requires type
def func(x):public static void func(int x) {Return type and access modifier required
return xreturn x;Semicolon
# comment// comment
Nonenull
True/Falsetrue/falseLowercase in Java

list.append(x)list.add(x)

Thought experiments for bridging:

  1. “In Python you write x = 5 and Python figures out the type. In Java you write int x = 5 and declare the type explicitly. Which approach do you prefer after using both? Which one would you choose for a large team project? For a quick experiment?”

  2. “Python lists can hold any mixture of types: [1, 'hello', True, 3.14]. Java’s ArrayList<String> can only hold Strings. What bugs does Python’s flexibility enable? What bugs does it prevent compared to Java?”

  3. “Python functions are first-class objects — you can store them in variables, pass them as arguments. In Java (before lambdas), this was much more complex. Java added lambdas in 2014. What does it mean for a language to add a major feature 19 years after it was created?”

16. Assessment Strategies

Alternative Assessment Forms

Code review presentations: The student explains their code out loud, as if presenting to a team. The teacher asks questions about design decisions. This tests understanding more authentically than multiple-choice questions.

Bug-hunting assessments: Provide a working program with 5–8 intentional bugs of different types. The student must find and fix them using only their screen reader and development tools. This directly tests real-world debugging skill.

Design walkthroughs: Give the student a problem and ask them to design the solution — class structure, methods, data structures — without writing any code. Assess the quality of the design, not the typing speed.

Pair programming sessions: Two students work on one computer. One dictates code; the other types. Roles swap every 10–15 minutes. This surfaces communication and reasoning skills that solo assessments miss.

17. Supporting Diverse Needs

For Braille Display Users

Java’s verbose syntax can be particularly burdensome on a braille display with limited width. Strategies:

  • Keep lines under 79 characters (PEP 8 applies to style; the Java equivalent is generally under 100).
  • Use shorter variable names for very long class hierarchies where the full name is unwieldy.
  • Test the learner’s chosen editor with their braille display and screen reader. Prefer the documented VS Code or Theia workflows and avoid adding IDE complexity before it is needed.

For Students New to Screen Readers

If a student is still developing screen reader proficiency:

  • Begin with JShell instead of file-based programming. Single-line interactions provide immediate feedback.
  • Use pair work more extensively until independent navigation is fluent.
  • Reduce the number of new concepts per session until screen reader fluency stabilizes.

Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);

String line   = scanner.nextLine();     // Entire line as String

// Same methods work; wrap in try-catch for FileNotFoundException
