20. Teaching AI Tools Responsibly

AI coding assistants can explain compiler messages, offer hints, compare designs, or suggest test cases. They can also invent Java APIs, use language features unsupported by the configured JDK, omit imports, produce incompatible types, mishandle exceptions, or create unnecessary class hierarchies. Treat generated answers as unverified drafts. The course must remain teachable without paid AI access or a personal account.

Instructor use of AI during preparation

Instructors may use approved AI tools to brainstorm examples, draft alternate explanations, suggest test cases, or identify likely misconceptions. The instructor remains accountable for correctness and accessibility. Verify APIs and language features against the target JDK and official Java documentation; compile and test examples; inspect dependencies and build instructions; and test the workflow with the intended access technology. Never upload identifiable student work, accommodation plans, credentials, assessment answers, or confidential school information. Do not use AI-generated feedback as the sole basis for grading. Disclose substantive AI assistance when institutional policy or the publication process requires it.

Learning goals and appropriate uses

Students should explain that generated responses can be plausible and incorrect, ask focused questions, verify claims against official Java documentation and compiler feedback, identify unfamiliar APIs and dependencies, review code for accessibility and security, and disclose assistance when required. When permitted, AI may explain a diagnostic, ask guiding questions, rephrase a concept, suggest tests, or critique a proposed class design.

Java-specific risks

Review generated Java for:

  • Language features or APIs requiring a newer JDK than the course environment.
  • Incorrect imports, package declarations, class/file names, or main signatures.
  • Incompatible types, unsafe casts, incorrect generics, and confusion between primitive and reference types.
  • Incorrect use of == for String content comparison instead of .equals().
  • Null handling that can cause NullPointerException.
  • Incorrect resource handling, file paths, exception declarations, or broad catch blocks.
  • Confusion among Scanner.next(), nextLine(), and numeric input, including the pending-newline issue.
  • Unnecessary frameworks, Maven/Gradle dependencies, or architecture beyond the lesson.
  • Long declarations, deeply nested code, and IDE-generated scaffolding that is difficult to navigate.

Compile with the course’s JDK, read the complete diagnostic, and run tests. Check API and language claims in official Java documentation and the Java Language Specification.

Screen-reader and IDE review

Review whether the learner can navigate package and class declarations, fields, constructors, methods, and main; identify braces and nested blocks; understand method names, parameters, return types, and access modifiers; and access diagnostics as text with reliable file and line references. Prefer a small number of clear classes and methods over elaborate architecture. Explain generated boilerplate rather than treating it as magic.

Privacy, security, copyright, and equity

Do not enter student records, credentials, API keys, private repositories, or confidential school information into public AI systems. Follow school policy, approved-tool lists, age requirements, and data-protection obligations. Treat generated shell commands, build files, and dependency recommendations as untrusted. Verify library coordinates and maintainers before adding dependencies. Do not assume generated code is original or correctly licensed. Provide a non-AI alternative and discuss assumptions about visual IDE workflows and graphical output.

Verification protocol: Ask – Inspect – Verify – Adapt – Explain – Disclose

  1. Ask: state the concept or error and what the student understands.
  2. Inspect: identify unfamiliar types, APIs, dependencies, and assumptions.
  3. Verify: consult official documentation, compile with the target JDK, and test normal, boundary, and invalid cases.
  4. Adapt: simplify, correct, secure, and format for the learner’s level and access workflow.
  5. Explain: have the learner explain each class, method, type, and exception path and make a modification independently.
  6. Disclose: record the tool and its contribution when required.

Activity-specific policy

  • Practice: hints, explanations, and test ideas may be allowed; full solutions should be reserved for explicit code-review activities.
  • Projects: define permitted AI assistance in advance; require disclosure, tests, and an explanation of design decisions.
  • Individual assessments: AI should not perform the skill being measured unless the assessment explicitly evaluates AI-assisted development or an accommodation requires it.
  • Accessibility: screen readers, braille displays, magnification, and approved access tools are not prohibited answer-generation tools.

Discussion prompts

  • An AI example compiles on a newer JDK but not on class machines. How can the learner identify the version dependency?
  • An assistant uses == to compare two strings. How can the student demonstrate the defect?
  • A generated program catches every exception and prints “Something went wrong.” Why is that inadequate?
  • How can a learner distinguish understanding an object-oriented design from merely running it?

21. Comprehensive Instructional Planning and Course Implementation

This section consolidates practices that apply across the philosophy, learner-context, classroom setup, spoken-code, unit, assessment, differentiation, and resource sections above. Use it as a course-planning reference from intake through capstone evaluation.

21.1 Course planning and alignment

Map each unit to prerequisites, learning objectives, practice opportunities, and evidence of mastery. Do not assume every unit needs equal time.

  • Identify outcomes: problem decomposition, code reading and writing, data representation, control flow, functions or methods, debugging, testing, and communication.
  • Separate programming prerequisites from access-tool prerequisites.
  • Record the operating system, editor/IDE, runtime, terminal, screen reader, braille display, magnification, and adaptive input technology used.
  • Identify essential concepts, enrichment topics, and material that can be deferred without breaking later lessons.
  • Plan checkpoints after each major concept group and adjust pacing using student evidence.
  • Maintain a map linking each lesson to objectives, practice, assessment, accessibility considerations, and likely misconceptions.

A suggested progression is environment and navigation; computing foundations; expressions and data; input/output; decisions and loops; collections; functions or methods; object-oriented concepts; files and errors; testing; projects; capstone. Preserve prerequisites when reordering.

21.2 Readiness and learner partnership

Ask about preferred access methods, prior programming experience, keyboard navigation, file management, and what makes technical instruction usable. Ask about functional access requirements rather than requesting unnecessary diagnostic details.

Use a low-stakes baseline activity to observe how the learner opens and navigates a source file, moves by line/word/character/symbol, creates and saves a file, runs a command, locates output, and reads a diagnostic. Record strengths and supports, not just deficits. Revisit the baseline to recognize growth. Keep the learner central to decisions about tools and workflow.

21.3 Repeatable lesson architecture

  1. Purpose: state the problem the lesson addresses.
  2. Prerequisite retrieval: revisit the prior concept needed today.
  3. Vocabulary: define technical terms and spoken symbol conventions.
  4. Explicit model: demonstrate a small runnable example and narrate navigation and code changes.
  5. Trace: read the code structurally and predict behavior.
  6. Guided practice: solve a similar problem with prompts and fading support.
  7. Independent transfer: apply the concept to a new requirement.
  8. Debug and reflect: examine an intentional error or unexpected result.
  9. Exit check: collect an explanation, prediction, code change, or test.

State one navigation action at a time, allow the learner to complete it, and confirm the result before continuing. Provide source files and commands in advance when possible. Narrate all actions in shared-screen demonstrations and provide an equivalent text-based route.

21.4 Explicit instruction for accessible code navigation

Teach file structure before reading every line. Identify current focus and how to return to a known location. Teach line, word, character, symbol, selection, search, and go-to-line navigation, plus navigation to functions, methods, classes, and diagnostics. Explain indentation and block boundaries. Use manageable line lengths and avoid unnecessarily nested expressions. Give students time to read diagnostics and output independently. Do not take over the keyboard without explaining the action and obtaining the learner’s agreement.

21.5 Language-specific instructional emphasis: Java

Java’s explicit types, compilation, and class structure require deliberate sequencing:

  • Teach the JDK, compiler, runtime, source file, class, and main method before IDE-generated projects.
  • State the target JDK version and explain when features require a newer release.
  • Contrast primitive values and reference types, assignment and comparison, conversions, and integer versus floating-point division.
  • Teach String content comparison with .equals(), not ==, and explain null references.
  • Model Scanner input carefully, especially the newline remaining after token or numeric reads.
  • Teach array bounds, ArrayList operations, generic types, and collection selection with small examples.
  • Separate method signature, parameter, argument, return type, and method call. Explain static versus instance behavior.
  • Teach constructors, encapsulation, inheritance, and composition as design choices, not just syntax.
  • Read compiler diagnostics before running; distinguish compile-time errors, runtime exceptions, and logic defects.
  • Keep build tools and external dependencies out of early lessons unless required. Explain Maven or Gradle when introduced.

21.6 Misconceptions and diagnostic teaching

Ask learners to predict behavior, explain their prediction, run a small experiment, and revise their mental model.

Common issueInstructional response
Confusing assignment with comparisonContrast operators and trace values before and after execution.
Treating input as already numericIdentify input type, convert explicitly, and test valid and invalid values.
Off-by-one loop or index errorsTrace first, typical, and final iterations; state the valid index range.
Choosing an unsuitable collectionDescribe access patterns and required operations before choosing a structure.
Writing one large function or methodDecompose the task by responsibility and test each part.
Treating a running program as necessarily correctDefine expected behavior and test normal, boundary, and invalid inputs.
Copying code without tracing itAsk the learner to predict a new case and make a modification.
Misreading an error messageLocate the useful diagnostic, identify file and line, and inspect surrounding code.

Language-specific pitfalls include: primitive versus reference values; integer division; String identity versus content equality; null references; array bounds; constructor and method signatures; static versus instance members; checked exceptions; and the Scanner newline behavior.

21.7 Differentiation without lowering the learning objective

Adjust the path, not the intellectual goal. Supports may include smaller task increments, additional practice, explicit worked examples, alternative information formats, extra navigation time, starter code with gradually faded scaffolding, oral explanation or accessible demonstration, pair programming with rotating roles, predictable routines, and enrichment tasks that deepen the same concept.

Do not assume all blind students need the same support or that all low-vision students prefer magnification. Ask, document, and review supports with the learner.

21.8 Formative assessment, feedback, and grading

Collect evidence frequently: explain a concept, predict output, trace a loop, justify a data structure, find and fix a bug, write a boundary test, refactor code, or demonstrate an accessible workflow.

A practical rubric can score each dimension from 1 (beginning) to 4 (independent and consistent):

DimensionEvidence
Conceptual reasoningExplains the problem, algorithm, and language concepts
ImplementationProduces a solution that meets requirements
Code comprehensionReads, traces, explains, and modifies code
Testing and debuggingUses test cases and interprets diagnostics
Accessibility and communicationProduces understandable interaction and operates the workflow with access tools
Independence and reflectionDescribes decisions, limitations, and next steps

Share criteria before assessment. Feedback should name observed behavior, explain its impact, and identify an actionable next step. Do not grade screen-reader speed, typing speed, or visual formatting as proxies for programming competence.

21.9 Debugging and classroom support protocol

  1. Ask the learner to describe expected behavior.
  2. Ask what actually happened.
  3. Read the complete error or diagnostic, including source and location.
  4. Identify the smallest relevant code section.
  5. Form one hypothesis.
  6. Change one thing and rerun the program or test.
  7. Record what the result taught the learner.

Distinguish environment failures, tool-access failures, syntax/compile errors, runtime errors, and logic errors. Maintain a troubleshooting record with environment, exact command, error text, attempted correction, and outcome. Remove credentials and private information before sharing logs.

21.10 Pair programming and collaboration

Use explicit roles: the driver controls the keyboard and implements the agreed step; the navigator reasons about the algorithm, checks requirements, proposes tests, and reviews the result. Rotate roles. Do not automatically assign a blind student the navigator role. Both learners should have opportunities to operate tools and write code. Provide shared source files and task instructions in accessible formats.

21.11 Project and capstone supervision

Require a proposal that includes the problem and intended user, functional requirements, out-of-scope features, input/output design, data representation, major functions/methods/classes, accessibility requirements, milestones, tests, and any libraries or AI assistance used.

Review milestones: requirements, design, first working slice, feature completion, tests, documentation, and final explanation. Encourage a modest, complete, well-tested project over an ambitious unfinished one.

21.12 Collaboration with families and support professionals

When appropriate and with learner consent, coordinate with special educators, teachers of students with visual impairments, assistive-technology specialists, interpreters, and families. Agree on who supports access technology, who teaches programming, and how the student obtains help. Keep the learner’s agency central, share only necessary information, and follow school privacy policies. Do not make aides the default operators of the student’s computer.

21.13 Instructor preparation checklist

Before each unit, complete the learner-facing activities; verify commands and versions on the classroom platform; test keyboard and assistive-technology workflows; prepare expected output and common error examples; identify vocabulary, symbols, misconceptions, and prerequisites; provide accessible instructions and assessment criteria; and decide how understanding will be observed.

After each unit, review student work and feedback, note barriers, adjust pacing and scaffolds, and record reproducible corrections. Document agreed accommodations rather than silently changing expectations.

21.14 Quality assurance and continuous improvement

Review links, software versions, commands, APIs, package recommendations, and assessment assumptions periodically. Test with actual screen readers and braille displays where possible; a successful build or visual inspection alone does not establish accessibility.

When reporting a barrier, include the page, reproduction steps, operating system, editor/runtime version, assistive technology and version, expected behavior, and actual behavior. Exclude personally identifying or sensitive student information. Submit corrections through the project contribution process.

Teacher’s Guide: Introduction to Computer Science with JavaScript

For Students with Visual Impairments — Complete Instructor Edition

How to use this teacher’s guide

This guide is a companion for instructors, not a script that must be followed word for word. Read the philosophy, learner-context, and technology sections before the first lesson; use the unit notes while planning; and return to the assessment, differentiation, AI, and quick-reference sections throughout the course. Adapt procedures to the learner’s actual assistive technology, operating system, course goals, and prior experience. Confirm tool-specific instructions in current official documentation because editor, screen-reader, and runtime behavior changes over time.

Plan for both programming learning and access to the programming environment. Establish what the student can already do independently, what access skills need instruction, what supports are already in place, and how the learner prefers to receive feedback. Never assume a diagnosis predicts a student’s preferred tools or level of independence.

1. Philosophy and Why JavaScript

The Case for Teaching JavaScript to Blind Students

JavaScript has a unique profile of benefits and challenges for visually impaired learners:

Universal relevance. JavaScript is the only language that runs natively in every web browser. A student who learns JavaScript can eventually build tools that improve their own accessibility experience — custom browser extensions, accessible widgets, automation scripts. This self-advocacy potential is meaningful.

Node.js enables accessible terminal programs. While JavaScript began in browsers, Node.js allows running JavaScript programs in the terminal — the same accessible text-based environment used for Python. This curriculum focuses on Node.js to keep all I/O in the terminal where screen readers excel.

Asynchronous programming is a real-world skill. JavaScript’s async/await model reflects how most modern software actually works — programs that wait for I/O, network requests, and user events. Learning this early prepares students for professional development.

The npm ecosystem. Over 2 million packages on npm provide pre-built solutions for almost any problem. This is a double-edged concern for beginners (dependency complexity), but the ability to say npm install and gain powerful functionality is professionally relevant.

JSON is native. JSON.parse() and JSON.stringify() are built into JavaScript with no import required. For data persistence projects, this reduces friction.

An Honest Account of Challenges

JavaScript’s permissiveness is a silent-failure risk. Unlike Python (which raises exceptions for type mismatches) and Java (which rejects them at compile time), JavaScript silently converts types. "5" + 3 = "53". "5" - 3 = 2. 0 == false = true. Without visual scanning of intermediate results, these silent failures can propagate through a program undetected. This must be addressed through defensive programming habits taught from day one.

Asynchronous programming is conceptually hard. The async/await pattern required for user input is a genuine hurdle for beginners. There is no way to eliminate it from a Node.js input-based curriculum. The approach in this guide is to scaffold it carefully and defer full explanation of the event loop to later units.

Multiple valid syntaxes. Function declarations, function expressions, arrow functions, methods — all do essentially the same thing. var, let, const — three variable declarations. == and === — two equality operators. This variety, which professionals call “JavaScript fatigue,” creates unnecessary cognitive overhead for beginners. The approach in this curriculum is to teach one style consistently (const/let, arrow functions, ===) and acknowledge alternatives exist without teaching them in parallel.

2. JavaScript-Specific Accessibility Challenges

Silent Type Coercion

This is the greatest accessibility risk in JavaScript for blind students. Unlike Python’s TypeError and Java’s compile-time type check, JavaScript silently converts types in ways that can produce wrong answers with no error:

ExpressionResultExpected by ProgrammerProblem
"5" + 3"53"8+ concatenates when one operand is a string
"5" - 322- converts string to number
"5" * "3"1515Multiplication converts both
"" == falsetrueMaybe?Loose equality coercion
0 == falsetrueMaybe?Same
null == undefinedtrueProbably not
NaN === NaNfalsetrueNaN is not equal to itself

Mitigation: Require Number() before any arithmetic on user input. Require === always. Teach typeof and isNaN() as defensive checks. Make logging intermediate values an explicit exercise before running any calculation.

undefined vs. null vs. NaN vs. false vs. 0 vs. ""

All six of these are “falsy” in JavaScript. Aurally, they are indistinguishable unless you call typeof or check explicitly. A student who hears console.log(result) and the screen reader announces “false” cannot know whether result is false, 0, "", null, undefined, or NaN without further inspection.

Teaching approach: Establish a diagnostic template:

console.log("Value:", result, "Type:", typeof result);

This outputs both the value and its type, providing audio context that console.log(result) alone does not.

Callback Hell and Asynchronous Confusion

Before async/await, Node.js input used nested callbacks:

// Confusing nesting --- avoid in teaching
rl.question("Name? ", (name) => {
  rl.question("Age? ", (age) => {
    rl.question("City? ", (city) => {
      console.log(`${name}, ${age}, ${city}`);
    });
  });
});

This nesting produces code that is confusing to read AND to hear — the indentation deepens with each question. The async/await pattern linearizes this:

// Clear and linear --- use this exclusively
const name = await askQuestion("Name? ");
const age = await askQuestion("Age? ");
const city = await askQuestion("City? ");
console.log(`${name}, ${age}, ${city}`);

Teach async/await from the start and avoid callback patterns entirely in this course.

3. Classroom Setup and Configuration

VS Code or Theia IDE for JavaScript

Theia IDE is an alternative editor with keyboard- and screen-reader-oriented workflows suitable for this course. It supports many VS Code extensions through Open VSX; check availability of ESLint, Prettier, and JavaScript language support, and verify each workflow with the learner’s screen reader. VS Code-specific settings and shortcuts may differ.

Required extensions:

  • ESLint — catches type issues, undefined variables, and style violations before running code
  • Prettier — auto-formats code consistently (run on save with editor.formatOnSave: true)
  • JavaScript (ES6) code snippets — tab-complete common patterns

Recommended ESLint flat configuration (eslint.config.mjs in project root; install the current ESLint, @eslint/js, and globals packages as local development dependencies):

import js from "@eslint/js";
import globals from "globals";

export default [
  {
    files: ["**/*.js"],
    languageOptions: {
      ecmaVersion: "latest",
      sourceType: "commonjs",
      globals: globals.node
    },
    rules: {
      ...js.configs.recommended.rules,
      eqeqeq: "error",
      "no-unused-vars": "warn",
      "no-console": "off"
    }
  }
];

The eqeqeq: error rule makes == a linting error — it must be ===. This is an automated enforcement of the rule that prevents the most common silent bugs.

Node.js REPL accessibility:

node                      # Start REPL
.help                     # List REPL commands
.exit                     # Quit (or Ctrl+D)

Windows Powershell

node                      # Start REPL
.help                     # List REPL commands
.exit                     # Quit (or Ctrl+D)

The Node.js REPL is excellent for early exploration. Results are printed immediately after each expression, providing audio feedback without the compile-run-read cycle.

Alternative JavaScript Environments

EnvironmentPlatformAccessibilityNotes
Node.js + VS CodeAllHighRecommended setup
Node.js + terminal onlyAllHighFor students who prefer minimal UI
Replit.comWebMediumNo-install; test with student’s setup
CodeSandboxWebMediumCloud editor; variable accessibility
GitHub CodespacesWebHighCloud VS Code; same accessibility as local
Glitch.comWebMediumProject-based; variable accessibility
ObservableWebLowNotebook-style; primarily visual
DenoRuntimeHighAlternative to Node.js; similar accessibility

4. Spoken JavaScript Conventions

Symbol/PatternSpoken Form
const“const”
let“let”
var“var” (avoid; legacy)
===“triple equals” or “strict equal”
!==“strict not equal”
==“loose equal” (should hear this rarely)
=>“arrow” or “fat arrow”
...arr“spread arr”
...args“rest args”
async“async”
await“await”
undefined“undefined”
null“null”
NaN“NaN” (say each letter N-A-N)
typeof“typeof”
instanceof“instanceof”
new“new”
this“this”
class“class”
extends“extends”
super“super”
import“import”
export“export”
require()“require”
module.exports“module dot exports”
Promise“Promise”
async function“async function”
() => {}“arrow function”
(x) => x * 2“arrow function taking x, returning x times 2”
#field“hash field” or “private field”
`template ${var}`“backtick template literal with variable var”

Reading an arrow function:

const doubleIfPositive = (n) => (n > 0 ? n * 2 : n);

“const doubleIfPositive gets arrow function taking n, returning: if n greater than 0, n times 2, else n”

Modern JavaScript and Node.js conventions

Teach the curriculum against the current Node.js 26 LTS line. Node.js 26.13.0 entered LTS on October 28, 2026; use the latest security patch in the 26.x line rather than pinning students to an old patch. Node.js 24 remains supported as LTS, but is not the current LTS line.

For new course examples, consistently use const/let, strict equality, explicit numeric conversion, async/await, and node: built-in module specifiers. Prefer the built-in node:test runner for basic unit tests; Jest is a valid optional framework, not a requirement. Keep the two module systems explicit: use a package.json type field and matching file extensions/configuration, and never mix CommonJS and ES module syntax in one file. Use current ESLint flat configuration (eslint.config.mjs) rather than the deprecated .eslintrc format. Check input and parsed JSON at runtime: JavaScript’s runtime values remain dynamic even when editor tooling or static analysis is used.

5. Unit 0–1: Setup and Foundations

Lesson 0.1: Installing Node.js

Instructional Cues

Verify installation at every step:

node --version    # Should print v26.x.x (26.13.0 or a newer 26.x maintenance release)
npm --version     # Should print a version number
npx --version     # Should print a version number (npx is bundled with npm)

Windows Powershell

node --version    # Should print v26.x.x (26.13.0 or a newer 26.x maintenance release)
npm --version     # Should print a version number
npx --version     # Should print a version number (npx is bundled with npm)

All three must work. If npm is missing, the student may have installed only the Node.js runtime without npm. Reinstall from nodejs.org (npm is included in the standard installer).

REPL first — files second: Begin with node in the terminal. Let the student type expressions and hear results immediately. This builds confidence before introducing the file -> run -> read cycle:

$ node
> 5 + 3
8
> "Hello " + "World"
'Hello World'
> typeof 42
'number'
> typeof "hello"
'string'
> .exit

The npm init conversation: When initializing a project, npm init -y generates package.json automatically. Walk the student through reading the generated file:

npm init -y
cat package.json   # or type package.json on Windows

Windows Powershell

npm init -y
Get-Content package.json

package.json is plain JSON text — fully readable with a screen reader. Understanding its structure is important for later lessons about dependencies and scripts.

Non-Obvious Accessibility Strategies

  • Node.js version managers: nvm (Node Version Manager) allows multiple Node.js versions. For a student who may work on multiple machines or projects, run nvm install 26 and then nvm use 26 to select the Node.js 26 LTS line. nvm is command-line-only and fully accessible.
  • Project-local dependencies: install course tools with npm install or npm install --save-dev from the project folder. Run local executables with npx or npm scripts. Avoid npm install -g for course tools; global installations can conflict across projects.

Thought Experiments

  1. “JavaScript was created in 10 days in 1995. What marks of that hasty design are still visible in modern JavaScript? (Think about typeof null === 'object', NaN !== NaN, 0 == false.) Why haven’t these been fixed?”

  2. “Node.js uses a single-threaded event loop to handle many concurrent operations. A traditional multi-threaded approach uses multiple threads running in parallel. For a web server handling thousands of requests, what are the tradeoffs of each approach? Which tends to be more memory efficient?”

  3. “npm has millions of packages. The average Node.js project depends on hundreds of packages, many maintained by single developers with no organizational backing. The ‘left-pad incident’ in 2016 broke thousands of projects when one 11-line package was unpublished. What does this incident reveal about the risks and benefits of the npm ecosystem?”

  4. “JavaScript runs in browsers, in Node.js servers, in mobile apps via React Native, in desktop apps via Electron, in IoT devices, and even in serverless cloud functions. What does this ubiquity tell you about the relationship between a language’s design and its adoption?”

Lesson 1.3: Variables and Data Types

Instructional Cues

const vs. let — establish the rule on day one:

“Use const for everything. If you get an error saying you’re trying to reassign a const, THEN change it to let. This approach produces cleaner code and prevents accidental reassignment bugs.”

Demonstrate the error:

const x = 5;
x = 10; // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

“This error is helpful. const is protecting you from changing something you said was fixed.”

Dynamic typing with auditory ambiguity:

Run this sequence in the REPL and ask the student to predict each output before pressing Enter:

typeof 42; // "number"
typeof "42"; // "string"
typeof true; // "boolean"
typeof null; // "object"  <- the famous bug
typeof undefined; // "undefined"
typeof {}; // "object"
typeof []; // "object"  <- arrays are objects!
typeof function () {}; // "function"

“Notice that both {} (object) and [] (array) produce ‘object’. How do you tell them apart? Array.isArray([]) returns true. Array.isArray({}) returns false.”

Template literals vs. concatenation:

const name = "Alice";
const age = 15;

// Concatenation --- confusing order of operations when read aloud
console.log("Hello, " + name + "! You are " + age + " years old.");

// Template literal --- linear, clean, easy to hear
console.log(`Hello, ${name}! You are ${age} years old.`);

Read both versions aloud with the student. Ask which is easier to follow aurally. Template literals are almost universally clearer when heard, because the variable values appear where they belong in the sentence.

Thought Experiments

  1. “JavaScript has only one number type for integers and decimals. Python has separate int and float. Java has int, long, double, float. What precision problems arise from having a single number type? When does 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 matter, and when doesn’t it?”

  2. “JavaScript has six falsy values: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy — including "false" (a non-empty string), [] (an empty array), and {} (an empty object). Design a quiz: ask the student whether ten different expressions are truthy or falsy. Which answers are surprising?”

  3. “var has function scope; let and const have block scope. What does ‘scope’ mean? How does a variable declared inside an if block with var vs. let behave differently? Which behavior is more predictable and why?”

6. Unit 2: Numbers, Input, and Math

Lesson 2.2: User Input in Node.js

Instructional Cues

The input helper module pattern:

Provide the input.js module in every project skeleton. Students should not need to re-create this boilerplate:

// input.js
const readline = require("node:readline");
const rl = readline.createInterface({
  input: process.stdin,
  output: process.stdout,
});

function askQuestion(prompt) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => rl.question(prompt, resolve));
}

function close() {
  rl.close();
}

module.exports = { askQuestion, close };

Walk through what each line does at least once so students understand the structure, but do not require students to write it from scratch until they’re comfortable with async programming.

The async/await mental model — teach this story:

“When your code hits await, imagine it puts up a ‘please wait’ sign and steps aside. Other things can happen while you wait. When the answer arrives, your code picks up exactly where it paused. The async keyword on the function declaration is your promise that ‘this function may pause at some point.’”

async function main() {
  console.log("Starting..."); // 1: runs immediately
  const name = await askQuestion("Name? "); // 2: pauses here until user types
  console.log("Got name:", name); // 3: runs after user answers
  const age = await askQuestion("Age? "); // 4: pauses again
  console.log(`${name} is ${age}`); // 5: runs after user answers again
  close();
}

main(); // Kick off the async function

Ask: “What line is running while the program waits for user input?” (None — the function is paused. The event loop can handle other things.)

Why main() must be called at the bottom: async function main() defines the function but doesn’t run it. The main() call at the end actually starts execution. Without the call, nothing happens. This trips up beginners — demonstrate it.

Non-Obvious Accessibility Strategies

  • rl.close() is mandatory: Without rl.close(), the Node.js process continues running after main() finishes. The terminal appears to hang — cursor blinks but no prompt. For a screen reader user, this is confusing. Teach close() as the final step of every program that uses input.

  • Prompt trailing space: Always include a trailing space in prompt strings: "Enter your name: ". Without the space, the cursor appears immediately after the colon with no separation, which some screen readers render as “Enter your name:cursor” — an awkward audio experience.

  • Input validation loop: Without validation, a blank Enter or a non-numeric string for a number causes silent failure. Provide this reusable pattern:

async function getNumber(prompt) {
  while (true) {
    const input = await askQuestion(prompt);
    const num = Number(input.trim());
    if (!isNaN(num)) return num;
    console.log("Invalid input: please enter a number.");
  }
}

Teach this pattern and require students to use it whenever they need numeric input.

Thought Experiments

  1. “The readline module uses an ‘event listener’ pattern — rl.question(prompt, callback) means ‘when the user answers, call this function.’ The async/await pattern wraps this in a Promise. What problem does the Promise solve that the raw callback doesn’t? (Think about reading the code linearly.)”

  2. “Node.js uses a single-threaded event loop. While your program is waiting for user input (await askQuestion), the thread is free. What else could the thread be doing? In a real application, this might mean handling a different request or updating state. What does this tell you about why async/await is important for scalable programs?”

  3. “Synchronous input (blocking until the user responds) and asynchronous input (doing other things while waiting) represent fundamentally different programming models. For a single-user command-line program, which matters? For a server handling 10,000 simultaneous users, which matters more? Why?”

7. Unit 3: Control Flow

Lessons 3.1–3.3

Instructional Cues

=== enforcement — make it automatic:

With ESLint configured to flag ==, the student will hear a warning whenever they use loose equality. Walk through the first warning together:

if (userInput == 5) {   // ESLint: Expected '===' and instead saw '=='

“ESLint is protecting you from a common silent bug. Change this to ===. The only exception is checking for null-or-undefined: x == null is sometimes used as a shorthand for x === null || x === undefined — but avoid this until you understand it.”

Truthy/falsy in input validation:

const name = await askQuestion("Enter your name: ");
if (!name.trim()) {
  console.log("Name cannot be empty.");
  // re-prompt...
}

!name.trim() is true when the trimmed string is empty ("" is falsy). This is idiomatic JavaScript. Read it aloud: “if not name dot trim” — ask: “What does ‘not an empty string’ mean? Why is an empty string falsy?”

Ternary operator — limit its use:

The ternary condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse is concise but can be hard to follow when read aloud:

const status = score >= 60 ? "pass" : "fail";

Read: “const status gets: if score greater-than-or-equal 60, quote pass, else quote fail”

Teach it but establish this rule: “If the ternary is easy to read aloud in one breath, use it. If it requires re-reading, use if-else.”

Thought Experiments

  1. “JavaScript’s == performs type coercion before comparing. TypeScript (a typed superset of JavaScript) was partly created to address this. What does TypeScript’s existence tell you about the real-world cost of JavaScript’s permissiveness? What did developers gain from TypeScript that JavaScript didn’t provide?”

  2. “Consider: if (userName) vs. if (userName !== '' && userName !== null && userName !== undefined). The first uses JavaScript’s truthiness; the second is explicit. In a code review, which would you prefer seeing? What are the readability and correctness tradeoffs?”

  3. “JavaScript’s optional chaining (?.) and nullish coalescing (??) were added to the language to handle null/undefined more gracefully. user?.address?.city returns undefined instead of throwing if user or address is null. Why did this feature take decades to add to a language created in 1995?”

  4. “The switch statement falls through by default in JavaScript. Modern JavaScript has been moving away from switch toward mapping objects for dispatch tables. const actions = { 'add': addFunc, 'delete': deleteFunc }; actions[command]?.();. What are the accessibility implications of this pattern vs. a switch statement when read with a screen reader?”

8. Unit 4: Arrays and Objects

Lesson 4.1: Arrays and Functional Methods

Instructional Cues

Introduce map, filter, reduce as a trio:

Don’t teach them one per lesson — teach the relationship between them first:

“These three methods each take a function and apply it to every element in an array. map transforms elements. filter keeps or removes elements. reduce combines elements into one value. Together they cover most array processing.”

Then give one shared example that uses all three:

const students = [
  { name: "Alice", score: 88 },
  { name: "Bob", score: 62 },
  { name: "Charlie", score: 95 },
  { name: "Diana", score: 71 },
];

// 1. Filter passing students (score >= 70)
const passing = students.filter((s) => s.score >= 70);

// 2. Map to get just names
const passingNames = passing.map((s) => s.name);

// 3. Reduce to build a report string
const report = passingNames.reduce(
  (acc, name) => acc + name + ", ",
  "Passing: ",
);

console.log(report); // "Passing: Alice, Charlie, Diana, "
console.log("Count:", passing.length);

Accessible printing for arrays of objects:

// Accessible: numbered, labeled fields
students.forEach((student, index) => {
  console.log(`${index + 1}. ${student.name}: ${student.score}`);
});

// Less accessible: raw object output
console.log(students); // Produces cluttered bracket notation when read aloud

Chaining — build up incrementally:

Show chaining as a composition of steps, each of which you can trace separately:

const result = numbers
  .filter((n) => n % 2 === 0) // Step 1: keep evens
  .map((n) => n ** 2) // Step 2: square each
  .reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0); // Step 3: sum

// DEBUG: break the chain to trace each step
const step1 = numbers.filter((n) => n % 2 === 0);
console.log("After filter:", step1);
const step2 = step1.map((n) => n ** 2);
console.log("After map:", step2);
const step3 = step2.reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0);
console.log("Final sum:", step3);

The debug version (step-by-step) is more accessible during development. Consolidate to the chain after confirming correctness.

Thought Experiments

  1. “map, filter, and reduce come from functional programming — a paradigm based on mathematical functions that have no side effects. JavaScript arrays also have forEach which is for side effects only. What is the philosophical distinction between map and forEach? Why does this distinction matter for reasoning about code correctness?”

  2. “The sort method in JavaScript sorts in-place and mutates the original array. filter, map, and reduce return new arrays, leaving the original unchanged. Why the asymmetry? What bugs could arise from sort’s mutation? How would you sort without mutating: [...arr].sort(...)?”

  3. _“Functional composition: const double = n => n _ 2; const addOne = n => n + 1; const doubleAndAdd = n => addOne(double(n)). How does function composition scale? What is the advantage of composing small, focused functions over writing one large function that does everything?”*

  4. “The spread operator [...arr] creates a shallow copy of an array. For an array of primitives [1, 2, 3], the spread copy is fully independent. For an array of objects [{name: 'A'}, {name: 'B'}], the objects inside are still shared. What does ‘shallow copy’ mean? When does this distinction cause bugs?”

Lesson 4.2: Objects

Instructional Cues

Destructuring — introduce before objects are complex:

const person = { name: "Alice", age: 15, city: "Portland" };

// Without destructuring:
const name = person.name;
const age = person.age;

// With destructuring:
const { name, age } = person;

// In function parameter:
function introduce({ name, age }) {
  console.log(`Hi, I'm ${name}, ${age} years old.`);
}
introduce(person);

Destructuring is ubiquitous in modern JavaScript. Teaching it early reduces the verbosity of object access code, which in turn makes programs cleaner to read and hear.

Object.keys(), Object.values(), Object.entries() as navigation tools:

For a student who cannot visually inspect an object in a debugger panel, these methods provide audio-accessible object introspection:

const config = { theme: "dark", fontSize: 14, notifications: true };

// What properties does this object have?
console.log(Object.keys(config).join(", "));

// What are all the values?
Object.values(config).forEach((v) => console.log(v));

// Both together:
Object.entries(config).forEach(([key, value]) => {
  console.log(`${key}: ${value}`);
});

Optional chaining for safe nested access:

const user = { profile: { address: null } };

// Without optional chaining --- crashes if address is null
const city = user.profile.address.city; // TypeError!

// With optional chaining --- returns undefined instead
const city = user?.profile?.address?.city; // undefined, no crash

// With nullish coalescing for a default
const city = user?.profile?.address?.city ?? "Unknown city";

This pattern is essential for working with real-world data where fields may be missing.

Thought Experiments

  1. “JavaScript objects can have properties added or removed at any time. user.newField = 'value' just works. Java objects have a fixed set of fields defined at compile time. Which approach is better for representing data from an API that might add new fields in future versions? Which is better for ensuring all required fields are present?”

  2. “Object.freeze(obj) makes an object immutable — you can’t add, remove, or modify properties. This mimics the behavior of a Java final field or Python’s frozenset. When would immutable objects be useful? What patterns become possible when you can guarantee an object won’t change?”

  3. “Prototype-based inheritance means JavaScript objects can inherit from other objects directly, without classes. Classes (introduced in ES6) are ‘syntactic sugar’ over this prototype system. What does this mean? What can you do with prototypes that you cannot easily express with class syntax?”

  4. “JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the universal data exchange format. It looks almost like JavaScript object literals but has stricter rules: all keys must be double-quoted strings, no functions, no comments. Why must JSON be stricter than JavaScript object literals? What security problems would arise if JSON allowed functions?”

9. Unit 5: Strings

Instructional Cues

Template literals for multiline strings:

const menu = `
--- Main Menu ---
1. Add item
2. View all
3. Search
4. Delete
5. Quit
-----------------`;

console.log(menu);

Template literals with newlines are much cleaner for building multiline output than repeated console.log() calls. Teach this pattern for menus and reports.

Regular expression basics — connect to real need:

Before introducing regex syntax, establish the problem it solves:

“You have user input that might have extra spaces, uppercase, or punctuation. You want just the words. Without regex, you’d call .trim().toLowerCase().replace(',', '').replace('.', '')... for every punctuation mark. Regex lets you express ‘any non-letter character’ once.”

const messy = "  Hello, World!   How are you?  ";
const words = messy
  .trim()
  .toLowerCase()
  .split(/\W+/)
  .filter((w) => w.length > 0);
console.log(words); // ['hello', 'world', 'how', 'are', 'you']

Teach \w+ (word characters), \d+ (digits), \s+ (whitespace), and the g and i flags. Don’t attempt to teach full regex — a basic vocabulary is enough for data cleaning tasks.

Thought Experiments

  1. “Template literals use backticks ` while regular strings use " or '. Backticks on a keyboard are typically in the upper-left corner. For touch typists, backticks are less natural than quotes. What keyboard shortcuts or text expansions might a blind programmer use to reduce the friction of frequently-needed but awkward characters?”

  2. “String immutability in JavaScript (same as Python) means every .toUpperCase(), .replace(), and .slice() creates a new string. For a loop that builds a long string incrementally, what is the efficient alternative? (Hint: consider Array.push() + .join() as a form of StringBuilder.)”

10. Unit 6: Functions

Extended Instructional Cues

The four function forms — teach one style, acknowledge the rest:

// 1. Function declaration (hoisted --- can be called before declaration)
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

// 2. Function expression (not hoisted)
const multiply = function (a, b) {
  return a * b;
};

// 3. Arrow function --- SHORT BODY (implicit return)
const square = (n) => n * n;

// 4. Arrow function --- LONG BODY (explicit return required)
const absolute = (n) => {
  if (n < 0) return -n;
  return n;
};

Teach style 3 (short arrow) and style 4 (long arrow) as the primary forms. Acknowledge 1 and 2 exist and how to read them. Do not attempt to teach all four simultaneously.

The implicit return trap — a critical accessibility issue:

// These DO return a value:
const double = (n) => n * 2; // [x] implicit return
const greet = (name) => `Hi ${name}`; // [x] implicit return

// This does NOT return a value (the curly brace requires explicit return):
const broken = (n) => {
  n * 2; // No return statement! Returns undefined.
};

// Fixed:
const fixed = (n) => {
  return n * 2;
};

When heard aloud, n => { n * 2; } and n => { return n * 2; } sound different — the return keyword is present in one and absent in the other. Teach students to listen for return inside block-bodied arrow functions.

Higher-order functions — connect to previous array methods:

// map() takes a function as argument
const doubled = [1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 2);

// We can also pass a named function
const double = (n) => n * 2;
const doubled2 = [1, 2, 3].map(double);

// This works because map expects a function --- it doesn't care if it's
// named or anonymous, arrow or traditional

“Every time you used array.map(...), you were passing a function as an argument. Higher-order functions — functions that take other functions — are normal JavaScript.”

Closures — establish the mental model before the code:

“A closure is a function that remembers the environment where it was created, even after that environment is gone. Imagine a letter in an envelope. The letter is the function. The envelope is the environment — it contains variables the function needs. Even if the person who wrote the letter is gone, the letter still has access to everything in its envelope.”

function makeCounter(startValue = 0) {
  let count = startValue; // This is the "envelope"

  return {
    increment: () => ++count,
    decrement: () => --count,
    reset: () => {
      count = startValue;
    },
    getCount: () => count,
  };
}

const counter = makeCounter(10);
counter.increment();
counter.increment();
counter.increment();
console.log(counter.getCount()); // 13 --- count persists!

Thought Experiments

  1. “Arrow functions don’t have their own this — they inherit this from the surrounding scope. Regular functions create their own this. This was a major source of bugs in pre-ES6 JavaScript. How many of the following do you think involved confusing this? (a) Typos, (b) Variable scope errors, (c) Async timing bugs, (d) this binding bugs. In JavaScript specifically, (d) is disproportionately common — why?”

  2. “Pure functions always produce the same output for the same input and have no side effects. Math.sin(x) is pure. console.log(x) is not (it has a side effect). Why are pure functions easier to test? Why are pure functions easier to reason about in a screen-reader debugging session?”

  3. “Memoization caches the results of function calls so repeated calls with the same arguments return the cached result. Write a description of a memoized fibonacci(n) function. What is saved? What is the tradeoff? When would memoization be harmful rather than helpful?”

  4. “JavaScript is a multi-paradigm language: you can write imperative code (explicit step-by-step), object-oriented code (classes and methods), or functional code (pure functions and immutable data). For the accessible data manager project, which paradigm produces the most maintainable code? The most testable? The most readable when heard aloud?”

11. Unit 7: Classes and OOP

Instructional Cues

toString() is mandatory:

class BankAccount {
  #balance;

  constructor(owner, initialBalance = 0) {
    this.owner = owner;
    this.#balance = initialBalance;
  }

  toString() {
    return `BankAccount[owner=${this.owner}, balance=$${this.#balance.toFixed(2)}]`;
  }
}

const account = new BankAccount("Alice", 1000);
console.log(account.toString()); // BankAccount[owner=Alice, balance=$1000.00]
console.log(`${account}`); // Also calls toString() implicitly

Require toString() in every class. Explain: “When your screen reader reads console.log(myAccount), it reads toString(). Without it, you hear [object Object] — completely useless. Define toString() to hear meaningful information.”

Private fields # — establish as the default:

class Dog {
  #name; // Private --- cannot be accessed outside the class
  #age;

  constructor(name, age) {
    this.#name = name;
    this.#age = age;
  }

  get name() {
    return this.#name;
  } // Getter --- controlled access
  get age() {
    return this.#age;
  }

  set age(value) {
    if (value < 0) throw new Error("Age cannot be negative");
    this.#age = value;
  }

  bark() {
    console.log(`${this.#name} says: Woof!`);
  }

  toString() {
    return `Dog[name=${this.#name}, age=${this.#age}]`;
  }
}

“Private fields starting with # are truly private — not just conventional privacy. myDog.#name outside the class throws a SyntaxError. This is real encapsulation.”

Thought Experiments

  1. “JavaScript classes are ‘syntactic sugar’ over prototype-based inheritance. TypeScript adds static typing on top of JavaScript classes. With three layers (prototypes -> ES6 classes -> TypeScript classes), is JavaScript’s OOP model more or less trustworthy than Java’s, which has only one layer? What does ‘syntactic sugar’ imply about the behavior of the underlying mechanism?”

  2. “The class keyword was added to JavaScript in 2015, 20 years after the language was created. In those 20 years, JavaScript developers built massive applications without classes using only prototypes and closures. What does this tell you about the role of syntax vs. capability in programming languages?”

  3. “Mixins are a way to compose behavior from multiple sources without inheritance. Instead of class A extends B, you copy methods from B onto A’s prototype. JavaScript supports this; Java does not (without interfaces). When would mixins be more flexible than single inheritance? What problems could they cause?”

12. Unit 8: Files, Modules, and Error Handling

Lesson 8.1: Files

Instructional Cues

__dirname and path construction:

const path = require("node:path");
const fs = require("node:fs");

// __dirname is the directory of the current file
const dataFile = path.join(__dirname, "data", "contacts.json");

// Path joining prevents slash vs. backslash issues on Windows/macOS/Linux
console.log("Data file location:", dataFile);

For a student who cannot visually navigate a file tree, console.log(__dirname) and console.log(dataFile) are essential diagnostic tools. Teach them to print file paths as the first debugging step when a file isn’t found.

fs.existsSync() before file operations:

if (fs.existsSync(dataFile)) {
  const data = fs.readFileSync(dataFile, "utf8");
  return JSON.parse(data);
} else {
  console.log("No data file found. Starting with empty data.");
  return [];
}

Always check existence before reading. The alternative — catching ENOENT in a try-catch — works but puts normal “first run” behavior in the error path.

Lesson 8.3: CommonJS Modules

Module design for accessibility:

A well-designed module has a clear exports interface. Teach students to think of their module’s exports as its “public API” — what other files can use:

// contacts.js --- exports only what other files need
const path = require("node:path");
const fs = require("node:fs");

const DATA_FILE = path.join(__dirname, "..", "data", "contacts.json");

function loadContacts() {
  /* ... */
}
function saveContacts(contacts) {
  /* ... */
}
function findContact(contacts, name) {
  /* ... */
}

// Export only the public interface
module.exports = { loadContacts, saveContacts, findContact };

“Everything not in module.exports is private to this file. Other files can use loadContacts and saveContacts, but they cannot directly access DATA_FILE. This is encapsulation at the module level.”

Thought Experiments

  1. “Node.js’s CommonJS (require) and the ES Module standard (import) are two different module systems in JavaScript. This creates confusion — some packages use one, some use the other. TypeScript can use both. Why did two module systems emerge? What does this history say about how standards develop in open-source ecosystems?”

  2. “Synchronous file I/O (readFileSync) blocks execution until the file is read. Asynchronous file I/O (readFile or fs.promises.readFile) allows other code to run while waiting. For a startup script that reads configuration before doing anything else, which makes more sense? For a web server that handles thousands of requests, which matters more?”

  3. “Custom error classes allow code to throw and catch specific, named errors: throw new ValidationError('email', 'Invalid format'). What is the advantage of this over throwing new Error('Validation failed: email field invalid format')? Think about code that catches and handles the error.”

13. Unit 9: Collections, Analysis, and Testing

Jest Testing

Instructional Cues

Jest output is accessible:

Run npx jest --verbose for maximum accessibility. The --verbose flag produces:

PASS src/math.test.js
  add function
    [x] adds two positive numbers (3ms)
    [x] adds negative numbers (1ms)
    [x] handles zero (0ms)
  getGrade function
    [x] returns A for score >= 90 (0ms)
    [x] returns F for score < 60 (0ms)

Test Suites: 1 passed, 1 total
Tests:       5 passed, 5 total

Each test name is announced. Failures include file path, test name, expected vs. received values, and a diff. All of this is plain text — fully screen-reader-accessible.

Add to package.json scripts:

"scripts": {
    "test": "jest --verbose",
    "test:watch": "jest --verbose --watch"
}

npm test runs all tests. npm run test:watch reruns tests whenever a file changes — useful during active development.

Test naming convention:

describe("BankAccount", () => {
  describe("deposit", () => {
    test("increases balance by deposited amount", () => {
      /* ... */
    });
    test("rejects negative amounts", () => {
      /* ... */
    });
    test("rejects zero amount", () => {
      /* ... */
    });
  });
  describe("withdraw", () => {
    test("decreases balance by withdrawn amount", () => {
      /* ... */
    });
    test("throws InsufficientFundsError when balance is too low", () => {
      /* ... */
    });
  });
});

The nested describe / test structure, when announced by Jest with --verbose, reads as complete sentences: “BankAccount > deposit > increases balance by deposited amount.”

Thought Experiments

  1. “Jest’s expect(value).toEqual(expected) performs deep comparison — it checks that two objects have the same structure and values, not that they are the same object in memory. Why is deep comparison usually what you want when testing? When would you specifically want reference equality (toBe)?”

  2. “Snapshot testing in Jest captures the output of a component or function the first time, then checks future runs against that snapshot. What are the advantages? What are the risks? When might a snapshot become ‘stale’ and mislead you into thinking code is correct when it isn’t?”

  3. “Code coverage measures what percentage of your code is executed by tests. 100% coverage is a goal but not a guarantee of correctness. Design a function with 100% test coverage that still has a bug. (Hint: think about boundary conditions — what if the test covers the case where x=5 but not x=0?)”

14. Units 10–11: Projects and Capstone

JavaScript Project Structure

my-data-manager/
|--- src/
|   |--- models/
|   |   +--- contact.js
|   |--- storage/
|   |   +--- dataManager.js
|   |--- ui/
|   |   +--- consoleUI.js
|   +--- utils/
|       |--- input.js         (the readline helper)
|       +--- validation.js    (reusable validation functions)
|--- data/
|   +--- contacts.json
|--- tests/
|   |--- models/

|   +--- storage/
|       +--- dataManager.test.js
|--- eslint.config.mjs
|--- package.json
+--- index.js

package.json scripts — teach as accessibility tools:

{
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node index.js",
    "test": "jest --verbose",
    "test:watch": "jest --verbose --watch",
    "lint": "eslint src/",
    "lint:fix": "eslint src/ --fix"
  }
}

npm start — consistent command regardless of entry point filename. npm test — runs all tests. npm run lint — checks for errors without running the program.

npm run lint as a pre-run check: Teach students to run npm run lint before running the program. ESLint catches undefined variables, unused variables, and == before the program runs — much faster than finding runtime errors.

Accessible Output Design for Capstone

Require students to design their program’s output to be navigable and self-describing:

// Navigation landmark prints
function printSeparator(title) {
  const line = "-".repeat(40);
  console.log(line);
  if (title) console.log(`  ${title.toUpperCase()}`);
  console.log(line);
}

// Numbered list with clear field labels
function printContactList(contacts) {
  if (contacts.length === 0) {
    console.log("No contacts found.");
    return;
  }
  printSeparator("contacts");
  contacts.forEach((c, i) => {
    console.log(`${i + 1}. ${c.name}`);
    console.log(`   Phone: ${c.phone || "not provided"}`);
    console.log(`   Email: ${c.email || "not provided"}`);
  });
  console.log(`Total: ${contacts.length} contact(s)`);
}

// Confirmation messages --- every action must produce one
function confirmAction(action, details) {
  console.log(`[x] ${action}: ${details}`);
}

Thought Experiments

  1. “Your capstone is a command-line program. Eventually, it could become a web application. What would need to change? What would transfer directly? Write a two-column list: ‘Can reuse as-is’ and ‘Must rewrite.’”

  2. “The accessible design principle ‘no visual-only cues for critical information’ means every status, error, or confirmation must be communicated through text, not color or icon alone. Where in your program have you relied on visual formatting? How would you replace it?”

  3. “Open-source your capstone project. Write a README that explains: what the program does, how to install it, how to run it, and specifically how to use it with a screen reader. What information would a sighted user find obvious but a blind user needs explicitly stated?”

Thought experiments for Python->JS students:

  1. “In Python, you use spaces to define blocks (indentation). In JavaScript, you use {}. Python’s blocks are invisible — they’re just the alignment of characters. JavaScript’s blocks are explicitly marked. Which feels more natural? Which provides clearer information when read aloud?”

  2. “Python’s None and JavaScript’s null/undefined both represent ‘nothing,’ but they behave differently. Python has one ‘nothing’; JavaScript has two. When is null appropriate? When is undefined appropriate? Under what circumstances would you encounter one vs. the other?”

  3. “Python’s type system and JavaScript’s both use dynamic typing, but JavaScript’s is more permissive — it coerces types rather than raising errors. After using both, which approach do you find more helpful for learning? Which is more appropriate for production software?”

16. Assessment Strategies

Alternative Assessments for JavaScript

Console output analysis: Provide a JavaScript program and 3–4 sample inputs. Ask the student to predict what the program prints for each input before running it. This tests reading comprehension without requiring writing.

Linting-first review: Submit code that is free of all ESLint warnings. A student who achieves this has internalized JavaScript’s best practices at the syntax level.

Refactoring exercises: Give a working but poorly structured program. Ask the student to refactor it to use functions, modules, or classes appropriately. Assess the quality of the architecture, not just whether it runs.

Test-first implementation: Give the student a set of failing tests. Ask them to write the implementation that makes the tests pass. This tests code comprehension and problem-solving without a blank-page start.

17. Supporting Diverse Needs

For Students Who Are New to Async Programming

Async/await is conceptually hard. For students who struggle:

  1. Provide the complete input.js helper and instruct them to use it without modifying it.
  2. For the first several lessons, treat async function main() { ... } main(); as boilerplate, not content.
  3. Introduce the conceptual explanation of async/await only after students are comfortable with the rest of the language.
  4. Consider deferring async until after basic functions are mastered.

For Students with Additional Cognitive Considerations

  • ESLint provides immediate text feedback for common errors — use it as a learning tool. Hearing “no-unused-vars” and then explaining what that means is a teaching moment triggered by the student’s own code.
  • JavaScript’s many syntactic variations can be overwhelming. Enforce a single consistent style (arrow functions, const/let, ===) and defer alternatives.
  • Use the REPL liberally for short experiments so the student gets immediate feedback without file management overhead.
