Input Helper Module (Copy into every project)

// utils/input.js
const readline = require("node:readline");

const rl = readline.createInterface({
  input: process.stdin,
  output: process.stdout,
});

/**
 * Prompts the user and returns their response as a string.
 * @param {string} prompt - The question to display
 * @returns {Promise<string>} The user's trimmed response
 */
function askQuestion(prompt) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    rl.question(prompt, (answer) => resolve(answer));
  });
}

/**
 * Prompts until a valid number is entered.
 * @param {string} prompt - The question to display
 * @returns {Promise<number>} A valid number
 */
async function askNumber(prompt) {
  while (true) {
    const input = await askQuestion(prompt);
    const num = Number(input.trim());
    if (!isNaN(num)) return num;
    console.log("Invalid input: please enter a number.");
  }
}

/**
 * Closes the readline interface. Call at the end of every program.
 */
function close() {
  rl.close();
}

module.exports = { askQuestion, askNumber, close };

20. Teaching AI Tools Responsibly

AI coding assistants can provide explanations, hints, test ideas, and alternative examples. They can also produce incorrect JavaScript, misunderstand Node.js module configuration, recommend untrusted npm packages, or conceal asynchronous behavior. Treat every response as an unverified proposal. The course must remain accessible without paid AI access or a personal account.

Instructor use of AI during preparation

Instructors may use approved AI tools to brainstorm examples, draft alternative explanations, propose test inputs, or identify likely misconceptions. The instructor remains accountable for accuracy and pedagogy. Verify every API and language claim against the target Node.js release and MDN or Node.js documentation; run examples and tests; review package recommendations; and test the learning workflow with the intended access technology. Never upload identifiable student work, accommodation plans, credentials, assessment answers, or confidential school information. Do not use AI-generated feedback as the sole basis for grading. Disclose substantive AI assistance when institutional policy or the publication process requires it.

Learning goals and appropriate uses

Students should describe the limitations of code generation, ask focused questions, verify JavaScript behavior using the runtime and official documentation, identify generated code beyond their current level, and disclose assistance when required. When permitted, AI may explain a diagnostic, rephrase a concept, suggest edge cases, critique an algorithm, or generate test inputs. Prefer hint-based prompts and have the learner describe their own understanding first.

JavaScript and Node.js risks

Review AI output for:

  • Confusion between CommonJS require() and ES module import, including package type, file extensions, and runtime version.
  • Incorrect claims about semicolon insertion, equality, coercion, truthy/falsy values, undefined, null, or NaN.
  • Missing await, unhandled promise rejections, callbacks that do not complete, or incorrect execution-order assumptions.
  • Browser-only APIs used in a Node.js lesson or incorrect Node.js APIs.
  • Unsafe file paths, command execution, network requests, or untrusted input handling.
  • Unnecessary npm dependencies, typo-squatted or abandoned packages, or packages with excessive permissions.
  • Dense chaining, nested callbacks, clever one-liners, and output difficult to review sequentially.

Run examples in the course’s declared Node.js environment, inspect values and types, and test success, boundary, and failure cases. Verify API claims in official Node.js documentation or MDN.

Screen-reader and output review

Review whether braces, nested callbacks, and asynchronous control flow are navigable and explainable; identifiers are descriptive; prompts and output provide context; results arrive in a predictable order; module style is consistent; and the AI interface itself is accessible. Prefer named functions and intermediate variables when they improve understanding. Make asynchronous behavior explicit.

Privacy, security, and equity

Do not submit student records, credentials, private code, API keys, or confidential school information to public AI systems. Follow institutional policies, age requirements, and approved-tool lists. Treat terminal commands and package recommendations as untrusted. Verify package names and provenance before installation. Provide a non-AI path and never make a paid account a prerequisite. Discuss how generated examples may assume mouse use, visual browser interaction, graphical output, or a particular operating system.

Verification protocol: Ask – Inspect – Verify – Adapt – Explain – Disclose

  1. Ask: state the problem and what has already been tried.
  2. Inspect: read the response and flag unfamiliar APIs, packages, syntax, and assumptions.
  3. Verify: check MDN or Node.js documentation; run a minimal example; test normal, boundary, and invalid input.
  4. Adapt: simplify, secure, format, and make code accessible to sequential reading.
  5. Explain: have the student explain control flow and make a new change without AI.
  6. Disclose: record the tool and assistance when required.

Activity-specific policy

  • Practice: hints and explanations may be allowed; request complete solutions only for code-review activities.
  • Homework/projects: define permitted assistance and require disclosure and verification.
  • Individual assessments: do not permit AI to perform the skill being measured unless explicitly included in the assessment or an accommodation.
  • Accessibility tools: screen-reader, braille, magnification, and keyboard access tools are not prohibited answer-generation tools.

Discussion prompts

  • An AI answer mixes CommonJS and ES module syntax. How would you diagnose the mismatch?
  • A suggested npm package has a plausible name but few trustworthy details. What should you check?
  • A promise-based program prints results in an unexpected order. How can you reason about await?
  • What must a student understand if AI generated most of a function?

21. Comprehensive Instructional Planning and Course Implementation

This section consolidates practices that apply across the philosophy, learner-context, classroom setup, spoken-code, unit, assessment, differentiation, and resource sections above. Use it as a course-planning reference from intake through capstone evaluation.

21.1 Course planning and alignment

Map each unit to prerequisites, learning objectives, practice opportunities, and evidence of mastery. Do not assume every unit needs equal time.

  • Identify outcomes: problem decomposition, code reading and writing, data representation, control flow, functions or methods, debugging, testing, and communication.
  • Separate programming prerequisites from access-tool prerequisites.
  • Record the operating system, editor/IDE, runtime, terminal, screen reader, braille display, magnification, and adaptive input technology used.
  • Identify essential concepts, enrichment topics, and material that can be deferred without breaking later lessons.
  • Plan checkpoints after each major concept group and adjust pacing using student evidence.
  • Maintain a map linking each lesson to objectives, practice, assessment, accessibility considerations, and likely misconceptions.

A suggested progression is environment and navigation; computing foundations; expressions and data; input/output; decisions and loops; collections; functions or methods; object-oriented concepts; files and errors; testing; projects; capstone. Preserve prerequisites when reordering.

21.2 Readiness and learner partnership

Ask about preferred access methods, prior programming experience, keyboard navigation, file management, and what makes technical instruction usable. Ask about functional access requirements rather than requesting unnecessary diagnostic details.

Use a low-stakes baseline activity to observe how the learner opens and navigates a source file, moves by line/word/character/symbol, creates and saves a file, runs a command, locates output, and reads a diagnostic. Record strengths and supports, not just deficits. Revisit the baseline to recognize growth. Keep the learner central to decisions about tools and workflow.

21.3 Repeatable lesson architecture

  1. Purpose: state the problem the lesson addresses.
  2. Prerequisite retrieval: revisit the prior concept needed today.
  3. Vocabulary: define technical terms and spoken symbol conventions.
  4. Explicit model: demonstrate a small runnable example and narrate navigation and code changes.
  5. Trace: read the code structurally and predict behavior.
  6. Guided practice: solve a similar problem with prompts and fading support.
  7. Independent transfer: apply the concept to a new requirement.
  8. Debug and reflect: examine an intentional error or unexpected result.
  9. Exit check: collect an explanation, prediction, code change, or test.

State one navigation action at a time, allow the learner to complete it, and confirm the result before continuing. Provide source files and commands in advance when possible. Narrate all actions in shared-screen demonstrations and provide an equivalent text-based route.

21.4 Explicit instruction for accessible code navigation

Teach file structure before reading every line. Identify current focus and how to return to a known location. Teach line, word, character, symbol, selection, search, and go-to-line navigation, plus navigation to functions, methods, classes, and diagnostics. Explain indentation and block boundaries. Use manageable line lengths and avoid unnecessarily nested expressions. Give students time to read diagnostics and output independently. Do not take over the keyboard without explaining the action and obtaining the learner’s agreement.

21.5 Language-specific instructional emphasis: JavaScript

JavaScript’s dynamic type system and runtime should be made explicit:

  • Teach let, const, and scope before elaborate function patterns.
  • Contrast === and == with concrete values; make coercion visible in REPL experiments.
  • Treat undefined, null, empty strings, zero, false, and NaN as distinct values.
  • Distinguish arrays from objects and explain property access, index ranges, mutation, and iteration.
  • Introduce asynchronous input deliberately. Explain promises, async, await, and output order.
  • Teach CommonJS and ES modules as separate systems. State module mode and Node.js version before troubleshooting imports.
  • Make error handling and file paths explicit; distinguish syntax errors, runtime exceptions, rejected promises, and logic errors.
  • Use ESLint and formatting tools as feedback aids, but explain each diagnostic.

21.6 Misconceptions and diagnostic teaching

Ask learners to predict behavior, explain their prediction, run a small experiment, and revise their mental model.

Common issueInstructional response
Confusing assignment with comparisonContrast operators and trace values before and after execution.
Treating input as already numericIdentify input type, convert explicitly, and test valid and invalid values.
Off-by-one loop or index errorsTrace first, typical, and final iterations; state the valid index range.
Choosing an unsuitable collectionDescribe access patterns and required operations before choosing a structure.
Writing one large function or methodDecompose the task by responsibility and test each part.
Treating a running program as necessarily correctDefine expected behavior and test normal, boundary, and invalid inputs.
Copying code without tracing itAsk the learner to predict a new case and make a modification.
Misreading an error messageLocate the useful diagnostic, identify file and line, and inspect surrounding code.

Language-specific pitfalls include: coercion and equality; undefined versus null; truthy and falsy values; array mutation; callback and promise ordering; CommonJS versus ES modules; and browser APIs versus Node.js APIs.

21.7 Differentiation without lowering the learning objective

Adjust the path, not the intellectual goal. Supports may include smaller task increments, additional practice, explicit worked examples, alternative information formats, extra navigation time, starter code with gradually faded scaffolding, oral explanation or accessible demonstration, pair programming with rotating roles, predictable routines, and enrichment tasks that deepen the same concept.

Do not assume all blind students need the same support or that all low-vision students prefer magnification. Ask, document, and review supports with the learner.

21.8 Formative assessment, feedback, and grading

Collect evidence frequently: explain a concept, predict output, trace a loop, justify a data structure, find and fix a bug, write a boundary test, refactor code, or demonstrate an accessible workflow.

A practical rubric can score each dimension from 1 (beginning) to 4 (independent and consistent):

DimensionEvidence
Conceptual reasoningExplains the problem, algorithm, and language concepts
ImplementationProduces a solution that meets requirements
Code comprehensionReads, traces, explains, and modifies code
Testing and debuggingUses test cases and interprets diagnostics
Accessibility and communicationProduces understandable interaction and operates the workflow with access tools
Independence and reflectionDescribes decisions, limitations, and next steps

Share criteria before assessment. Feedback should name observed behavior, explain its impact, and identify an actionable next step. Do not grade screen-reader speed, typing speed, or visual formatting as proxies for programming competence.

21.9 Debugging and classroom support protocol

  1. Ask the learner to describe expected behavior.
  2. Ask what actually happened.
  3. Read the complete error or diagnostic, including source and location.
  4. Identify the smallest relevant code section.
  5. Form one hypothesis.
  6. Change one thing and rerun the program or test.
  7. Record what the result taught the learner.

Distinguish environment failures, tool-access failures, syntax/compile errors, runtime errors, and logic errors. Maintain a troubleshooting record with environment, exact command, error text, attempted correction, and outcome. Remove credentials and private information before sharing logs.

21.10 Pair programming and collaboration

Use explicit roles: the driver controls the keyboard and implements the agreed step; the navigator reasons about the algorithm, checks requirements, proposes tests, and reviews the result. Rotate roles. Do not automatically assign a blind student the navigator role. Both learners should have opportunities to operate tools and write code. Provide shared source files and task instructions in accessible formats.

21.11 Project and capstone supervision

Require a proposal that includes the problem and intended user, functional requirements, out-of-scope features, input/output design, data representation, major functions/methods/classes, accessibility requirements, milestones, tests, and any libraries or AI assistance used.

Review milestones: requirements, design, first working slice, feature completion, tests, documentation, and final explanation. Encourage a modest, complete, well-tested project over an ambitious unfinished one.

21.12 Collaboration with families and support professionals

When appropriate and with learner consent, coordinate with special educators, teachers of students with visual impairments, assistive-technology specialists, interpreters, and families. Agree on who supports access technology, who teaches programming, and how the student obtains help. Keep the learner’s agency central, share only necessary information, and follow school privacy policies. Do not make aides the default operators of the student’s computer.

21.13 Instructor preparation checklist

Before each unit, complete the learner-facing activities; verify commands and versions on the classroom platform; test keyboard and assistive-technology workflows; prepare expected output and common error examples; identify vocabulary, symbols, misconceptions, and prerequisites; provide accessible instructions and assessment criteria; and decide how understanding will be observed.

After each unit, review student work and feedback, note barriers, adjust pacing and scaffolds, and record reproducible corrections. Document agreed accommodations rather than silently changing expectations.

21.14 Quality assurance and continuous improvement

Review links, software versions, commands, APIs, package recommendations, and assessment assumptions periodically. Test with actual screen readers and braille displays where possible; a successful build or visual inspection alone does not establish accessibility.

When reporting a barrier, include the page, reproduction steps, operating system, editor/runtime version, assistive technology and version, expected behavior, and actual behavior. Exclude personally identifying or sensitive student information. Submit corrections through the project contribution process.

Julia Teacher’s Guide

Purpose and course context

This guide supports instruction in the Julia curriculum for beginning programmers, including blind and visually impaired learners using screen readers, braille displays, magnification, and keyboard-first workflows. It supplements the complete lessons and topic index.

Julia is a high-level, dynamically typed, JIT-compiled language used for numerical computing, simulation, optimization, statistics, and research. The course baseline is Julia 1.12. Teach interactive experimentation while preserving reproducibility through project environments and explicit dependencies.

Outcomes and sequence

Complete the shared Computing Foundations Primer and Terminal Skills prerequisite, then follow Units 0–11. Learners should run scripts in a project, work with values and types, use control flow and collections, write functions, reason about multiple dispatch, model data, handle files and errors, test code, and complete the capstone. They should be able to distinguish interactive convenience from a reproducible project.

Use a predictable lesson cycle: objective and vocabulary; explain the code and expected data shape; predict the result; execute; inspect textual output; change one operation; explain the result. Encourage learners to state expected types and dimensions before running array operations.

Environment and package management

Verify with julia --version. Run a script with:

julia --project=. main.jl

Activate and manage the project with Julia’s Pkg environment. Keep Project.toml and Manifest.toml under version control when the course’s reproducibility requirements call for them. Teach that JSON3.jl and CSV.jl are external packages, not standard-library modules. Use the documented project environment rather than installing packages globally or relying on a learner’s personal default environment.

Teaching Julia concepts

Dynamic typing, multiple dispatch, and functions

Julia variables are not statically declared with a fixed type in the same way as C or Go. Values have types, and functions can dispatch on argument types. Teach multiple dispatch with a small set of methods whose behavior is easy to compare. Avoid introducing many overlapping methods before learners understand function calls and argument types. Explain that type annotations in method signatures participate in dispatch; they are not simply variable declarations.

Collections, arrays, and indexing

Arrays are central to Julia. Teach dimensions, axes, shape, element type, and indexing explicitly. Julia’s conventional arrays are one-based; use eachindex when iterating over arbitrary arrays. Explain broadcasting with the dot syntax as a distinct operation and teach learners to predict shape and element-wise behavior. Never rely on a visual plot or matrix layout as the only way to understand an array; provide a textual description of dimensions and representative values.

Performance and compilation

Julia compiles methods just in time. Beginners do not need premature optimization, but instructors should explain that first-call compilation can affect timing. Do not compare a first invocation with a warmed-up run as if the difference were algorithmic. Teach benchmarking only after correctness and reproducibility, and use established benchmarking tools in project scope where required.

Files, tabular data, and errors

Use explicit paths and deterministic data fixtures. CSV.jl and JSON3.jl are dependencies, not built-ins. Explain package APIs and version constraints. Teach exceptions and validation as different concepts; handle expected missing or malformed data intentionally. Keep output in text tables or labelled records where that is more accessible than a plot.

Accessibility and instructional delivery

  • Use the REPL and terminal as text-first learning environments; make prompts and output understandable when read linearly.
  • Explain parentheses, square brackets, colons, semicolons, transpose marks, and dotted operators when introduced.
  • Describe array dimensions, axes, and data shape in text. Do not make color maps or plots essential to an assessment.
  • Teach keyboard navigation and command history without relying on mouse-driven notebook controls.
  • Keep package installation, environment activation, and execution steps explicit.
  • Offer a text summary or tabular representation for any visualization.
  • Allow time for speech/braille review of dense expressions and nested array operations.

Test the actual REPL, terminal, editor, and assistive technology in use. A notebook or plot that works visually is not necessarily accessible.

Assessment and differentiation

Assess function design, type reasoning, dispatch selection, array shape/indexing, reproducible package use, and correct handling of files and errors. Ask learners to predict result types and dimensions, not only numeric values. Include empty arrays, boundary indexes, missing data, and package/environment failures. Evaluate correctness separately from performance; do not reward optimization that obscures a clear solution.

For additional scaffolding, use vectors and scalar functions before multidimensional arrays and multiple dispatch. For advanced learners, extend to parametric methods, performance measurement, and numerical stability while preserving the introductory learning outcomes.

AI-use policy

AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, refactor, or generate course code or assessment solutions.

Instructor preparation

Verify Julia 1.12, activate the repository’s project environment, and confirm required packages install from the documented manifest or project file. Run the current example checks if provided and separately validate expected results and assistive-technology access. Record package versions and whether performance measurements include compilation warm-up. Consult the shared accessibility guidance before requiring plotting or notebook tools.

Kotlin Teacher’s Guide

Purpose and audience

This guide supports instructors teaching the Kotlin pathway to beginning programmers, including blind and visually impaired learners who use screen readers, braille displays, keyboard navigation, magnification, or other access technology. It supplements the Kotlin curriculum overview, unit lessons, and complete lesson reference.

Kotlin is a statically typed language that runs primarily on the Java Virtual Machine in this course. It interoperates with Java libraries but has distinct syntax, null-safety rules, collection interfaces, and language conventions. Do not assume Java knowledge is a prerequisite.

Course outcomes

Learners should be able to explain the role of source code, compiler, runtime, project, and dependency; write, compile, and run small Kotlin programs; declare values and variables; use numeric types and explicit conversions; read input and produce output; construct decisions and loops; select and manipulate collections; design functions; explain classes and objects; work with files and errors; test behavior; and complete and communicate an integrated project.

Recommended instructional sequence

Follow the unit order in the curriculum. Do not skip computing foundations or the terminal prerequisite simply because a learner can use an IDE. The terminal provides a transferable route to running tools, interpreting diagnostics, and understanding project structure.

Use a predictable lesson rhythm:

  1. State the learning objective and prerequisite concepts.
  2. Define new vocabulary before using it in a code example.
  3. Explain the structure of the example before asking learners to execute it.
  4. Ask learners to predict the result.
  5. Run the example and compare actual behavior with the prediction.
  6. Discuss diagnostics and common mistakes as evidence about program structure.
  7. Assign a modification that requires reasoning rather than copying.
  8. Ask the learner to explain the result in their own words.

Teaching Kotlin’s type system

Explicitly distinguish a variable’s declared type from its current value. Kotlin’s type inference reduces annotation where the type is clear, but inference does not make Kotlin dynamically typed. Use examples that contrast val and var, and explain that val prevents reassignment of the reference rather than guaranteeing deep immutability of every referenced object.

Teach numeric conversions as explicit operations. Do not imply that an Int can be used wherever a Double is expected without conversion. Explain integer division, floating-point representation, and overflow at a level appropriate to the learner’s stage.

Teaching null safety

Null safety is a central Kotlin concept. Introduce nullable types deliberately and contrast a non-nullable declaration with a nullable one. Teach the following as distinct tools:

  • Safe call ?. performs an access only when the receiver is non-null.
  • Elvis operator ?: provides an alternate expression when the left side is null.
  • Not-null assertion !! asserts that a value is not null and accepts the possibility of a runtime exception.

Do not teach !! as the routine solution to a compiler error. Ask learners to explain why a value may be absent and choose a design that handles that possibility.

Collections and data modeling

Distinguish arrays, lists, sets, and maps by their behavior and intended use. Kotlin’s read-only collection interfaces do not necessarily guarantee that the underlying collection cannot be changed through another reference. Avoid teaching read-only as synonymous with deeply immutable.

Use named data classes when records have domain meaning. Pair and Triple are useful for small temporary groupings, but opaque positional fields can make a program harder to read and explain through a screen reader.

Object-oriented instruction

Kotlin classes are final by default. Explain that inheritance requires an explicit design decision and the appropriate open declarations. Teach composition and interfaces alongside inheritance rather than presenting subclassing as the default reuse strategy. Distinguish properties from Java-style field access and explain constructors, visibility, and member functions.

Files, resources, and errors

Teach file operations with explicit paths and predictable test data. Discuss working directories because relative paths are interpreted relative to the process’s current directory, not necessarily the source file’s location. Use resource-safe constructs such as use when appropriate. Learners should inspect returned values and exceptions rather than suppressing failures.

Accessibility and instructional delivery

  • Provide all essential content as selectable text.
  • Use semantic headings and descriptive links.
  • State code punctuation and nesting explicitly when introducing unfamiliar syntax.
  • Avoid instructions such as “click the green triangle” without a keyboard equivalent.
  • Ensure the learner can inspect compiler messages and program output as text.
  • Provide keyboard-first navigation paths for editing, saving, running, and debugging.
  • Allow additional time for screen-reader verbosity and braille review; do not interpret slower navigation as weaker conceptual understanding.
  • Test the actual toolchain with the learner’s assistive technology. Do not infer accessibility from a vendor statement or another learner’s configuration.
  • Do not make a visual debugger, diagram, or GUI-only tool the sole assessment route.

See Development editors and IDEs for the role of VS Code, Theia, and other professional environments. That reference discusses product purposes and accessibility evaluation but does not provide third-party IDE setup procedures.

Assessment

Assess both the program and the learner’s reasoning. Suitable evidence includes a prediction of output before execution; a clear explanation of variables, types, and control flow; a test that distinguishes normal from boundary or invalid input; a diagnosis of a compiler or runtime error; a justified choice of collection or data model; a function or class explanation in terms of responsibility and inputs/outputs; a demonstration of file handling and error reporting; and a reflection describing what was tested and what remains uncertain.

Do not equate a program that compiles with a program that is correct. Require expected-output checks or explicit behavioral tests where the lesson calls for them.

AI-use policy

Follow the repository’s course policy. AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement; it must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, refactor, or generate course code or assessment solutions for students or instructors. Instructors should provide the same policy consistently across language tracks.

Validation and maintenance

The course includes expected-output fixtures and an example-checking workflow. Before a teaching term, instructors should review the current compiler and JDK baseline, run the validation script from a clean checkout, verify relevant mdBook links, and record exact versions and results. Runtime validation and assistive-technology validation are separate activities.

Report corrections through the repository’s contribution process. When changing examples, update expected output and validation evidence together. Do not claim that the course has been fully accessibility-tested unless the exact supported workflows have been exercised and documented.

Lua Teacher’s Guide

Purpose and course context

This guide supports the Lua curriculum for beginning programmers, including blind and visually impaired learners using screen readers, braille displays, magnification, and keyboard navigation. It supplements the complete lessons, topic index, and Lua course overview.

The course targets Lua 5.4 and the standard library. Lua is a lightweight, dynamically typed, embeddable scripting language. Its table-centric data model and use in game scripting, application extension, configuration, and automation should be taught without making a visual game editor or graphical environment a prerequisite.

Outcomes and sequence

Complete the shared Computing Foundations Primer and Terminal Skills prerequisite, then follow Units 0–11. Learners should run scripts with the interpreter, work with values and expressions, use decisions and loops, model data with tables, write functions and modules, apply object patterns where useful, process files and errors, test behavior, and complete the capstone.

Use a consistent lesson cycle: objective and vocabulary; explicit walkthrough; prediction; interpreter execution; output review; one modification; learner explanation. Ask learners to predict both the returned value and any side effects.

Toolchain and packages

Verify with lua -v and run a script with lua main.lua. LuaRocks is optional for the core course; use it only when a lesson documents an external dependency. JSON and standards-aware CSV support are provided through packages rather than the Lua core. Explain package installation, module lookup, and runtime version requirements before assigning dependency-based work.

Teaching Lua’s distinctive semantics

Dynamic values and truthiness

Variables hold values whose types are determined at runtime. Only false and nil are falsey; values such as zero and the empty string are truthy. This differs from several other languages and should be tested explicitly. Teach nil as absence and distinguish it from false.

Tables and iteration

Tables can model sequences, maps, records, and object-like structures. Sequence indexing conventionally begins at 1. Teach the distinction between the sequence portion and arbitrary key/value entries. ipairs iterates sequence entries; pairs iterates key/value pairs without a guaranteed order. Do not write assessments that expect a stable pairs order. Explain that the length operator has specific sequence semantics and should not be treated as a universal count of every key.

Functions, modules, and metatables

Functions are first-class values and can return multiple results. Teach parameter lists, return values, closures, and module boundaries with small examples. Introduce metatables only after learners can explain ordinary table lookup; metamethod behavior can otherwise obscure the data model. Object-oriented patterns in Lua are conventions built on tables and metatables, not a built-in class syntax.

Errors and file operations

File functions commonly return a value plus an error message rather than raising an exception for every failure. Teach learners to check returned values before use. Use explicit paths and close files reliably; explain working-directory behavior. Keep external JSON/CSV dependencies documented and avoid implying that these formats are built into the core language.

Accessibility and delivery

  • Use the interpreter and terminal as the baseline, with text-only examples and output.
  • Describe punctuation including braces, brackets, dots, colons, concatenation, and the length operator.
  • Explain table contents as labelled key/value pairs or ordered sequence entries.
  • Avoid visual game editors, scene trees, and color-only debugging as required learning tools.
  • Provide keyboard equivalents for editor and execution actions.
  • Make iteration order explicit in examples; do not ask learners to infer order from a visual display.
  • Allow time to navigate nested tables and punctuation through speech or braille.

Verify the learner’s actual interpreter, editor, terminal, and assistive technology. If a game or host application is used for enrichment, provide a standalone text-based path for every assessed objective.

Assessment and differentiation

Assess truthiness, nil handling, table modeling, indexing, iteration, multiple return values, module design, and file-error handling. Include tests for zero, empty strings, missing keys, sparse tables, and unordered map traversal. Require learners to explain why pairs order is not a contract. A successful script exit does not prove correct data handling or accessible interaction.

Begin with simple sequences and records before nested tables and metatables. Extend advanced learners with closures, coroutines, or host-application scripting only after core language semantics are secure.

AI-use policy

AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, refactor, or generate course code or assessment solutions.

Instructor preparation

Verify Lua 5.4 and run the repository’s current example-validation procedure. Confirm all external package steps and test file operations from a known working directory. Validate screen-reader output in the actual classroom environment. See the shared accessibility guidance.

Teacher’s Guide: Introduction to Computer Science with Python

For Students with Visual Impairments — Complete Instructor Edition

How to use this teacher’s guide

This guide is a companion for instructors, not a script that must be followed word for word. Read the philosophy, learner-context, and technology sections before the first lesson; use the unit notes while planning; and return to the assessment, differentiation, AI, and quick-reference sections throughout the course. Adapt procedures to the learner’s actual assistive technology, operating system, course goals, and prior experience. Confirm tool-specific instructions in current official documentation because editor, screen-reader, and runtime behavior changes over time.

Plan for both programming learning and access to the programming environment. Establish what the student can already do independently, what access skills need instruction, what supports are already in place, and how the learner prefers to receive feedback. Never assume a diagnosis predicts a student’s preferred tools or level of independence.

Python 3.12+ baseline and current conventions

The learner materials target Python 3.12 and newer. Python 3.15.2 is the current stable release as of October 30, 2026, while 3.12 is the minimum compatibility floor. Teach and assess against 3.12-compatible syntax and standard-library APIs unless a lesson explicitly identifies a newer feature. Do not require prerelease builds or features introduced after 3.12.

Model current conventions consistently:

  • Follow PEP 8 naming and layout: four-space indentation, snake_case functions/variables, PascalCase classes, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE constants, readable imports, and short logical lines. A strict 79-character limit is a guideline, not a reason to create awkward wrapping; preserve clarity and accessible reading order.
  • Prefer built-in collection annotations (list[str], dict[str, int]) over legacy typing.List/Dict in new Python 3.12+ examples. Annotate function inputs and return values when it clarifies the contract; explain that annotations do not enforce runtime types by themselves.
  • Use f-strings for interpolation, pathlib.Path for paths, context managers (with) for files, and explicit main guards for runnable modules.
  • Use specific exception types, avoid bare except, avoid mutable default arguments, and compare absence with is None.
  • Use uv to create project environments and manage dependencies: uv init –python 3.12, uv add package, and uv run command. Commit uv.lock for shared projects. Do not install course dependencies with global pip.
  • Introduce Ruff for linting/formatting and pytest for tests only after learners understand the underlying Python and standard-library workflow. Do not make either tool a prerequisite for basic lessons.
