  Shift+Tab       Outdent selected lines
  Ctrl+D          Select next occurrence of word
  Ctrl+H          Find and replace

TERMINAL
  Ctrl+`          Toggle integrated terminal
  Ctrl+Shift+`    New terminal
  Up/Down arrows  Navigate command history
  Tab             Auto-complete filenames
  Ctrl+C          Stop running program

SCREEN READER
  Ctrl+Shift+P    Command Palette
  Ctrl+Shift+P -> "Toggle Screen Reader Optimized"
  Shift+Alt+F1    Accessibility help

22. Comprehensive Instructional Planning and Course Implementation

This section supplements the unit-by-unit notes with a full course implementation framework. Use it alongside Sections 1–21.

22.1 Course alignment and pacing

Map each unit to prerequisites, learning objectives, practice opportunities, and evidence of mastery. The sequence builds from environment setup and computing foundations through expressions and input/output, control flow, collections, functions, object-oriented programming, files, exceptions, testing, data analysis, and projects. Do not rush the transition from collections to functions or from functions to classes; learners need to trace and explain smaller programs first.

Plan time to learn the tools. Editor navigation, terminal use, indentation awareness, virtual environments, and reading tracebacks are course skills, not unrelated overhead.

22.2 Lesson planning template

For every lesson, prepare measurable objectives, a plain-language explanation, new vocabulary and spoken symbol conventions, a small example with expected output, a prediction question, guided and independent practice, a likely misconception or intentional bug, a formative check, and an optional extension.

Use a consistent rhythm: orient, retrieve prior knowledge, model, trace, predict, run, practice, debug, explain, and reflect.

22.3 Python-specific instructional checkpoints

  • Indentation: teach indentation as syntax and structure. Identify the suite belonging to each if, loop, function, and class. Distinguish tabs from spaces and inspect whitespace.
  • Names and types: ask learners to state the type and current value of important variables. Use type() for targeted experiments, not as a substitute for explanation.
  • Input conversion: reinforce that input() returns a string. Require explicit conversion and validation before arithmetic.
  • Loops and collections: trace index ranges, iteration variables, mutation, and empty collections. Distinguish iterating over values from indexing by position.
  • Functions: identify parameters, arguments, local variables, return values, and side effects. Test functions with multiple inputs.
  • Classes: connect each instance to its own state and distinguish class definitions from object creation and method calls.
  • Files and exceptions: teach working directories, relative paths, context managers, expected exceptions, and meaningful recovery messages.
  • Testing: begin with expected results and simple assertions; introduce a framework after learners understand what a test checks.

22.4 Accessibility and independence checkpoints

Ask the learner to demonstrate how to locate a function, identify the active indentation level, read a traceback, move to a reported line, run a program, and review output. If a step is inaccessible, troubleshoot the tool configuration and provide an alternate route before concluding that the programming concept is not understood.

Do not prescribe one screen-reader verbosity setting. Work with the learner to balance punctuation, indentation announcements, and speech rate. Ensure braille users can inspect symbols and line structure and low-vision students can adjust font, contrast, and magnification without losing keyboard access.

22.5 Assessment and feedback

Use low-stakes checks: predict output, explain a branch, trace a loop, select a collection, write a function with a clear contract, find and fix an exception or logic error, add a boundary test, or explain a design decision. Assess reasoning, correctness, code comprehension, testing, accessible interaction, and reflection. Do not grade speech, typing, or navigation speed as proxies for programming competence.

22.6 Differentiation and enrichment

Use starter code, worked examples, vocabulary previews, smaller practice sets, additional time, or alternative explanation modes where appropriate. Fade scaffolds to build independence. Enrichment can compare algorithms, improve validation, add tests, refactor repeated logic, or document trade-offs.

22.7 Project checkpoints

Require a problem statement, user needs, feature list, input/output plan, data model, and test plan before implementation. Review one working feature at a time. For a text adventure, test movement, inventory, invalid commands, and save/load behavior separately. For command-line tools and capstones, review persistence, validation, error handling, and the clarity of prompts and confirmations.

22.8 Collaboration and safeguarding

Coordinate with assistive-technology specialists and other professionals with the learner’s participation. Keep confidential student information out of shared examples, public issue trackers, AI prompts, and source-control history. Use synthetic data and remove credentials from logs before sharing them.

22.9 Continuous improvement

At the end of each unit, record outdated setup steps, unclear directions, inaccessible output, and concepts needing another example. Verify software instructions against official documentation. Report reproducible issues with operating system, Python version, editor, screen reader, and steps—without sharing personal student information.

Rust Teacher’s Guide

Purpose and course context

This guide supports the Rust curriculum for beginning programmers, including blind and visually impaired learners using screen readers, braille displays, magnification, or keyboard-first workflows. It supplements the complete lessons, topic index, and validation instructions.

The course uses stable Rust with the Rust 2024 edition and Cargo. Rust’s ownership and borrowing rules are not incidental syntax; they are a central part of how learners reason about memory safety, data access, and program design. The official Rust book recommends that learners with no programming background first study general programming concepts. Complete shared foundations and ensure learners understand variables, functions, collections, and control flow before expecting them to work independently with ownership.

Outcomes and sequence

Complete the shared Computing Foundations Primer and Terminal Skills prerequisite, plus introductory programming preparation where needed. Then follow Units 0–11. Learners should use Cargo, compile and run programs, interpret compiler diagnostics, work with ownership and borrowing, model data with structs and enums, use pattern matching and collections, handle errors with Result and Option, define traits and functions, test behavior, and complete the capstone.

Use a predictable cycle: objective and vocabulary; trace a small code example; predict ownership and output; compile; inspect diagnostics; make one change; explain why the borrow checker accepts or rejects the program. Treat compiler feedback as a source of information, not an adversary.

Toolchain and Cargo

Install Rust with rustup. Verify rustc --version and cargo --version. Create a project with:

cargo new course_app
cd course_app
cargo run
cargo test

Explain Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, crates, modules, build profiles, and the distinction between rustc and Cargo. Use the Rust 2024 edition consistently. Keep dependencies explicit and project-scoped. Teach learners to read the first relevant compiler diagnostic and follow the borrow checker explanation back to the expression or binding that created the constraint.

Teaching Rust concepts

Ownership, borrowing, and lifetimes

Teach ownership through concrete values and moves before introducing references. Distinguish Copy types from moved values. Explain shared references and exclusive mutable references, and connect borrowing rules to aliasing and mutation. Do not reduce lifetimes to punctuation or tell learners to add annotations until the code compiles; first ask what data must remain valid and for how long. Avoid presenting clone as a universal repair for ownership errors.

Structs, enums, and pattern matching

Use structs for records and enums for alternatives that must be represented explicitly. Teach exhaustive match expressions as a way to account for every variant. Explain Option for possible absence and Result<T, E> for operations that may fail. Encourage explicit handling rather than unwrap or expect in ordinary application paths; explain panic as a deliberate failure mechanism, not normal validation.

Collections, traits, and errors

Teach Vec, String, HashMap, and iterators with attention to ownership and borrowing of elements. Introduce traits as shared behavior contracts and generics only after learners understand concrete functions. Explain iterator adapters as transformations and distinguish lazy adapters from terminal operations. Use the standard error propagation operator only after learners understand Result and the caller’s responsibility.

Files and tests

Use explicit paths and deterministic fixtures. Explain that relative paths resolve from the process working directory. Check I/O errors and avoid panics for expected file failures. Teach unit tests, integration tests, and test assertions through Cargo after learners can explain function inputs and outputs.

Accessibility and delivery

  • Keep code, rustc/cargo output, and test failures available as selectable text.
  • Explicitly name angle brackets, ampersands, asterisks, colons, double colons, lifetimes, and pattern syntax when introduced.
  • Teach keyboard navigation by diagnostic, line, symbol, and file; avoid mouse-only IDE features.
  • Describe ownership changes as ordered events: binding, move, borrow, mutation, and scope end.
  • Do not rely on graphical ownership diagrams; provide text traces with named variables and lifetimes.
  • Ensure compiler diagnostics and test names are navigable with the learner’s assistive technology.
  • Allow time for dense compiler messages and repeated code navigation.

Test the actual rustup, editor, terminal, and screen-reader combination. Accessibility validation is separate from successful compilation.

Assessment and differentiation

Ask learners to predict whether a value is moved, copied, borrowed, or dropped; justify data-model choices; handle every enum variant; and explain how errors propagate. Include empty collections, missing map keys, invalid input, and file failures. Evaluate the quality of reasoning, not simply whether the learner found a way to silence the compiler.

Start with owned values and short scopes. Add nested borrowing, traits, iterators, and more advanced lifetimes only when prerequisite concepts are stable. Advanced extensions should deepen understanding without turning the course into a contest to satisfy the borrow checker.

AI-use policy

AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, refactor, or generate course code or assessment solutions.

Instructor preparation

Verify stable Rust and the Rust 2024 edition, run the repository’s rustc example checker, and separately test expected behavior and accessibility. The documented smoke checks establish compilation and process exit only; they do not prove capstone correctness or assistive-technology certification. Record toolchain versions and validation scope. See the shared accessibility guidance.

Swift Teacher’s Guide

Purpose and course context

This guide supports the Swift curriculum for beginning programmers, including blind and visually impaired learners using VoiceOver, other screen readers, braille displays, magnification, and keyboard navigation. It supplements the complete lessons, topic index, and validation instructions.

The course baseline is Swift 6 language mode with a current Swift 6 toolchain. Swift is used for Apple-platform applications, server software, and systems components. Teach Swift’s value semantics, optionals, protocols, structured error handling, Codable, and concurrency as language concepts. Do not conflate learning Swift with building a graphical iOS interface; the core course should remain accessible through command-line projects.

Outcomes and sequence

Complete the shared Computing Foundations Primer and Terminal Skills prerequisite, then follow Units 0–11. Learners should compile and run Swift programs, use types and control flow, work with arrays and dictionaries, write functions, define structs and classes, use protocols, handle optional and throwing operations, process files and Codable data, test behavior, and complete the capstone. They should understand the distinction between a command-line Swift package and an Apple-platform application requiring Xcode and platform SDKs.

Use a consistent lesson cycle: objective and vocabulary; code walkthrough; prediction; swift execution or package build; output/diagnostic review; modification; learner explanation. Encourage learners to predict both values and types, especially when optionals and inferred types are involved.

Toolchain and packages

Verify with swift --version and swiftc --version. Run a source file with swift main.swift; create an executable package with swift package init --type executable, then use swift build, swift run, and swift test. Xcode and Apple SDKs are needed for simulator and native application work, but not for the core command-line sequence. Use Foundation for file operations and Codable JSON encoding. The curriculum uses a standards-aware external CSV library where quoted fields and embedded newlines require full CSV parsing.

Teaching Swift concepts

Types, value semantics, and collections

Swift is statically typed with type inference. Explain that inference does not make the language dynamically typed. Distinguish let from var and explain value semantics for structs and enums. Arrays and dictionaries are value types with copy-on-write implementation behavior; teach observable value behavior without overpromising a particular copy timing. Explain dictionary lookup as optional because a key may be absent.

Optionals and error handling

An optional explicitly represents a value that may be absent. Teach optional binding, if let/guard let, nil coalescing, and optional chaining as separate tools. Do not normalize force unwraps as the default response to compiler errors. Distinguish optional absence from thrown errors: they represent different forms of control flow. Teach do/try/catch and throwing function contracts with explicit failure cases.

Protocols, generics, and concurrency

Introduce protocols as behavior contracts and generics as reusable abstractions with type constraints. Use concrete examples before protocol-heavy designs. Swift 6 concurrency checking can surface data-isolation and Sendable diagnostics. Teach async/await and task structure only after sequential control flow and function contracts are secure. Explain actor isolation and shared mutable state conceptually; do not dismiss concurrency diagnostics as compiler noise.

Files and Codable

Use explicit paths and deterministic fixtures. Explain process working directories and Foundation file APIs. Teach Codable as a structured serialization mechanism, not as a guarantee that arbitrary external data is valid. Handle decoding failures explicitly and test missing, malformed, and unexpected fields. Use a CSV parser that supports quoted fields and embedded newlines rather than splitting every row on commas.

Accessibility and delivery

  • Keep the introductory workflow command-line and text-first; do not require Xcode’s visual interface for core outcomes.
  • Teach VoiceOver and editor navigation appropriate to the learner’s platform; provide keyboard paths for build, run, and test.
  • Explicitly describe optionals, question marks, exclamation marks, arrows, generics, and closure syntax.
  • Make compiler diagnostics, test output, and program output navigable as text.
  • Describe collection contents, protocol conformance, and asynchronous event order in text.
  • Treat simulator and GUI testing as an extension with a documented accessible alternative, not the only way to demonstrate programming knowledge.
  • Allow time for punctuation review and verbose Swift 6 concurrency diagnostics.

Validate the actual macOS or Linux toolchain, editor, terminal, and assistive technology. VoiceOver and other screen readers differ by platform; do not assume a workflow transfers unchanged.

Assessment and differentiation

Assess type reasoning, value semantics, optional handling, collection selection, protocol use, error propagation, Codable validation, and tests. Include absent dictionary keys, empty collections, malformed JSON, file errors, and throwing operations. Require learners to explain why a force unwrap is or is not justified. Separate compilation, expected-output behavior, package tests, platform UI behavior, and accessibility evidence.

Scaffold with structs, simple functions, and sequential code before protocols and concurrency. Extend advanced learners with generic constraints, actors, or platform APIs only after the core language outcomes are secure.

AI-use policy

AI may be used only for personal conceptual understanding and reinforcement. It must not write, complete, autocomplete, repair, refactor, or generate course code or assessment solutions.

Instructor preparation

Verify Swift 6 language mode, run the repository’s example validation instructions, and separately exercise expected behavior and accessibility. Record OS, compiler version, package commands, and any platform-specific prerequisites. See the shared GUI and workbench accessibility guidance before requiring Xcode or graphical application tooling.

Teacher’s Guide: Introduction to Computer Science with TypeScript

For Students with Visual Impairments — Complete Instructor Edition

How to use this teacher’s guide

This guide is a companion for instructors, not a script that must be followed word for word. Read the philosophy, learner-context, and technology sections before the first lesson; use the unit notes while planning; and return to the assessment, differentiation, AI, and quick-reference sections throughout the course. Adapt procedures to the learner’s actual assistive technology, operating system, course goals, and prior experience. Confirm tool-specific instructions in current official documentation because editor, screen-reader, and runtime behavior changes over time.

Plan for both programming learning and access to the programming environment. Establish what the student can already do independently, what access skills need instruction, what supports are already in place, and how the learner prefers to receive feedback. Never assume a diagnosis predicts a student’s preferred tools or level of independence.

TypeScript and Node.js version baseline

Use Node.js 26 LTS (26.13.0 or a newer 26.x maintenance release) and TypeScript 7.0.2, the current stable compiler as of October 30, 2026. TypeScript is checked at build time and emitted as JavaScript; Node.js executes the emitted JavaScript. Keep the project’s module format explicit and use a local compiler version recorded in the package lockfile.

Teach strict type checking progressively. Prefer explicit function parameter and return types where they clarify contracts; use inference for obvious local values; use interfaces/type aliases for object shapes; prefer unknown over any for untrusted values; and keep strictNullChecks enabled. Explain that type assertions do not validate data and that types are erased from emitted JavaScript. JSON, user input, file contents, and network responses still require runtime validation. TypeScript’s compiler catches many classes of mistakes but does not prove program correctness.

  1. Philosophy and Why TypeScript
  2. TypeScript-Specific Accessibility Challenges
  3. Classroom Setup and Configuration
  4. Spoken TypeScript Conventions

  6. Unit 2: Numbers, Input, and Math
  7. Unit 3: Control Flow
  8. Unit 4: Arrays and Objects
  9. Unit 5: Strings
  10. Unit 6: Functions
  11. Unit 7: Classes and OOP
  12. Unit 8: Files, Modules, and Error Handling
  13. Unit 9: Collections, Analysis, and Testing
  14. Units 10–11: Projects and Capstone
  15. Bridging from Python/Java to TypeScript

  17. Supporting Diverse Needs

  19. Quick Reference Sheets
  20. Teaching AI Tools Responsibly
  21. Comprehensive Instructional Planning and Course Implementation

1. Philosophy and Why TypeScript

The Case for Teaching TypeScript to Blind Students

TypeScript has a unique profile of benefits and challenges for visually impaired learners:

Universal relevance. JavaScript is the language that runs natively in every major web browser; TypeScript is compiled to JavaScript before browser execution. A student who learns TypeScript can eventually build tools that improve their own accessibility experience — custom browser extensions, accessible widgets, automation scripts. This self-advocacy potential is meaningful.

Node.js enables accessible terminal programs. JavaScript runs on Node.js outside a browser. TypeScript source is first type-checked and compiled to JavaScript, which Node.js then executes. This curriculum uses Node.js to keep I/O in the terminal where screen readers excel.

Asynchronous programming is a real-world skill. TypeScript’s async/await model reflects how most modern software actually works — programs that wait for I/O, network requests, and user events. Learning this early prepares students for professional development.

The npm ecosystem. Over 2 million packages on npm provide pre-built solutions for almost any problem. This is a double-edged concern for beginners (dependency complexity), but the ability to say npm install and gain powerful functionality is professionally relevant.

JSON is part of the JavaScript runtime. JSON.parse() and JSON.stringify() are available without an import; TypeScript can type the values around these calls, but JSON.parse() returns untrusted data that should be validated. For data persistence projects, this reduces friction.

An Honest Account of Challenges

JavaScript runtime permissiveness remains a risk even in TypeScript projects. TypeScript’s compiler catches many statically visible type mismatches before execution, but its types are erased when JavaScript is emitted. Runtime coercion still exists ("5" + 3 produces "53"; "5" - 3 produces 2; 0 == false is true). Coercion can reappear at any/assertion boundaries and when data arrives from JSON, files, users, or APIs. Teach strict checking, explicit conversion, type guards, and runtime validation together.

Asynchronous programming is conceptually hard. The async/await pattern required for user input is a genuine hurdle for beginners. There is no way to eliminate it from a Node.js input-based curriculum. The approach in this guide is to scaffold it carefully and defer full explanation of the event loop to later units.

Multiple valid syntaxes. Function declarations, function expressions, arrow functions, methods — all do essentially the same thing. var, let, const — three variable declarations. == and === — two equality operators. This variety can create unnecessary cognitive overhead for beginners. The approach in this curriculum is to teach one style consistently (const/let, arrow functions, ===) and acknowledge alternatives exist without teaching them in parallel.

2. TypeScript-Specific Accessibility Challenges

JavaScript runtime coercion and static type checking

This is the greatest accessibility risk in TypeScript for blind students. Unlike Python’s TypeError and Java’s compile-time type check, TypeScript silently converts types in ways that can produce wrong answers with no error:

ExpressionResultExpected by ProgrammerProblem
"5" + 3"53"8+ concatenates when one operand is a string
"5" - 322- converts string to number
"5" * "3"1515Multiplication converts both
"" == falsetrueMaybe?Loose equality coercion
0 == falsetrueMaybe?Same
null == undefinedtrueProbably not
NaN === NaNfalsetrueNaN is not equal to itself

Mitigation: Require Number() before any arithmetic on user input. Require === always. Teach typeof and isNaN() as defensive checks. Make logging intermediate values an explicit exercise before running any calculation.

undefined vs. null vs. NaN vs. false vs. 0 vs. ""

All six of these are “falsy” in TypeScript. Aurally, they are indistinguishable unless you call typeof or check explicitly. A student who hears console.log(result) and the screen reader announces “false” cannot know whether result is false, 0, "", null, undefined, or NaN without further inspection.

Teaching approach: Establish a diagnostic template:

console.log("Value:", result, "Type:", typeof result);

This outputs both the value and its type, providing audio context that console.log(result) alone does not.

Callback Hell and Asynchronous Confusion

Before async/await, Node.js input used nested callbacks:

// Confusing nesting --- avoid in teaching
rl.question("Name? ", (name) => {
  rl.question("Age? ", (age) => {
    rl.question("City? ", (city) => {
      console.log(`${name}, ${age}, ${city}`);
    });
  });
});

This nesting produces code that is confusing to read AND to hear — the indentation deepens with each question. The async/await pattern linearizes this:

// Clear and linear --- use this exclusively
const name = await askQuestion("Name? ");
const age = await askQuestion("Age? ");
const city = await askQuestion("City? ");
console.log(`${name}, ${age}, ${city}`);

Teach async/await from the start and avoid callback patterns entirely in this course.

3. Classroom Setup and Configuration

VS Code or Theia IDE for TypeScript

Theia IDE is an alternative editor with keyboard- and screen-reader-oriented workflows suitable for this course. It supports many VS Code extensions through Open VSX; check availability of ESLint, Prettier, and TypeScript language support, and verify each workflow with the learner’s screen reader. VS Code-specific settings and shortcuts may differ.

Required extensions:

  • ESLint — catches type issues, undefined variables, and style violations before running code
  • Prettier — auto-formats code consistently (run on save with editor.formatOnSave: true)
  • TypeScript (ES6) code snippets — tab-complete common patterns

Recommended TypeScript ESLint flat configuration (eslint.config.mjs; install eslint, @eslint/js, typescript-eslint, and globals as local development dependencies):

import js from "@eslint/js";
import tseslint from "typescript-eslint";
import globals from "globals";

export default tseslint.config(
  js.configs.recommended,
  ...tseslint.configs.recommended,
  {
    files: ["**/*.ts"],
    languageOptions: {
      sourceType: "commonjs",
      globals: globals.node
    },
    rules: {
      eqeqeq: "error",
      "no-console": "off",
      "@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any": "error"
    }
  }
);

The eqeqeq: error rule makes == a linting error — it must be ===. This is an automated enforcement of the rule that prevents the most common silent bugs.

Node.js REPL accessibility:

node                      # Start REPL
.help                     # List REPL commands
.exit                     # Quit (or Ctrl+D)

Windows Powershell

node                      # Start REPL
.help                     # List REPL commands
.exit                     # Quit (or Ctrl+D)

The Node.js REPL is excellent for early exploration. Results are printed immediately after each expression, providing audio feedback without the compile-run-read cycle.

Alternative TypeScript Environments

EnvironmentPlatformAccessibilityNotes
Node.js + VS CodeAllHighRecommended setup
Node.js + terminal onlyAllHighFor students who prefer minimal UI
Replit.comWebMediumNo-install; test with student’s setup
CodeSandboxWebMediumCloud editor; variable accessibility
GitHub CodespacesWebHighCloud VS Code; same accessibility as local
Glitch.comWebMediumProject-based; variable accessibility
ObservableWebLowNotebook-style; primarily visual
DenoRuntimeHighAlternative to Node.js; similar accessibility

4. Spoken TypeScript Conventions

Symbol/PatternSpoken Form
const“const”
let“let”
var“var” (avoid; legacy)
===“triple equals” or “strict equal”
!==“strict not equal”
==“loose equal” (should hear this rarely)
=>“arrow” or “fat arrow”
...arr“spread arr”
...args“rest args”
async“async”
await“await”
undefined“undefined”
null“null”
NaN“NaN” (say each letter N-A-N)
typeof“typeof”
instanceof“instanceof”
new“new”
this“this”
class“class”
extends“extends”
super“super”
import“import”
export“export”
require()“require”
module.exports“module dot exports”
Promise“Promise”
async function“async function”
() => {}“arrow function”
(x) => x * 2“arrow function taking x, returning x times 2”
#field“hash field” or “private field”
`template ${var}`“backtick template literal with variable var”

Reading an arrow function:

const doubleIfPositive = (n) => (n > 0 ? n * 2 : n);

“const doubleIfPositive gets arrow function taking n, returning: if n greater than 0, n times 2, else n”

Modern TypeScript and Node.js conventions

Teach the curriculum against the current Node.js 26 LTS line. Node.js 26.13.0 entered LTS on October 28, 2026; use the latest security patch in the 26.x line rather than pinning students to an old patch. Node.js 24 remains supported as LTS, but is not the current LTS line.

For new course examples, consistently use const/let, strict equality, explicit numeric conversion, async/await, and node: built-in module specifiers. Prefer the built-in node:test runner for basic unit tests; Jest is a valid optional framework, not a requirement. Keep the two module systems explicit: use a package.json type field and matching file extensions/configuration, and never mix CommonJS and ES module syntax in one file. Use current ESLint flat configuration (eslint.config.mjs) rather than the deprecated .eslintrc format. Check input and parsed JSON at runtime: JavaScript runtime values remain dynamic, and static types do not validate external data at runtime.

5. Unit 0–1: Setup and Foundations

Lesson 0.1: Installing Node.js

Instructional Cues

Verify installation at every step:

node --version    # Should print v26.x.x (26.13.0 or a newer 26.x maintenance release)
npm --version     # Should print a version number
npx --version     # Should print a version number (npx is bundled with npm)

Windows Powershell

node --version    # Should print v26.x.x (26.13.0 or a newer 26.x maintenance release)
npm --version     # Should print a version number
npx --version     # Should print a version number (npx is bundled with npm)

All three must work. If npm is missing, the student may have installed only the Node.js runtime without npm. Reinstall from nodejs.org (npm is included in the standard installer).

REPL first — files second: Begin with node in the terminal. Let the student type expressions and hear results immediately. This builds confidence before introducing the file -> run -> read cycle:

$ node
> 5 + 3
8
> "Hello " + "World"
'Hello World'
> typeof 42
'number'
> typeof "hello"
'string'
> .exit

The npm init conversation: When initializing a project, npm init -y generates package.json automatically. Walk the student through reading the generated file:

npm init -y
cat package.json   # or type package.json on Windows

Windows Powershell

npm init -y
Get-Content package.json

package.json is plain JSON text — fully readable with a screen reader. Understanding its structure is important for later lessons about dependencies and scripts.

Non-Obvious Accessibility Strategies

  • Node.js version managers: nvm (Node Version Manager) allows multiple Node.js versions. For a student who may work on multiple machines or projects, nvm install 26, then nvm use 26 is a consistent way to set the Node.js version. nvm is command-line-only and fully accessible.
  • Project-local dependencies: install course tools with npm install or npm install --save-dev from the project folder. Run local executables with npx or npm scripts. Avoid npm install -g for course tools; global installations can conflict across projects.

Thought Experiments

  1. “TypeScript was created in 10 days in 1995. What marks of that hasty design are still visible in modern TypeScript? (Think about typeof null === 'object', NaN !== NaN, 0 == false.) Why haven’t these been fixed?”

  2. “Node.js uses a single-threaded event loop to handle many concurrent operations. A traditional multi-threaded approach uses multiple threads running in parallel. For a web server handling thousands of requests, what are the tradeoffs of each approach? Which tends to be more memory efficient?”

  3. “npm has millions of packages. The average Node.js project depends on hundreds of packages, many maintained by single developers with no organizational backing. The ‘left-pad incident’ in 2016 broke thousands of projects when one 11-line package was unpublished. What does this incident reveal about the risks and benefits of the npm ecosystem?”

  4. “TypeScript compiles to JavaScript for browser applications, Node.js servers, mobile apps via React Native, desktop apps via Electron, IoT devices, and serverless cloud functions. What does this ubiquity tell you about the relationship between a language’s design and its adoption?”

Lesson 1.3: Variables and Data Types

Instructional Cues

const vs. let — establish the rule on day one:

“Use const for everything. If you get an error saying you’re trying to reassign a const, THEN change it to let. This approach produces cleaner code and prevents accidental reassignment bugs.”

Demonstrate the error:

const x = 5;
x = 10; // TypeScript compile-time error: cannot assign to a const

“This error is helpful. const is protecting you from changing something you said was fixed.”

JavaScript runtime types and auditory ambiguity:

Run this sequence in the REPL and ask the student to predict each output before pressing Enter:

typeof 42; // "number"
typeof "42"; // "string"
typeof true; // "boolean"
typeof null; // "object"  <- the famous bug
typeof undefined; // "undefined"
typeof {}; // "object"
typeof []; // "object"  <- arrays are objects!
typeof function () {}; // "function"

“Notice that both {} (object) and [] (array) produce ‘object’. How do you tell them apart? Array.isArray([]) returns true. Array.isArray({}) returns false.”

Template literals vs. concatenation:

const name = "Alice";
const age = 15;

// Concatenation --- confusing order of operations when read aloud
console.log("Hello, " + name + "! You are " + age + " years old.");

// Template literal --- linear, clean, easy to hear
console.log(`Hello, ${name}! You are ${age} years old.`);

Read both versions aloud with the student. Ask which is easier to follow aurally. Template literals are almost universally clearer when heard, because the variable values appear where they belong in the sentence.

Thought Experiments

  1. “TypeScript has only one number type for integers and decimals. Python has separate int and float. Java has int, long, double, float. What precision problems arise from having a single number type? When does 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 matter, and when doesn’t it?”

  2. “TypeScript has six falsy values: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy — including "false" (a non-empty string), [] (an empty array), and {} (an empty object). Design a quiz: ask the student whether ten different expressions are truthy or falsy. Which answers are surprising?”

  3. “var has function scope; let and const have block scope. What does ‘scope’ mean? How does a variable declared inside an if block with var vs. let behave differently? Which behavior is more predictable and why?”

6. Unit 2: Numbers, Input, and Math

Lesson 2.2: User Input in Node.js

Instructional Cues

The input helper module pattern:

Provide the input.ts module in every project skeleton. Students should not need to re-create this boilerplate:

// input.ts
const readline = require("node:readline");
const rl = readline.createInterface({
  input: process.stdin,
  output: process.stdout,
});

function askQuestion(prompt) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => rl.question(prompt, resolve));
}

function close() {
  rl.close();
}

module.exports = { askQuestion, close };

Walk through what each line does at least once so students understand the structure, but do not require students to write it from scratch until they’re comfortable with async programming.

The async/await mental model — teach this story:

“When your code hits await, imagine it puts up a ‘please wait’ sign and steps aside. Other things can happen while you wait. When the answer arrives, your code picks up exactly where it paused. The async keyword on the function declaration is your promise that ‘this function may pause at some point.’”

async function main() {
  console.log("Starting..."); // 1: runs immediately
  const name = await askQuestion("Name? "); // 2: pauses here until user types
  console.log("Got name:", name); // 3: runs after user answers
  const age = await askQuestion("Age? "); // 4: pauses again
  console.log(`${name} is ${age}`); // 5: runs after user answers again
  close();
}

main(); // Kick off the async function

Ask: “What line is running while the program waits for user input?” (None — the function is paused. The event loop can handle other things.)

Why main() must be called at the bottom: async function main() defines the function but doesn’t run it. The main() call at the end actually starts execution. Without the call, nothing happens. This trips up beginners — demonstrate it.

Non-Obvious Accessibility Strategies

  • rl.close() is mandatory: Without rl.close(), the Node.js process continues running after main() finishes. The terminal appears to hang — cursor blinks but no prompt. For a screen reader user, this is confusing. Teach close() as the final step of every program that uses input.

  • Prompt trailing space: Always include a trailing space in prompt strings: "Enter your name: ". Without the space, the cursor appears immediately after the colon with no separation, which some screen readers render as “Enter your name:cursor” — an awkward audio experience.

  • Input validation loop: Without validation, a blank Enter or a non-numeric string for a number causes silent failure. Provide this reusable pattern:

async function getNumber(prompt) {
  while (true) {
    const input = await askQuestion(prompt);
    const num = Number(input.trim());
    if (!isNaN(num)) return num;
    console.log("Invalid input: please enter a number.");
  }
}

Teach this pattern and require students to use it whenever they need numeric input.

Thought Experiments

  1. “The readline module uses an ‘event listener’ pattern — rl.question(prompt, callback) means ‘when the user answers, call this function.’ The async/await pattern wraps this in a Promise. What problem does the Promise solve that the raw callback doesn’t? (Think about reading the code linearly.)”

  2. “Node.js uses a single-threaded event loop. While your program is waiting for user input (await askQuestion), the thread is free. What else could the thread be doing? In a real application, this might mean handling a different request or updating state. What does this tell you about why async/await is important for scalable programs?”

  3. “Synchronous input (blocking until the user responds) and asynchronous input (doing other things while waiting) represent fundamentally different programming models. For a single-user command-line program, which matters? For a server handling 10,000 simultaneous users, which matters more? Why?”

7. Unit 3: Control Flow

Lessons 3.1–3.3

Instructional Cues

=== enforcement — make it automatic:

With ESLint configured to flag ==, the student will hear a warning whenever they use loose equality. Walk through the first warning together:

if (userInput == 5) {   // ESLint: Expected '===' and instead saw '=='

“ESLint is protecting you from a common silent bug. Change this to ===. The only exception is checking for null-or-undefined: x == null is sometimes used as a shorthand for x === null || x === undefined — but avoid this until you understand it.”

Truthy/falsy in input validation:

const name = await askQuestion("Enter your name: ");
if (!name.trim()) {
  console.log("Name cannot be empty.");
  // re-prompt...
}

!name.trim() is true when the trimmed string is empty ("" is falsy). This is idiomatic TypeScript. Read it aloud: “if not name dot trim” — ask: “What does ‘not an empty string’ mean? Why is an empty string falsy?”

Ternary operator — limit its use:

The ternary condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse is concise but can be hard to follow when read aloud:

const status = score >= 60 ? "pass" : "fail";

Read: “const status gets: if score greater-than-or-equal 60, quote pass, else quote fail”

Teach it but establish this rule: “If the ternary is easy to read aloud in one breath, use it. If it requires re-reading, use if-else.”

Thought Experiments

  1. “JavaScript’s == performs type coercion before comparing. TypeScript adds compile-time checks but preserves JavaScript runtime semantics. What does TypeScript’s adoption tell you about the value of static analysis in large JavaScript codebases?”

  2. “Consider: if (userName) vs. if (userName !== '' && userName !== null && userName !== undefined). The first uses JavaScript’s runtime truthiness; the second is explicit. In a code review, which would you prefer seeing? What are the readability and correctness tradeoffs?”

  3. “JavaScript’s optional chaining (?.) and nullish coalescing (??) were added to the language to handle null/undefined more gracefully. user?.address?.city returns undefined instead of throwing if user or address is null. Why did this feature take decades to add to a language created in 1995?”

  4. “The JavaScript switch statement falls through by default, and TypeScript preserves that runtime behavior. A mapping object can be an alternative to switch for dispatch tables. const actions = { 'add': addFunc, 'delete': deleteFunc }; actions[command]?.();. What are the accessibility implications of this pattern vs. a switch statement when read with a screen reader?”

8. Unit 4: Arrays and Objects

Lesson 4.1: Arrays and Functional Methods

Instructional Cues

Introduce map, filter, reduce as a trio:

Don’t teach them one per lesson — teach the relationship between them first:

“These three methods each take a function and apply it to every element in an array. map transforms elements. filter keeps or removes elements. reduce combines elements into one value. Together they cover most array processing.”

Then give one shared example that uses all three:

const students = [
  { name: "Alice", score: 88 },
  { name: "Bob", score: 62 },
  { name: "Charlie", score: 95 },
  { name: "Diana", score: 71 },
];

// 1. Filter passing students (score >= 70)
const passing = students.filter((s) => s.score >= 70);

// 2. Map to get just names
const passingNames = passing.map((s) => s.name);

// 3. Reduce to build a report string
const report = passingNames.reduce(
  (acc, name) => acc + name + ", ",
  "Passing: ",
);

console.log(report); // "Passing: Alice, Charlie, Diana, "
console.log("Count:", passing.length);

Accessible printing for arrays of objects:

// Accessible: numbered, labeled fields
students.forEach((student, index) => {
  console.log(`${index + 1}. ${student.name}: ${student.score}`);
});

// Less accessible: raw object output
console.log(students); // Produces cluttered bracket notation when read aloud

Chaining — build up incrementally:

Show chaining as a composition of steps, each of which you can trace separately:

const result = numbers
  .filter((n) => n % 2 === 0) // Step 1: keep evens
  .map((n) => n ** 2) // Step 2: square each
  .reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0); // Step 3: sum

// DEBUG: break the chain to trace each step
const step1 = numbers.filter((n) => n % 2 === 0);
console.log("After filter:", step1);
const step2 = step1.map((n) => n ** 2);
console.log("After map:", step2);
const step3 = step2.reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0);
console.log("Final sum:", step3);

The debug version (step-by-step) is more accessible during development. Consolidate to the chain after confirming correctness.

Thought Experiments

  1. “map, filter, and reduce come from functional programming — a paradigm based on mathematical functions that have no side effects. TypeScript arrays also have forEach which is for side effects only. What is the philosophical distinction between map and forEach? Why does this distinction matter for reasoning about code correctness?”

  2. “The sort method in TypeScript sorts in-place and mutates the original array. filter, map, and reduce return new arrays, leaving the original unchanged. Why the asymmetry? What bugs could arise from sort’s mutation? How would you sort without mutating: [...arr].sort(...)?”

  3. _“Functional composition: const double = n => n _ 2; const addOne = n => n + 1; const doubleAndAdd = n => addOne(double(n)). How does function composition scale? What is the advantage of composing small, focused functions over writing one large function that does everything?”*

  4. “The spread operator [...arr] creates a shallow copy of an array. For an array of primitives [1, 2, 3], the spread copy is fully independent. For an array of objects [{name: 'A'}, {name: 'B'}], the objects inside are still shared. What does ‘shallow copy’ mean? When does this distinction cause bugs?”

Lesson 4.2: Objects

Instructional Cues

Destructuring — introduce before objects are complex:

const person = { name: "Alice", age: 15, city: "Portland" };

// Without destructuring:
const name = person.name;
const age = person.age;

// With destructuring:
const { name, age } = person;

// In function parameter:
function introduce({ name, age }) {
  console.log(`Hi, I'm ${name}, ${age} years old.`);
}
introduce(person);

Destructuring is ubiquitous in modern TypeScript. Teaching it early reduces the verbosity of object access code, which in turn makes programs cleaner to read and hear.

Object.keys(), Object.values(), Object.entries() as navigation tools:

For a student who cannot visually inspect an object in a debugger panel, these methods provide audio-accessible object introspection:

const config = { theme: "dark", fontSize: 14, notifications: true };

// What properties does this object have?
console.log(Object.keys(config).join(", "));

// What are all the values?
Object.values(config).forEach((v) => console.log(v));

// Both together:
Object.entries(config).forEach(([key, value]) => {
  console.log(`${key}: ${value}`);
});

Optional chaining for safe nested access:

const user = { profile: { address: null } };

// Without optional chaining --- crashes if address is null
const city = user.profile.address.city; // TypeError!

// With optional chaining --- returns undefined instead
const city = user?.profile?.address?.city; // undefined, no crash

// With nullish coalescing for a default
const city = user?.profile?.address?.city ?? "Unknown city";

This pattern is essential for working with real-world data where fields may be missing.

Thought Experiments

  1. “TypeScript objects can have properties added or removed at any time. user.newField = 'value' just works. Java objects have a fixed set of fields defined at compile time. Which approach is better for representing data from an API that might add new fields in future versions? Which is better for ensuring all required fields are present?”

  2. “Object.freeze(obj) makes an object immutable — you can’t add, remove, or modify properties. This mimics the behavior of a Java final field or Python’s frozenset. When would immutable objects be useful? What patterns become possible when you can guarantee an object won’t change?”

  3. “Prototype-based inheritance means TypeScript objects can inherit from other objects directly, without classes. Classes (introduced in ES6) are ‘syntactic sugar’ over this prototype system. What does this mean? What can you do with prototypes that you cannot easily express with class syntax?”

  4. “JSON (TypeScript Object Notation) is the universal data exchange format. It looks almost like TypeScript object literals but has stricter rules: all keys must be double-quoted strings, no functions, no comments. Why must JSON be stricter than TypeScript object literals? What security problems would arise if JSON allowed functions?”

9. Unit 5: Strings

Instructional Cues

Template literals for multiline strings:

const menu = `
--- Main Menu ---
1. Add item
2. View all
3. Search
4. Delete
5. Quit
-----------------`;

console.log(menu);

Template literals with newlines are much cleaner for building multiline output than repeated console.log() calls. Teach this pattern for menus and reports.

Regular expression basics — connect to real need:

Before introducing regex syntax, establish the problem it solves:

“You have user input that might have extra spaces, uppercase, or punctuation. You want just the words. Without regex, you’d call .trim().toLowerCase().replace(',', '').replace('.', '')... for every punctuation mark. Regex lets you express ‘any non-letter character’ once.”

const messy = "  Hello, World!   How are you?  ";
const words = messy
  .trim()
  .toLowerCase()
  .split(/\W+/)
  .filter((w) => w.length > 0);
console.log(words); // ['hello', 'world', 'how', 'are', 'you']

Teach \w+ (word characters), \d+ (digits), \s+ (whitespace), and the g and i flags. Don’t attempt to teach full regex — a basic vocabulary is enough for data cleaning tasks.

Thought Experiments

  1. “Template literals use backticks ` while regular strings use " or '. Backticks on a keyboard are typically in the upper-left corner. For touch typists, backticks are less natural than quotes. What keyboard shortcuts or text expansions might a blind programmer use to reduce the friction of frequently-needed but awkward characters?”

  2. “String immutability in TypeScript (same as Python) means every .toUpperCase(), .replace(), and .slice() creates a new string. For a loop that builds a long string incrementally, what is the efficient alternative? (Hint: consider Array.push() + .join() as a form of StringBuilder.)”

10. Unit 6: Functions

Extended Instructional Cues

The four function forms — teach one style, acknowledge the rest:

// 1. Function declaration (hoisted --- can be called before declaration)
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

// 2. Function expression (not hoisted)
const multiply = function (a, b) {
  return a * b;
};

// 3. Arrow function --- SHORT BODY (implicit return)
const square = (n) => n * n;

// 4. Arrow function --- LONG BODY (explicit return required)
const absolute = (n) => {
  if (n < 0) return -n;
  return n;
};

Teach style 3 (short arrow) and style 4 (long arrow) as the primary forms. Acknowledge 1 and 2 exist and how to read them. Do not attempt to teach all four simultaneously.

The implicit return trap — a critical accessibility issue:

// These DO return a value:
const double = (n) => n * 2; // [x] implicit return
const greet = (name) => `Hi ${name}`; // [x] implicit return

// This does NOT return a value (the curly brace requires explicit return):
const broken = (n) => {
  n * 2; // No return statement! Returns undefined.
};

// Fixed:
const fixed = (n) => {
  return n * 2;
};

When heard aloud, n => { n * 2; } and n => { return n * 2; } sound different — the return keyword is present in one and absent in the other. Teach students to listen for return inside block-bodied arrow functions.

Higher-order functions — connect to previous array methods:

// map() takes a function as argument
const doubled = [1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 2);

// We can also pass a named function
const double = (n) => n * 2;
const doubled2 = [1, 2, 3].map(double);

// This works because map expects a function --- it doesn't care if it's
// named or anonymous, arrow or traditional

“Every time you used array.map(...), you were passing a function as an argument. Higher-order functions — functions that take other functions — are normal TypeScript.”

Closures — establish the mental model before the code:

“A closure is a function that remembers the environment where it was created, even after that environment is gone. Imagine a letter in an envelope. The letter is the function. The envelope is the environment — it contains variables the function needs. Even if the person who wrote the letter is gone, the letter still has access to everything in its envelope.”

function makeCounter(startValue = 0) {
  let count = startValue; // This is the "envelope"

  return {
    increment: () => ++count,
    decrement: () => --count,
    reset: () => {
      count = startValue;
    },
    getCount: () => count,
  };
}

const counter = makeCounter(10);
counter.increment();
counter.increment();
counter.increment();
console.log(counter.getCount()); // 13 --- count persists!

Thought Experiments

  1. “Arrow functions don’t have their own this — they inherit this from the surrounding scope. Regular functions create their own this. This was a major source of bugs in pre-ES6 TypeScript. How many of the following do you think involved confusing this? (a) Typos, (b) Variable scope errors, (c) Async timing bugs, (d) this binding bugs. In TypeScript specifically, (d) is disproportionately common — why?”

  2. “Pure functions always produce the same output for the same input and have no side effects. Math.sin(x) is pure. console.log(x) is not (it has a side effect). Why are pure functions easier to test? Why are pure functions easier to reason about in a screen-reader debugging session?”

  3. “Memoization caches the results of function calls so repeated calls with the same arguments return the cached result. Write a description of a memoized fibonacci(n) function. What is saved? What is the tradeoff? When would memoization be harmful rather than helpful?”

  4. “TypeScript is a multi-paradigm language: you can write imperative code (explicit step-by-step), object-oriented code (classes and methods), or functional code (pure functions and immutable data). For the accessible data manager project, which paradigm produces the most maintainable code? The most testable? The most readable when heard aloud?”

11. Unit 7: Classes and OOP

Instructional Cues

toString() is mandatory:

class BankAccount {
  #balance;

  constructor(owner, initialBalance = 0) {
    this.owner = owner;
    this.#balance = initialBalance;
  }

  toString() {
    return `BankAccount[owner=${this.owner}, balance=$${this.#balance.toFixed(2)}]`;
  }
}

const account = new BankAccount("Alice", 1000);
console.log(account.toString()); // BankAccount[owner=Alice, balance=$1000.00]
console.log(`${account}`); // Also calls toString() implicitly

Require toString() in every class. Explain: “When your screen reader reads console.log(myAccount), it reads toString(). Without it, you hear [object Object] — completely useless. Define toString() to hear meaningful information.”

Private fields # — establish as the default:

class Dog {
  #name; // Private --- cannot be accessed outside the class
  #age;

  constructor(name, age) {
    this.#name = name;
    this.#age = age;
  }

  get name() {
    return this.#name;
  } // Getter --- controlled access
  get age() {
    return this.#age;
  }

  set age(value) {
    if (value < 0) throw new Error("Age cannot be negative");
    this.#age = value;
  }

  bark() {
    console.log(`${this.#name} says: Woof!`);
  }

  toString() {
    return `Dog[name=${this.#name}, age=${this.#age}]`;
  }
}

“Private fields starting with # are truly private — not just conventional privacy. myDog.#name outside the class throws a SyntaxError. This is real encapsulation.”

Thought Experiments

  1. “TypeScript classes are ‘syntactic sugar’ over prototype-based inheritance. TypeScript adds static typing on top of TypeScript classes. With three layers (prototypes -> ES6 classes -> TypeScript classes), is TypeScript’s OOP model more or less trustworthy than Java’s, which has only one layer? What does ‘syntactic sugar’ imply about the behavior of the underlying mechanism?”

  2. “The class keyword was added to TypeScript in 2015, 20 years after the language was created. In those 20 years, TypeScript developers built massive applications without classes using only prototypes and closures. What does this tell you about the role of syntax vs. capability in programming languages?”

  3. “Mixins are a way to compose behavior from multiple sources without inheritance. Instead of class A extends B, you copy methods from B onto A’s prototype. TypeScript supports this; Java does not (without interfaces). When would mixins be more flexible than single inheritance? What problems could they cause?”

12. Unit 8: Files, Modules, and Error Handling

Lesson 8.1: Files

Instructional Cues

__dirname and path construction:

const path = require("node:path");
const fs = require("node:fs");

// __dirname is the directory of the current file
const dataFile = path.join(__dirname, "data", "contacts.json");

// Path joining prevents slash vs. backslash issues on Windows/macOS/Linux
console.log("Data file location:", dataFile);

For a student who cannot visually navigate a file tree, console.log(__dirname) and console.log(dataFile) are essential diagnostic tools. Teach them to print file paths as the first debugging step when a file isn’t found.

fs.existsSync() before file operations:

if (fs.existsSync(dataFile)) {
  const data = fs.readFileSync(dataFile, "utf8");
  return JSON.parse(data);
} else {
  console.log("No data file found. Starting with empty data.");
  return [];
}

Always check existence before reading. The alternative — catching ENOENT in a try-catch — works but puts normal “first run” behavior in the error path.

Lesson 8.3: CommonJS Modules

Module design for accessibility:

A well-designed module has a clear exports interface. Teach students to think of their module’s exports as its “public API” — what other files can use:

// contacts.ts --- exports only what other files need
const path = require("node:path");
const fs = require("node:fs");

const DATA_FILE = path.join(__dirname, "..", "data", "contacts.json");

function loadContacts() {
  /* ... */
}
function saveContacts(contacts) {
  /* ... */
}
function findContact(contacts, name) {
  /* ... */
}

// Export only the public interface
module.exports = { loadContacts, saveContacts, findContact };

“Everything not in module.exports is private to this file. Other files can use loadContacts and saveContacts, but they cannot directly access DATA_FILE. This is encapsulation at the module level.”

Thought Experiments

  1. “Node.js’s CommonJS (require) and the ES Module standard (import) are two different module systems in TypeScript. This creates confusion — some packages use one, some use the other. TypeScript can use both. Why did two module systems emerge? What does this history say about how standards develop in open-source ecosystems?”

  2. “Synchronous file I/O (readFileSync) blocks execution until the file is read. Asynchronous file I/O (readFile or fs.promises.readFile) allows other code to run while waiting. For a startup script that reads configuration before doing anything else, which makes more sense? For a web server that handles thousands of requests, which matters more?”

  3. “Custom error classes allow code to throw and catch specific, named errors: throw new ValidationError('email', 'Invalid format'). What is the advantage of this over throwing new Error('Validation failed: email field invalid format')? Think about code that catches and handles the error.”

13. Unit 9: Collections, Analysis, and Testing

Jest Testing

Instructional Cues

Jest output is accessible:

Run npx jest --verbose for maximum accessibility. The --verbose flag produces:

PASS src/math.test.ts
  add function
    [x] adds two positive numbers (3ms)
    [x] adds negative numbers (1ms)
    [x] handles zero (0ms)
  getGrade function
    [x] returns A for score >= 90 (0ms)
    [x] returns F for score < 60 (0ms)

Test Suites: 1 passed, 1 total
Tests:       5 passed, 5 total

Each test name is announced. Failures include file path, test name, expected vs. received values, and a diff. All of this is plain text — fully screen-reader-accessible.

Add to package.json scripts:

"scripts": {
    "test": "jest --verbose",
    "test:watch": "jest --verbose --watch"
}

npm test runs all tests. npm run test:watch reruns tests whenever a file changes — useful during active development.

Test naming convention:

describe("BankAccount", () => {
  describe("deposit", () => {
    test("increases balance by deposited amount", () => {
      /* ... */
    });
    test("rejects negative amounts", () => {
      /* ... */
    });
    test("rejects zero amount", () => {
      /* ... */
    });
  });
  describe("withdraw", () => {
    test("decreases balance by withdrawn amount", () => {
      /* ... */
    });
    test("throws InsufficientFundsError when balance is too low", () => {
      /* ... */
    });
  });
});

The nested describe / test structure, when announced by Jest with --verbose, reads as complete sentences: “BankAccount > deposit > increases balance by deposited amount.”

Thought Experiments

  1. “Jest’s expect(value).toEqual(expected) performs deep comparison — it checks that two objects have the same structure and values, not that they are the same object in memory. Why is deep comparison usually what you want when testing? When would you specifically want reference equality (toBe)?”

  2. “Snapshot testing in Jest captures the output of a component or function the first time, then checks future runs against that snapshot. What are the advantages? What are the risks? When might a snapshot become ‘stale’ and mislead you into thinking code is correct when it isn’t?”

  3. “Code coverage measures what percentage of your code is executed by tests. 100% coverage is a goal but not a guarantee of correctness. Design a function with 100% test coverage that still has a bug. (Hint: think about boundary conditions — what if the test covers the case where x=5 but not x=0?)”

14. Units 10–11: Projects and Capstone

TypeScript Project Structure

my-data-manager/
|--- src/
|   |--- models/
|   |   +--- contact.ts
|   |--- storage/
|   |   +--- dataManager.ts
|   |--- ui/
|   |   +--- consoleUI.ts
|   +--- utils/
|       |--- input.ts         (the readline helper)
|       +--- validation.ts    (reusable validation functions)
|--- data/
|   +--- contacts.json
|--- tests/
|   |--- models/
|   |   +--- contact.test.ts
|   +--- storage/
|       +--- dataManager.test.ts
|--- eslint.config.mjs
|--- package.json
+--- index.ts

package.json scripts — teach as accessibility tools:

{
  "scripts": {
    "start": "npx tsc && node dist/index.js",
    "test": "jest --verbose",
    "test:watch": "jest --verbose --watch",
    "lint": "eslint src/",
    "lint:fix": "eslint src/ --fix"
  }
}

npm start — consistent command regardless of entry point filename. npm test — runs all tests. npm run lint — checks for errors without running the program.

npm run lint as a pre-run check: Teach students to run npm run lint before running the program. ESLint catches undefined variables, unused variables, and == before the program runs — much faster than finding runtime errors.

Accessible Output Design for Capstone

Require students to design their program’s output to be navigable and self-describing:

// Navigation landmark prints
function printSeparator(title) {
  const line = "-".repeat(40);
  console.log(line);
  if (title) console.log(`  ${title.toUpperCase()}`);
  console.log(line);
}

// Numbered list with clear field labels
function printContactList(contacts) {
  if (contacts.length === 0) {
    console.log("No contacts found.");
    return;
  }
  printSeparator("contacts");
  contacts.forEach((c, i) => {
    console.log(`${i + 1}. ${c.name}`);
    console.log(`   Phone: ${c.phone || "not provided"}`);
    console.log(`   Email: ${c.email || "not provided"}`);
  });
  console.log(`Total: ${contacts.length} contact(s)`);
}

// Confirmation messages --- every action must produce one
function confirmAction(action, details) {
  console.log(`[x] ${action}: ${details}`);
}

Thought Experiments

  1. “Your capstone is a command-line program. Eventually, it could become a web application. What would need to change? What would transfer directly? Write a two-column list: ‘Can reuse as-is’ and ‘Must rewrite.’”

  2. “The accessible design principle ‘no visual-only cues for critical information’ means every status, error, or confirmation must be communicated through text, not color or icon alone. Where in your program have you relied on visual formatting? How would you replace it?”

  3. “Open-source your capstone project. Write a README that explains: what the program does, how to install it, how to run it, and specifically how to use it with a screen reader. What information would a sighted user find obvious but a blind user needs explicitly stated?”

From Python to TypeScript

PythonTypeScriptKey Difference
print("hello")console.log("hello")Method vs. function

True/Falsetrue/falseLowercase in TypeScript
Nonenull and undefinedJS has two “nothing” values

Thought experiments for Python->JS students:

  1. “In Python, you use spaces to define blocks (indentation). In TypeScript, you use {}. Python’s blocks are invisible — they’re just the alignment of characters. TypeScript’s blocks are explicitly marked. Which feels more natural? Which provides clearer information when read aloud?”

  2. “Python’s None and TypeScript’s null/undefined both represent ‘nothing,’ but they behave differently. Python has one ‘nothing’; TypeScript has two. When is null appropriate? When is undefined appropriate? Under what circumstances would you encounter one vs. the other?”

  3. “Python is dynamically typed, while TypeScript checks declared types before emitting JavaScript. The emitted JavaScript still has dynamic runtime behavior. How do these differences affect debugging, flexibility, and runtime validation?”

16. Assessment Strategies

Alternative Assessments for TypeScript

Console output analysis: Provide a TypeScript program and 3–4 sample inputs. Ask the student to predict what the program prints for each input before running it. This tests reading comprehension without requiring writing.

Linting-first review: Submit code that is free of all ESLint warnings. A student who achieves this has internalized TypeScript’s best practices at the syntax level.

Refactoring exercises: Give a working but poorly structured program. Ask the student to refactor it to use functions, modules, or classes appropriately. Assess the quality of the architecture, not just whether it runs.

Test-first implementation: Give the student a set of failing tests. Ask them to write the implementation that makes the tests pass. This tests code comprehension and problem-solving without a blank-page start.

17. Supporting Diverse Needs

For Students Who Are New to Async Programming

Async/await is conceptually hard. For students who struggle:

  1. Provide the complete input.ts helper and instruct them to use it without modifying it.
  2. For the first several lessons, treat async function main() { ... } main(); as boilerplate, not content.
  3. Introduce the conceptual explanation of async/await only after students are comfortable with the rest of the language.
  4. Consider deferring async until after basic functions are mastered.

For Students with Additional Cognitive Considerations

  • ESLint provides immediate text feedback for common errors — use it as a learning tool. Hearing “no-unused-vars” and then explaining what that means is a teaching moment triggered by the student’s own code.
  • TypeScript’s many syntactic variations can be overwhelming. Enforce a single consistent style (arrow functions, const/let, ===) and defer alternatives.
  • Use the REPL liberally for short experiments so the student gets immediate feedback without file management overhead.
