Input Helper Module (Copy into every project)

// utils/input.ts
const readline = require("node:readline");

const rl = readline.createInterface({
  input: process.stdin,
  output: process.stdout,
});

/**
 * Prompts the user and returns their response as a string.
 * @param {string} prompt - The question to display
 * @returns {Promise<string>} The user's trimmed response
 */
function askQuestion(prompt) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    rl.question(prompt, (answer) => resolve(answer));
  });
}

/**
 * Prompts until a valid number is entered.
 * @param {string} prompt - The question to display
 * @returns {Promise<number>} A valid number
 */
async function askNumber(prompt) {
  while (true) {
    const input = await askQuestion(prompt);
    const num = Number(input.trim());
    if (!isNaN(num)) return num;
    console.log("Invalid input: please enter a number.");
  }
}

/**
 * Closes the readline interface. Call at the end of every program.
 */
function close() {
  rl.close();
}

module.exports = { askQuestion, askNumber, close };

20. Teaching AI Tools Responsibly

AI coding assistants can provide explanations, hints, test ideas, and alternative examples. They can also produce incorrect TypeScript, misunderstand Node.js module configuration, recommend untrusted npm packages, or conceal asynchronous behavior. Treat every response as an unverified proposal. The course must remain accessible without paid AI access or a personal account.

Instructor use of AI during preparation

Instructors may use approved AI tools to brainstorm examples, draft alternative explanations, propose test inputs, or identify likely misconceptions. The instructor remains accountable for accuracy and pedagogy. Verify every API and language claim against the target Node.js release and MDN or Node.js documentation; run examples and tests; review package recommendations; and test the learning workflow with the intended access technology. Never upload identifiable student work, accommodation plans, credentials, assessment answers, or confidential school information. Do not use AI-generated feedback as the sole basis for grading. Disclose substantive AI assistance when institutional policy or the publication process requires it.

Learning goals and appropriate uses

Students should describe the limitations of code generation, ask focused questions, verify TypeScript behavior using the runtime and official documentation, identify generated code beyond their current level, and disclose assistance when required. When permitted, AI may explain a diagnostic, rephrase a concept, suggest edge cases, critique an algorithm, or generate test inputs. Prefer hint-based prompts and have the learner describe their own understanding first.

TypeScript and Node.js risks

Review AI output for:

  • Confusion between CommonJS require() and ES module import, including package type, file extensions, and runtime version.
  • Incorrect claims about semicolon insertion, equality, coercion, truthy/falsy values, undefined, null, or NaN.
  • Missing await, unhandled promise rejections, callbacks that do not complete, or incorrect execution-order assumptions.
  • Browser-only APIs used in a Node.js lesson or incorrect Node.js APIs.
  • Unsafe file paths, command execution, network requests, or untrusted input handling.
  • Unnecessary npm dependencies, typo-squatted or abandoned packages, or packages with excessive permissions.
  • Dense chaining, nested callbacks, clever one-liners, and output difficult to review sequentially.

Run examples in the course’s declared Node.js environment, inspect values and types, and test success, boundary, and failure cases. Verify API claims in official Node.js documentation or MDN.

Screen-reader and output review

Review whether braces, nested callbacks, and asynchronous control flow are navigable and explainable; identifiers are descriptive; prompts and output provide context; results arrive in a predictable order; module style is consistent; and the AI interface itself is accessible. Prefer named functions and intermediate variables when they improve understanding. Make asynchronous behavior explicit.

Privacy, security, and equity

Do not submit student records, credentials, private code, API keys, or confidential school information to public AI systems. Follow institutional policies, age requirements, and approved-tool lists. Treat terminal commands and package recommendations as untrusted. Verify package names and provenance before installation. Provide a non-AI path and never make a paid account a prerequisite. Discuss how generated examples may assume mouse use, visual browser interaction, graphical output, or a particular operating system.

Verification protocol: Ask – Inspect – Verify – Adapt – Explain – Disclose

  1. Ask: state the problem and what has already been tried.
  2. Inspect: read the response and flag unfamiliar APIs, packages, syntax, and assumptions.
  3. Verify: check MDN or Node.js documentation; run a minimal example; test normal, boundary, and invalid input.
  4. Adapt: simplify, secure, format, and make code accessible to sequential reading.
  5. Explain: have the student explain control flow and make a new change without AI.
  6. Disclose: record the tool and assistance when required.

Activity-specific policy

  • Practice: hints and explanations may be allowed; request complete solutions only for code-review activities.
  • Homework/projects: define permitted assistance and require disclosure and verification.
  • Individual assessments: do not permit AI to perform the skill being measured unless explicitly included in the assessment or an accommodation.
  • Accessibility tools: screen-reader, braille, magnification, and keyboard access tools are not prohibited answer-generation tools.

Discussion prompts

  • An AI answer mixes CommonJS and ES module syntax. How would you diagnose the mismatch?
  • A suggested npm package has a plausible name but few trustworthy details. What should you check?
  • A promise-based program prints results in an unexpected order. How can you reason about await?
  • What must a student understand if AI generated most of a function?

21. Comprehensive Instructional Planning and Course Implementation

This section consolidates practices that apply across the philosophy, learner-context, classroom setup, spoken-code, unit, assessment, differentiation, and resource sections above. Use it as a course-planning reference from intake through capstone evaluation.

21.1 Course planning and alignment

Map each unit to prerequisites, learning objectives, practice opportunities, and evidence of mastery. Do not assume every unit needs equal time.

  • Identify outcomes: problem decomposition, code reading and writing, data representation, control flow, functions or methods, debugging, testing, and communication.
  • Separate programming prerequisites from access-tool prerequisites.
  • Record the operating system, editor/IDE, runtime, terminal, screen reader, braille display, magnification, and adaptive input technology used.
  • Identify essential concepts, enrichment topics, and material that can be deferred without breaking later lessons.
  • Plan checkpoints after each major concept group and adjust pacing using student evidence.
  • Maintain a map linking each lesson to objectives, practice, assessment, accessibility considerations, and likely misconceptions.

A suggested progression is environment and navigation; computing foundations; expressions and data; input/output; decisions and loops; collections; functions or methods; object-oriented concepts; files and errors; testing; projects; capstone. Preserve prerequisites when reordering.

21.2 Readiness and learner partnership

Ask about preferred access methods, prior programming experience, keyboard navigation, file management, and what makes technical instruction usable. Ask about functional access requirements rather than requesting unnecessary diagnostic details.

Use a low-stakes baseline activity to observe how the learner opens and navigates a source file, moves by line/word/character/symbol, creates and saves a file, runs a command, locates output, and reads a diagnostic. Record strengths and supports, not just deficits. Revisit the baseline to recognize growth. Keep the learner central to decisions about tools and workflow.

21.3 Repeatable lesson architecture

  1. Purpose: state the problem the lesson addresses.
  2. Prerequisite retrieval: revisit the prior concept needed today.
  3. Vocabulary: define technical terms and spoken symbol conventions.
  4. Explicit model: demonstrate a small runnable example and narrate navigation and code changes.
  5. Trace: read the code structurally and predict behavior.
  6. Guided practice: solve a similar problem with prompts and fading support.
  7. Independent transfer: apply the concept to a new requirement.
  8. Debug and reflect: examine an intentional error or unexpected result.
  9. Exit check: collect an explanation, prediction, code change, or test.

State one navigation action at a time, allow the learner to complete it, and confirm the result before continuing. Provide source files and commands in advance when possible. Narrate all actions in shared-screen demonstrations and provide an equivalent text-based route.

21.4 Explicit instruction for accessible code navigation

Teach file structure before reading every line. Identify current focus and how to return to a known location. Teach line, word, character, symbol, selection, search, and go-to-line navigation, plus navigation to functions, methods, classes, and diagnostics. Explain indentation and block boundaries. Use manageable line lengths and avoid unnecessarily nested expressions. Give students time to read diagnostics and output independently. Do not take over the keyboard without explaining the action and obtaining the learner’s agreement.

21.5 Language-specific instructional emphasis: TypeScript

TypeScript’s static type system and JavaScript runtime should be distinguished explicitly:

  • Teach let, const, and scope before elaborate function patterns.
  • Contrast === and == with concrete values; make coercion visible in REPL experiments.
  • Treat undefined, null, empty strings, zero, false, and NaN as distinct values.
  • Distinguish arrays from objects and explain property access, index ranges, mutation, and iteration.
  • Introduce asynchronous input deliberately. Explain promises, async, await, and output order.
  • Teach CommonJS and ES modules as separate systems. State module mode and Node.js version before troubleshooting imports.
  • Make error handling and file paths explicit; distinguish syntax errors, runtime exceptions, rejected promises, and logic errors.
  • Use ESLint and formatting tools as feedback aids, but explain each diagnostic.

21.6 Misconceptions and diagnostic teaching

Ask learners to predict behavior, explain their prediction, run a small experiment, and revise their mental model.

Common issueInstructional response
Confusing assignment with comparisonContrast operators and trace values before and after execution.
Treating input as already numericIdentify input type, convert explicitly, and test valid and invalid values.
Off-by-one loop or index errorsTrace first, typical, and final iterations; state the valid index range.
Choosing an unsuitable collectionDescribe access patterns and required operations before choosing a structure.
Writing one large function or methodDecompose the task by responsibility and test each part.
Treating a running program as necessarily correctDefine expected behavior and test normal, boundary, and invalid inputs.
Copying code without tracing itAsk the learner to predict a new case and make a modification.
Misreading an error messageLocate the useful diagnostic, identify file and line, and inspect surrounding code.

Language-specific pitfalls include: coercion and equality; undefined versus null; truthy and falsy values; array mutation; callback and promise ordering; CommonJS versus ES modules; and browser APIs versus Node.js APIs.

21.7 Differentiation without lowering the learning objective

Adjust the path, not the intellectual goal. Supports may include smaller task increments, additional practice, explicit worked examples, alternative information formats, extra navigation time, starter code with gradually faded scaffolding, oral explanation or accessible demonstration, pair programming with rotating roles, predictable routines, and enrichment tasks that deepen the same concept.

Do not assume all blind students need the same support or that all low-vision students prefer magnification. Ask, document, and review supports with the learner.

21.8 Formative assessment, feedback, and grading

Collect evidence frequently: explain a concept, predict output, trace a loop, justify a data structure, find and fix a bug, write a boundary test, refactor code, or demonstrate an accessible workflow.

A practical rubric can score each dimension from 1 (beginning) to 4 (independent and consistent):

DimensionEvidence
Conceptual reasoningExplains the problem, algorithm, and language concepts
ImplementationProduces a solution that meets requirements
Code comprehensionReads, traces, explains, and modifies code
Testing and debuggingUses test cases and interprets diagnostics
Accessibility and communicationProduces understandable interaction and operates the workflow with access tools
Independence and reflectionDescribes decisions, limitations, and next steps

Share criteria before assessment. Feedback should name observed behavior, explain its impact, and identify an actionable next step. Do not grade screen-reader speed, typing speed, or visual formatting as proxies for programming competence.

21.9 Debugging and classroom support protocol

  1. Ask the learner to describe expected behavior.
  2. Ask what actually happened.
  3. Read the complete error or diagnostic, including source and location.
  4. Identify the smallest relevant code section.
  5. Form one hypothesis.
  6. Change one thing and rerun the program or test.
  7. Record what the result taught the learner.

Distinguish environment failures, tool-access failures, syntax/compile errors, runtime errors, and logic errors. Maintain a troubleshooting record with environment, exact command, error text, attempted correction, and outcome. Remove credentials and private information before sharing logs.

21.10 Pair programming and collaboration

Use explicit roles: the driver controls the keyboard and implements the agreed step; the navigator reasons about the algorithm, checks requirements, proposes tests, and reviews the result. Rotate roles. Do not automatically assign a blind student the navigator role. Both learners should have opportunities to operate tools and write code. Provide shared source files and task instructions in accessible formats.

21.11 Project and capstone supervision

Require a proposal that includes the problem and intended user, functional requirements, out-of-scope features, input/output design, data representation, major functions/methods/classes, accessibility requirements, milestones, tests, and any libraries or AI assistance used.

Review milestones: requirements, design, first working slice, feature completion, tests, documentation, and final explanation. Encourage a modest, complete, well-tested project over an ambitious unfinished one.

21.12 Collaboration with families and support professionals

When appropriate and with learner consent, coordinate with special educators, teachers of students with visual impairments, assistive-technology specialists, interpreters, and families. Agree on who supports access technology, who teaches programming, and how the student obtains help. Keep the learner’s agency central, share only necessary information, and follow school privacy policies. Do not make aides the default operators of the student’s computer.

21.13 Instructor preparation checklist

Before each unit, complete the learner-facing activities; verify commands and versions on the classroom platform; test keyboard and assistive-technology workflows; prepare expected output and common error examples; identify vocabulary, symbols, misconceptions, and prerequisites; provide accessible instructions and assessment criteria; and decide how understanding will be observed.

After each unit, review student work and feedback, note barriers, adjust pacing and scaffolds, and record reproducible corrections. Document agreed accommodations rather than silently changing expectations.

21.14 Quality assurance and continuous improvement

Review links, software versions, commands, APIs, package recommendations, and assessment assumptions periodically. Test with actual screen readers and braille displays where possible; a successful build or visual inspection alone does not establish accessibility.

When reporting a barrier, include the page, reproduction steps, operating system, editor/runtime version, assistive technology and version, expected behavior, and actual behavior. Exclude personally identifying or sensitive student information. Submit corrections through the project contribution process.

Programming Code Glossary

A detailed student reference for Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, and the optional post-capstone Kotlin supplement. Find the term in the language section, then use that language’s INDEX.md to locate the teaching lesson. Definitions distinguish concepts that are easy to confuse.

Shared computer science vocabulary

Algorithm

A finite, ordered method for solving a problem. It defines steps, decisions, inputs, and expected outputs; a program implements an algorithm.

Argument

The actual value supplied to a function call. The parameter is the receiving name in the function definition.

Assignment

Storing a value in a variable or assignable location. Assignment is not equality comparison.

Boolean

A logical value that is true or false. Python spells literals True and False; the other languages use lowercase.

Bug

A defect causing a crash, incorrect result, or unmet requirement.

Class

A definition describing data and behavior for a kind of object.

Compiler

A program translating source code and reporting compile-time problems. Java compiles to JVM bytecode; TypeScript emits JavaScript.

Condition

An expression deciding which branch runs or whether a loop continues. Java requires Boolean conditions; Python and JavaScript also allow truth-value testing.

Constant

A binding that cannot be reassigned. This does not necessarily make the referenced object immutable.

Data type

A classification defining possible values and valid operations, such as integer, string, Boolean, array, or object.

Debugging

Systematically reproducing a problem, narrowing its cause, inspecting state, testing a hypothesis, correcting the defect, and retesting.

Declaration

An instruction introducing a name such as a variable, function, class, or type. Initialization gives a variable its first value.

Expression

A combination of values, names, operators, and calls evaluated to produce a value.

Function

A callable unit of code performing a task. It may accept parameters and return a result.

Input

Data received from a person, file, command line, network, or another system. Validate external input.

Instance

One particular object created from a class.

Iteration

One repetition of a loop body, or traversal of a sequence or collection.

Library

Reusable code packaged for use by programs. A standard library ships with a language or runtime.

Literal

A value written directly in source code, such as 42, 3.5, a quoted string, or true.

Loop

A control-flow structure repeating instructions. for commonly traverses items; while repeats while a condition is true.

Method

A function associated with an object or class.

Module

A file or unit grouping code and exposing selected names for reuse.

Object

A value grouping data and often behavior. Java objects are class instances; JavaScript and TypeScript also have flexible property objects.

Operator

A symbol or keyword performing an operation, such as arithmetic, comparison, or logic.

Parameter

A named variable in a function definition that receives an argument from the caller.

Return value

The value a function or method gives back to its caller.

Scope

The region of code where a name can be accessed. Local, block, function, and module scope rules differ by language.

Statement

A complete instruction such as a declaration, assignment, conditional, loop, or return.

String

A sequence of text characters. Strings are immutable in all languages covered.

Syntax

Formal rules defining valid source-code structure. Valid syntax does not guarantee correct logic.

Testing

Checking program behavior against expected outcomes. Unit tests focus on a small function or method.

Variable

A named binding used to refer to a value. Declaration, assignment, mutability, and type rules vary by language.

Python glossary

init

Initialization method called when an instance is initialized. Commonly assigns self attributes; allocation itself involves new.

name and main guard

Module attribute equal to main when run as entry point. The if name == main guard protects entry-point code from running on import.

append()

List method adding one item to the same list. It mutates the list and returns None.

break and continue

break exits the nearest loop. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and proceeds to the next.

dict

Mutable mapping of keys to values. Keys must be hashable; values can be any objects.

elif

Additional conditional branch evaluated only if earlier conditions are false. Python uses elif, not else if.

except and finally

except handles a matching exception. finally is used for cleanup and runs whether or not an exception occurred, subject to process termination.

float and int

float is binary floating point; many decimal fractions are approximate. int is arbitrary precision in ordinary Python implementations.

for and while

for iterates over an iterable. while repeats while its condition is true.

F-string

String prefixed with f that evaluates expressions in braces, for example f-string interpolation of a name.

import

Loads a module and binds names for use, such as importing math.

input()

Reads one line from standard input and returns a string. Convert it before numeric operations.

is and is not

Identity comparisons testing whether references are the same object. Use == for value equality; is None is conventional.

Iterable

Object supplying members one at a time, such as list, tuple, string, dictionary, set, or range.

len()

Returns number of items in a collection or code points in a string, not necessarily user-perceived Unicode characters.

list and tuple

list is mutable and ordered. tuple is ordered and immutable; a one-item tuple needs a trailing comma.

None

Singleton meaning absence of a value. Compare using is None.

open() and file modes

Opens a file. r reads, w writes and truncates, a appends. Prefer a with statement and specify UTF-8 encoding.

range()

Arithmetic sequence used in loops. Stop is excluded: range(3) yields 0, 1, 2.

return

Ends a function and optionally sends a value to caller. Falling off the end returns None.

set

Mutable collection of unique hashable elements; no positional indexing.

Slicing

Selects a sequence portion with start, stop, and optional step; start is included and stop excluded.

with and context manager

Managed context with reliable cleanup. File contexts close files automatically through the context-manager protocol.

Comprehension

Concise collection construction from an iterable, optionally filtered. Use a loop when clearer.

Docstring

String literal first in a module, class, or function, stored in doc and used to document behavior.

Exception

Object representing an error. Common types include ValueError, TypeError, KeyError, IndexError, and FileNotFoundError.

Generator

Iterator-producing function or expression yielding values lazily. Generator functions use yield.

Lambda

Small anonymous function expression containing one expression. Use def for multi-statement or documented functions.

MRO

Method Resolution Order: order Python searches base classes for attributes, especially with multiple inheritance.

Mutable and immutable

Lists and dictionaries can change in place; strings, integers, and tuples cannot. A variable can be rebound either way.

PEP 8

Python style guide recommending four-space indentation and snake_case names for functions and variables.

Property

Managed attribute commonly created with property decorator, allowing attribute-style access with getter/setter logic.

Type hint

Optional syntax describing expected types. Not generally enforced by Python at runtime; static tools can analyze hints.

Virtual environment

Isolated Python interpreter/package context. The course uses uv to create and manage the project’s .venv, install dependencies, and run commands without global pip installation.

uv

A Python version, project, and package manager. uv init creates project configuration, uv add package installs and records a project dependency, uv run command executes inside the managed environment, uv sync installs the dependencies recorded in the project files, and uv tree displays the dependency tree. uv manages the project-local .venv and can install Python interpreters.

JavaScript glossary

Array

Indexed ordered collection that can change length. Methods include push, pop, map, filter, find, reduce, and forEach.

async and await

An async function always returns a Promise. await waits for a Promise inside an async function without blocking the whole event loop.

BigInt

Primitive for integers beyond Number’s safe range. BigInt and Number arithmetic cannot be mixed directly.

const, let, and var

const is block-scoped and cannot be reassigned; let is block-scoped and reassignable; var is function-scoped legacy syntax.

console.log()

Writes values to the console; common terminal output in Node.js, not a file-writing API.

Destructuring

Extracts array elements or object properties into variables.

Event loop

Coordinates synchronous call-stack execution, queued callbacks, and asynchronous completions. Long synchronous work delays other tasks.

export and import

ES module declarations exposing and bringing in bindings. Dynamic import returns a Promise.

filter, map, and forEach

filter creates an array of passing elements; map creates a transformed array; forEach calls a callback and returns undefined.

for…of and for…in

for…of iterates values from an iterable; for…in iterates enumerable property keys.

Map and Set

Map stores key-value pairs with arbitrary key types. Set stores unique values.

NaN

Special Number value for invalid numeric results. It is not equal to itself; use Number.isNaN().

null and undefined

null represents intentional absence of an object value. undefined commonly means missing, uninitialized, or no returned value.

Number

IEEE 754 binary64 numeric primitive. Use Number.isFinite() and Number.isSafeInteger() where appropriate.

Object

Property collection. Ordinary keys are strings or symbols; use Map for arbitrary key types.

package.json

Node project metadata. Its type field selects ES module or CommonJS interpretation for .js files in that package scope.

Promise

Represents an asynchronous result that is pending, fulfilled, or rejected. Handle with then/catch or async/await.

readline

Node built-in module for line-by-line input from a stream such as standard input.

require() and CommonJS

require loads modules using Node’s CommonJS system; module.exports exposes values. ES modules use import.

Spread syntax

Expands iterables or object properties. Array/object spreads make shallow copies, not deep clones.

Strict equality ===

Compares without loose equality coercion. Preferred for most comparisons; objects compare by identity.

Template literal

Backtick-delimited string supporting multiline text and expression interpolation.

Arrow function

Function expression using arrow syntax. It has no own this or arguments; not interchangeable with every traditional function.

Callback and closure

Callback is a function passed to be called later. Closure is a function plus access to surrounding lexical variables.

ECMAScript

Standard defining JavaScript syntax and semantics. Node and browsers add different host APIs.

Hoisting

Processing declarations before scope execution. Function declarations and var differ from let/const temporal-dead-zone behavior.

JSON

Text format for objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. Use JSON.parse() and JSON.stringify().

Node.js and npm

Node.js runs JavaScript outside browsers. npm manages dependencies, scripts, and lockfiles. Use npm install or npm install --save-dev in the project directory to keep dependencies local.

npx

npm’s package-execution command. It runs a package binary from the current project’s dependencies when available, or can fetch a package into npm’s cache for one-off execution. Prefer project-local development dependencies and npx or npm scripts over global npm installs.

Prototype

Object used in property lookup when a property is not found directly.

Type coercion and truthiness

Coercion converts types automatically or explicitly. Falsy values include false, 0, empty string, null, undefined, and NaN; empty arrays/objects are truthy.

TypeScript glossary

any and unknown

any disables most type checking. unknown accepts any value but requires narrowing before use; prefer unknown for untrusted data.

as assertion

Tells compiler to treat an expression as a type. It does not convert or validate runtime data.

enum

Defines named constants. Numeric enums can create runtime objects; string unions or const objects may be simpler.

interface and type alias

interface describes object shape; type names a type expression including unions, intersections, tuples, and function types.

never

Type representing values that should not occur; used for non-returning functions and exhaustive checks.

Null and undefined in strict mode

With strictNullChecks, they are distinct types and must be handled or narrowed before non-null use.

Union and intersection

Union uses vertical-bar syntax for alternatives; intersection combines requirements.

Type annotation and inference

Annotation explicitly states a type; inference derives a type from values and context. Neither adds runtime validation.

Generic

Type or function parameterized by a type variable, preserving type information across reusable operations.

keyof and readonly

keyof produces a union of keys of a type. readonly prevents assignment through a type but does not freeze runtime objects.

strict and tsconfig.json

strict enables stronger checks. tsconfig.json controls source inclusion, target, module resolution, strictness, and output.

tsc

TypeScript compiler. Checks types and can emit JavaScript; prefer the project-local compiler.

Discriminated union and narrowing

A shared distinguishing property enables compiler narrowing based on control flow.

Structural typing

Compatibility based on members a value provides, not its declared type name.

Type guard

Condition or function giving evidence about a value’s type so compiler can narrow it.

Type erasure

TypeScript-only annotations, interfaces, and aliases are removed during compilation. Validate external data at runtime.

Utility type

Built-in transformations such as Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit, and Record.

Java glossary

abstract class

Cannot be instantiated directly; can contain implemented and abstract methods.

Array and ArrayList

Array has fixed length and one component type; use its length field. ArrayList is a resizable List; generic arguments use reference types such as Integer.

boolean, char, int, and long

boolean is true/false. char is a UTF-16 code unit. int is 32-bit signed; long is 64-bit signed.

break and enhanced for

break exits the nearest loop or switch. Enhanced for traverses array or Iterable elements.

catch and finally

catch handles an exception. finally performs cleanup; prefer try-with-resources for AutoCloseable resources.

class, constructor, and this

class declares a type. Constructor initializes an instance and has no return type. this refers to the current instance.

final and static

final prevents reassignment, overriding, or subclassing depending on use. static associates a member with the class.

HashMap, HashSet, and TreeMap

HashMap stores pairs without guaranteed order. HashSet stores unique values. TreeMap orders keys.

implements and interface

A class uses implements to satisfy an interface contract. Interfaces define member contracts.

JDK, JRE, and JVM

JDK provides development tools including javac. JRE describes runtime components. JVM executes bytecode.

List and Map

List is an ordered collection allowing duplicates. Map stores key-value associations.

main method

Traditional entry point: public static void main(String[] args).

null

Absence of an object reference. Calling an instance method through null causes NullPointerException; primitives cannot hold null.

package and import

Package organizes types and access. Import allows simple type names; importing a package does not import subpackages.

private and public

private restricts member access; public exposes a member wherever its declaring type is accessible.

return and void

return ends a method and may send a value. void means no return value.

Scanner

java.util input parser. Mixing nextInt() and nextLine() can leave a newline for the next read.

String and equals()

String is immutable. Compare contents with equals(), not ==, which compares reference identity.

switch

Selects a branch; Java supports switch statements and newer switch expressions.

throw and throws

throw raises an exception object. throws declares checked exceptions a method may propagate.

Try-with-resources

Automatically closes resources implementing AutoCloseable.

Wrapper and autoboxing

Wrapper classes such as Integer correspond to primitives. Unboxing null throws NullPointerException.

Checked exception

Compiler requires code to catch or declare it with throws, unless it is unchecked.

Encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism

Encapsulation hides internal state; inheritance extends a superclass; polymorphism lets a general reference invoke concrete overridden behavior.

Garbage collection

Reclaims unreachable heap objects. It does not replace closing files or sockets.

Generics

Type parameters provide compile-time type safety; Java implements generics with type erasure.

Maven and Gradle wrappers

Project-local scripts that run a declared Maven or Gradle version for a project. Maven commonly uses ./mvnw on macOS/Linux and mvnw.cmd on Windows; Gradle uses ./gradlew and gradlew.bat. The wrapper avoids requiring each learner to install a global build tool.

JUnit, overloading, and overriding

JUnit tests behavior with assertions. Overloading changes parameter lists. Overriding replaces inherited instance behavior; use @Override.

Kotlin supplement glossary

data class

Compiler generates equals, hashCode, toString, and copy based on primary-constructor properties.

fun, val, and var

fun declares a function. val is a read-only binding. var is reassignable.

Null safety and nullable type

Kotlin distinguishes non-null String from nullable String?. Java interoperability and external data may still require checks.

Safe call and Elvis operator

Safe call ?. accesses only when receiver is non-null. Elvis ?: supplies a fallback when its left side is null.

when and smart cast

when is a multi-branch expression or statement. Smart cast narrows a stable value after a type or null check.

Extension function

Function with a receiver type, callable with member-like syntax; it does not add a real class member.

object and companion object

object declares a singleton. Companion object provides class-associated members but is not identical to Java static.

Coroutine

Concurrency abstraction for suspending/resuming work. kotlinx.coroutines supplies the framework; suspend alone is not the framework.

BooleanTrue / Falsetrue / falsetrue / falsetrue / falsetrue / false
Functiondeffunction / arrowtyped function / arrowmethod in classfun
Null-likeNonenull / undefinedboth; strict null checksnull referencenullable types such as String?
Sequencelist / tupleArrayArray / T[]array / ListList / MutableList
Equality== value; is identity=== strict equalityJavaScript runtime ===equals() for objects; == for primitives== structural; === referential

Runtime and type-system distinctions

  • Python type hints are optional metadata; ordinary execution does not enforce them.
  • JavaScript is dynamically typed and its runtime does not enforce TypeScript annotations.
  • TypeScript checks types before execution, then emits JavaScript. Type annotations are erased; validate external data at runtime.
  • Java checks declared types at compile time. References can still be null, and generics use type erasure.
  • Kotlin distinguishes nullable and non-nullable types, but Java interoperability and external data can still require runtime checks.

Learning sequence

Lua Topic Index

Use this index with the Lua curriculum overview, the existing Lua course overview, and the complete Lua lessons.

Course sequence

  • Unit 0: Environment and workflow — interpreter, workspace, accessible editor workflow, terminal, and project dependencies.
  • Unit 1: Computing foundations — program structure, values, variables, and first scripts.
  • Units 2–4: Expressions and control flow — numeric computation, input/output, conditions, loops, and tables.
  • Units 5–8: Program organization — iteration, functions, modules, object patterns, files, and errors.
  • Units 9–11: Applied programming — testing, data processing, projects, and capstone record management.

Lua language concepts

  • Dynamic typing and the nil, Boolean, number, string, function, table, and userdata value categories.
  • Truthiness: only nil and false are falsey.
  • Tables as sequences, maps, records, and objects.
  • One-based sequence conventions.
  • ipairs for sequence traversal and pairs for key/value traversal.
  • Functions as values, closures, and multiple return values.
  • Lexical scope and local variables.
  • Metatables, metamethods, and prototype-style lookup.
  • Modules and require.
  • File handles, return values, and explicit error checks.
  • External packages for JSON and CSV workflows.

Important distinctions

A Lua table is a general-purpose data structure, not simply an array. Sequence operations conventionally use integer keys beginning at 1, while map-like tables may use strings or other valid key types. The iteration order of pairs is not guaranteed. The length operator is not a general count of every key in an arbitrary table; teach its sequence assumptions explicitly.

Lua’s falsey rules differ from languages where zero or an empty string are false. Functions can return multiple values, and callers may receive fewer values than a function returns. These behaviors should be explained through concrete examples.

Rust Topic Index

Use this index with the Rust curriculum overview and complete Rust lessons. The course introduces Rust’s ownership model and systems-oriented programming practices.

Learning sequence

  1. Rust toolchain, Cargo projects, and first program.
  2. Variables, mutability, types, and expressions.
  3. Input/output, parsing, and error reporting.
  4. Conditions, loops, and control flow.
  5. Strings, vectors, slices, and collections.
  6. Functions, ownership, borrowing, and references.
  7. Structs, enums, and pattern matching.
  8. Methods, traits, and generic concepts.
  9. Error handling with Option and Result.
  10. Files, modules, testing, and package management.
  11. Integrated projects and capstone.

Rust-specific concepts

  • Cargo manifest and lockfile.
  • Immutable bindings by default and explicit mut.
  • Ownership, moves, borrowing, and lifetimes at an introductory level.
  • Stack and heap concepts.
  • String versus string slices.
  • Vec, slices, and iterators.
  • Structs, enums, and exhaustive match.
  • Traits, implementations, and generics.
  • Option and Result<T, E>.
  • ? error propagation and recoverable errors.
  • Unit tests, modules, and documentation.

Introductory Modules Index

These modules introduce focused areas of computing that complement the full programming-language curricula. They are not substitutes for the terminal prerequisite or the shared computing foundations.

Modules

  • Git: Version control: repositories, commits, branches, merges, remotes, pull requests, and reading diffs as text.
  • HTML and CSS: Web structure and presentation: semantic HTML, CSS rules, document structure, and accessible web content.
  • Markdown: Technical documentation: headings, lists, links, code blocks, tables, dialects, and screen-reader-friendly authoring.
  • R: Statistical computing: R values and data structures, descriptive statistics, data import, and reproducible analysis.
  • Regular expressions: Pattern-based text processing: literals, character classes, quantifiers, groups, flags, dialects, and command-line tools.
  • SQL: Relational databases: relational models, queries, filtering, aggregation, joins, transactions, and safe data access.
  • Structured data formats: JSON, YAML, and TOML: syntax, data models, validation tooling, and format selection for each format.
  • Web accessibility: ARIA, WCAG, and accessible design: the accessibility tree, WCAG principles, semantic HTML and ARIA, keyboard and focus, forms, and testing workflow.

Suggested prerequisites

Complete the Computing Foundations Primer and Terminal Skills prerequisite before working through these modules. Basic file and folder navigation is assumed.

Learners new to version control should complete the Git module before modules that assume repository workflows, such as Web accessibility practice on hosted projects. The Markdown module is recommended before any module that asks for written documentation; the Regular expressions module and Structured data formats module are independent of the others and can be studied in any order.

Swift Topic Index

Use this index with the Swift curriculum overview and complete Swift lessons. The course introduces Swift’s type system and application-development foundations.

Learning sequence

  1. Swift toolchain, source files, and first program.
  2. Constants, variables, types, and expressions.
  3. Input/output and conversion.
  4. Conditions, switch, and loops.
  5. Strings, arrays, dictionaries, and sets.
  6. Functions, parameters, and return values.
  7. Structures, classes, properties, and methods.
  8. Protocols, extensions, and value/reference semantics.
  9. Optionals and error handling.
  10. Files, Codable, testing, and packages.
  11. Integrated projects and capstone.

Swift-specific concepts

  • let and var, type inference, and static typing.
  • Optionals, optional binding, and safe unwrapping.
  • Value semantics for structures and enums.
  • Classes, reference semantics, and inheritance.
  • Protocols, extensions, and generics.
  • Arrays, dictionaries, sets, and collection operations.
  • Codable for structured serialization.
  • throws, do, try, and error propagation.
  • Swift Package Manager and package structure.
  • Structured concurrency concepts where appropriate.

Contributors to this Curriculum

Michael Ryan Hunsaker, M.Ed., Ph.D. (he/him)

About Dr. Hunsaker

Michael Ryan Hunsaker holds a Ph.D. in neuroscience (behavioral/translational neuroscience focus) from UC Davis and a Master’s degree in Special Education from the University of Utah with a credential to teach blind and visually impaired students. His career uniquely bridges scientific research, clinical experience, and classroom practice-positioning him to design accessible educational materials grounded in both neuroscience and practical pedagogy.

Research & Clinical Background

Following his doctoral work at UC Davis (2012), Dr. Hunsaker completed postdoctoral research in primate neural development at the UC Davis MIND Institute, where he developed sophisticated research methods to evaluate developmental disorders. During this period, he gained extensive clinical experience working directly with children and adults across a broad spectrum of diagnoses, including autism spectrum disorder, cerebral palsy, genetic conditions (fragile X syndrome, Williams syndrome, 22q11.2DS, Down syndrome), ADHD, and Tourette’s syndrome. This diverse exposure to different neurological profiles taught him a crucial lesson: each learner’s disability uniquely shapes their cognitive strengths, learning preferences, and educational needs.

Transition to Education

In 2013, recognizing the gap between academic research and classroom reality, Dr. Hunsaker made a deliberate career shift to direct education. Rather than pursue traditional academic pathways, he committed to applying his scientific training to help students in real classroom environments. As a special education teacher, he focused on understanding the individual relationship between disability and learning-developing instructional approaches that enable students to access their full potential rather than working around perceived limitations.

Expertise in Accessibility & Inclusive Design

His specialization in teaching blind and visually impaired students, particularly those with additional disabilities, has given Dr. Hunsaker deep expertise in accessible pedagogy and non-visual problem-solving. He grounds all curriculum design in evidence-based practice informed by neuroscience, accessibility research, and years of direct classroom experience with diverse learners. He understands that accessibility is not an afterthought or accommodation; it is the foundation upon which effective education for all students is built.

Creation of Accessible Educational Resources

Motivated by observing persistent gaps in affordable, practical, and culturally responsive accessible educational materials, Dr. Hunsaker created TVI Resources, a collection of free, openly licensed instructional materials designed to meet the real needs of educators and students. This commitment to accessible education informed his development of this curriculum: a screenreader accessible computer science curriculum designed explicitly for blind and visually impaired learners, emphasizing independence, technical mastery, and real-world application.

Acknowledgements

This curriculum stands on the shoulders of innovators, educators, and open-source maintainers whose commitment to accessibility and open education made this work possible.

Open Education & Accessibility Movement

Finally, this curriculum is part of a broader movement toward open educational resources that prioritize accessibility from the ground up. It reflects the conviction that education should be barrier-free, that students with disabilities bring unique perspectives and strengths, and that accessible design benefits all learners. The work of accessibility advocates, neurodivergent educators, and disability justice activists informed every decision in building this material.
